I purchased this game for a chance at combat in space and on the ground, do not get me wrong, the game itself has great potential. The space battles are indeed fun, AI or players can pilot the capital ships, you can walk around these capital ships, man their turrets to attack enemy space craft or boarding craft, or simply walk around defending the ship from boarders, resulting in gun fights in a space ship that IS ALREADY ENGAGING WITH ANOTHER SHIP. Pretty epic idea, protect your pilots/gunners though.
Or if the capital ship/Frigates isnt for you, simply go to the hanger, board a fighter ship and launch from the hanger, attack enemy craft/boarding craft, or simply grind away at their capital ship. Not in the mood for flying? Get a squad in a boarding ship instead, launch from the hanger, have teammates on the guns (or let the AI do it), that are on the sides, vailiantly defending the ship from the onslaught of fighters and big ship guns so you can reach your objective. In the mean time a player/AI will pilot the boarding craft to the enemy capital ship, find a weakspot, dock, let the backdoors slam down in the breach and let the boarding commence from the soliders sitting patiently in the rear guns at ready. Board the enemy ship, do as much damage as possible, sabotage key points, disable ship turrets from within, take out the captain and leave the ship dead in space while its bombarded from the exterior, cause general havoc. BUT if you can... Take out the core reactor, bye bye ship...
Ground combat is a much more simpler flavour however, two game modes, both are similar to Battlefields Conquest and Rush. You have vehicles such as tanks. APC's and Heavy APC's etc etc, with quite a range of variety for modding each vehicle for each player. Unlike other games where you can camp a spawn point for a vehicle, this game not so much, you have to earn it by actually playing the objective, and listening AND following the commanders orders.
In a nutshell, a great game with a lot of potential however... the downside is, from my point of playing on and off for over an hour (even just booting up to cheack servers multiple times), the game seems dead. Absolutely no players in any of the servers, it is fun messing around with bots for a while, but it gets to the point where you need actual human players to contend with. I would suggest the developers perhaps launch this on sale, to get it on the steam front page even, maybe it could breath some life back into the game and bring it back from the abyss, hell, even launch an AD campaign for the game, the revenue it would bring would be great for you guys, and the development of the game. A game like this, if made big enough can easily find its way on to consoles too.

Update: The devs got the game going for most of the people that were having issues. I'm not too familiar with survival/rpg games, so I cannot really compare it to any. Initial Review (after 30 min of play)
-Introduction is painfully clunky - the text types out at a painfully slow speed that appears to engimatically pause and unpause with the user's clicking... with heavily pixelated slow fade transitions... I eventually had to skip it (which, thumbs-up, I was able to do so).
-Tutorial is bogged down with a tutorial message system which is burried under persistent action/interface menu windows.  The tutorial attempts to allow the player a choice of how they wish to accomplish the ambiguous goals... unfortunately, this allows the user to make some bad choices, which then bogs down the tutorial advancement.  Fortunately, like the bugged Into, it can be skipped, that is to say, you can quit to the main menu.  This is critically important, because unless you "attempt" the tutorial, you can not play the main game (which... is ok IMHO).
-Traveling is... confusing.  Am I sending my "boat" accross the mainland to a land-locked country?  Where Am I now?  Am I moving?  A better color-scheme with a persistent "Status windows" could help.
-Finding the best market is unpolished, but leaning in the right direction, IMHO.  For example, Intel from Russia says Sniper Weapons are the lowest price... Ok.  But all Sniper RIfles are the same low percentage?
-Loading up.  So I loaded my yatch up... it can hold 6? tons of goods.  Okay.   Wait, so 8 portable (breaks down for portability) sniper rifles takes up 12,000 pounds (6? short tons)? yeah... right...
-Selling weapons.  Which ones did I buy?  Where did I put them?  Okay... let me just sell from my boat, I'm sure it will be... where.... okay, let me see, I think I bought sniper weapons, let me choose that category... WHOA that's a lot of sniper weapons... which one do I actually own to sell... this one, nope, this one, nope, this one... YES, it says I have 8, okay, sell those... it says I just made a profit, that's good... forgot what I paid for them... guess that mark-down category was at least some kind of accurate...
-The interface does not "let" you know it worked, which leads you to wondering, did it work?  A simple animated color-change and the common "click" sound or some cool voice confirmation would be great... incl, cha-ching, vroom, zoom, clunk, etc.
-Some of the game's components are based on time... .  There is a pause, good... though, things going too fast does not seem that much of an issue.  No speed-up control is however severely missing.
-Saving... very unclear, I finally found it in the options menu.  Definitely needs to be more up-front.
My Final Verdict: Its sorely unpolished, but this could change with the future.  The concept is good, and fills a niche which hasn't been touched since a decade or so with the severely antiquated and not supported, "Guns Girls Lawyers Dollars".  Got some spare money, get it on sale, play it later...

Microtransactions added after 6 years is an instant thumbs down but my full review is below.
I found ways to have fun with Two Worlds 2 through all of its faults. Part of this fun came from exploring the (mostly) open world in the campaign, and playing the multiplayer with friends. There are plenty of features that could have been improved including the combat, voice acting, and story.
Pros -
-PvE can be fun with friends at first
-Exploring the world
-The magic system
Cons -
-Microtransactions
-The story
-The voice acting
-Seperating the largest campaign island
-The multiplayer grind
-Tedious quests
-Lackluster DLC
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-Campaign
The story isn't memorable in any way and there are plenty of tedious quests throughout. The voice acting is laughable at best, but it is an improvement over the first game in the series. My favorite part about open world games is the exploring aspect but unfortunately this game somewhat restricts you in certain areas. For example, you can a very large island on the map in singleplayer, but the campaign only lets you explore a small section of the it. For some reason the rest of the island was used for the multiplayer maps and was cut from the singleplayer experience. This was a major dissapointment back in the day, however nowadays there is a mod called World Merge that combines the world spaces from the main campaign, DLC, and multiplayer experiences. I do think that the recent patch may have broken this mod though so that's another disappointment altogether.
-Pirates DLC
It has been a while (years) since I've played this DLC piece so I can't offer full review on it. However one thing still sticks with me even today: tedious or pointless quests. I remeber the feeling of frustration while completing the quests, and honestly I can't see myself playing the DLC again.
-Combat
Playing as a warrior can be a little sketchy sometimes since your character might sometimes glitch out while fighting. The skill moves are interesting at first but quickly get old as you begin to use the same move in every situation. I never really played as an archer so I can't offer much of an opinion on that, but I can say that the mage spell system was pretty cool. It lets you combine different effect and action cards into a customizable spell. It was easily the most layered form of combat in the game, and I have to give them props for the creativity.
-Multiplayer
There are several different gamemodes available, mostly PvP, but I am going to focus on the PvE and village gamemodes. The PvE gamemode is a collection of quests that take you through the rest of the large island from the campaign. Again, the story is lackluster, but I did have fun fighting through the levels with my friends. I did enjoy the village mode at first, but after a while constatly being asked to defend it began to get tedious. Unfortunately there is another downside to the multiplayer, grinding. There is really no point to playing multiplayer PvE (if you're not interested in PvP like me) once you complete all of the campaign missions unless you want grind for levels.
-Overall
I did have some fun with this game, but there are many flaws. The story is unremarkable and quite frankly the voice acting kills the vibe. There are some weird dialogue choices throughout as well. The DLC isn't worth the price, but I still enjoyed exploring the island. The combat can be fun, but it is lacking in smoothness and polish. Multiplayer PvE was fun for a while but it quickly became grindy once all of teh missions were complete. I would recommend this game for people that like to explore openish worlds, but just remember that there are plenty of flaws on hand.

Disappointing. That's honestly the only way to describe this version of a once great series.
It's mired with grindy mechanics for getting cards for the deckbuilding, 90% of the time you get useless crap (as with paper magic), but unlike the cardboard crack you can't trade (that's reserved for MTGO) so your collection of rubbish grows. Also, there's no ratio of mythics upheld (the 1/8 packs for mythics holds more or less true in real MTG, but not here) so expect to see the same cards over and over and nothing good.
Of course you can always pay for the cards you want (and the very best cards seem to be locked behind microtransactions anyway) and that's not really what I play DotP for. I have to pay enough for real cards, if I wanted to buy digital ones, I'd do MTGO.
On top of this the UI is incredibly choppy and slow and quite bland. Everything is hidden in multiple depths of menus, which would be fine if the UI wasn't so slow. Furthering the problems beyond the campaign grinding and multiplayer there's nothing really in the game. There's no Archenemy or Two headeded giant or any of the cool features from the previous games that made them cool experiences and breaks from the campaign. Instead there's just the artificial slog of getting cards.
Overall I just cannot recommend this version. Stick with 2014, MTGO or even the cardboard crack and hopefully next year they'll learn from how badly this was recieved.

This game is pretty decent, as it's the first installment that allowed me to actually fiddle with the deck beyond just sideboarding things, and while it does lack some of the functionality of the previous editions (namely Two-Headed Giant), the sheer number of options is well worth it. My main gripes about it are the rather clunky menu interface that takes an inordinate number of clicks to get to anything, the somewhat odd card collection, the fact that the AI has access to alternate victory condidtions and cards that are denied to the player, some of them for no clear reason, and the the aforementioned lack of Two Headed Giant. On the other hand, you can eventually unlock all the cards in the game for your collection, the adventure nodes are a fun little challenge, and the fact that the game allows me to build decks that are more suited to my playstyle more than off-set the losses. While some may say that the game is P2W, it isn't. When you pay for the extra cards, you are just paying to speed up the unlock process and removing a fair amount of the challenge from the game.

This engine is actually around for quite some time. It is new on Steam and perhaps this is not the best place for it, but having used it on quite a few projects over the last years I can only say it is a very neat tool. I don't write that much reviews on steam, but I think the earlier review for this project are bit unfair. So I've decided to write down some thoughts of my own.
Esenthel is not easy. But keep in mind that 'easy to use' often also means less options. You cannot really comprehend the software fully when you've only spent a few hours on it. Evaluating a game engine takes months.
Yes, some engines will overwhelm with a few very cool tutorials and spectacular effects. But really, do you think this tells you anything about how fit the engine will be for your next big project? Perhaps a few months in, you'll discover that certain things you had in mind are just not possible or very hard to implement because of the way the engine is conceived. I think you need to complete at least one project with an engine before you really know if it's good or bad.
This engine is not very intuitive. But once you take the time to learn how everything fits together, the workflow is great. And there are a lot of video tutorials and manuals on the website to get to that point. Not to mention the forums, which are particularly helpful.
In the end you'll spend weeks or even months developing your first project. And hopefully more will follow. So ask yourself: how important is it that you have to spend a few more hours reading manuals before you're up to speed? Intuitive buttons save time when you're new. Lots shortcuts and a flexible toolset save time EVERY time.
Making a game is hard work on your own. Esenthel is quite good for teams. Working together on a 3d world works like a charm, art creators can import their work with drag & drop: syncing with other team members happens automatically. Code can be synchronized too.
Of course you'll be able to do this with most other game engines. Just saying it works just as well with Esenthel.
Ever tried to ask a question on a dev forum? Take a look at the esenthel forum. Almost every question that's decently phrased is answered. Devs are really trying to help you out.
You can also get help from the developer. He's quite active on the forum too. This is a big advantage compared with the big players out there. He actually listens (but doesn't always agree with you, of course :-)
I think that about 10 times over the last 3 years I needed a new feature added to the engine. Mostly it was added in a matter of weeks, sometimes even days. This matters a lot of you're depending on an engine. (I don't think Unity would have listened to me, but of course I'll never know for sure.)
The reason for using the Esenthel Editor instead of Visual Studio is that it does makes your work easier. Esenthel uses a precompiler which automatically generates your header files, constructors and includes. It also figures out by itself where you need a pointers instead of references. This takes away some of the more tedious parts of programming. But the output is still c++, making your code a lot faster compared to script based engines.
You can also link to every other c/c++ library you can think of. Most other engines don't allow that for the basic licenses.
Oh, and if you're serious about c++ programming you can also get the full source license for only double the price. If nothing else, you can learn a lot about how to create 3D software with this.
Esenthel has a quite permissive licence. You can do about anything you want, as long as you include the logo at startup. You're free to sell your software any way you want, with no extra cost. Esenthel won't ask for a sales percentage, unless you use the Esenthel store. You're free to create any kind of software (as long as it's not a game engine). By comparison, CryEngine will not even permit you to create simulations or serious games with the basic license.
I'm not sure if Steam is a good place for this kind of software. I recommend you visit the Esenthel website and start from there. The software is not easy to learn but very capable. If you're serious about game development and need an affordable option, you should consider this. Especially if you're a programmer with a preference towards C++.
Oh, and don't let the visual design scare you away. People seem to believe that good looks make you code faster or something. If you're one of those, you can always use another skin or even create one yourself. But of course it hardly matters.

I have been working with Esenthel for a few months now and my experience so far has been great, it's a well featured engine that is very easy to use, with a good amount of tools a clean API and over a hundred well documented tutorials that guide you through the use of most of the engine's functionality. The engine is receiving updates constantly, the developer has a zero bug tolerance policy and along with the rest of the community is very helpful on the technical side of things.
So to be more specific the user interface is very simple to use and functional. The Project Tab is where all the functionality starts, it is built around a drag and drop mindset and it reveals what tools need to be visible depending on the task you are working on without clamping the screen constantly with unnecessary information.
Importing assets is as simple as a drag and drop and the terminology used is self explanatory. A pop-up hint bar usually presents what additional information is needed so learning how to handle and navigate through the engine wasn't a problem.
The world editor offers all the functionality that is necessary to make good looking terrains such as heightmap, material/mask and colormap importing, all sorts of heigh editing tools along with the very necessary custom heightmap brushes, material, color and object painting tools with masking, terrain and grid align, translate, rotate and scale functionality.
But where the world editor truly shines is the very smooth built-in world chunk streaming system that allows for as good as infinite non-instanced worlds. One thing that is missing though and could speed up your workflow is the ability to group assets but last time i checked the feature was on the road map.
The object editor offers the usual transform tools along with a very useful Mesh LOD creation system with info on mesh logistics, collider and bone creation and manipulation tools, ragdoll tools, custom object parameter and class assigning system and mesh part specific functionality.
Finally the API is well written and documented and the engine has a well thought-out and clean structure. The supported language is C++ that is the industry standard for its performance and low level control but without a doubt you have to have a basic C++ knowledge or at least you have to be willing to learn in order to use it. The built-in code editor that is included features a powerful Auto-Complete system, an advanced search tool and is using a professional C++ compiler such as Visual Studio to compile the scripts for all the supported platforms. Along with the above the code editor acts as a pre-compiler that offers some very handy C++ Improvements in areas such as header (.h) usage, forward declaration, operators and more.
Esenthel as with any other software has its pros and cons in comparison to the competition and where it might lack some features it sure has other features that are lacking from other well-known engines so it's well worth evaluating before you end up on a choice for your product. As a final word Esenthel is a complete tool made with professional standards that is well worth using.

Swords and Soldiers is a goofy 2D real time strategy with simplistic gameplay and dead multiplayer.
You can play as three races: the Aztecs, whose leaders have awesome names like “Fulthrotl” and “Luvsbatl”; the Vikings, who can summon Thor; and the Chinese, whose melee unit, swordsmen, yell “ayyyy chop chop” when spawned. I laugh every time then feel dirty afterward.
The graphics are sprightly and pleasant. The music isn’t annoying—an important consideration when you must listen to the same set of tunes all game—and even catchy at times. The sound is funny—ayyy chop chop, damn it. The gold gathering units are all women whom are referred to as “gold diggers.” I giggled.
I feel as if I’m listing bullet points. I feel as if this stinks of dysphemism, as if I’m hedging my honesty though I’m not. One of the reviewers states that he has nothing negative to say about Swords and Soldiers; this is true for me too, but I also can’t find any salient positives. The game’s aesthetic, especially the humor, is its greatest boon. The gameplay is a bit shallow which betrays its mobile roots. I ENJOYED playing through the campaigns, but I also don’t desire to ever replay the game again.
Swords and Soldiers is simple: you gather gold to purchase units and spells, and units move ever forward until they’re destroyed or demolish the enemy’s base. Spells use mana, which replenishes at a steady rate which can be increased via upgrades, when cast and make up half of the S&S’ complexity. All “skill” in this game culminates in your ability to spawn or spam the rights units while using spells correctly. That’s essentially it; as long as you can spawn units with minimum deference to insuring the units work together (i.e., not spawning ten of the same unit but you know, mixing it up a bit!) and not spamming your spells so that you aren’t left high and dry to an ayyy chop chop invasion, you pretty much win. The campaigns squelch this flaw by hamstringing the player in some way. Objectives are often more than lolsmash the enemy to pieces. The story mode is entertaining because it works against the shallow gameplay.
Hence my conundrum. I enjoyed the handicaps and weird objectives of the single player, but without the constrictions as an impetus, Swords and Soldiers isn’t all that fun. Essentially, it’s the prototypical mobile game: fun in short bursts as the medium requires but without any staying power.

This is a game that may be similar to other's in some ways (think Warhammer: Battle March), but also contains a new and beautiful element of building your own Multiplayer Empire. The initial few sessions of the game may be a little slow if handled incorrectly, but if you focus on spamming workers and houses as much as possible in your first few logins - the game really picks up pace. Remember that every resource gatherer pays for itself in time and then adds to your empire FOREVER (or until you accidently run it into a pack of Orc Wargs whilst trying to run from a spreading forest fire...).
Resources are collected while you are offline so my advice is to dabble with the game and focus on raising the population cap, building a workforce and balancing your economy. Then when you find yourself with an excess of resources, build yourself a decent army ready to play co-op battles against surrounding computer-controlled cities. If you find yourself producing too much of one thing, carry it to an allied city and trade it. From here the game really opens up - your units start to level, your new vassel cities begin to gather more resources and your power snowballs.
The beauty of this game is that it ISN'T too easy. If you lose a unit (or an entire army), then, well, tough luck. You have to apply your mind, know when to pull out and heal your units. It is wise to build a "backup army" to replace losses and learn what is worth sacrificing for the potential gain. Losing a couple of fully levelled archer units will be worth it if you take a city in return, charging in 16 units of fully levelled knights suicidally is not.
Similarly PvP is where it really gets interesting. You may attack or be attacked by a human player with a balanced army, though this does seem like a fairly rare occurance. A few days ago I was attacked by a player whilst carrying looted resources back to my home city, I didn't want to pay out the forfeit for refusing to battle so after challenging his hero to single combat and buying myself some time, I simply led his army on a merry dance around the map. As he chased me, his army became strung out and I picked away at his front units until he simply surrendered, giving me 5500 gold in loot :)
The terror of losing his men made him pull back, making it feel like a realistic war experience.
So far my experience of this entirely free game has been positive. Whilst it is possible to buy a very limted amount of "booster packs" per-nation you create, it is no way game breaking or unfair. They can only be bought once and their contents can be reasonably attained anyway with a few sessions of play. Considering PvP is balanced by army strength - it should never really be a problem for people who don't buy them. Think of it as a small bump to help players get going (for a small fee to help keep the game running).
As far as reliabilty is concerned, I've faced a couple of heartbreaking bugs whereby my hard-earned gold disappeared in transit - BUT - within a few minutes of putting my problem on the General Chat channel, rather polite and decent Moderators refunded my resources and left me a happy elf, swimming Scrouge McDuck style in my pile of gold again. I only wanted to try this game in case I would prefer a refund, and after a few minutes playing, I really thought it wasn't worth the price and strongly consider it. Still, playing brought me almost at the end of the second campaign after two hours of pleasant playing -so that refund is now out of question.
Is it good ? That's not so easy to tell. It feels like a mobile game, and it is quite simplistic. You click on units to spawn them, and they walk relentlessly towards the enemies coming from the right. You can use spells also, which are crucial to succeed. In the campaign, there are two major kinds of goals: Hold on for some time as your base is continually attacked, or destroy the enemy base.
There are three available factions: Vikings, Aztecs, and Chinese. All of them are quite different and you have to adjust your gameplay, which is a good thing for sure. However there are not many different units per faction, but the fun is they are all different enough, so I guess it's okay.
Overall, it is fun, missions are less than 10 minutes long, which I deem as an advantage. Achievements also are creative and not so easy to unlock (there are not basic grinding or "end the game in difficulty mode i" for i from 1 to 5).
CONCLUSION:
Don't spend the full price for it, it's not worth it. But in sale, you might want to consider adding it to your library, as it is nice, fun, casual, and yet challenging enough.

Even with all its flaws, this game (with its restored content) is amazing. I enjoyed it much more than I did its prequel.
The primary reason for this is Kreia, who is by far my favorite [spoiler alert] villain in the Star Wars canon. She is definitely one of the most evil. Her obsession with the Exile resolves into being a hatred of the Force. To her, it forcefully imposes direction on an aimless and pointless reality. Even more glaring is when the Force leaves one who is accustomed to its presence. Having seen existence through the underlying fabric that connects all life, only to be betrayed by it: one is deserted and worse than blind. The Exile is a hole in the Force, beautiful to her. But more than this, the Exile herself abandoned the Force.
Kreia's ultimate plan is to achieve by the means of the Exile what was accomplished at Malachor V at the close of the Mandalorian Wars, but on a larger scale: to create a ripple in the Force that would never cease, deafening all of life to the Force's presence by further opening the wound in it. In the end, it seemed to me that Kreia was not much of the Sith that she worked under the pretense of being.
There are more worthwhile elements to the game, but Kreia was by far my favorite. As far as characters go, though, HK-47 was a close second. It is worth getting him as early as possible just to work your way through all of his dialogue. A few of them come to mind.
"Consolation: But I would not worry, Master, I imagine it will not be long before their murderous hands try to seize you by the throat. Twi'lek Metaphor: It seems like they are attracted to you like krek beetles during the Bright Land seasons."
"Statement: Oh, I am aware of that, Master. I simply use it to give you the illusion of control and obedience. Humans often need such comforts until the end comes." To which you can reply, "What do you mean, 'the end?'"
"Conclusion: You have just shown me your soft, meatbag-like underbellies, and said, 'HK-47, please shoot me repeatedly there until I die.'"
One final note: some people have said that this game is difficult. This is not exactly true if you know what you're doing. If you don't, then yes this game can be very difficult. Having a little background in the game mechanics goes a very long way. I've found that all you really need in order to very easily beat the game on the hardest difficulty is to have spent most of your attribute points in dexterity along with getting Master Speed, Master Flurry, and Lightsaber Finesse. You don't need these things, but I did and I faced all of the major bosses in my starting clothing as a Sentinel; I was basically untouchable. Really, if you understand the game mechanics, then you can play the game hundreds of different ways and still get through it without too much struggle on your part.
In spite of this, there are some extremely difficult parts where the game forces you to play as another member of your party. Here are some tips to make it much easier:
1. As you will have too many credits to spend near the end, breakdown a lot of your things rather than selling them and make the best plasma mines. Make sure Atton and Mira have good skill levels in demoltions so that you can defeat Darth Sion and Hanharr, respectively, by simply running away and setting mines.
2. The HK-47 mission can be difficult, so make sure that you have saved all of the droid shields you've collected throughout the game. You're going to need them. It would also be good to have made a lot of construction kits up to this point.
3. When you first defeat Hanharr with Mira (use plasma mines), you will have to fight a lot of Ubese. Save yourself the trouble and run away from them, going to the door that triggers switching back to the Exile. I cannot remember how to get to this door, but if you look up a walkthrough, it will tell you better than I could.
4. The one part that was difficult for me while playing as the Exile was leaving Nar Shaddaa after having talked with the Jedi there. You face tons of HK-50's. If you haven't gone to Dantooine yet, then you won't have a lightsaber. Blaster bolt deflection is a must-have, otherwise these HK-50's are extremely difficult.
5. Save yourself the pain of playing through Peragus for the first time and just use a walkthrough. The first turn-off most people have is how long and boring Peragus is. If you know what to do, though, it is not so long and, actually, not so boring as most people say.
Maybe I've dumbed this down too much. In any case, I don't have anything else to say. Buy this game!

A fun side-scrolling strategy game. You don't build any buildings (besides towers) so it's all about building units and research. There is a story mode that teaches you how to play and how to use the different units of the game. It's shown in a cartoony manner, with over-the-top characters fighting over stuff like a giant pepper.
The different races can play very differently so that adds some complexity to the game. But at its core the gameplay is simple and straightforward. Combat units automatically march towards the enemy base and will engage the first enemy they meet. You can gain magic skills that allow you to interact more directly in the combat.
So managing which units to build, which things to research, and which spells to use is how the game plays out.
A fun game with quick little missions that can entertain strategy game fans.

Now I'm going to try and do this game some good by submitting an honest, positive review. Absolutely DO NOT get this game if you don't have the proper PC to run it (see system requirements below), I am personally running the newest Alienware laptop and am having no difficulties with FPS. Those who have horrible FPS will have great difficulties playing the game, because the game tracks so and will kick if you have an extremely low FPS ( I know this from my friend having played it and kicked due to this).
That said, I also hardly experience these latency issues that everybody is spamming, maybe once or twice every fifteen rounds and have only been kicked from two rounds the entire eleven hours I've played thus far. I don't think that's too bad considering all of the spamming that's going on within the other reviews about peer to peer connection and I've only experienced visual latency of an individual once during a duel.
Now whenever it comes to the gameplay, holy crap is it freaking amazing. This is very easy to learn, and there really isn't a way of mastering. It's just basically getting better overtime and adapting to the varying playstyles of individuals that you may come across (however take advantage of external blocks and guard breaks like everyone else). The closest I can think of to this directional type of combat is Mount and Blade, yet this can be even more fast paced and enthralling.
The issues that I do have with the game is how money-grubbing Ubisoft can be, and this game DEFINITELY speaks that. By what it seems, you can unlock everything through grinding a lot, and ultimately can beat any kind of other players if you are experienced, but I loathe the ability to pay for skill progession. So, know that you're getting into a♥♥♥♥♥♥storm of financial overcharges if you decide to get the game and want to progress swiftly if you aren't too skilled. It's taken me a tad bit, but I've already unlocked all of the characters (could have unlocked faster if I concentrated on the missions to accomplish).
Overall, I do think this game is worth it if you find a good community to play with (or have friends willing to buy it). This game is extremely boring, in my opinion of course, if you're alone just doing your own thing with random people (yet the community hasn't been too toxic so far, only one round has been extremely bad in terms of bad-mouthing and emote-bagging). I absolutely love the complexity when it comes down right to it, don't let the rage-inducing reviews get your attention and sway you away from the game. Think critically whether or not YOU would enjoy it and can devote the time to getting good, make good use of the how to play section and fighting bots to train as new heroes. Have fun and good luck with your decision!

This is a great little game, but you need to understand what you are getting into.  I have two large warnings, I think you won't be happy if you are not comfortable with these:
- It is very much an indy title.  The interface is a bit rough, and sometimes difficult to interact with
- There are some bugs here and there, but the developers are responsive and a new patch just rolled out
The game is often described as a Business Simulator.  To be more specific, I liken it to a grown up version of the old DrugWars game.  Buy low, sell high, pay off your loans, evade the cops.
That is it in a nutshell.  Sounds simple, but there is a reason people still play DrugWars / DopeWars on every platform available:  It's a fun formula.  It replays well.
And Arms Dealer has a lot that it adds.:
- The variety of content and number of locations are huge.
- You have a wide selection of public and private transportation options.
- You can build and customize your transport vehicles
- You can involve yourself in global politics, and instigate wars to manipulate markets
- The metagame of evading law enforcement as well as headhunters adds a great layer of excitement
But I can't overemphasize my first two cautionary elements.  This is not a high-gloss title with millions of dollars behind its development.  It has some problems, and the interface can be a real challenge.  If you are easily frustrated or don't have the patience to learn something that is a bit counter-intuitive, this probably isn't for you.
If you like spending money on a game you will never get to play, this is the "game" for you.

This is one of my favorite games to date.
This game has been in development secretly(ish) for the past SEVEN YEARS, and has been released in EA format for about 11 months now. The devs are doing a fantastic job, maybe not as transparent as they should be, but they know about that, and they are going to get it done soon(tm).
This game is a passion project, and it's a hell of a project. This game brought be back to the battlefront two days, not the EA ♥♥♥♥♥ on your childhood with a reskin of Battlefield days.
These are the FOUR major issues with this game, though:
1. Lack of player base on a regular schedule, but the bots are fun as all hell, and it actually gets difficult to tell who's a bot sometimes.
The Reason for the lack of a player base? Simple. Lack of advertising. They haven't advertised because the game isn't finished, and they didn't want to blow their chances by releasing their game too early. Sometimes I wonder if these people have business degrees, I wouldn't doubt it.
2. The UI is clunky, buggy, and kinda confusing. This will not be a problem soon(tm) when the team develops a whole new UI, which they are in the middle of right now, if you check the most recent post, they posted screen teasers for possible UI models.
3. The weapons don't sound like weapons, or feel like them either. They feel like nerf guns.
Well old chap, the devs know that too, and they are also busy on new animations and sounds for the guns to make them feel like military grade weaponry.
4. Infantry combat feels clunky, TTK is too high. This issue has been talked about a bit, but it is still a concern, and I can guarantee you that the game won't be released without some change to infantry firefights.
If you grew up playing Battlefront I and/or II, this is the game for you, this is the sequel you've been waiting for. There's no lightsabers, but at least you can fly the cap ships.

Really wish that I could like this game, but my expectations are far from met. I was very hopeful to have a good minigame type of game on PC, but unfortunately I will have to wait a bit longer it seems.
Pros:
- Colorful vibrant graphics
Game looks very nice and I'm mostly a fan of the art style.
- Lots of fun/cool character customization
There are lots of cool hats to collect that add a bit of an incentive to keep playing that dont cost any additional money.
Cons:
- Most of the minigames feel the same
Most of the minigames feel the same with only a couple of genuinely unique and fun to play games here and there. A majority of the games youll play have the same kind of gimmick to them. Youll be put into some stage and punch of kick people while trying to do a somewhat samey tasks eacxh game has to offer. Some games are a good relief from this such as the food eating game the game in which you rapidly press a button to break as many pieces to a tower as possible and maybe 1 or 2 others which I cannot remember.
- Poorly designed UI
The game tries to be more unique and has a ui that is minimal and allows the polayers to mess around while waiting in lobby. While this idea sounds nice it ends up becoming players trying to ready up and then mistakenly unreadying when jumping around the lobby room. A more streamlined menu focused ui would be very nice for this game.
- Poor controls
Think of Gang Beasts, the characters movement is very unprecise and is kinda wonky in general, however unlike Gang Beasts the gimmick really does not work well for this kind of game at all.
- Terrible points system
Each minigame gives you points up to 1000 points and the game can be set to a few different limits such as 5000. Games often are easy enough to have multiple ties because the limit of each minigame and the fact that points are given to players as individual scores not based on how they placed in the match. Many games allow players to keep playing until each player has reached the max 1000 points and does not stop when one player hits the max so the other player can catch up in many cases ending in a 4 way tie for 1000 points each.

TLDR - It might be worth $10 for a few hours of gameplay, but that is all I would ever pay for this game.
Pros:
- Uh, let's see... it's MTG, I guess?
- Full deck building is neat, but at the cost of other gameplay mechanics...
Cons:
- Pay2Win
- Buggy/slow menus
- Worse AI/automation than before (land tapping is a b***)
- Doesn't feel like enough cards for a full deck customization game
- Loss of interesting game modes, like challenges. No archenemy, 2 headed giant, etc
- Very obtuse UI. Game doesn't tell you when you unlock decks (or how to), doesn't tell you the deck you start with 1) will suck and 2) you're stuck with it
- Single player campaign is very short and that's all the single player content there is other than grinding boosters
- Very grindy. You unlock cards only through boosters. Many cards are ONLY available by BUYING boosters
- Pay2Win (yes, it's on here twice)
Full review:
Well, I love the MTG Planeswalker games, but this one really missed the bar. It's still fun, but it lacks a lot of the things that made the previous ones better - there are no more puzzle challenges for one thing. And it's also horribly designed in that you have no clear idea how to unlock cards. When you start, a tutorial is offered. I know how to play MTG so I wanted to skip it but didn't see how. It wasn't until I finished the first one (which takes forever as there's a ton of "do this to proceed" things) that I found how to skip. At which point you chose a deck to start with but NO WHERE does it tell you that this is the deck you will be stuck with the rest of the game! So naturally I chose one that sounded interesting but of course sucked really bad. So Planeswalker difficulty was crushing me bad, and there's no way to get a "new" deck until you just unlock enough boosters (read: random cards) until you can build yourself a new one.
But I figured, well I can just unlock those other decks, right? That's how the other games worked. But it's not apparent how to do so -- other matches only unlocked boosters (random cards ftw, amirite??) I had to search the internet for a bit to find out you have to keep playing the "Explore [Planes]" matches until the Planeswalker (again, randomly) shows up to fight you. And then it doesn't even tell you that you unlocked a deck! You have to go to the Decks menu option, Create a Deck, and THEN you can create a deck off the ones you unlocked. And I'm pretty sure for a couple, like Nissa, did not even unlock a deck at all. Overall it's just a very baffling experience. And the unlocked decks aren't even that good. Or you can of course pay $20 to have all this work done for you! Because clearly we are all just sacks of money and will always throw it at Wizards.
I really miss the ability to unlock cards for a specific deck. Don't get me wrong, when I heard they had full deck creation for 2015 I thought that sounded great! But I also thought they would still have the prebuilt decks that you could work with. But they do not. Now it is ALL boosters. And the "prebuilt" unlock decks are rather poor.
So what are your options then? Buying boosters of course! So let's throw $2 a pop for a 10-pack booster just on the off-chance I might get one of those random cards! This is HORRIBLE. With the last games, I could pay $3 for a deck expansion that would unlock 3 FULL decks that I could then unlock 20+ cards for each just by playing the game. That is totally worth it. But $2 for 10 cards, that might not even be GOOD? No freakin way. This game just has GREED written all over it, and no consideration for the consumer.
Oh I should also mention that there are also cards that can ONLY be unlocked by paying for boosters! So yeah if you didn't think this game was just about sucking the money out of you, you might want to think twice.
As a final note, there are other bafflingly poor choices in the game design that are clear steps back from 2014. For instance, the toggle for "Automatically use optional abilities" is still there, but it's all or nothing now. Whereas in 2014, even if you had auto ON, it would still ask you for things like Draw a Card, because you don't want to millstone yourself. But this game it no longer does. So those card draws can bite you in the♥♥♥♥♥if you're not careful.
Also the mana tapping is HORRIBLE. Pay attention to what mana it says it will tap! Basically I've found it likes to tap ALL your mana of one color first, which makes the multicolor decks (which are pretty much all of them) a pain to play because it will always tap you out at the worst time. I have lost several matches because I was not paying attention to the mana tapping. In 2014 and previous games, the logic was smart enough to try and leave you mana for whatever spells you had in your hand. It may not have always been the best, but at least it was effective like 95% of the time. In 2015 it just screws you over constantly.
So basically this game... well the initial $10 isn't so bad for a few hours of gameplay. I've built some interesting decks but not as great as I would like them to be. So without spending more money, there's really not much else this game offers. It basically emphasizes multiplayer and microtransactions way more than the previous games did, which I do NOT enjoy. I don't know if I'd recommend the game. It's alright for the 10 dollars, but also a huge disappointment compares to the last games.

Game is ok overall. Trucking tycoon is a nice ideea. The economy and industry part are handled very well in my opinion. Unlocking various complex industries is a good game mechanic. Having the whol map of USA open gives a good growing feeling to a tycoon game.
Those being said, the game has some negatives:
- contract terms are too simplistic, makes planning routes in advance useless. Planning defines a good trucking company from a bad one.
- you are capped at 8 Schedules (call them delivery routes) each can contain 3 delivery contracts. At first when you start your company is not a big deal, later though when you are 5-6 levels as a Company, you feel silly having 90 trucks and the whole USA at your disposal.
- UI is bad. No mouse rightclick implemented in the game, to make it easy to navigate and give orders to your trucks, see details in contracts or any other objects on the map. And this is a 2017 game. Mind blowing.
- Lack of mouse-over tooltips which could help at least to see if a truck is loaded or empty when you hoover over them. All in all the game is too click intensive even for the most simplier orders.
-various bugs with quests and UI
Game feels like an early access which with good ideas but unpolished.
I recommend it but not for this price. Wait for a sale discount.

After being fired from a trucking company, you and your partner decided to open your own business. Only having your partner’s truck you decide to open your HQ in your hometown. From there you must manage your logistics and resources to continue to grow, while keeping the US economy running. If you enjoy management games and trucks then you’re in the right place! TransRoad USA by Deck13 Hamburg and astragon entertainment is listed at $24.99 on Steam for PC.
TransRoad USA has two modes: story mode and sandbox. The main difference between the two modes are that in sandbox you get to decide where to establish your HQ. I found sandbox to be more enjoyable, personally. Using different locations allow for different pros and cons. I also found that it was easier to distribute the money and gain it accordingly. Story mode also has only one difficulty setting.
Unlike most walk through tutorials, TransRoad USA only supplies you with tips. I found this very confusing and much harder to grasp how to play efficiently. My friend, however, thought it was only a little confusing and picked it up a lot quicker than me, so it may be different for every individual. Something that came in handy, because I was so confused by the tutorial, was that you could access the manual any time throughout the game. The controls for the game can be very laggy and buggy.
The art style is interesting. I feel like a lot of their aesthetic is playing off trucker stereotypes. The USA theme is definitely amped up by imagery of eagles and the classic dinner breakfast in the loading screen and menus. I personally find this cheesy and to be a weaker point of the game. I feel like it is too predictable to rely on trucker stereotypes. I wasn’t surprised at all, it’s what you would expect a trucker game to be. I wish there was a more professional feel, one you usually find with business related games.
The sound has its ups and downs. The story mode does have voice acting, which can be rare for 2D games, but the voice acting would cut out before the end of the written dialogue. For example, the screen may say something like, “Oh no! What are we going to do?” The audio would then only say, “Oh no! What are we…” For a PC game listed at this price, it is surprising how many audio errors there are. One really cool feature of the game is that you can “change the radio station.” At the top right corner there is a radio icon, when you click it you can download listen music to listen to in game. I think this is really immersive and an awesome detail.
Overall, I think if you enjoy the trucker aesthetic and logistic management then I think you will enjoy this game, though I’m not sure at the price it is listed for. I think this game has a lot to be fixed but isn’t a terrible game.

Now I'm going to try and do this game some good by submitting an honest, positive review. Absolutely DO NOT get this game if you don't have the proper PC to run it (see system requirements below), I am personally running the newest Alienware laptop and am having no difficulties with FPS. Those who have horrible FPS will have great difficulties playing the game, because the game tracks so and will kick if you have an extremely low FPS ( I know this from my friend having played it and kicked due to this).
That said, I also hardly experience these latency issues that everybody is spamming, maybe once or twice every fifteen rounds and have only been kicked from two rounds the entire eleven hours I've played thus far. I don't think that's too bad considering all of the spamming that's going on within the other reviews about peer to peer connection and I've only experienced visual latency of an individual once during a duel.
Now whenever it comes to the gameplay, holy crap is it freaking amazing. This is very easy to learn, and there really isn't a way of mastering. It's just basically getting better overtime and adapting to the varying playstyles of individuals that you may come across (however take advantage of external blocks and guard breaks like everyone else). The closest I can think of to this directional type of combat is Mount and Blade, yet this can be even more fast paced and enthralling.
The issues that I do have with the game is how money-grubbing Ubisoft can be, and this game DEFINITELY speaks that. By what it seems, you can unlock everything through grinding a lot, and ultimately can beat any kind of other players if you are experienced, but I loathe the ability to pay for skill progession. So, know that you're getting into a♥♥♥♥♥♥storm of financial overcharges if you decide to get the game and want to progress swiftly if you aren't too skilled. It's taken me a tad bit, but I've already unlocked all of the characters (could have unlocked faster if I concentrated on the missions to accomplish).
Overall, I do think this game is worth it if you find a good community to play with (or have friends willing to buy it). This game is extremely boring, in my opinion of course, if you're alone just doing your own thing with random people (yet the community hasn't been too toxic so far, only one round has been extremely bad in terms of bad-mouthing and emote-bagging). I absolutely love the complexity when it comes down right to it, don't let the rage-inducing reviews get your attention and sway you away from the game. I agree that this game has a lot of flaws, some of which eventually got patched out (like the dumb 3-weapon-limit ostensibly influenced by today's shooters).
However I don't think that this game is as bad as the press and people are making it. Sure, it's no masterpiece by any standard and not even remotely close to being an exceptional game, but at the end of the day I had a lot of fun playing through it.
The levels are really great and possibly one of the best features of this game. During the story, you get to see tons of environments. Unfortunately, not all developers do that anymore today. In today's games, you often get just one scenario and then they stick with that during the entire game. Not so in this game. You get a Casino, Las Vegas, the Canyon, some Burger-tower (which is kind of cool), a construction site, some alien world, and tons more.
The weapons are mediocre to me. Sure, you get "The Ripper" and the RPG, but all in all the weapons are nothing worth mentioning. As a fan of Duke 3D, that's disappointing.
The voice of Duke is really awesome. Like it's really great, as it has always been. I agree that the one-liners and what Duke is saying is really 80's-like, cheesy and macho, but anyone being surprised by that clearly has never played any of the Duke games ;) It's sad that so few of today's heroes lack a personality. In this game, Duke still got his. And that's really great!
The difficulty is a strange one. To me, the game feels kind of unevenly paced at times. Some parts I had to re-play more often than necessary (the first boss fight for example), while others were too easy. The pig "cops" are also extremely annoying in this game and jump around on speed. I liked the pig cops from Duke 3D way more.
Also what I think harms this game more are all these ""modern"" (yes, double quotes) elements like the weapon carrying limit (what the hell is the point of that anyway??) and the self-healing (why are medkits so taboo nowadays??). They should have left these elements like they were in Duke 3D. Nobody gives a damn anyway. And here the criticisms are most definitely justified. They should have left all "old-school" elements in there. It would have made the game better. Instead, there's an "old-school" component and a pretentious "modern" component. Apparently they tried to cater to all those Halo or CoD-players that don't know games without self-healing existed. It doesn't work.
In the end, it's by no means a bad game. I think it's a nice time capsule for what it is, if you ignore those pretentiously added "modern" elements.

I don't think I've ever seen a game as bad as this.
I'm not talking about the "humor" or the innuendo. Bad, as in "Mouse moves faster horizontally than vertically". Or bad, as in "during a scripted sequence a badly made monologue is repeated five times in a row".
I watched myself jump in the mirror - and regretted it immediately. Duke jumps with his feets - no movement of the torso or even hands - those just hang idly down...
The graphics are outdated, which is OK, but also uninspired and boring. The best part, sadly, was a room in the museum where screenshots of the old games could be seen.
The game either holds your hand, telling you what to do, or it just leaves you alone to figure out what the hell you're supposed to do.
"Press LMB for brake" seems simple, right? But does it mean "press and release" or "press and hold"? Actually it meant "press and hold until the F-Gauge is full, then release and immediately press and hold again. Repeat several times until the next part of the sequence starts."
In case you don't see the pattern, you'll be reminded every time you release the brake.
The voices are partly OK and partly annoying - this might be a matter of taste, but I found the shrill voices of the twins to be quite annoying and not at all sexy (which I have to assume they were supposed to be).
Did I mention that the mouse movement is quite unexpected? Apparently the mouse moves at a fixed speed while in the menu, and in a setable speed while in the game.
Which of course means you can change the mouse speed in the menu, but not try it.
I usually try to finish games, often with cheats, unless there are repercussions (i.e. no achievements - I'd rather not finish a game then, or try it without cheats, I'm stupid like that), but I'm not sure if I WANT to finish this game.
Sure, I'd like to know how the "story" progresses, but I'm not sure it's worth the pain...

I play games to experience the plot myself, not read it. The player spends the majority of the time wandering cluelessly between the same rooms trying to find the next boring piece of text. The slightly spooky atmosphere is gone after going back to the same room for the fifth time just to confirm that no, there's still nothing here. The physics based puzzles are pretty good, when you can find them, and just opening a door feels more realistic as you have to do the motion yourself with a mouse. The game tells you at the beginning that one should not play to win but to immerse into the game and atmosphere. Sounds pretty good on paper but it's poorly implemented in this game. Good concept wasted.

It took a few games for Wizards to realize, but finally we have open ended deckbuilding as promised. The game is enjoyable, and unlocking boosters by winning games versus the AI has a great feel of progression. There are quite a few achievements and portraits to unlock, and the battlefield looks nice and clean. You can save your custom decks, and you can unlock 5 sets of cards to create them with. There now is online matchmaking as well, it seems Wizards took the comments from the comunity to heart, and finally added the things to the game we always wanted.
There are, however, quite a few flaws with this game, including but (probably) not limited to:
1. If you want to equip another deck, you have to go back to the main menu to do so. In the campaign this is only a minor inconvenience, but when playing online this becomes quite bothersome. Speaking of which:
2. Earlier versions of MtG:DotP had Two-Headed Giant, a really nice way to play co-op. In 2015 it is gone. The reason for this? It would be really hard to balance, and one of the rules of THG is that the decks of one team combined may not have more than 4 copies of the same non-basic land card. I understand this, but still I think this is a step backward.
3. The amount of content has drastically decreased. Aside from there being no special gamemode (like Planechase or Archenemy), the game also lacks challenges and a revenge campaign, both of which were present in earlier versions.
4. You can create your own decks, but there are a lot of cards you simply cannot get your hands on. I am not even talking about the ridiculous paywall you have to breach before you unlock all the cards from the Premium set, I mean this: You will play against a lot of AI decks that will have interesting cards in them, whilst not being available to you. When you did grind yourself through the sets to unlock all the cards for a set, you will notice that about 70% of them are really bad cards. Like the standard 2/2 for 2, the 3/2 flyers for 4 mana, or that 3/4 vampire for 5 that will get flying as long as you pump 2 life in it each turn you want him to. And not only the creatures, the instants and sorceries as well. 5 mana for an instant speed destroy target creature, it cannot be regerated? No thank you!
5. Programming AI may be the hardest part of making a good player vs. AI game, but the AI sometimes makes really stupid mistakes. I have seen the AI sacrificing an unblocked creature to its Bloodflow Connoisseur before it did damage (and I did not cast spells at that time). I have witnissed a Boros charm being cast to make all his creatures indestructable, which is not a bad manouver, but it is questionable to do so in his end step (again: no spells cast from my hand). Also the AI sometimes simply won't attack you when clearly he would make a great trade, has twice the amount of creatures on the battlefield and has a great chance of lethal damage next turn, all because you have some mana untapped and one or two cards in hand. And not only the opponent AI is flawed, the automatic mana-tapping function is random as well, sometimes leaving you with all the wrong mana so you cannot cast the other spell in your hand (luckily you can turn this off). Same goes for auto-assign damage to blocking creatures, which you, and I urge you to do so, can turn off as well. By the way, I played the game on highest difficulty, so maybe it is their way to make the game harder, but this does not explain the AI behaviour.
6. The battlefield looks nice and clean, but every combat step it will slide apart to uncover some red moat. It's only a visual thing, and this is my own opinion, but I got annoyed by it after playing a couple of games. I don't  like the black border around selected cards in your hand either.
7. The menu, and speaking of which: the whole interface, is clearly ported from the console versions of the game. Scrolling through the menu is painful, and the sliding circles they are made up from are unclear. Scroll to zoom bugs out unless you replace your cursor away from the centre of the screen, and while the menu is usable with a mouse, I reverted back to using the keyboard for it most of the time.
8. When you first start up the game, the game asks you whether you are an experienced Magic player, and if you have played earlier versions of this game. All they do with this info though, is setting the difficulty. I clicked the equivalent of 'I know everything, I played Magic and the DotP games for years,' and after picking a starter deck the next stop was the tutorial. I played the first one, only to see if you would get some unlocks for them, but alas: No such thing. Then I clicked the 'Skip Tutorial' button, as for me it was more a torture than a tutorial, and I got the screen: "Congratulations! You have proven yourself worthy!" I liked the irony in that, I admit. Then I had to defeat a deck for real, using my severly underpowered starter deck. I say this because the largest creature I had was a 3/3. Most of the cards in the deck were borderline useless, and there was NO WAY to change the deck, or unlock more then a single card for it. It was hard fighting against 5/5 vigilance  angels, let me tell you. But then again, highest difficulty. And I was glad it was kind of difficult to get throught some encounters, losing a game sometimes was refreshing (and sometimes painfully annoying).
Final verdict: I don't really know. The game has much potential, but I am afraid we won't be seeing any of that until 2016. I have bought the game and had some fun with it, even though I knew much of the game was a step back compared to its predecessors. If you want to get some deckbuilding going, play against (not with, because of the lack of THG) friends or archenemies, then by all means go for it. Do not bother with buying the DLC though, it does not unlock anything you cannot get by playing the game, and the foil conversions... Well... Let's just say I don't like it when the cards in my R/B Vampire deck behave like Edward Cullen.

I've been reading a lot of bad reviews, or what I would call negative reviews on Magic 2015. I don't understand why this game is getting all the hate when I feel it's the best one yet. I get that a lot of people don't like the whole redesign of the game. Not having pre-created decks like it's predecessors. They think it's harder to get a good deck but it's really not. You still just gotta play through the campaign. Unlock your boosters and build a card collection, instead of a unlocking decks and building a deck collection, then you go and create decks out of the card pool. It's not even slower like some have said. Yeah you are kinda stuck to your starter deck color choice until you at least finish the first plane but it's no different then having 1 maybe 2 decks unlocked by the point in any of the previous games. Plus before you finish the final tutorial match you can change and re-choose which deck before you continue. A lot of people don't realize this and/or are too lazy to spend the time and practice with all the starting color combos then complain when they don't like their choice. That's your fault if you didn't. That being said all the decks can win just fine.
I think the redesign of the game was an eventual change and they should've done it sooner.
They finally added a Create a Deck feature that fans have been asking for since the first game. It was the biggest requested feature and we now have it! And yet people complain about it because it's not like the other games... Seriously? It doesn't restrict you to a pre-created decks and small card pools that you can change maybe 20 cards in and out but instead a much larger card pool of all different colors. The only restrictions are;
A) What you can make work. If you can make a viable 5 color deck nothing is stopping you from doing so. If you would rather  make a 3 color deck and it works nothing is stopping you. If you just want a simple mono color deck go ahead. Still if you want the standard two color combo deck you can do that too. They've opened up your options and give you the tools to make the deck you want, albeit even if it's from a limited card pool still but it's much larger than any of the previous games.
B) The unnecessary restrictions on card rarity and how many you can have in a deck. The official rule of having 4 copies of one specific card in a deck isn't how they chose to do it unfortunately. You are allowed the normal 4 of any one card as long as it's a common. You are only allowed to add 3 of any one card if it's uncommon, 2 if it is a rare, and only may have 1 mythic rare in a deck. I understand what they are trying to do by keeping it balanced or not allowing too many powerful cards but I disagree with doing so. It's balanced already if everybody is playing by the same rules and is allowed to have the same 4 of any card. If my friend puts 4 mythic rares of specific card in his deck for a better chance to draw that one it's fair because i can add 4 mythic rares to mine too if i so choose. It's all about creating a better deck, better card synergy anyways. What combos and what cards work together. I think they should reconsider this for the next game and just stick with the official rules of 4 of any one card.
Now I want to talk about this notion that they just want to suck more money out of players. "microtransactions." For as polished a card game as MTG is. With satisfying competitive card-duelling and great art $10 is more than fair price. And that's ALL YOU HAVE TO PAY. You can unlock every card in the game by doing campaign and going back and doing explore plane and facing a random opponent (this years version of challenges). If you just want to zip through the campaign and then jump on multiplayer you can unlock cards that way too. By playing multiplayer duels against friends and winning you get a random booster pack. All the cards in the game can be unlocked except the premium card pool, which is a small 50 cards or so side pool of cards they offer to players who want to further expand their collection and have more options when creating decks BUT i can tell you right now you don't need any of them cards to make plenty, AND I MEAN PLENTY of decks.
I have beat the game's campaign and am currently unlocking the rest of the cards, my friend already beat the campaign and unlocked every single card in the game and never had to pay anything but the price of the base game. We both have been making tons of decks with just the cards we unlocked and we're beating players who have boughten premium cards. So listen people if you put in the time with the game's campaign and play a lot of games you can definitely unlock the cards to make plenty of good decks, different colored decks, and not have to spend a dime extra than the price to buy the game. If you want to you can and that's fine it might let you make your deck better but It's definitely not pay to win. Trust me.
The other common complaint I hear is "fewer features than its predecessors,"  Yeah so they took out some modes like Planechase, Archenemy, and two headed giant but so what. Magic is mostly a 1vs1 game anyways and they still give you the ability to do a 3 or 4 player match, 1 vs 1 vs 1 vs 1 and 4 player matches are better that way than on teams. I too wish they would add in more casual multiplayer formats so we have more ways to play and maybe they will yet but it doesn't take away from the game.
Overall it's a great game, probably the best one yet, and I've had no real problems with the game. Except for a few issues with how smart it is by auto tapping the lands and not doing it right but they give you a option to choose which to tap so you can manage it manually yourself but I would think the A.I. would be smart enough to tell I have a green colored card left in my hand and to not use all my Forests in play but it don't. That and I have had issues with applying settings and the windowed mode not working right now but my friend hasn't had these same issues.
I just can't believe how overwhelmingly negative everybody is on this game. They finally give us the one feature everybody has been asking for and everybody hates the game. Full deck creation is the one feature everyone's wanted since the first game and now people complain because it's not as simple as previous editions where they made the deck for you? Pfft. GTFO

This game is really a miss. Slogging through the menus is an exercise in extraordinary patience, the "free" collection of cards is worthless. Don't get fooled into believing you can unlock all the cards through hard work and perseverence: certain cards are locked behind the money wall. Of course, these are the good cards. So if you want to play online with other people and not just the AI, then you're going to have to shell out.
But you can't really just play against the AI, either. Opponents get stacked hands and decks, and no matter what you do they play the same way virtually every time. Either you turn the difficulty up and play against an opponent with a stacked deck and the skill to wield it at almost perfect effectiveness, or you turn the difficult down and watch the opponent, half the time, defeat himself with absurdly bad plays.
Since starting the game, I have only seen my opponent get mana-screwed one time. I am mana- or at least color-screwed 9 games out of ten. With a control deck. With 27 lands. It could just be ridiculously bad luck, I know, but the sheer number of unplayable hands I see leads me to believe that there is something wrong with the game's "shuffling".
All things considered, this game is only fun if you want to buy all the cards and play online with other people. Single player is a joke and, honestly, an affront to a magic player with a decent level of skill, and the cards you can unlock in the base $9.99 game don't allow for any cool decks to be made--and certainly not a deck that can compete with other players online.

"Ancient Go" aims to be an app for total beginners to Go, which is great. Currently, outside of "Ancient Go," the only other app out there on Steam is "Crazy Stone Deep Learning -The First Edition-," which is $79.99. However, "Crazy Stone" is arguably meant for committed Go players, who are much stronger at the game. So, "Ancient Go" is a cheaper alternative for "Crazy Stone" that allows the Steam community to start playing Go at a cheaper price. That said, "Ancient Go" has its strengths and weaknesses.
+ A relatively flexible and potentially strong AI.
+ Access to the Online Go Server (OGS) via a free account, which allows for getting a rank.
+ Tutorials to get started.
+ Allows for changes in board size.
+ Can change scoring rules.
+ Beautiful GUI.
+ Steam achievements for encouraging beginners.
+ Can play against friends on Steam (I have yet to try this.)
+ The developer seems to listen to user input, judging by changes made in the past.
+ The app helps bring awareness of Go to the general gaming community via Steam.
+ Supports different rule sets.
+ The developer appears to be working on further updates for the future.
+ Visual hints included for weaker players.
+ Undo feature to allow players to learn from mistakes.
- The AI tends to play tactically, not strategically, even at stronger levels.
- The jump between the difficulty levels is too large for people to smoothly progress through.
- Does not allow players to add handicap stones.
- Currently cannot chose sides with the AI.
- Currently cannot vary the komi with the AI.
- Capture Go for beginners is not available as an option.
- Little advantage to the online play now, unless one's internet browser is broken.
- Only access to the OGS server is allowed. (KGS, IGS, TyGem, etc. are not available.)
- Does not teach Go terminology (i.e., atari, ko, tsumego, tesuji, joseki, etc.)
- Does not recommend/provide other resources (i.e., books, Go problems, etc.)
- Cannot change graphic settings.
- AI tends to play moves that make no sense (i.e., self-atari, keeps playing when no points can be gained), even at stronger levels.
- Does not explain the differences between the different rule sets.
- Does not have abilities that would help users teach, save, or review games natively (unless I am missing something here).
All-in-all, the app does what it sets out to do, but I would not say that it encourages players to keep playing for long periods of time and keep coming back for more. I recommend it only for the sake of the Go community to keep growing and going strong.

Ancient Go is a barebones Go client for Steam. If you don't know about Go, it's an abstract strategy board game that is thousands of years old yet still popular today. It is unique in many respects; you can learn more and try it out free at
. The rest of this review will focus specifically on this software, not the game itself, which is excellent.
Ancient Go features a 3D model of a Go game, a rudimentary AI, and can function as a basic client for the Online Go Server. OGS is a large and established community of Go players so you should be able to find a game at any skill level any time of day. I was not able to get that feature to work (it kept saying my username and password were wrong, though I was able to log in on my browser just fine) but I'll give it the benefit of the doubt and assume this is just a temporary bug.
This software has the features any Go client worth installing *must* have, but it lacks the features such a client *should* have. In order of importance, these include:
I'm not sure who the target audience for Ancient Go is. People who take the game seriously are used to the rich, efficient, and *free* clients that already exist and will likely not drop their features and cash just to get a render of a board and an additional potential point of failure in online matches. People who are new/casual Go players are going to need more help than "here's how to place stones, here's what 'ko' means, good luck!".
Even when one tempers expectations (a $5 price point, a dev team of one) Ancient Go is a letdown. I hope the developer continues to work on it and I can update my review to a more positive rating. As of now, it's just too bare; visit
for everything this game can do and 10x more, for free and without installing anything. Then, if you love the game and want to spend money to play in a cool 3D environment and let your steam friends know you're doing so, buy Tabletop Simulator instead.

Okay, guys, here it is.
If you want a puzzle game where you get to solve puzzles by resizing stuff, well, this is not that kind of a game.
The actual number of puzzles that require resizing stuff to solve them is close to zero. All you have to do is carry cubes around and place them on buttons. The size of those cubes doesn't matter at all, only if you use them to get to high platforms.
The developers' thoughts must have been like this: "Hey, let's take the idea of resizing and make a game with it, because someone else might have the same idea and make something good, but here we are with ReSiZe and lawsuits and stuff", and they made this game just for the sake of being the first to use this kind of mechanics. But the game is so bad and raw. You spend half the time carrying cubes, and the second half — waiting for incredibly slow platforms to carry you somewhere.
Not a single "puzzle" makes you think. And did I mention that puzzles don’t involve resizing stuff at all? I guess I have.
Here are some ideas for you, developers. I came up with them in about five minutes when I woke up in the night to go to the toilet.
1.	Size affects weight. When I step onto a button, I’m told “You’re not fat”. Apparently, a teeny tiny cube is fat enough. Why not make it possible to press a button with a big cube, but not with a small one?
2.	Let’s say there are magnets and/or floating platforms. The magnets can attract small cubes, but not big ones, and a platform sinks if you put a big cube on it. Cuz it’s heavy. Yeah.
3.	Or there are some systems that you have to balance using cubes of various size. To make it more difficult and interesting, let’s say cubes don’t weigh 4, 8 or 16 pounds/kilos, but 4, 10, 18, I don’t know. Something like the water riddle in Die Hard 3.
4.	Or, for instance, there’s a platform moving horizontally with a cube on it. It goes through a series of obstacles. A small cube can fit into a hole, and a big cube can push away something that blocks its path, cuz it’s heavy, remember? And you have to resize the cube accordingly from a distance. It would be fun, I guess.
If you spend a bit more time developing actual puzzles, you can do better than that. I hope.
And yeah, the optimization. I can’t say I have the most powerful PC in the world, but, for example, one of the recent games, the one that involves killing Nazis, gives me stable 60 FPS in FullHD with average quality. ReSiZe can’t even provide 30 FPS with the lowest quality possible in 1600x900. I would understand that if you had developed your own engine, but it’s Unreal Engine you’re using, so wtf?
Anyway, for all of you who consider buying this game — don’t. It’s so not worth $7 I paid for it.
