This game has some serious pacing and balance issues. Some levels are so easy they can barely be considered entertaining, others are so hard you're left wondering if there's some hidden mechanic you're missing that's necessary to play the game. Also the enemy in Story mode doesn't seem to follow any of the same rules the player is forced to in terms of gold or mana accrual. Even if you kill all of their workers they seem to have no trouble finding gold to spawn new units as quickly as possible (unit cooldowns also don't seem to apply for them). What this means for gameplay is that you have to follow the pattern they set for you or you're quickly overwhelmed. Which makes this not a game. It makes it a set of instructions. The graphics are pretty but not particularly so. The music is fitting but not particularly so. The story is amusing but not particularly so. Pretty much the entire game left me with that "Yeah, and?" kind of feeling.
If you're a superfan of tower defense games or really simple strategy toys, consider picking this up during a sale for at least 80% off of it's retail price (9.99 as of 7/7/15). Otherwise, I'd avoid this title completely.
Disclosure: I did not buy this game directly but instead received it as part of a Humble Bundle. This is not the sort of game I would typically consume, so I may not be the most reliable reviewer.

(Stay clear of the starter edition this game does go on sale , the starter edition is a mega grind to get anywhere)  So after 500+ hours of gameplay I can say I have never been addicted to a game as much as this. The previous addiction of mine was the free to play game planetside 2 which has a strong focus on team play and tactics. This game could been seen as an evolution of another game I picked up a year previous to this one. That game would be CS:Go a game which is a staple in the fps industry. The concepts of CS:Go are simple and I will not knock the game however the simple fps concepts have been expanded and adapted in this game.
The adaptation and evolution hasn't created a carbon copy like many other fps out in the market but adds a lot more elements and variables. The biggest element of all as advertised in the destructive and interactive maps offered this adds a whole new level of tactics and gameplay that CS:Go never offered me. The gadgets are unique to your chosen operators which can been seen as loadouts, they all add something different when attacking or defending that is refreshing to see. The devs continue to work on the game and bring out new content, however they made the choice to pause on such content to work on the overall health of the game. In this I say in part has been very useful but given the size of the dev could have been done in a greater and better way. This game is a solid fps game however isn't a perfect execution, it has a few grievances with me personally that need to be addressed, these issues have been addressed in a much preferable way in CS:GO. The content should also get a reworking at present all new operators are unlocked through an in game currency you can earn from playing the game. This currency is rather easy to obtain but the operators are all priced the same, apart from the original operators. They should at least think about decreasing the amount needed to unlock operators each year so the most recent ones cost the most and so on as that would be fair. There are a few other issues but I feel overall in time these will be addressed the devs are very active and hope to keep the game alive for years to come. I can only recommend this game to people looking for an evolution of this genre and want a game that require more thought.

Okay well let me say firstly these are just my first impressions, the game is very new and I've not got many hours on it so some of this stuff may be inaccurate.
Arms Dealer is in my opinion a very good game with a lot of promise-and with future patches and such I can see it being a very complex sim that you can sink hours into. However right now at this moment it seems very shallow.
So let me explain a bit.
Arms Dealer is a business sim where you whizz around the world selling weapons illegally trying to beat the competition and stay ahead of the law while getting $tack Bundle$ of dolla dolla.
So let me focus on some of the actual buisness and economic aspects of the game seeing as they are it's core mechanics.
Well it all seems a bit two dimensional and areas that could be incredibly deep seem very vauge and not properly explained or disfunctional.
Firstly- supply and demand. Basic economic principles. Certain countries are called Arms Suppliers, and they, suprisingly, supply you with guns. Nations like France, Switzerland, the Uk, Russia, China and the USA and a few others. Each supply thier own national models of firearm and they differ in price based upon assumed quality (though this isn't an ingame value and it abstracted rather crudly I feel to simply "PRICE" reflecting it's supposed quality)
Every other country in the world is an arms buyer. Yup thats right- except for maybe 8 or 9  nations no-one else is selling or making any sort of firearm in the world. No-one.
You can't even buy surplus stock of other countries weapons from them. This seems a little unrealistic seeing as countries like Syria, Iran and others are major suppliers of weaponry. Secondly, over-abundance of supply seems to have little or no effect on price. I sold 265 crates of grenade launchers to the Netherlands during thier War with Ukraine (thus taking those weapons off the market effectivly as i bought up all of Russia's supply of them)
However a few in-game days later I returned to Russia, the supply had magically regenerated so i bought them all again and went back to The Netherlands and sold them for the exact same price. Now I know weapons break and degrade ect but within an in-game week and half I had sold a massive $400,000,000 worth of Grenade launchers to the Netherlands which would be fine. Except I basically flooded thier market with them and just raked in massive profits. Surely someone at Netherlands HQ (tm) was sat thier doing stock take thinking "♥♥♥♥ we have a lot of Grenade launchers we don't really need to pay much for them anymore" and why was no-one in Russia going "♥♥♥♥ Grenade Launchers are popular lets double the price"
It broke the game and was a simple exploit. In a month of back and forth trading I made 1.2 BILLION and jumped from being the worlds number 100 arms dealer to 18th. It's not really providing any depth or challenge is it? And this is all before The Agentcy (the law enforcers baisically) even were aware I existed. In fact they didn't try to activly stop me until i reached 11th on the table.
After that it was easy sailing, I could go to any country I wanted and buy up thier entire stock and sell it all en-mass to The Netherlands and make huge profits. All this time I didn't sell a single gun to Ukraine, but this didn't seem to affect the war at all. No there are potentially 99 other arms dealers in game, (but so far I've only happened to chance upon 1 of them while I was chillin in Cuba waiting to make the trip to the USA.) So maybe they sold the Ukraine guns but that data, if it exists, isn't easy to find. In fact I didn't find it. So I have no idea. But surely selling almost the entire arms producing worlds stock to one country would end the war pretty quickly?
So to spice things up a bit I decide to become a war maker. The game has a feature called Black Umbrella where you can manipulate nations into going to war with each other. But this seems overly complex and abstracted, I didnt; really know what I was doing except green numbers good, red numbers bad in creating war desire. It broke immersion a little bit, and it was also ridiculously easy. After making so much money from my arms dealing I could withstand the price of any of the triggers needed to start the war. 3 million is all it took to make Ethiopia and Poland go to war, I make double that in a single Russia-Netherlands Grenade Launcher run these days.
Ethiopia and Poland. WTF. How would that even work? Geo-politics doesn't seem to exist in Arms Dealer on a sort of level. You also cannot make Arms Suppliers go to war, despite the USA, Russia, China and Israel being probably the most likely countries to get into a war.
There seems to be a bit of an attempt at alliances though with COMAX, NATO and NA opinions changing of you with every purchase and sale but frankly this all seems a little pointless. I have no idea who is in any of these factions beyond simple guesswork as faction lists don't exist or if they do I couldn't find them and no tool tips existed to tell me where to look. No do I have any idea what they affect. At first I thought price. Russia is probably COMAX and Netherlands is probably NATO, but the prices of Russian weapons didn't change nor did the quantity despite the massive sales and -6000 COMAX opinion i was generating on each trip. So I have no idea if thats a bug or what.
So thats a lot of negatives and you're probably wondering why I recomended this game. Well frankly it is a lot of fun. I really enjoyed the idea of using a freight ship to move hundreds of tonnes of munitions to Mexico and then manipulating them into a war with Finland and getting insanely rich. It's also very addictive and I stayed up way too late these last few nights thinking "I'll just do one more trip" or "I'll just make one more war"
Secondly, the potential for depth is there. With a more in-depth economic system and geo-political system this game could be fantastic. It could be highly complex with a very large challenge attached to it. So for the moment I'd say buy the game and enjoy it for what it is but pay attention to it and it may develop into something amazing.
EDIT: I'd also say that the dev's are really fast at trying to fix things which is a refreshing change given the current tidal wave of utter♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that has swamped Steam lately. Permanently unfinished Early Acess games that sit vacant for months are strangling Steam and overcrowding it with medicority, the comitment of the devs is a true breath of fresh air.
Secondly a lot of people are complaining of bugs and crashes, i've not had any crashes or obvious bugs so far. The tutorial is very clunky though.

This is the game that I have wanted since I was little kid, playing Star Wars Battlefront 2. It is absolutely amazing.
The space combat involves both small fighters and large captial ships, fighting it out either for control points or to destroy/defend targets.
The ground combat has the same objectives, and also a multitude of vehicles (including APCs, tanks, and even a gunship!).
The level of customization is incredible; there are a lot of weapons and upgrades, meaning you can play just about however you want. And that extends into most of the vehicles and fighters, too!
The combat itself feels both organic and tactical, with either a player or the AI acting as a commander for the entire team issuing orders to be carried out by squad leaders, who have two squad members to help them.
I wish there was a better system for giving commands, though; it sometimes is a little tricky targeting objectives to order your team to attack them.
And the UI isn't the best; it often feels a little clunky, and new; however, this is a big thing the devs are working on.
Also important is that the devs have devoted and continue to devote a lot of time and energy into improving this game; the most recent update took a while to come out, but it was also a very large update with a lot in it.
I find that I experience quite a bit of lag sometimes, especially in ground battles; but that's another thing the devs are devoting time to fixing, and it has improved quite a bit since I started.
My only other complaint is that it has a small player base for some reason; I don't really know why, it is an amazing game that is so much fun to play with actual people instead of bots.

No issues with fatal errors here, game is running rock solid. I actually forgot it on for like 6 hours (most of the "play time" I had so far, haha - I haven't had a chance to play it as much as I have wanted to) and came back to it still running without any crashes.
Gameplay seems very fun so far. It's a fairly traditional trading sim with some nice twists. You have to pay money to get intel to determine the market for different guns since you're working on the black market. Or you can just buy guns and try to sell them blind. You can make a little money just selling from supplier countries to buyer countries. Or make your own demand - initiate black ops jobs to start wars between countries, then make bank selling the countries weapons at higher prices.
Several official organizations are trying to catch you and you can be tracked and build up a bounty and become wanted. You can also work to either track and do bad things to your competition, or make alliances with other arms dealers. I haven't gotten far enough into that to see how it all works. I know you can bribe officials to stave off bounty hunters, but I haven't dealt with them yet either.
The only issue I have had is the economy breaking and demand becoming static (which lets me dump ridiculous amounts of weapons at high prices without dropping them) but other people I've talked to haven't had that issue. I contacted the devs about it and they seemed very surprised to hear about it and are currently working to fix it, so if you have the same issue know that they're working on it (although extra reports wouldn't hurt I'm sure).
-edit- The patches fixed the above issue I was having.
I'll come back and update the review once I have time to play the game a bit more, but so far I don't see any reason for the negative reviews.

To me this is the closest thing to Star Wars Battlefront 3 that we are likely to see for a long time. It's got everything I want, land battles (with infantry, tanks, gunships, etc. all in an objective based environment), space battles (with ship boarding, frigates, capital ships, cruisers, etc.), loadout customization, and even light squad command (which I hope to see greatly expanded on and streamlined).
That being said it is in Early Access and being developed by a small team. The development is slow, the playerbase very small (which the devs aren't worried about because they don't want to get their marketing into full swing until the game is more complete), the UI clunky (which is will be fixed very soon),  and the graphics kinda bad (they went for a realistic style which I personally think was a bad move).
The only really big gripe I have with the game is lack of singleplayer profile. I play games on the go a lot and last I checked my profile isn't persistent when offline (which is important because you need to level to equip more stuff). I do not know if this will be changed ever.
Despite its shortcomings I highly recommend this game. It's price is reasonable, the devs are nice and responsive,  and the gameplay is very fun.

Thanks to Dev Saxxon for his reply, I appreciate his quick response and I'm reposting his comment here:
That sounds good. However, what really matters in this kind of game is resources and territory.
You want to have a real player driven world, with incentives both to conquer and to defend, giving value to virtual stuff and, eventually, making gameplay emerge ? Then you have to have a simulation of RL economics and resource management.
A river, a strategic point, a source of easy income, etc… should be things to fight for, and not giving access to everything to everyone is what creates the need for player interaction, be it conquest, trading, theft, agreements…
Most sandbox RPGs failed because they tried to focus on other aspects of gameplay before laying this groundwork, ultimately creating a giant with clay feet which would clumber as soon as the hype faded, or as soon as something came unbalancing the fragile balance of the more refined gameplay systems.
On the other hand, take the example of a successful sandboxe like EvE : it survived through to good and the bad versions, through the hard drive erasing patches, through the Goons (mad props), through the watergate-like revelations, etc… because everytime remained the incentive to play, to fight, to interact.
If you take player interaction from EvE, it’s a very boring game. And if you erase resource scarcity and territorial value, there’s no player interaction to that game.

This game is really fun. There is a huge variety of gameplay here - both the infantry combat and space combat are well executed, which is a commendable feat. I often find myself enjoying a couple rounds of space combat, then switching to a ground combat map and enjoying myself just as much - neither aspect of the game has been left out or recieved less attention than it deserves. Many space combat maps also involve boarding objectives.
I think the space combat deserves special mention, plodding around in the larger ships is a blast. I am not really into twitchy space fighter combat so I usually avoid those, instead deploying as a corvette, destroyer, cruisers, or even battleship when they become available. Flying the larger ships is a lot of fun as you get to think about how to position your ships (for the AI controlled turrets) and when and where to use the ship spinal mount weapons (big forward firing ion beams) and missiles (which often fire in salvoes of 4 or 6) which are directly under your control.
The AI is very good. It does a decent job at acting believable and seems able to take and defend objectives and perform most tasks in game - which as far as most games go is spectacular. My AI squadmates don't seem to follow orders particularly closely but that hasn't really bothered me, I just let them do their thing.
Many reviewers have mentioned a general lack of player population however I have enjoyed the game regardless because the AI is pretty good. Even with only 2 human players on each team (the rest being AI) the game is fun, though I am sure the experience must be very different with more human players.
If you try this game, don't make the mistake I did - go straight to multiplayer. As mentioned it is very fun even without any other human players. The AI is smart but only when set to the highest settings, which on my (admittedly older computer) is laggy - so join a multiplayer server and let the server take care of all the AI processing. Multiplayer is smooth and is the same thing as singleplayer anyways. I almost gave up on the game after the first hour because of singleplayer, then I joined an empty multiplayer server and got hooked for the entire evening. A few other players even joined after a little while.

For as far as the game goes, cars drive realistically and playing with a keyboard is a pain. A controller or a decent steeringwheel gets that out of the way flawlessly. Like real life you shouldn't flat out the gaspedal and you don't exclusively steer hard left or right.
It's not a racegame (yet?), but still more of a physics and crash engine show off. Not only is it very impressive, good lord is it fun! From cruising past landscapes to folding your car around a tree and watch metal deform in slow motion.
Gamemodes seem to get added and updated over time. Like I said, unlike most early access games the developers keep adding depth to the game rather than a new car or 2 before abandoning the project. I for one am eager to see what the game will grow in to.
Highly recommended if game mechanics and sheer dumb fun is your thing!

Having played the sequel on the Wii U at PAX 2014, I was excited to see how Swords & Soldiers HD held up to its younger brother. It’s not as fancy as the sequel, but still has all of the charm that grabbed me when I played Swords & Soldiers II. The factions feel different from each other and each need their own tactics to be played well. Without anymore babbling on, let’s get into it!
The Swords & Soldiers series come off as basic and cartoony. It’s almost a little too basic to grab my attention if I had just seen a video. This is another example of why you shouldn’t base your opinion on a game solely on looks. (I’m going to have to get over that since it appears that I’ve said that a lot lately.) I know it’s getting harder and harder to do with how graphics are shaping up these days, but with all this good content out there with simple graphic schemes, it’s important to try a game out before one blows it off completely.
So without all the fancy-schmancy HD-ness of its sequel, Swords & Soldiers HD focuses on fun gameplay with some deep gameplay/tactical decisions. You’ve got to carefully manage how you work your available options because the slightest misstep could cost you the game. (That sounds overly dramatic, but it has happened to me.) Do you need to create more gold miners or get some research done to build some fighters to apply pressure onto your opponent. What type of unit do you research first? Want a slow heavy-hitter or a ranged (but low HP) user? Eventually you’ll have everything researched, but you may find it in your best interest to not do everything up front lest you find yourself with all the options in the book, but no money or defenses when the enemy comes a-knocking.
All of the factions feel completely different and I like that. As impressed as I was that the sequel not have reskinned armies with the same abilities, the same applies here. You’ll obviously have a few units that play similar, but with enough differences to make you wish that your unit could either poison others or rush into fights. It’s give-and-take all while each army has their appeal and that’s what’s so great: having options. Not only are the units available different, but how your basic game mechanics work are also different. Everyone has passive mana regen, but how you get more differs from faction to faction.
The Aztecs have to sacrifice units in order to gain more mana faster. Personally, they are the hardest to play. I just can’t seem to strike the balance between building my army/defense and figuring out how to get the 350 mana needed to pull off my super move. I’m also not used to sacrificing my own units. The Chinese run almost similar to the Vikings except they abandon defensive towers in favor of towers that help regen mana quicker. I get it, and I’ve actually won matches as both factions, but two out of three factions just don’t do it for me. I’m not sure if it’s the fact that the Vikings look like Dwarves or that they are simple in execution. The Vikings are pretty straight forward: economy, defense, damage. I know that tends to be my thing, but I do believe no single game has pigeon-holed me so well into one specific faction.
Score: Gewd.
Swords & Soldiers HD is a solid game. All three factions offer distinctively different ways to play the game and that’s very cool. The fact that I can’t very well play two of them is more on me than it is the game itself.  I know this is more of a multiplayer game for those competitive sorts, but the campaign does offer a good fun story packed with humor and is worth the purchase in and of itself. While the game is pretty good, it’s getting older now since the sequel is coming out and having played both, Swords & Soldiers II will probably be the favored son. I’d recommend picking Swords & Soldiers HD up when it’s on sale to play it as well as support a good developer.

This is an exceptionally well done game. The attention to detail is outstanding.
It basically follows the 16-bit (SNES, Genesis, Amiga, etc) style of platformer except here everything is in HD. The levels are colorful, well drawn and most important there is a good amount of interaction.

When I die I want to be able to immediately get right back to the start of the level and start playing again.
Besides that this game is excellent! Oh another thing I want to mention is the music & sounds. Both are superb. The music puts me in a sort of fun lazy mood. Overall the entire game is very well done and it is easy to see the developer spent a lot of care and time creating this game.
Highly recommended if you enjoy platform games.

This game gets a lot of hate for the P2P network connection the games use. Personally, the only network issues I come across are when the host of the lobby leaves, which more often than not end up successfully transferring to a proper host within the time available, and a few occasional hiccups which are met with a game pause to avoid any unfair moves during the hiccup.
With the network connectivity aside, I have never played a game similar to this, or at least extensively. My playlist of games includes MOBA's and FPS games, with some Open World type games. And I love this game. People say the combat can get boring, but if you start to get worn out, switch queue types. There is the fast paced dominion capture-the-point mode, the potentially stressful 1v1 and 2v2 game types, the hectic skirmish mode and the larger scale 4v4 mode.
I expect to be playing this game for a long time, and hopefully the P2P connection, some slightly over/underpowered heroes and various launch bugs don't scare people away, because this is a great game and deserves live out as one.

So, a lot of people call this game "the scariest game they've ever played", and go on and on about the scariness, but I am evidence that it is totally possible to play this game without really being scared! Most of the "horror" of this game is just gross things (read: fleshy things) in dark rooms, which isn't really horrifying, it's just... gross stuff in dark rooms, and if that's not something that bothers you, then you'll be just fine in this game. Honestly, Daniel (the main character) is much, much more freaked out than I am! If you play this with the idea that it's a video game, and play it the same way you'd play any other video game, then it's more fun than scary! It has a cool back story and very interesting puzzles, and interesting mechanics involving keeping Daniel's mental health from deteriorating by keeping him out of the dark (which he seems to be very afraid of), and from observing disturbing events. So this is not a game where you can just run from point a to point b, you really have to think and strategize about your movements and where you go/stand to keep Daniel in a functional state. It's pretty cool and I've not played anything quite like it before! Also, rather than fighting monsters, you have to make them go away, which is also quite interesting (though there were no monsters for the entire first hour of the game and that was a bit disappointing to me), by hiding in the dark, no less! And either action, getting too close to a monster, or hanging out in the dark, will lower Daniel's sanity, so it requires some careful planning and knowing when it will be okay to come out. As briefly mentioned earlier, the story is presented in a very cool way, Daniel gave himself amnesia at the beginning and you basically have it right along with him, as you obviously don't know anything that he used to know. And as the story unfolds its like unravelling a mystery. Very cool! I also found the game a bit educational, as it takes place in the 1800's and is faithful to the time period, so I was able to look up some of the objects that are in the game and learn about what they were. All in all, this was a very enjoyable experience for me, so I give it a full recommendation! I didn't find it as scary as most people seem to, but I enjoy the gameplay and find it to be a very unique experience. I've had a lot of fun!

Early Access Day 1 review:
Edit: Thumbs up because it looks promising. (I'd hold off getting it until counting method issues are resolved, hopefully.)
Project seems promising. It includes basic tutorials for rules and scoring, a VS. AI mode and an Online multiplayer mode.
The AI is not particularly strong on any setting (Hard is when it starts playing slightly better moves, maximum tends to take a bit more time to play moves, but not a LOT of time.) So (at least at this stage) the AI is really meant for beginners. It would be nice to get a stronger one later down the line, but I'd rather see good multiplayer added than the focus be on AI.
The UI is polished and pretty. It seems simplistic, but in the same way that Go is "simple", giving it a nice "relaxed", almost elegant look.
A few notes:
At the current stage, it does NOT appear as though you can do the following:
*You cannot Select custom Komi values (7.5 is way too much on small boards! I usually play with 6.5 komi on 19x19 anyway...)
*You cannot Choose to play Black or White (It always made me black? Maybe the Host is always black?)
*You cannot Choose different scoring methods (Japanese and Chinese (area counting) being the most important of these. Are points in mutual life counted as points? I haven't encountered this yet so I'm not sure...)
*You cannot Choose different timing options for the game (e.g., Canadian Byo-yomi or Japanese Byo-yomi)
All of these will be vital things to add, in my opinion, to make the title complete and robust. The lack of scoring methods really stuck out to me, as requiring people to capture "dead" stones in their territory may teach them the value of filling in dame, or "neutral" points first, but not all scoring methods will allow you to play stones within your territory without penalty.
As a side note, I am not a fan of including "two eyes" in the tutorial. I believe needing "two eyes" is an emergent property of groups, which are not made until they are needed, so they should not be taught as required... Teaching the concept of "two eyes" being required for life has often made beginners I'm teaching/facing over-concentrate, allowing me to gain the upper hand everywhere else on the board. This is a bad habit I have to try to knock out of them. "Two eyes" isn't a rule, it's just something you learn a group needs space to 'eventually' make in order to live 'if' required.
I look forward to seeing what this project becomes in the future! I am very excited to be able to share and play Go with friends on steam!

First, I would like to say that you will either love or hate this game, and you will know it within the first few hours of playing. I dont see anybody that just sort of plays this game here and there for fun. This game simply does not work that way. However, I will dissagree with other reviews in regards to playing alone. I play alone, and have my own little medieval farm tucked away surrounded by forest. It took me many many hours to get to that point, and the server does not skill cap anything, so people can level up as much as they want. Those types of servers, one can go solo and thrive.
With that little background, the game is for the most part realistic. Almost everything in this game is time consuming, and Im not going to lie... perhaps a little too time consuming. I have a small hut, back yard garden with wattle fence surrounding it, and that literally took me three days to build. However, during the time of construction, I had to stop and go looking for food because the last thing you want to do in this game is die.
So what is the goal of this game? What ever you want it to be. My goal was to simulate a nice little medieval farm, tend to it, improve it... etc. I am very pround of what I have built, and this game has some lasting rewards. Some may strive for control, the amount of weapons and possibilites in this game is ridiculously huge thus allowing them to control by force is neccessary. However, you will not really find players like Reign of Kings, just running around killing people. You dont do that in this game because their is just too much to lose, too much progress, and too much hard work being put in by people. With that being said, the community is awesome, very mature, and helpful.
Buy this game if you......
1. Want realistic medival simulator
2. Are a dedicated player
3. Willing to actually learn the game, because the learning curve is huge!
Do not buy this game if you...
1. Are a casual PC gamer
2. Think progress in Rust, or Reign of Kings is too slow
3.  Cant deal with a little bit of bugs, not game breaking... but complete lack of understanding for early access games.

Do not buy this game!
If you enjoyed Duels of the Planeswalkers (dotp) 2014, do not buy this game!  If you like Magic, do not buy this game!  No one should buy this game!
Besides the slow and clunky interface is the fewest and weakest card pool since dotp began.  I was interested in this game as it was the first dotp game to have comepletely open deckbuilding.  No more pre-built decks forcing you use to use suboptimal cards to update them to a slightly better deck, I thought.  Well, I was correct about the pre-built decks being gone, but not about the sub-optimal cards.
Issues:
1) Card pool - The card pool is 400 cards.  This may sound like a lot, but spread across five colors, artifacts, multicolored, and lands and it is far too few.  Did you want to play an archetype beyond aggro, mid range, and control?  Too bad.  There's no support for ramp, dredge, or reanimator.  Also, since there are no pre-constructed decks, seeing fun blasts from the past are gone.  No mono W Humans aggro, no more GW enchantments, no more equipment deck.  There are no buildling blocks available to build anything but what you can build in a normal, boring draft.
2) Card power level - The entire card pool is about the power level of M 2015.  As you unlock cards, all you'll see is more and more limited chaff that you'd be emberassed to play in a deck you constructed.  It honestly feels like you're playing M 2015 block constructed.  Yeah, that awful.  Gone are the days with powerful removal, wraths, cheap reanimator cards, good counterspells, or efficient creatures.  Most of the decks from dotp 2014, fresh from being unlocked, could beat the best thing I could build in dotp 2015.
3) Microtransactions - Sure, the game costs only $10, right?  WRONG!!  A list of select cards are hidden in premium only packs, which can only be purchased from the cash shop.  There is no other way to get these cards other than to spend money.  I've seen reports it costs $50 to unlock 4 ofs for each of these cards.
In conclusion, don't waste your money on this greedy, shallow, weak product.  Buy any of the other dotp games, at a fair discount these days, and enjoy those games.  Whatever you do, don't waste your money on this.

In a battle of The Good, The Bad, and ugly, this game defiantly comes out on top. It has a very unique style in its class, a great community, and Devs who listen and respond to its players. The game provides plenty of features, lots of different tactics to try, and does a good job rewarding you for hard work. Let's break it down:
The GOOD:
- Lots of units to mix match and unlock
- I love research, upgrading, and expanding. Everything from buildings to individual units
- Crazy epic and awesome units are immortal. Meaning when you save up all your crowns to get that dragon. You love him, pet him, and feed him, give him a great home and BAM! Some glory dragon slayer slays your dragon! (Noooo) But no worries, he may lose a few levels of experience, but he is not lost forever!
- I love how epic my cities feel. In the early stages of the game things feel slow. A little humpty-Dumpty, but the pace quickly picks up. Especially when you start sieges.
- Siege Battles!
- The real money exchange system isn't a pay to win. They have boosts to help get your city going, but most everything else is aesthetics.
- Co-OP options are awesome. When doing something that you need a little extra oomph… Go Co-Op!
The Bad:
- What can I say, games got bugs. While Kingdom Wars has eliminated most of the 'Show Stoppers' an occasional boot out of a battle, or a vanishing GUI can still provide headache. Even though the developers have done a great job reimbursing any lost time / effort, it's still a hassle.
- Friends / Guilds / Chat system is a little clunky. Sometimes it's hard to tell when someone is online, or directly chatting with you.
- I have mixed feelings about the map. Part of me wishes we could see other player cities, while another part says this is a very interesting setup. I like not being camped, people sitting outside my city waiting for protection to fall, but on the other hand. I kind of miss doing it?
The Ugly:
- The biggest complaint I have about the game is some of the weird, jerky movement in battle. I hate having to issue orders multiple times to get a unit to perform a special task.
- Though I love Co-Op, sometimes finding someone to help you perform a task is… troublesome. Sometimes I sit for 15+ minutes looking for someone to siege with me.
- The popup messages are troublesome. They ask or provide you with certain information. "Would you like to vessel a city, or loot it for xx crowns." If you don't answer before another message is triggered you lose both options. Being invited to a Co-Op is sometimes confusing. Yes it tells you the name or quest, but it zooms so far into the map, it's hard to tell where you really are.
Overall, I would highly recommend the game. The units, city building, and unique features add a very refreshing spin on the RTS genre. The Free to play is truly free as you will not find a hidden 'Pay to win' market. The community is helpful, and the Developers are extremely repsonsive. Raise a mug to Kingdom Wars!

Greetings steam comunity,
5cents on why this game is recommendet by me and why you should waste a part of youre precious livetime playing it.
First of all - why should one play it?
- its fun
- its free
- its got castels
- its got dragons (some of them slightly three headed)
- its got mad magics
- its not a pay2win
To give this a more serious aproach - the pro stuff:
+ The game is a fine mixed castle building, army training and stuff wrecking experience(, a little of what i wanted as a stronghold fan :) ).
+ Three playable races - elves, man and orcs.
+ The gameplay of the battles is well done. Whyle the overal controling mechanism is rather simple one may invest some energy into the micromanagement of unit stances and rotations to gain the best from the troops efforts.
+/- The castle is limited to a few number of designs and placement spots - which are nicely done to alow the player a rather wide range of tactical options.
+ The Armys consist of up to 60 units, including sige engines and workers to get all those shiny coins from the corpses. As the units gain experience they may be upgradet to fit the players needs.
+ The KI citys are chalanging and differ greatly in theyr designs
+ The pvp system seems promising, presenting some late game challange, interesting battles and army compositions and the rather easy and fair mechanics of avoiding it by paying a part of ones ressources to the attacker.
+ The overal unit ballancing seems to be sound and while its not perfect the developers are working to improve it.
+ The comunity is alive and quite friendly.
To play it is a little like....
One may upgrade his camp to a formidable stronghold. While the walls rise high the troops may march to complete the first quests and plunder some stuff on the way. By doing so one aquires the in game currency of crowns - and even if there is a rather great heap of those in the in game store, the number one may get there is limited.
In time the army will get experienced and gain enough power to take on the great citys of the world. The choice between looting a vanquished city or taking it on as a vassal is rather rewarding - more so if you just managed to gain a victory inside the walls of the capital :).
On the dark side ther are a few things to be said:
- The KI is just not up to the task. While the unit KI is ok with only some minor *whydoyoustupidhealersengagetheogersinmeeleagain >.<* kind of problems the KI troops on the battlefield remain stationary until engaged, most of the time. Most of the movements an enemy will do are rushing his remaining troops into the keep, if you break don its gate, and some counter charges if this gate did not belong to the keep. The odd exeption is a charge of the reinforcement troop. Those apear after half an hoer into a KI sige and are pathetically easy to block, by disengaging your troops from the city and mincing the reinforcements.
- The ballancing of the fractions is not finished yet. The orc race seems to be a little on the downside, in the overal army performance.
- There are few end game challanges out of pvp matches. If one has put some thought into the army composition and the upgrading of ones troops there will be next to nothing left to stop this army.
-/+ The game is still in the making. While not essentialy bad, one may get slightly annoied by a few bugs and gliitches. Also ive experienced two mayor bugs up until now, of the *dude where is my castle?* kind. On the other hand: those where solved in a matter of one or two days and the mods did theyr best to recompensate the losses. Also one may hope to see some further improvements to the gameplay and some more content to come.
oh, and cookies, because.... you know....
In summa summarum i recommend this game.
Hope to see you (try) torching my city some time :),
best regards,
Cyraion.

I downloaded Adventures of Fluzz as an experiment. I wanted to play a game that had absolutely no review on it, and do my part for the Steam community by writing a comprehensive review that will help inform others before purchasing.
My expiereince of Adventures of Fluzz:
In the world of FLuzz, not everything makes sense. YOu're not told all the controls (or even given the option to look them up) but that does add to the sense of adventure somewhat. It's also not quite clear why you are a luminous pink rabbit, running round collecting apples and oranges, rather than carrots....either way, I salute you for trying to break the stereotype of Rabbits always wanting carrots. You will also come up against dogs shotting tomatos, spynx's shooting lasers out of their eyes and mosquitos trying to defecate on your rabbit head. (also hedgehogs in the desert, but please let me if this is actually common IRL)
Despite the somewhat strange concept of this game, it is quite and entertaining distraction and it borrows alot from classics such as Mario and Sonic.
It's not quite as polished as it could be (i had difficulty returning to menu etc when dying) but it was a relatively fun 45 minutes for the price of a large Mc Donalds. And who can say that's not good value.
I also got to number 39 on the worldwide leaderboards! With some more practice and real commitment, you might even be able to beat Frodo, who is currently holding the number one spot.
Overall, I would recommend this game for a fun light hearted 40 minutes - 1 hour, but would recommend that the dev lowers the price to entice more players.

Picked this up whilst it was free recently and I can safely say I'd be disappointed if I'd actually had someone snipe my wallet for the privilege. The X-ray kill-cam is a nice feature as are the relatively 'realistic' rifle physics (just don't expect the same from any of the other weapons), but the rest of the product just doesn't live up to expectations.
There's no planning involved or freedom to explore. You're dropped in tiny, linear levels and lead by the nose via a sequence of gold 'coin' (for want of a better word) style markers. Don't get it into your head to think about wandering off either - it might look like you can explore bombed out building 'x' or mysterious street 'y' to ferret out a cunning back route but the Nazis / Russians (they're fairly indistinguishable as enemies) have deployed their secret weapon - the invisible wall.
The cover mechanic is only applied to certain objects and it's never really clear which - some windows you can hunker down beside or under, others not. Why? Who knows, perhaps 'snipers knee' becomes an issue after a while preventing bending low. The environments are littered with detritus as befits the bombed out setting but none of it is movable or interactive in any way (other than the obligatory exploding gas / fuel cans), which becomes an issue with the restrictive level design. Many a time I've had my wily sniper prevent from pressing gallantly onwards because he'd got stuck on a fallen lamp post and couldn't step over it - another symptom of early onset 'snipers knee' perhaps. You can't dive under tables for cover or behind bars for a quick pick-me-up even when there's clearly room, they're not part of the prescribed route and way you should be playing so they're basically set-dressing.
The gripes and odd design decisions are many and bizarre but most annoying has to be the enemy AI and the snipers in particular. No matter how careful your supposed plan may be or how forward thinking you suppose you're being, most plans (mine at least) were defeated because the enemies have a habit of spawning in behind you, but inside the perimeter of defences you set up earlier. Many a time I was assailed by waves of repetitive dialogue spewing Nazi goons only to murder them all in inside-out graphic detail and then discover all my traps untripped. Bloody Nazi super-teleportation technology I reckon.
The enemy snipers are almost precogniscent in their abilities to spot you and get the first shot off and thanks to the previous mentioned teleportation technology it doesn't matter how carefully you scan the rooftops and abandoned buildings for them, because they aren't there until the game decides they need to be there. Thankfully though the Americans have their own version of precognition and in this game it's called the 'restart checkpoint' button. The general Nazi grunts seem to be telepathically linked. Once one is alerted the entire Nazi army knows exactly where you are, what you had for lunch and when you last changed your stars and stripes underwear; in fact I wouldn't be surprised if Hitler himself got a call apprising him of your whereabouts. Even enemies that can't see you or even have a clear shot will open up with great gusto at the nearest piece of crumbling stucco between them and you, although this actually makes locating them quite straightforward.
So to sum all that up in one word: 'frustrating'. Frustrating design, frustrating implementation and frustrating because it could have been so much better. Still, there's always V3. Note: I was playing this on the 'sniper elite' difficulty setting, it might be more forgiving on a different setting.
Sniping mechanics fun for a while but as an actual game and an enjoyable experience it just doesn't stand up (which would probably get it sniped in the forehead anyway).

So, a lot of people call this game "the scariest game they've ever played", and go on and on about the scariness, but I am evidence that it is totally possible to play this game without really being scared! Most of the "horror" of this game is just gross things (read: fleshy things) in dark rooms, which isn't really horrifying, it's just... gross stuff in dark rooms, and if that's not something that bothers you, then you'll be just fine in this game. Honestly, Daniel (the main character) is much, much more freaked out than I am! If you play this with the idea that it's a video game, and play it the same way you'd play any other video game, then it's more fun than scary! It has a cool back story and very interesting puzzles, and interesting mechanics involving keeping Daniel's mental health from deteriorating by keeping him out of the dark (which he seems to be very afraid of), and from observing disturbing events. So this is not a game where you can just run from point a to point b, you really have to think and strategize about your movements and where you go/stand to keep Daniel in a functional state. It's pretty cool and I've not played anything quite like it before! Also, rather than fighting monsters, you have to make them go away, which is also quite interesting (though there were no monsters for the entire first hour of the game and that was a bit disappointing to me), by hiding in the dark, no less! And either action, getting too close to a monster, or hanging out in the dark, will lower Daniel's sanity, so it requires some careful planning and knowing when it will be okay to come out. As briefly mentioned earlier, the story is presented in a very cool way, Daniel gave himself amnesia at the beginning and you basically have it right along with him, as you obviously don't know anything that he used to know. And as the story unfolds its like unravelling a mystery. Very cool! I also found the game a bit educational, as it takes place in the 1800's and is faithful to the time period, so I was able to look up some of the objects that are in the game and learn about what they were. All in all, this was a very enjoyable experience for me, so I give it a full recommendation! I didn't find it as scary as most people seem to, but I enjoy the gameplay and find it to be a very unique experience. I've had a lot of fun!

But really though, this is impressive on so many levels.
The AI is like a real living creature: it makes mistakes but remembers what you do and this may come back to hurt you. ie: you injure a random tribe-based creature by accident, they will hunt you down when they find their friends, or if you do befriend the rest of the tribe, the one you attacked will be much more likely to act aggresively.)
The creatures do not just wait around like in Skyrim, or any other RPG, but they roam around, hunt for food (you if you're not careful), fight for territory, and live their lives perfectly fine without you. You are not needed nor wanted and that is part of what makes everything feel so real!
You are weak and frail, and you stay that way the entire game. You NEVER get new techniques, or skills, or anything. You start off with everything someone who has been playing since beta, but you learn how to use all of them through experimentation.
Failure is always waiting around the corner, and that is fine because you learn from it. When you finally do learn how to defeat a creature that's been harrassing you all game, you feel amazing because you didn't need anything besides what you already had to do it. When you overcome a difficult section, you always feel like you barely made it because you never become "too strong" for an area.
Final notes: Is more than a game, is a living, breathing world. Is very hard and stays that way if you do not adapt. If you want to know what it is like to truly survive in a world where you're not the focus, get this game. You will not regret it.

*Short Review*
I dont think I need to mention that this is the sequel to Knights of the Old Republic, but can the follow-up surpass the origional in the hands of a new devloper? Overall, I don't think so. But Nontheless, KOTOR2 is not just a great game, but a great KOTOR game. I worthy sequel that tries some new things and does some things better then the prior game, but not everything :)
*Long Review*
Like I said before, Do I think KOTOR2 is better then KOTOR1? No way in Hell! But KOTOR2 does handle some things better than KOTOR1.
The Combat remains unchanged, and team building gets an 'infulence' mechanic where you can bring your party memebers to follow along in your force allignment (and sometimes train them to Jedi classes!), but other then that, the actual party mechanics remain the same from both games.
I'll start this review off with what I feel KOTOR2 did better.
1, Overall Scale
Mother of God is the scale of KOTOR2 SO MUCH BIGGER then KOTOR1. More Maps, Larger Maps, More Items, More quests, longer main quest and Overall a longer game. While I feel this is a plus, but its not without its flaws and ends up creating problems down the road (More on that latter).
2, Jedi Classes
Unlike KOTOR1 where you pick from one of three jedi classes once you get to a certain point in the game (Guaridan, Sentinel or Concuilar), when you make your charactor in KOTOR2 you pick one of these three classes to start with. They are exactly copy and pasted from KOTOR1 and play the exact same way. But once you get to a certain level point (and enough light side or dark side force allignment points) you can pick another Jedi class to 'Evolve' to. They are roughly the same as the previous three jedi classes, but they have several tweaks and differences. It is also worth noting that the advanced jedi/sith classes have different names and abilities depending on if your charcter is light side or dark side aligned.
The Lightside and Darkside comparable classes play/handle near the same, but the exact abilities of each class between light and dark sides are different.
It is also worth noting that you do not have to pick the advanced class that is an upgrade of your starting class. For example, Lets say you started playing as a Jedi Guardian. You are playing dark side, and you meet the requirments to advance your class. You do not have to pick the Sith Maurader (Dark Side Jedi Guardian Upgrade), You could also go with the Sith Lord (Dark Side Jedi Consular upgrade) and etc. So upgrading your jedi class can either be an upgrade of your current/starting class, or a total 'respec' of your character.
3, World Detail
Like I said above, there are more maps and areas in KOTOR2 then KOTOR1, they are also larger, But they also feel more detailed and polished. The areas are filled with more unique NPCS, things to do, Shops to Shop at, Sidequests to do, Etc. More work was spent improving the art of the new maps as well. Each location has its own look and feel to them, but they are all so beautifully done!
Now for what I did not like about KOTOR2
1, It is easier to get lost doing side-missions or just exploring in the larger maps. This really can be considered a plus or minus depending on how you look at it, but I feel it was a flaw. I feel there was too much side content and that KOTOR1 had just enough for you to get satisfaction out of doing the side missions, but there were not so many side missions that you could make several new questlines out of the side content.
2, The Story... (This is no doubt my biggest problem with KOTOR2)
Overall, I feel KOTOR1 had a MUCH better story. Long enough to be entertaining and satisfying, but not too long where you got bored and felt trapped in endless build up. The Longer story of KOTOR 2 also felt much less polished and rushed to me whereas KOTOR1 story felt more polished and consise.
I also did not like the main vilian of KOTOR2. Darth Treyia. She has two henchmen that your find and fight earlier in the game than her. The Henchmen are Darth Sion and Darth Nihilus. I found myself liking the story of Sion and Nihilus more and appricating them as characters, Their fights are also satisfying and difficult (But never unfair!). Darth Treyia Herself had a weak story, her fight felt cheap and unfair. You could have re-written the story where the 'final duel' was between Sion / Nihilus and your PC and I feel it would have been more satisfying then what we got.
KOTOR2 also tried to pull a KOTOR1 sort of Plottwist at the end, but by the time the twist comes it has been teased to much, and you dont really have that much interest in the story of Treyia to really care (They start teasing it within the first hour of gameplay...) So no 'I Am Your Father' or 'You Can Not hide what you once were' moment in KOTOR2.
They also somehow made the back story of your PC weaker and less interesting. You play as a jedi exile with a wide-open backstory for you to fill in (and story to play through in the game), but this felt less interesting and impactful then the story of your PC in KOTOR1. The Story of your KOTOR2 PC is linked to the first game and your PC from KOTOR1, which I will give mad props for
But at the end of the day, all my problems with KOTOR2 are just little nitpicks. All and All, I would totally recomend KOTOR2 to anyone who loves Star Wars and KOTOR esspessaly!

Keep up the good work, at this rythm, this rough but beautiful gem will become a marvelous jewel only asking to be discovered.

Con:

Don't buy if you dont like indies, wait if you are not sure about the state of the game, or buy if you know like me that this underdog is much worth supporting; i'm already having great fun with it :)

Arms Dealer version 16.0.3
Subjectively, as someone who loves military hardware, trading sims, and political theatre, this game scratches all the right places.
All products, weaponry, have unique descriptions and stats that makes you weigh aspects like supply, capacity, distance, and per unit profit in each planned trade. The idea of being a shadowy merchant of death who bribes generals, puts nations to war, and sells every sort of imaginable weapon to make disgusting amounts of blood stained money while evading authorities is endearing and fun to role play. I love it. Because of my subjective enjoyment alone, I reccomend this game.
Objectively, the game shows promise, but needs a lot of work.
The interface gets in the way quite a bit. A prime example of this is travel. Say you want to move to Poland with a bunch of cheap machineguns from China. Click Poland right? Now you have a window for Poland. Ah! A travel tab! I want to take my private yacht so I'll click private travel. That....made a minimized window. Close the window for Poland. Unminimize. Poland is not selected. Choose private yacht. Now I have to click a button to plot course. Window minimizes. I can't click Poland, I need to click a chain of countries leading to Poland. That makes sense, some countries may have investigators or might not be paid off enough and could intercept my shipment. click click click. Okay, I have a path to Poland. Wait, I need to load my machineguns into the transport to be taken with me when I travel. Okay, got my machineguns loaded, I've told it to sell them instantly when I get there, I've bought intel to tell me how much profit per unit I'll make. Good to go. My yacht turns into a plane and flies through the countires I've plotted to Poland. There's a quick travel option too, but it never brings cargo and can take you on ridiculously inefficent paths, and a Public travel option which is great if you'd like to wait 7 minutes to go to one of 5 or so countries you've never heard of with 45 tons of Israeli pistols.
Several aspects of the game are incomplete or still being worked on, though it seems that they are being diligently updated by the developers. Some hidden menues don't do anything, a great portion of products are missing portrait graphics, Quite a few gameplay systems are implemented but seem to not be fully flushed out. There's definitely a lot of behind the scenes variables and factors that impact gameplay which are kept obscured from the player. The tutorial is also a slog you have to troubleshoot your way through.
Overall, I love the game personally, but you might not if you're not willing to tolerate its shortcomings. The game does show promise for future versions, but at the moment it can be a hassle to play through for someone who doesn't absolutely love the kind of game it is.

I'm recommending this game if you're one of those freaks like me who crave any kind act of masochism you can inflict upon yourself, but I also DON'T recommend this game if you're impatient, easily frustrated (whether it be by difficulty, getting lost, hidden mechanics you'll never know of unless you look at a guide, etc). All of the latter happen a lot, and it feels like it's pushing me to my limit. But I love the most basic premise here much more than the mechanics I've mentioned: MUCH more, considering how much trouble I'm having even getting out of the very first area of the game.
Rain World is all about your survival in a broken ecosystem, in some kind of post-apocalyptic world (however overdone concept) where you'll uncover past sins and regrets where Humanity is responsible for...whatever the damn history of his game has in store. Just look at the screenshots and watch the trailer, because I REALLY can't tell you a lot about it, because it's infuriating and I can't power through it like I do most other challenges I take on in games.
The game's controls are unusual, but moderately easy to get used to — you move with the arrow keys, jump with 'Z', pick up pebbles and rocks and all that kind of stuff with shift, throw that stuff with 'X', and eat food that you either find or catch by holding shift. And you can hold the space bar to remember the layout of the world: see where you've been, where you've died, where you can take shelter from the rain that can crush your squishy little Slugcat body. And goodness mention all those hidden moves you can pull off again. But look at that Slugcat cutie! Oh, I love him/her ^3^
But if you're looking for tense gameplay, harsh punishments for falling prey to the unfair amount of predators there are, don't look any further than here: it's got it's own special kind of difficulty. And there IS an alleged 'easy mode', but it's horribly humiliating with how easy it is, and I choose not to take it on. Each loss isn't full-frontal, hard-hitting failures like the ones Dark Souls and the like show you, but rather, it feels deeper than that. For me, anyway. It feels like it's genuis in that sense, and I always come back to it every few days, just to try harder. Eventually, I will succeed past the beginning, and hopefully NOT get cockblocked by another vast and difficult wall, or spike.
And it's $20, too; I don't believe it should be priced like that, for what you'll most likely get from it. Another reason not to recommend this game, but it's so freaking beautiful in it's own way, and people like me see the beauty through and through, even through struggle and strife. That is why I'll never give up in the end, when you're defeated — it's why YOU should never give up in the end, when you feel defeated.

Star Wars Knights of the Old Republic II - The Sith Lords
The game is set 5 years after the original. The Republic has since been weakened from the Jedi Civil War and the Jedi have are being hunted down by the remaining Sith. You play as the lone Jedi Exile who throughtout the game reconnects with the force. This game unlike it's predecessor is set in a more darker tone. If you're familiar with the first game you will know that your actions in the game will affect whether you lean towards the light or dark side. Though with this game, it is more grey than black and white. It can be hard to tell whether doing a good thing is actually the right thing to do.
The game's story is not as straight forward as the original. As it may have a defined story, but there are generally two or more sides to most of the game's plot points. As like the first game, there are multiple endings. There are also some nice side quests you can play that add some extra play time although they are optional. Another large part of the game is the party system. Throughout the game you gain party members, some may be familiar if you have played the predecessor while others are new. The game includes an influence system. The influence system works by increasing or decreasing the influence you have with your party by performing actions that they either agree or disagree with. Having a good influence with party members can give benefits, those that you will have to play the game to find.
Although this game is 10 years old and may be a little dated by current game standards, it is still quite enjoyable. Also due to the fact that this game was rushed and is unfinished, there may be an assortment of bugs but nothing that is too game breaking, as well as missing story points. Although with it's unfinished state it is still a pretty polished game as all the features from it's predecessor have been upgraded and refined. Though if you want to play a more finished game I recommend getting the Restored Content Mod as it adds the cut content that was originally supposed to be in the game.
My personal rating for this game is 9/10 and was one of the most enjoyable games in my childhood.

Kingdom Wars, a fantasy RPG game based around 3 races, the Elves, Humans and Orcs. This game is an ''Open-World'' RTS with RPG Elements here and there, with a great execution on Mass-Battles it can be kind of unbalanced here and there, in PvP for example if you have a highly trained army of 25 people you will be easily killed by a weak army of 10 units. The game still requires alot of scaling in many different aspects but the developer team which by the way exists out of only four people who are working very hard to provide you the best possible RTS game they can make out of this.
Gameplay,
the gameplay aspect of this game is still wonky and outbalanced by bugs or mistakes in the ''Scaling'' system but overall it is still a solid part of this game and most ''Hardcore-RTS'' players will be able to look past it. This game is  not very competitive because of a simple mechanic called: Battle protection. It allows you to not get attacked by anyone at all for a long time. In most FTP RTS games the Battle Protection timer continues even when you are Offline, but in KW
Battle Protection pauses removing the Competitive aspect of this game by a lot. Luckily though, you can never be matched against an army bigger than your own. After some mishaps here and there and unbalanced features the gameplay is still solid and since it will most likely be improved in future updates it isn't such a big issue. I give the gameplay in this game a 6/10. Which will most likely become an 8/10 or a 9/10 if they fix these issues.
The biggest problem in this game so far are the graphics and the countless bugs that keep appearing, while this may sound like a stupid thing to say, in this case it really isn't. The resolution in this game is incredibly low, I have seen games from back in 2001 that look better than Kingdom Wars. And Kingdom Wars was made in 2010. The bugs though are far worse than the Graphics. People are constantly reporting in that they crash during Sieges or that they bought something with real money and didn't get what they bought an even bigger issue is that the resource counter doesn't work. For example, sometimes I make 10 food per minute and 95 wood per minute and then 10 minutes later I make 29.9 food per minute and 63.5 wood per minute, the Resource counter is by far the biggest issue. Small things like this can be quite irritating at times but it is also to be expected from a WIP game and will most likely be fixed eventually.
Cons include:
-Outdated graphics
-Several unbalanced gameplay elements
-Lots of bugs
-Huge amount of dialogue can be a bit overwhelming at times
However this may sound negative, the pros in this case outnumber and outscale the cons by far. Pros like:
-Solid gameplay
-Lots of detailed lore
-Frequent updates usually containing lots of bug fixes
-An ever growing, non-toxic and friendly community
-Great and active staff members
-And most importantly, NOT pay2win
This game has a lot of potential. As long as the developers get rid of bugs and expands upon its pros, this game will have a bright future ahead of it.

I very much loath using "promising" to define a game in development, so I'll say this: AFF is a game with soul. It combines the team-based gameplay of Battlefront 1 and 2 (not that god awful EA garbage), The feel of Unreal Tournament (sans being too "fraggy"), and the ground-up customization that feels unique and amazing. There are no weapon unlocks, but leveling the three traits (Combat, Support, and Command), allows you to add more to your kit. There are several jaw dropping moments when I first started playing that, as a game developer, made my jaw drop. The interior of capitol ships, for example, is instanced as what I assume to be a separate part of the map, but the windows (what I assume to be camera textures) add the convincing illusion of scale. You can stand on the bridge of a battleship and actually see the battle in real time. I don't want to spoil all the little goodies that make this gem unique, though.
But speaking of it being a gem, it might just be the roughest diamond I've ever adored. The audio is a HUGE work in progress to where all the guns sound like pea-shooters, speach is gritty and "filler-esque," and other sfx are off or of low quality (the devs have acknowleged this, and it's a minor issue). Optimization has come a long way since infant-alpha, but there are still a few hic-ups to iron out. Textures that were borrowed from UE2's stock library have almost all been replaced by nicer looking maps, but there are still some grimy clashes when new and old textures are next to one another. The HUD used to be a cluttered NIGHTMARE, but has since been brought to tollerable levels (again, the devs have acknowleged this). And while the bot AI isn't terrible, there definitely needs to be a little tweaking to make it feel more human.
So, why would I recommend this? Because it has SOUL! And if the past few months of early access is any indication, the devs are working around the clock to turn this into an indie-multiplayer jewel of a game. If you want to wait for a few more updates to see what happens in the future, then I don't blame you, but Strangely Interactive, I tip my hat to you guys. Keep doing what you're doing!!!

This game is being given my rating of a current 4/5 due to good performability. I will explain the reasons why I like and feel a recommendation to the game as well as the defects and failures in this game, let start with the failures first as most people like to read the Good n Bad in order, yeah...I don't do that.
----BAD!!!
#1: The Current Cash Shop Model allows you to literally buy your way to victory for only 10-20$ USD and is practicly forcing players to do this if they want to get their walls' up before the peace-timer ends. Not only that, the daily transaction limit on crowns should be removed, 30 Crowns a day is about 2 Upgrades of the lowest pool, not even remotely worth it.
#2: Sieging requires a very large force or a very small for of units you could simply buy from the Cash Shop, Simply buying 5 Minotaurs grants you 280 Power for your army and is in no way fun to deal with as a single minotaur can kill 5 ogres by itself, let alone an entire 8 battalions of cavalry. My gripe on this is, you can also buy army power by making nothing but archers and catapults, buying fire arrows and siege munitions then stacking stone and sitting back and not doing anything as your archers have 700 range and infinite ammo.
#3: Respawns are an issue when fighting other players and in missions, I play as Orcs personally because I like their resource system, it reminds me heavily of LoTRBFME, But as I could clearly see, if you buy a ton of goblins, get them all to level 20 and then max out their health regen and HP, they can literally die in combat and be instantly replenished, this obviously needs to be fixed, Goblins are in no way weak, Why buy a bunch of slayers when I could just mass so many goblins it causes the opposite player to lag out?
#4: Marketplace, Oh god...This eats my RTS time soo much, Unlike "Age Of Empires" where you can setup an auto-transaction pool, you have to click the icons manually, I wish this game gave you the ability to say: "If a resource hits this  much, sell it into gold" or add a "Always keep this much on hand"; I hate having to manually click the sell resource button multiple times only to be rewarded with a deselection of the marketplace or barely any outcome.
#5: The Pathing Engine, Oh lord, I broke this on the first day, apparently you can only have 3-4 Orcs harvesting a single deer, and I have about 40 Marauder Squads gathering food, problem is, there is only like 20 Marauders of the 200 collecting anything, the rest are rumbling and grumbling around like idiots, Its like watching turkey vultures trying to take turns pulling a carcass off a busy intersection, Everyone wants a stab at the corpse. This dissapoints me heavily and I believe the Pathing AI needs to be adjusted for better efficiency, because of this, I cannot bring my food income above 90.0.
#6: The Resource System, Yay! not so bad now, but still underperforming. The amount of resources players are given per map, at an interval of every 3 days of respawn is stupid, If I build in a Desert, I expect far more stone than gold. And the worst part about this is the fact that the resources can only be optimally harvested by 2 harvesters each turning this into a "Starcraft 2 SCVs per Mineral Field Moment" Overrall, I either think the amount of resources per minute gathered from these needs to be increased, or increase the movement quality and gather rate of all harvesters, even with upgrades, they are still snails at this time.
#7: The Upgrade System, Okay this is my final gripe, as it stands, you can literally train units to get certain skills and passives that make them sometimes, in wording of Goblin Hordes; Unkillable and other times just plain ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. How would you feel if someone's hero walked into your army and started 1-shotting all of your men and you couldn't even do more than 1 dmg to him while he regens 80/sec? Or if someone bought a set a Archers and got their movement speed, health regen, range, damage, and resistances maxed out? and just solo'd all your cavalry with arrows? Say...aren't archers supposed to be weak vs melee? It sure doesn't look like it to me. Another issue with this system, is not every unit can be upgraded, which bothers me, I cant increase the replenish rate of my Wargs, Yes I use wargs as outrunners to kill runners, and I can upgrade my laborers, even though they spawn at level 5. I would love to improve their movement speed. I realize this game is not done yet, but seriously?
------GOOD STUFF!!!------
#1: Performance = The game performs very well on my crappy computer, I have everything that is below the minimal requirements listed for downloading the game, my Graphics card is even out of date by 8 years. I'm suprised I can run the game at 60-113fps in terrain that would normally eat my computer, however there is one terrain that drops me below 30fps, and that is the swamps, that terrain is either high on particles or overrun with reflections. The graphics options are lack luster and need to be evaluated, but if this game turns into another 64x system required game, I swear I'm going to break a kneecap.
#2: Animation Quality = I love the chopping down of trees and the maiming of overly maimed corpses, the arrow firing and ring-rung animations of swordsman swinging their swords in 4 different ways at least gives heart to this addition, I hate games like "Rome Total War" where there is literally 1-2 Animations for everything except pre-scripted cinema gestures. The only thing I noticed is the level attack animation, it looks like there is no attack speed pool between attacks as soon as the target engages within melee range. This might need a look into.
#3: Map Movement Speed = I like this system, however I have seen it in many other F2P and B2P titles and some of which are much faster, this system prevents sieges from occuring too-often which is nice as players have to constantly run back and forth from their major city to replenish supplies and then run back, the only problem I see is when you are doing campaign or single player effects like quests, I think your movement speed should be increased for these and only these, especially if all your going to have to do is talk to some old fart.
#4: Unit Composition = I love that you have brought back the obvious, Archer vs Swordsman vs Cavalry vs Pikeman vs Siege effect, but there is alot of balance to be had and as it is clearly obvious, Archers are the best. I also want my Trolls, what Orc army doesn't have a giant Cave Troll? Ogres are not as good as Trolls. I think if you were to add a Troll which you should, it should replace the useless Meat-Grinder and cost crowns to make.
#5: Heros = Many games don't have a natural hero system, as it is very hard to balance, "IT IS" but either way, kudos to the Devs for adding it, however I would rather be given a choice on what type of hero I am interested in, it gripes me that  every Hero I've gotten so far has been melee, I would atleast like a "Switch Weapon" effect or be able to choose if my hero was a Mage, Archer, or Warrior, this would give the game more variation and would make buying Vanity for the individuals more effective as you would have more to choose from instead of 3 pathetic pieces of army that look the same.
----FINISHED----

I've very much enjoyed this game.  I chose to go Elves, and much like another review I read some time ago they have a very Protoss-esque feel to them.  Their units are individually stronger than all the others, however they train slower and cost more.  Their buildings also give great benefits, yet generally seem to be on the fairly costly side.
Yet the cost usually isn't an issue as their economy is entirely trickle based, well actually it's mostly trickle based, the single glaring and strange exception to this is stone.  The lack of any way other than through alchemy or manual mining to get stone is honestly a pretty big issue, especially since I've been getting a resource boost already and was only making about 4 stone per minute if I didn't use alchemy - contrast that to the ten food per minute and the 25+ wood per minute.
The balance of resource gathering, at least for Elves, is off.  You have a resource cap, however most of your resources are going to be wood considering it takes zero effort to get lumber as an Elf.  As a matter of fact you start off the game getting 10+ wood per minute, compared to the paltry sums of about 1 to 3 per minute of everything else.
Despite that issue the game was absolutely still worth trying and playing and, for those looking for a slower-paced gameplay or an RTS that didn't take up all your time, the Elves would have been right up your alley.
The main benefit of the Elves, I feel, is the ability to log off of the game and come back some hours later to build your buildings and military up.  As resources continue to trickle in whether or not you're logged on it feels like a game that doesn't force you to pay attention to it every waking second of every day in order to progress, which, honestly, was a breath of fresh air.
Furthermore it's really nice not to have to worry about being attacked while logged off, unlike some games.  While it's a little clunky and has a few issues every once in a while the dev team is very active and clearly working hard to bring the best experience they can.  In such I really do suggest trying this game out if you're in the market for a fantasy RTSMMO.
