It's refreshing to see a game like Rain World that gives you so little direction and yet gives you everything you need to succeed right at the start of the game. Other games pride themselves on having fantastic character progression that keeps a player wanting more, but Rain World does things a little differently. Game mechanics may seem a little wonky at first, but the true joy of playing the game is watching those mechanics gel together so well as you survive in a strange world. The character progression is not you gaining more abilities, but you better learning to utilize the abilities you already have in order to defeat the ever-increasing dangers you must face. It is a matter of brain over brawn, adapting to your environment instead of changing it, remaining ever-cautious in a world that will swallow you whole if you let your guard down for even a second, because Rain World is an underdog story. It's about a small creature with a decent throwing arm beating the odds and making it to the top, and it's about a person who, given only the minimal tools required, managed to overcome every obstacle in their path by being the most adabtable, the most cautious, and the smartest in a world that values strength over all else.

My personal oppinions about this game are mixed. I do think that there are many things about the online play server systrem that could be improved (Peer to Peer why) but I still think that the good outweighs the bad and would reccomend this game to people who like a challenging skill based combat system in their games.

There are tons of thing to be said about this game, both good and bad.
One of the first things I was confronted with, per example, was the long wait time to get my purchase to actually go through. Apparently this was a 'one time' thing that had happened twice now, and was caused by a huge increase in people suddenly buying the game.
But, once the purchase went through, I was dropped in a game.
I played around for a bit, until my first character died, and here's my first real impression:
the game has a long road ahead, but has a solid roadmap to be able to reach the finish.
First of all, it's more a shooter than an RPG, considering there's no real 'progression' as of yet. But the developers do actually listen to players, they communicate better than most AAA title developers, so who knows what they might change/add in the future.
And the lack of character progression gives it a little bit of a pointlessness to it, but then again, the atmosphere, the setting, the horrible monsters and the occassional other player do make for a weird mix. I took a couple of shots at another player, without 'luck' of killing them, and considered if this was the road I wanted to take with my character. It wasn't, but still, it was tempting to just try and shoot someone, to get some loot. As I had been looking all over the place, and had yet to find some decent goodies.
This was one drawback that I hadn't expected, the endless search for bounty, be it food, weapons or ammo. Could be realistic, but it just made it more attractive to shoot some random player fighting Nether...
At some point, I decided against it and ran off. I saw a Nether and thought I'd quickly shoot it, before it'd notice me and start screaming. It teleported, I killed it with my knife, and I thought I'd be safe for a second to spend my newly acquired skill point. All of a sudden 3 other Nethers had teleported into the building and I was getting killed. No way of fending these off with a kitchen knife, so I tried running. Alas, their teleporting skill showed superior to the speed at which I could move my feet...
So I died a horrible death, but yet, it didn't sting as much as when dying in many other games, even ones where dying doesn't mean losing anything. It sort of even gave me a feeling of accomplishment, however weird that might sound. I had survived for a while and I didn't do too terrible, considering the safe point had been unavailable for the entire duration I was in the game.
Anyway, the 'good' and 'bad' according to me summed up:
+looks decent, although I expected a lot better graphically
+feels realistic
+atmosphere is just amazing
+has lots of potential
+devs seem truely interested in listening to the community and giving them what they want
+great for team and solo play, room for all different styles and for both short and long sessions
-is it really worth the 20 bucks? It is worth the 11 bucks I spent during Winter Sale...
-it's lacking quite some balancing
-there are missions, but there might be some 'goals' missing on the long run
-if only there was more information about what you're 'supposed to do' while playing, regarding missions and otherwise...
UPDATE: February 2014
They have just updated the game, wiped all characters, added crafting and introduced 'tribes'.
At first, this seems like a step into the direction I wish to see this game going: survival.
But after playing around with it a bit, it's still the same game: walk around searching for loot, come across your first human contact and die because you thought you could be friends...
Worst part of this one time, I was right about to enter the safe zone, the guy was just waiting outside the safe zone for someone to come back fully packed...
I can't say this ruins the game completely, but it's still a while before this game really is a survival game instead of just another FPS...
Currently, I would not recommend buying this game for anything more than 10 bucks.

Summary: Unpolished. But Okay.
Caveats: I have only played through the Single Player campaign with No DLC
The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly(Or the Ugly, the Bad, and the Good because thats the order Im going to put it in)
Forgive my language but... Unpolished as FRAK.
Movement can be sticky at times. I get stuck on the strangest things like pieces or rubble, door jambs, small ledges. Its game breaking at times because it can easily get you killed.
Enemies can see you through walls, Enemies can shoot you through walls. At one point I was seeing the tracer fire come through a solid brick wall. Let me repeat that.
Enemy fire was coming through a SOLID. BRICK. WALL. It wasnt like I could shoot back either. My bullets hit the wall but his came through the other way just fine. Enemies can see you through smoke but you cant see them. So I guess the soviets and germans invented thermal vision really early in world war 2 because they can see you just fine and they'll let you know it. But riddling your body with bullets.
Some of the items that you start the mission with are frankly quite useless. Dynamite for example. I've never used dynamite. I've never had the occasion to use it. You're supposed to set it up. Set up somewhere else. And then shoot it. But I never had the opportunity to do that. The game doesnt give you the situation to do so. I found frag grenades from both sides, land mines and trip mines the most useful of the bunch.
Rocks are also singularly useless. You throw it the enemy turns around for about 3 seconds. Then promptly turns around, sees you and kills you dead. They dont even walk too far to check out where it landed either. Its usually about 2 or 3 steps in the direction it landed, they look around, and then turn back usually seeing you trying to crouch walk your slow butt to the other cover that you wanted to get to with out them seeing you. So much for that plan.
Stealth or the lack thereof. For a game that purports to be a game about a sniper and slowly sneaking past enemy patrols, covertly taking out enemies, you sure dont have a lot of incentive to do so. In fact you're actually actively punished for doing so. Stealth kills get you 10 points. head shots? I think the lowest I've seen is 75 points with the silenced pistol.
In fact it seems like you're encouraged to start head shotting fools. Screw stealth just start busting heads.
Not to mention this game loves, LOVES to put you, a sniper with a long rifle, in close quarters, in tight cramped spaces where your slow bolt action/semi-automatic rifle, is a hindrance. Forcing you to switch to your ♥♥♥♥♥♥ smg with its hilariously wide spread.
Did I mention that you're really squishy? Like it takes about 3-5 solid hits for you to die? And that the majority of the enemies you face either use smgs, which will pretty much melt your face, or sniper rifles which kill you even faster? Cause you are. And they do.
Enemy acquisition is annoying as all hell. You have a pair of binoculars which is great if they ever allowed you to survey your battlegrounds before being dropped right into it. You can tag enemies but there's no real point to it.
In fact the only use I found for binoculars were to tag enemy counter snipers. And thats because I couldnt find them in the first place. Why couldnt I find them in the first place? Well Im supposed to be watching for the glint of their sniper scopes. Problem being? Their scope doesnt glint until they've already shot you once.
Did I mention that enemy snipers have laser accuracy? And that their aggro time and range is ridiculous?
Normally when enemies see you they take a little time to go from white to yellow to red(ie, they see something, they see you?, They see you and are now shooting at you.)
Enemy snipers? It goes from white yellow red in about a second. Comapre that to regular soldiers in which it takes about 5.
And this is at long range. Im not even talking like you're right next to them and they take a while to realize you're the enemy. Im talking like Im on the other side of the courtyard. In a building. On the roof. type of range where it can be understandable they take a bit to figure out what the hell I actaully am.
But no snipers, they instantly see. And instantly take a laser accurate snap shot. They usually kill you in about 1-2 hits too.
Cover system: AKA Cover? Whats that? In most shooters, if you're in cover, you're pretty much safe from all incoming fire. In Sniper Elite V2? Dont make that assumption or you're going to end up dead very quickly and very often.
Its a good thing the game tells you not to rely on cover like that... Oh wait it doesnt.
You cant even take cover standing its either crouched or nothing. What Sniper Elite here cant stand behind door way and peak out that way?
Thats the other thing too. When you go to fire from cover you present your entire body. I can understand that if you're firing from the left but Sniper here is right handed. He has to present his entire body?
The Sniper shooting is supeeerb. Depending on your difficulty bullet drop is simulated fully, simplified, or not at all and boy is  it fun. Sometimes I didnt even empty my lungs to get the aiming reticule I just calculated it myself through the notches. And when that bullet cam activates you know its a sure shot.
Bullet Cam. It is great fun to see that bullet launch out of the rifle and just fly across the map to hit the enemy sniper right in the eye.
Last Thoughts:
Its like the game was two different games. One wanted to be a special ops world war 2 agent going in solo commando style and the other wanted to be a stealth sniper game where you sneak past patrols to set up at a vantage point and then snipe the enemy commander at the right time and place. Combined together and well... you get Sniper Elite V2.
Not. Especially at 30 bucks. 5? def yes. 10? Yes Even at 15 I'd say go for it. 20 is stretching it. 30 is a haha no way man.

Just going to say this up front, Rain World is currently my favorite game of all time. You play as a slugcat (adorable alien creature) in a VERY hazardous world, where you meet many different creatures (both good and bad, but mostly bad), explore different regions, and dissect a hidden story. In order to survive you must use the various tools around you, your own intellect, and knowledge learned while exploring.
This game is best enjoyed with time and patience. If you are not willing to give either, you may not like it. Despite being given basic instructions on basic controls at the start, you have to learn how to survive on your own. You learn by experementation and observation.  Unlike a lot og games similar to Rain World, you don't get upgrades, and your progression and survival is completely based off of skill and knowledge of your environment. Simple things like knowing how a certain creature is going to react to you, or if a creature can be befriended, or knowing if you can outrun a creature or not. The AI are AMAZING and fun to play with when you know them well enough. If you ever get bored of the single-player storyline, there is an arena and sandbox where you can goof off all you want.
The regions in the game are very different from each other, and present you different challenges to overcome. In order to progress to the next area, you NEED to know how survive in your environment. This game also has a ton of hidden lore, which you can only find by thoroughly exploring the map.
The game is also VERY CHALLENGING, especially when in hard mode. A problem is that it's easy to get stumpted when you are new to playing, and unfamiliar with the mechanics. The game can get fustrating, and this is why I don't recomend this to you if you aren't very patient. If you have time and patience and love survival games, I highly recomend this game. The time put into the game is very visible through the beautiful backgrounds and expressive atmosphere.  I have spent many hours playing this game, and have had an awesome experience playing.

Star Wars Knights of the Old Republic II - The Sith Lords
The game is set 5 years after the original. The Republic has since been weakened from the Jedi Civil War and the Jedi have are being hunted down by the remaining Sith. You play as the lone Jedi Exile who throughtout the game reconnects with the force. This game unlike it's predecessor is set in a more darker tone. If you're familiar with the first game you will know that your actions in the game will affect whether you lean towards the light or dark side. Though with this game, it is more grey than black and white. It can be hard to tell whether doing a good thing is actually the right thing to do.
The game's story is not as straight forward as the original. As it may have a defined story, but there are generally two or more sides to most of the game's plot points. As like the first game, there are multiple endings. There are also some nice side quests you can play that add some extra play time although they are optional. Another large part of the game is the party system. Throughout the game you gain party members, some may be familiar if you have played the predecessor while others are new. The game includes an influence system. The influence system works by increasing or decreasing the influence you have with your party by performing actions that they either agree or disagree with. Having a good influence with party members can give benefits, those that you will have to play the game to find.
Although this game is 10 years old and may be a little dated by current game standards, it is still quite enjoyable. Also due to the fact that this game was rushed and is unfinished, there may be an assortment of bugs but nothing that is too game breaking, as well as missing story points. Although with it's unfinished state it is still a pretty polished game as all the features from it's predecessor have been upgraded and refined. Though if you want to play a more finished game I recommend getting the Restored Content Mod as it adds the cut content that was originally supposed to be in the game.

A few years back, I saw Lord of War for the first time. Nicholas Cage aside, the movie was fantastic. Watching other series such as Jormungand only served to heighten that interest. Something about the allure of traveling the globe selling weapons sucked me in; the money, the danger, the thrill of closing a deal, and the power looming behing it all. I have been looking for a game like Arms Dealer ever since, so needless to say I was thrilled when I found it on Steam. This game gives you the same power and control of an arms dealer. Nothing feels quite so satisfying as closing a multibillion dollar sale of AK-47s to Columbia while narrowly avoiding the law enforcement hot on your tail.
That said, this game is definitely not for everyone. It takes a certain amount of patience, so if you're looking for some kind of fast paced, Call-of-Duty esque game, look elsewhere. This IS a business management game, so managing the interface (which is incredibly detailed and takes some time to master) is just a part of what you're signing up for. Some negative reviews have called this "counter-intuitive," but for a game so large in scope, it is going to feel unwieldy at first until you learn to master it. Also on that note, the tutorial is... lacking, but despite that I still caught on fairly quickly.
Another aspect I would like to note is that yes, the game is still early on in the developmental stage. You can expect crashes, and my game save was erased whenever the game updated, forcing me to start from the beginning again. That said, I expected that coming in. This game is still early on in development. There are going to be bugs. None of these errors took away from my enjoyment playing the game, and from the way I've seen this developer work, I have faith that this will get fixed in a timely manner.
In short, know what you are signing up for: you will be getting into a detailed, entertaining management game where you feel like a badass mastermind, and as the game is still being worked on and updated, you as a community member have a huge say in how the game moves forward.
If you have a few bucks to spare and are a fan of Lord of War, Jormungand, or feeling like a global badass, this game is certainly worth it.

Updated Review
As requested by the developers in my comments I have now played the game again and I am updating my review accordingly. It's worth noting that this is written 9 days after the games release from Early Access - so supposedly a finished product.
The biggest change is that they have now fixed the fatal error bug that was making the game unplayable - I played the game for over 5 hours straight without a single crash. Crate auctions also now seem to work.
Unfortunately my assessment of the game remains the same, great idea, poorly implemented and now finally having been able to play it is my opinion that the gameplay itself lacks any substance.
Things that I believe are poorly implemented:
- The tutorial is awful, and even the biggest defenders of the game admit this. You can get the basics from it but its clunky.
- The UI / Menu system is also awful. Its particularly a problem for the tutorial where the tutorial instructions get obscured by pop up windows. In the actual game itself core functionality, such as saving, wanted lists, achivements / perks, missions / plot aren't accessible at all through a menu instead you need to use key bindings.
- One of the most common tasks you'll be doing in game is loading your transports with cargo and setting destinations and this is badly implemented, the interface for it is clunky and illogical requiring you to switch between a minimised window, but I also encountered a number of bugs where transports locations were incorrect i.e. listed as travelling when in fact in a country, and also when plotting the route only to find it thought the transport was in a different country. The pathing for the movement itself is also inconsistant e.g. its signigcantly quicker going from Russia to North Korea, than North Korea to Russia - as it takes a different route. Unless stationary your transports will more often than not appear as planes on the map, even after obviously traveling through a port and taking a sea route.
- There is no explanation of the target finder missions, and they are not built into the plot.
- The main story arc was broken for me when I purchased some discounted weapons but was intercepted causing me to automatically dump my stock so I couldnt complete the mission.
- The text e.g. "no longer for sell" is either written by someone who has English as a second language or... well lets not go there.
- It looks like a whole bunch of stuff that was planned hasn't yet been implemented in game i.e. reputation system doesn't seem to have any impact (and isn't explained anywhere), meeting demand doesn't impact sale price, wars don't seem to resolve as you'd expect, and a general lack of missions.
- There's a huge disconnect between sound and the game, what happens in game has no effect on sound at all that I could tell. Its just a sound track on loop alternating between things such as street noise and music. The only time sound comes into play is if you sit like an idiot and allow the countdown to a hunter catching you to get low.
- Not really important but as I made myself sit through it for the purposes of the review, the intro is the most boring and cliched crud I've ever come across. You sit there in complete silence for the intro too, it could have perhaps done with some voice acting, even if it was done badly by the dev team themselves.
Game play:
I played the game on normal difficulty and it was ridiculously easy. The forumla to progress is straight forward and repetive and offer no challenge or depth of strategy:
1. Buy interl for countries around Russia.
2. Repeatedly go back and forth between Russia (your starting location) and the country with the best sale price until you have enough money to upgrade your hull (capactity).
3. Complete the sale mission, and shortly after an order request.
4. This gives you enough money to may out your transport, buy another and bribe some generals.
5. At this point you'll have a couple of routes to choose from, and you just grind back and forth selling weapons to the same country listed on your intel.
6. Eventually you'll have enough cash to start a war. You can normally cause it to war with two otehr countries.
7. At this point you just go round to every supplier nation, buy everything up and then ship it to the warring nation.
That really is all there is to it. It quickly becomes repetitive and boring. The game could badly do with a complete overhaul of the story with the inclusions of missions to break up the grind. I enjoy games of this genre such as the orginal Uplink, but there's just not enough variety in Arms Dealer to keep it interesting for me. Some people clearly do enjoy it, maybe you'll be one of them.
I do have a huge problem with the developers of this game. They clearly made a choice to move from early access knowing that this would cause people such as myself to buy it. They then complain on the steam forums, direct quote:
"We do not ask for free positive review,how ever we do ask for you guys to be less eager at giving negative reviews, if theres something you dont like, hey post it here, we are almost 24/7 checking the forums,"
I think it illustrates a complete lack of respect for customers that they are pointing the finger at people reviewing a supposedly release ready game, when it was their eagerness to take our money that made them take it out of early access. They whine that EA didn't turn up all the bugs and necessary feedback to get the game right, and that they don't have money for "a room full of testers", not my problem I only care about the product I paid for. They've adopted an "everyone elses fault but ours" attitude, even blaming the Steam review system, whilst themselves trying to manipulate it by encouraging people to only leave positive reviews, saying planned DLC wont be free unless they get the needed sales. Hypocracy.

I grabbed the game in Early Access, thought it looked promising and decided to hold off a review until the full version came out. It is now upon us and, my word, it looks amazing.
The opening sequence was a good set up and sets up a story behind your inception as an arms dealer (text went by a little fast for me tho). It looks like a simple game, but having grown used to the Early Access version, it looks pretty amazing. It a fairly simple game to pick up: you buy arms, travel to other countries, preferably those that are at war and turn a quick profit. Bribe generals to expand your network, gain access to new types of weapons and hopefully, you'll start to understand why arms dealing is a lucrative trade. Hopefully you'll be just waiting for a conflict to break out so you can sell your new anti-tank weapon.
You're not alone in this though. You'll be competing against the machinations of agencies who would love to put you out of business. You're also encounter other arms dealers who can spy on, ally with or even kill.
One of the best things about this game is the developemnt team itself. Looking at some of their forum posts convinced me that this game would be worth buying since they really do listen to the community. They've already released 3 patches since the full game was released and all through Early Access, they've always listened to the community and their suggestions, answering all questions put to them and fixing any issues as fast as possible.
Fair warning tho: there are some bugs in the game, some of the weapon descriptions are incomplete and there are still some UI problems. If you encounter them, don't throw the game away or rubbish it instantly. Go to the forums and tell the team. They really care about this game and your opinion.

Team Fortress 2 is a free class based first person shooter with cartoonish graphics managing to stay alive after 10+ years of its release. The game features  9 classes with their own unique playstyles, weapons, characters and stereotypes, wich might seem small compared to other similar games like Overwatch's 26, however the big number of weapons wich can totaly change a playstyle are what makes it stand out, along with its customization. The game puts you in a random team in a random map where you are presented with the objective of that map's gamemode, you then will make the choice of class based of what your team needs and make different strategies for different maps. The game also has an alternative CO-OP gamemode called Mann VS Machine where you fight off hordes of robots, utilising different upgrades and powerups, however, I recommend you play this mode after you become at least semi-competent at the core gamemodes. Current problems with it include the small team behind the game, general balance in some matches and the neglection of it by Valve. Don't let that affect you tho! It is a very fun game wich easily becomes an addiction and introduces you to an amazing community and its branches. If I had to rate it from a scale of 1-10, I would and give it a solid 8.5/10, the minor problems still remain but they are getting slowly fixed, the game just had a major update, even after 10 years!

UPDATED REVIEW:
Regrettably, I find the game ultimately boring and repetitive.  Some gameplay design is also dubious, to say the least. I love herbalism, the feel of it, but to do it without a huge strain on your eyes, you have to actually downgrade graphics. Clever.
Other than that, everything just takes forever to do, and the end result is not that impressive either. Not a bad game per-se, but just...disappointing.
A no from a guy for whom it used to be a yes.
If so you wish, you can now read the original review below. When I had played it for less.
Allow me to say this first.
The game is in early access, and is by all means flawed. There are bugs. There are things you will dislike. There are parts you mind find amazing, but sadly not yet implemented. All of this is present.
But besides that, I do honestly believe that if you have ever shown a liking towards the idea of being a medieval peasant, who can maybe work himself out to be a capable warrior, skilled farmer or perhaps a prized alchemist, this might rock your boat.
Let us first summarize the pros. The game presents and open world with other players, but you must not worry about getting stabbed with a nearest stick as soon as you find another human being. Not only is this forbidden on most server, it also has negative consequences. As I mentioned above, there are several profession you can do, and freely combine if you for example want to do basic farming as well as basic smithing, though such merging will prevent you from being a master in either. The game requires you to play in groups of multiple people, which could be considered a downside, but I like this feature, since it can create a friendlier atmoshphere, forge possible friendships and makes it feel much more like a medieval town that you work towards. The various professions have quite a bit of depth in them and all are equally important to the community.
Very importantly, I find the developers to be fairly active and helpful, despite some fearing an unknown studio will fail. The updates are surprisingly common and you can also track what they are up to from a number of videos on their channel.
Now about the bad. It might be very easy for someone to find the game repetitive, as you are often required to amass a certain amount of resources before you can focus on something perhaps a bit more desirable. To add to the injury, you will see a lot of progress bars, which might be fast, but are frequent. The game is not the most optimized in the world, though it went up a lot lately, and is surprisingly stable. The combat system leaves a lot to be desired, mainly in precision. This will hopefully (and likely) be changed in a later update, yet as of now, it must be mentioned.
The recollection.
The game has an incredible atmosphere, bringing you to the harsh world of feudal times. If you ever wanted to be a medieval smith, hunter, farmer, alchemist or perhaps a builder, you will find this game quite pleasing. The long time it takes to complete various tasks such as building houses or creating complex tools can be infuriating, but if you manage to find a friendly group of people with whom to work on a village and get to speak with them on, say, teamspeak (which is very common, no worries), a lot of this boredom will dissipate, thanks in no small part thank to having people to talk with as you do your things. With all that, the game deserves your attention and perhaps further investigation.
And that is my recommendation.

AFF (Angels Fall First) is one heck of a game. I have never played any FPS with nearly this level of balance and enjoyable gameplay. The fact that you can jump into a fighter, change to a capital ship, then be part of a boarding party or play a planetary invasion where you pilot fighters or tanks or just run along as a ordinary soldier adds to the experience. The graphics are fine, the movement and "feel" though, are excellent.
If this game has any drawback, it is the lack of a dedicated single-player mode with story elements, and the comparatively few (ground, as I prefer this aspect of the game) maps. There is a lack of people playing online (which in all honesty is not the game's fault, but the playerbase), but even this is something you can look past, because the bots that fill out the teams in single or multiplayer mode are really quite good.
The story is fascinating, the weapons are different enough to make your choices interesting, yet the game is pretty well balanced and no weapon is overpowered. The developers have (yet at least) not broken anything, just improved on everything, and they do so at a decent rate. I have faith that this game will continue to become better and better!
Why are you still here? Click that "Buy" button, this game is a solid 7.5 / 10 -worth the price!

If growing up you were a fan of 'Duke Nukem 3D'...and boobies, then you'll love...erruhh...should...erruhh...might enjoy this game. Or maybe you won't, I mean who can really tell with this one. Over however long in development, with countless engine updates, and one or a million developer changes, I still to this day, have no idea why so many knuckleheads held this game to such high standards. I suppose it was their undying love and fond memories for the Duke Nukem of the 90's, but still, how good could this game have been when it was passed around more times than some lame joke about a girl who is very promiscuous? Actually...pretty damn good, if you ask me!
This game was destined to fail ever since year five in development, so it really doesn't matter now, but like I said, if you were a fan of the original 'Duke 3D' game, then this game should be pretty enjoyable for you. Or maybe it won't be, who cares, either way get f'd and buy it cheap. But still, 'Forever' manages to be more imaginative than 75% of new shooters out there today and maintains some of the humor and feel of gameplay from the original. The storyline is the same 'save the world from the aliens' but what else did you expect, and each map feels fresh and fun to play through each and every time, with small puzzles and challenges along the way.
Overall, this is a game most people have most likely already forgotten about, but it's still incredibly fun if you ask me. And even though it's probably not the game that the developers originally set out to make, I'm still thankful to have been able to play this version. So pick this one up for a few bucks during the next sale if you're a fan of Duke Nukem or shooters in general. Because 'Forever' is a pleasant change from the mundane, everyday shooters that most people play day in and day out.

Kingdom of Aurelia is a fun casual adventure game with a hint of hidden object gameplay in it. Its story and level structure is especially praise-worthy, because it manages to eliminate pointless backtracking yet still provides enough challenge.
Kingdom of Aurelia: Mystery of the Poisoned Dagger is the direct sequel of
—and by “direct”, I mean it: it starts almost right at the moment that game ended.
This time around, we play as the quirky sidekick kid of the previous game, who needs to rescue the princess from a magical poison. I guess nobody else in the kingdom had time (after all, the streets are empty). Joking aside, the story is enjoyable for a casual adventure, even if we get it in rather small doses.
Gameplay follows the generic adventure game/hidden object hybrid Shaman Games is known for. Except for the backtracking: by dividing the plot to 9+3 chapters with only a handful of locations in each, they created something that feels like one long adventure, but the self-contained areas make sure that the player never gets lost. This is such a strong point that I could forgive the game for its numerous small bugs (of which one forced me to restart completely). I hope anyone who tries it will feel the same.
I was not happy initially, but there are constant updates coming, so I recommend it if you like local coop party games.

Kingdom of Aurelia: Mystery of the Poisoned Dagger has the feeling of a sequel with a backstory introducing the world and characters from what could almost be a previous game, but it's an original game from Shaman Studios, as you set out on a quest to save the princess from a deadly magical poison.
The game, although a HOG, features a beautiful steam punk world to explore, interesting, but not a lot of, Hidden Object scenes, some puzzles that range from easy to challenging, and a decent story. The voice acting is ok, but not strong, and the game also introduces some elements that have been done before, but rarely, in providing you with a dream catcher to read other character's thoughts, and a flying robot that helps you with some tasks. This game is a gem and for $17, has more replay value and content then some AAA titles (battlefront).
AFF delivers an excellent space combat experience. The starfighters, bombers interceptors carry customizable loadouts, with each of the two factions having unique weapons. On top of the starfighters dogfighting and attacking larger vessels, drop ships can board enemy capital vessels and wreak havoc on the enemy team.
Where the selling point is at though is the capital ship warfare. Each side (depending on the gamemode) starts with one large capital ship, and as the battle progresses, depending on your teams performance, additional corvettes, frigates, and dreadnoughts can be warped in.
The combat between these large ships is unique and due to the slow maneuverability your moves must be planned ahead of time. Don't think just because the capital ship is so large and mighty that it can't be destroyed, bombers, boarding partys, and other ships make for very tense space combat.
Land/infantry combat is surprisingly just as satisfying. Fans of battlefield will feel right at home with the difference being that instead of vehicles spawned right at the onset; similar to space combat depending on your teams performance additional and stronger vehicles will drop in. This encompasses lightly armored scout vehicles, apcs, tanks, mechs, and aerial gunships.
Where I put the least attention too but had the most surprisingly enjoyable time was the infantry combat. There is a plethora of weapons and attachments to be used. The firing of each weapon feels unique and powerful. The infantry combat is hectic and at times just plain brutal. Enemies and friendlies alike are not squishy but not complete bullet sponges either. Which is good cause the sheer intensity of some battle will leave many spawning round and round.
The ai is also great. Not without issues with occasional pathfinder/reaction issues. Occasionally I'll see a vehicle or ship get stuck or enemies run right past me, however considering the complication of there tasks and the rarity of these occasions, this is easily overlooked. It's also a plus that when you play ai matches you can be given a stud of ai that will follow and aid you in the fight, it's such a cool experience to have a wing of three other fighters flyin in formation while I lead the charge on an enemy group of ships. Or having my team ready to jump out as we board the enemy vessel.
To break down my review,heres some bullet points.
Pros:
-fantastic space combat
-pilot everything from star fighters to capital ships
-surprisingly equally fantastic land warfare
-high level of customization to gear, weapons, vehicles.
-offline ai in all game modes
-intense combat both infantry land and space.
-very active devs/community
Neutral:
~ while graphics aren't bad, they aren't next gen. Imo they are still very good. The tracers and explosions create an epic feel.
~physics engine is a little dated, some land vehicles have a clunky feel, odd collisions, still encompasses rag doll, and collisions but not as dynamic, again imo not negative/easily noticeable.
~ai has some path finding/targeting issues, however when comparing to modern shooters ai and or lack thereof, and considering the complicated tasks the ai performs it's easily overlooked.
Cons:
-sometimes low server population (can't really blame the devs for that).
-It would be nice to see some gamemodes that have ships/vehicles spawn at the beginning of the match or ability to cusomtize the match to have this.
(I actually posted this idea on a thread and the devs responded and explained why this would be difficult, but did not rule this out.

The game is about being a rat in a maze of steel and vegetation, and finding out where to go and how to survive while trying to find shelter before the rain starts killing and drowning everything.
But you're not the only one trying to survive in there, all sorts of creatures also leave their shelter once the rain is gone in search for nourishment, some will be your prey, others, your predators, but they're all part of an eco-system that doesn't wait for you to make your move.
The magic of Rain World is its emergent AI, every single creature has its own agenda, they move around the map by themselves, hunt what they perceive as easy preys, and hide from danger. While their behavior follows these guidelines, their position can be unpredictable and that's where the RNG mentioned in many reviews comes into play.
You're the rat with the human brain, for you there's a solution around every single obstacle, all the tools are here, you're only missing the expertise.
The game expects you to experiment, to explore, to figure out things by yourself, there's no hand-holding, no upgrade or hint. It's a brutal game that takes its sweet time to deliver one of the most unique experience, there really isn't anything like it. No other game that captures the feeling of being a rat-sized animal in man-made environment full of a living and breather eco-system better than Rain World does.
I'll recommend the game to anyone curious about its premise and willing to suffer a bit.

Flying Wild Hog are still working on bug fixing, balancing, enhancing and updating the game along with the rumored release of all new content and modes.  Currently inventory management is pretty terrible.  You'll end up with hundreds if not thousands of upgrades if you're not taking care of selling upgrades or using them to forge new upgrades.  The multi-player that was described and advertised as being a big part of the game launched with quite a few issues which still exist.  There is no voice chat and there wasn't in game messaging either until a recent patch which makes no sense for the co-op MP experience they advertised.
As for game play length.  I beat the single player in around 35 hours.  If you go through quickly without exploring or doing the side missions or trying to complete the achievements then you'll be disappointed with the length of the game.  This is the type of game you'll want to play the new game+ mode on after beating it to finish out the achievements or find the guns that you didn't get on the first play through.  FYI, there are over ~75 weapons currently with a lot of variety in their characteristics. Weapon types include melee, swords, shotguns, assault rifles, rocket/grenade launchers, bows, etc.  Weapons can be customzied with upgrades which modify firing modes, add elemental damage, boost character stats etc.  Also there are "Chi" based magic attacks that can be upgraded.
There is an RPG like player leveling system that lets you assign skill points to many different areas including magic, special attacks, ammo capacity and various other attributes.  The developers will be adding additional functionality for more upgrades later and due to this, there is type of currency that you get in new game+ mode that is unusable in the game currently.  You can collect it to be used later.
In summary:
Pros
--Nice graphics and good performance on average computers
--Lots of weapons
--"Chi" based magic system
--Lots of loot (upgrades for customization)
--Forging system for creating custom upgrades
--"Karma" based progression system that lets you upgrade many player and game play attributes
--Has procedural environment generation so levels are supposed to change when you replay them in free roam mode
--Going along with the procedural environment generation is a random weather and day night system which adds more variety to the game
Cons
--Does have bugs but the developers have been good so far about balancing and patching
--Co-op MP needs quite a bit more work seeing as how there is no voice chat, balance issues, issues with how the game handles items, shops and host/guest interaction and saving, etc
--Seems like the game could have used some more time for polish and adding/finishing features
I hope Flying Wild Hog adds in more MP features like a last stand/horde mode with randomly generated levels.  Also, I really think a co-op game needs to have in game voice chat from day one!!!  Not even having in game messaging from day one just makes no sense too!?!

This game is hard. I've sunk hundreds of hours into Isaac, Gotten Over It with Bennett Foddy, conquered Cave Story's Running Hell, and completed the entirety of the Soulsborne series, yet Rain World still manages to uniquely frustrate me. Perhaps that is just another virtue of this quirky game. Slugcat's movement is very clunky, unlike that of any well-received modern platform game, but that's clearly by design. Over time, you learn to maneuver Slugcat more and more gracefully, but some of the later areas in the game are platform-precise and can get really tough. Because of the organic randomness of the enemy AI, you will occasionally suffer an unfair death. It's certainly annoying, but that feeling of helplessness establishes a mood seemingly antithetical to the medium of video game: You really do feel weaker than the world around you, in a "food-chain" sense rather than an "underlevelled" sense.
That reservation aside, the other (beaming) reviews have more thoroughly described the myriad of Rain World's strengths. It's innovative and organic and incredibly deep and I can't get enough of it. If you're willing to delve beneath the off-putting surface of this game's difficulty and cryptic mechanics, you'll be deeply rewarded with the most lifelike environment I've ever interacted with in a platformer.
Finally, the animation of Slugcat tightrope walking across poles is so darn cute that it warrants the pricetag by itself.

You buy cards, you make your own deck, and improve it from there. Also these may be weak decks but if you're smart enough and skilled enough it's not THAT hard to beat the beginning enemies and start earning cards. I'm not sure what people are looking for with this game, but they're not looking for a Magic the Gathering experience.

Third: You need a good computer, I have a e6540 with a dual core Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-4610M CPU @ 3.00GHz CPU, AMD Radeon HD 8790M and 16 GB RAM and it still runs a bit oddly on normal graphics, though I think my issue is my CPU.
Forth and final: None of the vehcles are actual brand names, they can't use brand names because they can't get permission to use namebrands, vehicle manufaturers don't want their vehicles shown with damage, because apparently their vehicles aren't able to be damaged in real life....
Anyway onto the review.
At the time of writing you don't get a ton of vehicles, there is a simi-truck, a pickup (that has a full covered version that reminds me of a SUV) and a van, that makes up the trucks.
You get a few sports cars (I'm thinking just two and the rest are just kind of race conversions of normal cars)
This strange three wheeled death trap called the Pigion that is more silly that anything else.
There are 2 drag cars in the game, the Moonhawk drag and the Barstow drag (the Barstow is new).
But like I said, most of the vehicles are what you would see in the parking lot at your supermarket.
Come to think of it, the first part was more of a review than the last part, oops.
What you should take from this rambling: This isn't really much of a game yet, it is really more of a tech demo or physics simulator, it isn't really for the faint of heart, I personally really like it and can't wait to see where it goes.
Keep in mind it is early access, actually early access, some things might not work right and things might be buggy, and  they haven't added multiplayer yet, but from what I've read they will add multiplayer.

After spending quite a few hours straight since I bought it, I think this game is a great game. However, there are flaws that I must state in the current version of the game.
Pro's:
The game is very community friendly. You don't have to worry about getting non-stop attacked or killed. Most servers don't allow random and no reason killing. Where as in games like DayZ, or Rust you have people who just constantly kill for no reason.
This game is very relaxing. Those nights you get off from work and don't feel like just running around and gunning people down in FPS games. This game is great as to where you can just sit, listen to the very relaxing and beautiful music, and build while maybe watching a movie or something.
Can do and build what you want, and how you want. If you want to take a week or so to build a huge underground fort, you can. If you want to build a stronghold, you can. Or perhaps a beach farm, you can. You can pretty much do what ever you want in this game, if you have the time and patience.
Great and beautiful graphics. They are just stunning and beautiful to sit and stare at. Very fleshed out as well.
-----------------------------------
Cons:
Optimization is not great. If you run it on medium or low, you can roughly get around 20-30 FPS with a mid tier PC. If you want to run anything above that, you'll need to have the most modern and updated gaming computer. Even then, there's no telling if you'll get anything above 30fps.
Worlds are just dead, and rely too much on player to player interaction. The servers are not dead, just the world feels really empty. There's hardly any wildlife, and the map is so big, you'll rarely come across other players, even on 64 player servers filled. The building feature even revolves way too much on player interaction, because how many items you need to build certain things, and how long they take to aquire them.
Obtaining weapons take a very long time. You can almost immediatly get tools, and a sling with rocks, however if you want to use a bow, crossbow or sword it, takes a whole town to wield them, because first you have to build a smithy, which requires all these other objects that require skills, and the skill like contruction take a very long time to level up if you're by yourself.
The requirement for a friend/s to play with you. If you want to get anywhere without taking a few weeks to build a small town, you need atleast a friend or two. The length it takes to collect items from things like tree's, rocks, ores, and even food is so long, and most items you get is only 1 every 15-20 seconds, which is not a lot seeming as how you need around 10 things you may or may not get from searching for a simple fence.
Some skills like fishing is very obsolete because of how they were implemented. I spent over 45 minutes trying to catch one fish, because somehow in 1,000BC fish are so rare. Then when you get a fish and cook it, your campfire somehow gets broken, and the fish only gives you about 20 hunger regen, when something like an apple which is pretty common and you collect around 23 in 5 seconds gives like 17-20 hunger regen.
Hunting is also pretty obsolete because of how hard/long it takes to get a bow and how little wildlife there is.
------------------------------------------------
Anyhow my total ranking is, 7.5/10. There's a lot of potential here, and I hope we get more patches before the september release.

Progress comes along at a snail's pace, and the game is still years from being finished or even being playable. Combat is uninteresting and dull and developers have all but abandoned any form of combat that isn't wild swinging and running in circles. Gone are their Mount and Blade roots. This game was received from a friend of mine who wanted me to try this. So, in otherwords... I RECEIVED THIS GAME FOR FREE!!!!!!  Now, onto the actual review of the game.
This game is based in a BattleField like setting where several factions are fighting for resources (Just like most games styled after massive battlefield games) and kind of reminds me of a very beefed up version of BattleField 2142.  The only thing is, they took it a step further.  Not only are there small craft in which you can play around with, you also have Carriers and such in which you can also fly and use to the team's advantage.  Your unit you play as is also VERY customizable from Armor Size and Resistance to Weapons, Utilities, ect.  Developers are always finding ways to fix bugs, performance issues and add new stuff to the game.  Recently, there has been a HUGE overhaul on the game maps and ships and they are soon to be adding more maps and such (As of the current date of the reveiw).  Now, lets get to the Pros and Cons section.
Pros:
* This game allows for customization of just about every aspect of the player.
* The game is still very balanced despite certain weapons and ship controls, ect.
* Maps are very open but still allow for coverage of players.
* The game looks beautiful even with certain low resolution textures added.
* Continuing support of dev team to push the game further on.
* Game is very easy to pickup and play even without customization of game character/ships.
* Always have patches to fix issues in game (Just about every other day at this point)
Cons:
* Depending on age of PC Hardware, optimization only goes so far with this game.
* Not a large player base yet as most are waiting for the game to progress further.
* User Interface seems somewhat clunky.
* Almost too many maps to choose from if you just like to play "Instant Action" and just play.
* Stat balancing of weapons in-game seem to be a little lacking but I know they do it for a reason so others done annihilate you with their OP Weapon Modifications.
All-In-All, the game is very solid for being Early Access and can be picked up and played easily enough.  There are always updates to fix optimization and or glitches.  I recommend picking up this game if you are in to BattleField Type Games.

, probably one of the most anticipated and hyped up games of all time, but did it live up to the expectations of Duke Nukem fans? Not exactly. Does that mean
is a bad game?
Unfortunately,
was not very well received by critics and fans when it was eventually released in 2011 after
. The most popular places to read PC Gaming reviews all shunned
shortly after it's official release and it was deemed as the worst game in the series. Despite all of the negativity and bad reviews surrounding the game, I decided that I would try it myself to see whether or not it is as bad as everybody makes it out to be... After playing it through a good number of times, I do not think this is a bad game at all, in fact, I truly believe that this is a game worthy of the
title, even though I seem to be very alone with that opinion. I believe that this is a really great game, flawed mainly by it's release date, if it was released back in 2004, it would have been considered a much better game as it doesn't really meet todays standards.
Sure, it's not the most phenomenal game ever released, nor is it revolutionary like
or
were, but it's not a bad game either. When it is looked to as the "successor" to
, the game will naturally be compared to it's originals, but if you look past that,
is a good game within it's own right.
It's lengthy, fast-paced and very interactive single-player campaign is an example of what modern games should be looking to set as their goals, it's very, very rare you will find any singleplayer games with any more than 8 hours of singleplayer game-play in this day and age, so that is a big bonus. The game is also very atmospheric, comedic and  varied, you can tell this game has come from an era from the past, though unfortunately many years too late.
All of your favourite weapons from
make a return, so there is no problem there, excluding the fact that you are limited to how many you can carry now (more about that below), there are a few more new weapons to play with such as the Railgun and the Enforcer Cannon which are both satisfying to use, there are a few more but nothing glorious.
Graphically, the game isn't exactly groundbreaking but it's still a very pretty and well-made game, you can tell that a lot of work has gone into it. The humour is the same as it's always been, cheesy and crude, but funny (most of the time). There are also endless references and easter eggs that you will come across throughout the campaign that are bound to amuse you.
The game has it's flaws, as most of you will already be aware because the critics love letting you know about it, but there are only two things that spoil this game for me. The first issue is that some of the maps feel linear and relatively simple, especially when compared to
... General exploration is limited and there are little to no secrets to discover in the game, which is a shame given how much fun it was to explore in
, but health bonuses are non-existent anyway now so finding a secret area may not be as great as it once was.
Secondly, the two weapon limit is frustrating and can ruin the experience more often than not, there is an option to enable a four weapon limit as opposed to the two, but this is still an issue, the reason being is that some weapons are mandatory to destroying certain enemies, with a limited inventory, you are constantly made to pick and chose between the weapons you want on the spot rather than keeping everything at once like you could before. This ultimately damages the singleplayer quite a lot, it also makes exploration and any secrets feel a bit pointless as ammunition and hidden weapons are now more of a burdening choice than they are a bonus.
So, flaws aside, I will stand by and defend
by saying that it is a good game. Rather than avoiding it based on what most critics had to say, you should ultimately decide for yourself if you like it or not after playing it through, I know lots and lots of people are on a bandwagon preaching hate to the game when they haven't even given it a chance, and that's just lame. Rather than paying full price, I do recommend buying the complete set (DNF & DLC) during a sale. Don't believe everything you hear, try things for yourself before you make assumptions.

Kingdom wars is actually a pretty nice RTS, and while the MMO aspect doesnt have all that much yet (its mainly just PvP against other players or working with them to take NPC cities, alliances also dont do much yet) from an RTS standpoint i would say its pretty fun. The game takes a while for you to start up, and its certainly not the kind of game you'll "finish" in a week or so. Units actually matter as resources take time to collect and when most units die they are permanently gone (exceptions to that include the starting "Hero" unit and special units like wizards and dragons that simply lose levels upon death) Speaking of levels, as your units kill enemies they will gain levels, these can be used from simply increasing max HP to extending an archer units sight/amount of arrows. The units that you level over time actually matter as they will be the most powerful units in your army and form the backbone of your fighting force. Tt feels like battles actually mean somthing in this game, win or lose you will be affected. Currently there are only three races in the game, Humans, orcs, and elves, but talk of adding an undead or dwarvern faction is being discussed. I would say if you are into strategy games you should at the very least give this game a try.

The shooting mechanic is rough, but once you get used to the jumpiness of the controls I personally found it not only acceptable but completely fun. Don't expect this to be CoD, and ESPECIALLY don't expect Halo. There's no aim assist here. If you pick up a railgun and start shooting, your aim better be pixel perfect.
Sniping is a niche role, both difficult and not fully rewarding. However, in combination with other roles a sniper can still be a formidible enemy.
The usefulness of bombers in the game is the one thing I would like to spotlight above all else: I never really played a game where the bomber wasn't just an inferior choice. In this, a single well-piloted bomber can completely cripple an unguarded capital ship, and with enough time, even destroy some of them. It's a role you can really dedicate to.
At $18 this is a -steal- for any shooter, sci fi, or spcae combat fan. If you are all three, you would be wrong to not at least add it on your wishlist and wait for a sale/full release.

This is a great game, it has many casual gameplay elements taken from Rome total war, and some building elements from The Settlers (7?). Controlling your army, and leveling them up on the over world is great fun, building your city and aquiring upgrades also plays out well. The timers on building buildings don't hit as hard as I initially thought they would, with twenty minute build timers on some of the larger buildings passing by quickly as I focus on other portions of the game
I have to say, that by far, BY FAR, i enjoyed the first part of the game the most, the psuedo tutorial. Running around with my hero and a few units, clearing my lands from bandits, coming back to find a messenger had arrived, or a lord wanted me to do something was thrilling and immersive.
The game looks fantastic for how many units are on the screen at once, and every battle I find myself Roleplaying as my hero, and ordering my units to take the field and feeling the loss of every man in all of my squads.
The only thing I really dislike are the crown earning systems, I find the process too slow, where PvP may net you the most crowns the fastest, that can come at the total loss of your army (save for maybe one or two units if you are lucky), which means it's back to the drawing board to re level up your units. (You can also buy your units levels at nearby towns with in game gold)
You could also take your leveled army, and farm the overworld maps for crowns, but after the third run through of a map, I find myself getting tired of the same placement of units, the same patrol paths, the same spawn point. Vary up the maps a bit more, is all I ask, make the single player overworld a bit more varied for map selection, instead of relying on the same one or two exactly the same maps per section.
It's a great free to play game if you are into city builders with PvP elements. Enjoy it while it lasts.

EDIT: You know, thinking about what someone else said, "based on a deceptively simple concept," I thought about the old addage I have at the top here, and it had me realizing that it applies to the whole game in a number of ways. One day food might be plentiful. Other days there's little. Same goes for weapons, monsters, and other things (
)
I get tired of seeing reviews complaining about difficulty. The whole point of this game is balls-hard, white-knuckling survival and learning on your feet. Dealing with the physics engine with movement is like learning to walk again. You'll be learning a lot by being forced to try something different or getting it through your head that the other creatures are basically people, too, and of course the golden rule. Some creatures cannot be reasoned with, others can, and all of them have unique personalties as well as an opinion of you. You can feed the lizards other creatures about your size, for one. Some have to do certain things in order to hunt that you can use against them, and other creatures are especially vulnerable to a particular weapon
. Some people compare it to a nature documentary. I'm inclined to agree.
Most games give you tools, techniques, a mission, and a world to explore. This game breaks the mold and gives you none of those.
Want tools?
Find them.
Want techniques?
Figure them out.
Need a mission?
Make one.
Want to know more about your world?
You're gonna have to earn understanding. (
)
You'll probably clock at least 20 hours
before you get used to dying all the time, then end up dicking around and finding that one spot and go "you know, this actually looks really cool" and start noticing all the artwork poured into this game. Best example I know of is a part of The Wall that's just over the cloudline (meaning it doesn't rain there) where you can climb an old antenna array and watch them go by for hours on end. And you won't even get to the lore without exploring everything and finding some folks to help you out. You don't have a written or spoken language. You don't understand the Scavs. You don't even understand the lil gold hologram when you first meet her real self. To you she speaks nothing but gibberish.
The whole game is kind of a metaphor to real life, and it's harder to enjoy if you take it to seriously. A little seriousness, a little tact, a little patience. In fact I'm pretty mad I used a guidebook and now have a fully loaded Pilgrimage karma bar.
Not like literature passages but
of Passage. Each one is gotten a different way. Some from experimentation, some from persistence. Each one will earn you a warp to any shelter and max out your karma. The first one you should earn is "Survivor."
On a lighter note, slugcats really do move like thicker, heavier cats. In almost every way, including some more nature-defying stuff. Basically Charlie's
line, less personified due to lack of range of control, but more in that the physics engine leads to some weird antics. Speaking of the physics engine, it's incredible well built. As simple as it is, it works very well for itself and the movement setup synergizes too well with it, giving every creature even more personality than AI alone can provide.
The world, too, has tons of personality. Even before you can understand the world around you or talk to the one who can tell you about it, there's tons of graffiti, old wreckage, and plenty of things that you can deffer yourself. When you DO finally gain the ability to speak, some of the things you can find out about range from "hey bretty gud" to "WAIT WHAT?!" The sheer amount of little things hidden in the background alone is staggering. Even a small, unassuming pearl can reveal things to you, provided you have the right tools, or know the right person (
).
To top this off, the world is basically alive. I didn't remember this before I read another review, but while in a region, all the other creatures' lives are playing out. In the whole region. While some things are randomly generated, including on each cycle, other things are not, and I get the vibe that you don't always wake up right when the rain ends, but maybe some time after, and that's why things can be a lil different or wildly different than the day before.
As for the music, it speaks for itself. It's designed around what your character is experiencing, from entering a new area and being bombarded with a number of new sights and smells and feelings, being in danger, or just mucking about. No music tells it's own story, too. There's almost three times as much in-game as there is on the selection, and it's not entirely modular, either.
The last thing I want to talk about is the graphics. No, it's not HD. The max res is Wide-XGA, or 1366x768. Yes, it's pixelshit. No, it's not half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ It is not one♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ either, but
. There's so much love in this game. From the gorgeous intro's fully parallax'd panels, to the artwork within the game. The creatures manage to stay pixel-perfect despite using the physics engine, and what I think might be vector graphics??? as opposed to sprites, but doing so requires a lot of coding skill, so my ♥♥♥♥ing hat off to them. Areas are greatly fleshed out by pallets, lighting, architecture, and the creatures therein. Different species and their races and castes have little variations that also might clue you in to their personality and habits. There's no end to the amount of detail in any one area. Even the empty can tell you a story.
All in all this game is a ♥♥♥♥ing experience and is not meant to be played by someone who wants a book that explains everything. Expect something open-ended, expect a lot of unanswered questions. And IMO, it is on par with
in terms of the ART GAME trope and just how much the little details in it play into the mechanics.
Last words:
This game is one of the most confusing things next to addititon, but besides that the point is that this game is terrible, don't buy it. Period.

Rain World is a multi-layered Darwinian experience; most superficially the visuals bring to the mind images of murky, primordial swamps where creatures struggle for the most basic means of survival; food, shelter. Some creatures form the beginnings of social hierarchies, working together to scavenge and hunt. Other creatures strike out a kind of solitary territorial dominance, giant beasts that dive from the sky sending the other critters scurrying for safety. Some life forms lie in wait, such as large seaweed-tentacles that grab their prey, and vast fields of living grass that devour any unfortunate animal to wander into their midst.
But perhaps more interesting is the Darwinian nature of Rain World that transcends the computer screen. Unlike most video games, you are not special in Rain World. This isn’t just a sentiment or a design decision, this is technically the case: Rain World loads and runs it’s world like a true simulation. Most games load their world around the player; actors only exist and act when the player can observe them. This is a technical necessity for most games, especially complex 3D worlds like those of the Elder Scrolls or Assassin’s Creed. Rain World however runs the entire area you are in (areas are quite vast), every creature, all the time, whether you can see them or not. You might stumble upon a room full of dead scavengers, with a giant lizard scurrying away with one in its jaw. You’re witnessing the aftermath of something that actually happened.
All of these conditions serve to create a world where the Darwinian mantra of ‘survival of the fittest’ applies to all actors, including the player. It should be apparent by now that Rain World is hard. Many have gone so far as to call Rain World unfair. But this is actually not true. Doom, Halo, Skyrim; these games are unfair. They are unfairly skewed towards the player, with the other characters as simple extras, cardboard targets to be knocked over. In Rain World a vulture may swoop down without warning and snatch up a lizard; it may swoop down and snatch up you. Rain World is possibly one of the most fair games to ever exist.
So here comes the kicker: Is this level of completely unfair-fairness actually fun? Does Rain World actually work as a video game? This question does not have a simple answer, and a lot of it depends on the kind of person you are. Bear in mind, the idea of the player as a powerful, god-like killing machine is so widespread because it is based on some pretty good design principles. People often play games to escape mundane reality, and a power-trip in a fantasy world can be amazing. (Don’t misread my earlier comments - Doom 2016 was indeed a blast). Rain World offers a different kind of escapism, which is admittedly less palatable for most people than Doom.
It is possible to fly to the top of a mountain in a helicopter. The helicopter ride may be fun, the view will surely be beautiful. And when you get to the peak, you may smile, put a flag down, and fly off to the next mountain.
This being true, why do people still climb mountains? Why go through all that trouble and exertion? If this question baffles you, Rain World may not be your game, and that’s fine. But if you know the answer, then for you Rain World might be the closest thing that a video game will ever come to a religious experience.

Not much to say other than it is "GG ez" in a nut shell, so here is a recipe for banana bread...
Banana Bread
3/4 cup sugar
1/3 cup vegetable oil
2 eggs
1 cup mashed ripe banana (~2 large bananas)
3/4 teaspoon grated lemon rind
1&1/2 cups all purpose flour
3/4 teaspoon baking soda
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 cup chopped nuts and/or chocolate chips
Heat oven to 325F.
In large mixer bowl, beat together sugar, oil and eggs. Stir in bananas and lemon rind.
Sift together flour, baking soda and salt. Then add to banana mixture and stir until
combined.
Fold in nuts and/or chocolate chips.
Pour into well-greased 9x5x3 inch loaf pan.
Bake for 50-60 minutes or until done (toothpick test).
Remove from pan and cool on wire rack.
Makes one loaf.
Enjoy!

If you've played through the 'Duels of the Planeswalker' games through the years, then you will know it has gotten better and better (albeit little by little). Moreover, when Wizards announced the availability of a deck-builder feature in the then to-be released 'Magic 2015' most fans seemed overjoyed. However, picking up the game and trying it out quickly came down to a series of letdowns and shortcomings. It seems deck building is the only feature present in this game, with the complete removal of pre-constructed decks like in previous installments; although you are given a simple deck based on your mana color preferences (especially for newcomers useful, but enthusiasts all the same) Now, that in itself shouldn't be reason to abandon ship, since the sets featured (some of which are Ravnica, Theros, and Zendikar) are pretty awesome, but it turns out not even half of the cards featured in the set as we know them in real life can be obtained - which is a major letdown (Theros without Gods? Really?)
All in all, if you're used to the previous games in the series and you liked them, then it might be better to stay away from this title. You have to admit that the step towards deck building is a good one, but there's still a major way to go before this can be really called successful.
If you don't mind all of this (and more, just read some other reviews) and you're willing to try it out, perhaps even willing to spend money on it to get all the cards instantly, then by all means. At the end of the day, it will probably still leave you with an empty feeling.

This is a first person shooter that closely resembles battlefront's gameplay.  As of 5/7/2016 there are 18 maps. Some of the maps are reskins where the only gameplay difference is the objective.  It should also be said that maps are mostly broken into ground and space combat with a few having a little bit of crossover.
The space combat itself is incredibly designed, you start off inside a captial ship and can go to the docking bay to take a ship to pilot.  You can even take command of the cap ship as long as it's not in warp.  In fact it'ss only in space that the players have classes.  Theres a couple of ships broken into classes like fighter, bomber and dropship.
Once you fight on foot there is no class system what so ever.  You can take whatever role you want by picking your equipment, and unlike Battlefield you start with everything unlocked.  As you rank up you can resource points that work similar to a weight system.  Each piece of equipment has a "weight" value so as long as you have enough room to work with you can mix and match any weapons and gadgets you want.  This works the same way in vehicles as well.
And the system promotes teamwork.  You have a separate score based on following orders or giving support to other soldiers.  So in order to get the combo of gear you want you'll have to play as a team, which is a good thing thats missing in a lot of team based games.
Pros
- Lots of customization in terms of weapons and vehicle loadouts
- Progression system that lets you have all unlocks available from the start
- Varied maps in term of style and design
- Promotes teamwork through increased score
Cons
- Low player count
- UI is bad
If you enjoy Battlefront you should definitely pick this game up.

Duke Nukem Forever. What can I say, well the answer to that is that it's a HUGE disappoinment.
When I first played the game I was heavily blinded by nostalgia, thus ignoring many of the games issues until I played through it the second time, to which only then did I realise what a colossal piece of sh*t this game was.
Negatives:
.Low quality textures for a modern game which is not surprising considering it uses the Unreal 2.5 engine but even than I've played games (such as MK vs DC universe) that have utilised the potential of the engine to higher standards
-For those who are console users I've heard that the console versions of the game suffered from texture pop-ins (essentially the textures are not rendered fast enough on whatever you appear to look at the time.
.Gameplay, rather than have the fast paced gameplay from its predocessor, DN Forever moves at a more sluggish pace similar to that of most modern FPS such as Halo or Call of Duty, even worse considering that when Duke sprints he tires out within 8 seconds.
.Regenerative health, aka. the Ego bar.
.Two weapon limit (Four on the patched version for pc)
.Linear level designs, which eliminates level exploration.
.Boss battles are ridiculously easy as you are essentially given limitless supply of ammunition for the either the rocket launcher or the devastators.
.Terrible driving mechanics (not surprising since Gearbox were the ones to develop the driving mechanics)
.Terrible ending.
.Wall b**bs, WTF!
Positives:
Most of Duke's one liners are still awesome
From what I've seen from the expansion pack "The Doctor who cloned me" it actually looks fun.
The fellow who is friends with Duke is rather funny even if some of his lines are vulgar.
The "Content" that a lot fans have wanted to see again in the series.
Overall the game was just a let down and I hope that when 3D realms (The creators of the Duke Nukem series) make the prequel to Duke Nukem 1 known as 'Duke Begins' that they learn from their mistakes so as to avoid making another DN Forever because every fan of the series does not want a bad Duke Nukem game, no fan does.
Overall a 4 out of 10

I like the idea of this game, but I sadly can’t recommend it in its current state. However, from what I was able to play (due to the sluggish performance & low FPS) I liked what I saw. I think it has potential, but it needs some serious work on the performance front. Based on the reviews and discussions in the forum, this is a common issue for practically everyone that’s played the game. Hopefully the devs will take notice and correct this ASAP. As far as the review, in short – my low down quick & dirty is: if you liked playing TransOcean 1 & 2, you'll probably like this game. It's made by the same devs and is basically the same game, just with tractor trailers carrying freight from Point A to Point B. My advice is to wait for a few updates to roll out that fix the performance issues before buying. If and when they do, I’ll change this review to a recommended / thumbs up. My PC specs are listed on my profile for review & comparison. Note – I’ve only tried this on my gaming laptop at the time of this review.
UPDATE #1: I've tried it on all my computers, and I get the same performance issues on the others as well. Is it playable? Just barely…not sure about you, but I don’t like to waste my cash ($21.24) on a just barely playable game. To be honest, 4 days now since release and we are yet to have a patch. Due to this, I'm honestly considering a refund, as well as never purchasing a Deck 13 Hamburg or an astragon Entertainment GmbH product again. I think these issues should have been addressed before releasing. I mean what were their test machines, and on what settings did they try the game on?? If you (I do) compare other botched releases to this one, others have worked hard to correct the issues pretty much IMMEDIATELY (i.e. CMS 2018). I for one am not at all sympathetic to these developers having to “research” the cause of their issues. There really shouldn’t be any excuses - it’s practically the same game they’ve produced before (TransOcean), just on land, and…it uses the same ENGINE (Unity)!  I’m really not sure why it’s a big surprise to these folks all of a sudden?? At the time of this update, I still stand behind my review as “Not Recommended.” Caveat Emptor, eh?!
UPDATE #2: I've recently been playing the Beta update, and things seem to be improving. I'm now seeing better performance while playing, but I'm also getting locks and crashes. Obviously I'm now over my time limit to refund, so I guess I'm riding it out. I seriously doubt I'll update this review again, unless I'm just blown away with future updates & changes.
My final verdict - if you really, really like trucking logistics or management games, AND can live with issues that may never be fixed.
