Basically Robot Arena (you construct a robot) but instead of a fighting robot you make a robot which would climb over some obstacle, e.g. stairs, a wall, a narrow passage etc.
Pros:
- a unique idea (though arguably it's still much more fun to fight with robots in Robot Arena than just climb over obstacles here, unless you really are into non-violent games)
- interesting story
So-so:
- the puzzles are varied but solving them didn't feel satisfying. Most often I'd just either randomly stumble on a solution, or iterate on a supposedly incorrect solution until it would (clumsily) still perform the task. The whole puzzle is physics-based, so even with a wrong vehicle you can sometimes reach the goal. It would be great if the game had an option to show the solution which the author had in mind, e.g. after the level is solved.
Bad:
- there are some annoying useless animations which slow the game down, e.g. the character needs to step on a plate, then "covert" into a robot (long animation), then you can build the robot. In fact, the whole running thing with picking up the story pieces feels somewhat out of place since it's just a puzzle game with robots. The running part should have had more gameplay (not just running), or maybe it should have been taken out altogether. The story could just be told in briefings before/after puzzles or whatever.
A unique physics-based puzzle where you construct robots to climb over obstacles. You will like it if you enjoy physics-based puzzles and like to construct/engineer mechanisms.

While I'm saying "NO", I don't want to give the impression that this is a bad game, because it's not a bad game.
The only real problems I'm seeing are that the controls are unresponsive, i.e. "Press  *A* to jump" but pressing *A* does nothing.
The other thing is the UI; I like how it's customizable, but you can't tell what information it's telling you, if anything, so while I can see how much ammo I have left, I can't tell what's health, armor, shields, or even if I can board the enemy ship.
I've never been one for multiplayer with other people, so the "lack of community" doesn't bother me much.
While the tutorials are helpful in saying what is supposed to happen: "Board the Tank to take control, but first you need to customize it", it doesn't always tell you HOW to make it happen, (in this case, there's little "hardpoints" you click on and then a list pops up, but nowhere does it tell you to do that.)
While I understand that the flight controls are meant to be realistic (and I think they are), I can't tell the difference between the two modes.  I imagine that they are something that's meant to be switched around as the situation dictates, i.e. boarding an enemy ship VS making planetfall.
-------------
To clarify, I am in no way saying that this is a bad game.  The premise is strong, the setting makes sense, and there's plenty of maps/systems to choose from.  The gun/vehicle customization is there and it's plentiful, so there's something for every playstyle to make it work.
But to put simply, it needs just a smidgen less "Realism" and just a smidgen more "Rule of Fun" in the way of streamlining menu, tutorial, and UI
Even more simply, I can't get this game to work for me, but I'm putting it back on my "Wishlist" and will be following it, eagerly anticipating the finished product.
Keep up the good work.

Okay, so this one is kinda complicated. It's a good game. Basically, you have to build a little machine to help you get past certain obsticles. Sounds good, right? Another huge problem I have with this game is that fact that they never seem to give you enough parts to let your creativity run wild. I get the fact that they didn't want to make the game too easy for you, but what they should have done was make a system that gives you points based on how many parts you used. Definitely a must for all RTS fans. Especially since it is free, right? Unlike most game's that are free, this one also comes with the guarantee that it isn't pay to win. Wait one second. Free game not being pay to win? That's right! Paying in game with hard currency does not give you an outrageous advantage over people who choose not to pay and many options are simply for visual effects like battle standard and the like. Ha I'm gonna make my army bear the picture of an electric guitar. What? There weren't electric guitars back then? Darn.
Well anyways, This game is in my words: "A more drawn out MMO version on Age of Empires." Set in the medieval time period. Here you get to build your city, raise armies, capture enemy strongholds then choosing whether to control them or simply plunder them, and that's just the tip of the iceberg. As for you mythical lovers, there's also dragons, and wizards, and dwarves, Oh my! Choosing between three races is pretty cool, but here you can also select unique traits to focus your race on. Oh no, another underestimated indie gem! I really don't know why this kind of games don't get the attention they deserve. Is it the puzzles? Is it the price? Maybe the lack of promotion?

I found the human mode and the plot useless/uninteresting, but above all I miss leaderboards for each level that would give this game a competitive edge and probably more players. All in all, a fantastic physics based design/puzzle/action game that I strongly recommend.

This is going to sound like heresy, but Rain World does Dark Souls better than Dark Souls.  Wait, hear me out before you smash your monitor.
What made Dark Souls great (for me, anyways) was that if you wanted to beat it, you had to get over yourself.  You couldn't just hack and slash your way through like in so many other games.  You had to accept that those other games never really required much skill or thought.  In Dark Souls, you had to learn to predict enemy behavior, how to anticipate traps, and how to conserve health.  It had intentionally clunky controls that punished you for button-mashing.  It would occasionally throw a cheap shot at you to keep you on your toes.  But Dark Souls didn't fully commit to this concept.  You still could power up your stats and equipment, and because enemy placement never changed, you really only got surprised the first time you entered an area.
Rain World takes this gameplay philosophy and runs with it.  Even just walking or jumping feels awkward until you figure it out.  You have no weapons or equipment other than the spears and rocks you find littered around.  Every enemy kills you in one hit if you get too close.  And enemies often have just as much freedom of movement as you - leading to moments where you enter a room, find yourself face to face with a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off lizard, and have to run for your life across multiple rooms.  Killing these enemies is extremely difficult and time consuming, so you have to use the environment and other enemies to escape them.  The result is that nearly every minute of gameplay keeps you on your toes.  You have react to situations organically, often surviving by the skin of your tiny slugcat teeth.  When you combine that with the beautiful and oppressive setting (sprinkled with hints that something terrible that happened long ago), you have a game where you feel almost compulsed to keep going - just to see where and how you'll die next.
Oh, I should probably mention: I've played this game for over 20 hours and made zero progress in the plot.  That sounds horribly unrewarding, but I keep discovering new little mysteries, gameplay tricks, and environments, and I'm so invested that I can't .  It's time consuming, but it doesn't feel like a waste of time.

Rain World is a captivating experience. You are a mere slugcat, surviving in a desolate environment full of deadly creatures.
DISCLAIMER: At the time of writing I haven't beaten the game yet; I'm about 1/3 of the way.
Like many others have said, the game is challenging. The enemies are brutal, and you're constantly on the run to collect food and find shelter. The game explains very little about the mechanics of the game, which can be frustrating if you're left scratching your head for a couple of hours trying to progress, but I think this is actually one of the game's greatest strengths. It forces you to adapt, and learn from your experience. Just like in nature, there are no "easy paths to success". Sometimes you'll get unlucky and get ambushed by enemies, fall off a ledge, or fail to find food/shelter, but the fact is that if you're skilled enough, and think ahead, you can avoid death 95% of the time. What's really fun about this is that there are no "levels" or "upgrades", just you as a player learning to survive in this world.
With that said, some of the cues in the game are easy to miss. I accidentally took a really difficult path early on in the game which lead to me getting stuck in a difficult area before the game had a chance to teach me a key mechanic. I was stuck, so I put the game down for a few months, and came back to it this week. Thankfully, I got some hints from viewers in my Twitch chat, and was back on track within a couple of hours. My advice is that if you
go in blind, but if you get really stuck, join the official discord channel for the game and ask for tips, or check out the wiki and get hints from there. Just be careful not to tread to deep and spoil too much! The more you learn on your own, the more satisfying the experience will be!
Difficulty aside, the game is absolutely beautiful in its presentation. The world has a pixel-rendering style, but feels very organic due to all of the rust, grime and dirt blended into the scenery. You can tell how much effort went into the art direction of the game. The lighting, color palette, and effects all blend together seamlessly. The character animations also seem very natural, especially for slugcat who looks and feels very soft.
Overall, the game is a weird, ecosystem sandbox that demands your attention. You will get unlucky, suffer, and lose progress. but if you persevere, you'll adapt, and have plenty of fun. It's definitely one of my favorite games of 2017.

tl;dr: This game is a waste of your time unless you're OK randomly dying with no fault of your own.
I've played lots of metroidvanias and lots of tough platformers, but most are deterministic.  Most don't have you relying on dumb luck to make a single step forward.
The difficulty in this game is fully ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, and there's no real defending it.  If you're OK with being cockblocked at least 1/3rd of the time, not being able to proceed because the only way forward was randomly filled with enemies that you don't have enough items to kill, or enemies sitting in a chokepoint and refusing to move, or the next savepoint is literally too far away for you to make it there in time, then you're probably just fine with this game.
But when the supposed 'easy mode' still has these flaws, where there's literally no chance of success, it just leads to a ♥♥♥♥ton of wasted time.
It's overall really well made, I like not knowing exactly what to do - but it's so incredibly often that the only way forward is clogged with enemies, and you have nothing to deal with them, you just have to die repeatedly and hope that the next time you revive the way forward is clear, which, due to its Karma system, actively sets you back every single damn time.

More than a good game, more than a bad one, I prefer an INTERESTING game. With its dark and clever metacommentary on the Star Wars universe itself, its multilayered characters, and a truly bleak atmosphere that conveys the horrors of war far more than any weepy montage of Jedi Knights getting gunned down, Knights of the Old Republic 2 (KotOR2) more than fits the bill.
HOWEVER, IT IS VERY IMPORTANT THAT YOU DOWNLOAD SOME KIND OF CONTENT PATCH FOR THIS GAME. KotOR2 was rushed for the holidays, and a ton of vital content was left on the cuttng room floor, from characters scenes to incredibly important plot details. The Sith Lords Restoration Patch is one of the best. DO NOT play this game without something like that.
Following closely the heels of the first game, KotOR2 examines in more depth exactly what would happen to the people of a galaxy after decades of war, and it isn't pretty. From the protagonist to the party members, everyone has been scarred...and the scars are more subtle than some bomb-scorched landscape. It takes a simultaneously more mystical view of the Force and a more critical view. After all, has the Force really done anything in the Star Wars universe but perpetuate years for its thousand-year history?
Of course, the game has some clever "outs" built into the story to keep the deconstructions from getting too heavy--some unreliable narration, though you'll have to play for yourself to see what I mean. And while the game plays well enough, it's essentially more of the same KotOR we got last time...along with the same massively overpowered character you get by the end of the game. All these goes with the afformentioned fact that the game really isn't done--the pacing can be a mess towards the end, even with the patch.
Ultimately, it's up to you whether this makes the game worthwhile. As for me, this is one of my all-time favorites. It made me think--not just about Star Wars, but about the world outside of it. And I say that if a game can do that, it's damn worth a few hills of bugs.

Magic 2015 is a money grabber and pretty much a slap in the face to anyone who bought it.
I know this is long, but you should read it.
Especially if you haven't bought it yet.
Right from the start you play through the campaign.
Every Planeswalker you go up against in the campaign has the max quantity allowed for each card that make their deck strong. Some Planeswalkers have cards that aren't even IN THE GAME.
Examples: Terramorphic Expanse, Phantasmal Bear, a bunch of Extort cards and more.
That's not a challenge. It's an un-fair advantage.
So after going through the simply annoying campaign you decided to start playing online against other players.
"Finally, I can now start getting to the fun of all this."
BAM!
You're hit by a bunch of players who have paid $36, $56 or $76 for cards so again having the max quantity allowed for each card that make their deck strong. When you only have 1 or maybe 2 of the max quantity allowed for each card that make your deck strong.
By this point I can almost assure you that you will feel the need to buy the premium boosters, or the all the base cards so that you can have a deck that is capable of not getting completely slaughtered.
So what the hell, you go for it. You spend the $56 on the cards while mouse wheeling threw an annoying and buggy menu obviously made for tablets, and non-stopping mouse over sounds from their menu buttons that make you wish you were deaf...
You try to make you're deck how you want it and notice that you can only have 3 of the same uncommons, 2 of the same rares, and 1 of the same mythic. Completely changing the way decks are built in magic.
So not only did they give the A.I. a bunch of cards you can't get (even if you pay the $76 you don't get the cards the A.I. has access to), not only did they set up the campaign to be un-fair and limit your deck to almost trash to push you towards paying for cards, not only did they design a complete pay to win model no better than StarTrek Texels, but after paying the $36, $56, or $76 they significantly reduce the limit of customization and what you can do with the money you just spent compared to Magic: The Gathering's official rules.
Do not buy this game!

Sometimes the back seats are missing because the previous owner wanted less weight, sometimes the dashboard is cracked from years in the sun, sometimes there are just problems that don't need to be there.
Duke Nukem Forever is a used project car that you can't finish. You can see the tape on the wiring, you can see where parts were spliced into it, It's a mess.
First off, enemies are bullet sponges. This was a problem in DN3D, but not at this level. Good news is that headshots do seem to work on some enemies, and they do an entertaining cartwheel ragdoll. Some enemies like the floating fat guys and the octobrains are given way too much significance and are almost boss battles.
The game offeres a few  modern FPS no-nos, like limited weapons, limited enemy count, Regenerating health, Corridor levels, it's really sad to see these anti-fun measures applied to duke.
The game's humor is pretty good, Some pop-culture references fall a little flat in this age of the internet, but they're really no better or worse than classic OJ Simpson trial references found in Duke3D. The DLC campaign is another story though. The humor is god awful, and they even try and work some social justice into it, but with anthony burch writing for the game, Just like his wife by other men, it's going to get messed with. in particular there's a part where you're supposed to reject a "slap-a-hoe" arcade machine, then the game celebrates you NOT playing it. Why was it even put in in the first place? There's no reason for it to exist.
Which brings me to another point. Much like classic dook, there are tons of interactables in the environment. Sadly, these are often more fun than the rest of the game. Duke Nukem was never an original game. It was always a pop-culture spouting rip-off game. Duke 1+2 were contra/metroid rip-offs, Duke 3 was a doom/ROTT clone. This duke you can trell when it tries to emulate first HL2, then Halo, then CoDMW respectively. And the problem with emulating 3 games is, it doesn't know what it wants to do. Duke 3D took the platform of Doom and made its own adventure. These newer ones don't stray a terrible lot and are really bland.
This game DOES have multiplayer, the multiplayer IS dead, but when it was alive, it was absolutly fantastic. It was fun, Fast paced, challenging, and had a ton of unlocks that don't really affect gameplay, but unlocked activities for you to do in your hotel room, like pool, or darts or pinball. So there's no one who slogged it out and got the super ultimate gun and beginners are scared off. But, the MP is dead so it's a moot point.
On it's own, if this game was called Mr. shooter guy, had NO ties to duke nukem, this would be a forgettable, mediocre game. But this game was a sequel to one of the best games of the 90's. This game is an insult. It's a tragedy that this will be Duke's last adventure. This COULD have inspired a whole new generation to love dook with his witty humor and great gameplay, but instead it's a lazy hodge podge hastily thrown together from years of most likely rejected content.

Still Early Access, but this game shows potential!
Having read a bit about the game, and watched the standard YouTube videos about it, I decided to give it a try. Now admittedly I haven't put in a whole lot of hours, because there still are some things that needs to be polished, before a final release is due.
That being said, the game as it is now, is a lot of fun. The physics are unlike any other car game, which really is what sets this game apart right now.
The handling of the cars is very unique, and not two cars feel the same. Depending on the type of car you have chosen, a simple task like driving down the road can become a challenge. I'll bet ya', you'll be wrapping your car around a few trees before you get the hang of the in-game handling.
The game in its current state, already lets you do a bunch of different customization options, and I'm not talking about rims, speakers or the likes here, but stuff like removing parts of the body, removing a wheel, stripping the vehicle down to its core etc.
All things that make the game kind of nerdy, but nerdy in a good way.
The graphics are quite good too, and once you get the hang of controlling your car, you can start venturing into more advanced manuevers like handbrake turns, burnouts and whatever your heart desires.
So for now, in Early Access, the game is for anyone looking to drive around some beautiful scenery, all while tinkering with different setups on your virtual vehicle, and just goofing around basically.

April 2015 Review:
Great concept, but AI and GUI are well behind industry standards.  Yes, it is early access, but there were enough frustrations and rough edges to discourage me from recommending this game.  I hope the money spent is worth it and I will continue to check back every several months.  I want this game to succeed, but can't recommend at the current stage of development and price point.  Rating:  5.5/10
UPDATE June 2016:
AI and GUI are still sub par, but there is now a useful functional tutorial to help things out and the game engine is much better optimized and the AI isn't nearly as horrible, in some cases it is quite decent.  Before when you started shooting an enemy in the back, he'd just go on his merry way and die.  Now, they actually turn around and return fire.  Animations seem to have made progress and damage modeling on soldiers while not pretty, is well done.  Sound and ambience are much improved and on par with what I would expect out of a game labeled as version "0.9."
I have played only a handful of maps, but I must say that the map design is actually quite good and the addition of tactical briefings that explain objectives is a huge plus over a year ago.  There are also a few new weapons to choose from and as opposed to a year ago, there's probably enough variety to keep the "armory enthusiast" happy for a good while.
In summary: a year later, the devs still have the same awesome concept but have now demonstrated they can put forth the effort to make a fully playable product.  This game is far from perfect but could be an example of faith ultimately well-placed for those of us who put in the money at the get-go.  Definitely worth picking up on sale if you have the extra little cash and interest in a game with significant upside.  Rating 7.2/10

Just because I like reminders : remember to do your homework before purchasing any early access games. This includes videos of the game itself, searching discussions and forums and checking out the developers reputation. If there is a road-map included, all the better.
Welcome to Party Panic where chaos is met with a smile. Like most Humans, I saw this game and instantly made a comparison. I compared it to Mario party and was wondering if it could be just as good. Unlike Mario Party, Party Panic does not have a board system. Rather, mini-games are played back to back while scores are displayed after each game. The way the scores are displayed is beautiful, and whats even more beautiful is the fact you can punch or kick a buddy off a higher pedestal than yours. As your score grows, so does your pedestal.
The player has almost thirty mini-games to choose from with the addition of a gauntlet mode. Of the thirty mini-games, some that are included are sprint orientated games (such as smacking a post or running for your life), sumo ball orientated games (such as collecting coins, a soccer mimic and classic sumo), dodge-based games (such as running from an avalanche, jumping over a rotating blade, dodging ghosts and dodging falling rocks or players), fighting-based games (such as scoring points for landing blows), collection based games, racing orientated games and finally coordination sort of games (which involves pressing the right buttons at the right time).
There is a decent amount of variance so far within the mini-game realm. The
feels very classic to me. Meaning, even though the objective or dynamics are simple the game is still quite challenging. When playing with friends, the atmosphere becomes even more intense when everyone is rushing as fast as they can to get the combination down. This is a breath of fresh air in a sense as it evens the playing field for anyone. Expert gamers to n00bs are sure to get enjoyment. Any game that someone can perfect is nice, but having a game where everyone has a fair chance is golden. Moreover, there is a pretty cool gaming feature included that attempts to keep all players involved at all times. In certain mini-games (not all yet I'm hoping), when a player is knocked out they still have a chance at redeeming themselves and sometimes scoring points. For example, in an boulder-falling game or falling-tiles game, players that have been knocked out from active game play can still attack other players from the grave. In these two games, the fallen players can aim and sometimes control the projectile they fire out. This is an amazing feature as it attempts to keep everyone involved even when they are out! Successful games (virtual or not) are successful for the sole reason everyone is still participating. This is a step in the right direction and I encouraged it to go even further! I hope to see this continue and a lot more variances and new stages in the future.
Gauntlet is a series of linear mini-games back to back. This is a solid addition and gives players a break from playing mini-games. Unlike mini-games where there are pauses, players are competing in real time and with one another. Players can choose how many stages to have prior to starting the gauntlet. The stages don't have too many variances at the moment, but the concept is on the right track to creating a fun alternative to mini-games. Some stages include dodging spikes, jumping platforms and avoiding spinning blades. Players are participating with other players and can interfere with one another. This is fun and annoying as landing on someone's head gives you an extra bounce up into the sky. To win the gauntlet, players have to make it to the end. Progress can be tracked by viewing the middle of the screen; the heads of the players will appear in the middle and as the player progresses further, so will their icon. There is also a death count that keeps a toll of how many times you fell off the stage. The game will end when one player reaches the very end and comes into contact with a stepping stone.
, the style suits what the game is about. Cartoony, funny, playful and emotional. The cartoon and comical aspect are reciprocal to one another. It's funny seeing these things getting bounced around everywhere. The expressions on players faces is the icing on the cake. Whether they are getting rocks thrown at them, running from a whale trying to eat them, snow trying to crush them, or lava trying to burn them, the players are laughing, showing signs of worry, straight faced or sticking their tongue out. This is just a pleasure to watch when everyone is going full speed and the players in the game are making faces.
are OK as of the moment. They are accurate, but a little more umph and emphasis needs to be added. Key sounds are always important to making an impact. I can still hear the ping from the game WCW vs NWO revenge when a wrestler runs into a steel ring post. My suggestion would be to diversify the sounds between different characters... maybe even using different voices like worms did? Moreover, the music is on the right track and does a good job giving a little bounce to the mini games. I'm curious to see what else is to come in this domain. Although sound and music may be considered a brush up touch to the final product, it can really enhance the experience.
Overall, the game is fun and engaging. Because it is in limited regarding development, there may be only so much replayability for certain players. Depending on the crowd, I can see people easily throwing a couple of hours per session (especially with the drinking game mode turned on). The games and gauntlet are still in development; adding more inclusive and dynamic games will ensure Party Panic's success. There is online capabilities at the moment, but finding a game is a bit difficult. I recommend playing with local players to maximize this games effect.
To the developer, I have a few suggestions :
>Keep adding mini-games. New stages may bring new ideas and game-modes. On the other hand, the stages you currently have are also open to modification. Small objective, player or terrain changes can fuel these new modes. The best games (be it virtual or not) can be in the form of modified games. A soccer game can be broken up or modified in many ways to make it fair or even more fun. Try to keep an open mind!
>Personalizing characters is great. I think adding whatever designs come to mind in regards to hats or color should be added. I do like how the characters make faces throughout the game. You could potentially give the player some control over this.
>Gauntlet is a really cool feature that gives the player a break from mini-game sessions. This linear and continuous game is pretty sweet, but can still use some tweaks. More stages, modifications and variances definitely need to be added here. It would be interesting perhaps to add items or some sort of "X" factor that rattles all players wherever they are on the map.
>I would recommend making the classic sumo mode less mobile. This is not to say restrict movement, but add some weight to the sumo balls. Flying around everywhere at full speed is fun; adding some weight or momentum can add some difficulty and strategy to the movements.
>Continue to add elements of inclusiveness; when players die allow them to compete in one way or another.
EARLY ACCESS RATING : 6.9/10

There's something soothing and peaceful about the crafting and farming side of this game.  You have very few storage options, and none at the start, so you have to get into the habit of only taking from the land what you absolutely need.  You can optimise the trees you find by paying attention to their quality, and before long you're surrounded only by big, green, healthy looking trees.  As long as you start somewhere close to water, clay, and game you'll have what you need to start your little settlement.
The game needs a lot of work and refinement still, and has a lot of minor but recurring issues with its GUI setup, but once you get the hang of that it's pretty smooth sailing.  There are some issues with very basic things (like once you close the pop-up message box, which you almost have to, you can only exit the game by commanding the server to stop with "quit();" and then ending the process for the client through Task Manager) and there are problems with you needing to know so much about how to start before you do.  Tunnels are never clear exactly how they'll end up when you start them (so you might not be able to get out without the /stuck command), you need granite to make castle walls (the only way to level up your architecture skill--besides half making the walls with just the rocks then destroying them--which you need to build the keeps) which is only found in the centre mountain.
All that said, it is a very enjoyable game once you get going with it.  After you make your  first full volley of mistakes, anyway, and are willing to start again in hopes that you'll make fewer of them and actually be able to get somewhere.

I played Dawn of Fantasy back in its early closed beta. It was...horrible. So many game breaking glitches, errors, units disappearing, the hero disappearing...just so many things. Luckily, the developpers are always on the prowl so they listened to everything we had to say...and they still do today. I've rarely seen developpers being so active, especially for such a lengthy amount of time.
Now...I have yet to find a single bug. It took some time, but the game is in a great functioning state. There are a little jitters here and there, but they don't cause any real problems.
This game has three races: Orks, Elves, and Humans. There is also the rumor of the possible coming undead race, but let's not get ahead of ourselves. (See...See what I did there? Ahead? You know...un...undea-Headless Horseman...)
Unlike many other RTS games where the differences are just aesthetical or very minor, all three races are heavily different from eachother. Where humans use peasants to mine, chop wood, and kill livestock, elves need wood spirits to gather wood. And the other races do not have the same form of livestock as the humans. Elves have unicorns and Orks have a type of 'boar'. Both can be used in combat and, while the boar can be killed and have its meat taken, the unicorns give a steady trickle of gold (and can be used to protect your gatherers from wolves).
When you create a new race, you have the option to choose from three different regions of that race's territories. The only thing that changes, I've noticed, is the landscape. This affects the placement of your soon-to-be walls and will create different kinds of tactics when attacking and defending players/npc towns. Afterwards, you have the option of choosing between different traits that will become permanent for that city, although the region you choose already possesses a few natural traits that will be added to your two choices. This makes some strategic decisions on developping your region change, as the traits affect ressource income, training, building, and stats of units.
Units are also varied. Where humans have a good balance between unit types (melee, range, siege, cavalry), orks are more centered around melee, health, and anger issues, while elves are more centered around range and speed. I might be mistaking, but this is how I've percieved all three.
Some units have abilities specific to them, such as human knights being able to heal nearby units or the elves ranged cavalry being able to use an arrow volley (accelerates their firing rates).
For you, the player, you are represented by a 'hero' (that you can rename with crowns. More on those later). This hero allows you to interact with NPCs on the maps, allowing you to buy and sell ressources, buy mercenaries (this is the only way to get units from the other factions), or train your troops (including your hero). To travel on the world map, you need your hero to lead the army that you create. Depending on what units you bring with you, the amount of ressources you can carry with you increases. You can only carry a certain amount of wood, meat, and stone, so be cautious. As for your gold, you can carry however much you want! Except 'thieves' will start stealing the amount that exceeds your ressource cap. This also happens in your town.
You have several options when travelling on the world map. You can set up a camp (with three defensive levels depending on the ressources that army possesses) which allows you to attack player cities. These camps can let you mine for ressources (if you have gatherers) and recruit units from your race to bolster your sieging force. You can also fight on the map, allowing you to see what is in the region. If you do it from a camp, you'll have a place to retreat to if you're overwhelmed. If you have no defences, well...
This is a great way to see the regions without towns or cities. Sssilistra, for example...Nah. Why would I spoil that for you?
You can also siege the npc towns on the map and conquer them, they become 'allied' with you. Plus, you get to loot the corpses on that map if you have gatherers and won. Hooray for corpse desecration! Otherwise, there's not much use with allying with npc towns apart from trading, but that only gives you a fickle amount of ressource income.
Sieging can be slow, especially with the accuracy provided by your trebuchets/siege catapults/ bolt throwers, and with the many defenses that can be placed in a city or town, you best be wise on where you go to fight as you can be annihilated in just a few seconds. The fun part is when you enter the city after tearing down the walls and the defenses.
Now, there's the matter of crowns and special units. Before you ask; No. The special units do not cause a pay-to-win situation. They can killed just as easily as any other unit...sometimes. It depends on the unit. First, let's talk about crowns. Crowns are the special currency bought with in-game money, but they can also be obtained in-game via combat and completing quests. These are used for research and constructing certain buildings. The demands for the buildings are minor and will certainly just take you a single trip on the world map and 'entering the region' to get the crowns needed. A few bandits and there you go. You got your building plus some extra. You might've gotten enough for the beginner's research too!
Now, for the special units. Before the game became free to play, you just needed enough crowns to buy a dwarf unit or a dragon from the market. Now, you need not only the crowns, but the building as well, and these take a CRAZY amount of ressources to build! Not only that, but you have the crowns that are eaten up by the buildings. This prevents everyone from having too many of these units seeing how powerful they are. I find it both logical and crippling when thinking about the research needed to unlock the spells for the three mage types (provided you even manage to recruit one). You can no longer get tons of dragons or hydras as, to do so, you need to build several of the buildings dedicated to recruiting them seeing as only one beast cage can sustain one dragon or hydra. This is a good thing as, before the regulation of its power, a dragon could annihilate entire groups of units with a single fireball, not to mention the fire spreading in the town and destroying everything but the walls.
Now, it's reasonably powerful, but cannot do anything on its own. It can't. Don't even try. I'm serious. Don't make it walk over there on its own. Because of these extreme limitations on the special units, you're still depending heavily on your regular units. Not only that, but player towns might harbor a dragon, so I would advise you to carry a dragon slayer, if you can get him out of the tavern.
Another feature related to PVP is the protection time. You can buy this from the barracks for crowns. There's a large amount of different times, so don't worry. The timer does not keep going when you've logged out. It resumes when you continue playing in that town, however. Building and ressource gathering continues.
As for the simpler things, I cannot percieve graphics the same as other people, so, for me, these are still pretty good. The music fits the time period this is set in and doesn't disappoint, although more variety would be needed.
The game isn't perfect, but perfection leads to stagnation.

There is the option to replay levels to come up with different solutions, and a sandbox level is also available, but I do wish the game had more content.
The content that's there though is enjoyable, and I certainly don't regret buying the game. I just want MORE of it! :)

I actually bought the game back in the day, stumbling upon it during a massive sale. At the time, I wasn't particularly impressed, as it lacked a lot of the freedom of your typical city-builder, and the progress seemed slow enough that I wondered if I'd ever see my town grow into a city before losing interest in the game.
In retrospect, I think I had largely missed the point.
As it has gone free-to-play, firstly, I'm glad it avoided the pittfalls of becoming a pay-to-win game in the process, as the two more often than not go hand-in-hand. My town is still small and undeveloped, and as more of a city-builder myself, I have yet to really go deep into the siege/warfare aspects of the game. The controls for that, in what little of it I have engaged in, were a little clunky and troops were difficult to manage, but it seemed that it was surmountable, and that with time and experience, one could probably master the warfare system, should they be inclined to do so.
As a city-builder, which is where I'm coming from, it is a bit limited, as you don't really choose where buildings go as freely as you do in most others. That said. it has been fun seeing my town grow, and stocking it with a large enough garrison to defend myself against any potential attackers. In fact, the game is probably more comparable to an online game I used to play called Travian, but it is very polished graphically in comparison, and much deeper in terms of variability and different units/buildings.
The slow pace of the game might deter some, but I've come to enjoy stopping by every so often to see how many resources my villagers have accumulated. I check in once every other night or so, and in that span they've usually cobbled together enough stuff for me to be able to signifiantly add to my town with each log in.
All-in-all, it's not a game for everyone, and it limits the freedom of both the city-builder and the strategy/siege models, however in return it provides both of those in one game, doing something unique and playable, to me anyway. There's a lot in here for one game, and not necessarily too much, as is so often the case these days.
The price is right, these days, so it's certainly worth giving a shot, and remember to log in a few times before giving up on it, if you're not enjoying it so much. It wasn't until my fifth login or so that I started realizing that I was actually having fun with the game. Be that a critique or not, I recommend the game as it currently stands.

It is what it says on the tin: build robots, solve puzzles. I helped test this game and honestly I'm not a puzzle game guy but the building aspect in the puzzle context works... MechoEcho is a nice break from the wildly free form crafting sandboxes zombie horde survivals I'm use to. Here you're faced with a task: get from point A to point B. And do that using a limited set of blocks and your imagination. At first the game is a tutorial explaining basics but before you know it, you're playing levels that force you to question if it can be solved at all with the limited pieces and this turns into a fun challenge.
This is where the game gets it right, it will challenge you to think outside of the box. Usually after a break from the game a new idea will pop in your head to go back and try. Even after you solve a level you'll likely find yourself going back to solve the level again with a new configuation and this aspect of replay surprised me, as I'm use to rushing through games and moving on.
If you like puzzles and building things, MechoEcho is for you.

More than a good game, more than a bad one, I prefer an INTERESTING game. With its dark and clever metacommentary on the Star Wars universe itself, its multilayered characters, and a truly bleak atmosphere that conveys the horrors of war far more than any weepy montage of Jedi Knights getting gunned down, Knights of the Old Republic 2 (KotOR2) more than fits the bill.
HOWEVER, IT IS VERY IMPORTANT THAT YOU DOWNLOAD SOME KIND OF CONTENT PATCH FOR THIS GAME. KotOR2 was rushed for the holidays, and a ton of vital content was left on the cuttng room floor, from characters scenes to incredibly important plot details. The Sith Lords Restoration Patch is one of the best. DO NOT play this game without something like that.
Following closely the heels of the first game, KotOR2 examines in more depth exactly what would happen to the people of a galaxy after decades of war, and it isn't pretty. From the protagonist to the party members, everyone has been scarred...and the scars are more subtle than some bomb-scorched landscape. It takes a simultaneously more mystical view of the Force and a more critical view. After all, has the Force really done anything in the Star Wars universe but perpetuate years for its thousand-year history?
Of course, the game has some clever "outs" built into the story to keep the deconstructions from getting too heavy--some unreliable narration, though you'll have to play for yourself to see what I mean. And while the game plays well enough, it's essentially more of the same KotOR we got last time...along with the same massively overpowered character you get by the end of the game. All these goes with the afformentioned fact that the game really isn't done--the pacing can be a mess towards the end, even with the patch.
Ultimately, it's up to you whether this makes the game worthwhile. As for me, this is one of my all-time favorites. It made me think--not just about Star Wars, but about the world outside of it. And I say that if a game can do that, it's damn worth a few hills of bugs.

**RELEASE DAY UPDATE**
Bottom line up front:  Still underwhelming.
The UI has gotten better but is still not good.  The popup dialogs are still obtrusively large and don't close/minimize in a common sense kind of way.  The tutorial popup is particularly bad as it's opaque, unmovable and stays behind most the other popup dialogues.  The other UI element, the world map has gotten slightly better but is still lacking.  You still can't scroll the map at all (arrows, WASD, or mouse drag) and can only do point zooms with a scrollwheel.  Some of the countries are so small that you'll be pixel hunting to click on "The Random Islands" (ingame country name for the Maldives, no clue why).
Some new mechanics were introduced.  Building and upgrading vehicles is actually interesting.  Bidding on blind crates is a decent mini-game.  So are the "Black Umbrella" terrorist acts to trigger wars.
Still the overall game is painfully dull.  It takes a certain lack of vision to make arming Iran with Israeli arms for an invasion of Central America boring.
The single player campaign is not very great, but I really like playing it multiplayer with friends.

Some games just don't appeal, or have a few nagging issues that bog down an otherwise passable experience. And then there's games that make a person angry just by thinking about them. For me, KOTOR II is in the last category.
While initially I thought of it as an improvement over the original KOTOR with its more interesting characters, its improved character models, its expanded game mechanics, its awesome Sith Lord concepts (a rage-fueld zombie and a human-shaped hole in the Force) and its admittedly very well done opening level. The ENTIRE REST OF THE GAME proceeds to♥♥♥♥♥♥all over these expectations.
It creeps in slow, with only a few nagging concerns. Telos is basically Taris only smaller, darker, and with even less personal motive to get involved with the plot. But at least there you know exactly what you need to do to get back on track to your actual goals (even if it means playing toadie to a completely irrelevant power play between two factions).
Then you realize that the overarching goal is vague at best. The Sith are trying to kill you, and you've developed an inconvenient Force bond with the most unapologetic author avatar in the history of videogames. Somehow, hunting down the survivng members of the Jedi Council and either gathering them or murdering them will somehow resolve one or both of those issues.
On two of the four planets you visit (discounting Telos), this is simple enough. There's a big fat Force user landmark on both of them. On the other two, not  so much. One, you just sort of know where the Jedi is without explanation (unless your character somehow saw the expository cutscenes too), and the other you have no choice but to wander around prodding side quests with a stick until the game decides that its ready for you.
It's the latter that finally pushed me from "ambivalent" to "hate." Nar Shadda is the ♥♥♥♥♥iest ♥♥♥♥ing place I have ever been in an RPG. It's worse than Taris. It's worse than the ♥♥♥♥ing Catalyst, because at least the Catalyst is mercifully direct. Rather than being given any sort of obvious plotline to follow (even the other planet where your goal isn't obvious in-character, Onderon, the plot at least directs you down the right path), you're left to just wander around the city, with completely uninteresting side quests dangled in your face that have nothing whatsoever to do with your to main goals of "talk to the Exchange to get rid of the bounty on your head" and "find the hidden Jedi master" until you've tripped over enough cutscenes playing a sped up bounty hunter drama between a smug redhead and a psychotic Wookiee that the game is willing to let you in on the plot too.
Unfortunately, when that happens it's the single stupidest ♥♥♥♥ing part of the plot. You're sent a message asking you to come alone to a lowlife bar with a poisonous-for-humans (why only humans? I've always been confused with KOTOR's weird humans-and-every-other-species seperation that is in no way hinted in the actual films apart from the Empire being 99% human, which seems to mostly be because their leader is a card-carrying evil overlord who felt racism would round out his ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ resume) atmosphere, and to come alone. Obviously it's a trap and everyone knows it, so of course you have no choice but to go alone.
You can visit this bar beforehand with a gas mask and be totally fine, mind. But, because the game has some character schilling to do, you're accousted by the smug redhead and knocked out with poison gas (even if you happen to be wearing an air filter while the smug redhead explains that anyone not wearing an air filter will be knocked out), and she promptly goes and gets herself captured. The Jedi you were looking for turns up and says he's going to get involved and runs off, so you have no choice but to run into the bar after him. And now, again, EVEN THOUGH YOU'RE WEARING A GAS MASK and EVEN THOUGH YOU WERE FINE BREATHING THIS EXACT SAME AIR EARLIER, you get poisoned. Because Kreia decided she wants to come to the rescue and nobody steals her spotlight, damn it. So she teaches you a way less effecient method of being immune to poison and you're allowed to continue.
If you don't like the smug redhead, I hope you kicked enough puppies before this point because once you go in there you can't leave until the dungeon's finished, and if you're not strongly Dark Side aligned you get stuck with her in your party, forcing you to play her for a section while you duel the psycho Wookiee you could've had to the death. This is around the point where I closed the game and began to write a lengthy rant of why this game pisses me off in many, many ways.
Of course, no criticism of this game can come without bringing up Kreia. Where to start? She's been openly admitted to be Chris Avellone's author avatar and vehicle for him to complain about everything that rubs him wrong about Star Wars. And of course this means that she is invariably proven right about everything that comes out of her ♥♥♥♥ing mouth and characters who would never take her verbal abuse from anyone else in a thousand years are miraculously cowed by her audacious and scathing remarks. And of course she's the main villain, and is really, really ♥♥♥♥ing obvious about being up to something from minute one and you still can't do a damn thing about it. It wouldn't bother me so much if she wasn't praised as a brilliantly written character and not acknowledged for the self-assured Mary Sue she is.
I'm not going to complain about the ending here, because I recognize that its bare-bones status and confusing continuity is the result of executive meddling and not a design choice by the devs. But that doesn't excuse the author avatar nailed to your ankle, or the laughably thin illusion of choice whenever forwarding the plot requires you do something incredibly stupid or out of character, or the complete lack of narrative direction, or the convenient lapses of competency whenever you're scheduled to fall into a trap, or anything else this game does atrociously.
In summation, the first hour or so of this game is great fun, with an atmosphere that sets the mood nicely, a nice little conspiracy, and varied gamplay, but the game does its absolute best to♥♥♥♥♥♥all over those positive first impressions over the next 20-odd hours by being as determinedly obnoxious as possible before running out of breath and collapsing into its own mess at the end. Don't bother.

I expected very little of Swords and Soldiers (S&S), as it was an extra, unknown game in a Humble Bundle that started its life as a console game. I was pleasantly surprised!
S&S is a curious blend of two genres I don't usually enjoy: 2D side scroller and RTS. However, five minutes into the game, I could see through the cutesy graphics and I found a game of surprising challenge and deep gameplay. S&S is now available for tablet play, but it's far more challenging than the average casual tablet game.
Without going into the game mechanics, I'll briefly say that the challenge of S&S is about recruiting the right balance of each unit type into your army to make your forces competitive in groups. Also, staying focused on the big picture while also assisting your units at the strategic level. The game plays at a very brisk pace, which makes it difficult to manage all aspects of your forces at once.
The levels are bite-sized; about 5-15 minutes each, perfect for a game that was born as a mobile app. But the levels become increasingly more complex. A couple of hours into S&S, and you'll find a staggering number of things that you have to manage simultaneously. You have to juggle more and more types of units and one-off attacks to reach victory in each new level.
S&S also includes an online mode for playing competitively against friends.
If you like RTS games, give this a go. It's a pretty good game at a budget price.
As for me? Lesson learned: Play every game. I expected little, but Swords and Soldiers impressed me.

I just have to say: If I was going to recommend this game, it would be a hell of a challenge at the moment!
Much like the other Duels of the planeswalkers games, I can find ways to get fun out of it. But this one makes it quite a bit
more difficult then the others I have played!
Now to what I like and dislike about this.
The Decks!
Positive: You can build your own decks: This has its enjoyable moments and it feels good to "Build" your own deck as-well as
having freedom to do what you want and use or add what-ever colour you feel like! so long as you have the right cards of course. It was also good for them to do Tutorials before jumping you right into the decks and give you a chance to understand what the colours do!
Negative: The starting deck experience I thought was fine at first. But you eventually realise that the starting deck you get is just garbage and can't really compete against half the decks reliably. It doesn't help that the cards you get almost feel like they are intentionally designed to not help your deck (I'll get to that later)
Negative 2: Be careful what Starting colour you pick, because you cannot change once you accept it! You can build others yes, but good luck with that!
______
Boosters!
Positive: I really like that they have done it much like MTG in real life (Bunch of commons, 3 uncommons and a rare or mythic rare!) the mystery of the boosters is always something I am a fan of. It is also nice that you get a booster everytime you finish a campaign mission (Not sure about Multiplayer; haven't touched it yet)
Negative: As much as I like the mystery of the cards, I swear it is Designed to NOT pick cards for your starting deck! the amount of cards from boosters I have gotten that have been every colour BUT Blue white (Which is the starting deck I chose) Is a bit silly now! This
does makes me guess they done it for the next Negative...
Negative2: PAYWALL, GUYS! PAYWALL! This I was originally worried about because we already pay money for the bloody game, and it feels like you're forced to pay more, Which is just bad design! I did by two just to see a difference. Thankfully I just got draws I couldn't use, because that is exactly what I needed (Insert Sarcasm here!)
_____
Visuals
Positive: The menus and the game over-all game looks nicer and more modernised! It is good to look at and easy to find most things.
Positive: When actually playing the game, everything not only looks better and is easier to see but they made it more interactive. It was a cool Idea that the Environment actually shifts tone and the battlefield gets modified as-well as some other minor things which is just neat to look at!
Negative: As much as I like the look of the menus... They couldn't make it more annoying to work with! In a nutshell, you can only look at one thing at a time (Single player, multiplayer, decks, shops ect..) and when things are locked off, it doesn't allow you to look at them AT ALL! It is especially annoying in the Deck area, where you can see these different decks, but cannot get a clue of WHAT THEY ARE!
Negative 2: This isn't really a visual thing, but it kinda does fit in. TRANSITIONS! And boy do they like making you look at fading white fog with a white background... Slowly! If they didn't take so bloody long, they would actually be pretty cool and would fit well with the theming of 2015. But no, they had to be unusually slow and annoying to watch! You even have to stare at the start menu! "Yes, they must look at our glorious 'Enter game' button" A Genius developer said (Insert Sarcasm here)
-----
Finally, Gameplay
(NOTE: I haven't done multiplayer yet, only single player, so I wont judge the game there)
Positive: Because of the ability to properly make your own deck, the game has that extra level of enjoyment. It is that feeling when in real life, you made your first deck away from a starter deck and won against one of your friends (Which is a fun♥♥♥♥♥feeling!)
Positive: I don't know if I am frequently lucky or not. but it feels like the drawing system is more designed so you actually get cards you can use so you can actually play the game! I do know from the previous DotP games that you can quite oftenly just draw abysmally and you'd be better off leave or restart half the games you play.
Negative (This is campaign exclusive) : I have grown to really hate the campaign in this one! It isn't like the others where they add some stupid mechanic that you have to get a good draw to beat it.. That still exists, but from the ones I've seen, they are at-least acceptable and only slightly annoying. What is annoying that relates to that is the AI drawing the same cards, or always having the same cards. This would be fine if the deck you were given and the boosters weren't so bad that you likely can't do a thing about what they do. I'm almost content to not play the singleplayer at all because of it!
-----
CONCLUSION!
I can say for a time you will get enjoyment out of this game much like the others. How long that lasts, will likely depend on how full your wallet is... or your Patience to tolerate some of the issues this game has.
It does sadden me a little, because I was looking forward to the boosters, the deck building and just a freash change from the usual DotP Formula. It is just a classic case of "Taking one step forward, but two steps back" Which is really unfortunate.
Thank you for reading my Rambling! Hopefully I did well for a first review on Steam!

I've seen a few negative reviews on here so I feel the need to throw in my two cents. Overall I really love this game and I look forward to the full release more with every update.
First off, I've fallen victim to abandonware and incompetant devs before but this is most definitely not one of those cases. The dev team has a public update schedule that they do their absolute best to stick to and while the updates might have seemed minor lately, it's most likely because of the massive upcoming graphical overhaul that they'll be implementing soon. The game is very much playable in its current state, however. Combat is similar to Mount and Blade, and I really like the skill progression system. The player base is a LOT better than most of the other sandbox survival games I've seen and there are always whitelisted servers if that's a concern.
This game requires people to work together and it seems like a lot of the problems that people are having stem from not finding a good group to play with. I lucked out in that regard and there is no better feeling than having six people all pull together to finally put up that big plaster house. Server choice is also incredibly important; as an example, some servers are still banning mining and tunneling despite the fact that the devs have optimized that aspect so those don't cause the same lag problems anymore. The judgement hour/ guild update has removed a LOT of griefing that was happening before. It's also good for groups since it gives a single hour every day for everyone to sync up and pull together to defend the base or conduct raids of your own.
TL;DR: Don't try to solo this game; especially important for herbalism. Pick a server carefully. Past that, everything is good and only getting better.

Hardly the shambolic mess people pretend it to be, DNF is the result of mixing a more traditional FPS experience with the modern features and trappings of the same genre. This combination was not fruitful and its positive effects mostly tepid, but the game is still polished, free of bugs and mostly very entertaining. Pacing is a serious issue, with the "meat" of the gameplay taking over one hour to properly arrive. Good weapon and enemy variety, multiple interactive objects and minigames, competent vehicle segments and even considerably high challenge on the highest difficulty - There's definitely fun to be extracted from this game, and occasionally you'll even bear witness to brief flashes of genius. Just don't expect anything more than what it is: a solid but uninspired linear shooter, yet not without its own share of cool rollercoaster thrills.

Having played several "free to play" games, this one actually delivers on not needing to pay to win. The in-game currency called "crowns" is obtained through multiple ways from questing to pvp. With premium, gains are doubled but even without a player can amass wealth from sieges and quests in a matter of two or three hours.
City management is simple and straightforward as resources are close at hand and placement of buildings is set by building plots scattered around the landscape. Time and crowns are all that is really needed to construct a powerful castle and the time goes by quickly as you fight to gain crowns.
There are a diverse number of troops to choose from. Recruitment can include the troops of your own race as well as mercenaries when camping in foreign lands and dwarves and beasts from special buildings. Only three playable races are available: elves, orcs, and humans. Hopefully dwarves will be added in the future and possibly dragons (please).
Battles and troop management are split between the world map and specific battlegrounds and are fairly easy to grasp. The only complaint towards troops in battle is their refusal to listen to certain orders. When you send cavalry in to feint an enemy into charging and the cavalry doesn't retreat when you tell them to, your strategy gets ruined and you are forced to en masse charge or risk losing part of your army.
Aside from the troop command issue, the game is both fun and addicting as one could spend hours trying to earn crowns, conquer cities, and improve his/her own. Coupled with the game actually being fair and not requiring real money to be good, I would recommend it to any seeking a fun, free-to-play strategy game.

I'm emerging from the weird trance state that I've been in for the past few days, dozens of hours of leaping and snatching and throwing muddied together in the rains of time. Rain World sucked me in deep. And now, having broken free from its fierce world, I can finally put together my thoughts into something coherent.
... I guess I'll start by saying that yes, the game is tough. Tougher than most. It holds your hand for approximately three minutes, and then throws you bodily into a world full of things that want to eat, drown, or otherwise end you. Controls, at the start, are cumbersome. Slugcat feels slow, uncoordinated. Jumps appear to be impossible. Food outruns you. Your spear hits only the air over a lizard's head and you barely escape sharp-toothed death by quickly climbing a pole.
All of this, I must insist, is part of the learning process. A few cycles in and you will find yourself more reliably making those impossible jumps, and not because slugcat is actually growing stronger, not because you're leveling up, but because you, as the player, are learning how to better play the game. You'll learn tricks you would never have thought possible, clamber your way into parts unknown, figure out a way to make that weird hard-shelled fruit edible.
This is not to put myself above the anger that comes with failure. I came to many a point of frustated table-slapping as I missed the same jump for the third time in a row. Or got nabbed by a lizard that was sitting right outside the exit to a pipe. What I'm trying to say is that the difficulty barrier exists for you to overcome it, to test you. The world wants you to see it, but you just have to stick with it.
I won't tell you to git gud. But I will tell you to keep trying.
Enough of me rephrasing the same thing multiple times. Should you buy Rain World? Hell yes. Full price, even. The game design choices are excellent, the soundtrack is wonderful, and the art is spread gloriously across every screen you scurry through. It's full of beauty and horror, hardship and triumph. It is a nature documentary about the bravest creature still breathing in this savage land, and you are the star.

is a very good game, one of the best I've ever played.
From the art to the music, from the atmosphere to the story, everything is deeply fascinating and touching. The feeling of danger is permanent, and you quickly identify with the little creature you're playing. You don't share its struggles or its needs : you feel them, you live them.
The game is so immersive thanks to its music and its beautiful apocalyptico-industrial environnemen, the creatures and their behaviour are so credible that you quickly cease to be the player and become the cute little slugcat fighting for his survival in this brutal world.
Finding food and shelter, avoiding dangerous lizards, carefuly befriending other sentient animals, all this becomes your main goal. This and, of course, exploring. What is there to see this way ? Is there more food ? Are the creatures less hostile ?
And while crawling or running for your life, trying to progress without being attacked by other predators, you'll surprise yourself by stopping in a safe place to admire the view, you'll stop in a corner and enjoy this wonderful feeling of still being alive and in a place where nothing wants to kill you. Your shelter, small and empty, will become a place where you feel at home, shielded, calm.
- Beautiful art, music, story
- Credible and menacing wildlife trying, just like you, to survive
- Very very very immersive
- Full of interesting and intriguing secrets and lore
- Simple gameplay and nice movements of the creatures (you included)
- The dev team is here and listen, help, update
- You character is incredibly cute, a little speck of softness in a brutal world
- Like I just said, the game is BRUTAL... I mean, it is very very VERY hard (the "Monk" mode makes it a easier but let's be honest, it is still challenging), and you'll need patience and skill (and a bit of luck)
- The story is very mysterious, you'll have to search and guess a lot ; honestly that mystery is part of the charm, but some players who want easy and clear answers may find that part afrustrating
- No co-op for now, meaning you will feel very very very lonely in front of all these lizards, carnivorous plants, huge centipedes, creepy vulturs etc...
: buy it, its price is way below its real value

I really enjoyed Knights of the Old Republic (KotOR), and I also really like this one, too. You might think of it as a Star Wars franchise precursor to Mass Effect with a Baldur's Gate-styled combat system where you can pause during real-time to change weapons, queue up items/weapons and force powers. Unlike Mass Effect, it is a dice-roll system and you can't control the weapons, so the combat isn't quite as gripping but that doesn't downgrade the overall quality of the game. Character development and alignment are a big focus in this game, and so like Mass Effect 2 & 3 you'll find your decisions have consequences for you and your crew. Just like KotOR, this game has a massive amount of story and plot which can be explored in as much depth as you want. If you want to just focus on finishing the main storyline, you can; if you want to go digging up lots of information and do lots of side quests, you can do that, too. This is a great title for any Star Wars or RPG gaming fan to add to their collection. *****

The world is massive and open ended, but you need to find shelter/save points before the days timer runs out. This occasionally left me feeling like I was on rails a little bit. Even though the world was so huge and open, some areas I didn't want to explore because I was so focused on staying alive. It's an odd choice to mix those two gameplay dynamics together, and it can be VERY frustrating, but it definitely has a feeling of magic to it. I wouldn't change it, but some might not be able to stomach it.
Overall I felt like the game was hard, rewarding and a one of a kind experience.

Nether is one of those games where you will rgaequit for 3 days after losing a 20 hour progressive character, nd for a little while, you despise the game. But, i always seem to come back to it because of its replay value in being multiplayer. I wasnt going to compare it to dayz but in a few regards, i must. I loved the open-worldness of dayz and am a fan of it, but one thing that nether has is a more urban, close quarters experiance. Now this is not better or worse i feel than dayz, but it does offer something different. there are still scenarios in which you must watch for snipers across an area of 300 yards for example, but because of the urban environment, you arnt just a sitting duck until he finally hits you. In other words, it gives new players a simple chance. Don't get me wrong, there are a few areas in which an accidental misstep can put 20 killer machine nether and a player on you, but unlike dayz, a new player isnt doomed to being sniped or gunned down by helicopters as is he in other games. Admittedly, i bought the game when the base value was 30 dollars. It has dropped dramatically to 20 dollars, and is currently on christmas sale for a mere 12 dollars. Would i say this game is worth 30? no, 20? maybe, but for 12 dollars, i would buy the game for a few hundred hours of fun. And as Markiplier has once said "about 60% of a horror game is about ambiance" and in his playthrough, he was quivering and terrified the entire time.

This game.....is bad. Compared to the previous Duels incarnation this one decided to remove features rather than add them. When I started out I was pretty glad I could skip the tutorial since I've played Magic for longer than I care to admit. I was pretty perturbed that you only get the deck that you randomly choose based on whatever colors you like.
From there the game is pretty impossible. You start with a limited deck with no synergy, and your opponents have quite a bit of synergy built into their decks. When you start to accumulate cards I must say that I enjoy the amount of customization you are given. Anything and everything that you want to do with the cards you've unlocked, you can. Having such an open deckbuilder is a pretty awesome feature. Unfortunatly, that's about the only positive thing I can say about this game.
My biggest gripe is how the mana is tapped for you. The game, for whatever reason, thinks that when you cast a green spell you want to tap all of your green mana. Okay. Sure. Well, if you have a creature with a green activation cost and another green spell you were planning on casting....sorry. I guess you shoud have been babysitting the left Ctrl button a little closer. The fact that the auto land tapping went from somewhat intuitive with a mis-tap here and there to "Oh, I'm sorry I did that. I guess you should have hovered over your spell and waited. Tee hee!" I have been so frustrated by punting a game away due to the ridiculous way the game decides to tap your mana that I have tried to ragequit on several occasions. Well. Brings me to my next point.
The UI is this game is bad. Really bad. Unspeakably bad. It was clearly designed for a mobile platform and moved over to PC. I can't say how it plays on xbox, but I'm guessing it plays pretty awesome on mobile. The menu icons only repond if you clock a tiny square at the bottom. The menu is a left to right swiping sort of thing, which is great if you are using your finger, and awful if you are using a mouse.
If I could get my money back for this game, I would. I don't under any circumstances reccomend this purchase. Perhaps in the future they fix this, but given WOTC's recent track record with terrible changes (MTGO, DailyMTG) I doubt they will.

The terrible microtransaction system this game has in place ruins what would be a fun game.  Unlike the past duels of the Plansewalkers games, right off the bat at the end of the tutorial (that the game forces you to finish to progress through the campiagn), everyone who already put money into buying the game is on uneven footing.  This is because once you beat the tutorial, you get a single "premium" booster pack.  In order to get a premium booster pack after that, you must purchase them for the small fee of $2.  Well those $2 purchases add up and after youve spent around $30, youll be able to have every card in the premium booster set.  What makes things worse is that the cards in the premium set are all amazing.  The developers purposely put some of the best cards to build decks around into the booster set that you have to purchase after already buying the game!  So in order to fully compete or even to have fun against the other players in multiplayer, you HAVE to spend that extra $30 to get the cards you need since, chances are, youll run into a bunch of people who have already paid the extra $30 or so to beat on people who dont want to pay to unlock mandatory content in a game theyve already purchased.  Maybe in the future theyll fix this issue with the dlc, but until they abolish the premium booster pack model, this game is broken and not worth its $10 price tag plus whatever the dlc will be.
This is the perfect example of a pay to win game model.  Stay away unless you are willing to throw an extra $30 down the drain to be able to have a fair match with other players in multiplayer.  If you really have an itch to plays a duels of the planeswalkers game, go buy the 2012, 2013, or 2014 versions.

WOW. Bohemia has come a LONG way since the Flashpoint days.
Operation Flashpoint was the original that started it all and the move to the Arma series was quite a significant improvement on Bohemia's part. I didn't play Arma very much or very long but I was impressed with what I saw and thought it was a worthy successor to Flashpoint. If I recall the jump from Arma to Arma 2 though was mediocre. I remember there was more of an impressive jump when installing Operation Arrowhead but regardless Arma 2 was a source of countless hours of fun for me in the editor and I loved Arma 2 so much that I gave my physical copy to a friend and bought it all over again on Steam.
I finally got off my butt and installed Arma 3 and like I said above, WOW...impressive.
The main map is gigantic and beautiful but moreover the optimization is incredible. It took years to build a PC strong enough to handle Arma 2 at decent settings and Arma 3 runs even better despite being SO MUCH BETTER IN EVERY POSSIBLE WAY.
We will start with the obvious which is the gorgeous landscape and environmental visuals. The sun glaring through the beautiful trees brought to life with alpha to coverage anti-aliasing is a majestic sight.
The audio, my god the audio! Earlier titles always needed mods to make the game interesting to the ear. This is the exact opposite. The weapon, vehicle and explosion sounds are terrific and as close to perfect as one could be! Even the voice acting, though still not "great" is heavily improved.
The editor, my god the editor! They FINALLY got the editor successfully converted to 3d. Arma 2 had a secret 3d version of the editor but it was experimental and had numerous bugs making it useless to me.
I still haven't put enough time into this to truly explain how cool this all is but I am so blown away so far that I feel like I needed to share these thoughts before I get lost in this amazing game and forget to come back. I still haven't explored the underwater atmosphere or even tested to see how nightvision and lighting look when compared to the previous titles.
I have 2 more things to mention and then I will finally shut up.
1) The controls are 'simplified' but in a good way compared to Arma 2. The previous titles had complicated controls that seemed to get worse with time and the character movement was always sluggish. This has all been remedied! The controls are glorious now and character movement is better than ever before. While still not geared towards close quarter battles, the game simply isn't designed for close quarter battles which are rather rare and unrealistic. (I forgot to mention the animations are vastly improved and coupled with the ragdoll physics the improvements are night and day when compared with the previous titles)
2) There is competitive shooting! There are these awesome shooting courses set up where you run through them timed and shoot at pop up targets. Some are timed to be up a while, some move, some are friendly targets, some are bonus targets. You can switch weapons and treat it like a 3 gun competition but with only 2 guns instead. Incredible feature and highly addictive! As though the campaigns and editor weren't already enough they went and dropped this feature on us.
Fans of previous Arma titles or the original Flashpoint title will seriously respect the evolution that this title brings and I can't recommend it enough.

Finally a real Party Game!
This game is a perfect example of how party games should work! Too many of the party games on steam have such a steep learning curve that they scare my casual gamer friends, or mechanics that make the gap between noobs and veterans unbridgeable. This one however just fits. It has that nintendo couch party feel that I have missed since I gave up on Nintendo consoles (read: saddest day of my virtual life).
To be quite honest it is Mario Party without the frustrating slow (and seemingly rigged ha) board game in between! The mini games and game modes are tons of fun, and the AI is plenty compitent and ends up dominating me at times.
Excitement aside this is still an early access game and there are components that need strengthening. Some of the mini-games are definitely not as strong as others, and some just need tweaks to reach their full potential but for just being released there really is just a ton of content here, and the Developer has been super responsive and is dedicated to doing a whole lot more before the final release of the game. I'm excited to watch the game grow, in the mean time it already made my top 5 couch party games.
If you like couch party games and enjoy the EA part of steam games, I really recommend this one.
TL;DR: Is Mario Party, Super Approacheable game, Tons of content, Room to grow
