text: I think this game is a wonderful example of what a game classed underneath the "Horror" genre should really be. The graphics and the style of this game is top notch. I found myself so in awe in the beauty of the areas I was able to go through. This game sticks in my mind to this very day, and no doubt in future ones, because of it's brilliant and mysterious story. There are hidden plot arcs that you can find out through reading what comes on the screen during loading times, after you go through a safe door. One of these great stories ends up changing on what decisions you make, ****(Possible spoilers into Daniels past)**** for example whether you choose to save some people on your journey or do the "right" thing. These things could determine Daniels past, as you sort of create his character. Though very strictly limited, I found it really touching ****Ending of Spoilers****. As I stated I think this game is an example of what you should be expecting from a Horror game. This is because, especially when you enable developer commentary in the game, the developers I think were very masterful at setting atmosphere and the pacing of the horror. You sort of share the same feelings as the character you play, Daniel, when it comes to that. For example the player needs time to recollect their feelings after going through a very scary event. You make them feel safe, and then you make them slowly go into the next area, making sure the atmosphere is appropriate and when the time is right, go "balls to the walls" and let the monsters roam. Amnesia the Dark Decent is a wonderful game and I really hope I get the opportunity to play more games like this. I really love Daniel's character and everything in this entire game and world! I look forward to seeing the new game coming out from these developers which I think is called "Soma". I recommend this game to anyone really as there is either great scares or beautiful story. This is a 10/10 for me though I am possibly biased for this game, though I think its okay for me to be that way. Take care everyone.

Interesting game... I will explain.
First off I highly recommend you do the tutorial and actually take the time to read the texts. There is never to much written but there is no voice acting. But the tutorial gives you a lot of needed knowledge to get the hang of the game. Also you might want to start as humans first, the other races, elfs and orcs. have confusing build structures.
Now when it comes to explaining this game I would have to say, it is stronghold kingdoms map combined with a sort of Total war style combat / with age of empires sort of peasantry. Read bellow this for a further explanation.
Stronghold Kingdoms - When in the main world map you will see separate borders. Your settlement will be one of several in a sort of county, with several other faction areas in a province type area. A border separates these which makes it easy to know whose who.
Total War - When it comes to units in this game, you do have large formations of units instead of single soldier running about. When you construct a unit 20 come out inside of one. So when you enter war or move your units to investigate a camp, you will have the different archers in their group, soldiers, knights, so on.
Age of Empires - When it comes to building structures in this game it feels like Age of Empires. Granted you wont find yourself having the peasants build the buildings, but instead you select an available spot on the ground to construct a building. Now the peasants are used to gather materials around the town area, Gold, Wood, Stone, and food are all the average resources you need to have them gathering.
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Things to know when you start!
- You have a 24 hr peace period, meaning other players cannot attack you until after 24 hours.
- Your selection of traits and plains where you build will decide a lot of stuff. Such as if wood is plentiful (plains area) , if stone is easily accessible (In mountains) , Also lastly is wooded areas (In Forests).
- Doing the quests at the beginning will advance your story line, get you free resources, and decent experience towards the game as well. They are easy and actually very fun to complete.
- This is a Stronghold Kingdoms style rts. Which means buildings will start building slower and slower the more you construct. If you don't want to put much time in a breathing game you may want to steer clear.
- I have done little castle work, besides in the tutorial. My reflection on it though is like a Total War style castle. You build the wall then garrison the unit squads along the walls. You also build single siege weapons to attack the walls, making it easier to maneuver or attack different sections of the walls.
- I did not access the market as of yet, though I clicked on it once to view it. It did seem a bit pay to win, as you purchase crowns like on stronghold kingdoms. Then you use the crowns to get resources , fast building , though it does not seem to allow unit purchase. You can purchase dragons though... not sure how OP they are.
--------------------------------------------------------------------
My Impressions
- Early stages of the game I am enjoying. It feels like Age of Empires as my units charge around to wreck the wicked soldiers and goblins about. Making gold and other resources depends completely on how many peasants you send to that specific resource.
- The late game makes me nervous, I really cannot tell if the game has the system like Stronghold Kingdoms that sort of punishes higher lvl players for attacking lower , newer players. But I guess that will be something we see in a few days if I just get rolled by some troll.
- So far I do like this game, its worth continuing to play and I hope to see the population on the game grow.

The story moves along quickly enough to keep you interested, allowing you to take missions in the order you prefer, as they become available. A solid game of the golden age that holds up well to the test of time.
However, gameplay aside, there are issues with the Steam port of this game. As many have noted, there are issues whenever trying to fly through a Lagrange jump point. You can pilot your corvette up to the very point of the jump, at which point the whole game crashes. It's very disappointing to be able to get just a taste of this fantastic game, but to be stymied at one of the core game mechanics.
5/10, Steam.

This game is fantastic and while I would normally complain that the game is a bit at odds with itself as to the genre (combining quick-paced closely-timed survival with gorgeous and necessarily slow exploration) the Beta completely removes that obstacle. There are a few issues that ought to be attended to though.
First, with the positive!
- The game is gorgeous with this very vivid and pleasing artstyle both in game and in the cut-scenses and menus.
- The sound design is superb! There are many audio cues that one needs to listen for, the music is very pleasing and everything sounds in just the right way as to be immersive.
- The controls are (mostly) intuitive and very well handled.
- The enemies are interesting and are all puzzles to be solved, none of them feel distinctly unfair.
- The game is (mostly) fair. Many obstacles that are presented to you have subtle ways in which to circumnavigate them.
- There multiple avenues of play.
- I'm sure the multiplayer would be fun if I had anyone to play it with, I'm quite excited for the arena mode.
- The 3 singleplayer modes (not difficulty settings, though they may seem like that) appeal to different ways to play and are quite satisfying.
The negative
- Some of the visuals are misleading, especially in swimming segments. More effort should be taken to clearly distinguish what is and isn't an accessible air bubble for the player. Such visual deception helps no one and it puts artificial difficulty there.
- Swimming controls are abominable. If that's the intention, well done.
- There are secret commands. There is no obvious presentation of different maneuvers (sliding, backflips, or even dropping objects in comparison to tossing them). Even if that was the intent there should be a solitary button just to drop an object instead of automatically throwing it. It is quite annoying.
-While in tunnels (not the automatic ones) everything is awful. The ease of movement is dependent on the orientation of the slugcat, of course, but the fact that it is so hard to see is inexcusable. Artificial difficulty via obscured visuals is below a game of this quality and really ought to be removed.
- The camera not following the slugcat in rooms that are larger than the screen. It happens quite often where the room is quite large and when you cross the edge of the screen and the next screen pops up do you realize that it's a cliff edge and momentum takes you tumbling over, or you get snared by a predatory plant, or some creature snatches you up. Again, artificial difficulty via obscured visuals.

I really enjoyed Knights of the Old Republic (KotOR), and I also really like this one, too. You might think of it as a Star Wars franchise precursor to Mass Effect with a Baldur's Gate-styled combat system where you can pause during real-time to change weapons, queue up items/weapons and force powers. Unlike Mass Effect, it is a dice-roll system and you can't control the weapons, so the combat isn't quite as gripping but that doesn't downgrade the overall quality of the game. Character development and alignment are a big focus in this game, and so like Mass Effect 2 & 3 you'll find your decisions have consequences for you and your crew. Just like KotOR, this game has a massive amount of story and plot which can be explored in as much depth as you want. If you want to just focus on finishing the main storyline, you can; if you want to go digging up lots of information and do lots of side quests, you can do that, too. This is a great title for any Star Wars or RPG gaming fan to add to their collection. *****

EDIT: This review originally was focused on the sole fact that the game was unplayable for the better part of last week due to a Steam / playnether sync error. Below is my updated review based on the game-- which is now playable (you can log in). Steam did not give any refunds for this game so please keep in mind that with potential future log in issues, you will not be able to receive a refund.
Graphics: 9/10 - the graphics in Nether are pretty amazing considering it's a first person MMO. The environment is filled with skyscrapers, subways, deserted cars and debris. When you walk through the devastated city, you really get a good sense of lonliness and the need for survival. The nether are violent creatures that can warp all around you and the animations are done very well. The first-person perspective looks really great when running; changing weapons and using the various different melee weapons on nether. There's really not much better in terms of graphics on an MMO, in my opinion.
Gameplay: 7.5/10 - Moving around the city is pretty fluid. If you've played shooters like call of duty, the controls will certainly feel natural to you. If you're hoping to use an Xbox game controller, as of right now it seems phospor has only half implemented the controls for it. You can shoot, run, and move around using your controller; but access to the map, inventory, and quick-slot items are not available. The movement seems well thoughtout, in that it is pretty simple but effective. You can jump  over obstacles, climb ladders, sprint to outrun nether or bandits, and crouch/prone for the stealthly approach. There is an option when leveling up to increase your jumping height so that you can access higher areas, which I thought was very cool. The melee system is pretty good. You can block and power attack when leveling up the melee skill. Often times you'll find yourself wanting to melee nether, so that you don't have to make much noise -- avoiding other confrontations. The nether themselves can be downright scary! If you're wearing a pair of headphones and walking through one of the cities subways in the dark, you'll know what I mean. I found myself more than once turning around to see a huge Golem Nether charging right for me. The nether aren't perfect, though. They tend to get caught on things when dealing with elevation, like scaffolding. You won't mind too much though, since you can beat the heck out of it without it warping behind you then. There isn't a huge amount of Nether roaming around; maybe a few per block. The real danger, as with any survival MMO is the other survivors. There are multiple Safe Zones, in which you can trade(courier missions from 1 SZ to another), sell, and store some items in a global inventory. When you die, if you can make it back to a safe zone, any items that you put in your global inventory you can have access to. The problem with these safe zones is that they are very easily campable. Make it to a high-level and just pull a nice sniper rifle out of your bank? Step three feet outside a safezone and get stabbed by a level 1 hiding in a bush. But this sort of thing is to be expected in these type of games. Really the only gripe I have with gameplay so far is that the current playable zone is quite small, there isn't a lot of variety in loot, and the game gets pretty old - fast. These are all good complaints, considering this is in fact early access. The adrenaline you can get by finishing courier missions, while fighting off bandits and nether is pretty awesome.
All in all, I still can't recommend this game, yet. Despite the high gameplay & graphics review, this is too early in development for MOST players to really enjoy. I've spent a lot of hours playing alpha & beta games, including DayZ, and this one is certainly well polished, but not as well developed. I think most players would play this for a week and move on, and I'm feeling mostly the same way. With the account sync problem taking a while to get sorted out, it worries me for the future - sync or swim. The good news is that phospor games seems really into asking the community what they want for future updates (motorbikes!?) - so stay tuned.

I recommend this game in particular to people who like experimenting with new approaches to similar challenges or those who are looking for a new kind of platforming experience, something familiar yet new.
Additionally, expect a healthy dose of failure, since this is very much a game about learning and trying different solutions while pressed for time and under duress.
The eye to detail in both graphics and design is impressive, as well.
This game is first and foremost an ecosystem simulator crossed with a platformer.
Everything moves according to its own ability to utilize the physics of the game.
Everything has unique behaviours and opinions, even similar looking foes, and individuals within that genus.
Rushing ahead may lead to an early death or a trap.
Without observing, applying your knowledge and learning/using your own memory,
, as other creatures have memory spans and individual opinions of you.
Cowardice can be more lethal than daring or even passiveness.
Keyboard and controller have their advantages and disadvantages as a control scheme both in this game.
A Keyboard will probably be more consistent for when it comes to climbing and similar movement.
A Controller will probably give you an edge in rougher, more open terrain.
Your results may vary, but this is my experience with the two choices.
Despite the RNG being unfair at times and despite the unreliability of factors like some food spawns, the time per 'day' (or rain cycle, in this case), this game is at worst, a frustrating game that still manages to instill wonder and awe and makes me come back despite some unfairness.
While, at best, it's still a really interesting game that gives you a rush at narrow escapes, a sense of accomplishment even if you don't make concrete progress and, at its core, it has a surprising amount of freedom in a dense package, even down to how you want to complete the game itself. Your journey is yours, your experiences are yours, and the amount of time I've spent on this game just makes it seem better.
It's just a shame it's not for everyone, because it's well made and animated for something that might invoke a retro feel.
Rain World is a deceptively simple game with a surprising amount of depth to it.
The graphics may look 'retro' but it is a very beautiful game and makes good use of the whole "the apocalypse is green" aesthetic. By which I mean that it's not just a lot of grays and browns.
The game rewards exploration and observation in equal measure, but also punishes dawdling and recklessness. I think, going in to this game you ought to be aware of two things: you're going to get stuck somewhere on your first run and restart, if not twice. The game has more replayability than I can give it credit. The way you progress from beginning to end is, in fact, extremely open-ended, and will only be limited by you, the player's, experience and knowledge of the world. How you navigate each area and deal with each obstacle is entirely up to you, there are a few awkward bottlenecks but on the whole, there are a lot of alternate paths and  the amount of exploration required and lore acquired in a playthrough is, at the end of the day, left up to how you decide to progress.
If you follow iggy, your little worm-shaped guide in its clumsy attempts to point you to a task, your playthrough can be both one of the short ones or extremely long ones. A lot of the time, the way forward is hidden enough to be a bit obtuse until you find it, and then it becomes second nature when you pass through the next time.
Enemies will come at you in ambush, camouflage and head on both, some will hear you, some will see you, some will only sense you by your intensity of movement. There's even an enemy type that reacts only to you physically interacting with it (as opposed to walking past) and the game gives you a great many tools to deal with each obstacle. you can even have enemies duke it out between one another.
This game has a lot of freedom, freedom of movement, freedom to explore, and, technically, freedom of choice, in the form of your progression path.
That said, there is going to be a lot of times where you're either stuck or feel like you died an unfair death.
The RNG can screw you over and unless you've amassed enough experience as a player (not as a character), chances are you're going to feel like there is no progress, or no point.
At its shortest, speedrun strats/sequence break notwithstanding, the game may last you 3 hours if RNG is extremely kind and you know what you're doing.
At its longest, even under the same circumstances, it can easily last you fifteen for one run.
This game is beautiful, harsh, well made and deceptive. The controls seem unkind until you have learned them. And while the story, such as it is, is interesting and fairly well precented, I have just as much fun, if not more, just fooling around practicing tricks and messing with critters around the map. The purpose of karma as an arbitrary progress lock can be a bit frustrating but at the same time, it is often the game's way of telling you to slow down and re-evaluate. Those enemies blocking your path? can they be scared? can they be befriended?
There are few games today that relies on the player getting better and better to the degree rain world does without being about pressing a button combination perfectly and memorizing the exact pattern and beat of a thing.
That said, for a game that might seem frustrating, I don't really ever get upset with any of my deaths.

First, the bad:
So far i've only got a few complaints about this game. firstly, the UI really needs work. there are things that i thought were buttons, but werent, and some of the text is so small that it was hard to read (this is coming from a guy who has a 36 inch television set up as my monitor, so you know it's a problem.)
another thing, i have no way of comparing weapons. none of them have useful tooltips. for example, there are two SMG's available to each faction, and all the tooltips basically say is "this is an SMG. it fires little bullets and is small enough to carry as a sidearm." theres no stats displayed, and no way to know which of the two would be better for me unless I use them a bunch and try to get a feel for both of them.
Third complaint: the aircraft controls are a bit awkward, and dogfighting is incredibly difficult, for me at least. the system itself is easy enough to pick up, you pint the mouse where you want to face, and the keyboard controls your felocity in various directions, and as a whole i like it far better than the flight controls in planetside 2 and other games, but i just couldnt seem to get ahold of it. sometimes when i move the mouse, the ship turns slowly, sometimes when i turn the mouse my ship pulls a U-turn so fast that i go crashing back into the hanger and immediately explode. all in all, i just find it very difficult to keep the reticule on an enemy fighter long enough to do any significant damage. part of my problem might have been how choppy the game was, which is my last complaint.
this game needs some optimisation before release. i'm running a airly good rig. it's kinda old but it was the best you could get when i built it a few years ago, and no matter what i do in the settings, the game always seems to have just a little bit of stutter. it might have something to do with the fact that there were 63 AI's running around with me in all of the missions i played, but even in the tutorials it got a little bit choppy.
Other than those four things, though, i'd say this is a pretty great game, and it's exactly the kind of thing that i've been looking for for quite a while now. I personally cant wait to see where the devs go with this, and i'd be happy to go right along with them.

Duke Nukem Forever (DNF) was the follow-up to Duke Nukem 3D from over a decade prior, which means nostalgia and high expectations played a large part in how the game was originally reviewed. As Duke says himself near the beginning of the game “after 12 ♥♥♥♥ing years, it better be (good).” Sadly, the game was thoroughly mediocre and nobody was impressed. Strangely, DNF has a 55 metacritic rating which is rare for a big name game but the Steam player reviews for the game are “mostly positive.” I’d guess that’s because no matter how disappointing the game is, it still isn’t “horrible.”
It’s been so long since I played the old DOS game Duke Nukem 3D (Or Duke Nukem 1 & 2 before that) so I can’t really recap it. Fortunately, you don’t need to have played to older games to get what’s going on in DNF. An alien fleet is looming over the Earth and the US president is confident that peace negotiations are going well. It’s a good chance these are the same aliens from the previous Duke Nukem games so the president is worried that our hero Duke is going to pick a fight and start a war. Naturally, the aliens attack (and start stealing Earth’s hot women) so it’s up to Duke Nukem to kick their asses once again.
Gameplay for Duke Nukem Forever is straightforward first person shooter with no real innovations, except a few places in the game where you get shrunk down to the size of a Barbie doll and need to navigate terrain puzzles while avoiding the huge (normal size) aliens. The puzzles in the game are not too difficult to figure out, which is a good thing because DNF doesn’t have a “hint” system (where you hit a button and it shows you where you’re supposed to go next). Usually the door you’re supposed to go through has an orange flash, but it is still possible in a few places not to know what to do next (like one level in particular involving a crane wrecking ball).
When I first played through the game about a year ago, one of the gripes I had was the limited weapon inventory. For a first person shooter there’s actually an adequate variety of guns to choose from, both human and alien (pistol, shotgun, machinegun, rocket launcher, etc.) The problem was that you could only carry 2 weapons at a time like in Halo 1.  When you run out of ammo, you can drop the gun you’re holding and pick one up from a fallen enemy. This would have been fine except that one of the game’s Steam achievements requires you to carry the pistol for the entire game, leaving you with 1 other weapon. I believe the developers patched it though, so now you can carry 4 weapons at any given time. The game’s health system is the now standard regenerating life system except that instead of being called health, it’s called ego. You can raise your maximum ego by doing various environmental things like looking a porno magazines or lifting weights that you find lying around on various levels. Most of your ego boosts will probably come from killing bosses though.
Pros:
+Fights with giant alien bosses are always a plus in my book. Unfortunately, only a couple of these fights involve outside the box thinking. For example the giant alien queen requires pipe bombs and dodging alien impregnators. Most boss fights just require spamming rockets and circle strafing. All bosses can only be hurt by turrets and explosive weapons.
+Decent variety in enemies and environments. The game’s graphics aren’t bad when it comes to the grotesque alien enemies that you’re facing. You get an up close look at a few of the melee enemies. I wasn’t a big fan of the alien hive level because of the weird night vision system that the game uses (Duke Vision) but at least  it changes things up a bit. The underwater level was kind of fun where you need to swim from air supply to air supply.
Cons:
-Outdated humor. The game makers tried to keep the feel of the old Duke Nukem games by having Duke constantly spit out one liners and other macho stuff. The problem is that he seems to say something every time you kill an enemy so some of the quotes keep repeating over and over (“Wonder how many pork chops I can make out of you” after killing a pig alien which is one of the most common enemies in the game). Since you’re killing aliens every few seconds a ton of the quotes are heard about a hundred times by the end of the game. Have you seen the Expendables movies with Sylvester Stallone and Arnold Schwarzenegger? You know how all the old washed up action heroes keep using quotes from their successful movies? The DNF humor feels kind of like that.
-The game just doesn’t stand out in any way. If this wasn’t supposed to be the glorious return of Duke Nukem, the game wouldn’t have been such a disappointment. People would have just said, “meh nothing special about the game. Play it and forget it.” But of course the fans seem to feel like the 12 years since the previous game should have been spent perfecting Duke Nukem Forever.
A friend was using the Steam family sharing thing to play DNF off of my account and I asked why of all the available games he would be playing a game so mediocre. He said it was because he hadn’t tried it but had played the previous Duke Nukem games. I guess it’s like the Aliens vs. Predator movie franchise. Everyone seems to think the movies suck, but I like Aliens and I like Predators, so might as well see the movie once. Make sure that you don’t pay too much for the game though (less than $5). As for the game’s DLC “The Doctor Who Cloned Me,” the DLC is actually pretty long (about 5 hours I think) and doesn’t really add much new to the experience. I think there’re only a couple new weapons, but there are a few new bosses to fight.

A Fantasy free to play non pay to win fairly slow-paced RTS game with PvE and PvP elements, with an ever growing community
If that sounds interesting to you then this is the game for you
My first time playing this game I had mixed feelings. Low res graphics, buyable units, premium accounts and Purchasable city plots. All of it was too Pay-to-Winesque for me. But after having spent quite some hours into the Game by talking and bonding with the Community I very rapidly discovered how wrong my assumptions were. Buyable units are easily stomped on by non-buyable units. Premium is merely a small bonus. While it may not be Pay To Win on the gameplay part it does have a few knacks of its own, for example: ''Starting another city'' with another race and settings requires a payment of 4.99$ or by deleting your current City. This feature is very stupid as it limits you to only 1 race which limits the player from sinking more time into the game without sinking money into the game. A very positive change would be if they gave you 2 slots instead of 1, maybe when they release the Undead race they will give everyone a 2nd slot. HINT HINT
Updates are pumped in weekly so expect bugs/glitches that you might encounter to be fixed soon
Next to bug and glitches fixes new content is added to. Such as skins, units, buildings maybe even a whole new race.
On a side note, this game is still pretty unstable, on a daily basis people come in and complain about how they crashed during big battles or that certain things aren't working. One of the Major malfunctions in this game is the fact that Online gameplay isn't fully server hosted causing bugs with Resource gathering from time to time, but that is simply because they don't have the financial support to make everything more server dependent. Which is where you come in.
Gameplay itself is very solid. While the Army management is pretty flonky because of bugs with manual Army mapping and you can only select 18 Units at once, it is still fun and massive, there are some performance issues with big armies moving around and large fights (FPS drops and sometimes Crashes) it is still very fun, competitive and enjoyable. A few issues here and there make the competitive part of this game ALOT less... competitive, such as Battle protection pausing when going offline. But it is still carried forward by the massive rewards PvPing and PvEing give, especially late game.
The best part of it, when you start PvP you can't be put up against opponents with a larger or smaller army then yours, making it completely skill reliant.
Pros
-Solid game
-Solid experience
-Lots of dialogue
-Wide open-world with lots of provided Lore
-Updates are sinked in on a weekly basis
-Lots of playability
-Fun and growing community
-Lots of content
-Beautiful design
Cons:
-Bad AI
-Inconsistent unit collission
-Workers not always doing what they are told to until you manually send them
-Extremely buggy
-Not enough is server hosted
-An extreme amount of dialogue (This could be a Pro depends on how you look at it)
-Extremely low res (Ruins the design part by quite alot)
-Some Pay to Win elements that do need to be removed
-Pretty hard learning curve for newcomers
-Unit management is not that good (HD patch would help xP)
This may look very negative but as a whole the Pros outmatch the Cons by far, since the Developers of this game are working very hard to take charge and improve this game as a whole. While some issues may not be fixed in a few weeks, months or even Years it still is a solid experience and a must play for Hardcore RTS players that want to enjoy both sides of an MMORTS, the Town management and PvP without PvP taking the cake like in most MMORTS games.

So, here's the thing... It's Duke Nukem. You can't expect it to seem good to you if you're expecting something serious.
While I wasn't a fan of the Duke Nukem games before, because I was born a bit too late and I missed the "Golden Era of DOS Games", I became a fan now. I had finished the game once before, when it just hit the market, but I wasn't very impressed, mostly because of the reason mentioned earlier.
However, the game grew on me, and I decided to buy it for myself and finish it on the hardest difficulty - which I'm currently working on.
I always choose to play 3D shooters on the hardest difficulty because the harsh challenge makes the game extremely fun, and the more difficult it is to finish the game, the more rewarding the feeling you get when you finally manage to do it. Besides, even when played on "Come Get Some", the game seemed pretty easy to me, most of the time. The real challenge comes when you're able to play it on Insane. A piece of advice: arm yourself with a very good weapon besides the rocket launcher or the devastator when you're going to fight the Octaking. It is by far the most difficult boss battle in the entire game.
So, why didn't I like the game when I first played it? Well, like I said, it had to do with the overall immature style of it, but I wasn't aware it was supposed to be immature. If that was also your first impression, give it another chance and play it on a hard difficulty. Trust me, you'll love it! Played like that it's an old school shooter at its finest.
Oh, and by the way, I think the shrink ray is actually trying to make another reference - like many others you will find during your playthrough, and it's intentionally made to look like something right out of Portal. It's Duke Nukem humour... I guess you have to be a fan to understand it. :)
Being a fan of old school 3D shooters, I'd give it a 10/10.

The requires a realization that teamwork is key. Don't expect to launch the game and do everything by yourself like you can in other survival games. As soon as I bought this game, my first impressions were rather poor. I was saying "Clunky UI" and "Horrible skill progression" Although it might seem like that at first sight, I realized it was actually very intuitive. The UI is allowed to be placed freely and wherever you like. It's wonderful in fact!
There is a lot of grinding to per se "unlock" options to craft/expand on what you are leaning for. For example, want to be a blacksmith? First you need to prospect and figure out where some ore is. Keep doing that until you reach the 30 mark on Prospecting and now you unlock mining. Depending on the server, grinding can be fast or slow.
This is where working together with fellow people is essential. As for I, we play on the RP Clif Server which raises the cap just a little over the default skills progression cap. This forces joint operation such as someone being a blacksmith, farmer, contruction builder, herbalist (Which is the most grinding of all the skills as well as animal lore which is under farming), carpentry, ect.
Many people find this off putting but this is exactly what I look for a survival/building medieval game. The social bonds and interaction on this game is like no other. In your average surival game like Ark or Rust you will most likely be killed on sight and get a few laughs out of little things. In LiF: YO however, you forge your own destinies and bonds with each other. It's epic!
Thank you for this game and I can't wait until it is fully complete.

Some mining can cause server lag/freezes annoyances

Hello, Rhoken7 here.
I wanted to try and explore the game a little more before i tried to write a review for this game. I feel that it is a very well thought out game, I enjoy it. The battles are pretty epic in most points. The original sounding names of the places, the lore, the size of the game itself, and how you get to build your city the way you want, for the most part. I did the tutorial but i felt it lacking. I dont know if i missed a advanced stage or what, but some things you find out later in the game that you wish you knew at first. For instance, i wish i knew that my population cap didnt go over 90. I wouldn't have wasted my time trying to get it even higher and spend my earned recourses that i got in game on expanding building plots. the only positive out of doing so gives oyu the ability to increase your storage capacity. But i was a little let off when it told me that i could build more houses but when i got back to the game my population cap did not increase. Also i have knoticed that the PvP notifier is a little lacking as well. I dont spend all my time playing the game, once I finish what i can at that very moment. I may send an army out to a mission and i will go check something like youtube or Facebook. Which brings me to another point. Sometimes it can be very slow going. Which has caused some friends of mine to not give it a chance after one day. The times it takes to build, travel, or even gather enough recourses can take you days. (days of real time, not in game time). But back to PvP. There has been times I alt tab out of the game. or even while in game, im told there is someone at the gates for a fight, and nothing happens after that, the game will automatically "pay off" the person coming to my little town. I would much rather take my chances at fighting the person instead of the game automatically paying them off. Last thing i would like to point out is the graphics of the little characters running around. It can be horrid at times to see a horse that has no eyes. Just saying. The landscape graphics and buildings graphics are good for this game, I jus tthink the NPC's and other Characters in the game need a little bit of sprucing up. Other than those points i find this game to be very fun. I plan on playing it for a long time and would recommend it to anyone who likes something like Clash of Clans, C&C, or even Star Craft. It takes elements from a game like Clash of Clans where you build buildings and train units, upgrade those buildings, and go fight people. It takes a RTS point of view during battles and out of battle as well through out the game like Starcraft and C&C. If you like being a Commander of some sort of army and like to make a pretty cool little kingdom as well. this game is for you. Because of the bad character graphics, long wait times, and un-locatable PvP indicator at times, i give it a 7 out of 10. its a good game, just needs a little work.

All in all this is probably the best mideval strategy game I have ever played.

OK, first, and most importantly, do not buy this game if you are not willing to wait for it to become a proper game. It's still very much Early Access. It's mostly a vehicle sandbox to show off the amazing crash physics. Do buy this game if you are keen to support the developers, and can see the potential this game holds.
Now to the game itself. The menu is confusing. The game runs very poorly. It looks beautiful. The car crashes are second to none. The soft Body physics are the best you will ever see outside of an actual Goverment ran crash simulation laboratory. They really are that good. Amazing. The driving physics are a little weird though. I drive IRL, and the only vehicle I ever drove that started bouncing when pushed to hard in a corner was a Go-Kart. Most cars just understeer, the others oversteer. In this game, all cars start to boiunce sideways in quite an ungainly fashion, and once oversteer has started, it can quickly degenerate in to a harsh pendulum motion. On the plus side, the game has great mod support, from the community and the developers, which is fantastic, as some developers 'look down their nose' at modding, even though it's keeping their game alive (I'm looking at you Oovee). Anyway, there is still quitre a lot to play with as of right now, and updates are pretty frequent, and so is communication from the developer. By comparison, Bugbear who make Next Car game haven't blogged in neasrly 2 months, and the last one was to tell us they were having a great time in Finland.
All in, buy this game if you have patience. Do not buy it if yuou want a lot of driving game right now. Recommended.

Developer Obsidian Entertainment was born of former PC RPG giant Black Isle Studios’ closure, and with the name Chris Avellone affixed as lead designer/writer there was an expectation that we’d be seeing something transcending the low standard of video games—even if they were stuck using flippin’ Star Wars (of all things: Really?) as a starting point.
What Obsidian’s crew ended up doing was to look at Star Wars, at all Lucas and BioWare and every EU author had accomplished to manipulate the monomythic structure in the creation of something palatable and brilliantly addictive, and just…wrench a knife somewhere in them there guts and twist, twist until everything that gives the Star Wars appeal is torn apart. Piece by piece, the Sith Lords subtly begins feeding you each and every tired expectation, and, as they come, what you feel is this growing sense of relief, this subconscious drive to be satiated on your own literary comfort food—but: There’s always that moment—and you come to expect that too, come to rely on it as the antithesis to your prior highs—there’s always that moment the game asks Why? Of this path so often repeated, what accomplishments do you imagine?
A beggar family, torn apart both financially and physically by war, asks for your help--a paltry sacrifice on your part to ensure their safety; maybe, just maybe, nearby stands a man asking for the same outcome, but in place of your own personal sacrifice he offers great monetary gain. It’s either-or, here, and the tendency of players will be towards “good” over “evil," so the sacrifice is made, the family hobbles off pitifully to presumed safety and bright futures. You yourself positively reflect on the morality bonuses given for another day saved--and the game stops you dead in your tracks, voicing—almost exclusively through your mentor Kreia—its frustrations with the ignorance inherent in your actions.
No matter your in-game answer for Why?, the result is always the same; your choice, perceived as the moral high ground, was nothing but a wasteful performance of ignorant folly. Drawing parallels of your actions to vampirism, your acts of kindness, of Jedi charity, do nothing but steal what power the helpless may hold for your own use (i.e., the experience points gained by your choice, an idea reflected in Star Wars lore itself without any game-y statistics). No matter how buried motives are under the guise of self-sacrifice, helping the needy only serves to weaken them, altering their perceptions on universal modality and, in some cases, making them targets to others more desperate and lethally-driven towards the same goal.
By following the ‘goodness’ of the Jedi code—a lie fabricated for self-preservation and personal profit—it's suggested you just led an entire family to their death.
This deconstructive direction outside the realm of predictable comfort is what makes the Sith Lords such a massive improvement over BioWare’s excellent predecessor, and, really, the story is just too dang good for Star Wars; its goals far too high and self-aware, but also something the Star Wars brand has desperately needed for a long time.
Yet, while the writing of the Sith Lords is far stronger than its prequel, I rate both titles the same, and may, personally, even view the first as a better game. Achievements aside, the Sith Lords is riddled with bugs, moments of atrocious pacing issues and literally a quarter of the game unfinished. Many of these issues have been repaired by dedicated fans over the years since release, but that’s still not enough: The long intro segment and Nar Shadaa still feature pacing issues that stem from more than a rushed development cycle, but simply clumsy planning and writing.
Kreia’s continued domination over the players’ own emotional turmoils are what champion this game ahead of so many others, her words forever scarring views of Star Wars as fluffy entertainment. Amidst the wealth of coding error that would come to define Obsidian’s games, it’s that writing--that twisting of archetypal norms and the assumption of a moral compass built from her presence that make this journey so darn good. In the rush to finish this game under a holiday development schedule, she’s written out as Darth Traya, but despite the new name’s implications, despite the donning of black robes, she's never convincing as a villain. (It’s hard to buy her shadow mask when she’s always right, even if she is pushy and demanding. Her role as a mentor is far more believable.)
It’s long before she makes her name in betrayal that she raises the avatar and herself from the dead. Five years have passed since Revan redeemed herself and saved the galaxy (the pawn of a Star Wars cliche repeated almost by the decade), and the next galaxy-wide threat is already in full effect. It’s unfortunate that not many seem to know it. This behind-the-scenes orchestration of tragedy is defined by absence in TSL: The concentration of power so great, so abnormal even by Star Wars standards that it threatens itself strictly by persisting, every moment needed to devour the essence of this life that connects every living being. Sith Lords Sion and Nihilus, Kreia’s guiding hand, the avatar herself—exiled by choice from the Jedi Order for her own acceptance of rational, necessary darkness—are all representative of the ultimate consequence of the power sought by good and evil in Star Wars lore, each in their own way black holes eating away at what seems, on the surface, like a coherent system guided by a familiar mythos born long before ’77.
The rest of the supporting cast lends a helping hand in reinvent the Star Wars universe, too, with the best among them following the same route the game’s overall quest system takes. The first to join your cause is--of course--a clone of Han Solo even down to the predilection for familiar catch phrases, but as the story progresses his character is turned inside out, his snarky personality made merely a coping mechanism for his horrific past. Another is a twist on the now-stereotyped wookie: A psychopath tortured by his own culture, he adheres under a broken sense of honor to life debts--you know, that cultural norm handed down from his homeworld that would bind him to anyone who saves (or spares) his life--that also drives his psychopathy. He’ll fight alongside those owed such a debt, but not without the constant reminder that his only wish before dying is to gleefully dismember them.
It’s this team of equally-lost souls the avatar and Kreia influence and guide on their mission to remove the devouring endgame. Since the conclusion of BioWare’s epic, Revan’s vanished and the Jedi Council lie in ruins. Barely a handful of members still live, and that persisting, devouring force quietly ravaging the galaxy has them in hiding. It’s the Exile’s job to pull these hiding Jedi out of their inherent selfishness either by hunting them down or banding them together to Save the World.
Fantastic characterization and dialogue aside, story progression doesn’t bring the same joy or discovery BioWare gave players, due possibly to overcomplication or ridiculous ambition beyond TSL's budget. The series has since become an MMO, and the characters’ fates removed from the postmodern, deconstructive tone of TSL back into comfortable, anticlimactic Star Wars fare.

This is only time when I had high expectations for a game and having those expectations exeeded.
At first it felt harsh and unfriendly (now devs have nerfed difficulty curve a bit to adress that), I could barely go anywhere without being torn to shreds by pesky lizards. But I kept pushing forward and little by little I got better. Where RPG's make you feel like you are becoming more powerfull through unlocking more high level abilities and increasing stats for your virtual avatar, this game gives you the same feeling through your own skill as a player upgrading. Slugcat is weak and fragile and there are no ways in game to upgrade it into a stronger creature. The only way for it to survive is to be smart and agile and for it to become that you'll have to observe, experiment and learn. It feels like game is constantly stacking all odds against you leaving you with only cubic centimeter of chance, and when you learn to use that cubic centimeter it's the greatest feeling ever.
Another thing - AI is bananas in this game. It really feels like living breathing world full of creatures trying to survive, killing and eating eachother.
Also worth mentioning - the visuals and music are delightfull.
This kind of game is not for everyone, obviously, but it's at least worth to give it a fair try. And I higly recomend this game to anyone who finds joy in beating seemingly impossible odds.

BeamNG.Drive is a rather interesting concept. It uses an advanced physics engine alongside .jbeam skeletons to simulate realistic damage in a collision, which is the main selling point of this application. (I'm not exactly going to call this a game yet, it's still mostly a game engine/simulation)
TL:DR: Has lots of content and modding support, advanced physics, and constant updates, but can be slow and buggy.
PROS:
+Realistic damage, suspension, aerodynamics, traction, etc.
+Multiple vehicles, all with different customization options (which do greatly affect the vehicle's performance and handling)
+many large, open maps, with varying terrain types
+Full modding capability
+Development is quickly progressing, bugs are getting fixed and content is getting added at least once a month, the game is continually evolving with each update
+Built-in terrain/level editor
+Plenty of different debug modes
+Lets you see the .jbeam skeleton in-game
+Slow-mo for the more dramatic collisions
+Support on the forums is very helpful for resolving issues
+Ibishu Pigeon
Cons:
-Very CPU-intensive, can run very slowly on older/slower systems (If you have problems with this, check the forums)
-Can be somewhat complex for someone new
-Lots of bugs (Many are removed each update, though)
-Just like GRID, it's very, VERY difficult to drive at speed without crashing on a keyboard

Nether has a lot things going for it.  Great atmosphere both in the sounds and visuals.  You're always scared and constantly scanning for either monsters or, far more dangerous, other players.  You never have enough supplies, be it food, ammo, or just a decent weapon and that lack always keeps the edge on.  The first half hour of play was for me some of the most enjoyable i've ever had.
There are cons though.  Once the initial wonder of a new game world and its mechanincs wear off what the game boils down to it searching.  90% of what your doing is looking for glowing items on the ground.  Food becomes critical as the games veiw of realilism is that every character is a hypoglycemic diabetic who dies if he doesn't eat a full meal ever half hour. The monsters beomce something to avoid rather than engage because they drop nothing useful.  The XP you get from them isn't a good trade off for the ammo your spending.  The PVP is tense, visceral and immidiate but again, simply becomes tedious as if both player have guns, the one to see other first wins.  Almost zero cooperation exists because no one can trust anyone.  I'm not an exception to that.  When i was starving i shotgunned 4 different players to death hoping one would drop food.  (Game needs a cannabilism option because i would totally eat people.)
However this game is not feature complete and with the ground work they have i expect this to become something truly great.  If your on the fence then wait for actual launch to make up your mind.  I'm liking the game as it stands but short of some major content increases it's probably not worth your money.

(TLDR? This review is also available in video format for your convenience below.)
Magic the Gathering; Duels of the Planewalkers has become a yearly franchise, and with the recent success of Blizzard's Hearthstone, they've attempted to step up their game with Magic 2015 by allowing players the much-desired ability to finally create their own decks.
After a brief tutorial, you're able to pick a starting deck and begin the campaign. From there, you're able to unlock booster packs as you defeat opponents, allowing further customization of your decks. If you don't feel like endlessly-grinding the single player, you're also able to purchase additional cards via micro-transactions and collecting every card will run you about $50. If you factor in the initial cost of the game, Magic 2015 will run you about the same price as a full-price triple AAA title.
There are nearly 300 unique cards to choose from or close to 1000 if you include duplicates, allowing for a multitude of options when it comes to crafting your deck. You're also able to adjust the amount of land in your deck for the first time, which is recommended as leaving it up to the game to do this automatically isn't ideal. Often assigning lands with no rhyme or reasoning behind it, such as giving you mountains in a blue deck. Infact the AI in general is greatly diminished in this installment as it will often tap the wrong lands by default if you're not careful enough to use the toggle key. Such as tapping all of your swamps for colorless mana instead of any other lands you may have available.
The campaign features a bit of a narrative where one of the Planeswalkers; Garruk Wildspeaker has gone rogue and has been hunting down other Planeswalkers.  It's your job to track him down and stop him. The campaign's story is nothing extraordinary and chances are you've purchased the game to play with friends.
The Multiplayer allows for you to use your crafted deck against your friends as well as other players online. Unfortunately, it's been stripped down from previous games of the series, featuring a lot less gametypes. Two-Headed Giant, Archenemy and Sealed Deck have all been removed, with the only option being a 1 on 1 duel or free for all. The user interface is also completely unintuitive as there's no lobby for multiplayer matches. Once a game is concluded, you're forced to exit to the main menu where you'll have to jump through a few separate menus in order to change your currently equipped deck or to host another game. Also a search function would be a welcomed addition for the deck builder, as it can sometimes be a little tedious searching for the cards you want.
This isn't the only area of the game that is lacking content as the single player challenge mode has been removed as well. There are also a lot of cards that are only available in the single player campaign and inaccessible when it comes to crafting your deck. One could say this is a result of balancing issues, but the game has definitely been designed from the ground up to cater towards micro-transactions. I wouldn't mind spending money for constant DLC card packs and additions if the game was self-contained like Hearthstone but the fact that it's simply a yearly release that will only be supported for a limited time, makes it feel somewhat pointless.
Magic 2015 also has quite a few bugs and glitches. I found that I was unable to change my resolution to 1920 x 1080 without going in and manually editing the config file in wordpad. I've also experienced quite a few freezes in the multiplayer where the timer will disappear, forcing us to leave the game. Not only that, but it does randomly crash to the desktop as well.
Ultimately, Magic 2015 is one step forward and two steps back, it's enjoyable if you're a fan of Magic the Gathering. The deck creation tool is a much welcomed addition, however micro-transactions, an unintuitive interface, bugs, and a lack of features in general holds it back. While the initial game provides a great base to build on, chances are the DLC will be aimed at making as much money as possible from the consumer before repeating the same formula with Magic 2016.
This review is also available in video format:
Pros:
+ Deck creation tool finally allows you to craft your own decks.
+ More customization options, such as being able to adjust the amount of land in your deck.
Cons:
- Challenge & Multiplayer modes removed when compared to previous entries.
- Lots of bugs
- Unintuitive Interface
- Lackluster Campaign
- Microtransactions

Ok. This review is going to be a little long, so here's an overview:
I have some issues with AFF. But, it is in early access, and the pros mostly outweigh the cons, so recommended review. This game has major potential (more on that later) and it seems like it's in active development, so good job devs! Even considering - if you like what you see here, maybe follow or wishlist the game to see if it goes on sale. If you aren't convinced, go look it up on youtube and look at some gameplay.
Alright, on to the meat of the review. Here are some of my recommendations to help kick this game out of "cool" and into "LEGENDARY."
1: I put this at the top because it is the thing I want most out of this game: GROUND TO SPACE COMBAT. The tools are there, devs! Battlefront III was going to do it, BF Elite Squadron did do it (on a PSP!), Space Engineers has done it - YOU CAN DO IT!
2: Remove the arbitrary limit on the number of classes. It's kind of dumb.
3: STREAMLINE AND CLARIFY THE LEVELING PROCESS. I have a hard time figuring out what upgrades I've gotten to my loadout limits.
4: Make the starcraft less floaty. The space combat is something I want to view as a privilege, not a chore.
5: Make clearer the things that earn you command and support XP.
6: Make clearer what I have to do to get a vehicle on my next deployment.
Ok, pros and cons list, as is standard.
PROS:
+ Tight combat with intense, largescale firefights
+ Incredibly awesome, unique, and diverse weapons
+ Cool vehicles
+ Lots of class and vehicle customization, allowing for fine-tuned specialization
+ Fun boarding mechanic
+ Great team play
CONS:
- I have often lost track of friendlies and enemies during firefights
- Vehicles are "par for the course": Jeep with gun, APC with bigger gun, Tank, Gunship (which I have never flown)
- Needs to be streamlined
- AI is dumb
- Games are generally biased (long game timers throw games for the attackers, short timers for the defenders)
TL;DR This game has great potential, but requires streamlining. Good Night.

is a Sci-fi FPS with the look of games like Unreal Tournament and Halo, and is based on the Unreal 3 Engine.  The game itself is a series of matches you can customize to your liking vs. AI, or play multiplayer.  I don't really enjoy multiplayer games all that much, so I can't really comment on that aspect of this particular game.
Here's what I think so far:
I like the style of the world, and for some reason the sci-fi art never gets old for me, and I enjoy the blending with FPS genre.  I am a bit biased on that, since the more realistic ones are usually boring to me.
Neat vehicles and aircraft, again, very customizable, and the ability to change spots inside them.  Moving around on the big ships too and getting in various large gun seats is pretty cool too.
There is a ton of customizable options you can save out for future loadouts, which is a really nice feature.  The ability to add more to your player and vehicles overall loadout opens up as you gain more experience as well.
There is a good bit to do on this game as far as goals and sub-objectives.  I like the diversity it offers here.
The AI options are nice.  You can move sliders around in the options to find the right balance for whatever type of combat and game you are looking to get out of it.
I would really like more of a campaign or story mode.  It feels a bit lacking, and I don't really enjoy multi-player on most games.
I don't like how many buttons are used for various things.  It seems quite inefficient, and it's a bit of a pain for me, and I would enjoy a simpler layout, or buttons being able to do more than one thing depending on what you are doing in the game.
The tutorial mode was a little confusing, and I found myself having trouble clearly understanding some things that were briefly mentioned.  A lot of buttons were not mentioned at all that can be used in-game as well.
While basic movement was supported by the controller I'm using, I could not keep consistent buttons mapped for the controller.  There just aren't enough buttons either for various functions I would need.
I can't return to the game once I alt+tab out of the game or change any screens without it freezing up on me so far.  This is a little frustrating.
I would prefer unlockable vehicles, or more weapons available as I gain more experience.  This feels rewarding, so I would prefer that system to just getting more space to carry or add to my vehicles.
For early access I am enjoying what I have played so far.  The sheer customization is pretty daunting for me, since I have not put a whole lot of hours into it yet.  I would imagine getting nice setups and gaining more options by gaining combat experience will really open this one up!
While I wish there was a campaign mode, it's still fun playing against the AI, and tweaking it to ones liking.  I have had a hard time with this so far, but I am still just starting out.  I feel like there is quite a learning curve here, and it's not something I could just start playing with guns blazing.
The ships have interesting physics, and it was not so easy for me to steer these well.  There are two modes, one with more stopping ability, and another for speed and better movement.
The mix is really great between the combat, capturing objectives, controlling of vehicles, and overall high energy FPS style gameplay.  I like the mix going here so far, and I look forward to trying more, and probably updating my review as it goes along.
I didn't use the commands for squadmates very much really, and when I did, I didn't notice a drastic difference overall.  Possibly more investigation is warranted to find out the depth of what it offers at this point in time.  I know on some other games it has been vital, but I did not really get that on this one yet, so far.
This game is well put together for early access, and I have found only positive things to say about it.  I'm not a huge FPS fan, like many seem to be, but when it has the sci-fi elements, I really like to see what sorts of variety it offers, especially when there is the space blended in too.  The graphics are very nicely done as well.
If you are into FPS genre, especially geared towards space or sci-fi, and you are not looking for a story or single player campaign type mode, then I would definitely give this a try.  I am very amused by what it has thrown at me so far, and I look forward to finding out more!  The customization is another boon for anyone into that sort of thing.  I'm sure there are a number of possible combinations with loadout menus, especially as you gain more clout by undertaking the various scenerios offered, or playing multiplayer.  It has some light strategic elements to it, but I would say at the core, it's mainly just a great action-packed FPS.

So, before I begin my review let me just say that I'm a huge fan of Magic the Gathering. Been playing it for a few years and I've played prior Magic the Gathering titles: 2012, 2013, 2014. With that said, let me delve into my review of the game.
THE EXPERIENCE
From the beginning you have the option to play through the entire tutorial or skip to the final battle (a nice option for those familiar with the game). I skipped to the final battle and was poised with choosing a deck to play with; I ended up rolling with black/blue since I love being mean and figured it would get me through the campaign fairly easy with the lifesteal/control combo I was thinking up in my head. I beat the the final stage in the tutorial and that was when my fate was sealed. I had no way of changing decks, and I had to win my way through with the deck I chose. I was stuck on the first Plane and first opponent for quite awhile; once I got past that though I was on a winning streak and unlocking more and more cards. Several hours later, I've completed the campaign and have unlocked a good amount of cards to deck build with, as well as improve my original deck. After completing the campaign there are still several cards to unlock through random booster packs that you win as you defeat opponents, and each Plane has a "Explore" level that pits you against a psuedo-random opponent to test your mettle and wit. Although it was a rocky start, I'm really hooked now.
THINGS I LIKE
1. Unlocking cards through boosters, and being able to have complete control over deckbuilding: choosing the number of lands you want (dual/basic) and how many colors you want to run in your deck, choosing your own spells to create your own synergies, and the amount of cards available (running a WUB lifegain/control deck like I originally wanted thanks to the cards available)
2. Replayability is high for me personally. I haven't finished everything that I can possibly finish in this game yet. Also, being as OCD as I am I'll probably want to unlock 4 of every card thats available just to maximize my deck building options and build that perfect deck.
THINGS I DISLIKE
1. In game purchases - I just never liked them to begin with, and I think it's a terrible idea. If anything, maybe they could have added a thing where you earn points when you win matches, and you can use those points to buy boosters or something like that. Besides, using real money to unlock cards kind of takes away from unlocking them the good ol' fashioned way.
2. Unlocking decks - being stuck with a single deck in the very beginning can be brutal depending on which one you choose, they should have let you switch between a couple at first like they did in the previous iterations of the game. My suggestion with that is to look up the deck lists online (which I think someone already mentioned in the comments) before you decide which one you want to use.
I enjoyed my time with it, and I recommend it. It's not so bad once you get a little further in the game.
P.S. make sure you manage your lands manually with the Left CTRL button, otherwise it's going to use lands in a truly terrible and unefficient way.

I played a lot of the early Battlefield and Call of Duty games but I found both series quickly became stale and repetitive bringing nothing new to table and using the same game mechanics over and over to farm money. I tried a few other FPS's after those but they all felt like they were trying too hard to be similar to the big name titles so I gave up trying new ones...until Angels Fall First.
AFF is the game I've been looking for.
The game starts with a tutorial which guides you through the main different elements of the game. It teaches you about command (whilst playing, the commander can set objectives, if you follow these you are rewarded with command XP points), weapons use and vehicle types (ground and air). You can revisit the tutorial anytime if you missed anything like I did. Once you've learnt these you're ready to start playing.
Once you've picked your server you'll be dropped in the deployment room where you can check and change your load-outs, view stats and a few other things then 'ready up' once you're ready to go (you can still do all these things once ready). Once both teams are ready or the deployment timer reaches zero the game begins.
There are two types of maps, space maps and ground maps and the play style of each is different. Ground maps are gun and ground vehicles and involve no flying at all. There will be various objectives to defend and capture whilst taking out the enemy team with your highly customizable loadout.
Space maps are more air vehicle oriented and involve a lot of flying but also some on-ship ground work such as defending your main base ship when it's under attack and has been breached, repairing the weapon systems when they've been taken offline and assaulting the enemy base once you've breached theirs. All the maps I've played so far are massive.
The space combat is fantastic though and I think that's what mostly keeps me playing. You can choose from various ships (scimitar bomber for me 90% of the time) and customize your loadout before flying out and engaging in combat. At first I struggled a little with the controls but they are fairly easy to pick up once you actually start playing.
The game already features a lot of customization from your weapons, ammo (fire, acid and more) and armour to the vehicles you drive or pilot and the weapons in them. There are plans for more maps, more weapons and more customization so that's a huge thing to look forward to.
Angels Fall First focuses heavily on teamwork which I LOVE. It doesn't focus that much on your kills and deaths, but more on three categories: Commander, Support and Combat. You level up each individual element which is a lot better than the usual KDR/MVP in my opinion.
AFF also has beautiful graphics, I had a friend comment on them whilst I was playing and I have to agree. I'm not saying the graphics are the best thing I've ever seen, but they are pretty great for a fairly unknown FPS.
Now onto the cons. My biggest problem with the game so far is the lack of players. The game currently only has a handful of players on at a time which means there is a little less of the teamwork element BUT the community I've encountered so far were all friendly and helpful. Also having bots fill out the servers helps as the AI is pretty impressive. Whilst playing a lot of the time I can't tell who is a bot and who is a real player. Hopefully when the word gets out there will be an influx of players because it really is a game worth playing. But don't expect full servers now. Another little gripe was some of the objects I ran into or jumped onto were in-fact not solid, causing me to plummet to my death. As I said though, this is really minor as it was aesthetic objects and not walls or floors.
Badly Optimized.

This is an outstanding game; easily the best one of the series.  It has a strong card pool, it's a lot more balanced than previous versions, and it allows full deck building.  Playing your own deck vs. someone else's unique deck online really can't be beat.  There are other games that try - namely Hearthstone and Might and Magic: Duels of Champions.  Both of those are decent games, but they lack the overall depth, strategy and quality of Magic by a large margin.
There are a lot of negative reviews (generally from people with very little actual play time) - and they mostly fall into two categories:
1. people who are upset Wizards removed two-headed giant from the game modes.  If you primarily play DOTP for two-headed giant, this is not the game for you.  It is, however, the best 1v1 game there is.
2. people who are upset at the premium content, and who label it 'pay to win'.  Basically, there was day one DLC, and it was very expensive (28 dollars for all of it).  However - this content is not necessary - it enables a greater number of deck archetypes, but doesn't actually imbalance the format - at least not by much.  The base game card pool is quite strong.
There are other negatives to the game - the user interface is not as good as prior versions, and there's a difficult battle at the end of the tutorial that's difficult to beat for some players so they are frustrated (hint: pick a deck with white or red in it and you'll be fine).
But on the whole, the game is outstanding.  I've already built 10 distinct decks from the card pool, and I feel like I've barely scratched the surface.  It is the most fun I've had with any Magic game ever.
I do not recommend.

Hi guys, Hellbound Commander here.  I think i've possibly found the best medieval strategy game that is Free to play, maybe even in general.  I was searching in the f2p tab on team and i came across this game.  I got interested and I downloaded it.  It was worth it.  Kingdom Wars is the best game i've played in a long time!  The level of depth to the game is almost unparalleled in anything I have seen.  There are so many features that I really can't fit into this review, so I want to ask you guys to download this game and start playing it so that you csn get a feel of what i mean.  The graphics are amazing, the battles and wars going on all around you add so much content to your experience that there is really no way to get bored of it.  You have the campaigns and the quests and everything that are sitting right there to become available to you as you build up your castle and venture out into the world of Mythador.
There are so many features, one of which is what the devs cleverly labeled the "Home Warfare" law which was passed by King Erian IV (I play as a human lord).  It offers you the chance to attack your neighbors and also other players to gain more resources, get some battle experience under your belt, or just simply entertain yourself.  To protect new players however, as on many other games your castle/town is not attackable by other players until you've spent 24 hours of real time on the game.  I've still got almost 18 hours left on mine.  It closely resembles the Stronghold crusader series because of its real-time combat and detail to the units, structures and features.  As you progress in the game you eventually become more attuned to your surroundings.
It is important to start with a strong workforce and a small army, as well as a desire to do the quests you are assigned.   That usually opens up doors to more quests, campaigns, and other features of the game.  There is a special currency in the game, called Crowns, which are used to buy some elite units, make castle siege defenses, upgrade buildings, etc.  You can buy these crowns with the in-game money called Coins, which are obtainable through Gold Mines, battles and quests.  You can also get coins by bringing a group or two of peasants along with you and tasking them for 'Corpse Looting'.  This enables them to loot corpses, whether they be your's or your enemy's, for materials and Coins.  Other ways to get Crowns are to do quests and win battles, for each you receive a specified number of crowns.  Crowns are essential in your ability to progress through the game as a successful player.
This game, unlike most 'F2P' games out there is not a pay-to-win game.  The success of players isn't determined by how large their wallet is, but rather how much patience and perseverance they have.  If you Persevere you can eventually rise to the top and become one of the strongest players throughout Mythador.  I bid you all farewell future lords and ladies, and I wish you good fortune should you choose to join me and many others on Kingdom Wars.

Imagine star wars, now remove the Jedi Powers, add in Marines, and what you'll be left with is Angels Fall first, a fun game which looks like a lot of different things, but ultimately stands alone as it's own unique, addictive and fun game.  Looking at Angels Fall First you'll be reminded of Battlefield, you'll be reminded of Titanfall, (maybe even be reminded of Call of Duty, but shhh...  we don't really mention call of duty on the internet, it was after all the cause of the great flame war of 2006).
Angels fall first is your typical story, of Marines vs other Marines, in outer space, using all manners of weapons and vehicles.  The possibilities are endless when it comes to weapons.. You want a shotgun with a high powered scope.. have at it. You want ammo that burns enemies to a crisp...  no problem.. you want to spit acid from your sniper rifle directly into the faces of your enemies and watch them melt into a primordial pool of fizzling slime?  Yeah well me too, not so much the slime, but the acid is a sure thing, and the enemies being dead.... ALL the way..  Weapons aren't the only way to fit, you also have vehicles, both land and air.
Obviously the game is huge on pvp, but that portion of the game is rather lacking on players at the moment..  Don't fret you can still play single player with bots... I know, the word single player and bots has been synonymous with horrid AI, and games that cease being fun almost immediately after picking them up.  I still remember playing COD Black Ops on Nuke Town, highest difficult setting, and watching the Carnage play out hiding in a corner killing bots left and right..  The AI in this game is actually pretty decent, I'd say it's right up there with some of the best AI I've seen period..  The game has 5 difficulty settings or AI level slider.  *hint*, you may find yourself pulling out hair on level 4...  on level 5 you might as well crawl up inside the fetal position and start sucking your thumb..
Numerous other slider options exist as well, most of them are rather basic though, how many teammates, how many AI per team, etc etc etc..    The game has a fairly large selection of maps, which from what I've seen during my playing time, large and well built.  A few points exist which would be beneficial to your team to control, and will probably be the hub of fighting.  Although it's certainly not necessary to lock yourself down in a corner to spray and prey, but rather hold down these points with your teammates.
So would I personally recommend this game?  The answer is yes I would, while the multiplayer or PVP portion of the game is rather empty at the moment, once the word gets out on how well put together and fun Angels fall first is, I predict that population will increase quite significantly.  Also being in early access has probably been a slight detriment to the player base, I'd look for a spike in population once the game leaves Early Access..  Even if the pvp never picks up, the bots are probably better than the average player you'd run into anyway.  Picking up the game now will surely help with development and lock you in as an early adapter, but no shame exist in waiting if you feel skittish with the game being in Early Access, just remember to add it to your wishlist because you'll want to give this one a try for sure..
