What happens if Battlefield 2142, Section 8 Prejudice and Starwars Battlefront 2 have kinky threesom? Angels Fall First
In short:
If you liked any of the prementioned games, you will like this one. A good subjective number /10, would join hot ship on ship action again.
In long:
THE GOOD
Everything you want in space combat is there. Bombing, dog fights, boarding/repelling action and huge ships pounding away at each other.
Well rounded ground combat, from tanks duking it out on open planes to CQC in a city.
Customisation, customisation everywhere. This game rewards those who experiment with loadouts, you dont even have to shoot people to win with the right builds. And all the stuff is available to you right from the start.
10 maps that all play differently with the 2 game types so far.
Friendly community, who will offer advice and guidance if you ask nicely. You will need to, at this point  the tutorial isnt all that helpful.
Intuative Friend or Foe marker system. Exactly what you would expect in the future. Easy to see effective engagement ranges, clear indication of where the actions at and what your objective is.
Colour blind options. You can edit the UI colouring to your preference.
Good command system that rewards players for following orders, but not restrictively so.
Rewards team play more than mindless killing. And the AI is good at being a team with you.
THE BAD
The space ships have induvidual speed limits. Why cant there be a good space combat game with realistic physics involved?
Almost too much information is thrown at you in play, you will quickly get used to and take advantage of this but it can be overwelming to start with.
If the AI is the commander, you can be ordered to defend a drop pod at the back of the map where nothing is going on. You dont have to follow the order but still.
If you are looking for PvP, look else where until full release. The devs have been treating EA exactly as it really is, a paid beta where you get the full game in the end. This means not many people know of this games existance as all efforts have been on development and not marketing. This is actually a good thing in my books.
THE UGLY
These are the things that are problems now but should be solved before full release.
The UI needs work, both in providing more contextual information and layout (the devs have said they are working on this)
Balancing issues. To be honnest this game is well balanced for the most part, just some tweeking here and there like a certan railgun cannon needing a nerf.
Minor bugs. This is EA so bugs are to be expected, however i haven't come across anything game breaking yet. The worse ive seen was the last member of the enemy team being a bot, in a tank stuck on a rock in the corner of the map. Took 10 minutes to find and kill it.
THE WIERD
A lot of players love to play as the AIA and at the start of the match text shout on chat things like "FOR THE EMPEROR!"... i think there are some 40k nerds here.

One of my favorite RPGs and probably the best story I've experienced in the Star Wars universe aside from maybe Empire Strikes Back.
This story gives you a completely fresh set of characters (aside from HK-47 from the first game but his return is most welcome) and a fresh story that isn't simply copying wholesale from the movies. The game challenges the broad themes we see in other Star Wars stories while still absolutely feeling like its a part of that setting.
I don't have a lot to say about the game play. Obsidian did the best they could with what they were given. I like the way you can unlock abilities for yourself and others in your crew through repeated interactions. If you've played any old school rpgs, the gameplay should be adequate, being based on d20 rules. You at least get some choice for how you level but you always have the option to autolevel if you don't want to fool around with it. You're really here for the story anyway.
And I have to tip my hat to the makers of The Restored Content Mod which, as other reviewers note, is absolutely essential. Google it, download it. I'm on my third playthrough coming back to this game after some months and the Restored Content Mod has been updated to version 1.8.3 in the interim. With this version of the mod, the experience is very minimal on bugs. The only crashes I've had could be attributed to other improperly installed content mods. Aside from this, I recommend googling to find the widescreen solution for this game. It takes a little work sadly to get this game to support modern monitor resolutions (if your monitor is 4 by 3 aspect ratio, you should be fine but if you're using a 16 by 9 or 16 by 10 and you don't want your characters to look bloated, google the widescreen fix and then the minimap fix for the widescreen fix.) So yeah, some up front work to be done but this game is 10 bucks and IMO, even with the extra work, its going to be the best ten bucks you'll spend on an rpg outside of Fallout New Vegas.

Slightly more than a hundred hours later... time to write a review. Two thumbs up!
The game is still early access at this time, but very playable--it's the best of the five survival building games that I bought on Steam. There are very pretty places to see in the game--prettier than any of the other games I have--but also deserts and volcanoes for variety. This game rarely lags, and when it does, it is 'fixable' by logging out of your current world and logging back in.
No early-access game is bug-free--but this game has good bugs as well as bad ones. Even in survival mode, some items are currently free to build--like the TNT! Other bugs aren't so much fun, so avoid the worst of them with this list of three things not to do:
Don't quit the game if you have magically-created creatures following you. They'll quit playing as well, but don't won't return.
Don't drop things by right-clicking on things in your inventory. Sometimes I've dropped one sword and found two on the ground, and sometimes dropped items disappear (especially storage crystals). Put useless things in chests instead. Never try to drop armor! It disappeared the one time I managed to do it.
Don't expect magically-created critters (Awakenlings?) to follow you though transporters if they will land on blocks or slabs. They'll show up on natural dirt or stones only--sometimes much later!
This game has a creative mode that I've barely touched, so there's plenty more gameplay left!
I really only have one question... the animals and creatures I create cast shadows when the sun sets... but my avatar does not. Perhaps it's because I've died so many times in this game, but it's still spooky!

Huge fans of micro-transactions and console parity afficionados aside, you've been duly warned.

First thoughts...
It's a pretty cool game so far! It needs a tutorial, but you can figure things out fairly easily.  It's still in Early Access (EA), but it is one of the better EA games I have played!  It isn't nearly finished, but it is already fun to play!
The world that was generated for my first experience is beautifully rendered is high quality graphics.  I set the anti-aliasing from 1x to 2x (your only two choices) and it slowed the game down a bit.  It wasn't that much better, as the graphics already looked awesome!
Sound is good without any pops or glitches.  There was a storm brewing and it sounded awesome!  Creature sounds were great and scary at times.  I was being persued by a beastie and thankfully I found a building to hide in! I let my pet do the fighting while I ran away! lol  He died, but he showed up later when I was building stuff, so I guess he respawned?
It looks like a good deal of work has been put into this game already and it has some really great working ideas!  It still needs work, but it is playable and I never felt I couldn't advance in the game due to an unfinished part.  The map generated for me is HUGE!  It will take some time exploring this map! You can enter you own seeds for map generation.
There are beasties to fight, if you can figure out how to build a weapon! lol  I'm not that far into the game yet. If you die you just respawn, so it's not that punishing.  You'll build things like windmills and lightning rods to capture and harvest resources.  It's pretty cool!
As I said, there are some really great ideas here and many of them are already working and playable.  KUDOS to the dev's as this is looking to be an awesome game!  Please don't stop developement on this game as it could be one of the GREAT games here on Steam!!!  It's already fun and interesting! :-)

What happens if Battlefield 2142, Section 8 Prejudice and Starwars Battlefront 2 have kinky threesom? Angels Fall First
In short:
If you liked any of the prementioned games, you will like this one. A good subjective number /10, would join hot ship on ship action again.
In long:
THE GOOD
Everything you want in space combat is there. Bombing, dog fights, boarding/repelling action and huge ships pounding away at each other.
Well rounded ground combat, from tanks duking it out on open planes to CQC in a city.
Customisation, customisation everywhere. This game rewards those who experiment with loadouts, you dont even have to shoot people to win with the right builds. And all the stuff is available to you right from the start.
10 maps that all play differently with the 2 game types so far.
Friendly community, who will offer advice and guidance if you ask nicely. You will need to, at this point  the tutorial isnt all that helpful.
Intuative Friend or Foe marker system. Exactly what you would expect in the future. Easy to see effective engagement ranges, clear indication of where the actions at and what your objective is.
Colour blind options. You can edit the UI colouring to your preference.
Good command system that rewards players for following orders, but not restrictively so.
Rewards team play more than mindless killing. And the AI is good at being a team with you.
THE BAD
The space ships have induvidual speed limits. Why cant there be a good space combat game with realistic physics involved?
Almost too much information is thrown at you in play, you will quickly get used to and take advantage of this but it can be overwelming to start with.
If the AI is the commander, you can be ordered to defend a drop pod at the back of the map where nothing is going on. You dont have to follow the order but still.
If you are looking for PvP, look else where until full release. The devs have been treating EA exactly as it really is, a paid beta where you get the full game in the end. This means not many people know of this games existance as all efforts have been on development and not marketing. This is actually a good thing in my books.
THE UGLY
These are the things that are problems now but should be solved before full release.
The UI needs work, both in providing more contextual information and layout (the devs have said they are working on this)
Balancing issues. To be honnest this game is well balanced for the most part, just some tweeking here and there like a certan railgun cannon needing a nerf.
Minor bugs. This is EA so bugs are to be expected, however i haven't come across anything game breaking yet. The worse ive seen was the last member of the enemy team being a bot, in a tank stuck on a rock in the corner of the map. Took 10 minutes to find and kill it.
THE WIERD
A lot of players love to play as the AIA and at the start of the match text shout on chat things like "FOR THE EMPEROR!"... i think there are some 40k nerds here.
Not exactly as awesome as in the intro movie on the sales page.

- Is this game fun?

Its one of those games were you throw it on for abit, do some stuff then switch it off to come back tomorrow to           more troops, resources, etc. Constant quests will be given so you'll be busy unless you have to siege, which later on you will be doing a lot.  Battles can scale from a small skrimish to full on siege with a wide selection of troops, monsters, war machines, heros, dragons , etc.  Though choosing your battles is the most important because you can be quickly overwhelmed and overrunned.
- Is this bad?
- In some areas, yes. Combat is very clunky and fights are one big bloody orgy at most.(Blood for the Blood god!!) That and most units if left unchecked will run around chasing god knows what and probably die. Mostly peasants which you'll be lossing left and right when exploring or fighting. No real tatics in open battles or quests. Just send your army in one direction and loot the dead  as they go.(This isn't Total War guys). It comes down to who has more numbers though the more veterans you have the better for you or it can worst because a high level unit of knights can 3 v 1 and win. Seiges you have to plan or you will loss your army fast and retreating is, at times more costly. So once you start theres no going back. - No. Its there but IT CAN be avoided completely. Daily rewards can help in some areas depending on what you get. Plus quests often give you tons of loot, crowns, food, troops, etc. The store is there but name one MMO out there that doesn't have a store. Plus if you do want to sink some money into this game it's really cheap. The most expensive thing is about $30 bucks.  Which isn't bad for what you get out of it.
- Should I try this?
- If you like Fantesy games and city management games, try this. And for ♥♥♥♥ sake this game is free so you're not spending a cent on it. If you liked Stronghold(The orginal, not the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ ones) and would like more city management then this a game for you.

Now the question is, do you want this game? Do you enjoy a massive experience put together by a small team? Does the Early Acess tag blow your opinion away? Do you enjoy supporting Early Acess games(EA's so to say) that actually deserve recognition? I will try to help you understand most of this as this game is anything short of a "good" game.
TL;Dr? If you want a good itch scratcher for the games of 2016 to come , get this! When I saw the Devs of Stangely Interactive shelling out an ACTUAL(not saying that their previous ones were bad. Most EA games have horrible updates) update I cried. Space Battles With Flyable Capital Ships, Ground Combat, Customization on a deep level.
The Gameplay
You fight as either a soldier for The United League or Empire. There is technically no story except for the little bits given to us during briefings, but from what I can tell play Ixion and Ixion teriitories first. The gunplay implements recoil, overheating and gun stances. The game implements a psuedo rts system if you are the commander on the battlefield and a nice squad system. The gameplay runs smoothly, for the exception of the intrusive UI(oh god we will get to that) In space battles you can fly a fighter or comandeer a capital ship, inside each ship is a whole new map. Its pretty cool.
Graphics
Think about last gen, but now think about team that has pulled every single love juice out of last gen. The enviroments are stunning if fighting in space, while ground textures could use some work(in my opinion) its look pretty nice. Now do not expect Battlefron or Call of 12 year Old graphics. I want you to remember that this is made by a small dev team that has poured their time and soul into this.
Multiplayer
So I do not really spend time in mp but when I do, me and my friend enjoy it. Regardless of master elite players or bots. Its the gameplay that matters, not crapping on some twelve year old. The community is small and the devs know that, but just remember, you can always swittch sides. Servers are ok but remember what I said before? You can play completelely offline with up to 64 bots/players. Sapce battles and ground battles can both be played in mp.
The UI
The devs are working on it, they really are. Its just kinda garbage, but thats becasue the game does have a semi complex loadout evaluation.
Suggested updates
Better tutorials
Something in the vein of Battlefront II's galactic conquest
A UI focused patch only
An infantry patch only
A space battles patch only

Disclaimer: I really shouldn't have to write this, but it should be obvious from the beginning: This is my
experience with this game. It is not necessarily representative of what the game is like, and your mileage my vary. However, if you're reading this review, then you're interested in my opinion, and this is what it is.
The game is a highly ambitious work in progress that needs a bit more reworking in order to be truly successful. I have no doubt that this game will be successful on its launch, though it needs  just a few tweaks for some longevity.
I had previously outlined three major issues with the game that stopped me from giving it a positive review. As of the current patch on the beta branch, I can proudly say that all have been addressed.
With a wide variety of ships, starfighters, infantry weapons, and vehicles, the game is well on its way and is a worthy Early Access investment. With all that being said, it's time for me to get critical of the game.
As far as infantry fighting goes, the camera works just fine. If, however, you're on the ground and driving a fast-moving buggy over hilly terrain, the camera will constantly wobble in order to keep the vehicle upright. If you roll the vehicle, the camera will attempt to go underground.
Aiming with the camera becomes more difficult in space. The ship will always attempt to turn to where your cursor is, but your ship turns slower than your cursor moves. This means that insofar as gun dogfights in space goes, it's nearly impossible to get a kill on a target as either it or you are turning. Capital ships are much slower and thus have this problem less, but due to their size, the weapon can fire out of alignment. This has been temporarily resolved in game by having a marker indicate where your ship is actively aiming, but it's not intuitive.
Nowhere is this issue more apparent than when you're piloting either the Velius or the Gheist mechs. Because their weapons are arm-mounted, you can attempt to fire at a target that is directly in front of you and have the shots land in the dirt metres in front of the target because of the aiming system. To be fair, however, the devs have stated that
.
Experienced players have no problem going and doing what needs to be done. However, new players are going to be oftentimes stuck wondering what is going on. This was an issue from previous builds, and the issue persists now. There aren't any voiceovers or big arrows telling you what to do and how to do it. Each game does have a commander, but the default AI commander is not very intelligent and will often tell you to defend an objective while on the attacking team (which is fine if you have other humans attacking the objectives, but not when you're alone).
The addition of voiceovers will help the game in this regard, but the best way to know what to do is to read guides, ask the game's Discord channel, or have a mentor help you out.
Of course, AFF can be the most top notch game in the world, but like any multiplayer game, it's only as good as its community is.
My experiences with the community have not been positive so far. While it would be unfair to compare the AFF community to a larger one such as Call of Duty or Planetside due to size alone, the community I have encountered have mostly seen fit to stack the teams in their favour.
I had previously estimated that the community would rally around a negative review and downvote it into the ground to keep new blood from finding the game and thus keep their own egos going.
I am willing to admit that portions of that review were influenced by my own frustrations from the aforementioned issues compounded with the actions of a few.
Toxicity happens all over the internet, and I have no doubt that it has made its way into AFF already. It's unfortunate that in order to get past such toxicity, you sometimes have to be abrupt, to the point, and "salty". I gave StrangelyInteractive too little credit in this regard previously, and for that they have my apologies.
Does AFF have its bad eggs? Definitely. Every game does. With the game being in early access, however, it is very easy for those bad eggs to become extremely apparent, especially given how very few people actually play the game on multiplayer. Organized community-made matches are set up on the Discord server, and people wanting some community action should definitely join it to find a group. Without Discord, it'll be a very, very long time before you'll find a populated server.
$20 is a very cheap game, and I have wasted far more money for far less quality games. As far as early access goes, this is well on its way and is a fun game to play. It's highly varied, and if you're looking for a first person space war, then Angels Fall First has you covered for a good price.

I'm propably going to get roasted for what I have to say on this one, but I'm willing to change and edit my review as the game matures and as I myself try it out more. These are my initial expressions though:
This game has ALOT going for it, almost too much to be believable. Massive battles with almost everything you can think of:Mechs, squadrons, fighters, bombers, Capital Ships, tanks, ground units, the list goes on and on: customizable gear and weapons and all in completely realtime environment. At one moment you're on the bridge of a capital ship that's carrying weapons, soldiers, fighters, bombers, heavy assault weapons etc, at the helm of the ship, actually piloting it, the next minute you can choose to stroll down to antiaircraft weapon unit and shoot some incoming hostiles or then take off from bay on a fighter and join space combat and so on, in realtime. basically you can choose whatever to do in this game, even just stand around and just spectate the battle going.
But, where is the soul of the game? To me it feels lifeless and boring, even with tonnes of activity on screen. It's got so much going for it, and yet it feels lifeless. It does not feel uber cool to play it, though the content in this game should make you go WOOOOOO!!! I can't put my finger on it but it does not feel enjoyable for some weird reason, for me at least. Something is missing but I don't know what it is. All is there that should make this one of the most badass games ever.. But the feel is not there. Maybe it is too huge of a project to try cram in everything that's uber cool in an effort to make a game to dream for and somehow the feel of gameplay got lost somewhere in translation..
I have to say I have not played this that much, but just for the reason it does not feel all that great. There's no lure making you want to dive back in. There's none of that 'can't wait to get home so I can play that game' feeling.
Anyway as I said that all is subject to change and I'll happily edit this if it does. Also it just could be I'm a moron and other ppl really like the gameplay.

This game has problems, yes. There's no denying that. I mean, the humor of Duke Nukem was that we always knew he was a complete tool, but here, we're supposed to think he's actually a righteous dude. That makes his treatment of women, his terrible one-liners and everything else feel less like satire and more like, you know, things that are okay and cool. Certainly, that's one of the biggest cruxes here.
But as for everything else? I've never understood, and likely never will, the hatred the rest of this game gets. The level design is remarkably creative, and the core gameplay is visceral and satisfying. And while, perhaps, the graphics are a bit dated, good graphics don't make a good game. Ah, yes, and the sound design is actually pretty good as well. The guns sound great, the music is 90's cool, and Jon St. John delivers as Duke... as always.
So, yes, as a guy who considers myself a feminist, a lot of the humor is kind of screwed-up in a way that doesn't feel ironic, and that's definitely a knock against it in my book. But it doesn't make me hate the rest of the game. On a sale, if you can overlook some issues, this is a fine way to spend 8-10 hours, and I'd recommend it to anyone looking for a fun, brainless shooter.

Kingdom wars is an Innovative kingdom builder.  I like the economic system, the more peasants you have working the fields, the more resources you get.  There are also upgrades for said peasants to make them more efficient, as well as upgrades for your military.  I like the fact that you don't need real cash to make crowns, which you get by completing missions, reaching accomplishment milestones or trading for gold in the game.  Trading is probably the fastest way to make gold in game, as you can create an army with a few horse carts and peasants to carry goods to market, plus add farm animals to the army to sell those in different cities.
Creating an army is easy enough, just need to go to the world map.  You pick the units you want in it, military, peasants, animals and send it on it's way.  The combat leaves a bit to be desired, I think the AI needs a bit of work, as I leave my force sttationary, send a unit of archers up to snipe at the enemy.  As soon as the enemy starts moving toward my army, I run them back and wait for the slaughter, as the enemy only sends in a few units without archer support.  After their melee units are dispatched, rinse and repeat on their archer units, who blindly follow into oblivion.  Send in the peasants to clean up the corpses and you get a nice bit of loot.  I also like the wide variety of units allowed in the game, the fact that you don't need to worry about using real money to buy the better units, as they cost resources and crowns and are available to everyone.
I haven't gotten to build up my castle yet, as I have been concentration on my economic upgrades, but from what I've seen, it really looks worth building a castle as soon as you can afford the crowns, stone and/or wood for it.  I haven't tried siege warfare yet either, so I really have no knowledge of it other than the turtorial I played.
Overall, I find the game a lot of fun, it's a kingdom builder that really allows you to build a kingdom.  You have diplomacy to ally yourself with npc's or other players, forming guilds/clans.  It is an awesome experience.

Shadow Warrior 2 is a follow up to a reboot from 2013, however for those who were familiar with the first game of the reboot series Shadow Warrior 2 may turn out to be something quite different than they expected.
Entire game went into diablo 3-esque design direction where entirety of the game is oriented towards cooperation although it's still possible to play from start to the very end alone. Death in classic FPS definition is no more, once you die, you seamlessly teleport to nearest checkpoint without any loading screens and only penalty is loss of cash and the fact that all enemies that you didn't manage to finish off will have their health restored.
Additionally, main "meta" focus of the game is the loot which although being generously given by the game is mostly meaningless (aside from 70 or 71 weapons you can collect). Collectibles are split onto few groups:
-Upgrades
-Lore pickups
-Chinese fortune cookies
And classic FPS pickups like ammo/health/etc.
For many the upgrade collectibles are going to be main issue with the game as they somewhat represent "RPG-ification" gone not quite the way it should be. You will get
in upgrades, upgrades for weapons, upgrades for player, upgrades for skills, upgrades for coop. After 20+ hours i've managed to collect over 500 upgrade gems, 95% of which are of minimal difference as the main functionality of the upgrade gems are mostly percentage improvements (which by default are very marginal). Only upgrades that most of the players will find viable would be ones that actually modify weapon behavior (dual wielding, turret mode, explosive ammo  and such). Rest of the loot is either a living hell for most of the players or as close to paradise you can get if you happen to be someone who enjoys min-maxing your stats by manually sifting through 1000+ upgrades you may have collected in order to find that one gem that gives you 0.001% to a stat you care about.
Another aspect of bringing the game closer to RPG border is it's gameplay design, unlike first entry in the (rebooted) series, SW2 is mostly non-linear, basing it's gameplay on a hub world and characters that will send you both to main story and side missions (and much like most RPG games, you can return to hub at any time during the mission).
Main reasoning behind calling certain missions "side missions" is the fact that you are not obliged by the game to finish them, however by their very design you'd be a fool to ignore them (at least during first playthrough) as they offer both equipment and skillpoints that you're going to need during later stages of the game (especially on higher difficulties or when playing in coop). With that said, side missions are few notches above classic MMO/RPG "fetch" quests, at the very least they provide an animated and voiced dialogue with character telling you what to do and why you need to do that, but beyond that core of 99% of those missions is either "bring something back" or "kill something".
Main story missions offer more variety (and of course more lore for those who care), however due to free-roam and non-linear nature of the game, it's very easy for the player to feel disconnected from main story as he puts giant time gaps between doing each of the story missions, making him less invested into main story. By the time you get bored enough doing everything else than main story, you might already forget what happened in the main storyline up to the point where you decided to pick it up again (of course it all depends on player and the issue is remedied to a degree by existence of in-game encyclopedia that can bring you up to speed to a certain degree).
As far as the levels go, "procedurally" generated is a great marketing euphemism, all levels are hand-made however they're split into bigger or smaller parts that get randomized each time you load in the level - if you've played Left 4 Dead 2 you already understand core of this system. As of the date of writing this review, amount of levels in the game isn't astonishing,
each and every one of them both looks and plays great. I guess, depending on each one's individual attention span it may be possible to get bored with handful of levels being repeated over and over again, though personally i don't think i'm going to have any issues with it until i've put at least more than a 100 hours into the game. Additionally future DLC's might also bring more levels to the table.
The FPS mechanics are mostly top-notch, movement is smooth and so is shooting. There's a variety of enemies and even within each type it's possible to find a "superior" or "elite" version. The only "real" issue (and possibly the biggest one) regarding gameplay are balancing issues. As i've mentioned earlier the blending of FPS and RPG didn't exactly go perfect in case of Shadow Warrior 2 which is very apparent on higher difficulties and in coop mode. It's very easy to run into enemies that are bullet sponges. If you expect to be able to completely ignore RPG elements of the game and survive entirely thanks to your FPS skills, you're going to be sorely mistaken. As the game goes on, you will need to keep on micromanaging your skills and stats, squeezing out every possible percentage in order to stay afloat.
Difficulty is split into two parts: First one is base difficulty (easy/medium/hard/insane) and player multiplier (always 1 for SP and from 2 to 4 in MP). As you go up both scales (difficulty and player multiplier) enemies turn into incredible bullet sponges (unless you have extremely well micromanaged character, and in case of coop session you have a team of people like that). Which results in fights being more time consuming rather than more challenging.
-Looks great (Not groundbreaking but it looks great and runs at high framerates)
-Plays great (FPS mechanics are mostly top notch)
-Wang is back (Classic SJW triggering jokes)
-Full, start to end Coop (for those who miss the old times)
-Lots and i mean LOTS of unique (non copy-pasta) guns
-Free roaming for those who want to quickly drop in, bash some skulls and drop out
-Main story is very short and not very engaging (but then again everyone liked DOOM and nobody played it for the story)
-Design shift from linear story-driven to free-roam/coop based gameplay
-Character models (mostly human ones) really stick out visually from the rest of the game
-Really poor balance at the release (though again, this is a subject to change)
-Lots of loot that's mostly meaningless
Overall, i'd give this game a solid 8/10, possibly 9/10 if all of the major issues get sorted out. With possible content drops (more maps, quest and enemies) it'd easily be a 10/10 and if developers ever decide to give us mod tools i'd say it's 11/10 must Wang.

Put 18 hours into the open beta, and I definitely don't regret my purchase, 9 hours into the full game. The singleplayer, while not having the most gripping story, is fairly well written with good voice acting. The game has few balance issues, but, most complaints about balance can get chalked up to "get good". If you want a deep fighting game with a unique combat system, gorgeous visuals, and you can handle a loss or 2, I can't recommend For Honor enough.
EDIT: After more hours in the game, I feel like I should touch on something I didn't. The matchmaking, and connection errors. The connection errors can be ridiculous, as games can just be a flip of a coin whether you'd finish it or get booted for no reason other than "Ubisoft". There are also many times where you are queued with players with levels in the single digit, while facing off against teams of multiple-prestiged players. Ubisoft really needs to fix these issues if the game's going to be around longterm, which it should, since the game mechanics are stellar. Despite these connection issues, and matchmaking issues, I still recommend the game, since when it works, boy it works.

That's actually the inherent problem with this game - you see, unlike the previous entries, it now offers complete customization of your decks, which is a "step up" but with the pitifully limited library of cards and limited number of copies of the more powerful cards, you soon realize that, sure you can make your deck however you want, but in the end it's not really how you actually want.
DotP 2014 sent you in with a prebuilt deck with coherent themes and strategies - DotP 2015 sends you in with a janky pile of commons and uncommons that ultimately aren't as interesting, powerful or exciting in any way.
Again, you can make your deck however you want, you just have to do it with the pile of junk they've seen fit for you to be allowed to use.
Infuriatingly more still, some of the most exciting cards are locked behind a premium barrier - seriously, you pay for the game, but you have to pay more for some of the more decent cards.
Rather than making a unique and interesting game, we get "starter deck simulator 2015". Save the $10 and go play some FNM.

Pros:
-Bought the game for $32 on release. Can't really say that about any other big name AAA these days.
-Removal of the horrible stamina meter and the insane fall damage now makes movement incredibly fun and satisfying during combat as well as allowing you to traverse entire stages in mere minutes
-Lots of new weapons that have a Borderlands-esque feel to them, but also don't feel entirely random
-Many new ways to customize your weapons as well as providing a handy weapon wheel for quick access
-Leveling up is generally easier and there are many more skills to choose from as a result
-Multiplayer mode can be pretty fun with friends and allows you to grind outside the main campaign
Cons:
-With the addition of semo-random weapons and randomized weapon mods, the game menus just feel way too "busy". Sometimes I can spend up to 10 minutes at a time in the menu trying to arrange my mods and read all the logs I pick up. I want to dash around and shoot things, not micro-manage the procs on my weapon mods.
-Lo-Wang's dialogue gets old really fast, they really should not have given him so many lines in this game
-Multiplayer with randoms usually results in following the host rush each objective without stopping once to kill anything, completely defeating the purpose of multiplayer
-Ammo is ridiculously expensive at the main hub, but in each level there at least 3 ammo shrines that will replenish all my ammo for free, so why is ammo so expensive then?
All in all the game is still really fun, but when I think about having to scour menus and manage mods I immediately get turned off sometimes. Play it with friends that you know for the best experience.

Date: 07-21-14 posted after 10 hours of play.
Magic 2015 is the latest instalment of the Magic CCG franchize. It a reasonable $9.99 USD.  This edition has some improvement over Magic 2014, you can build your own deck, and you unlock a whole booster pack when you win a game, instead of just randomly unlock one card for your pre-built deck. That being said there is a lot of downsides to the game, It honestly feels a bit clunky after playing 2014 including a fog around the edge of the screen, and general slowness in changing between steps.  There is no true window mode, which means if you're playing on dual screens it is stuck on the primary monitor.

It is also irritating to  see  your opponent play a card and think, ‘That would be perfected for White Red deck’, only to find out you can never have it. Though apparently you can hack the game to allow access it. The starting deck is also very low powered, though once open a booster pack or two you can start amping up. I am ambivalent  towards this, as this fit most CCG style games i have played, you buy a fairly basic starter deck’  and then buy booster packs to upgrade or modify it to suit your gameplay style.
The multiplayer almost seems to have taken a step back, as there is no longer a two headed hydra (two on two) game play, you have to leave the match to change decks, and you have to beat the first camping boss to unlock the multiplayer.
Finally it still has some of the issues I had from 2014 including no option to turn off the timer in multiplayer. If i’m playing against my friends, we’re chatting and hanging, no need to feel rushed, let me set the game up with no timer, I can just yell at my friends to go. Where as if I am playing against a random person then I should be able to choose to set the game up with the timer on.
All in all  a solid if generic Magic game for the price. If you don’t have Magic 2014 then get this game, otherwise you might want to wait for a sale.  3 out of 5

This game is hard.  This game doesn't tell you much, really anything, right up front.  The story is opaque, and only becomes clear after hours of play.  Movement can be difficult and finicky, the obstacles can be frustrating, and you can get repeatedly crushed by random factors out of your control.
Personally, I absolutely love it.
This game isn't for everyone.  If you need clear progress and rewards, if you want complete control over your experience, if you want things completely explained without the possiblity of you missing something, with reguards to both story and sometimes gameplay mechanics, then you probably should avoid this game.
If you love exploration, hard struggles fought through trial and error and luck, and you want facinating lore and beautiful artwork with stirring, minimalist music, then you might be in luck with this game.  If you've every wondered what being a sewer rat is like, then this game is 100% for you.
The story in this game is one that requires patience, and an appreciation of asthetic rewards.  Or in other words, you might play for an hour or two with multiple failures and all you'll be rewarded with are a couple lines of information that reveal a few details about the backstory of the world, and it can be incredibly easy to miss this information.
That might not appeal to you.  I think the world is really cool and fully realized, and fighting through for those rewards was worth it for me.  This was largely because everything has so much character to it that I wondered what had happened to this world.
Gameplaywise, it takes some effort to master, but there's a lot of fun to be had once you're use to it.  Movement takes some getting use to if you want to be precise in your movements, so the plateforming elements can seem overly hard for a while, but it gets easier when you learn your limits.  Combat is difficult and dangrous because you're as much prey as you are predator, but it's really satisfying when you down a lizard for the first time.  There are somethings you'll only learn are dangerous by them killing you for the first time.  This game loves nasty surprises, but that's part of the challenge and part of the fun.
To sum it up, what you can do takes some time to learn and become proficient at, but once you do it's fun and engaging.  Wanting to learn those things depends on you wanting to explore and learn about the environment, and that requires you have an aesthetic appreciation for the world it's trying to show you.

Based on the limited amount of time I have spent with this game I am sure there will me more to explore. Given that its only EA at this point in time, there will be more to come. I got the game on sale which is going on right now for a little less than half the original price and I am liking it. It does not feel as mature as Creativerse, but what it has already got the better of my curiosity.
What I liked about it.
- Its premise is based on fantasy and magic. (This was the main thing for me. I was looking around for a minecraft like game with better graphics and based on magic. BINGO!!)
- It has a unique way of crafting in the game, through assembling blocks into shapes then casting a spell on it.
- There are some very powerful functional controls given to players where creative mode crafting is involved. You can even make your own customized weapons, and other items. (I have not explored this area much yet, but from watching the available video I thought it was really facinating.)
- You can make your own golems of various shapes and sizes by assembling the blocks into a recognizable shape and casting the spell (I doubt there is another game out there that lets you do this). And, you can command said Golem to mine for you.
- Lots of blocks, colored blocks, materials, to allow you to get creative with your creations.
- You can fly, throw fireballs, and shoot lightning.
- Graphics definitely looked better than the pixilated stuff you see in minecraft and its clone.
- The ingame map where you actually see all the activity going on in an area around you, including where the mobs are, what they are doing, where are the resources for you to go mining for, and where are the guarded chests-o-loot which you could go killing for.
What I didn't like (it is my greatest hope that they exist now because its in EA)
- Even though the graphics are better that minecraft, it could still be better.
- There are some annoying bugs but not totally game breaking at this point.
- Not much of a tutorial going on at this time.
- Not a whole of lot content in terms of fun and interesting encounters.
- The mob AI could be drastically improved on.
- No caves and dungeons to explore ("Yet", I hope).

A hugely rewarding, deeply engrossing experience almost ten years on from release. This is my second time all the way through (first time on the xbox) back in 2004/2005.
The best thing about KOTOR 2 is the writing, and the characters. It is deeper, and definitely darker (but perhaps with more profound moments of light and redemption due to contrast), than the first KOTOR. As expected the game looks a little out of date, but the sound, voice acting, and as mentioned, excellent story carry things along very nicely. The presentation is really quite cinematic, with nice pacing, good use of dramatic pause, and a poignancy that is rare in computer games.
It is an excellent RPG to play driven by your own moral compass etc, intentionally selecting and ignoring the threads to form your character, and party relationships. This is a MASSIVE part of the game, and in many ways is far more interesting than the grinding and combat etc (which is fine, and quite entertaining). Some of the outcomes of choices are a little tired/naff/obvious. For example there are so many problems ultimately solved with violence etc, but hey it's star wars and a computer game... what can I really expect! On the whole the dialogue and outcomes are very enjoyable, especially as you come to understand the personas and motivations of the party members, and learn to pick the threads that yield the best reactions.
I highly recommend installing the missing content patch, which is now very clean and tidy, and adds considerably to the experience and sense of completeness. That said it would be nice to see a clearer round up of what you acheived from your choices/acheivements in the wider universe (minor niggle).
An indellible experience, and I would love some more.

This game really is terrible. It's too intricate to be played casually, and it's so under-developed and broken it's maddening to try to take it seriously. I purchased it a long time ago and never really got into it until 'Operation Health', the season dedicated to fixing the game. Higher tick servers have really only help you watch in more detail how broken the game is. This is largely due to two issues.
The first, client sync is absolute trash in this game. Hit registration is utter garbage. What you see when you die will not be the same thing you watch in the deathcam. I have a fiber to premises connection in the Bay Area, and a rather well built computer so hardware is not the issue. Regular inconsistancies inclue dieing by what appears locally by a single inexplicable shot from someone who is not even visible, then you watch the killcam which will show your killer peeking a corner and shooting you 3-5 times before the server even lets you know they are there. If you find yourself in close combat with somebody, their location becomes erratic, and their movements completely impossible.
The second is map/game design leading to the issue of 'spawn peeking'. While on the attacking team you will frequently be shot as you spawn or shortly after from a fist sized hole someone bashed in a barracade before you spawned. Defenders spawn inside the building, Attackers outside with little cover and few preset spawn locations. Unscrupulous players will use this to end your round before you get 5 seconds under your belt.
It's really a shame, I loved the old R6 games, Frankly, Rogue Spear on 56k was far and away a smoother experience than this game. As it stands this game is a broken mix of CS:GO and early TF2. I recomend you pass this one by, despite UBI's claims, its highly unlikely this game will ever be properly developed.
TLDR:
Great concept ruined by poor netcode, poor game design, and lack of polish.

I bought this game earlier today. I was sceptical, obviously, given the amount of negative reviews surrounding the game; too much emphasis on PvP, poor design... you get the picture. But, I do love myself some good ol' survival horror, so I bought two copies (One for myself, one for my friend) and we gave the game a go.
Before I continue, I'd just like to emphasise that this game is indeed early access; it is not yet completed, and has a long way to go before it will be a finished product. With that in mind, here's my opinion,
I was amazed. Genuinely amazed. The graphics are on par, if not better, then some high-budget releases these days. The games map style feels, to me at least, like a cross between Fallout 3 and The Last of Us; rubble and destroyed cars cover the streets, and nature has rapidly regained a foothold, with entire streets coated in near man sized weeds and grass. Building lay desolate, and fires were abundant. I felt as though I was stepping directly into a destroy, crippled world, which felt surprisingly fresh when compared to the relatively clean map design (that is to say, not destroyed) of such other survival games, like DayZ and WarZ (or whatever it's calling itself now). I had to constantly remind myself that this wasn't even the finished product, and that it could only get better.
Secondly, the gameplay. The premise is simply, and has been done countless times before; you wander, looking for supplies to stay alive, whilst fending off other players and the enemies, which in this case were the bizzare, almost alien 'Nethers'. The Nethers are implemented great; there isn't too many, or too few of them. One moment, you could be walking down an abandoned street with nobody in sight, whilst another you could be sprinting up towards a rooftop with a whole host of those creatures after you. I've only played for a fair few hours, but the Nether didn't seem to grow tiring or tedious to fight at all, which is more than I can say for certain other survival games (*Cough* DayZ Zombies *Cough*).
Walking around is still pretty buggy, but that's to be expected; sometimes you might walk through a pile of garbage or a desk, whilst others you might lag sligtly while jumping over something.These things need to be addressed, but they are no where near game breaking by any means. The loot system seems to work well so far as well; whilst at first I felt as though there was nothing to be found, once I got the hang of the game, I quickly learnt where to search to get my character going.
And finally, we have what seems to be the biggest complaint I've seen about the game so far; its insistance on PvP.
Look, this isn't the kind of game where you're going to walk around and find a group of people to join up with. That might happen, but it'll be rare. Finding people isn't as rare as it is on DayZ, but is still uncommon. People will shoot on sight. The game feels best when played with friends, people you already know and trust; don't go expecting people not to kill your for your knife, cause they will. So yeah, I can understand why people playing alone would complain about the PvP, because it honstely doesn't feel like a game you should play alone. Grab a friend or two and meet up, and you're bound to have a good time.
This game isn't perfect by any means, but claiming that it's a 1/10 is just rediculous. As it is now, I'd give it a solid 7/10, and it really can only get better. At £8.99  as I'm writing this review, it is definately worth the cash.

After playing this game for 12 hours it's clear this is a free to play, or pay to win game (just about pay to play).  The developers say they aren't going for that pay to win game however the time it takes to build anything is staggering without paying.  Everything in the game costs crowns which you earn by completing quests, killing a players army, playing co-op, or defending your keep.  By no means a small amount of crowns either so basic upgrades cost 10~120 crowns each.  Note that defending your keep doesn't happen often enough to make gathering crowns in that manor a viable option.  You can purchase crowns which makes the game go quicker as you also get gold when you do this to boot.  Thus making the game actually playable if you pay.
The delevopers give out a starting bonus deal to help new players get into the game.  Compared to how slow the game moves, the bonus didn't make that much difference.  The issues is simple resource generation bonus for 10 minuts at the x10, x8, x6, and x4 level, and a 5 hour x2 resource generation.  I stopped playing before that ran out as I couldn't imagine playing the game at normal resource generation without pulling my hair out.  You also won't get attacked by anything for the first 24 hours.  To be honest I cancelled the protection as soon as I started to see if I would even get attacked at all.  I didn't at 12 hours of play get attacked once.  Which kind of makes having a walled village pointless.
The game itself has a good concept.  The graphics are okay but not great, the sounds, and music is garbage, the game play is kind of interesting.  The bugs are many.  The biggest issue is that it's a 100% server sided game.  I can log out and get more resources than I can while playing due to the lag between the server and my game.  I have an above average rig that can handle any game out on ultra settings so no it's not my computer.  If your army dies there is a glitch that doesn't reset your population count at your home base cuasing some issues trying to rebuild an army.
The main reason I don't recommend this game is becuase there is so much work involved with building an army after you get defeated, or even just play and win a battle.  Compaired to the loot you receive from a battle the cost of building an army is crazy.  An army can cost around 1,000 resources per unit with an army cap of 90 units it can get expensive.  The first major battle in the game requires around 25 units to beat.  However the losses are about 20 units.  The treasure gained is around 2,000 gold and about 400 wood and a crown or 2.  The 20 units cost around 30,000 food, and about 15,000 gold.  You don't gain land, units, or anything else in the first major battle.  It was cool to watch just not cool enough to waste 5 hours rebuilding another army to go on the next mission.
The peasant AI is horrible as well, and the gathering of resources is limited at best.  Some of the peasant resource gathering upgrades are bugged and actually don't improve what they say they will.  Which is similar to placing buildings, some locations are even bugged and you can't place anything there.  You have to choose wisely what you will place as you are limited to so many slots unless you get an upgrade to the slots of buildings you can place.  Which also requires crowns, and a lot of them.
The population cap in town might be to blame for everything wrong with the game.  With a glitch that doesn't calculate the population correctly, to not showing you all of your peasants when you click on the view all button it would seem the developers haven't finished this game yet.  The population cap is sitting at 90.  While I was able to max mine out at 50 in town after having to use population for animals to get extra food resources I found that I couldn't generate enough to build an army of 30 in a day.  It took about 5 hours to get a army of 25 going.  After that main battle which lasted about 5 minutes.  Having to rebuild all but 4 of those units there simply wasn't enough motivation to continue playing the game.
If the developer reads this I would recommend focusing on fixing any bugs the game has.  I would also lower the cost to upgrade anything with crowns in the game.  I would also rewrite the treasure you get after a battle to match the size of the battle, and the losses you will take on at an even matched battle.  If you lose you get nothing, if you win you get enough to at least repair, or rebuild most of your army.  The resource generation is so slow that it would take weeks to get anthing interesting going not to mention all the crowns I'd need just to upgrade my town hall to a castle might take months.  I would recommend changing the population cap to 100 for peasants, or fix the resource generation to make the game pace faster.  Playing 1 battle every few hours is dull and boring after all.  As the name of the game isn't kingdom building it's kingdom war. Compared to other games out there I can play that in this genra this game comes in as boring, and slow at best.  It has a ton of potential to be great, it just simply isn't at this time.

The strum of a lute serenades my ears as my peasants dutiful mine on my homeland, carrying sacks of stone and gold, tending my fields, butchering livestock, and working hard in the forests surrounding my large keep with it's mighty stone walls. A babbling brook works through my stronghold as my men patrol the walls with crossbows, blunderbusses, and bows at the ready. Bubbling oil gurgles away at the top of my gatehouses waiting to pour onto those who'd dare breach the sancitity of my realm. Trebutchets sit atop round towers waiting for the drums of war. My quiet management of my fief is piereced by the panoply of trumpets hearlding a welp who dares to raze my homeland. So I herd my peasants in and lock the gatehouses. I assemble my personal guard to the outer courtyard and lock the inner gatehouse. The enemy arrives at the edge of my walls and my trebutchets begin to sing with the whistle of flying boulders and the "swipp" of arrows leaving their strings. My men bubble out from a far gatehouse and make battle with the enemy on the fields and ruins of my homeland's outfields. They are bloodied but are victorious, the enemy driven before them.  The gates open and the peasants return to their tasks. The lutes play again and the once again peace falls over my land. It feels good to be lord.
Kingdom Wars is a PVE/PVP oriented MMORTS where you are lord of a tiny homestead on a vast and deeply detailed world of Mythador. Populated with Orcs, Elves, and Humans it reminds me deeply of Tolkien's Lord of the Rings but with a distinct Reverie Worlds spin. You can choose a race, two traits, and three different homelands that help give your kingdom a unique feel as well as mechanical benefits. You can engage in PVE quests or PVP content with additional Co-OP offerings. By far my favorite MMORTS to date and has hours upon hours of enjoyment.

I don't have that many hours under my belt yet, but my first impression was similar to some other players who gave negative reviews, although as I played more of the game I warmed up to it.  Like som others on the forums, I also assumed that there was a glitch preventing me from using the decks I paid for until I looked up that you had to progress through the capaigns to unlock them.  The campaigns are relatively easy though, and it isn't hard to unlock the cards.  If you get stuck on one of the later campaigns try switching your booster cards around.
Unlike other players, I like the interface, and don't mind the slight delay between menu switching.  Once you get used to it, you start to adapt by hitting escape instead of using the mouse to back out of some menus.  Using both the keyboard and mouse made the navigation more fluidic for me.  If Stainless Games decreased the time it took to switch menus, that would be even better through.
The AI isn't perfect, and makes mistakes when you solo, but humans make mistakes too.  The AI rarely makes miskes though, and I haven't played any other game where the AI is flawless anyways.  The deck builder is excellent, and the gameplay interface is also superior to many other card games out there.
Overall, this is a solid game, and worth my money.  Some of the criticisms about Magic 2015 I have read are valid, but for me at least, those problems are not game breaking enough to post a negative review, and depends on how sensitive you are to interface details, profit models, and minor gameplay mechanics.  The argument against pay-to-win isn't baseless, but ignores the fact that almost all card games you download on a computer have a similar profit model at heart.  In this market it would be highly unusual for any other profit model to exist.  As a result, it is to be expected, and shouldn't be a shock to players at all unless this is their first time buying a game that uses microtransactions.  Selling a NEW game with a relatively popular title for $9.99 should be a clear indication that the company intends on using microtransactions to pay for the rest of their overhead in making the game.  There are also other clues such as player defined tags in Steam, and forum comments, so I am not sure why so many people were surprised about this, and reeled so hard against it after they bought it.  This is how the real card game works as well, right?
If you are on a budget, and can't afford anything more than $9.99, then you most likely will still get $9.99 of enjoyment out of the game before you get bored of the grind or how the interface works.  If you can afford the microtransactions, or even the $19.99 or $34.99, then you will get that much more enjoyment compared to other games with similar price tags.

Before review, I'll talk about some of the critisim I saw in others' reviews:
1)
.
Seriously, do me a favor and just down-rate any review you see that complains about this. Just go compare the screenshots of this game from community hub with other games, even the triple-A games. This game has beautiful graphics comparable to other much more expensive titles. Not to say that this game is the pinnacle of gaming graphcis but there's very little to complain about if you're being honest with yourself.
2)
.
To be honest, inventory management aren't well designed and took about 10-15% of my gaming time. Do keep this in mind if you don't like to plan or look at fine prints of a game. You can play the game at a lower difficulty setting and completely ignore this portion of the game if you hate inventory management or looking through a list of available upgrades.
3)
.
The difficulty descriptions are detailed when starting new game so much so they even give the exact % increase in received damage, enemy HP and exp gained. But if you haven't started playing I highly recommend you to play this game near the highest difficulty level. Normal feels like easy and Hard doesn't feel hard. Insanity level 1 feels more like somewhere between normal and hard of a typical game. Keep this in mind when you start a new game. If you like a challenge just keep changing difficulty level to the highest one available based on your character level. Only at insanity level 4 did I feel like the game is at hard core mode of a typical game.
4)
.
As most story and artisitic appreciation goes, this is very subjective. Shadow Warrior 2013 wins in terms of the raw feel it deliveries. In particular the humor and x factor if that's even a thing. And Shadow Warrior 2013 has a stronger ending. But due to all the added dimensions of the story in SW2 I feel that the story here is more rich and there's alot more lore building. There's alot of small notes you can find and collect and read when the game ends. Its nothing as ground breaking as Resident Evil's "Fever gone but itchy. Hungry and eat doggy food. Itchy Itchy Scott came. Ugly face so killed him. Tasty.". But to be fair they are interesting to read anyway. Oh and SW2 ending suck.
5)
.
There are 2 sets of element. If enemy is immune to poison, it is weak to electric and vise versa. If enemy is immune to fire, it is weak to ice and vise versa. Very simple mechanics and yet people feel it keeps them from enjoying the game. I feel its interesting and prevents gamers from bulldozing through the game mindlessly. So, I like it.
6)
.
The quests actually adds abit of story and conversation between Lo Wang and NPCs so its not all boring. Honestly, you can literally rush through the level without fighting and finish the quest quite quickly. Problem solved. You know a complaint is stupid if its solution is one only sentence and doesn't require any sacrifice of any sort. Also, no idea why such a subjective opinion get repeated in the exact same phrasing so many times. Feels almost like its the same guy who bought many copies of the game just to lower the rating of this game to below 90%.
7)
.
Another stupid complaint. The game is actually very interesting due to high customizability to gamer's perferences. See point "8" of my review of this game below and you'll see why.
Before I go ahead and review this game, I'll just go right ahead and mention the following:
1)
.
You get 10% upfront for pre-order or 20% if you already own the previous game. I'll be lying if I said it didn't affect my impression of this game and their dev team and management. Doing so not only win fans' hearts, it also kinda shows how they're not here for the money. Also reminds me of some of the cool people I've met in my life who I wouldn't mind buying them drinks every once in awhile.

.

In short, looking beyond the game itself. These guys are a good bunch of fellows who did their job well and aren't here just to make money. Not say that they don't wish to profit, but obviously they don't do so by doing questionable things like selling out on people's trust in them.
Wow, I've already said so much about this game I'm feel sleepy. Anyway, here comes the review:
1) This game has a 89% rating. So, if you're not picky as hell there's a good chance you'll enjoy youself playing this game.
2) Good graphcis.
3) Fast pace awesome action game.
4)
.
Yup, your eyes aren't playing tricks. I'm going to go ahead and say that this game is so good that I feel that its better than Doom. Down rate this review if you disagree but this is how I feel honestly. From story to game design to environment design to just how the game generally feels.
5) Good story. But bad ending.
6) Good music. I mean like seriously good. But you may need the Deluxe Upgrade to enjoy it fully.
7) Good value for money. This is literally a AAA game at a B game price. Definitely must buy.
8) Notable improvements above Shadow Warrior 2013.
8a) Ammunition used to be insufficient at high difficulty due to high enemy HP. Less of an issue now. Basically you are not forced to use melee weapon at high difficulty levels.
8b) Interest factor. Getting new weapon, skill etc constantly allowed me to constantly enjoy the game in a new light.
8c) Customizability. You can spec your character to DPS Build (High Crit Change and Dmg Bonus), Tank Build (Dmg resist and HP), Invisibility High Dmg Build (Raw Damage without Crit), High Mobility Build etc etc. You can abuse the mechanics of the game in a very forcus specific way using upgrades and they are fun in their own way. Btw, high dps means you can hack and slash and make use of high DPS. Invis however means you have to hit enemies one hit at a time as invisibility bonnus damage only applies for one attack and then you will have to go invis again so Crit chance and damage doesn't apply with consistency here.
8d) Free Roam. I like how I can go back to stages I've completed before.
8e) I know how many people say its like Diablo or Borderlands but is that necessarily bad Subjective if you ask me.
8f) Also the elemental system. I think I find it fun. I like how I can poison and burn enemies to death, freeze or paralyse enemies with ice or electricity. I like especially how corpse of poisoned enemies explodes and poisons + damage other enemies near them. Fun to see a chain of explosions. Disagree if you like, then just ignore this point as an improvement.
8g) No need to find all secrets for achievement. I think you only need to find about 70-80% to unlock achievement which I think is much more reasonable than having to find them all.
9)
. I love how I can take photos of scenic views when I see one. Might even say the whole gaming experience feels like a vacation in Lo Wang's world.
10)
Didn't actually try. Seems like there's a friendlist and a public mode.
So, to conclude just buy the game already. I'm sure its obvious that you will very likely enjoy it and find every dollar spent well worth it.

A lot of people will criticise this game for several reasons. Allow me to summarise them and spare you the time spent scrolling through identical negative reviews.
Here's what people don't like:
1. The controls are imprecise
2. The enemies are unpredictable
3. The ending is weird
4. The difficulty is too high
Can I disagree with these? Not at all! Rain World is a hard game. It will frustrate you. Several times I have had to stop myself from injuring my laptop after my 43rd ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t death against the blue octopus things that hang around the zero-gravity area. I have angrily quit this game at least 7 times. Does this mean it's a bad game? Of course not.
The game is hard. But don't you remember when all games were as hard, if not harder than this? When did we collectively decide that hard=bad? I understand the concerns, though. Rain World is not hard in the same way that Super Meat Boy is hard. The difficulty comes from factors you often can't control. Enemy placement, unclear platforms, unreliability of food spawns, all contriubte to the difficulty. It's tough, I won't understate that, and often not for the right reasons.
However, I keep coming back. Do you know why?
It's because frustration from continually missing that ♥♥♥♥ing jump fades. What remains is the sense of wonder and awe at the beauty of the environments, the immersiveness of the world, and the absolutely stunning visual design. Simply looking at this game is absolutely entrancing, and finding new and varied environments is very rewarding. People complain about the ending- That's a personal issue. I thought the ending, and the lore surrounding it that you can organically work out was a very interesting conclusion. It leaves questions, but, to anyone familiar with the game; Wouldn't it be a bit underwhelming if you just found this super secret area with all your family there, reuinted with them, and then ended the game?
The world sets up something much bigger than that. The architecture of the levels is clearly intentional, clearly alluding to a fallen civilisation- one you are able to find out. The world of this game is bigger than you, bigger than your family, and the ending creates a very enthralling conclusion to that, giving a hint into what became of the world at large.
Essentially, exploring the world and finding out the lore is fun and rewarding, if sometimes frustrating. I would highly recommend this game. Give it some time, give it some effort. You will be rewarded.

The world and atmosphere of Rain World didn't interest me enough to keep play after the initial hour I played. There's probably a good, maybe even great game hidden under the many problems rain world has, but I think for many it isn't worth the tedious and unfair design decisions that plague this game. You start the game as a slug cat seperated from its family and you now must use your smarts to stay alive with the help (?) of a strange eyeball creature and find your lost slug cat brethren.
Rain Worlds greatest asset is its beautiful, rustic world, overtaken by nature and the cat-astrophic (ha puns) rain that is presumably the reason for this post apocalyptic setting. From the very get go Rain World nails this sense of being lost in a world you don't quite understand. You want to explore this place, you want to see what Rain World has to offer. The game's apperance and sound design only amplifies this feeling. It's a gorgeous looking game. The abandoned factory setting overtaken by lush flora is engrossing and pulls the player in. The only sounds the player hears in the beginning for the most part is subtle, but effective. Vibrant bells ring through the air while the wind tunnel effect plays in the background almost all the time, making everything seem so much more empty and larger than it really is. Sadly, despite this amazing visuals, it falls flat on its face almost immediately.
Right out the gate you feel lethargic and weak. The controls are hard to grasp and the slug cat jumps, moves, and responds slow. The controls are sluggish in the worst possible way, even if its fitting for the slug cat, and even if this was intended by the devs. No part of the control scheme is fun or intuitive. The slug cat's annoying controls makes for tedious platforming and bug catching, which are core parts of the game. The game tries to handicap you with bad controls to force you to think and use resources around you to get through obstacles. Unfortunately the platforming sections of the game become overly difficult and frustrating, especially when making a mistake such as missing the jump or not grabbing a pole in time results in dying as well and sends you back to the last place you hibernated.
The hibernation mechanic is an important part of the game but it has many flaws. You can only hibernate once you have eaten enough bugs and you may only hibernate in specific locations. Hibernation is important for three reasons, the first being Karma (I will touch on this in a second). The second reason is to avoid death by rain. One of the interesting mechanics in the game is the rain mechanic, but in my opinion it's implemented badly. After a certain amount of time the screen will begin to shake and then it will start to rain until the screen fills up with water and kills the slug cat. You can stay safe from the rain by hibernating until it goes away which also resets the timer until the next rain storm. The problem with the rain is it discourages exploration and taking your time, but the game is naturally an exploration game with a heavy emphasis on thinking your actions through instead of charing head on. The rain conflicts with these ideas and makes the game seem like its not quite sure what it wants to be. Fast paced survival or slow, ambient, atmospheric, exploration game? The third reason hibernation is important is because it acts as a save spot. If you die you start at the last place you hibernated. If you die, all the way back to where you last hibernated. Close to the next hibernation spot but got lost or stuck on a platforming section and died to the rain? Back all the way to the last hibernation spot. It's frustrating to lose so much progress and doesn't feel like it's done well.
The karma system in this game is nothing more than stupid padding. In order to progess to a new area you must have enough karma. Gain karma by hibernating, lose karma by dying. There's no reason to have karma in this game at all. It doesn't test your abilites or skill or anything. It's tedious and only functions as a barrier that punishes you for the games already unfair mechanics.
Last but not least the enemies. The enemies in this game are the worst part about this game. Worse than the controls, worse than the hibernating system, worse than the rain, even worse than the karma. Everything about the enemies is frustrating in every way possible. The monsters in this game have the ability to move freely from room to room with no absolute pattern. At first this sounds interesting, you always have to be on your toes, you never know where the weird yellow lizard creature might be this time. You play cautiously but all of it was for nothing because a lizard was waiting for you right on the other side of the pipe and there was nothing you could have done to prevent it. The next time you come back to that area you think of a new strategy. You wait until the lizard comes out and you can go around it. The lizard comes out, but instead of leaving the pipe it just sits there and you end up dying after it finally moves because of the rain. Nothing about the random nature of the enemies in the game is fun or interesting and creates some of the infuriating gameplay.
I wanted to enjoy rain world, but I couldn't. I really couldn't. After dying offscreen because my camera didn't move into the next area when I did I had it with this game. I know some people think the world of this game, and I'm glad they could, but I couldn't even play it for 2 hours without wanting to bash my head against the wall. If you can endure the random movement of the enemies, the stupid karma system, bad controls, and the rain that constantly rushes you in a game where you want to take your time, then give rain world a try. As it is, I can't recommend it. If you want a game with great atmosphere and platforming then go play hollow knight. It's even $5 less than this game.

The FPS aspects are absolutely brilliant, as the game's two factions have an asymmetric balance across the board, from guns, to vehicles, and space vessels. On top of that, the weapon customization is absolutely obscene, being able to choose ammo types, scopes/sights, different barrels,  body modifications (such as weight, holster speed, and reload speed), and three unique armor suits that cater to different playstyles. The armor itself is even modifyable, with slots for motion sensors, jammers, explosives sensors, additional armor, faster armor regen, or faster sprint speeds.
Add this customization to the vehicles, and you have a game where you can literally play however you want. Sneaky sniper? Check. Heavy weapons? Check. Fast shotgunner with a rocket? Check. Repair specialist with turrets? Yep, you can do that too.
The only thing stopping you from whatever you want is the points system, of which there are three. Combat, Command, and Support. THe more points you have, the more stuff you can use. Earning the points is pretty easy too. Combat points come from dealing damage, murdering enemies, and blowing stuff up. Command Points come from playing objectives set by either the Squad Leader, or the Team Commander. As either of these, you get Command Points for objectives you set being completed, and winning a game as the Team Commander gives you a 2x bonus to earned Command Points. Finally, Support points are done by resupplying teammates, healing them, reviving them, repairing armor or vehicles, keeping teammates safe from gunfire with certain gadgets or attachments, and having deployed turrets score damage/kills.
This game is huge, in scope, ambition, and customization.
It is only lacking in the price tag department... so what are you waiting for?
