I've barely played an hour and a half of this game, and already it's given me an experience more exhilarating and awesome than any big battle AAA I've played. Even the new Battlefront, which is admittedly much more accessible, still can't meet the level of emotional havoc and panicked, adrenaline surge that AFF invokes in me.
Rather than a Pros and Cons list, which could mislead you about the quality of this partocular title, I want to answer three questions potential customers probably would like to know:
1. What makes the game so good?
2. Then, what's the catch?
3. Can you explain what an average session is like?
Let me explain:
1. What makes this game great is the ambition that's already been realized. Rather than worrying first about graphics and polish while adding actual content later, Strangely Interactive have got the content DOWN. The gameplay is exactly what the target fan base has been looking for for years, and in some folks' case, for decades. Let's be honest, development of AFF was probably catalyzed by the limbo and cancellation of Star Wars Battlefront 3. When DICE took on the project, fans of both battleFIELD and battleFRONT were pretty thrilled. That end product was a gem to look at, but like gems, it lacked any inherent value. AFF devs Strangely Interactive know that fans love epic battles with massive cluster♥♥♥♥s of players, large choice in loadouts, large choice in roles, and high strategy at a footsoldier level. And they focused on that first and foremost.
2. The catch is that the game's more aesthetic and superficial elements have taken a big hit. The graphics, while certainly passable and playable in, could stand to receive an upgrade. The ships are well-designed structures with logical interiors. I was escaping a capital ship I'd just rigged to blow, and the whole thing was collapsing and igniting like some kind of alien disaster film. Meanwhile, the ship had so many corridors to actual engineering levels and crew Quarters that my thwarted escape was delightfully frustrating. This is a breath of fresh air after Battlefront 2 decided that the highly vulnerable shields, engines, and weapons system cores should be located immediately adjacent to a very accessible hangar. Delight aside, what's far worse than the underwhelming graphics are the overwhelming UI and clipping bugs. At one point, in my capital ship's hangar, I fell into a massive pit that appeared to be a fighter ship elevator. I didn't die, and so had to wander around in there until I predictably found a hole in the map through which I fell out of the game and was able to respawn. The HUD is a mess of miniscule print, unexplained symbology, and in-battle tips that all seem to fight for space with abandon. I tried to command the battle at hand. While I think that feature is a great concept, it absolutely fails in execution. You simply can't be a commander and a soldier. What would make more sense is that the commander stay outside the battle to observe and issue orders, much like in Natural Selection. Unless you're on the bridge, battles are two chaotic to use the current system. The Loadout screen has a lot of great ideas - a points system that let's you choose from a wide array of gadgets and upgrades without becoming too OP in a single match - but, navigation of this screen is confusing and a hassle. These UI problems could be solved by taking a gander at the first Battlefront's command system. It was underused, but the simplicity was essential to what AFF needs today. I get that big battles are usually long and complex, but being able to issue orders on the fly and select a Loadout quickly reduces critical downtime. Players don't want to lounge around in a Loadout screen, they want to get back to the action! Additionally, Battlefront and Battlefield also had UI that I consider intuitive and reasonable. It also looked pretty flashy. I have no doubt, however, that this early access title will have a very well-considered UI element upon release. The devs seem to have thrown all the goodies in already. Now they just have to organize them.
3. So, let me give you a few examples of an average match - keep in mind I only played with AI. The setting is always futuristic, and the map is either a big city, an outpost city, or in space with some nebula, planet, or space station as a reference point for scale and orientation. You start in a large briefing chamber with some sweet♥♥♥♥♥holograms and a bunch of bored soldiers watching a description of mission objectives (you can always skip this part, but it still takes a minute for the mission to load). The overall mission will either be a spawn point tug of war or a defense/assault thing, the latter of which might involve various more detailed objectives for the assault army. In either mission type, you can use spawn point capture strategically.
You then choose a loadout, choose a spawn point, and show up on the battlefield. If you're among the vanguard, there will likely be an eerie silence as you hustle to the first objective. You shoulder past fellow infantrymen. You nervously keep an eye out for enemies. When you see your first enemy, all hell breaks loose. Shells start going off, turrets spring up at the command of your brothers in arms. Smoke grenades fly and make the laser sights all the cooler. The noise is inescapable. And beautiful. A symphony of laser fire, bellowed orders, and fighter ships criscrossing overhead. Like a ballroom with a wall of mirrors to give the appearance of greater space, the sound and sight of the battle around you says, "This isn't a skirmish. This is war." It's intoxicating. Then, you die. You come back, muffled gunfire in the distance, you leap back in. My favorite moments are finding a forgotten alleyway or fire escape in these abandoned streets of Scifiville that I could use to flank or snipe. You have a moment to yourself where the enemy has no idea where you are. You regroup. You take a breath. Then you begin taking pot shots.
The battle's with individual objectives are divided into stages, in the same way Battlefield's are. As each stage ends with an objective completed, the battlefield either shifts focus or changes shape.
For instance, in a space battle, you'll start on the capital ship, in hyperspace. You can fly out on a fighter and take down the enemy's main guns and shields. Once the way is clear, the next objective becomes entering the enemy space station. Your capital ship drops out of hyperspace, and youre free to take a drops hip full of space marines over to the space station for boarding. Meanwhile, the capital ship itself carries it's own game changing firepower.
The game isn't flawless, but it's got the meat already there to show everyone that these devs can pull it off. I'm looking forward to the final product. Meanwhile, I'll be enjoying a campaign of massive battles from one end of the Galaxy to the other. Hope to see you there.

Shadow Warrior 2 is very strong in a few critical aspects, moderate in story, and very, very weak in map variety.
Strengths:
Maps & graphics look beautiful. Everything looks fantastic. The built in screen shot system lets you capture a scene exactly how you want - all games should have such a robust built in capture system.
Combat - You have a wide variety of weapons & abilities that you can combine on the fly. Depending on your difficulty level combat can become hectic extremely quick. It easy on some maps to find yourself flying nearly 1/4 ways across the map while attacking mid air. Combat feels smooth and reactive. This is some of the funnest, most dynamic combat I've came across in a game. The AI generally offers a fun opponent
Optimization - Personally for me with everything at nearly ultra game ran extremely smooth on a - Evga 1070 GTX, Win 7 64, 32 Ram, SSD. And actually my 1070 suffered a short halfway through the game so I had to temporarily replace it with my 980 GTX 4 gig vram. I noticed very little difference on the same settings and turning off depth of field and one or two other settings but no texture quality reductions gave me the same performance.
Moderate - Story. Both the story itself and the pacing were very middling. Story of about the same quality as the new DOOM but much more choppy. At the beginning of the game you find yourself suddenly in different locations with was jarring and affected the continuity of the story. You will always find yourself back in a central hub and basically teleport to each new location.
Weak - Map Variety. This is easily and by far the weakest aspect of Shadow Warrior 2. Its so ridiculously poor I'm surprised the game was released with so few maps. Almost immediately in the game you will find yourself repeating the same 3 or so maps over and over again. Theres about 3 or so unique ones that never repeat and 3-4 others that you constantly repeat. Sometimes the areas are shuffled around a bit but its very clear its otherwise the same map. This contributes significantly to the sometimes grindy feel of the game.
Crafting System - This is nearly complete garbage except for Elemental upgrades. All the other upgrade types can end up being completely random. Even when you take 3 upgrades with identical names or identical traits or both you can end up with complete junk. At high levels 130,000$ of junk and 3 good upgrades wiped out can be very frustrating. I most consistently received upgrades of the same type with elementals. Don't expect taking 3 identical elementals will give u the same exact but upgraded one. You will only get the same elemental type. I had luck with with piercing and turret ones also but found they would sometimes spit out a level 1 upgrade instead of the identical types i put together.
Store - Ammo is super over priced - makes no sense. Most of the stuff in the store isn't better then what you pick up either. Mostly just a waste of time except for selling stuff off.
Loot System - So much loot! Just endless piles of loot everywhere and the system for managing it is far from efficient. Much of it has mixed attributes - that is some positive and some negative but there is no way to sort out the ones with negative qualities. Sorting and managing this junk was a real downer, made the game drag very bad but you need to swap your upgrades every map or so to stay scaled up to the next challenges.
I also get the impression the devs had a hard time balancing the game difficulty out. I started out on Insane 1 but the updates kept changing the gameplay so its difficult to say how it will be when you purchase. I recommend just finding the difficulty level you have fun at and adjust later if it becomes too easy / hard. As I say I started at Insane 1, finished the last big fight at Insane 2 and it was way too easy - about 30 seconds or so.
Also if you choose too difficult a setting the game becomes extremely grindy. You may need to replay some maps over to get more Skill points from Karma. If you want to max your skill points faster I recommend putting in the Karma perks as soon as possible and also use Karma increasing body armor as soon as possible. You can about double your Karma points doing this.

Shadow Warrior 2 is a fun romp of a game that draws from several wells of inspiration. Firstly, the game looks and feels a whole lot like Shadow Warrior, the original rehauled version. It plays lightning fast, has smooth graphics, and though the character models seem a bit off, everything else aesthetically looks great. They reworked the control system so special moves are easier to pull off, instead of the mortal kombat style of hitting a direction twice and pushing a button. The weapons and character upgrade systems are robust and add variety to one of the many different weapons. Seriously, I have 48 different weapons and i'm still going.
That being said, Shadow Warrior 2 does have a few flaws. The mission variety is rarely more than go here, kill this, report back in. I, personally, don't mind, as long as it does it well (which it does). However, some may find that a turn off, so it's worth mentioning. The free roam for mission areas is nice for loot and scoot running, but they don't have the random objectives that Diablo 3 performed in it's adventure mode. This game NEEDS an adventure mode for end game content. It would be perfect. Something that drops a boss monster or collection objectives just for the fun of it, and the loot of it of course.
Those notes aside, this game does a lot really well. The action is a hyped up speed fest where bullets and swords move as fast and smooth as you would expect. It draws inspiration from games like Borderlands, Diablo, and sets them in a cyberpunk world that you would swear is Shadowrun in design. The voice acting is mostly great, though a little hokey at times. The jokes are always hit or miss, and i'm pretty sure they do it on purpose. When your games main protagonists name is a play off of being a hung low♥♥♥♥♥♥...you can bet seriousness was taking a back seat to fun. Still, even in it's ridiculousness, the game finds a serious enough story to make it feel like it's not all a joke. Just most of it. It develops Wang as a character, along with his new sidekick in his head. A snotty brat that eventually comes to be justified (mostly) in her mood. A well spun legend of the smith, and the goddess who saved the world are all fleshed out both via game story cut scenes and collectable books that i'm still picking up after twenty hours.
Overall, this games great if your not looking for a Deus Ex or Mass Effect level of storytelling and design. Someone's Half Life 2 homage took a dump all over Duke. Face-palming ensues.
The Good:
+ They nailed Duke's persona spot-on
+ Jon St. John is back voicing Duke
+ The "go mess around" levels are sometimes funny
+ The gratuitous T & A fit Duke perfectly
The Bad:
- puzzles
- platforming
- driving
- the fact that the above 3 are even in a Duke 3D game
- the "go mess around" levels got old fast (slow-paced & no action)
- unintuitive maps, puzzles, etc ("where do I go?", "what do I do?")
- short oxygen meter & forced situations using it (cheap deaths)
- short action sequences that force you into killzones (cheap deaths again)
- short action sequences that are a joke (infinite ammo and rocket launchers)
- action / gun-fights in general are treated like side dishes instead of main course (argh)
- DLC has more of the same, but replaces Duke with another person doing all the trash-talking (!)
Before I get started, the Duke of old, 2D platforming days is gone. When they released Duke Nukem 3D they totally rewrote who and what Duke was. THAT is the Duke that this game was meant for. However, I suppose for nostalgia's sake, they decided to push him back into a 3D version of his old 2D game world.
It doesn't work.
When you think "Duke" from Duke 3D days you think action. So, what should have been a straight-forward run-n-gun (a la Serious Sam) was instead developed as a puzzle / platformer / driving / mini-game / turret-shooter with action elements thrown in. Duke is thrown in the middle, and is forced to flounder around like a fish out of water.
As Angry Video Game Nerd (AVGN) would say "WHAT WERE THEY THINKING?!"
The irony is when Duke voices your frustration as if he, too, is insulted to be a part of this game:
EG1: Duke approaches a puzzle with pipes and valves. "I hate Valve puzzles." Oh, lol, a quip about Valve's puzzles in HL2. So hilarious. Yeah, screw that. Duke's gonna punch his way through this one instead of doing the stupid puzz... oh... ok, nope, Duke has to do the flipping puzzle. Wut? (Even Angry Joe beat the game for that one.)
EG2: In the DLC you get done with another stupid puzzle and Duke spouts "FINALLY!" Yeah, finally! Why am I stuck doing stupid puzzles?! Where's the flipping action?! If Duke himself is tired of this garbage, how do you think I feel?
I'm not ticked off at Duke, though. I'm still a Duke fan, because this game merely mis-uses the Duke Nukem IP ... horribly ... and doesn't represent Duke well. Duke was thrown into the middle of this mess, and you're stuck feeling sad for him having to muck through it. You're frustrated at the game, but you're empathetic of Duke being stuck in it.
Duke fans went in with certain expectations, and the game defied those expecations in ignorance, spite and / or neglect. But, that's not Duke's fault. That would be like buying a game that has Barbie in it and finding out it's a Mortal Kombat clone. It's not Barbie's fault, it's the fault of the ignorant developers / publisher.
The sad part is this isn't a bad game; it's just not a good Duke game. It would have done better had it been a stand-alone title starring a different lead character. Instead, Duke was shoe-horned in, and it doesn't work. As I said, they should have emulated Serious Sam, not Gordon Freeman.
The DLC is even more disappointing then the main game.
Dr. Proton (who? ... he was your antagonist from Duke 2D platforming days) starts as your chief antagonist, and it seems like a novel concept. But, they don't leverage his robots or Duke clones much, and you waste him 1/2 way in. What's left? Oh, you're stuck fighting more aliens like in DNF ... how original.
And, they took everything that grates about DNF and put more of it in the DLC ... more puzzles, more driving, more platforming, more ball-scratching as you try to figure out where to go and what to do (which makes you feel like an idiot).
In addition, they neuter Duke mid-way through of his last, remaining machismo (his mouth) by having  some jack-a** side kick making all the wise cracks. So, the DLC is just insult to injury.
Basically, if you're looking for a decent Duke Nukem 3D sequel, then go play Serious Sam. Sam picked up the baton that they made Duke drop, and has been running with it for the past years. Even playing Duke in Bro-Force is more entertaining than this. At least there's more action and more explosions.
Likewise, look at my play time... 20 hours in 2 weeks. I'm on winter break from college; lots of time on my hands to catch up with my gaming. I spent ten hours a week on DNF. That's sad. When I really like a game I'll make a day of it. But, I found myself making excuses to not play this game... laundry, dishes, folding, vacuuming ... my apartment has never been cleaner. I started playing the game to see what all the fuss was about, and once I started I wanted to see it through. But, I found myself waffling hardcore getting there. That speaks volumes.
If you get this game, go in with expectations set per above. Don't go in thinking Duke is about action. In fact, don't have any expectations. Even 12yo's are ranting about how they're insulted that they used a lot of T & A to lure them into this stinker. That's saying something, too.

DOTP 2015 changes several things about the DOTP experience.  Some are for the better, but overall, I think the series took a step backward with this installation.  The new single-player card collecting experience is nice, but restricting some of the best cards to microtransactions leaves a very bad taste in my mouth, making it difficult to recommend the game overall.
So, let's talk about the game.  Well, it's magic.  There's a great variety of cards and the "booster collection" system actually lets you put together a deck of your own creation, rather than relying on the premade deck templates of the previous series.  Unfortunately, this system is let down by some arbitrary limitations, both in the variety of cards, and how many of each card can be unlocked.
The menus are preposterously slow.  They look fancy, sure, but it quickly becomes frustrating to navigate the menus as you have to watch the wispy animations.  Hell, it takes the game about 10 seconds to get to the main menu after you click "start" on the title screen.  There's just no reason for this.
The core game is good though if you're a fan of MTG.  The duel interface is great as always.  There are a variety of encounters in the single player experience and the acquisition of boosters does a nice job if creating a sense of progression.  One criticism I might levy - which could be said to some extent of all DOTP - is that increasing the difficulty really just makes it so that the AI has ungodly luck.  That is to say, if their deck has an answer to a card you just played, it's a surefire bet that they will draw it in short order.  It definitely amounts to an increase in difficulty, but it never feels like you get outplayed; it just feels like you lost to impossible luck, and that can be frustrating.
Now, perhaps the most vehement criticism levied against this game is that it is pay to win, and to an extent, I would tend to agree.  While there are some very good cards that you can collect in the single player experience, the premium booster packs (purchased with real money) contain several extremely powerful bombs.  While these cards may not win a duel by themselves, there is an obvious difference in a deck without them than a deck with them.  For example, G/W tokens with doubling season is far scarier to me than G/W tokens without doubling season.
So, I will say that as a fan of MTG I enjoyed the single-player experience.  I liked the card collecting and the ability to create my own decks.  But overall I have to recommend passing this one up; I think the previous DOTPs were superior, and the money-grab scheme in DOTP 2015 leaves a sour taste in my mouth.

There are a lot of reviews that liken the game to Shadow Warrior (2014) plus Borderlands. While fair from a high level, you really need to understand some nuances to make sure you'll enjoy the game. SW2 is a well-optimized, edgy, bombastic blast of fun whose graphics are refreshing compared to Borderlands 2. The custom gun system is endless fun for creating the exact batch of toys you want to use in this slaughter-fest. In the end, I'm happy with my purchase, but consider the following to make sure you will too:
Coming from SW1:
-Levels don't really feel like levels you're used to from SW1. In an effort to provide re-playability there's random conjoining of level sections each time you play. Plus, you'll re-visit certain areas which makes it all kind of a wash level-wise in the classic sense. I began to recognize set pieces by the end of just one playthrough.
-By default you'll be led where to go via  your mini-map and I'm not sure why you'd even turn it off. The levels are HUGE open areas, but there's not much else to discover other than a few extra pieces of loot or bullets. No sidequests or such.
-There was a LITTLE bit of strategy in SW1's enemy tactics. Some were really hard and unique. Here.. every boss, every enemy.. strafe or kite and hold down fire. It's fun, it's a blast, but even on difficulty 4/4 (+2) I got up to, I don't see the strategy needed. It's just a Pew-Pew fest. Here, you might make sure you don't shoot something with acid that is resistant to acid, but you can still get by. Sometimes you'll just suddenly be dead and wondered WTF happened, but that's it. All or nothing.
Coming from BL2:
-You're going to have side missions and story missions, but you have two hubs. That's it. Otherwise, you fire off into areas that are not connected in any way... nor is any attempt made to create that illusion that they are connected. In BL2, you would hit "gates" to the next area which were visually consistent -- so even when you needed to switch areas, you could tell where you were and where you were going.
-Coming from the interesting choices of the skill trees in Borderlands 2's unique abilities, here we can carry more bullets, more health, more running speed, more damage with fire, more damage with acid, more damage with frost... Zzzzzz. It borders not even bothering.
-Story here is not much to speak of. Again, it's a short ride compared to BL2, with no areas to explore or reasons to go about places, so you never settle in and get into it. Put another way, you won't have as much longevity here as you likely did with BL2.
Remember to keep in mind, this is just a review trying to highlight some differences not spoken about too much. It's a great game and I agree with the praise. A definite thumbs up for the money, the devs did a great job and I look forward to their next effort. It's a unique product that definitely holds its own in my collection.

First off I recommend you watch gameplays and what not to see if you'll enjoy it. You may think it's not worth $60 right now and while thats a respectable reason, but if 60 big bux isn't a big deal for hours of fun just go ahead and buy this game.
Pros:
Solid game in general.
Nice graphics w/ good amount of settings and no crazy requriements. No issues on that spectrum whatsoever.
Story mode isnt awful but don't expect Witcher or New Vegas levels of writing. I like it because it lets you try a good amount of heroes. Took my friend and I 9 hours to complete on the hardest difficulty.

There's gear and feats (ie perks) you unlock as you level up heroes and play the game, which really helps you set your playstyle for each hero. All gear adds to a stat while taking away from another. Higher level gear gives a bigger bonus while taking away more. For example you can make yourself do more damage at the cost of less defense etc
Everything in the game shop can be bought and earned via in game currency (steel) Steel is earned by daily objectives in multiplayer or bought with real money.
The ai's in multiplayer are great as in they show no mercy but are beatable. They aren't idiots. Difficulty scales from 0-3.
Cons:
P2P for match hosting. There's servers for matchmaking players but each game is P2P hosted. Which isnt that bad but when a host leaves and it crashes the match because it was unable to migrate it can get a bit annoying.
I think this game would benefit greatly from a server browser w/ a community hosted/rent a server system.

A breathtakingly beautiful exploration and puzzle game with a world and story to really draw you in.
There really isn't much to say about the game that can't be gleaned from the screenshots and videos on the store page. What starts out as a well-executed puzzle game with some light platforming will quickly draw you in with its world building, story and varying mechanics, and turns into what I have no trouble calling a piece of art.
While the gameplay suffers from a little bit of a slog around the late middle of the game, don't discount it, don't quit. If you're going to play this, see this through until the end. The atmosphere and setting should easily help you with that.
I will put a caveat about my recommendation, however:
The game not only suffers from performance issues, but is also quite short, and aside from catching up on collectibles offers almost no replay value. With less than 6 hours of playtime it is hard to justify a 35€ price point for this product, especially if you're looking for lots of content for your money. Only buy this full price if you absolutely value a short, focussed and directed experience.

Hoo boy, Rain World. It's fairly successful at what it sets out to do: have the player survive the predator-prey dynamic in a hostile and unpredictable world in the role of a weak, vulnerable creature.
The problem is... that didn't translate into a good
. At all.
The keyword here is unpredictable, which applies specifically to the enemies. To put it simply: they do as they please. They'll never be waiting for you at the same spot, instead roaming around across screens, maybe fighting each other, maybe hunting other prey, or
(okay, it's not common, but it has happened).
So you might already see where this is going. You play as this wimpy♥♥♥♥♥white jelly thing that depends heavily on wits and resources around it to outsmart and survive some grumpy boys and the occasional eldritch abomination. Only, there are a few issues:
1- the random nature of enemy behavior means that if the game is having a bad day and won't take any of your jellybean sass, you WILL die
2- the controls and enemy AI are not very consistent (yay for lizards spinning in place for no reason, among other things) and will screw you over from time to time
3- your resources and big brain, many times, won't be enough to overcome the clusterfug wrought by 1 and 2
But "hey", you may be thinking, "I can just be very careful and take the time to work around all the crap being thrown at me!". Haha. No, darling. You're on a timer, which means if you don't hurry your♥♥♥♥♥up to a shelter after getting fat enough to hibernate you get the privelege of becoming the test subject for the rate of survivability of a massive water nuke (spoiler: it's 0%).
That brings me to the next point: Karma. Each time you hibernate, you gain a Karma level, and lose one each time you die. You need those levels to go through gates separating areas, meaning that whenever the game decides to “prank” you a bunch of times in a row you’ll need to do some level grinding depending on where you want to go. Now, that’s not really as bad as it seems at first: new players might feel like they’re losing progress, but most of the time you won’t have to worry about karma, since each area is pretty sizable. It’s kinda like souls in Dark Souls: not that big of a deal. It can turn into a pain, though; particularly when you go through a gate into a new area and are trying to reach a shelter (i.e. save point), only to die and get sent back all the way with lower karma to boot, likely forcing you to spend at least a whole cycle just to build up enough karma and try again, praying to slug jesus the game won’t kick you in the mouth this time.
After some time of
playing you might start asking yourself “wait a minute, what’s the end game here? It can’t be just endlessly eating and sleeping over and over like some disgusting neet steam reviewer”. And you’re right. Like the intro shows us, in a twist of fate, little Slugcat gets separated from its loving family and thrust into the wilderness to fend for itself. It must now journey through perilous landscapes to
So this is Rain World, more or less. Explore tunnels, eat bats, throw spears, do the nirvana and get brutally murdered hundreds of times in BS situations on the way. Being a big fan of platformers and exploration, I
I can say I enjoyed my time with this game; its world is huge, beautiful and intriguing. But would I recommend it to most people? No way. Rain World turns out to be extremely frustrating thanks all the random chance involved in surviving predators and annoying inconsistencies in its design (most of which I didn’t even touch upon here because this thing is already huge as it is).
Dice rolls, man. They can really mess up your♥♥♥♥♥♥ so only venture in if you have really high tolerance for trying things over and over again.
There is an upcoming update which will add an easier mode and some improvements, however. Maybe that’ll convince me to change the recommendation here? Who knows.
On a final note, I have absolutely no sympathy for Slucats. They clearly demonstrate above-average intelligence and are able to use tools with no problems,
Please. It’s like they deserve to die at this point. I would say the same for Scavengers, but they at least are competent enough to craft decent weaponry and have the common sense to form small communities and spread around. They’re obviously the master race of Rain World but get relegated as goofy NPCs instead. What a shame.

A game targeted at all Stronghold, LOTR:BFME, and Age of Empire fans.
Task villagers to harvest resources, build up your castle/stronghold, raise armies to go questing/clearing areas/sieging/pvp, all while the units in said armies gain ranks and can become quite powerful.
Battles take place Total War style, the only setback is the fact that unit collision has little to no effect, battalions don't stick together, so tactics have a somewhat reduced effect here. Bringing villagers to battle is actually mandatory, because looting the fallen yields amazing amounts of resources, especially from PVP.
After any PVP (field battle or siege) you get some PVP protection time, so you're not overwhelmed from annoyingly nonstop PVP. Although, keepi in mind that the rewards from participating in PVP are quite bountiful. If you don't want to participate, a small bribe is possible, which is proportional to the army size. Smaller armies = smaller payouts. You do get PVP protection after a payout so it is possible to skip the whole PVP deal alltogether.
There is a special resource (crowns) which is necessary for all upgrades and high level units. It comes quite slowly at the beginning, but are most certainly attainable without paying real money. Ammasing gold is the way here, because crowns can be bought for gold at a rate of 1:5000. A solid economy is key, which is a must for any player of this type of game.
Solid game, If you loved Stronghold, BFME, or Age of Empires you should definitely try this one.

5/10 Got it for free, so I can't complain... but I really wouldn't recommend it to anyone.
TL;DR The two player cooperative gamemode is entertaining enough, and there's alot of room for two people to synergize. Singpleplayer brings you through the same missions. I've not touched PVP multiplayer, so I can't give any opinions on that.
If you have a friend its a pretty fun coop game, albeit with some obvious shortcomings.
As for the full review,
The premise is rather engaging; A lone sniper, deep within enemy territory, assassinating high priority targets. Lightly armed and completely unarmored, you have to rely on the advantage of range, stealth and traps.
Unfortunately the game isn't nearly as fun as it sounds.
Though the shooting mechanics are quite sound - the game features bullet drop and wind direction affecting the trajectory of your shots - shooting your enemies is not exactly rewarding. The AI is bad, and your enemies move erratically or stand in the open abruptly.
Stealth is not an option, which is a shame. There are some neat mechanics in the game, like periodic ambient noises masking any sound you generate, and ghostly images of your character as an indication of where you've last been seen by the enemy. Failing to kill an enemy in a single shot immediately results in them going on full alert, and they instantly know where you are. Enemy snipers may choose to engage you over infantry skirmishes infront of them, while you scout the area from far.
The game gives you many traps to fight an enemy with superior numbers. There are occasional explosive barrels and intact vehicles littered around the map. You can leave dynamite on the ground and shoot it when enemies walk by. Land mines and trip mines can be set up to watch your back. Unfortunately you rarely have any real opportunity to use these. Unless the mission requires you to hole up somewhere for a while, you're mostly on the offensive, and have no real need to cover your back. Even when you're on the defensive, your enemies make no real attempt to storm the building you're in, they just find some cover outside and try to return fire with their submachineguns. If the mission requires you to backtrack, enemies will just spawn where they should have had to walk past your traps to get to. There is no real place to survey the area and lay down these traps, and its far easier to just shoot everyone you see.

TL;DR what EA's Battlefront should have been, and more. Buy it for combined arms space war, but don't expect constantly populated servers.  This game is a ton of fun and I wouldn't regret buying it even if it were abandoned tomorrow.  Developers are highly active on their Discord room and not reliant on sales for funding.
(updated after update 17)
Gameplay is similar to Battlefield and Battlefront II, team based combined arms warfare on a pretty big scale - not Planetside, but none of the crippling bugs PS2 is known for, either.  Weapon customization is a huge deal here, as is budgeting equipment.  Easily worth the $18 of early access, this is a solid $40 game on release in my eyes
In-depth on ground warfare:
AI is in a great state, able to go toe to toe with players without cheating.  Bots feel natural and will flank, take alternate routes, and try to use splash damage
TTK in this game is relatively slow, which I enjoyed since it forced players to think more about what they were doing.  Netcode could use a little work - you have to lead targets to hit them.
Equipment has depth and is (mostly) without pointless options, but squad command is somewhat limited: "follow," "free roam," "interact with target," and "move" are the only commands, there is no way to indicate class or equipment preferences.
Visuals: a bit eh compared to AAA games, but servicable, consistent, and not ugly by any means.  For a small team, this is great.  The actual visual design is really cool, just don't expect the latest and greatest effects.  It's unreal engine 3, after all.  Postprocessing effects are also on an upward trend, with the latest update improving lighting and adding options
Sound: as of the sound update, every gun feels like it can ruin someone's day.  Not high fidelity, but very fun
Menus and options: The menu scales well on 4K and presents all the information you could want clearly.  However, it isn't as "atmospheric" as the previous menu.  Currently, the UI is very bland, but very practical.  The game has all the expected Unreal Engine options.  There is no tutorial right now.
Should you buy it?
It's almost in a finished state now, and most certainly playable.  You won't be wasting your money if you like space combat or Battlefield, even without further updates to the game.

Duke Nukem Forever is one of those odd little games that are usually overlooked because of it's flaws.Yes the game isn't perfect . The storyline is very predictable and the game isn't exactly a graphical powerhouse. This game is however one of the most satisifying first person shooters I have ever played. Almost all of the games weapons are unique and fun to use and this game makes one of gamings greatest sins, backtracking, actually enjoyable. This is done with clever implementation of a device that shrinks Duke to action-figure size. You will go through a level as tiny Duke, and then go backwards as the normal sized Duke. Each version of Duke (tiny/normal) will face different obstacles. This is level design done right.
The game does have a few new weapons to play around with, but most of them aren't very interesting or just plain underpowered, but they make up for this by always having ammo within reach, thus making it an expendable weapon, and also the ultimate backup in case your main weapons empty out.
Some things are just downright stupid in this game. Duke can only carry 2 weapons at a time. This can be icnreased to 4 on the pc version. A Duke Nukem game should let you carry lots of weapons. Just look at half life 2, Gordon Freeman can carry 10+ weapons, so having a maximum of 4 is just unnacceptable.
The game has plenty of references, as you would expect from a Duke Nukem game. None of them break the immersion from the game too much, and it's actually really nice to see them in there. You can tell the developers had fun with this game.
Even after the long wait, Duke Nukem Forever is still just a Duke Nukem game. Aside from it's flaws, I'd say its a pretty fantastic game that many people can enjoy. Duke Nukem Forever, is a game I would recommend. Just don't go in expecting it to be perfect.

So many knee-jerk reaction reviews for this game.  Please disregard the majority of the negative reviews you will see for this game.  I'll be honest, I'm a little embarrassed at the community right now.
This is not to say that there aren't legitimate criticisms to be levied against this game.  Clearly there are.  First and foremost, the non-intuitive mana tapping REALLY throws a wrench into the dynamic of this game compared to other entries from the series.  In previous Duels of the Planeswalkers games, it wasn't perfect, but the game was pretty good at determining which mana to tap based on the other cards in your hand.  This is not the case in 2015, and it's not clear why this mechanic was changed.
Secondly, people aren't wrong about the menus being clunky and slow.  I want to play the already, dammit!  Stop making me sift through waves of menus that are overly animated and take way to long.  It won't be annoying at first, but after you've restarted your campaign match for the 10th time, it's incredibly frustrating that it takes sooooo long between when you press a button and when something happens.  Watching the screen slowly fade to white will become an agonizing exercise.
That's really the only two bad things that stick out to me in this game.  The main thing that everyone seems to be complaining about is the fact that there is a premium group of cards that are not available to unlock in the game without purchasing them separately as DLC.  To be clear 43 of the 298 cards are locked behind this "premium pay wall."  Every other card in the game is able to be unlocked through normal play.  The 255 cards that don't require payment are perfectly diverse and varied.  Enough so, that a wide variety of strategies can be utilized through the use of custom deck building with all of those cards at your disposal.  The irony of this whole situation is that if one were to buy the 255 cards that aren't DLC, they sure as hell would be paying a hell of a lot more than $10.  And sure, one might make the case that actual physical cards can be re-sold, and to that I say, "sure, but it's only $10 for 255 cards.  You're still saving like over a $100 (possibly more), so I'm a little unnerved by the overwhelmingly negative response here.
I think it serves to mention, that there is custom deck building in this game.  The thing that most DofP players have been clamoring about for years has finally arrived, and what is the response from the community?  A resounding "♥♥♥♥ you" to the developers behind this game because of the "day 1 DLC."  Don't get me wrong, I'm not crazy about the fact that 43 of the cards are locked behind a "pay wall" either, but the game itself still plays very well.  Part of the reason that they have included the "premium deck" has to do with the fact that that you can actually play this game just like traditional M:TG with deck building and all.  a 255 card series is pretty commensurate with standard M:TG series blocks.
Getting access to an entire block of cards for $10 is still a ♥♥♥♥ing steal, and them putting an additional group of cards behind a "pay wall" is frustrating, but they're certainly not ripping you off.  The game is still a great value at the MSRP price tag, even without the additional premium cards.  And it's not like the "premium cards" give any player an advantage over players using standard (non-premium) cards.  It's just for added variety.  I'm sorry but usually I side with you guys on situations like this, but those of you muckraking are just dead wrong here.

Wizards of the Coast and Stainless Games have listened to hardcore fans and finally given them what they want: a sales funnel.
I'm having a hard time grasping how Magic 2015 became such a mess. Previous games in the series have been wonderful, offering the components and mechanics of the Magic: The Gathering card game without the overly involved meta-game. Choose one of the pre-configured decks, play a quick game online, then step away from the computer and enjoy the other passions in your life. I contend that it is one of the most enjoyable ways to play Magic: The Gathering, if only because you don't have to interact with the sort of people who play Magic: The Gathering on a regular basis.
A common criticism of Magic 2015's predecessors was "Why can't I build my own deck from scratch using all of the Magic cards ever made?" This is similar to walking into a coffee shop and asking for a porterhouse steak. No one will argue that it's what you'd most desire at that given moment, but the resources exist for you to have that experience without making the world collapse and conform to your immediate needs. There is a game called Magic: The Gathering Online that allows players to have the "complete" Magic: The Gathering experience, such as spending hundreds of dollars to build the same deck that everyone else is using because of a mechanical exploit. That is it's own thing. You can go out onto the internet and type "Magic: The Gathering Online" in a search engine, with or without quotes, and spend lots of money on digital trading cards. The Duels of the Planeswalkers series has offered a different experience, more akin to a fighting game. It was a well balanced game that afforded many different play styles and allowed players to have fun regardless of their skill level.
Magic 2015 does away with pre-configured decks almost completely. You play a tutorial and then choose from a list of different decks. None of them are very good. You can not change your deck after choosing without deleting your save file and starting over. You must use that deck for the first section of the campaign. If you are patient you will eventually unlock the ability to build your own decks, but only after slogging through numerous battles with the starter deck.
When you win a battle, you are rewarded with a booster. This booster contains a few cards that are almost certainly worthless to you. Maybe you are playing with a black zombie deck. Your booster might contain three green cards that are not zombies. And you'll say, "Wow, I wish I could get lucky and open a booster with some good zombie cards in it!" The solution to this is to purchase a premium booster. These premium boosters contains the Good Cards. They cost $1.99 each. You can buy as many as you want. The only way to get the Good Cards is by buying premium boosters. If you buy enough of them, you might get a Great Card that wins the game when you play it. If you don't buy enough of them, you will be at a disadvantage when playing online against the people who did buy enough of them. These people will play a Great Card and you will lose the game.
It is important to remember that you have paid at least $9.99 for this experience.
Design decisions like these have turned a reasonably solid series into something foul. You should not buy this game. You should not play this game. If you want a casual game of Magic: The Gathering, buy Duels of the Planeswalkers 2014. It is well balanced and fun to play. If you want to spend exorbitant amounts of money building whatever deck is dominating the Magic: The Gathering meta-game, play Magic: The Gathering Online. If you want a real challenge, open a coffee shop that sells porterhouse steaks. Let me know how it does.
One additional item that I absolutely must mention as part of my "See Something, Say Something" campaign against offensive user experiences: the menus in this game are presented in a slideshow fashion, where you can only see one menu option at a time and have to cycle through each screen. This results in the inability to view menu options that are currently disabled. So it's impossible to judge your progress in the campaign, which is unfortunate because most of the game's content is hidden away behind various milestones. FAQs online told me that deck building was unlocked after beating Avanyc, but due to the poor menu system I was unable to determine how many more events I needed to clear before I reached that point. The "unnumbered list" menu system used in the previous games, as well as almost every single piece of interactive media produced since the beginning of time, would have been a much better solution for content navigation.

RiME is a wonderful adventure, a game I didnt think I would enjoy but after finishing the game, and finally piecing everything togheter it made the whole thing a really great experience.
Just as Hob and other games, RiME does not tell you the story by dialogue or text, but instead it tells you by visual queues or by soundtrack, ultimately revealing the whole story at the end. Its hard to describe without spoiling but I will say this, you wont expect the ending. I enjoy obscure story telling and RiME did a good job at it.
Visually, RiME looks incredible. You will progress through lots of varied zones, from sunny beatiful islands, to dark caverns. Whats great about the levels is that every single one is tied to the story and once you finish it, you'll understand in what way. Theres also a time of day in the first map which was fantastic.
Gameplay basically consists of platforming and puzzle solving. All are incredibly easy and straightforward. I would've enjoyed a bit of a challenge though. Still, it never gets dull and it always feels cool.
Soundtrack, as with everything else in the game is tied to the story as well. The more you progress the soundtrack shifts its tone. The songs are well made and arguably touching.
Overall, what I was expecting to be just an okay adventure game, turned out to be a really great experience. Highly recommended 8.5/10.

Upfront I will admit that this is one of my favourite games on PC. I have currently sunk over 2300 hours into it.
That may mean that I have become so enamoured with it that I will not be objective, but come on. If you've played a game for that long a time, there must be SOMETHING good about it.
At it's heart Team Fortress 2 (TF2) is a first person shooter (FPS). The key difference to a lot of other FPS games is right there in the title. You play this game as part of a TEAM, not to pwn every other person in the server.
There are nine classes you can choose to play, and as you get better at the game you will choose to play a class based on the situation that you find your team in. Changing can be done once you die, or if you run back to spawn, so you aren't locked into a class for the entirety of a match.
The classes are all very distinct although, as time has progressed, different weapons have changed this somewhat eg. slower classes can now get a speed boost, ground classes can now fly, etc.
There are a huge variety of weapons to choose from, with new ones constantly being added, mostly through fans who have designed them.
You can slowly achieve all the weapons over time just by playing the game, or you can buy them in a shop if you want to widen your arsenal quickly.
Luckily all the stock weapons supplied as the starting ones for each character are often the strongest ones to use, so it's not really pay to win.
Besides having a variety of weapons to collect, the game has another more controversial collecting option.
As you may have already heard, it is all about the hats, and other various miscellaneous pieces of attire. You can either purchase these, craft them, trade for them, or earn them.
There are an almost infinite number of item layouts you can use for your various characters. What this means is that you can dress your character in a fashion that shows off your personal style.
This can range from whacky, to serious. You can actually save 4 different sets of items to each character, making it easy to switch from a very professional looking Soldier for Competitve play, to a Halloween costumed robot.
Some find the TF2 market has dilluted the purpose of the game, making some people get more interested in playing dressups rather than killing people, but I think it has widened how people interact with the TF2.
I must confess, I have a very large collection of TF2 hats and other cosmetic items, so I am probably more in favour of enjoying the collection aspect.
Items that are rarer cost more to purchase from other players, in the Steam Market.
These include items that were produced in limited quantities, or items with special effects, referred to as Unusuals.
The game has an aspect of fun not only in letting you choose what to wear, but in giving each character dialogue to say that reflects their unique personality, and also by making Taunts available. These let you do stuff like start dancing a conga, that other players can join even if they don't own that particular Taunt.
There are many other things you can do in TF2 than collect cosmetics or weapons, and kill other opponents.
You can play a variety of different types of games.
Some of these are:
* Mann vs Machine where you and a small team of players try to destroy teams of robots
* Saxton Hale maps where it is one team vs a boss
* Seasonable maps such as ones that come out every Halloween, and include such things as bumper car racing
* A hide and seek style of map
* Maps where you play a deadly sport-like game with other players
* Duels against one other person on a regular server
* Melee only games
* Rocket jumping maps where you suffer no damage
There are so many that I'm not going to describe them all. You can even make a private server to play in with friends, and create your own type of fun with games like Rocket tennis, Heavy boxing, etc.
This gives you an endless variety of different TF2 pursuits, which in turn gives the game so much extra value.
New maps are usually released at least once a year, most of them designed by members of the TF2 community. They are usually excellent, and extend the life of the game.
Valve also opens up Contracts for players to purchase from time to time. They reward players for completing certain objectives, usually in the form of unique skins or paints for weapons. This feeds back into dressing your character to reflect your personality.
I could go on and on about this game, as there are so many other things it allows you to do.
It's core is team against team, and that is honestly where I spend most of my time, and have the most fun.
You may not score very highly on the board, but it might be your essential play that gets your team over the line to win a match. That means that less skilled players still contribute to the final result, making them not feel like they are just "bad git gud scrub".
Once you have played for a while you start to know which classes you are best at playing, and it is easier to get the most out of what each one does.
If you like to be a support, offensive, or defensive class you have lots of different characters to play in that style.
Some classes can also be used in more than one of these ways eg. you can play as a Battle Medic who doesn't heal other players, but instead attacks with his syringe gun and trusty knife.
The community isn't too toxic, although there will always be elements of that in most FPS games. There is the option to mute annoying players and you can choose just not to read the in game feed if it is annoying you.
When I think about Team Fortress 2 I think about all the fun I have had with it over the years, and continue to have eight years after I started playing it.
If you like also like to have fun, while playing as a team and testing your FPS skills, this is the game for you.

I loved this game as a kid. It is one of those games where you can waste hours without even noticing it. It is still interesting nowadays, although the graphics, etc. are a little bit outdated.

Similar in sense to Limbo in that both games have strong starts and then, after a certain beat is resolved, they just meander.
RiME builds a beautiful world with stunning cel-shaded style artwork and a soaring soundtrack, and entices you with early ideas about where things might go. But then, after a memorable area of hide-and-seek (like Limbo's spider), the plot gets lost. Mechanics that are introduced get a little bit of iteration and then are never used again.
You're supposed to be climbing a tower, but then randomly you'll just be in some other area entirely. One part has a groundhog day-esque section, then in another you're really just following some magic robots. The forest area was a confused mess, with no clear goal. Neither does the rainy area have a sense of place - it's just an arena to run around and solve four simplistic platforming puzzles. Where is it? Is it on top of the tower? It looks too big to be there. If these were meant to be inside the tower, it sure didn't feel like it. If these were meant to be around the tower, the tower should have been there in the background as a reminder of where we were and what our main goal is.
The game tries to give a sense of emotional weight to its narrative, but it doesn't spend enough time developing it. The fox for example, you bring it into being at the start and then it just acts as a guide of where to go. You don't really interact with it further, and then it rushes through its beats at the end. The nameless spirits are sometimes scared, then they're dangerous, then they're indifferent. Sometimes the soundtrack perfectly picks up the pace and setting, other times it's curiously absent.
With a better sense of progression of the tower, more interaction with the few characters so that their stories carried more weight, it could be greatly improved. It's an enjoyable experience, maybe a 6.5/10. Worth playing, but certainly a game with many rough edges that loses its direction in the later acts.

~The games does not explain almost anything to players. Exploring the world and moving forward will take a lot of experimentation, observation and wit. But unlike some games that love to hide information from players just for the sake of it and punishing them with trial and error, Rain World encourages curiosity. To a reasonable degree of course ( "What will happen if I throw a rock in the face of this big and mean-looking lizzard? OH GOD I REGRET EVERYTHING!" ) There will ALWAYS be signs of danger, if you are paying attention. I never encountered cheap traps or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t deaths. Just remember to be observant and listen to your little friend - hologram worm (or whatever that thing is).
~The game is a constant race against the clock - to do all your business during the cycle and get back to your safe spot and hibernate to wait out ruthless rainstorms. Different cycles, however, have different duration. So, again - pay attention and everything will be fine. Some people might not like the constant threat of time running out.
-There is no difficulty selection at the moment. (I've heard that developers are aiming to add this feature in soon-to-come-out update.) While for me the game is fine as it is, I can understand if some people will get frustrated with it. Sometimes, Rain World can be brutal and unforgiving.

I find myself a simple person. I like amazing graphics, exploration, feeling successful, and solving puzzles or otherwise feeling witty and special. I, having had family deaths in my history, do not like stories where a person or animal you become attached to passes away. I do not like admitting that the cycle of grief exists or that I have problems accepting the past. I especially didn't like the symmetry between my mom passing away and the scene witnessed through the keyhole.
Still, I like this game. It throws trials at you that may require some poking at times, but are simple enough to enjoy the scenery. I love the way you move through the water, considering few games realize how difficult it can be to be partially in the water.There's also the way the grief cycle is represented; it hit the feels. I'd love to talk about it more, but I'm also trying to be vague and let you figure it out yourself.
I recommend looking into it; the puzzles aren't as tough to solve as those presented in The Legend of Zelda, but it's got a way more complex story than rescuing a princess from a tyrant. Besides, it's beautiful; story and graphics-wise. I would put this at ... probably a nine out of ten for recommendation.

Rain World is one of the most unique games I've ever played; you won't find the same experience in any other game. Seriously, there's nothing else like it. Every aspect of the game: the sound, the art, the gameplay and world design are nothing short of excellent.
I could write an essay on everything I like about Rain World, and in my opinion, the game is virtually flawless (besides a couple bugs here and there). That said, the game is kind of niche; not everyone is going to enjoy it, so rather than rant about how great the game is, I'm going to explain what kind of experience to expect from this game.
The central idea of this game is to simulate an ecosystem that you are actively a part of. All of the creatures interact with each-other, you, and the world as a whole. The AI is quite advanced, for example: each creature has their own opinion of you and will react to how you behave. It is actually quite fun to just watch all the creatures AI interacting with each-other. If you're a fan of emergent gameplay, this game has a LOT of that. Another cool thing about this game is the procedural animations, they're quite impressive and I haven't seen another game attempt them on the scale that Rain World does. They look silly sometimes, but that is a part of the game's charm. The procedural animations combined with the dynamic AI make the game (and ecosystem) feel very alive.
If most of that sounds good to you, then I would highly recommend this game.

In
, you find yourself gathering wind power and expending it to fly; burning wood in an oven to afford blowing up your foes with fireballs; building with blocks and bringing those constructions to life.
What initially seems like a
is much rather a craft-and-animate title where you will find yourself trying to come up with shapes that the game can bring to life in one form or another. The tutorial starts out with you turning blocks into preset door and chest models, which by itself is not particularly spectacular, but after you experience dynamic windmill construction, where you give life to a windmill with a blade length of your choice, you'll notice that the game has some truly special potential along those lines.
It gets even better with giving life to NPC bipeds, which can have almost any shape you want, and are animated convincingly. The true potential of the game definitely lies in detecting and uniquely animating more things than just bipeds. Tripeds, spiders, birds, fish and so on would all be wonderfully jolly additions.
The author has been quick to add in
, and hopefully it will at some stage be possible for users to expand the available 'dynamic' objects/creatures. So far skins, buildings and some slight object changes are possible.
Multiplayer unfortunately does not have feature parity with singleplayer and is a much buggier affair overall.
With enough development time, there's a lot of promise here. The required triumvirate is polish, content and moddability.

Forewarning:  Prepare for a grind.  With that being said, you can also prepare yourself for feelings of accomplishment and pride.  I fully recommend this game despite the "Mixed" reviews.
All right, so I've had this game for a while now.  I can't recall at what point I purchased it, but I can tell you there have been MANY improvements and implementations into the game since.  I love this game.
The devs are open with the community, they're actively tracking and fixing bugs, and I can't help but love the crazy Ruskis behind it.
On with the Pros/Cons:
Pros:
You can terraform anything.  With a big enough group, you can level a huge area pretty quickly, or make your own plataeu village.
Requires seamless cooperation from multiple people to achieve amazing ends.
Certain resources are actually area-dependent, promoting trade between towns.
Settings can be adjusted - You can max out all the skills in a short time, or play something closer to realistic.
Animals will kill you if you're not properly prepared for it.  Don't chase down wolves with your bare hands.
Everything is player made.  I LOVE crafting and the way it was implemented in this game.
My favorite aspect:  EVERYTHING HAS QUALITY!  Your end-game here is producing perfect materials and items.
Cons:
Requires seamless cooperation from multiple people to achieve amazing goals.  If you don't have a group, I bid you good luck in finding some Canadians to take you in.  They're nice people.  Really.
Combat takes a lot of practice.
Worst thing I can think of:  The grind can be a little too realistic.  While you're going to want those awesome stone walls and towers put up, you're also going to have to spend your "down time" shaping stone and moving logs.  It's like snapping peas, though, make it a social thing.  It can be very zen sometimes.

The heart of Alchemist's Awakening is an open-world creative sandbox that has a lot of possibilities for the future. Only time and more users will determine exactly what the world becomes. There is potential for it to be a PVE survival with more advanced enemies to fight, requiring different elements, new attack methods, etc. With more active users, there is a chance it will become more of a PVP survival game, where your only safe haven is your home.
All possibilities aside, what the game is right now is a beautiful open-world sandbox where you can build almost anything you want in your section of land that you claim. You can work together with other players, share resources via community chests and element generators, and enjoy the pleasant visuals of the world. The crafting system is why you are an alchemist: the UI allows you to mix elements that you've collected to essentially have a menu to create tons of other objects, elements, and other interactive tools. Want to harness wind you collected from the windmill to fly around the clouds? You can do that. Combine the wind with fire you collected from your oven to create a fireball? No problem.
One reason I mention possibilities in addition to the features that are already included is because the developer is very active and responsive. Updates have been released consistently to include bug fixes, new features, and even the implementation of user feedback. This is an Early Access title that hasn't stopped development.
Another really nice feature of this game is Steam Workshop support. You can create or have access to many buildings and characters that have been created.  By subscribing to skins on the workshop, you can have your character appear as popular figures such as SpongeBob or Link, or self-made designs, including a polar bear with a jetpack, which is my personal favorite.  The developers recently offered to export user-created buildings as they migrated to a new back-end that would allow endless worlds.  This is the type of support and care being provided to the current users.

I'm writing this review because some negative reviews led to me almost not buying it.  I am sincerely glad that I did.  This is the game that I've always wanted.
Let me tell you about my first night on LiF.  I logged into an RP server and was almost  instantly greeted by experienced players who were not only willing to help me with every question that I had - but also fillled me in on all the political happenings that were revelant to that evening.  the community, if nothing else, makes this game worth playing.
Before I knew it, they outfitted me with a basic sling and some sling ammo and I was marching off to battle.  We arrived through the woods to a small fort in the north which seemed relatively empty - I was disappointed at first: This was it?  Little did we know that the enemy was crouching behind their walls equipped with heavy plated armor and bowmen galore.  After about 20 minutes, two concussions, an arrow through the chest, and general astoundment that I was still alive - I heard that the enemy king was knocked unconscious and his nobles lay dead around him.  Opposed to killing the enemy king, our king inisisted that we let him regain consciousness so he could role play his reaction to the embarassing defeat.
While waiting patiently around him, celebrating our clear victory, we were ambushed by almost a dozen of the fallen king's allies from the west.  They streamed in behind us and we fled with our tails behind our legs.  By the time we hobbled back home, bloodied and broken, we had only lost one ally - a clear victory if you ask me!
Since then, peace has been negotiated and I've decided to make a pacifist character. - dedicating  my time to building a religious school on top of a mountain.  That's the best part of this game, you can literally do whatever you want.  Want to be a cook? Someone needs you in their guild.  Want to be a warrior? Someone wants you for their realm.  Want to dedicate your time to stacking wood, mining deep into a mountain, watching wheat grow? Well, you're probably going to have to do it anyway.
Admittedly, I've only been playing LiF for 15 hours (and that is not much for this game!) but i felt like it was my duty to defend it at least a little bit.
Yes this game is still in development, yes there are many features that haven't been implemented yet.  But I promise you that if you connect with the right people in-game then its not something you will regret contributing to.  There's a steep learning curve but once you get a hang of it everythings really intuitive and well thought out.  I can't wait for final release.

Review:
Angels Fall First give a unique game where you play with marines (may I add they look very much like models from Titanfall, pretty close anyway) for The Emperor or its opposition across many different maps whether it be on a planet or in space, the action never stops. The customisability is absolutely endless, you can take a 7x scope and put it on a Shotgun, or have a Sniper Rifle without a scope, then change the ammunition to become Incendiary - wait, no, make it become Corrosive to fight against shields - and  then just add a bunch of other equipment; such as a turret. There's many maps to choose from; they range from space dog-fighting (no, not THAT illegal dog fighting, I mean planes vs planes or whatever you'd like to call it) to close quarters combat. The weapon selection is pretty endless, too. Snipers, grenade-launchers, assault rifles, shotguns, boomsticks (more OP shotguns) and many more to come, many different guns in each category can make up for tons of different play-styles to suit everyone. Are you very precise with mouse movements? Great, you can take a sniper. Are you great with flanking people? Great, take an assault rifle, you should be good to go. Are you great with flying giant ships? Take one from a large selection of ships and have fun.
Many hours of crying because you can't beat Difficulty 4 bots (There's 5 difficulties, 1 being the easiest, 5 being the hardest). AFF has very smart AI technology being used due to lack of players in the game, so you have to play PvE most of the time, sadly. So these aren't your average below bad player skill rank bots, these are ones which actually can complete the whole game without any of your help due to strategies. Certain bots will support others which are in need, others will push if given the chance depending on their position in the battlefield. You can play however you want to, be a sniper or not, use grenades or attachments, become a lone wolf or team player, kill or be killed (maybe this isn't such of a choice, you're gonna die... a lot). The maps are large, open and designed for fun play; there's many strategic points in the maps, so you should be on the look for them if you want to win but not to lose in the process. Players who play this game  are quite skilled, it has to be said; but the bots are definitely better than many. At the end of every match you will get to see your (depressing) statistics such as your Kills and Deaths, saviour, nemesis and so on.

It's going to be a bit long so here's a TLDR: This is the first draft of a fantastic game.
Here's the whole thing:
It's a FPS on the scale of Battlefield or Battlefront, and utilizes combined arms detailing use of infantry ground vehicles, aircraft, and space born capital ships.
Infantry combat is very smooth and well done, and gunplay seems very well balanced initially.
Ground vehicles work well with simple auto-control for unmanned turrets and a small, useful variety of secondary weapons.
Aircraft is a third person style of combat that reminds me of Strike Suit. It works well, though the point of view of the helpess soldiers in the back of the drop ship could use a bit of work as they easily get confused on what is happening.
Capital ships are the bases and seem generic but functional.
Gameplay styles are mixed and show depth and inventiveness, having to not only clear a minefield with fighters while bombers knock out station guns, followed by an assault phase where dropships need to be escorted and every fighter that escorts them is one less fighter guarding the mothership, while needing troops to actually take part in the assault the dropships faciltate a feeling of being immersed in a war not a  battlefield.
Combend it makes me feel absolutely wonderful and makes me think that this is what Battlefront should have been.
The UI needs a ton of work. If you know what you're doing and what's happening it functions as an update for issues around you, but for anyone that isn't particularly adept and figuring out the UI style (or has poor eyesight as words and symbols are small and smashed together) you're confused the entire time.
Overall it's osmething that makes me wonder why EA and DICE screwed up Battlefront and Hardline so much if they had so many people and so much money. This is done on a shoestring budget and less than two handfuls of people and plays much smoother and better than either of those games in my opinion.
Bottom line is: Play it if you're willing to sit through an intense learning curve of UI management while waiting for it to be their next target for polishing. Buy it if you love large scale FPS with combined arms tactics, such as Battlefield, Battlefront, or Planetside (the good one). Avoid it if you don't have the patience to watch a work in progress proceed with the miniscule budget and manpower they have. It's something that, when done, you will want to be able to brag about having been a part of from the beginning.

So I've finished this game after just 17 hours of rather slow gameplay and I have to say that compared to the first one I'm kind of disappointed.
I've played it in single player since I do not care for co-op or multiplayer.
This game can be characterized by two words: repetitiveness and over-complications where it does not have to be.  We've got about five different environments.. well more like 5 maps where all missions happens, you'll find yourself going to several locations multiple times and what's worse all story and secondary missions are kind of the same. There's more of "deja vu" moments than "wow" moments. In first game every mission was kind of original, you've visited the same place only in few specific occasions.
There are only 3 bosses and the last one is laughably easy.
Death means nothing in this game... yes you lose some money and xp but it does not matter since you have more than enough of both. Takes away the challenge. You cannot die when you fall. No save/load...
And the story which was especially latter part of the first game something that made me go forward, to see how it will all end... yes there is story, but all characters are unlikable, no strong moments, no powerful finale like first game.
Authors added gem crafting which is absolutely useless, a lot of weapons that sadly crushed the feeling of happiness of finding or upgrading a weapon to a more powerful one... Also weapons are terribly unbalanced: Mele weapons almost useless, good pump-up shotgun, gauss gun and good machine gun with RPG for bosses were all that I had used, the rest I've tried but found useless.
Graphic and sounds were fine, except for that hi-tech city environment - too much lights.
Overall this game failed where the first one ruled: mission design, weapon design and balance (I've loved katana and what I could do with it in the first game) and most of all story. Even Wang had better character design in first one, in this he was written as a immature brat...
For me it is 4,5/10 for those who liked first game and thus not recommended, for those who did not play the first game it would be 6/10 but I'd recommend them to go and play the first one, it is much better.

I tried... I really REALLY tried. I absolutely LOVED Duke Nukem 3D. I even had the whole Kill-a-ton pack with all of the add-ons. Needless to say, I was quite excited for the ever delayed Duke Nuke Forever. I waited till I could purchase it and proceeded to play through it.
I will start off saying that I really did enjoy the never shorted cheese factor (something I loved about the Duke 3D game). I also enjoyed most of the wide interactivity of many things in the game world.
Now for THE REST OF THE GAME; horrible, just horrible. The constant attempts at creating advanced puzzles based on all the hard work in making most of the world interactive lead to needlessly complicated puzzles that either took far too long to figure out, or were infinitely frustrating in dealing with doing EXACTLY what they want, step by step, or sudden demise. This would not even be much of an issue if the game supported quick saves... but alas, this is another game that employs the ever so frustrating "check point" way of saving. There were way too many times that there were large stretches of the game between check points, then other times where the check points were close together... and of course the further stretched check points always came way after an absurdly over drawn and stupidly difficult puzzle full of far too many frustratingly easy ways to die.
Again, I really REALLY tried to like this game, I really did! Hell, I even argued and fought in the name of the Duke series... but I was proven wrong and forced to agree with the masses; this game just sucks. It is frustrating, annoying, and generally just left me feeling angry as I rush to quit the game as fast as possible.
