RiME is an extraordinary little game full of charm. There is not a word of dialogue (that is comprehensible), yet it knows to tell a story and guide you along through a beautifully designed world. What struck me the most is that you could feel the passion of the developers, there is a lot of raw emotion injected into the game which reveals itself slowly but surely and leads to a satisfying conclusion. The game itself is not difficult, it has fairly straightforward puzzles but the pacing is great. It's relatively slow, but it suits the vibe of the game and it builds the intrigue more and more as you go on.
The game starts out in a world that's seemingly open and ready for exploration, which it is to an extent, but it's mostly secrets and collectibles that hide in the corners of the world. The game itself is linear and that's okay. The world is interesting enough that the exploration feels satisfying just to make your way through the beautifully crafted design. I definitely felt drawn to investigate the nooks and crannies and interact with all the objects that allowed it.
The main character is part of what makes the game awesome. The entire game revolves around this boy that finds itself in this mysterious place, guided by a little fox while the full story gets revealed through flashbacks and symbolism throughout the course of the game. His design is absolutely adorable, with a bright red cape and an innocent appearance. There is a dedicated 'yell' button (which activates certain objects in the game) which is the best. I love yelling at stuff. I love how flames flair up as he screams and I basically couldn't stop screaming (or humming depending on the situation). His animations are also just lovely. He feels genuine and lovable in a world that caters to his mystery.
All in all a very recommended game. It takes obvious inspiration from Team Ico games, especially Ico. If you enjoy those types of games then this is right up your alley. At times there are some janky moments with the camera or controls, but honestly it's not to the point of frustration. I just frigging loved playing RiME.

It’s five years after the end of the first KOTOR and the galaxy is still in turmoil. The Republic is struggling to recover from three wars in less then a century and the Jedi seems to have been wiped from existence but there is you an exile cast out of the Jedi Order for following Revan to the Mandalorian Wars and now the Sith are back and trying to kill you.
The story this time around is a big improvement over the first KOTOR and you get more information on the Mandalorian Wars and the effect it caused but first you are on the Ebon Hawk and its in pretty bad shape after getting attacked and after the prologue tutorial you wake up on the Peragus mining facility where everyone seems to have been killed by the mining droids and you need to find out what the hell is going on
The first thing about your character is that you are a Jedi from the start so you can get some more powers early on and you can become a higher class of Jedi by choosing one of three classes depending on your alignment the light side ones are like Jedi Weapon master but when you’re evil it’s pretty much the same class but with different names like Sith Marauder and now you can go up to level 30. There are of course new moves and powers but my personal favourite is when you go evil and get Force Crush with this you lift someone up and crush there body and most of the time it’s a one hit kill and is very useful for tough bosses.
Also as you will see early on your skills have more effect this time like the computer skill is good for hacking terminals to see some useful information or killing enemies without the hassle of a fight, with repair you can get some droid help or see some funny stuff like on Dantooine with some ‘friendly droids’, treat injury actually gets some uses like healing sick people or seeing medical related dialogue and so on.
Another big difference this time around is influence, if you have someone who likes kindness and you do something kind when they are in your party then they may reveal more information to you about themselves if you have enough influence and others will like cruelty and being agreed with, so it’s good to pay attention to each member of your crew to learn more about them and more about the story as another chapter in the Star Wars saga unfolds. This influence can also be used to make some party members into Force users if you choose to go that route.
You will get a different character depending on your gender and alignment so it makes for more difference every time you play through, I’ve played through five times already as male and female and of course good and evil and I’m still finding new things after playing it so much.
There are a lot of great new features in this sequel but it is also missing deeper missions that go beyond of kill that, get me that but hopefully this may be implemented in KOTOR 3 if it ever gets made and it may be shorter then the first KOTOR (without the TSLRCM
Mod)  but because of such difference which each different choice then this is easily twice as long as the original.
In the end nothing is perfect but if it was then you wouldn’t want anything else so let me just say KOTOR 2 is a huge improvement over the original and is made even better with The Restored Content Mod that adds in many things that were cut from the original release as Obsidian was forced to rush the game for the holiday season.
So if you enjoy Star Wars and RPG’s then give this one a go and you will find a very well crafted game that is still fun and interesting to play after ten years of being available to buy.

One of the best gaming experiences I've had. This game is definitely not for everyone, especially not people who:
1. Are easily frustrated.
2. Are looking for fast-paced progression.
Pros:
A very beautiful art style
The soundtrack is great
The lore of the world is intriguing
It's TOUGH. Not just "hard" but actually really really tough. Most things kill you in a single hit, and you get punished rather severely for dying (explained in cons). Of course this won't be a pro for everyone, but it was for me.
Managing to get through a difficult area feels amazing every time.
Neutral:
Overall progression is slow-paced, though encounters with the flora and fauna can get extremely tense.
All movement is based on the physics engine which makes everything move around super smooth.
Since all movement is based on physics, you can expect to see some buggy/wonky movement of the creatures in the world (Including the character you play as).
There's barely anything telling you where to go, which can often make you feel lost.
Cons:
To be able to progress to new areas, you have to have a certain amount of karma. Every time you hibernate (or save) without dying, you get an extra karma point, which caps at 5. Though every time you die, you lose one. If you want to progress to another area but you don't have the right amount of karma, you sometimes end up having to hibernate in the same area 4 times in a row, which can get rather repetitive, though I never had huge problems with this myself, I can certainly see people struggling with this mechanic. (NOTE: They are adding a new character who does not need karma to progress to other areas)
It doesn't help that "cheap" deaths happen occasionally. (Getting instakilled by an enemy you couldnt see)
Though it is without doubts one of my favorite games on steam, it's not meant everyone.

Kingdom Wars is a amazing title to play if you are into the rts genre. Taking the scale of the total war series and stronghold games it is a game you are sure to play for hours. Going off of graphics they have a very sound sound engine (pun intended) that has very realistic effects and ambience.

The devs and mods are on all the time with their fanbase and players supporting and helping when they can. It can also be a little on the hard to run side if your computer is a little on the lower side. With the amount and time the devs put in this game can only get better in the future.

rain world is a beautiful game with gorgeous environments, amazing music, wonderfully-designed worlds, and unique enemies. exploring the regions laid out for you is rewarding if only for the experience, and discovering new things and finding out more and more about the world of the slugcat is the focal point of this game, and it is masterfully done. each new discovery feels awe-inspiring as you slowly crack open the mystery of this world you've been dropped into. it makes you want to continue searching, and when you're on a good streak, you won't ever want to stop admiring the game's beauty and beholding its lore.
however, the game's downfall is that the controls feel sloppy and poor at times, leading to accidental deaths, and while they might be loose on purpose to give the slugcat a wobbly, marshmallowy feel, it's an unfortunate choice for a game such as this one in which you'll be running away from predators, performing hairpin turns, leaping across chasms of death, and trying to pinball your way into tiny holes in a mad effort to escape being another critter's meal. in addition, the difficulty is punishing, and you will die a lot. this is a trial-and-error game that, sadly, punishes you for trying, which makes it very difficult to get very far in the game very quickly.
this is a game that you absolutely must take your patience with, and if you don't love it from the start, you probably won't end up enjoying it as you continue burning through this slow, exploration-based platformer. the trick to enjoying rain world is to stop focusing on progressing and just take it easy and enjoy the scenery. when the time comes to progress, then it's time to move on, but forcing a deadline on yourself is going to make the game feel ridiculously unfair. it's a game meant to be taken at a snail's pace, much like the little slugcat, and pushing forward at the speed of light is only going to get you a swift death and frustration.
this is a good game to take in tiny chunks and not burn through all in one night.
also, thankfully, we are getting difficulty levels hopefully, so the difficulty curve is being addressed. we'll have an easy, normal, and hard mode, so take my commentary on the difficulty with a grain of salt. hopefully it will be resolved with an upcoming update.

I love MtG, but I can't in good conscience recommend this game to anyone. The Duels of the Planeswalkers games have always existed more as a product primarily targeting a casual/former/new Magic player audience, but even when I still avidly played the physical game, I could find something to enjoy in a DotP release. This year's edition makes the welcome change to allow deckbuilding to give more advanced players a meatier experience, but it does so many other things wrong that it ends up not being a product that is casual/new/lapsed player friendly, but isn't going to appeal to most avid MtGers either.
Pros:
Adds Deckbuilding
New UI graphic design is nice
Cons:
UI drags, even on a high-end setup
Removed challenges
Removed sealed play
Removed revenge campaign
Removed Two-Headed Giant format
Card unlocking system is horrendous
Not all cards unlockable without additional purchases (totalling almost $30 for everything, on top of the $10 for the game)
Locks you into the starting deck you initially choose, with no way to view the decklists or try them before choosing
Starter decks seem weak and have little synergy
AI doesn't seem very intelligent
Some enemy decks seem overpowered (despite poor AI), attempting to force you into the booster microtransactions
As much as I love Magic, this just isn't fun. It's like WotC wanted to go the Free-to-Play route, but didn't want to make it actually free to play. Some of this could be patched away (though I'm not holding out hope), but a lot of it seems to be problematic at the game's core. Between my Xbox 360 and Steam, I've bought every DotP release as they've come out. Without significant (and unlikely) changes, this will be the last one I purchase.

There are lots of complaints being thrown around about this game. The removal of 2v2 matches, the microtransactions, the awkwardly designed UI (clearly made with the ipad version in mind), but in truth none of these really bothered me. What really makes this kind of a worthless product to me, and I tried hard to like it, is the extremely limited and poorly chosen card pool. You can't really build......any of the classic archetypes of magic. It seems all the colors are missing major elements of their design.
White has no oblivion ring, or equivalent. This makes dealing with certain threats outrageously difficult, and building white/blue control really impractical.
Green lacks cost effective low mana creatures. They're bogged down with 5+ mana drops, usually without trample.
Red has absolutely no instant speed 3 damage burn spell. No Lightning bolt, strike, searing spear, or similar. This makes burn largely unviable, and izzet control/burn awkward at best.
Blue has negate but no essence scatter, putting their already weak creatures in an even worse spot. They get Inspiration instead of Oppurtunity, a huge downgrade.
Black has no doom blade or equivalent. The closest they come is assasinate, which is more expensive, at sorcery speed, and doesn't work against creatures who aren't tapped.
All of this doesn't make the colors imbalanced, just extremely awkward and clunky. Its particularly irritating when some of the needed cards are actually in the game, but not unlockable. The AI only decks have many cards permanently unavailable to the player, even after you pay extra for the premium booster packs. The Duels series has always been designed for newer players, and this should be taken into consideration. Sadly though, I'd have to reccommend 2014 instead. It may not teach you how to build decks, but at least the decks you see will be a little more represenative of what you'll see if you go down to your local Friday Night Magic. I'm hoping the card pool issue is fixed with updates and dlc. I don't want to wait another year for them to have a shot at getting this right.

This is a game that I can genuinely defend now having played it, I had some apprehensions similar to many other people, "It just looks like a more expensive Chivalry: Medieval Warfare clone" is a great one for example. What makes this game worth the foreboding $60 cost and unique is explained in a couple simple concepts the game provides, Interesting Combat, Genuine Intuitive Story, and the Hero System.
Combat: It's an interesting system really, every hero has a separate weapon and every weapon has different combos, locking on is relatively simple and really draws you into the fight, and on top of that what you get is a comprehensive blocking system that makes this combat simple to learn but difficult to master.
Story: I've just started the story and it's actually interesting to aviod spoiling anything you go through the lives of the various starter heros starting with the Warden and the lore and simple story are kinda pulling it leads you to feel as your character and you want them to succeed from the get go. On top of that it really does teach you the combat skills you're going to need for multi player, to be honest the first time i dropped into a duel and a dominion I got creamed but the story is slowly teaching some interesting strategies.
Hero System: Well on top of that which I already mentioned it allows people to have variance in a game that seems like it would get old quick, each character has their own combos, movesets, and feats leading to unique expeiences every time you pick a new hero. This really shines in the duel gametype in multiplayer you can take full advantage of your character's moveset and observe how the opponent is using their hero and counter strategize leading to a unique duel every time.
Now for my negatives and some of the things the community has brought up that I haven't seen.
Peer 2 Peer connection: Yes, the online is peer to peer (unless something has changed since the beta) however I haven't noticed it to serious affect and I live in Alaska with a 3mb/s up speed, I fought an individual from NY in the duels and joined an East Coast server and experienced near to no problems, so this may be on a case by case basis but don't use this for a reason to drop the game.
The price tag: Yeah, ouch 60 bucks, that hurts alot in terms of what it is and how much entertainment you may get out of it, but it really is worth it, for the reason's I've explained earlier in my positives section, it really does feel like what a AAA title should be (That has been given attention to) and that's a nice feeling considering the history of Ubisoft.
Overall it's an excellent game even from just first impacts and a negative sort of bias I had coming in, if you like complex and unique combat style and a reeling story I would certianly pick it up.
TLDR: good complex yet simple combat, story is actually interesting, don't buy the season pass and you'll do fine.

After reading relatively mixed reviews, I balked at the price, as I usually try not to pay this much for a game nowawadays. In the end, being a sucker for art styles of this kind, I bought Rime expecting a gorgeous puzzle game with a relatively balanced difficulty and clear nods to ICO, an old PS2 favorite from my college days. What I got was an unexpectedly emotional journey, told mostly through level design alone, about loss. Having recently had a family member pass away, I can only say that this game cut deep, and while the conclusion hurt like hell, it feels oddly providential to have played it this close to my family member's stepping beyond the Veil. Granted, I also did not see this story coming and only in hindsight does the way this game is built, make sense.
Good old hindsight. Life is always a little clearer looking back. Rime is no different. I've played a few games similar to this one. Again it reminded me of ICO and Shadow of the Collosus and Journey and a few other expected note strikers lots of critics have hit in their reviews. With this game though, the epic setting and mythical atmosphere, really touch on a sense of loss and the process of grief that frankly, hit much closer to home for me than any of the previous titles, because it isn't a prince trying to save a princess by killing Gods, or a boy leading a blind girl out of a fortress. This is about a broken family, and the peices that must be picked up after that breaking occurs. You may be guiding this boy through a quest, but you're also piecing something together, that was broken, all so that you can let it go.
Being a puzzle platformer that is more about the amtosphere of the journey than the puzzles themselves, this kind of game is not for everyone and for others, it may be best to wait till it's on sale. For me, this was a kind of catharsis, that I guess fate decided I needed to experience at this point in my life and given the love the devs put into it, as well as the thank you's they write in the end credits, well, that kind of heart ended up being worth $30.
I feel like this game shouldn't make me wish I was playing the prequel from 2013, but it does.

When RiME was first announced it went way under my radar. However when I won a giveaway for this game I decided to give it a try, and boy was I happy I did. I personally love these types of games, and RiME definitely filled a hole in me that I didn't even know I had. RiME is not for everyone, but for the niche audience it is for, you are in for one ride, and it is one hell of a ride.

RiME's artstyle and visuals are the best I have every seen. Every frame is awe-inspiring, with crisp textures and an amazing artstyle that is reminiscent of Abzu or The Witness. I found myself stopping and admiring the environment every minute or so, it's that good. Animations look amazing and feel extremely smooth. RiME also focuses on letting the player take a high ground and observe the entire area that they just explored and that only adds to how beautiful this game already is.
SCORE 10/10
RiME is a game mostly about exploration and puzzle solving. Puzzles are fairly easy and don't require too much thought to be put into them, but they are enjoyable and have some great concepts behind them. Puzzles feel like they are built into the environment, which makes them feel natural. Exploration is enjoyable, mostly due to the fact on how amazing the graphics are. However, most of the game is a walking simulator which might be a problem for some people, but not for others. RiME is also a fairly short game, only being 5-6 hours long, which wasn't that big of a problem for me since it's obvious to see how much the developers tried to put in into those 5-6 hours.
SCORE 8/10
The musical score in RiME is fantastic. The music is incredibly relaxing and matches the tone of the game perfectly. I'm not a big fan of classical music, but RiME's soundtrack obviously has so many emotions thrown into it that it's hard not to appreciate it. I'm not really a music guy so there's not much else I can say other than the music really is amazing.
SCORE 9/10
After playing through the game and reflecting on the story I am truly amazed. There is no real lore about what is going on around you, but the characters and the deeper meaning behind the story are extremely well made. There is no dialogue, just the environment and a few cutscenes. That only makes the story more interesting and makes you want to find out about the world around you. The only gripe that I have with the story is that it is way too cryptic. It's ok to have your story just be the environment and few cutscenes and to make you think about the story, but there is a real lack of explanation for a lot of things, at least a point in the right direction would go a long way to helping everyone understand the story.
SCORE 8/10
RiME is one of the most beautiful exploration game that I have ever played, with great music and an interesting story. However, the story is a bit cryptic and it's a bit short. Apart from that though, I would say RiME is one of the coolest games I've played in 2017.

I'm not sure i 'get' Midnight Ultra. Is it style over substance? Is it hipster? Is it a masterpeice? Maybe it's none of those things.
All I know is that after about 5 minutes my eyes and ears hurt. The graphics are bizarrely offensive, looking sort of like one of those blocky pixel-art peices made on a C64 in motion. Stunning and evocative in screenshots, stomach-churning in motion. It's also not very condusive to a twitch FPS. Half the time I can't see what I'm shooting until it's a foot in front of me gouging my bowels from my gut. Generally finding it hard to visually understand the game world is something I can't give a thumbs up for really.
The music is a matter of taste. I think it's garbage but you may enjoy a repeated guitar riff attempting to envoke Wild West themes. The other sound is in keeping with the visuals but does nothing too exciting.
I'm not sure who Midnight Ultra is for. My gut tells me this is an art school project made by Hotline Miami and Superhot fans who gave up halfway through and decided to sell what they'd managed to cobble together. My head tells me that's probably not the case and I'm biased.
So in conclusion, Midnight Ultra is a Tesco ham sandwich. Tasty to a point, affordable and satisfying if you absolutely love ham sandwiches and need one RIGHT NOW.

Darksiders is a pretty solid hack and slash game. Set in an apocalyptic Earth, after the "End War" between Heaven and Hell has started, you play as War, one of the four Horsemen of the Apocalypse. The story starts with War being sent to Earth during the Apocalypse, only to be accused of causing it himself; he must then embark on a quest to clear his name, by finding those responsible.
The gameplay is pretty solid; I've seen it mentioned as a mix of God of War and Legend of Zelda; while I'm not familiar with Zelda games, I can see the similarities to God of War, which I've played. The combat is great, there's three different weapons, plus several enhancements that you can equip your weapons with. There's also exploration and puzzle-solving, which make a good portion of the gameplay, and it's very well implemented. And that's without mentioning the collectibles, as there's lots of them, going from the already mentioned enhancements, to special items that grant you souls (which work as currency).
The story is excellent. While it draws inspiration from the biblical tales of the Apocalypse, having four horsemen and all, it still has its own spin to it. A creator is mentioned in passing, but has no real relevance to the story; War works for the "Charred Council", which seeks to maintain a balance between the forces of Heaven and Hell, and each of those factions has its own leader. The soundtrack is another solid point for this game, with some pretty good tracks.
Well, I think that's all I have to say about Darksiders. It's a pretty good game, so I recommend it.

This game offers a wealth of freedom in strategy and tactics.  The game is played turn-based on the campaign (strategic) map, and pausable RTS on the battle map.  Difficulty is independently scalable for the strategic portion and for the tactical portion of the game.
Terrain in the campaign map translates directly to terrain on the battle map; and terrain and weather can have dramatic effects on battle.  For instance, arrows fly farther if your archers are uphill of the enemy.  Bridges can be used as bottlenecks to block an enemy's crossing, while your archers decimate them.  Friendly fire is possible, and in many battles I have lost more men to my own archers than to the enemy.  Rain reduces archer effectiveness.  Open fields allow cavary to have more effective charges.  Uphill soldiers fight more effectively against their downhill opponents, Some troops gain a battle advantage in snow, and etc.
Music fades in and out nicely, and always seems appropriate for what is happening on the battlefield or the campaign map.  Voice acting of the advisors, and of the generals before the battles is well done, and often hilarious (there are some really funny audio "Easter eggs" in there).
It is possible to win battles against much bigger armies by exploiting the strengths and weaknesses of units.  Just one example: An enemy of infantry attacking your cavalry can be exhausted by using the superior stamina of the horses to evade the footmen for a time.  Attacking exhausted footmen usually results in a rout of the exhausted troops.
Replayability is high.  Different factions (most are playable after defeating them in a previous game) have different strengths, and playing them really is a different experience.  For instance, all the Roman factions are very well rounded and have an excellent infantry and tech tree.  Carthage has devastating elephant troops, but weak archers.  Other factions, like Partia, rely on heavy cavalry.  Gaul has a weak tech tree and economy (they are barbariaans, after all); but their troops can get big boosts from their religious system, their fierceness can induce morale penalties to their enemies, and they can field, by far, the best archers in the game.  Egypt has chariots, a well tounded military, and an excellent starting position on the map, allowing it to become an economic powerhouse without much opposition in the early game.  And the list of meaningful differences goes on...

A beautifully immersive experience that captivates with it's "Show, don't tell" philosophy of game design. Rain World presents an organic storytelling experience where you explore a vast ecosystem that has carved itself out of the ruins of a long-dead civilization. The huge non-linear world, fascinating interactive environment, and intelligent unique creatures lead to an emergent form of gameplay that offers an interesting story that allows you to fill in the gaps to interpret your own meaning for the Slugcat's experience through this amazing alien landscape.
The gameplay itself has a fluid-like sensibility to it where your actions and the reactivity of the environment to those actions works in an artistic harmony instead of more familiar reactivity. This may come across as undesireable to players seeking a more mechanical rigidity to their controls, but make no mistake the control scheme of Rain World is not poor, merely different, and with time comes it's mastery.
A truly breathtaking experience that truly allows you to go an epic adventure in a unique world. It is quite unlike anything else out there, definitely worth experiencing either first hand for yourself, or via Let's Play.

It's like playing Super Metroid for the first time, except with clunky physics based movement and a world that is even more engrossing and full of mystery.
Best played without any knowledge going in other than the karma system and how to swim. Everything else you should discover on your own, and there is a lot to discover.
Use a dpad or keyboard for most things. Do not use a stick unless you enjoy not being able to input precisely and in a reproducible manner.
Cons
-Physics based movement for everything means that sometimes you get screwed over or luck out
-A few very important things are so obtuse that you will probably have to look them up (how to swim long stretches without drowning)
-Sometimes it's hard to see certain small details
-Starts a bit slow
Pros
-Lush and living alien world
-Full of strange and often terrifying creatures, each with their own manner of living and placement on the food chain. Most of them seem to exist outside of a need to simply kill you
-Excellent at giving your that feeling of being low-middle class on the food chain.
-it is NOT SHORT. Don't expect a quick one and done CINEMATIC EXPERIENCE, this is a game that you'll be coming back to
-Instead of gaining new skills and powers, you gain knowledge and muscle memory that helps you survive in a brutal and hungry world
-The randomness helps with making the world feel alive. Creatures are autonomous and interact with each other.
-despite the obtuse nature making some things unfun, the feeling of discovery and just outright getting lost in an immense and new world is something I've never felt quite so strongly
Not for everyone, but if any of this sounds at all interesting, I would strongly recommend giving the game a try.

I've decided to completely rework my review for the current status of the game. The game I was telling everyone would be fantastic as it went on. The game I told my friends I'd rather play than DayZ. The game I bought myself, my brother, and two of my friends.
At first, everything was just fine. It was an Early Access game with little content, but good bones. The environments were often lovely to look at, even being a dirty, gray apocalypse. The engine it used certainly had potential, however it ran like garbage. To this day, with my 780ti, AMD 8350 and 16GB of RAM, the game stuggles to maintain above 30FPS in some areas. The game makes almost no effort to use the power available to it, even after an entire year of patches. The only graphic option available to make a difference is turning off shadows completely, which just makes the game look flat.
Combat has always been floaty. Melee, while having a bit of impact, is hard to determine. Will you hit the enemy in front of you, or your friend by accident? Who knows if you'll hit anything at all, despite being right in front of them.
Guns are also hit or miss, literally. They also have little to know sound travel. A sniper rifle cannot be heard in the middle of a dense city only 3 streets away? Yeah, not likely. That thing would echo for blocks.
Despite the Early Access warning being completely removed from the Steam page, everything about this game is still completely buggy if not broken.
Since day 1, don't use vehicles, or at the very least the motorcycles. They sort of just...slide across the environment and can barely climb over tiny obstacles, and if you try there's a 99% chance you'll just flip completely over and even die.
The Nether themselves, probably the most promising aspect of this game, aren't even well implemented. Don't get me wrong, their ideas and designs are fantastic, even terrifying, but all the promise is shattered when they see you through walls, you can't judge their range of sight or hearing at all, and 9 times out of 10 they will just instantly swarm and warp to you causing your death.
I know the point was to make them terrifying and deadly, a real challenge, but there's a difference between challenge and just being completely unfair. I love a challenge, but I hate how this game offers it.
Then there's the other players. This is the most obvious case of a survival game turned into complete deathmatch I've ever seen, and it's partly the devs fault. They continued to add things that encouraged kill on sight rather than encouraged teamwork. How loot spawns, how XP works, and then...territory claiming? Really? Did we need the game itself to encourage that? In games like DayZ, claiming a piece of land was implied. If a player set themselves up there, it was up to them to protect it. They didn't need extra XP or in game cash as incentive.
If this game was still labeled as Early Access, I'd still be able to forgive most of this since it had an actual chance of being fixed, but now since I can't find any evidence that it's still being developed and there's no warning that it's still not finished, I can't help but feel now they're just trying to trick unknowing gamers out of their cash and run.

I've seen a lot of reviews describing this as Shadow Warrior + Borderlands, but this game has much more in common with something like Diablo than Borderlands. Shadow Warrior 2 is what you get when you take Shadow Warrior and forcibly integrate Diablo style socketable gems and randomly generated levels. It might sound great at first, but the implementation is sloppy and uninspiring.
The Good:
-Melee combat is probably the highpoint of the game. You can get surprisingly tactical with it when combined with the various skill moves and fast paced movement system, and theres a good variety of weapons to use.
-Decently optimized for the most part. Graphics are decent, but not nearly as good as shown in the screenshots on the store page.
-Some of the banter between characters was amusing. Some of is also cringeworthy. Thats all subjective though.
-Nice variety of enemies.
The Bad:
-Guns range from being somewhat satisfying, to what the ♥♥♥♥ is this goddamn piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥
-Upgrading weapons is a huge pain in the♥♥♥♥♥thanks to a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ menu system. You're going to be picking up A LOT of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥in gems throughout the game, but to know what any of them do, you have to hover over each one with the cursor. They are categorized in tabs which helps somewhat, but all the accuracy/reload/damage/genericstats are in the same tab, and they are mostly what you pick up. Theres no way to filter them, and you can only sort them by rarity and level. You have to go through 3 slots for any of the 8+ weapons you'll eventually be using, look through a bunch of gems to see which one might be an upgrade, maybe stumble upon one that makes you consider replacing another gem, nope actually having 2% more fire rate is slightly better. Its just tiring. If you're super into min/maxing you might enjoy it, but even then you'll still have to navigate this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥menu system that feels like it was made by some amature developer making his first Unity engine game.
-Most the gems themselves are incredibly boring stat boosts or elemental effects. A lot of the more fun ones are restricted to certain weapon types. It was a major buzzkill for me when I couldn't apply flaking ammo to my minigun for maximum daka.
-Randomly generated levels that get old quickly, and lack any real variety or character. There are essentially 3 tilesets and you'll find most, if not all the pieces to them in any one mission area. Enemies spawn randomly in the level with no rhyme or reason, other than scripted mission encounters.
There are some other minor things, but those are the main ones that really killed the game for me.

Honestly.. Though i do have issues with a developer adding non-functional features to a game (The backstab and Pickpocket skills NEVER worked in multiplayer, save yourself 16000-20000 Auras and dont bother buying the skills) This game IS currently STILL the single best game i've ever played in terms of freedom in magic casting. Better even than Morrowind which only had a rudamentary customization ability for its spells. If you are a Spindly magey mage at heart than this game is something you simply MUST play at least one time in your life, that or wait for Two worlds 3.
All together i'd give it a spot in my top 10 favorite multiplayer games and as i personally never really played the single player as i've always felt that it should have been a Co-op experiance, and i highly value character creation in games which the single player doesnt have. I only ever bought it on Xbox 360 and PC for its Multiplayer so I simply wont rate its single player experiance, though i've heard it is quite good.
The game does have one particularily annoying thing about it you aught to know before picking it up, The signup/registration for multiplayer is kind of a pain to fill out, and also I STRONGLY recommend you avoid using third party content, even something so small as using player created maps as i've heard of GM's banning players for it as recently as January this year so... yay! Active GMs in a Seven year old game banning players who just want to get to level 40 without farming marshlands for a solid week and a half!
Its multiplayer is however also somewhat stunted at what is essentially a soft cap of level 40 content. There are players who are in excess of 200 levels, but they are only getting more skill points really, and the time they must have invested to get there is rediculous. Also to my knowledge level 40 is the highest gear in the game so I doubt there is any point to leveling that high.
And I simply must dock a point for their removing a bug that allowed you to stack an area Carrier for magic onto an enchant carrier for magic which gave players much more magic crafting freedom.
I should add that the multiplayer in the game IS map based rather than open world meaning you will constantly be opening and closing games from and into the lobby.. which is basically a 30-50 square meter town with a brick in the center that is just lined with shops.. a bit dissapointing, but I would still recommend you pick the game up for yourself and a friend if you have a day or two you want to burn playing something fun and a bit different from other games, you can even turn friendly fire on for a laugh. but i assure you the monotony will catch up to you on this one, so dont buy it expecting to play it for a massive period of time unless you really like being a wizard.
All together I would give this game a 7/10 which for being over half a decade old is pretty damn impressive, That and the fact that they are adding new DLC to it shortly on top of it being a fairly cheap game you can just pick up and play I see no reason not to get this game, even if you end up hating it i feel like you would be able to move past the sting of it fairly quickly.
Final thoughts : If more game developers created games that allowed in depth spell crafting or for stealthy co-operative gameplay and in essence let its players truely play their games how they would like while playing together (For me it's got to be earth magic.. so many games hate to add Earth magic.. I'm Looking at you Elder scrolls, and practically every MMO release outside of Guild Wars 1) in an open world There would be little to no need for any future games. That is my oppinion.

Shadow Warrior 2 makes some major changes from the origonal while still keeping the fun base shooting and sword...ing mechanics intact The biggest change is the game is much more loot focused a'la borderlands, but i find the actual gun and swordplay found in SW2 ten times more fun and satisfying than that found in the Borderlands games. There are now more than 10 times the guns than in the origonal and all can be inmbude with gems that drop from enamies that increase damage, attack speed, reload time, imbue them with elemental effects, and even alternate fire modes. almost all gems can be slotted in and out of any weapon at will and this this allows for an unparalled level of customization. Graphicly the game is good but nothing to write home about, charecter models and speically faces are pretty lacking but the enorinments and abundance of partical effects are a sight to behold and the multiple high quality animations make combat look as fun as it feels. Movement has also been greatly improved and you can zip arround the battlefeild at breakneck speed leading to some really fast and fun firefights. The game runs great too on a GTX 1070 i can max out everything and get 60fps pretty consitently but the options menue is very fleshed out for people with lower end machines, There's also some cool new Tech called Multi-Res Shading that can give you a real bost in performance with very little visual impact so i hope that's implimented in more games coming up. The story like the first game is nothing to really write home about but you'll probably want to watch the cutscenes because of the great one liners and back/forth Lo Wang has with the other charecters. if i had one complaint it's that a lot of the envoirments are re-used multiple times, and while the game does 'randomize" levels to adegree they still look pretty similar to one another, and many of them are so large it's often hard to find the optional bosses that frop weapons and high end loot. Overall Shadow Warrior 2 might be a bit too much of a departure for some fans, but if you're willing to accept something new it's still as much fun as the previous.

going into RiME, i expected to love it. everything hinted at something that i would enjoy - a mysterious island, a cryptic story to uncover, and a challenging or at least perplexing puzzle game.
unfortunately, the game failed to deliver on all of those parts.
i had major issues with this game, but i'm still recommending it for a couple reasons. one, the final sequence of the game's story almost made the game worth my money - without any spoilers, it was emotional, heartwrenching, and wondrous. it was the perfection that i had anticipated from the game beforehand. and two - even with these major flaws, i still ended up enjoying RiME and what it had to offer, an beautiful artwork and art style that it presented so wonderfully.
one of the main problems i had with RiME was the lack of what it promised to offer. story clips were only found at around 5 points within the 8-hour game and never lasted more than a minute or so, and were often disappointing and had so little emotional impact. most seemed like they were sped up and went by so fast that the watcher had little time to wonder and realize what was going on. even the final sequences, which i loved, were so short and felt like they could definitely be much longer and magnify that impression of emotions on the player.
but that's not to mention that the story didn't have its good parts either. i enjoyed the plot and how the events of the story were implied and ultimately left to the player to figure out. the final sequences almost had me in tears, and it was nice to see a story that was definitive but also left some details up to the player to decide on what had happened.
another problem i had were the puzzles. for a puzzle-game that even developed its own interesting mechanics and puzzle devices, the puzzles themselves never really developed beyond go-get-that-block or pull-this. they clearly were thought to be second-hand to the story, which was disappointing because the story didn’t really live up to its expectations. increasing the puzzle difficulty a little more i feel would interest the players a little more, and especially make the game more interesting in its slower areas.
then there are the collectibles. these are interesting and fun to find in your first playthrough, but the sheer amount of them (about 30-50 i would hazard) made me annoyed as i went through the 8-hour game again to find them, and my reward was often nothing more than a worthless sentence in the final moments, a brief song clip, a playable costume, or even simply an image on the menu screen. there needed to be a better reward system in place besides some simple achievement that made these worthwhile to the player.
a final problem i had were some faulty mechanics and frame rate issues. The art and shadow quality is automatically set to high, which stifled the frame rate even with a fairly good computer (i'm no expert on computer specs). i had to lower both to medium quality which was ultimately weird as when playing i didn't seem to find any major difference between the medium and high quality. and with the mechanics, there were about three major problems, and all of them had to do with ledges. RiME, for some reason, has a "boundary" on edges of cliffs and such where the character wobbles around like he's about to fall off a cliff whenever he's on a ledge, which was helpful in some cases where i would rather not fall off, and not helpful in others where i was purposefully trying to jump down. and the fact that the player controls the camera on some ledges made the controls very weird depending on the camera angle – almost like the forward button meant left or vice versa, and somehow when the camera control was fixed it was also annoying, as i either couldn't see where i was supposed to go or i missed that lack of freedom with the camera. and that's not even mentioning the problems i had RiME's death animation. pretty much the only way to die is to get your soul sucked out by vicious passive-aggresive dementors or to jump off a cliff. the soul-sucking is fine, i guess. but when you jump off a cliff, within a millisecond the game realizes that you're gonna die and the screen goes black and you respawn. there's nothing interesting about the animation. for example, what if, when you fell off a cliff, you could watch the boy fall right until he was about to hit the ground and then the black screen? this gives the player more emotional connection with the character and a better reason to not try and jump off cliffs.
but that's not to say i didn't love RiME. again, without any spoilers, i loved the final moments of the game, and i really enjoyed the atmosphere, artwork, and even the story at times. i'm not so certain that it's worth its full price of $30, (maybe at $20 or $15 is a better price) but i enjoyed my time with RiME overall, and i'm certain that if you're into these types of games that you will, too.

My 1.8 hour tally for this game may make my review seem a tad pre-mature, however I will review it regardless. Granted of course, my laptop doesn't do too hot with Unreal Engine-made games, so naturally, my gameplay experience was horrendous compared to what the average PC gamer could experience on their twice-as-powerful rig. I also was unwilling to try multiplayer, also due to the fact I suffered horrible framerates of 3-8FPS in singleplayer, and fared around 10-12FPS in the tutorial, alongside some rather glitchy sound issues in regards to the AI speaking.
Angels Fall First, where do I start? Well, it is definitely what it says it is, a combined-arms, sci-fi wargame. It goes full scale with combat, perhaps the most in-depth I've seen with a combat game. You literally can do just about anything in this game. From being a commanding player, ordering your troops to attack/defend objectives on a ground/space battle, to being a footsoldier in the force, either apart of a dropship for boarding an enemy battleship, or a squad on the ground to hold a position. AFF literally provides players full freedom over how they play the game. You can even modify loadouts for just about anything from the gun you're holding, to what armaments go on your ground vehicle or ship. You can even personalize the UI with colors, among other things. The maps also look beautifully detailed, and the gameplay seems fairly solid, even in singleplayer.
Of course, due to lack of playing multiplayer, I have no idea how the community of the game is, but basing it off previous reviews before me, I am to assume it has a rather small playerbase, with some latency issues in space battles.
To wrap the review in a nutshell of course, it's what Star Wars Battlefront III could have been. It's what the new Battlefront should be. This game drives home the class-based gameplay that made Star Wars Battlefronts I and II live for so long, even beyond the noted GameSpy shutdown of 2012 (seriously, those games are still alive guys). I hope to see this game become great like that someday (and I hope to have a better computer to actually play it on as well). It has so much potential to become something big. But of course, the game is in Early Access. It doesn't quite have all the quirks worked out of the system, and still needs to be smoothed out around the edges before it can truly become something great.
Overall, do I recommend this game? Well, if you grew up loving the class-based gameplay of Star Wars Battlefront, or like the gameplay of PlanetSide 2, I would recommend this. Plus, the game will only rise in price the more polished it gets. For me, this is one of those games where I'll buy it to play it later on (mostly due to my hardware). However, I do support the developers, and so I would say if you have the hardware for it, play it.

Midnight Ultra is a quick, fun run-and-gun love letter to old-school FPSs that's light on mechanics and goes all-in on aesthetic. It gets most of its mileage out of its unique look, squeezing everything into a jagged flurry of four colors while making smart use of its palette and textures to make sure you can still see what's going on at all times.
The combat is fairly straightforward but is paced out well and has a satisfying ramp in difficulty. By the end of the game, you're running frantically through hordes of familiar enemies, trying to figure out the best order to take them down. Ammo is sparse, and even with secret stashes scattered throughout the levels, I often found myself relying on the often-finnicky melee attacks towards the end of several fights.
This game's double jump is a godsend.... it just feels right, and is used for light platforming sequences that break up the action. However, falling to your death can be incredibly frustrating, as dying is a forced restart of the entire level--no checkpoints here. There are a few other cracks in the paint--the occasional AI bug, some misleading invisible walls and leaps of faith, sounds stacking or dropping out, and a lack of visual feedback on dealing or taking damage--but none of these are dealbreakers in the slightest.
It's immediately apparent that Midnight Ultra was made with a lot of love. It's rough around the edges, but like any good indie game, those little flaws end up adding to the charm. The pacing feels really nice throughout. Took me about an hour and a half to complete, with my fair share of continues, and its tough final encounters leave you with a real sense of accomplishment. All in all, there are way worse ways to spend three dollars and a chunk of an afternoon.

If you are brave enough to put up with the absurdity, then continue with the review.
KOTOR II was released as a severely unpolished and unfinished game following the release/success of KOTOR I. The sequel lacked a coherent ending, many of the quest lines vanished into bleak nothingness, and the game was riddled with technical mishaps. The story it told, however, was one of the most mature and horrifying side stories ever told in the Star Wars universe. Whereas everything post-prequels in Star Wars attempted to paint the universe as bright, full of raging emotion, and cataclysmic battles, KOTOR II provided the dead hulk of a galaxy that lacked any of that vibrancy. KOTOR I was a radiant beacon of hope compared to how sordid the affairs of KOTOR II are, and it's so valuable as a result.
Here is a product that tells exactly how dirty a civilization can get; how terrified a people can be; and more to the point, it presents a beloved franchise as a vulnerable, almost derelict enterprise. A few quick google searches can net you the proper mod scene to install some of the unfinished content, but even viewing the game in its naked, broken state will get you the proper experience.

This is a masterclass in bad game design.
The art is lush and the characters endearing and lovable, which makes the experience of playing the title almost heartbreaking in its tragedy. Every single design decision used to create this game seems to have been made to turn the process into as big a chore as possible.
The game didn't even start the first time I ran it because I'd mapped my Steam installations to a different folder. Take note that little "?" boxes imply the game is trying to load assets it can't find from your Program Files directory. A prompt would have been nice but would also have required a level of foresight I have learnt not to expect.
The controls are a continual source of contention. The title apparently has baked-in support for DualShock 4, but the button prompts are wrong and it doesn't support the D-Pad. You can hack together something in Steam but you'll also need to map the keys yourself in the interface; more on that later.
The visual design – that is, the way the images come onto your screen – is dreadful. The entire title plays at 1366x768, making the image blurred on any device where the picture needs to be scaled up as there is no support for proper pixel scaling. This makes finer details difficult to see and makes navigating the interface a chore.
The title itself demonstrates numerous examples of form over function, giving gameplay the impression of an afterthought.
When you're underwater your player sprite turns black, making it almost impossible to see. This oversight works in conjunction with the title's heavy use of rain, the falling of which causes the screen to shake about so violently that navigating the area becomes little more than guesswork.
Control prompts, done in a similarly lush and minimalist style, abound the first few minutes of gameplay, but suffer from the same planning; beyond a legend that is supposed to appear when you pause, but doesn't if you've mapped your own controls, the only time you're told what buttons to push is via an unhelpful spectre who follows you about, giving wonderful-looking but unhelpful advice in tiny images you can barely see. He vanishes if you get too close to him, and when he re-locates you have to wait a second for his unhelpful prompt again, if it appears at all.
When he finally does, you quickly realise that the button prompts he regurgigates are hard-coded images that pay no attention to the custom mapping you have been forced to do to compensate for the title's lack of testing; if you had mis-mapped the prompts in the configuration, the spectre gives out the wrong cues, and you are left to fend for yourself.
It appears as if very little of the title was ever actually play-tested and the whole thing seems to have been rushed out the door very quickly to meet a deadline.
The title attempts to tell the story wordlessly as the player moves through it, but this too is a half-measure; while some aspects of the story are delivered silently (such as the Spectre giving out his microscopic prompts), other mechanics are delivered lifelessly in text at the bottom of the screen. One would think a devoted arts team could have figured out a way to display hunger in the character beyond simply writing "You are hungry! Find food" at the bottom of the screen.
To those debating picking up this title since it is on sale, I would suggest eyeing the Community Forums first. There are over a hundred individual bug report posts, with most ending with someone mentioning a mythical update patch intended to alleviate the issues the title should have fixed in beta. There has been no ETA for this patch, nor any indication of what it intends to fix. Unless it is a re-make of the title in a new engine and compiled by people with a solid idea of what it is they are trying to produce, I would hold off on this one.

Kingdom wars is not only an RTS with in-depth leveling system on units, it is an MMO. The ability to co-op seige npc towns to gain bonus resources and crowns (used for upgrading technologies, and advanced units) is remarkable.
Combat system - Each group of soldiers has a number of units inside it, and as long as 1 lives the entire group can be healed. The abilities of each group of soldiers also come with abilities which help in the midst of battle, some are more defensive abilities while others can deal heavy damage or movement speed in tough situations. In all the combat is well rounded with units that counter other units, and ways to win if strategically done.
Building and Resources - This game is not a win in 1 day game, it takes patients and time to succeed into being a king. The resource gathering is per minute, which draws the building out but is worth it. During the time it takes to raise walls and gather resources for other builds you can spend time doing the Unlimited quests in the game for Crowns (In-game currency). Each building takes time, but you can build it all at once if you have the resources for it, or if you become impatient on a nessecary building you can rush the build with Crowns.
Questing - The game has unlimited quests, this gives you a never-ending pve aspect to a largely pvp game. From Quests you recieve Crowns, and/ Resources. Some quests are very challenging but with co-op quests it notifies you that you can get assistance doing the quest (either from a random player, or from a friend off of your friendslist).
PVE - I enjoy the pve the most. The battles in each of the zones is different, elvens fought in elven zones, humans in human zones, and orc's in the orc zones. Beyond that there are zones not allocated to a race. These zones have harder creatures to fight like orges (a unit of the orc's but the entire zone is ogre's), Dwarfs (a style of unit bought with crowns), goblins (another unit of the orc's but the entire zone is goblins), and even an extremely hard zone of Dragons!
PVP - The pvp is setup as matchmaking, you will never fight someone much bigger then your army/town and you will never be able to pick on the weak. Its balanced so that you can enjoy fighting without the fear of being slaughtered. If you choose not to fight a player who is trying to fight you then you can do a "payout" option and sacrifice some resources or a few units to not have to battle them and it allows you to return to what you what to do (Quest, farm, pve, etc).
Not pay to win - I want to state that in no way is this a pay to win game. There is options for buying packages, and being a Premium account but it gives only crowns, resources, and a bonus daily reward for premium accounts. These are all things you can aquire very easily in game but by buying a package you are not spending 30+ minutes gathering the resources or farming the crowns. Buying premium not only saves you time gathering crowns, it also helps the game grow and gives incentive to play. As a closing statement to this i will repeat - Its not pay to win, its free to play. Buying only helps you grow faster and helps the game grow faster.
In all I must recommend this game to anyone who enjoys RTS games, this breaks the mold of what RTS use to be and brings a new light on the future of RTS. I have enjoyed every aspect of the game and hope to see more content in the future.

One Last Chance is an alright little visual novel.
+ The art style is nice on the eyes, though combining anime character art with filtered photo backgrounds was an odd choice.
+ The in-game music was fine. While the songs were nothing particularly special, they did fit the scenes well and didn't make me want to turn the sound off.
++ The voice acting, for the scale of the project, was actually rather good. All of the voices were pleasant, and I didn't notice any off inflections.
+ The story, while really short, was alright. The game hit all the obvious story beats, but is also didn't do anything particularly wrong.
- However, while the story was perfectly fine, most of the endings were not. In some of the endings the characters didn't act as they probably should have. Others were just annoyingly cryptic to reach, causing me to have to look at a guide to get all the endings.
-- After each ending you are given the credits, and it’s the worst thing in the game. The song that plays in the credits has vocals preformed a vocalist who cannot sing very well. She's not the worst singer I've ever heard, but that still does not mean that the song pleasant. This would not be a big deal if you could actually skip the credits. Even if you manage to glitch the game and get the menu open so you can load a saved game, the credits just stay overlaid on the screen you loaded to, making the music in that screen overlap with the credit's music. So, every time you get an ending, be ready to either sit there for a few, or close and reopen the game.
While the game does have issues, these issues do not make the game unplayable. If you have four bucks and the game seems vaguely interesting to you, I'd say go for it.
However, I would not suggest buying the sound track. There are only seven tracks in the entire game. Six of them are just some piano/guitar that, while nice in-game, I would not listen to in my free time, and one of them is the credits song.

I've been hearing a lot of negativity towards this edition of magic the gathering etc etc long title blah. I'd put this into a list but screw lists, they're classist and I dont dig that, maaaan.
So some nice things in no particular order are that the game looks pretty sweet sometimes. If you never had to touch the menu I'd say the menu was great, but you do so that kind of ruins it. Seriously. Dont even TRY to menu with the mouse.
Continuing on this sweetness, the cards themselves are great looking as usual, and the customization of avatars and deck boxes are pretty wide and pleasant.

I got like 30 hours of this game (as of writing) by making all sorts of decks that I can and seeing what works and what doesnt. I bought this game on preorder, let's get this out of the way beforehand, so take that as you will.
This game is down to the core a fluid mechanical fighting game, That is all you are going to get. Don't buy this game if you are not ready for that, It's beautiful and just feels very refined in terms of the combat however there are some glaring issues that hint at the game being rushed to completion.
Lets talk about the single player mode or Story mode. This game mode is so hapharzardly done that it becomes glaringly obvious that they did not put much stock in it's completion after the E'3 trailer for it came out. The writing is something that might be out of a coloring book, the voice acting minus the main antagonist is awful and choices for coding are questionable at best. The observables in the game are really a great Idea but very poorly executed as they are always cut off by the unneccessary dialague that your antagonist quips about constantly. I would find one only to have the explanation cut off during a cutscene or abruptly stop when a enemy hero shout's his/her battlecry of 4 year old variety only to find after killing that character it wouldn't let me go back and view it.
But let's look at the upside of the story. The background story is mysterious and full proof. I was coaxed very willingly into viewing objects around the map that piqued my interest and found myself (if I had the time to due to the fact I was nearly  being shoved from one mission to another) standing and looking at all the beautiful sometimes morose scenery. this game had a depth to it that due to poor execution will go unnoticed and that makes me sad that only a few people will enjoy that. but the campaign is pretty easily seperated and leaves alot of room for people to go back and enjoy without trudging through the first completion pains.
The story will likely leave you wanting (in the bad usage) for more.
Now for the multiplayer.
This is this game's bread and butter. They fixed alot after the open beta and balance feels  better and there are moments where I feel like it's a real battle. However due to connection issues in the bigger gamemodes 4v4's specifically there are some moments where I feel like the battle is lost and we have been winning the entire game. This never becomes unjarring. I hope that they try to implement a different system, for if they are want some competive rank ladders they will need to adjust this seemingly archaic peer to peer setup.
But what about the good things? you might ask?
The game feels right. you can feel the effort put into the models from start to finish even if the viking minions look silly. and combat  just sinks in and feels so intoxicatingly good once you find a character that you enjoy playing, that I can see myself playing this for a long time. The ganks feel manageable even from a 3 on 1 standpoint with good positioning however this kind of combat where every millisecond counts in blocking dodging ducking and weaving can be hampered severely by a poor connection to the host. a player will guard break me and i will mash the X button to break at the appropriate time only to find I have almost predeterminatly lost the exchange.
This game has some growing pains to adjust to, and with the ubisoft label I fear that they will only determine that a sequel is the best option instead of letting this game grow and right itself.
So if you are looking for a cool medieval fighting sim. you've come out to the right place, if you are unsure wait for a discounted product before purchasing.
Otherwise this game is pretty decent.

Let me start by saying that I'm not really that much of a shooter fan, but I did love the first game and I'm also a fan of co-op stuff like Left 4 Dead and Borderlands.
That being said, this game in its current form just isn't a very good sequel to Shadow Warrior (2013) and not a very good loot-based co-op shooter either.
The main problem I think is that the game is hurt by too much randonmess: rather than a tightly crafted and challenging corridor shooter, you get a a game in which nearly everything is random and as a result of that, more often than not just not very compelling.
Despite of the random nature, pretty much every fight and every level feels exactly the same, and apart from very basic tactics regarding various elemental weapons, there just isn't too much to most of the fights - sure, they can be fun and fast and frantic, but the majority ends up feeling far too easy and far too long. This is made worse by the fact that especially in co-op dying rarely feels like it matters and it's far too easy to use cheesy kiting techniques.
On top of that, exploring the levels just isn't very much fun since all they will ever offer is more of the same, and the game throws so much  and such poor loot at you that running around collecting everything is rather pointless - pretty much all the cool stuff is obtained automatically or very easily found by killing the mini-bosses and the endless slew of weapons mods that you get is more of a chore to sift through (using a horrible interface) than something to get excited about. This is probaby the first game ever, also, in which low level common or rare upgrades are often better than ultra expensive and and rare legendary upgrades, further adding to the sense of pointlessness of it all.
And to top it all of, the system with a quest hub and numerous fetch quests adds very little to a game of this type, other than constantly keeping you out of the action with endless loading screens and boring cutscenes. I simply started skipping them halfway through.
I'm not ruling out the possiblity that this game can be ultimately saved by a gigantic patch that overhauls the loot system into something meaningful and rewarding, but even then I feel that the repetitive and random nature of this game will not lead to something memorable. It's OK to play in short bursts if you just want to have something colorful to look at without having to think to much, but it feels far to much like busywork to be compelling for long periods of time.

It's a good FPS. Lots of fun, but it feels like it lacks content. The ending is also a problem. 7/10.
Pros:
- Fun combat and different weapons.
- Nice story. Not the greatest, but it gets the job done.
- Scoring new loot is always fun.
- Modifying weapons, armour and abilities. You can also combine upgrades for better quality ones.
- Lots of monster to kill. They don't go down easily.
Cons:
- Game is a bit too easy. I nearly died a few times, but that was due to negligence. You can always sprint away and heal. I admit I played it on the standard difficulty.
- Managing your resources can be a chore. Having to scroll between screens to find the right weapon or upgrade you're looking for can be annoying.
- The ending was not well thought out. You'll see...
- The game feels short on content. There are side quests and such, but you can burn through the game in a few hours.
- Be prepared to revisit places you've already been to. There is not much variety. You essentially cycle between a handful of different places and complete missions there.
- The world is practically barren save some baddies to kill. It would have helped immersion if there were actual people about. I believe humans are living alongside demons, but you never see that. Instead the only people you encounter either help you or are people you have to kill. Same with demons.
Instead of these small "open world" locations, they could have gone with more linear design or provided more location options. The developers could have fixed the ending a bit too and provided a little more content, such as a second map. Another option would have been to allow players to drive to different locations. Was actually looking forward to it. I don't mind teleporting, but if they really wanted the "open world" feel, they could have done this instead.
The game is essentially a string of small sections that are supposed to add up to a map of activity that never really feels connected. You are teleporting somewhere, to fight new baddies in the same area you've been to before, to retrieve something so that you can get paid...only to repeat it. Between all this, you're levelling up and deciding what skills to invest in, but before you know it, and just when things are getting really interesting and even a bit more challenging, it ends. Hell, they coulda offered missions or challenges you could redo for money or prizes. That would have given it some longevity. But once you've finished the game, it has little replay value.

s of all time, I'm here to tell you why that's unfair, and why you shouldn't cheat yourself out of this experience.
But first we must list the cons:
Dated graphics (understandable for a 6 year old game at time of writing, but they lacked fidelity even at launch)
Numerous bugs and glitches
Shoddy animations
Shoddy voice acting
Poor multiplayer
Two Worlds has always been a series that lacks a certain amount of polish, the first game using in-house staff as voice actors because they couldn't afford professional talent, is just one example. While I personally enjoyed the first game for reasons I won't divulge in this review, many did not, however Two Worlds II is proof that the developers at Topware have improved upon themselves.
So onto the pros:
Expansive world
Fantastic combat system
Rich and fulfilling loot
T H I C C atmosphere
I recommend Two Worlds II because it stands as a monument to video game innocence, it is honest in its presentation, and flawed. But its flaws while often frustrating are part of the allure, and the game handles certain aspects of its creation very very well. To me, Two Worlds was the first game to utilise really satisfying hack and slash gameplay, it's heavy, but not too heavy, light where it needs to be, but not floaty (like Skyrim, and it is varied; Two Worlds has always had TONS of weapons and armour types. It is a precursor to the combat Demon Souls created, but far less punishing and enjoyable. Exploring the world of Two Worlds II might not have the same recognisable landmarks and features of classic games like TES, or The Witcher, but the detailed and varied environments make for an enjoyable romp on horseback with some of the most satisfying mounted combat since Mount and Blade.
The charm of Two Worlds lies in the moments the developers at Topware hit the nail on the head, it is a game that is so so close to achieving perfection, but is let down by developer inexperience. What is encouraging however, is that Two Worlds II was such an improvement over the first (and already enjoyable) game, that with this trend, Two Worlds III could be even greater, and that excites me a great deal.
So do buy Two Worlds II, if you are a forgiving gamer, who isn't looking for a polished AAA title. Buy it if you're looking for an experience, with ups and downs.
If you're looking for the perfection of a multi-million dollar budget then you may want to look elsewhere, or at least wait for Two Worlds III, maybe that will be the one.

Despite what some people say, Nether is a really good game. This game is a survival game and they have ensured that it stays balanced and fair towards new players and veterans alike.
The levels you have gained reset upon death - This is a good feature because it promotes cautious play and it means that you won't have any max level players steamrolling everyone else.
Name tags only show up if you are close to a player and aim at them for a few seconds, so there is no chance of being seen because somebody spotted your name tag popping out of the undergrowth!
Nether is a game about surviving, some new players may find this unfair due to being killed by other players but it really isn't. It is much more realistic that in these situations your hand is not going to be held by rules and people are going to attack you for two reasons. To take your gear and because they don't trust you. How do they know that if they don't shoot first they won't get a bullet in the back?
Please think about what you are buying before clicking the checkout button. If you can't handle the type of game where there are no rules to protect you then this may not be the game for you. This is also an EARLY ACCESS GAME! This means that yes there will be bugs and glitches. You are paying for an incomplete version of a game, that's not saying that it won't get better, because it will. The Devs are constantly making improvements to the game and it is far from unplayable. Think of it as more of a fully functional game without all of it's features.
That said, I really do recommend Nether to anybody who is a fan of the survival genre. Because the scenery and graphic effects do a great job of making it a really creepy experience. The Developers have also made the smart choice of making the cash shop cosmetic items only and there is no conversion rate for Nether Gold into In-game cash.
So yeah, I'd recommend Nether to anyone who enjoys this kind of game.
EDIT: After coming back to the game i can't recommend buying this. The devs ruined it and made it pay to win.

While on the surface, this may look like your average bargain-bin humble bundle pissall of a video game, but there are layers of depth here that I've never experienced in a video game before.  This game was gifted to me by a friend who found it at the very light entry fee of 70 cents.  70 cents is the barrier of entry into this elegantly crafted piece of interactive art.  I wasn't even prepared for the world I was about to be thrust into.
Pros:
-Rock collision detection is solid.  Popular titles like Bethesda's "Fallout 3" have failed time and time again with world geometry.  This game hits it on the head.
-Weapon variety is one of the strongest traits of this game.  Through my 3 hours of full gameplay, I've experienced both a rod and a halberd.  I cannot put into words my experience (seriously, try it out for yourself)
-Enemies!  You've got wolf.  See?  You've got skeleton.  See that?  Rumor has it there's bear.  Do you enjoy bear?  Look no further.
-You can purchase this fine title online for two quarters and two dimes.  A steal if you ask me.
-Developer support is top notch with DLC coming out seven years later!
-AI is on par, or better in some aspects, than AAA titles.  Two Worlds II outshines the original Two Worlds.  Town guards are responsive to the tinest of player actions.  Pull a weapon out around the wrong neighborhood?  You better believe you're as good as dead.
Cons:
-Not enough stat points.  While the enemy variety and combat is the highlight of this game, the skills were lacking.  There are only two skills, strength and vitality.  You can raise your attack strength and your health.  This is somewhat of a let-down!
-Menus are hard to navigate.  I would have suspected that I could've found more skills hidden in some far off menu, but there was nothing to be found.  The upgrade paths leave me wanting more.
-Magic system is unintuitive and poorly designed.  Healing magic doesn't do anything and it's not a problem to go along without a mage in your party.  Combat magic is laughable.
-It might be hard to get a party together if your friends can't afford the game.
-This game may lead to mental instability in the spectrum-bound.  Be wary about playing this game around your cousin.
Overall, this title is highly recommended, if not for the price of entry alone.  This title has it's flaws, but for only 70 cents, what do you have to lose?  After three hours, I'm satisfied to say the least.  Hope you enjoyed!
