The list of good singleplayer first person shooters released in the past 5 years isn’t long. There’s Doom 2016, Wolfenstein: The New Order 2014, Shadow Warrior 2013, and Serious Sam 3 in 2011. As a fan of Shadow Warrior, I had high hopes for this. I got worried when I learned they’d added co-op, and especially worried when I heard levels would use procedural generation. Unfortunately the game is even worse than I had feared. This is a review of the game viewed only as a singleplayer experience, and it’s possible it’s more fun in co-op. But that’s not how I was interested in playing this.
To be fair, Shadow Warrior 2 has fixed some things from the last entry. Bosses are way better, which is important as they were a joke last time. Also, the last game had inconsistent performance, whereas this game runs incredibly well, while looking way better. In general, the look of the game is its greatest asset. Human characters look like they were thrown together by a complete amateur, but the environments are nice. It’s also the first game on PC to support HDR10, so if you have a HDR TV the game doubles as tech demo.
But apart from those positives, Shadow Warrior 2 is bloated and vapid. Almost none of the qualities I look for in a singleplayer FPS are present, and it’s all because of the change in direction of the game and level design. You get quests from a central hub, and then select missions on a map. These maps are generated based on a few visual themes, and enemies are randomly placed on them. The effect this has on level design is that you walk around general purpose buildings and arenas, which might or might not be populated with enemies.
Unlike a properly designed game, there’s no sense of pacing or drama to the levels. Enemies just kind of mill about randomly in the levels, and there’s never any sense of surprise or tension. Even worse, there’s so few pre-built assets used for randomization that you’ve seen everything halfway through the game, just like Halo 1! You run up the same giant tower in the city three times, the same dungeon two times, the same everything over and over. And somehow, even with this amount of padding, the game is 5 hours shorter than the last one. How much time was wasted on this system? And for what? To make replays slightly less tedious in co-op?
To further ruin any sense of excitement when you play, the story is total garbage. The whole adventure feels like it doesn’t matter. This is in stark contrast to the last game, which successfully created not only a drama curve for the general story, but also character arcs. It wasn’t brilliant, but it was good enough to pass as acceptable. Shadow Warrior 2 is so far from the last game that it’s worse than the 1997 Shadow Warrior. When this little care is put in the story, you might as well not have one. I skipped several cutscenes for side quests, because they were the most torturous tedium I’ve ever seen in games. And I have a high tolerance for cutscenes, being a fan of Metal Gear Solid 4.
I don’t hate this game, but I’m disappointed. It’s 10 hours of generic paste, only slightly more interesting than Borderlands 1 and 2. This isn’t what I wanted from Shadow Warrior 2, at all. I guess if you really love the Borderlands games this might be fun. But I’d like it if these co-op based first person RPG shooters became more ambitious. I want to play a real game, not a collectathon. “Oh, I got a new weapon! Oh it’s♥♥♥♥♥♥ just like the last hundred.” “Which skill should I pick? Oh it doesn’t matter, there’s a hundred of them, so it’s balanced in a way where you don’t need to pick any.” No thanks, I’m fine.

Hey kids! Do you like Zelda? Do you like artificially progress gates until you get a thingy? Do you like to backtrack a lot to complete your game 100%? Yes? Okay. Now do you like the fact that your game is extra safe? Do you like the fact that its kept hostage on an underpowered gimmicky console that you will never touch with a 10 feel long pole? No? Okay. Ladies and gents who answered those questions, heres the best non Zelda Zelda game ever. Welcome to Darksiders.
This game is probably one of the better examples that you can mix 2 absolutelly different things together and come up with something nice. Being a child of Zelda and Devil May Cry, Darksiders manages to capture the feeling of both while still being its own thing.
We begin with the end of the world. So Tuesday really. Our protagonist, War (who is imo the most boring out of 4 horsemen of the apocalypse) lands on Earth where all hell break loose. Literally. During the shenanigans of the first mission we learn that we ♥♥♥♥ed up. But not really. Someone framed us. Time for revenge! The story in this piece is very bare bones but its still pretty interesting so no more spoilers. Its worth it.
Sound design in this game is really well made. Hit sounds, grunts, everything has the right feel to it. Probably the only sounnd that i havent enjoyed was war himself, as he is pretty much the most boring person in the entire game. And thats not because of the voice actor but rather the writing. War character is your average Kratos type of deal but without any edge other than revenge. He has no comebacks, no nothing. War Smash! Boring. Music on the other hand doesnt have a flaw imo. No matter where you go, its nice to just stop and listen. And every single score match the tone and the area we are in.
Graphics are okay. This game aged well-ish. There are still some low res things here and there, but that might have something to do with the fact that this game is quite old. Theres remastered version which i might tackle later on, for now, its okay but not the best. Console roots really shows is all im saying.
Gameplay. Imagine this. Imagine you are playing Zelda with DMC fighting mechanics. You get an item which counts as both weapon and puzzle solving thingy. You go throu the dungeon and play with its gimmick, maybe get an item which opens up another gimmick and way to the boss. Boss also utilise gimmick of the item you just found. Its Zelda, BUT you get to do all of that with combos and style points. So DMC. This mashup, and I cant stress this enough, is so refreshing and unique, that i really want to have more of it. And there is second (and third coming up) installment of the franchise which i approve. That being said, what about the controls? Well, for a port, Darksiders plays on keyboard well. It still doesnt hold a candle to the controller, but its playable and really good tbh. So points for that.
Achievements in this game are both fun to earn and somewhat challenging so if you like your artificial numbers to be well deserved, its a title for you.
One last nitpick before i wrap this rewiev up. For a game about HORSEMEN of the apocalypse, we get Ruin way too late in the game.
Strong recommendation if you like Zelda gameplay. Strong recommendation if you like DMC style of fighting. And overall its a nice piece. Get it on some sort of sale or jump straight into the Warmastered, whatever suits your fancy. Darksiders 3 is coming next year, dont rob yourself out of knowing the full scope of the story.
Zawisza out.

I'm at a loss why Steam responds to certain games with absolutely overwhelming support, and then lets other games like Fossil Echo or Papo and Yo just sit there. Seems like the arthouse crowd is sometimes too lazy to buy anything on this platform, and some people have absurd expectations with budget titles, which is a shame because games like this deserve better sales. Rime is an amazing experience. It's as simple as that. I played this on PS4, and all I can say is the graphics are even better here, and the FPS is a solid 60 on my setup. 1070 and 2600K. A true beauty.
It's totally acceptable that this game wears its inspiration on its sleeves, and yet who cares when it all comes together this well? Miyazaki films, Joaquín Sorolla paintings, and the game Journey come to mind, and this world is so profoundly lovely and attractive that I can basically overlook almost any flaws with the game.
The gameplay experience is actually soothing and fun to me, and I enjoy a very wide variety of games and difficulties across genres. No, you aren't going to be challenged like some SMB platformer or a PUBG gun game. It's not meant to be that way. It wouldn't even work that way. This is a relaxing puzzle game that swings toward the easier side, but it makes up for it with a decent amount of collectibles, and the game never overstays its welcome.
The graphics and world here are like some amalgamation of a Miyazaki film, Wind Waker, and ABZU. Honestly, I wasn't sure I was going to be impressed by their world, as there is limited interaction, but it is actually a breathtaking accomplishment. I am injecting SMAA at 1080p and the image quality is fantastic. While not overly detailed the bloomy resonance of the island recalls games like Ico and Shadow of the Colossus in tone.There is just something wonderful about running around a deserted place that has no equivalency in the modern world.
I cannot help but love this thing. It's too charming to hate, too pretty to leave behind, and overall the experience is something that the whole family can enjoy. It's puzzling that this game has under 1K reviews on Steam. You would think there would be a bigger audience for such an indie.
Anyone looking for a beautiful world spanning day and night that wants to solve a few puzzles and gaze at some gorgeous visuals is in for a treat here. Some of the collectibles are hidden fairly well and will take some logical thinking to collect. It's all very peaceful and heartwarming. Highly recommended.

I understand the concept of testing a game, providing the appropriate feedback for future fixes, but it's been quite obvious to most testers that the developers found themselves more immersed in the MMO version than the YO version in the previous years. Now, the story has changed as of 17 November 2015 that the devs have put a pause on the MMO to get YO out the door.
I love the concept of the game,  it's a bit of a grind, but man I have to be frank, the release (aside from graphics) is far worse than what was done before hand in the terms of bugs.
The mechanics of the game is great, terraform to your hearts content to make the perfect multi-tiered lanscape so you can build what ever you want. Be a farmer, build an out post, slowly create your own village and much more!
Combat is solid, face movements/body strafes guide your swings and can complete 'combos' to pull off different feats with each particular weapon.
Sadly, the bugs, even the ones identifed previously from the 'release' are still there and can seriously damper your gameplay experience.
I'd say nay on this game until the game breaking bugs are finally addressed and you can play appropriately. Just needs to be ironed out.
Just a bit sour to call it a 'release' when clearly it's been a rough one in hot fixes. I deeply wish to keep playing this game but until the bugs are fixed, it's just not going to happen.

It's beautiful, has an amazing concept and core mechanics, generally very well executed, but it has a fatal flaw:
It's way, way, way too damn hard. And that's coming from someone who thoroughly enjoyed Super Meat Boy.
The karma system makes death extremely punishing, and death is extremely common (try, die and repeat style), keeping you in loop for hours on end without making any trace of progress, and therefore, makes the game hardly rewarding to play. Also, the fact that ennemies have such random placement and behavior makes it prety much impossible to master your fate. Ultimately, the game can kill you at any moment with cheap deaths (e.g. getting snapped by lizard located under you in another, unseen part of the map). If I get through where I want to go unharmed, It's not even rewarding, because you rather feel like you were lucky rather than competent.
This is compounded  by the floaty controls which makes controlling slugcat unsatisfying at best. Platforming itself is also quite hard and with those controls, it's infuriating.
I really, really want to like this game, and keep getting back to it for 20-30 minutes at a time to just try to do, well, something, but I can't say I'm having fun playing it.
A sad example of the concept overriding actual fun gameplay.

Having invested slighty more than 40 hours in Rain world at the time of this passage, I come to you, the public, at this late hour to deliver a most urgent plea.
I was once of a mind to decry the game for its unceasing brutality and unforgiving, unrelenting, unfair cycle of desperate survival and unforseeable death. Though I recognized its unique beauty and loved its dynamic, fluid, and yet cohesive mechanics, I was repulsed by its difficulty. I am in regret for this.
While I can't place blame on those who persist in disliking Rain World's foundational difficulty (I empathize with them, in fact: my first 20 hours were hell), I can offer a nugget of advice for those who would consider providing the game another opportunity: have patience, and learn of the world and your capability in it before establishing a "lifestyle" as the Slugcat.
My principle mistake when initially playing Rain World was permitting my expectations to override my actions. I occupied nearly 20 hours with practically no progress and an abundance of futility, and all because I was awaiting some firm directive which never came. In my frustration with this interminable cycle, I began to condemn certain aspects of the game, most notably the karma system. In time I became so desperate for some means of enjoying the game that I sought out a mod which rendered this scapegoat, the karma system, inconsequential. The result was... hollow. With nothing to penalize me, I was no longer obliged to inject purpose into my actions, and the game's value evaporated.
This was a moment of revelation for me. I realized that, in order to enjoy Rain World, I needed to seek its rewards and venture into its world and mysteries rather than flit axiously from one hibernation chamber to the next in perpetual fear of the consequences of curiosity. I needed to accept that this alien wilderness was harsh in excess, and that to survive it I must accomodate it and, at length, begin to predict it. I had been humbled to a slugcat and flung, directionless, into a world eager to swallow me. My sole guides were my intuition and ambition to explore, and my immersion in Rain World was contingent upon my willingness to exercise both. So I did.
My advice as a "veteran" is this: do not allow your fear of penalty to succeed your will to explore. Learn to live, not just survive, and perhaps you, too, will leave your heart in the hostile yet beautiful lands of Rain World.

One time the enemy might bite its own tail and fall off a cliff, the other time it'll manage to get a surprise speedboost due to the way its body contorted and wipe 20 minutes of your progress. Sometimes you'll trip over your own body or randomly lose momentum mid-jump. Wall jumping is a mess.
Oh, did I mention enemies spawn quite randomly? Yeah, one time one screen will have 3 enemies, sometimes they'll be on another one. Navigating around enemies in some areas is just mindbogglingly stupid. I've had a few spots where an enemy was sitting on top of the only way forward and refuses to move. And you can't afford to just wait it out, either, because every damn run is on a timer.
But by far the worst is the save system. You can only save at special checkpoints, and you need to eat a bunch of food before you can do that. Oh, and you get 'karma' for saving, which you need for unlocking new areas. But you lose a point if you die. And you will die a lot. The scavenging aspect is a cute idea, but in this game it becomes a tedious and frustrating routine to pushish you for trying to figure out the game.
And you need to figure out the game, because boy does it tell you jack all after the first few hints. So you'll die while doing that. A lot. And every time you'll watch a 5-10 seconds animation of your save-room unlocking. And then you'll have to backtrack. And you'll have to grab some food on the way. And then you'll die. And then you will repeat the process. Or quit and find a more enjoyable game.
If you enjoy making no progress for hours on end and rerunning the same areas, this might be the game for you. But it ain't for me. I honestly wish this game had some sort of 'easy mode'. Yeah yeah, yada yada 'casul, git gut'.

Tl:dr: Backdrops are beautiful, the controls work, multiplayer is challenging and fun, single player is worth at least one run through from what I've seen so far. Microtransactions aren't that big of a deal, P2P functions but still meh, steep learning curve for MP, a nice challenging melee game that I'm surprised Ubisoft backed as it's more complex than just mashing buttons
Adding my $0.02 to the positive pile here. (Disclosure, took part in open and closed betas so add at least 3 extra hours to gameplay time) I can understand most of the complaints lobbied against the game (especially P2P...smdh Ubisoft). The story (from what I've seen so far) really only serves to teach you how to survive the multiplayer. Which isn't necessarily a bad thing in and of itself, Titanfall 2 did pretty much the same thing but it managed to tell an interesting story in the process. I can handle a 6 hour story in a multiplayer based game as long as it serves its function (ie teaching the player how to play multiplayer effectively) whilst telling a decent story in the process. As far as I can tell atm, it does that decently enough. Is the writing GOTY material? No. Is this The Witcher 3? No. Should you buy just for the single player? NO. But you should've seen that going it. This is a multiplayer focused game.
As for multiplayer, it's a blast if you take the time to stick with a class and learn how to play it effectively. The balancing isn't perfect right off the bat but if you learn your role and stick to it, you'll have fun slicing and dicing (or crushing) your enemies to bits. I appreciate the up left right approach to combat. It's Mount & Blade esque, while leaving enough room for fighting game style combos and movesets that are gratifying to pull off. Be warned though, if you run headfirst into multiplayer without looking at your move list or practicing you WILL get crushed. You WILL be frustrated. You WILL say the game is broken. This is not Chivalry, and for that, I give Ubisoft a pat on the back. (Though you shouldn't be button mashing in Chivalry either, you team killing pleb)
Yes there are microtransactions, but they don't serve much of a purpose. Mostly cosmetics and feats, which you don't need to win a battle if you fight well enough. Should they be in the game at all? I'd say no, grind it out son, but meh. That's a design choice I'm not too upset about.
Beyond all that, the optimization is done well. I run it totally maxed out with an i5-4790k and a GTX 970 at 1080p with very few frame drops. Is this game a masterpiece? No. Is it one of the better multiplayer melee combat experiences? Yes. Do I recommend it? Yes, IF you're willing to take the time to learn to play.

There are so many bad reviews of this game, it's ridiculous.  Most of it is about petty stuff overblown.  For some you'll have to go into the config file and change the defaults for display.  I had to do that with all the Magic for PC releases.  It's not something outside the average PC gamer's accumen to have to open the config file in notepad and change resolution, fullscreen, or refresh rate so that the game opens properly.  It's also not uncommon to have to complete a tutorial (for which they reward you with with a few cards.), or have to complete at least the first tier of campaign to get access to your premium unlocks or boosters.  That being said, if you bought the complete bundle your collection was stocked the moment you defeat Avycyn at the end of the first tier of the campaign.   It's so well stocked in fact that there's almost no use in buying premium boosters.  There were more than enough cards to build many good decks.  So i was relieved to not be riddled with microtransactions.  I don't see where people who buy premium boosters will have much advantage over anyone who had bought the complete bundle, or were patient enough to slowly unlock it all in the campaign.   Bottom line...buy the complete bundle, and pay to play issues won't be a problem.  Many complaints were also out about having a starter deck at first.  Once you've finished the first tier you can go build custom decks from scratch from the collection.  Plenty of cards for good decks, and cards in decks share to other decks automatically.  The deck builder is decent and filterable.  If you don't like some aspects of the interface and ai (like auto lands or lengthy animations) the settings panel lets you turn them off. Aside from not having customizable backgrounds, and acknowledging no mp 2hg... i'd say this edition has lost little and gained much.  Deckbuilding and multiplayer make this worth the price at the complete bundle...cheaper than buying real cards.  If you liked the last edition, or just enjoy MTG, then this is pretty awesome after about an hour of tutorial and tier 1 of campaign.  I'd give it 4 out of 5 stars...

SIX MONTH UPDATE (5/13/2016):
Six months later, and I am still thoroughly enjoying Shadow Warrior 2.  Like a fine aged whiskey, it's only gotten better with time, and I'm convinced that Flying Wild Hog somehow figured out EXACTLY what type of gamer I am and what I enjoy, because this game hits the mark for me on so many levels...hence the 71+ hours I've put into it.
Since my review back in November of last year, the developers have released 4 DLCs, including a hilarious Xmas event, a trials area, a PayDay crossover add-on that includes two weapons and a multiplayer skin, and a new bounty mission board, all at no extra cost to the player.  I don't really think I've ever seen that done before.  These free DLCs award players with even more weapons and ways to make your Wang stronger...and there are more DLCs to come!
The crafting system in the game is interesting, but you'll need to finish the Way of the Wang DLC in order to take full advantage of it.  Depending on the difficulty you're playing on, the level of your character, and the weapons you have equipped, completing those trials will either be a piece of cake or the bane of your existence. Either way, there will be blood.  Once completed, you'll be able craft gems, embed additional gem slots to your weapons, purify your upgrades by removing negative attributes, and even infuse them with greater damage, lower reload times, and higher rates of fire.  I love this because essentially, you can turn a sub par weapon into a weapon that does very high damage.
At level 67 with a myriad of skills and weapons equipped, I've been farming Insanity I difficulty for experience and Orbs of Masamune.  A lot of people despise that endless, Diablo III-esce grind, but personally, I love making my character stronger and stronger and putting basketball-sized holes in demons or slicing them into shreds.  I use invisibility to increase my damage when I stealth kill, and I use the Arm Of Orochi because it can't be blocked.  This is conjunction with Cerberus, Grip of Darkness, and Fury has made me pretty unstoppable at this difficulty.
In short, this game is still my favorite, and the longer I play it, the more I love it.  Power to the Wang!

Two Worlds is one of the most critically maligned video game series of all time, I'm here to tell you why that's unfair, and why you shouldn't cheat yourself out of this experience.
But first we must list the cons:
Dated graphics (understandable for a 6 year old game at time of writing, but they lacked fidelity even at launch)
Numerous bugs and glitches
Shoddy animations
Shoddy voice acting
Poor multiplayer
Two Worlds has always been a series that lacks a certain amount of polish, the first game using in-house staff as voice actors because they couldn't afford professional talent, is just one example. While I personally enjoyed the first game for reasons I won't divulge in this review, many did not, however Two Worlds II is proof that the developers at Topware have improved upon themselves.
So onto the pros:
Expansive world
Fantastic combat system
Rich and fulfilling loot
T H I C C atmosphere
I recommend Two Worlds II because it stands as a monument to video game innocence, it is honest in its presentation, and flawed. But its flaws while often frustrating are part of the allure, and the game handles certain aspects of its creation very very well. To me, Two Worlds was the first game to utilise really satisfying hack and slash gameplay, it's heavy, but not too heavy, light where it needs to be, but not floaty (like Skyrim, and it is varied; Two Worlds has always had TONS of weapons and armour types. It is a precursor to the combat Demon Souls created, but far less punishing and enjoyable. Exploring the world of Two Worlds II might not have the same recognisable landmarks and features of classic games like TES, or The Witcher, but the detailed and varied environments make for an enjoyable romp on horseback with some of the most satisfying mounted combat since Mount and Blade.
The charm of Two Worlds lies in the moments the developers at Topware hit the nail on the head, it is a game that is so so close to achieving perfection, but is let down by developer inexperience. What is encouraging however, is that Two Worlds II was such an improvement over the first (and already enjoyable) game, that with this trend, Two Worlds III could be even greater, and that excites me a great deal.
So do buy Two Worlds II, if you are a forgiving gamer, who isn't looking for a polished AAA title. Buy it if you're looking for an experience, with ups and downs.
If you're looking for the perfection of a multi-million dollar budget then you may want to look elsewhere, or at least wait for Two Worlds III, maybe that will be the one.

Review:
At the time of writing this, I've only thrown about 10 hours into the game, but so far it's been quite fun. I bought the velvet edition on sale for something like $5, but I have yet to play the DLC. For a quick summary, this game is very open world and free-form. The tutorial is really the only part so far that forces you to take a specific path.
GAMEPLAY:
TL;DR:
-Combat is a bit clunky but it's still fun. Plenty of customization and upgrades. If you use a controller, the aiming is pretty rough but you get used to it pretty quickly. There is actually an auto-aim option but I turned it off so I couldn't tell you if it's any good. Plenty of places and items to find. You can sell or break excess materials into pieces for upgrading your gear, too.
Explanation:
-Maybe this is a pro, maybe this is a con but the game has an interesting, albeit probably not intended, platforming mechanic that allows you to sequence-break pretty easily and skip some quests that you would otherwise need in order to progress (but you would miss the xp and items from them if you did). I usually end up trying to skip things and then go back to complete the quest anyway just for the gold and xp. In some places, you actually have to use it to reach some hidden items which are fairly useful.
-The combat is certainly nothing to compare to the likes of skyrim but it's not terrible. You can use a range of melee weapons, bows, magical staves and upgrade them in a few ways. The game allows you to sort of "counter-attack" after blocking a string of hits, which I quite like. You are also provided with a few moves such as a guard breaking attack to knock shielding opponents back and you unlock several more as you progress. The spell system is interesting and I appreciate the novelty in the system used for this game. Essentially, you have several cards for making unique spells. You can mix and match and nothing is permanent, so you can change them at any time (even mid-fight). You have effect types, area of effect, buffs, projectiles and modifiers for damage, attack type, etc. There is plenty of customization for magic users. The bows are pretty simple. You have a few abilities like different arrow types, multishot, long range, ect.
-Also, the game has plenty of loot to grab, locks to pick, fencegates to leap over. You can hunt animals in the wild and use their drops for lots of things like healing, buffs, alchemy, etc. On another note, I encountered a table for gambling with dice and it seems really easy to win almost every time. I played maybe 6 or 7 times and won 5 of them. All around, it's a good fun and there are plenty of other things to do even in the first town.
STORY:
-Haven't been through the entire story yet, but it's pretty standard. Some evil guy has your sister and you need to go rescue her and do a bunch of things along the way. That's really as far as I've been. The voice acting is hilariously unnatural and the character animations during speech are no different.
DECISION:
-Haven't played much, but for the first 10 hours it's been a good time. Certainly worth the price I got it for, but maybe even the full 20.00. If you like RPG's and old, slightly-buggy games then try it out. If you can catch the game when it's on sale, I would surely recommend playing it. I wouldn't necessarily choose to buy this game over another similar game. But, if you've got the cash and extra time on a weekend or whatever, then it's worth checking out.
Thanks for reading my review,
James

Alright, time for a change of pace here!
Nether is a recently out-of-alpha PVP/PVE zombie-apocalypse survival-horror FPS (try saying that five times fast). The game hasn't officially been released, but if you pre-order it now, you gain access to the (semi)open beta. That being said, it's only been out of its alpha state for about a month. "Really? Only been out of alpha for a month? This game is probaby LOADED with bugs and glitches! Who would want to spend money on something that's not even finished?"
The answer? You do.
Here's the deal, many of you have at least heard of - if not played - DayZ. For you unlucky folks, you can compare it to WarZ. At any rate, the game is pretty straightforward: you customize your character (albeit in a limited fashion), then you spawn in a random location on the map with naught but a kitchen knife and you must scavenge the city of Chicago for food, medical supplies, and weapons whilst avoiding and/or slaughtering the Nether - a strange, extradimensional type of zombie-like creature that has very keen senses and the ability to teleport.
Doesn't sound much like DayZ, right? The similarities here are in game mechanics. Every character is victim to permadeath...you die, you lose all gear and stats for that character. It's like Dungeons of Dredmor, only easier to croak! Oh right, and while you're trying to survive the Nether, you must also survive other players on the server. Who knows, maybe they'll show you mercy. But if there's one thing you learn in this game, it's that no one can stay their hand for long.
Much to my excitement, Nether has one key difference from DayZ/WarZ. That difference in a skill tree. Whereas DayZ focuses entirely on your equipment and a good stroke of luck, Nether incorporates experience points and level ups. Granted, many of the attainable skills aren't enough to mean life or death in a fight with a PC. But, it does give a certain amount of reward for managing to stay alive long enough.
Nether also has locations called Safe Zones. In these places, you're free from all harm (with a rather thrilling exception at the main haven). You are allowed access to a store through which you can buy and sell goods. Most importantly, though, is access to a Global Inventory. If you're lucky enough to get good loot and make it back to a Safe Zone, why not save it for later? Putting something in your Global means that any of your characters have access to it...until you pull it out to use it, of course.
Obviously, beta is beta. I will happily attest to the game's numerous issues with items that you can't pick up or Nether who decide that they've had enough of our mortal physics. Hell, I had one of them b**** slap me because I walked up to him and swung my baseball bat......which subsequently "whooshed" right through him. But know that these issues will not be in the game upon official release. And, even if they are, they can be seen as inconvenient - but entertaining - features.
Lastly, we can't forget about the actual horror aspect of this game. I'll be the first to admit that Nether doesn't grip me in terror. It doesn't make me white-knuckle my mouse nor do I scream like a little girl while playing it. To be honest, Nether doesn't do too well in the "horror" category. It does, however, provide a glorious feeling of suspense. No matter where or what you are. No matter when or with who..SOMETHING will happen to you. It's only a matter of time.
And that feeling, ladies and gentlemen, is why you're willing to look past the floating PCs and rocks that splash like water when you run. THAT is why you want to pick up one of the most addicting games I've played all year.

Arma is one of the best games on steam. The sheer amount of content the game has from the massive range of guns, to the crazy amount of mods is enough to keep you occupied forever. The base game itself is a very tactical military game, so if your not into the military style of game I wouldn't buy it. However there are dozens of gamemodes to choose from that can fit your style. The singleplayer aspect is fun but extremely hard and tedious. The missions are filled with AI that can instantly spot your location from hundreds of meters away and pretty much have auto aim at the lowest difficulty. But the multiplayer aspect is where the game gets really fun. As I stated there are several gamemodes which you can choose from, some mission based, with clear objectives, others with a style of free for all combat in massive open world. The base game uses plenty of mechanics in the gun play which can be very tactical. Zeroing distance, How far the target is away from you (in meters), Bullet drop, ect. are all very realistic and an important aspect in the gunplay. Arma 3 is typically not a run and gun game, you have to pretty tactical at times and always stay aware of what's around you. There are a large amount of guns to choose from, you have several Snipers, Rifles, LMGs, Pistols, DMR's, and SMGs to choose from as well as a large amount of attachments such as scopes (dozens of different kinds each with different ranges and configurations), flashlights/laser pointers, bipods,  and supressors. The guns and attachments also have several different kinds of skins. There is also a large amount of character customization. The main areas of character customization are as follows: Uniform, Vest, Backpack, Headgear, Glasses, and Nightvision. The Uniform, the Backpack, and the Vest can all hold a varied amount of gear, and there are several kinds of clothing in each area providing different appearance and different armor protection in the case of vests and headgear. There is also a large amount of vehicles, there are cars, mopeds, trucks, armored vehicles, tanks, helicopters, and jets to navigate the massive open world of the 3 main maps that are included in the base game: Altis, Stratis, and Malden. These maps are giant and would take hours to run across without a vehicle. There are also DLC, although a bit overpriced they do contain a lot of additonal content, inclding guns, clothing, vehicles, and even a massive tropical map. All of these aspects of the game come without the use of mods, and are just the core elements of the base game. The best thing about this game in my opinion, is the massive amount of mods availiable. Once you get bored with the base game and the DLC you can delve into new modded versions. There are several launchers for the game (A3Llauncher, CCGLauncher, A3Sync) which display modded Arma 3 servers and have the mods required for these servers ready to download. Many of the modded versions create entirely new games with the Arma 3 mechanics at the core. Some of the mods include DayZ mods, Survival Mods, and (my personal favorite) Arma 3 Life mods. They can add entire new maps to the game, with a bunch of new items. Some of the downsides of this game include the fact of the massive FPS drops that can occur. The sheer amount of  details in the game plus its massive map can be a huge strain on your PC. Even if you have a pretty good computer you can still experience a ton of lag in the game. I have a GTX 970, I7 Core, with 8 gigs of Ram and I get some lag, especially when starting up the game. And the gunplay can be frustrating, because it can be hard to hit someone from longer distances. Otherwise if you have a relitively good computer, and like more tactial, realistic-style war games Arma 3 is a great game which I highly recommend. 10/10

Wow. Quick question: have you played a horror game beyond the first Silent Hill or Resident Evil? If no, you might think Amnesia is pretty scary. If yes, I hope to God you don't. On the plus side, this flop is now free to shame your Steam library with its presence. On the negative side: everything else. For something made in 2011, it looks like it crawled out of Sega Dreamcast. I've played lots of indie horror games before, but the production quality here is just inexcusable. The sound design makes me laugh. You might seriously hear spookier noises in mobile-game Slender rip-offs. The ambiance could have very well been pulled from a CD of Halloween noises made for a haunted house with spaghetti worms and gelatin brains. Sounds include gusts of wind, creaky footsteps, and honest-to-God "Ooooo"s set on a mechanical loop. But the "horror" doesn't stop there. I hope you like stone walls, because that's all you're going to see here. The entire game takes place in a dark castle that looks like a dungeon from ES: Oblivion. Speaking of darkness, your character is afraid of the dark. Yes, he will lose his sanity if you stand two feet away from a candle. But he can't pick UP candles - just everything else in the world. Want to throw around boxes? That would have been cool in 1999, right? Well, throw away! The Havok engine's overly-sensitive brother is here to fulfill all your random-object-tossing fantasies. What happens when the main character loses his sanity? The screen gets blurry and everything starts to wobble back and forth. Mortifying, I know. But not nearly as scary as the enemies. I couldn't even get through one hour of the game, so I decided to Google the baddies to see if their monstrous appearance might offer some incentive to keep playing. Nope. The main villain looks like a fish man with a droopy jaw. If that scares you, I recommend staying away from any horror movie that isn't Paranormal Activity. Nothing about this game made me want to continue. The story comes from scraps of paper on the ground. How original! It involves an old man and some sort of curse - oh - and the protagonist has amnesia. Do I care if the protagonist rediscovers the pieces of his shattered psyche? No, because I only learn about him through random bits of flashback that force themselves onto the screen for a few seconds. And the voice acting. Oh, buddy, someone's community theater is going straight to Hollywood for this one. Look, every enemy requires the same strategy: run from it. And you're not very fast, so don't expect a lot of pulse-pounding action here. If you want to play a game with originality and creative monsters, try DreadOut. Give one of the horror mods for Half-Life 2 a whirl. Shrink from Alma in F.E.A.R. 2. Break out the old Fatal Frame series. Just don't believe the hype about this dud. 3/10.

Let me start off by saying I'm not a fan of open-world games, and nor am I a fan of God of War's hack 'n slash genre. But this game finds a perfect balance between those two. I really enjoy 'limited' open-world games, such as The Witcher 2, where you get a big hub to explore, but it is still possible to explore the entire map without sinking hundreds of hours into it.  I didn't enjoy The Witcher 3 or games like Skyrim.
First, let me explain how the game works exactly without spoiling. You play as War, one of the Four Horsemen, and you've basically been summoned to save the world from demons. Killing enemies and finding certain chests reward you with Souls. Souls can be spent on Life Essence (Health Potions), Rage Essence (which fills you with Rage, allowing you to use a super-ability, there's like 5 you can choose from) and permanent life increases, ability upgrades, new attacks,...
The game is semi-open-world, meaning you get to reasonably big hubs across the world and get to explore them one by one, much like the first two Witcher games.
So what exactly makes this game good? Well, here's a list of pro's & cons that came off the top of my head.
Pro's:
-Visually fine, it's clearly outdated but it doesn't look like complete rubbish and is still appealing
-Entertaining combat
-Travelling: Running across the world with your horse can be entertaining, but also boring. There's 'serpent holes' in the game, which is pretty much just a quick travel feature, making it easy to go to objectives around the map.
-Parcour: The parcour in this game is quite smooth and entertaining. Just climbing walls, but also using your grappling hook, portals,... is fun.
-Puzzles are fun!
Cons:
-Repetitiveness and drawn out: At the start it's not much of a problem, but towards the end, when you've unlocked all skills, the combat does get a bit stale. The last 6 hours or so are all with the same skill set, and unless I'm terrible wrong, you always perform the same, optimal combo. The surroundings and opponents cause for the same issue. There's a lot of gray and sand/dust around the world, with the exception of a small jungle and a few bits of snow. The story felt drawn out towards the end, when I thought I was near the ending, I had to do another few long quests that felt a bit unnecessary. I should add that I played through this entire game like 8-10 hours a day, but when I got to the end I got stuck and quit the game for a good month because it started feeling repetitive.
-Serpent holes: though the quick travel is fun, for some reason you always have to run and jump across this weird path in some kind of space environment whenever you want to quick travel, and it felt really boring after a while.
If you have any questions, feel free to ask!

After spending so long in development, Angels Fall First is finally a standalone game, and boy was it worth the wait. Frankly, there isn't much I can say that you don't already know if you've read any other review: the game is a lot like Star Wars Battlefront 2 or Battlefield 2142. Yet at the same time it benefits from a lot of the technical advances games have made since then. The scale is much larger than anything its forerunners could have accomplished, yet at the same time it retains their fun, easy to get learn but hard to master arcadey goodness. Simply put, you know a game is good when the only thing you want is more of it.
That being said, it is an early access game with early access problems. Even after their "Patch 2." I still have issues in the matchmaking lobby with the game connecting me to the wrong server. There are clipping issues in some of the level geometry, with falling through the map being a rare yet present occurance (IE. its only happened to me once in the 10~ hours I've played, but it did happen.) Some of the HuD elements are written in too small of font, and sometimes its all a bit cluttered, Finally, I just wish there were more maps. The game so far has a decent amount but more would be wonderful.
All in all, if you want a game like this one, you could jump right in as it is and have a blast. If your on the fence about it, give it a few updates before commiting. Either way, I do strongly reccomend it.

A fun game, but very difficult to get into. Is it a platformer? Survival? Stealth? Soulsborne?
It's a little bit of everything, and it does most things well. You are a small, mostly helpless animal trying to gather enough food to survive and avoid being eaten yourself. The game is mostly about climbing and exploration, with a series of interesting and frightening enemies along the way. It is also very, very hard.
The game boasts that its climbing controls give the player "Natural fluidity and a unique sense of weight." I think that's true for the most part, but it also makes the controls very difficult to get used to. You are taught basic controls and one advanced leap manuever by the game. Do yourself a favor and read a guide on the rest, because there are a lot of them. Sometimes the controls feel exactly like the devs describe them, and sometimes they feel ackward and obtuse. Something as simple as climbing up a pole, releasing onto a ledge, and jumping to the next one will take about twice as many button presses as it would in another game. But once you get into the flow of the controls, they feel great. I can jump over a monster, scramble over a nearby ledge, and leap across a chasm instants before the monster can turn around and bite me in half. It's all very breathless and organic.
The game often doesn't tell you what to do or where to go next. There's one or two secrets worth finding, but mostly what you will be looking for is food, shelter from the periodic rainstorms, and the next area to find. You will sometimes have a little yellow creature to point you in the right direction, other times you will not. I have to be in the right frame of mind to play the game, since it can be frustrating. If I play it for 15 minutes, probably the only thing I will have accomplished in that time is find several dead ends and a new place to find berries.
Progression through the game is made by passing through certain gates. In order to open them, you need to have high "karma." Every day you manage to leave your hibernation save point, gather enough food to keep living, and return to a shelter without getting eaten or washed away by the torrential rain, your karma increases. Survive long enough and you will be able to open these gates. The progression is similar to Dark Souls, you need to either find a new shelter or return to your old one or all your progress will be lost. It can be very frustrating at times.
The enemies in the game are varied, colorful, and interesting to overcome. Your ability to fight is practically nonexistent, and you're usually better off using stealth to get past enemies or just running for it. Each area has some unique enemies, and you need a different approach to each one. Different enemies have different senses, and will require a different approach It's a huge rush when you finally figure out how to get past an enemy and they no longer pose a threat to you.
There is a plot, and a few goals, but with almost 19 hours in this game, I have no real clue what it is. For me the push is to overcome whatever the curret challenge is and to see what new strange thing the game has to show me next.
If you're willing to take the time to unravel this game's mystery for yourself, I can highly recommend it. But you might want to have something easier installed to help you unwind once this game gets you so riled up.

RIME is a slow burn even for a game of this brevity, which may come across as an undesirable trait however it is very intentional. The story is told without any dialogue whatsoever, leaving atmosphere and emotional suggestion with most of the heavy lifting. The design will feel almost random as you piece together the hints within, a form of ordered chaos if you will. I found it difficult to feel invested in the game until the latter levels where the entire vision begins to come together and you understand and appreciate the how and why. While you may begin to figure out the general concept about halfway there are certain details that do not truly hit home until the game is finished.
That being said the game sometimes felt like a chore to play, with the reward and satisfaction being reserved for the final scenes, but I am glad I carried on. If you play the game and feel uninspired to finish I urge you to push through, it is worth the effort and may just prompt a second playthrough. While nothing in the game is particularly difficult the brilliant story telling through the game world is a lost art in interactive entertainment in recent years, an art that Tequila Works has shown can still be powerful and effective.

Might be a bit rambly. TL;DR: Love the aesthetic. Beautiful and lovable character. Quality of life is garbage. Backtracking for food is garbage. Goes over the line of difficult but fun to this is wasting my time and patience. It is very frustrating and needs better quality of life. That said, in short bursts, it is an alright game to play. It is worth checking out for its relatively modest price, but the payoff is VERY QUESTIONABLE. You can always watch a let's play for the ending I suppose... That's where this game falls short.
Pros:
-	Beautiful aesthetic. They did the pixel art wonderfully.
-	Organic, if not a little floaty and frustrating at times, controls. You feel like a slugcat.
-	Rewarding* progression through tough areas. (Up to a point… more on this in cons)
-	A very challenging experience for those who are brave (and patient) enough.
-	I love exploring the different places and dystopian architecture and I want more of it!
-	Interesting variety in enemies that challenge you.
Cons:
-	It’s a slog. Takes up a lot of time to make very little overall progress.
-	The physics of the game… While rather organic like the controls, they leave much to leave desired in the consistency department.
-	Randomness of some deaths: 1. Entered a room and suddenly eaten out of  a pipe exit. Not too big of a deal. 2. Falling. Good lord the falling. If I get knocked off a ledge and fall again I am going to die in real life. 3. Getting shanked with a spear by the natives across a great distance. What did I do to deserve this. Ow.
-	Backtracking = Frustration (after the first couple times). You will die a lot. Like dark souls. Except you have to backtrack through the level and hope that you can find some food or god help you, you are going to be stuck in the area for a looooong time. So instead of trying to overcome one or two challenges that are straight ahead of you, you are trying to overcome the game trying to actively screw with you and make things inconsistent all over the map.
-	Once you get beat down too many times, progression simply leaves you with an empty feeling of getting lucky that one time. It’s very hardcore and I have to take it in shorter bursts.
Things I would change:
-	Give the game an easy mode. I just want to have fun in the world at this point. I want to know the story and gather the lore. Have it respawn you at the last pipe you exited before death and allow teleportation back to checkpoints you have visited or something.
-	A more helpful UI. The current one is rather vague and doesn’t give information on how to get achievements or how to finish the current ones you have done SOMETHING for. Trips to the wiki are irritating.
Summary thing:
This beautiful, interesting, and rather deep game requires more patience than I have. While in the beginning it is a wonderful adventure, making you feel like a small, mostly defenseless creature making small steps towards a goal, this can be detrimental to overall progress. After a long and arduous journey through 4 of the maybe 12 areas the game has to offer, I simply do not feel that the payoff is worth any more of the struggle. It's a very interesting world that I would love to explore more, but it simply is too difficult to justify for  the most part. The small steps become a constant anxiety-fest instead of a fun pseudo-prey/survival simulation. I enjoyed figuring out some of the mechanics and it made me feel rather smart for doing so, but after that I was left with these ‘new’ mechanics and the same backtracking and hoop-jumping.
The cons outweigh the pros currently, but I will keep playing it. It's definitely worth checking out if you can deal with the cons.

An amazing game.
It can be frustrating, at times - it took many tries to pass through certain areas - but I loved this from start to finish.
Having curiosity and a willingness to experiment is a big part of what can make the game click with you or not, I think.
It was a really wonderful experience, and I'm so glad for it. It's like a kind of platform game I've always wanted to see, one with a large world to explore, playing as some sort of animal creature, potential friends along the way..
I think the best way to describe it is that it's all about the experience of the world. Curiosity. Playing as the slugcat, becoming one with the character.
It's all about you against the world, learning how it works, learning the layout of the world, what's right and wrong, friend or enemy, what's a useful tool for what, how and where to get food.
The game is all about this learning. It's all about your skills, your memory of the areas (though there is a map that builds up as you explore).
The game only teaches you a few things for survival, and the rest is up to you to discover and learn on your own. This is very important.
If you were to start all over, you'd be pretty much as powerful then as you were when you finished.
You aren't granted new moves. You don't gain stats. It's all about learning how best to use what you have to work with, whether it be the rocks and spears you often find, or how to kill something, the interactions between different things, the idea of doing certain things... You have to plan on your own, improvise, be curious, and not rush into a situation without thinking.
It rains every so often. Hard enough to kill. You have to eat enough to be able to hibernate in a sanctuary area, sleeping past the rain. Other creatures have to hide elsewhere, so if you're having trouble getting somewhere, after you sleep, that creature may not be there. Or something else could be.
This means exploration has a timer until you have to sleep again, but with planning, this isn't bad at all.
You'll find other creatures hunting, too, moving from area to area much like you are, just trying to survive and get by, wherever on the food chain they may be.
Platforming usually works well, though climbing on top of horizontal bars can be a little frustrating in some spaces. Other than that, every time I've messed up, I've known it's because I did something wrong. There was this one spot I kept falling, but I realized, wait, I don't have to hold down, just tap down once.
Precision (on the player's part) is important. I found keyboard to work far better than gamepad, personally. I was clumsy at first, but was soon zipping around with ease.

Given all of the terrible reviews this game has had, and being a guy who gets his jollies from deck-building specifically, I had to buy the game and see for myself. I just beat the game, so I've definitely given it 'a chance,' and I'll probably play it a bit more. Why am I packing the gun so tight? It's very simple: this game is someone's idea of a Pay to Pay to Play.
First off, the good points: I'm fairly happy overall with the deck-building aspects in the sense that you can literally build versus only unlock and substitute. I'm also really happy at the base price of the game: at $10 it means that more people can get in and that makes for more diversity in the meta. Despite complaints to the contrary I'm actually okay with the UI and just wish there was a way to turn off all the fancy effects to get the game to run better.
Now, the stuff that really annoyed me: The complete edition isn't complete; you're short-cutting your way through most, not all, of the card collection aspects. The game, had it wanted to capture the casual audience, should have allowed for card trading, which this game doesn't, because that's what keeps most people in the community, not just playing the game. That's some seriously lost opportunity, Wizards. The entire reason I started spending real money on Magic was because one man talked to me about deck building and gave me a bunch of commons, giving me the sense that I was now part of something much larger.
The card diversity in the game is exceptionally limited. This may have initially been to prevent 'power building' (there are also limitations on the number of duplicates you can have in a deck that don't follow standard) but it really keeps people from feeling the potential of certain sets, particularly Zendikar's 'man lands.' The fact that NPCs in the campaign use some of these missing cards furthered the feeling of frustration.
Overall, I'd recommend the base game to someone who was interested in seeing what Magic: The Gathering was all about, but would steer someone who's actually played the game before away to another product. The complete version left me with a terrible taste in my mouth.
Rating: 6/10, I would NOT recommend buying the Complete Edition

Kingdom Wars is a very interesting game. At first I had a very low opinion of it, but if you can overcome the first hour of the game and look past its shortcomings you'll find a very addictive experience with so much potential.
Negative impressions:  Visually it looks as if it made in the early 2000s, and the combat leaves a lot to be desired. Once battle is joined unit formations devolve into disorganized mosh-pit like globs with very poor unit collision detection (if any at all.) The animations are primitive and very basic, not just in combat but for walking, idle, and cutscenes dialog. There are also a host of bugs, many of which are highly destructive and infuriating. The worst I encountered was when I lost an entire army, 28 units, because a quest sent them into a void and left me with an empty army on the map- without even starting the quest. I was left without my hero unit, and an entire day worth of invested resources that I used to build said army.
Positive Impressions: The economic system and a load of fun, and by far the best part of the game aside from the general idea. You can make profits by trading, harvesting resources, looting battlefields, and questing. Each option presents its own benefits and challenges. If you decide to harvest resources at home then you will looking at the safest and most reliable way, but it also means you need peasants working the land which drags on your unit cap. Trade is the quickest way, but it also means you’re at risk of losing caravans and thus your cargo. It also requires more management and the natural risk of losing money on a trade if you’re too hasty.
The game has a pretty mild pace, which is certainly a positive in my opinion. You won’t become powerful overnight, and all buildings and soldiers take quite a bit of resources and time to make. There is also a healthy variety of units and plenty of defining traits to pick from. Units gain experience from battles which lets you upgrade them, in addition to researching new technologies and equipment. From what I can tell there is no pay-to-win advantage either. The cashhop is purely aesthetics and speeding up the process of questing rewards.
If the combat would be overhauled then I think this would be an easy game to recommend, and if animations and visuals where modernized then it would be a jewel. However as it stands it’s a give and take. If you can overlook its issues there is a lot of fun to be had, but not everyone can do that.

Mostly positive? WHAT? The game has excellent campaing that lasts for about 18 hours. Seriously story mode is 15-18 ♥♥♥♥ing hours and it's well made. The story itself is quite interesting and the characters presented to us are believable. Even the main villain is relatable to some degree. You play as most of the characters in each faction during the story mode so you could use it as a tutorial to learn basics of almost every character,which is nice. Reason to learn at least the basics of every character is that in pvp mode you really need to know what you and your opponent can do. For example if you have no ♥♥♥♥ing idea how Conqueror works and you're playing against decent conqueror he will probably flatten you in few seconds since you don't know how to respond to the things he does.
The main focus of the game is pvp,and it's excellent. This game has the best combat system I've ever seen in a videogame so far. It even trumps the Soulsborne series,which I am a huge fan of. The combat system is heavy,it's fast,it's impactfull and you really get the feel for the action. The skillcap in this game is extremely high. There are no noob characters even when some unskilled player might say that simply because they personally are not good enough to deal with said characters. There really is no cheese in the game,if your opponent keeps spamming 1 combo all the time and you can't deal with that you quite simply just suck at the game. Every attack can be avoided in one form or another. Even unblockable attacks can be parried,which is something everyone should learn. If you don't know how to parry you're quite simply a mediocre player. Quite a lot of players even fail at blocking,which is so easy I wonder how it's even possible.

Difference between 4v4 elimination and skirmish is that in skirmish you respawn until one team reaches score limit,and after that they need to take down entire team to win,whereas in elimination you win as soon as one team dies. 4v4 Domination is the main mode you've probably seen in gameplay trailers,two armies fight one another and players capture and hold objectives. The feeling you get after you kill 3 guys that came to the point you're holding and you're still standing there victorious is incredible.

The original Duke Nukem 3D has a linear format, you go from one stage to the next. However those stages are large, varied, and include numerous optional paths, secret areas, and methods of exploration(jet-pack, steroid-boosted jumps, etc). Duke Nukem Forever is entirely linear. For the most part in DNF you're either shooting a handful of aliens in quasi-arena areas, doing some ridiculous puzzle, partaking in a vehicle-section, or doing some ego-boosting activity. Oh and for the entirety of the game your sensibilities on what makes for quality game-design or at least in-offensive content are dragged through horse manure.
Vehicle sections - All too often FPS developers feel the need to include vehicle-sections. They use the word "variety" which is short for "we decided the actual game wasn't compelling". Some developers can rise above, and that's because they use vehicles in an intelligent manner. Half-Life 2 is a good example, well I think it is at least. Yes a good chunk of the game is spent on a boat, but there are occasions where you have to be on foot to get things done. It feels organic, and makes for good pacing. The Halo series is also a good example, since vehicles feel like very much a part of the game, and are even optional depending on the circumstances.
Duke Nukem Forever just didn't care. The developer looked at a checklist of what popular FPS titles did and said "We need this, but let's not put in the effort to make it quality." Vehicle-sections are a constant in DNF, and none of them are entertaining. Early on you're controlling an RC truck, a stage or two later you're driving an RC truck, not long afterwards you're driving a monster truck (that runs out of gas at specific points), then you're riding in a mine-cart, driving a forklift(wtf?), and so on. I'm probably forgetting a few instances but that's probably for the best. The main point is that DNF has vehicle-sections because they needed to pad the game out somehow.
The combat/gun-play - When you're making a first-person-shooter the shooter aspects should be compelling. There are several games that get this most basic element right. Duke Nukem Forever...doesn't. For a 1996 game, Duke Nukem 3D still holds up in the shootin' department. It's fast-paced, crunchy, and aliens make all kinds of nasty and gratifying noises when you splatter their guts. Shooting aliens in DNF isn't fun because there's no satisfying feedback. The over abundance of pig cops are the perfect example. They barely react when you're firing away at them, until they just sorta collapse when they die. If feels disconnected, like Duke didn't really kill them. What's also ridiculous is the lack of new enemies. Fifteen years should have been plenty of time to come up with some new aliens to design. With the technology available we should've seen some really creative stuff that pushes the envelope. Instead it's mostly the same enemies we saw back in 1996. Everything's the same, just crappier. This is especially apparent with the final boss fight against the Cycloid Emperor. He's the final boss of Duke Nukem 3D, the first boss of Duke Nukem Forever (in a nod to the first game), as well as the final boss. Good Lord.
Puzzles - When it comes to puzzles in an FPS, I'm firmly in the neutral camp. A little something to break up the action never hurts, as long as it isn't overbearing and doesn't screw with the pacing. DNF fails in this regard as well. Duke Nukem 3D was never the "thinking man's" shooter. Yes there were puzzles but they were more along the lines of flipping certain switches. The most elaborate puzzle took seconds to figure out. Naturally DNF has lots of puzzles. Alot of the time I felt like I was playing a seventh-rate Half-Life clone. None of it fits, very rarely is it clever, and it's just not fun. Defeating the Alien Queen requires bouncing pipe bombs off of trampolines. This is terrible. Every second Duke is hit by something that puts him into critical health. This is terrible crap.
The most bewildering addition is the ego system. In this game Duke recovers health (aka ego) when not taking damage. Boosting ego is done through a variety of actions, and they're almost all ridiculous. I can understand pumping iron giving an ego boost, but looking at pictures of women? What? It's a nonsensical system, but it's also kinda necessary because otherwise Duke dies too easily. This is the same guy that says "power armor is for♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;. Yeah, and taking cover almost constantly just to recover health is totally badass.
What really gets under my skin is that the humor in DNF is forced, painfully unfunny, and oft-times just plain awful. The timeliness of most of the jokes are just brutally bad, like the Olsen-twins esque pop-stars in the intro, "America, ♥♥♥♥ Yeah!", and well..you get the idea. Over the course of DNF's development hell, all of the jokes were kept in, even though most of them ceased being funny almost a decade ago. There's also this secondary character named Dylan. I still can't believe anyone thought he was a good idea. When he got killed off I kicked his corpse into a pool of electrified water. Naturally he returned in the expansion alive and well. I hate this game.
And yeah I played through the expansion. I'll admit, there were some neat moments (the clones mainly). The final boss is a vehicle section however and that's just unforgivable. Multiplayer is also available and uh...it wasn't that bad, at least compared to the rest of the game. It's not saying much sure, but at least it says SOMETHING.
There's a lot more I could be discussing about Duke Nukem Forever. There's that dream sequence where Duke is in a strip-club doing menial tasks for a lapdance, the plot(?), the misogyny, the--- eeeggghhhAHAHghhh! Forget it, I'm done talking about this mess.

Tomb Raider Underworld is the most awful game I have finished to date. In about all aspects apart from graphics it is a massive step back from both Anniversary and Legend and about the only good thing I can say about this game is that there are a few nice views to be enjoyed that just for a few seconds lessen the pain of playing this otherwise terrible game. I wish I didn't finish it, but at least I can now say with full confidence that this game isn't worth any money or time.
By far the most important elements of the Tomb Raider games I can think of are the camera and movement controls, which ideally enable you to get a good look at the level, work out where to go and then actually get there without much trouble. Sadly, Underworld does not even get close to a passing grade in either of these two categories. The camera has, especially in cramped environments, a mind of its own that often gets you close-ups of irrelevant pieces of scenery or Lara's butt while refusing to give you a workable perspective to conduct your next jump from. A couple of times the camera's incessant need to reposition itself even against your will resulted in a complete loss of orientation while standing perfectly still. After playing the first two hours or so I for the first time in my life felt dizzy from just playing a game.
The movement is another complete disaster. I am not exaggerating when I say that Lara got stuck in random bits of terrain at the very least
times, a state I could only get out of by frantically wiggling and jumping around until in a rare display of mercy the game let me break free. Trying to move with any kind of precision is a task that takes the utmost concentration and care since Lara moves like she's on rollerblades, so frequent use of the slow walk is advised. A problem that is absolutely ubiquitous is the difficulty in orienting Lara towards where you want her to look since she, just like the camera, will often do anything but what you want her to do. The animations that in other games provide you with important feedback to your inputs here provide you with none of that. While some of them look nice enough on their own, they have a tendency to react erratically to the most basic of challenges, leading to many preventable and frustrating deaths. Even standing near a ledge or other obstacle will in some cases cause the idle Lara to go absolutely haywire.
The puzzles are uninspired, forgettable and hardly a challenge and the story is expectedly bland and uninteresting, though some of the cutscenes and voice-acting are alright. Besides being a passionate archaeologist that's completely fine with destroying centuries-old pots and vases found in unexplored ruins for the occasional collectible, Lara is also (still) a murderous psychopath that has no qualms at all about killing droves of humans and members of endangered species alike. A detailed and coherent story was not the strong suit of Anniversary or Legend either, but they at least had some good gameplay in between. The combat in Underworld still has zero depth, zero weight, absolutely zero consequence to anything you are doing and does nothing but waste your time, it is almost a perfect copy of the combat from Anniversary and Legend, which means the same mindnumbing and utterly irredeemable combat system has now appeared in three games with close to zero changes to it. Additionally, the game now provides you with a weapon selection before and during each level, which because of the shallowness of the combat system is an absolute joke that could not be more irrelevant to the game if it tried.
What I find the most insulting about this game is that even with a studio of professionals and an experienced publisher working on it, they've learned nothing from their past mistakes, have no regard for the customer's money, time and intelligence and deliver a game that has that big-budget gloss, but is shockingly lacking in the departments that actually matter, it is the epitome of a polished turd. As far as I am concerned, this game is an unholy abomination that should not exist. Stay as far away as you can from this dumpster fire.

CLIFFS: Contender for worst/laziest PC port of all time, still one of the deepest, most involving games of all time.
For those who have never played the KOTOR duology, you need to know that you are absolutely missing out on some of the best moments in gaming.  These are the games that paved the way for the Mass Effect series and the "play as a good or bad person" mechanic seen in many games since.  You don't even have to be a big Star Wars fan to really enjoy them.  If you're like me, though, you will be one by the time you are finished.
Gameplay mechanics are similar to Mass Effect.  You and up to two other characters on your team at the same time. Run into some enemies, and the default setting is for the game to auto-pause while you issue your commands. Unpause and the battle commences.  The battle mechanics has a ton of stuff going on in the background that you don't even see.  This is good if you have terrible reflexes or just want a nice, enjoyable game to play without getting all tensed up.  The game uses a "D&D" based system to calculate how battles will play out.  Stats, saving throws, etc.  The game does not really get into depth on how certain stats and attributes affects gameplay, but it isn't too hard to figure out the basics.
Character development is like a classical RPG and is really in depth.  This allows you to tailor each member on your team and there are a lot of different paths to take.  For melee characters, you can go unarmed, one handed single-handed weapons (duelist), dual wielding single handed weapons, or a single dual-handed weapon (like a staff).  And then there are the variety of light sabers: short (for off-hand dual wielding), regular, and the double-bladed badass. Despite the dated graphics, the light sabers still look great.  Next up is the ranged build with an equal amount of variety.  Blaster pistols, blaster rifles, bowcasters (Wookiee weapon), and heavy blasters. Many of the weapons can be modified with various upgrades that you can tailor to your liking. For example, strong vs droids, can destroy shields, light vs dark powers, fire, ice, sonic, ion, and electrical damage, etc.  Same thing with armor.
At every level, your characters are awarded skill points to put towards various skills. The number of points varies upon the character's intelligence and class. Skills are Computers (slicing/hacking), Security (bypassing locks), Persuasion (can alter certain conversations), Repair (fixing things, "healing" droids), Demolition (disarming mines, effectiveness of grenades), Healing, and a few others.  In addition to skills, there are techniques to unlock.  It varies by class, but you will often get one point for every 2nd/3rd level to put towards techniques.  This is where you can tailor your character for a certain fighting style.  Adding points to dual wielding, for instance, can reduce the penalty recieved from using two weapons.  There are a ton of these things to unlock, giving you the oportunity to grow each character exactly as you want.
For the characters who can use The Force, you get one (sometimes two) points per level to unlock/upgrade Force Powers.  This is the fun stuff and there are a ton of different ones to choose from.
The absolute best part about this game is the depth of the story and how well-thought out the Star Wars universe is. There is so much to learn about the different planets, species, and factions in the Star Wars world and it can totally suck you in and make you want to watch the movies again (axcept for the one with JarJar; ♥♥♥♥ him!).  The story is very deep and has many interesting twists and turns.  If you have a short attention span and usually skip dialogue, you will not get the full experience from this game.  There is an incredible amount of dialogue here.  As you are walking around, you will have many opportunities to speak with others and even your own teammates.  You can guide the conversations by choosing your responses and this leads to one of the most interesting mechanics in the game.  Be a good guy (Light Side) or an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (Dark Side) and the game reacts to that.  This also affects your character development.  Some of the Force Powers are Light or Dark side.  You can still use any powers you want, but a fully Light Side character trying to use the Wound/Choke/Kill Force Power will require a lot more Force Points (like MP).  Force Points regenerate over time, but youcan easily run out in a battle. Dialogue is a huge part of this game and thankfully, the voice acting is terrific.  I have no idea how they managed to record so much and still fit it on the original disc. For every line of dialogue you hear, there are often one or more lines you don't hear because of the way you selected your response.  It's brilliant.  The "non-English" languages sound just as good as they did in the movies.  Ditto the light saber and blaster sound effects.  The music is also really good.
And now for the RANTS: Let me get this out of the way first. This is, without a doubt, the WORST and LAZIEST console-to-PC port I have ever seen! So much disappointment, and the frustration is compounded because the game itself is so deserving of a good port. It is so good, in fact, that if they gave it a modern refresh and re-released it, I would totally pay full price for it. How bad is it? How about this: This game, which was designed for consoles, HAS NO CONTROLLER SUPPORT! Instead, we are left with some mediocre keyboard and mouse controls. It's not that they are bad, but if you are in the mood to recline on your couch and play with a controller, you're out of luck.  Oh, and the resolution? Hope you're still using a laptop from 10 years ago. You can download a program and edit an .ini file to give you 1080p, but it should be able to be selected in configs. More bad stuff: the character AI and path detection is, for lack of a better word, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Since combat is automated, characters wil run around on their own.  More often than not, two or more characters will try to occupy the same space at the same time.  They usually end up stuck on each other or will just do-si-do around like they're dancing. This isn't Riverdance, morons! Go hit that enemy with yor light saber! Queueing up commands can be frustrating, too. You meet an enemy and the game auto-pauses.  You input your commands, then unpause.  More often than not, the characters will perform one default action first before doing the commands you ordered.  Huge pain in the♥♥♥♥♥if you issued your commands to buff the party up before going to go head to head with a Rancor, but your idiot teammates decide to run up to it, hit it once, then carry out your commands. Great, not only are you getting your stool pushed in, but the characters are out of buff range and don't share the effects you want. Oh, and often upon finishing a battle, the active character would not respond to inputs.  I would have to either switch to another character or quick save/quick load.  I was nearly finished with the game before I figured out that enabling V-sync can fix that bug.
Lastly, the fact that their are no Steam Achievements or Trading cars is like one final flick to the nuts while wearing tight jeans.  I know Space Channel 5 was recently updated to fix it's many shortcomings of being a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ PC port, and they even added Achievements.  Hopefully someone will give this game what it deserves in a much-needed update and fix the mistakes.  It's just unforgiveable.
I know the list of negatives is huge, but it absolutely should not deter you from playing this game.  You really are missing out. KOTOR 1 & 2 are two of the best games ever made and still stand up today.
