Technically, I've been playing this game since 2010, as I played it but never completed it. So it's been on the back burner for around 7 years. But during the summer sale, I decided to buy it on my PC, rather than playing my xbox copy, and finish this great game.
This game has an amazing and unique story, which can captivate your attention for long periods of time, making it almost impossible to turn off. I have been a great fan of Lara Croft and the Tomb Raider series in the past, and until recently, I hadn't played a game in years. It feels great to playing this old gem.
Alongside this, the game has really fun and satisfactory combat, and fantastic level design. The puzzels are really well thought out and fantastic, although I have to admit, sometimes I found it was not clear what I needed to do. I felt some puzzle parts were a little tedious but otherwise they were great!
The environment created in this game is so good. I love the locations, and when inside a tomb, you're kept on your guard for the next enemy to attack. There's always a feeling that's you're not quite alone.
However, this isn't completely perfect. It has it's imperfections, for definite. One thing I hated was the eratic camera function, which can get really annoying when in some tight spaces in the game. This is prominent at the start of the game, but seems to disappear as you progress through. Also, this game has a few little bugs, which are quite funny to begin with, but get very annoying, very quickly.
At one point in the game, you have to put a block on a platform, but everytime you do this, the block goes flying out of your grasp flying somewhere randomly. Also there are some large FPS drops at different parts in the game, especially underwater (I found). If this happens, then either turn v-sync off or on; fixing both issues.
Other than that, I found this game very enjoyable, and very nostalgic, expecially with the soundtrack (which is awesome).  It's a very mystical game, with supernatural events and features, but don't let that put you off, because it really is fantastic!

Definitely a confusing game at first, but once you put some time in to it and understand what's going on, it gets very fun.  The number of unique mechanics and different playstyles availbable is great, and makes it easy for anyone to find something that appeals to them. I don't review too many games so bear with me on this one.
Let me be up front and say that this game needs work, and that is very evident when you play it; however this game has a lot of promise and if you're into survival games, and don't mind Early Access development, then this game should suit your fancy.
The game consists of post-apocalyptic, urban combat. Currently (12/9/13) the game is very heavy on Player versus Player, but has the end goal aiming at a balanced Player versus Player versus Environment. This is something that will take time since the game seems to be in its earlier stage of development, but if you give it time it will become a very solid game that will be well received. If you're not one for sitting around and waiting for the next patch then avoid this game until it comes out.
I could talk about what's in the game right now, but that changes frequently enough that I would just be covering some of the core concepts, which most of the previous reviews have already stated.
Here is just a very quick breakdown of what to expect.
**PvP and PvE**
The Player versus Player right now is where the game has a lot of focus, not because the game specifically want's players to kill each other in a death-match style game, but because there is currently little incentive to not kill another player--just personal choice. The Player versus Environment aspect is lacking, as of right now, but they hope to add more to the game to help make this game-play much better. If you were to jump into the PvE only aspect, and decide to not kill other players, then you'll find out that you'll be just running around killing Nether, and trying to avoid players like the plague, which really narrows the experience.
**Small RPG Elements**
You can specialize your character's play-style through leveling up by either killing players, nether, or selling items. You can reach a max level of 30 and gain one skill point per level. You can place these points into the skill tree to improve your Gun, Melee, and Stealth play-styles as well as put points into stamina and survival aspects (I.E. You can run farther or jump higher, and food and medicine are more beneficial. You gain experience quite easily right now so even if you die and lose the levels you're able to get them back fairly quick.
**Perma-death**
Be ready for it because you lose all your levels and Items when you die (Even to other players killing you). You're going to die...a lot... Just take the death with a grain of salt. It's not that hard to find guns in this game, and you can attain any item--other than most cosmetic items--just from playing the game. You can spawn in and find a gun, or new melee item within mere minutes of playing so when you die the lose really isn't all that dramatic.
**Random (Drop-in) Spawns**
You'll spawn randomly on the map, and from there you can do anything you want. You do not have a saved location when you log-out, even when in a safe zone. They plan on adding some sort of log-out spawn point once they find a way that would not cause an imbalance in the game, such as server hopping and the like.
**Global Inventory**
This is where you can store items for all of your characters to use. You access it through being in the safe zone, and opening your inventory. It has very little room in it, so you have to make a choice of what to put into it rather than just filling it to the brim with guns and ammo. This part of the game is actually fairly well balanced. By balanced I mean that people are less likely to hoard items. This lack of hoarding provides a better experience for new players jumping in, and not being overwhelmed by the existing player base.
**Currency**
Currently there are two types of currency Gold Coins, and Dollars. Dollars are in-game currency that are found randomly through out the map, and drops off from other players. You use Dollars to buy food, medicine, ammo, melee weapons, and some cosmetic items. Gold Coins are bought through micro-transaction and are only used for the purpose of cosmetic item purchases. There is no pay to win aspect about it, so don't worry yourself about that.
**Cosmetic Items**
As previously mentioned the items consist of hats, and braces currently. They will not drop when you die, and once you've bought them they are yours forever. They are going to add a separate global inventory for these items, so that your other inventory will not be full with items you can't get rid of.
**Store**
Most of what could be said was said under the Currency block of text. You can go to a show in the safe zone(s), and once there you can access the shop through your inventory menu. You can buy ammo, food, medicine, back-packs, and melee weapons. You can also purchase cosmetic items, which consist of hats and bracers, but might branch out into more.
**Community Feedback**
The developers have been very attentive to what the community has been asking for. They have added, or changed content to suit that of the community, and are actively looking for its feedback about game-play and mechanics.
**Character Customization**
The game currently doesn't have all that much customization right now. The developers have noted that this is because of the need to focus on more important aspects of the game, rather than aesthetics. They also noted that they are planning on adding a female player model to the game, but have not done so as due to the previous statement.
I find this game a lot of fun, worth at least looking into. If you're not willing to drop the money on the game then just keep an eye on the following thread. They give out Guest Keys like candy in there, and all you need to do is active the key using your PlayNether account. I give the game a solid 7/10 right now, but as the game keeps developing I plan on changing that score to reflect the changes made.

Review Rewritten: February 10th, 2016.
While updates aren't as frequent as some other Early Access games, BeamNG's staff has been hard at work ironing out the seams and providing their userbase with a fun game with reasons to keep coming back. They could easily lay back and let the modding community add their own vehicles and maps to the game, but they continue to produce cars that are fun to drive. With the latest update, we've been given access to the ETK 800, a luxury estate wagon shaped like a Jaguar XF Sportbrake or Audi A6 Avant wagon. They've also fixed bugs and tweaked a huge amount of code for the game.
The game runs better and looks better, too. It's still a lot of fun to mix and match parts to build your own trim for all the cars in the game, and it's still the same ridiculous game of driving with reckless abandon. A perfect game for people who love destroying things, or enjoy customizing their vehicles. Furthermore, this is beginning to shape up as a legitimate tool for Hollywood's stunt engineers to use on the job for testing stunt schematics.
///
PROS:
+ Most realistic damage modeling I've ever seen in a video game.
+ The feeling of driving a quick yet fragile mass of plastic and metal is invigorating.
+ The car selection is a bit small at the moment, but is still quite diverse.
+ The maps are also very diverse, but again the selection is a bit small.
+ The modding community is very active, and produces very good content!
+ $30 is a good price for driving fans and sim racers.
CONS:
- A good computer is needed to play this game at reasonable frame rates.
- $30 might be a bit steep for people who only want to destroy cars.
- The cars seem to feel a bit too floaty with miles of understeer unless you adjust the suspension.
- The engines all sound exactly the same, as if a Slant 6 sounds exactly like a race-modded V8.
SCORES:
If the game were released as of this update, my score: 6.5/10.
As the game stands, in beta form: 7/10.
///
Get it when it goes on sale! This game is definitely worth the investment; I've had a lot of fun since I purchased the game, and I've never regretted my purchase. Whenever you feel bored with the game, you can just go to the forums and download a car to bang around with or download a track to cruise through. There is lots of fun to be had within the game's stock content and in the modding community!

An amazing game.
It can be frustrating, at times - it took many tries to pass through certain areas - but I loved this from start to finish.
Having curiosity and a willingness to experiment is a big part of what can make the game click with you or not, I think.
It was a really wonderful experience, and I'm so glad for it. It's like a kind of platform game I've always wanted to see, one with a large world to explore, playing as some sort of animal creature, potential friends along the way..
I think the best way to describe it is that it's all about the experience of the world. Curiosity. Playing as the slugcat, becoming one with the character.
It's all about you against the world, learning how it works, learning the layout of the world, what's right and wrong, friend or enemy, what's a useful tool for what, how and where to get food.
The game is all about this learning. It's all about your skills, your memory of the areas (though there is a map that builds up as you explore).
The game only teaches you a few things for survival, and the rest is up to you to discover and learn on your own. This is very important.
If you were to start all over, you'd be pretty much as powerful then as you were when you finished.
You aren't granted new moves. You don't gain stats. It's all about learning how best to use what you have to work with, whether it be the rocks and spears you often find, or how to kill something, the interactions between different things, the idea of doing certain things... You have to plan on your own, improvise, be curious, and not rush into a situation without thinking.
It rains every so often. Hard enough to kill. You have to eat enough to be able to hibernate in a sanctuary area, sleeping past the rain. Other creatures have to hide elsewhere, so if you're having trouble getting somewhere, after you sleep, that creature may not be there. Or something else could be.
This means exploration has a timer until you have to sleep again, but with planning, this isn't bad at all.
You'll find other creatures hunting, too, moving from area to area much like you are, just trying to survive and get by, wherever on the food chain they may be.
Platforming usually works well, though climbing on top of horizontal bars can be a little frustrating in some spaces. Other than that, every time I've messed up, I've known it's because I did something wrong. There was this one spot I kept falling, but I realized, wait, I don't have to hold down, just tap down once.
Precision (on the player's part) is important. I found keyboard to work far better than gamepad, personally. I was clumsy at first, but was soon zipping around with ease.
Intuition and experimentation is a lot of it, too, learning how to do different moves. Trying different things to see if they work.
There's a lot of personality to the animations. Music and sound design are great, too.
Each room has unique graphics (that I recall).
It feels like a lot of care and love went into this game.
The game is a really fun puzzle/adventuer game, but I do think it is a little pricey for the game length I do recomind the game, but I might wait tell you can grab it at a lower cost.

This game has an ....interesting save system that spoils the fun. It's a moody metroidvania-platformer with high difficulty and randomized enemy placement, so sometimes you'll just die. This wouldn't be a huge problem except for the aforementioned save system which undoes progress every time but starts you back at the same checkpoint. Basically, you have a "save counter" attached to your character that goes up by 1 when you save and down by 1 when you die.
Progressing past gates requires the counter to be at a high enough number. So you'll get to a new area, die, and then be unable to return there until you go save somewhere else across the map. It's not just difficult, it's time consuming and mindless. I'm pretty sure the designer just put it there to try and force backtracking since they don't have unlockable upgrades like most metroidvanias, but it's just  a completely unfun system that becomes the majority of time spent in this game.
It's a real shame, you can tell a lot of love and time went into this game, I don't know why they felt the need to add in this awful mechanic. Hopefully the devs put in an "easy mode" that does away with it and makes the game way more enjoyable in the process.
(I understand it's supposed to immitate survival, but it does so at the expense of basic enjoyment IMO).
Edit: So I've spent more time with the game, and after the first couple areas the larger amount of save point minimizes the amount of time spent having to retread ground. It's still a needless save system, but the extra room makes it less tedious. The other parts of the game are showing through more now, and they're still lovely. I've changed my review to a recommendation, with a strong caveat. THIS GAME IS STILL FRUSTRATING, but the positives outweigh the negatives, and apparently they're adding a mode that makes things a little easier, but for now just expect to be killed by the RNG gods every once in a while and have your progress erased in a way that requires tedious backtracking.

Rain world is the worst kind of game; A game with amazing potential, something that could have been a monumental success... only to find itself dragged down to mediocrity by the horrid design choices the developer made.
There's a lot of good here.  The game is extremely pretty, has great music, and very advanced Predator/prey AI.  Where it shines at its most, though, is it's setting.  The world is dark and dreary, with a constant threat of monstrous flood rains.  However, the setting's maze-like overworld, bizarre plants and animals, and eerie post-apocalyptic relics encourage you to risk your saftey to explore.
The big issues stem from the gameplay, which ranges from dull to controller-throwing.  The character's controls are imprecise and clunky, enemies have randomzied spawns and sometimes block your only path through a level, and the games 'flood-rain' mechanic forces you to save in brief intervals or die (something that discourages exploration and frequently leads to unavoidable deaths).
Worst of all, though, is that you are not told ANYTHING about the game.  All Rain World gives you is an extremely barebones tutorial in the beginning; gameplay features like the death-karma system, slugcat's abilities, protection flowers, and gate progression are flat out never explained ONCE.  I wouldn't even have known about any of them had I not caved in and turned to google.  Hiding information is something that games like Dark Souls and Hyper Light Drifter did pretty successfully, but Rain World takes it in the entirely wrong direction.  It's one thing to create a vague story for the player, and something entirey else to not explain your game's core gameplay needed to progress.
Had I purchsed this game for full price or kickstarted it instead of getting it in the Humble Bundle, I'd be much more furious than disappointed.  As it currently is, this game is gorgeous but just plain not fun to play.
Even at a discounted price I could never recommend this game to anyone.

* Played through the game and found it at least more enjoyable than Borderlands 2 or BL the Presequel, which it is more similar to than Shadow Warrior 1
* Game gets very easy & boring if you use the right weapon, skills and upgrades, unless you play on hardest difficulty available (depends on your level)
* # of upgrades is ridulously high, most are entirely useless, forcing you to sift through an endless sea of junk, to find that one upgrade that actually makes sense (my favorite are the whole "+2.5hp per enemy killed" upgrades: +2.5hp is the same as zero, given the amount of damage you take, so why are tons of these useless upgrades even in the game ? The same goes for a whole upgrade category, which you will most likely never touch again once you found the upgrade that starts with "-100% on health packs heal effect...")
* Same goes for weapons: Most simply do not deal enough DPS - if it weren't for elemental weaknesses/invulnerabilities by enemies, you could play the whole game with 1 to 2 weapons
* KIlling opponents (including bosses!) is a very non-tactical business: Go in with beefed up weapon slicing em' up, if health drops too low, disengage and heal yourself OR go invisible and heal yourself, repeat. I'm not saying it in't a franctic-kind-of-fun experience, but compared with SW 1, where you had opponents with shields, etc, it alas really lacks tactical depth
* Just read after completing the game that supposedly the leves have some procedural component - I never noticed any of that; quite the contrary: I thought multiple times, oh, yea, I've been here before - and here come the shrieking-fan-ladies...
* Further game design glitches:
** No compare weapons/upgrades support in the game
** Some communications at the start of a level are optional, then you get attacked immediately on entering the level and overlook the message to press a button to hear the conversation - you can then listen to it in a menu, but you cannot do it while walking around
** At one point nearly missed 3 side missions, since the previous mission suggested to continue directly with the main missions, and the "press T to teleport" (to home base) message was not shown
** Nearly all people you communicate with (mission givers and shop keepers) are like stiff robots when not inside a cut scene - this feels very much like a game from the 90s in this regard...
** Crafting system in game was completely useless, only tried it 3 times then gave up
* Overall conclusion remains: Alas everything about this game apart from the graphics is worse than its predecessor: Level design, combat, skill tree, story, boss fights - you name it. Since Steam continues to force reviews to recommend yes or no, I am forced to keep the game at not recommended.
Score would be 6.5/10

* If you have not played its predecessor, by all means do so :-)

Biggest letdown was the 2 guns carry limit, but other than that I had my fun and felt that I got my moneys worth - even though I pre-ordered it and as such got it along with all the hype.
Biggest shame is that 3DRealms didn't manage to release this themselves, they had a lot of it done and I cannot help, but wonder what went wrong. This game marks the end of a special era in video game history, before it became incredibly commercialized and big money. The whole way of doing business as 3Drealms was unique and I feel somewhat saddened looking at their website now and remembering what could have been if they hadn't spent 12 years on a title they ultimately never finished themselves. Its a darn shame, but Duke Nukem Forever will always represent the spirit of the old - though more in name than in game.
Buy it, play it and consider what it went through. Its a slide down in memory, that features multiple roadbumps, but its a slide worth taking in my opinion.

makes effective use of its game engine, having graphics that holds up well with its competitors of 2008. The environment of each level is beautiful, as the player can see how ancient civilization’s architecture degrade and allowed mother nature’s natural forces take over these inhabited areas. The audio has a faint stuttering across the entire game, which is bothersome if the player decides to wear headphones. Speaking of bugs, they’re more frequent when it comes to the physics of the game. Playing as Lara, she needs to be agile, nimble, and adequately on the move—not stuck in some areas of the game. It’s a constant occurrence, where the player should have to wait for a couple of seconds for Lara to free herself from the area. Nonetheless, the levels of this game are honestly way too big for a non-open world, linear story game. It could be forgiven if there were multiple routes of platforming; however, that as well is also linear. The reason behind this is for the collectibles, which isn’t useful in-game or give the player a network achievement at all. The game should’ve focused more on multiple paths for the player to platform for more replay value of the sort or different perspectives. The game is roughly around 9 hours to finish, and only has the replay value of Treasure Hunt Mode, an end game feature.  As the title explains it all, it allows the player to scavenge the remaining collectibles of the game, thus unlocks a bathing suit for Lara for underwater levels.
Controlling Lara is actually very clunky and has delayed responses.
Half of the time playing this game, Lara’s dying due to the faulty of controls. It often becomes a problem whenever she's rotating or jumping whilst platforming
of Lara’s controlling abilities. Combat can be irritating since Lara’s handguns don’t deal enough damage; furthermore, her secondary weapon runs out of ammo way too quickly. This subjects the player to use the game’s adrenaline system to perform effective headshots. Which is also unreliable since the only way to build it up is to shoot enemies, and Lara must get up close and personal. 90% chance of the time, Lara will take damage trying to perform this ability. The camera angles of the game aren’t up to par as well, especially in confined corners of the game. Nonetheless, whenever Lara’s maneuvering her way and must platform to a further area—the obvious thing for the camera to do is to zoom out for a better view of the map. Nope, it just zooms right up to her gorgeous♥♥♥♥♥ After one set of bad controls, there’s another set by simply introducing Lara’s motorcycle where she takes it along into the tombs and platforms with it. Motorcycles aren’t meant to be rode in tombs, especially when the corridors are dense and compact. Finally, the game doesn’t have objective markers for the player, so they’ll often have to scour the whole entire map whenever they’re stuck on a puzzle or level. This becomes an issue in later stages of the game,

For a game about raiding tombs, this game has a lot of water
The game offers a couple of options for Lara to use, the most useful one of them all is the sonar system. Unfortunately, it doesn’t show any of the objective markers or key items besides her motorcycle. It just shows a simplified geographical grid area for the player to view.  Clothing and weapons are recycled throughout the levels and can be selected each level. Just keep in mind that if the player desired an outfit that shows more skin—the less HP Lara will adorn. The only items that Lara is able to unlock as the game continues are Thor’s hammer, Mjölnir and the swimsuit after completing the game. Finally, collectibles are only useful for “Extras”, which are concept art, character designs, and the storyboard behind the game.
story is slim to none. The entire game is honestly a total of 30 minutes of cinematic cutscenes and platforming gameplay. The game focused more on the gameplay rather than story. Short Review: If you loved Eternal Silence during the golden age of Source Mods, you'll fall in love again with this game.
Long Review:Okay.. so.. I want you to take Battlfield 2142 and blend some Star Wars Battlefront II. Now, you're to add them into the Unreal 3 Engine and give a heavy stir, and onces that is done bake it for two hours.
Now that it's all done, you'll be pleased by this little charm of a game. It may not look pretty, and it's in alpha but it's one of the more stable alpha builds.  While a population is truely needed to play this game in mutliplayer, and it's riddled with too many menus I can say the fustration is worth the trouble.
This game gives you a rather extended amount of customization to your load outs for everything you'll be using, from your firearms and suit, to the vehicles you'll be operating in the theatre of war.
I haven't had this customization and NOT require to grind/pay for it in a very long time, which makes this leagues more enjoyable than other games. If I were to complain about one thing it's that the game is in an outdated engine, but something tells me if it was on a more recent Unreal engine the game wouldn't function due to the scope and size of the fights.
I recommend this game, but as it stands with the current build and bugs I'd say hold off for a sale.

Why am I writing this up? It's Amnesia. It's the game that everyone points to first when someone asks "What's a scary game?" People that have never played it recommend it to people who will buy it and never play it. What am I even doing here?
The truth is, I needed a reason to revisit this one. I'm a terribly jumpy person and genuinely scary games can wear me out good. The first time I played Amnesia, I never even made it to a monster. I knew I needed to give it another go and this was the perfect time to do it. And while I was playing, a thought occurred to me. Amnesia's been around for years at this point. How does it hold up in a post-Alien: Isolation world?
Amnesia casts you, unsurprisingly, as an amnesiac in a drafty old castle back in the 1800s. You soon find a missive from yourself, assuring you that you didn't want those memories anyway and there's someone in the castle you really ought to kill. As you begin exploring the darkened, crumbling halls, you find that there are other residents of the castle that are none too pleased to see you. There's no fighting in this one, it's pure stealth or fleeing. The cornerstone of Amnesia's gameplay, much like Penumbra before it, is sanity. Looking at monsters, seeing freaky things happening, and being in the dark make you lose sanity. Of course, if you stand there in front of a torch, the things that want to turn your insides into outsides will have an easy time spotting you. Encounters with monsters are all about balancing your stealthy skulking against your dwindling sanity, which is only restored by progressing through the game. It's a finite resource system like food in Lone Survivor, and works to layer urgency on top of your horror. I must admit it's a bit of a bother here though, because it puts some irritating visual effects on you when it gets terribly low.
The sanity effects are about the only misstep in the aesthetics, though. The graphics still hold up and manage to be rich and varied while still maintaining the dark, oppressive atmosphere. The level design is simple but effective, sending you through lavish halls and crumbling cellars and stranger places still, pacing out the frights and creatures. The big standout here though is the sound design. There is a lot more going on here than in most games, with your character making all sorts of breathing sounds and whimpers, footsteps for everyone being accurate to the surface that produces them, and even light sources making their own realistic ambient sounds. The castle itself is full of creepy sounds as well, most being apropos of nothing, but that just makes it all the more effective when it DOES signal something.
I was very pleased with the pacing of the game, and found it had little to no contrivances to get you where it wanted you to be. Enemy encounters are infrequent enough to keep you on edge when they're not around, and absolutely terrify you when they are. Dealing with them is obviously less involved than in Alien: Isolation but much more free-form than, say, Outlast. I could see some of the terror being lost if you have to repeat certain sections a few times, but the game is balanced well enough with pacing and items that it shouldn't be a concern unless you're really trying to pull back the curtain for yourself.
To my surprise, I found myself getting scared more often with this than in Alien. For me, Alien is much more about constant tension and the battle of wits with the xenomorph, whereas Amnesia is more about the terror of being helpless and confused. Not many games have managed to pull off the powerless protagonist angle without it becoming grating, but Amnesia owns it. Simple sounds and sudden visual effects will chill you to the bone, not as cheap jump scares but as payoffs to the incredible atmosphere the game maintains at all times. I feel confident in saying that no matter how far the genre progresses, Amnesia will always have a place of honor among the games that truly terrify.

I wanted to love Rain World so, so badly. As someone who has worked summers as a Naturalist and who loved the idea of a platformer/survival game that was based around a food chain and ecosystem it just didn't deliver for me, because of its mechanics and lack of visuals. To be fair to the developers and the game; I didn't play this game for more than 2 hours at most.
The platforming is done in such a way that the Slugcat feels very weak and it results in arbitrary difficulty. I appreciate the attempts at making Slugcat feel like an organic creature, but all it did was create frustration. Slugcat has slow movement, can't jump high, and has very few means of survival via combat. I know this is intended and is part of what seperates this game from others in the genre, but it does so in a bad way. I think they could have increased Slugcat's movement speed and jumping height very slightly and it wouldn't have hurt the realism while still making the player feel like its fun to be the Slugcat.
The levels are extremely sparse, and while initially I enjoyed some of the pixel art, it gets kind of bland with the lack of color and the simplicity of the creatures' designs. Having to slowly trudge around and get to the next screen over and over gets tedious quickly. There are indie games like Owlboy that have come out that are just so visually appealing and have such fluid mechanics; that I find it hard to recommend this game if it is competing for your wallet.
There may have been a good chance that had I stuck it out longer I may have come to enjoy this game, but I won't be finding out. It just didn't do it for me, and I found it too unpleasant to sink more time into it out of hopes that might change. There are lots of positive reviews of this game; and it may well deserve them as these things are subjective, but I felt the need to put in my voice as an opposing perspective.

If you like Collectible Card Games, you will probably get some enjoyment out of Magic 2015. This review is from my experience playing the game on the PC.
Even if you know nothing about Magic The Gathering (referenced as MTG from this point on), but always wanted to learn, the tutorial does a very proficent job in breaking down all the basics of the game, such as understanding the cards, the stages of play, tapping lands for mana, and so forth. For that part alone, I would recommend it to a friend that asked about a game that would teach them the basics of MTG.
To be candid, I wasn't impressed with this portion of the game. Your getting a deck that you will be stuck with, and you have to accept it sight unseen without knowing anything about the deck. You only know the decks color (such as White / Green), and some obscure hint as to how the deck will function. There is no reversing your decision once its made, and all decks are not equal. You would do well to research the starting decks online and pick the deck that will best appeal to your preferred play style.
The single player component of the game is hard. Be prepared to feel like your a soldier in a modern day conflict, that has been equipped with WW1 era equipment; it's doable, but you feel disadvantaged. Lets face it, the starting decks are weak, and the A.I. is playing with far superior, synergistic decks.
Win a single-player match, and you are rewarded with a booster pack you can open. After winning a few, its highly recommended you leave behind your starter deck, by either building a new deck, or improving your decks focus with the new cards you've added to your collection.
In single player there is an explore mode that you can keep playing until you unlock all of the available cards for that segment of the game. For example, Theros will unlock a set amount of cards, Ravnica a set amount, and etc. The best way to build your deck is to explore all you can and unlock all of the cards your able too.
One tip to consider.. if you get stuck exploring the first area, trying putting together a Red Mono deck with goblins, direct damage spells, with a few low mana cost buff spells, treason spells, or whatever you can piece together. The faster the deck the better, because you want to overwhelm the A.I. before it can get its overpowerd deck rolling. That should grind you through the first three explore areas pretty fast, resulting in several cards added to your collection.
To see if your missing any cards and need to grind more, in the menu, click on "Collection" and view the cards you can get for each zone.
The biggest complaint I have seen about single player is the difficulty, therefore grinding through those first three explorable areas will make a big difference.
For the purpose of reviewing the game, I did attempt several times to play multi-player. At the time of the review, I was not able to join any games, because they were either full, or would simply never join and then time out.
I will update this portion of the review if I ever get some experience with the multi-player portion of Magic 2015.
However, while on Multiplayer, I understand several  people are upset about the lack of a multiplayer feature that had been in the 2014 versin of the game. It was a very fun feature, and I was surprised by the design decision to leave it out.
If you have never experienced any of the previous offereings of MTG - Duel games, then you most likely will not notice any misgivings. However, to me the interface was a huge step back from the previous releases. It is slower, and annoying with its repetitive slow fade outs, that you will see over and over. This design decision really left me scratching my head.
Not sure why they lost the snappy, efficent, clean design of some of the previous releases??
To answer my own question, maybe because it was easier to port to Android and Console?
Now if you could adjust the fading speed, the menu speed, and some of the more annoying interface actions, it would appease alot of the negativity reviewers have towards Magic 2015.
You may make purchases to unlock some of the cards. There are also Premium booster packs you can buy that will give you cards that are not available in game. One reviewer estimated you would have to pay $38 dollars to unlock all of the premium booster pack cards, as it will not give you duplicates of any more cards than you are supposed to get via the booster packs.
Also if you purchased the core game, you can pay to unlock the cards you get from explore matches. It is a personal decision, but I actually have not minded grinding through those.
However, I will admit, originally I did pay to have those cards unlocked, but I never did receive them and am still waiting on a three day old support ticket with Steam to be refunded the extra money I paid. So keep that in mind if you are about the pay for those cards to unlock; they may not and you will just be out the money.
I did buy four premium booster packs to test it out. I did receive the boosters, and the cards were nice upgrades.
Ultimately, not sure how I feel about paying for more content in this game. The difficulty of the A.I., and the superior cards they have, does appear to give validity to the complaints that state, it was a decision, with purposeful intent, to force players to 'pay-to-win'.
While that could be, you CAN win in Magic 2015 without them! Before I purchased the four booster packs, I was grinding my way through just fine. Admittedly, the start was rocky and frustrating until I got a few cards unlocked.
To me this is the meat of the game. If you enjoy building your own decks, trying different color combination builds, putting together decks with as much synergy as possible, you will enjoy Magic 2015.
I loved this portion of the game, and have spent alot of time going back and forth to the Deck Manager component, scheming and tweaking my decks.
If you have some ideal of what to do, and add some cards to a new deck, but then your not sure how to complete it, the Deck Manager even has a nice "Auto-Complete" button that will fill out the deck for you.
I have tried it out a time or two, and did end up trading out a few cards here and there that Auto-Complete added in, but it did get me pretty close to a workable deck.
Of course, there is nothing as rewarding as building your own deck that ends up winning alot!. So spending some time on forums asking for help with your deck, researching a litte, and watching some vidoes on YouTube on building decks, will in the end give you the most rewarding experience and teach you the most about MTG.
Additionally, you can tweak your own lands, but that takes going into the Options menu and enabling it, as it is disabled by default.
If your considering purchasing the game, and you can over look the annoyingly slow interface and its even more annoying slooooww fade effects, somewhere buried under that UI is a pretty decent game. I recommend the game for its greater control over your deck builds, its tutorial for any newbies, and even its challenge and grindy design (I like unlocking cards so don't mind the grind, others may).
Overall not a bad game, but not a great game either. If you can see past the UI and dig down to the meat, you may come to the same conclussion. I would give it about a 7 out of 10.

I feel some of the reviews I've seen are a little unfair, so here's my take on a game that I'm enjoying, despite some teething pains.
The early game is certainly very frustrating, you're playing an underpowered deck and it feels like you're never going to get anywhere. After pushing hard through the campaign my little Red/Green deck is actually starting to do quite well.
I've read a lot of reviews about how you have to grind for cards (or suffer the dreaded Micro-transactions!!). My two cents on the matter is that part of the fun is winning games and opening packs - had I had the entire library at my disposal from the start, opening packs wouldn't matter. At least this way when I open a Booster pack there's enough anticipation to make it a fun experience. Unfortunately it does seem like this aspect is a detriment to the start of the game.
The game seems to do a
job of telling you what your starter deck contains. I chose Red/Green which was described in-game as a deck to ramp into big creatures. Imagine my surprise to find there were no such card in the deck itself!\.
I bit of research shows that pretty much all the starter decks suck, and this is the major failing of the game. It can take a couple of frustrating losses to get past an encounter and start modifying your deck. Again, it seems the plan is to give you a lame deck so that opening your first few boosters is a good experience. Perhaps a little misguided but not a reason to write the game off.
This really where the game shines. Sure you get a crappy deck, but opening boosters is fun... and the reason it's fun is that you can take whatever awesome cards you get and try cram them into your deck!
Just open up an amazing creatue? Put it in your deck, splash the land colour you need (or let the auto-builder take care of it) and take your new deck out for a spin.
At the time of writing I'm halfway through the campaign and loving it. Should anything come up of note I'll provide an update.

Magic 2015 ... One step forward, ten steps back. Firstly, I haven't put a ton of time into this game, so much of this is a reaction after only about a few play sessions, but this game really takes the cake for stupidity in design.
The UI is the first major step, back... glitz over usability. Slow, and unresponsive, though I do have an older computer. The menus are nested in a way that makes them even slower, then they should be.
The game first asks your skill level, so I chose Planeswalker, the highest, which then immediately goes to a tutorial. So, this seems to be the theme of Magic 2015, ask what people want then ignore that info, and give us what you think we wanted.
They got rid of old model, which while limited, in that you had many premade, but customizable decks, into you get a deck that you can customize. Now, when this deck fails misarabley because of design restrictions, there are no falling back to another deck that's more appropriate to the challenge, this is frustrating, and leaves you feeling screwed.
Now, when I checked years ago, MTG had over 11k cards in it's catalog, but here they give you access to around 300 after you unlock them through cash or play. It's just greed, even the orignal PC game that came out last century, or last millenium, if you prefer, had more, but your left feeling like the game should be a lot more satisfying then it is.
I realize Magic 2015, and the others are part of an effort by Wizards to get people to go to Magic Online, but I'm thinking that won't happen. What's the benefit, people can pay and pay for virtual cards they have no ownership of. Now, you may say you're doing the same with this, but that hasn't been true in the past. You pay an amount you have access to a mostly workable game with other unlockable cards. This game was dissapointing in the pay aspect of the bonus cards. Really you should be getting a lot more for what they're asking, since these cards won't move to the next Magic.  Magic cards are expensive IRL, so you really are paying for nothing when it comes to virtual cards. You don't own them, can't trade them.
I'm not going to bother with the rest of this review. Maybe, I'll just play an older versions of MTG when i need a fix, or find a new card game that's going to be more inclusive. I think if Wizards wants my cash in the future, they should seriously consider easing up on the stupid restrictions that these game artificially put in. Use the computers ability to take away restrictions and give us freedom, and decent priced addons not stupid packs.

In many ways, I view Rome Total War as the high point in the Total War Franchise.
Set in ancient, take control of one of many factions (Italian, Barbarian, Mid-Esteastern) and conquer the world!  It's a large game with the map covering Europe and parts of Asia and Africa, and a single game takes more than a small investment of time.
The core gameplay focuses on war and empire management. Battles allow for auto resolves, but the real charm and strength of Total War relies on taking to the field and commanding large numbers of troops in massive combat.  It controls great, even when the scale of the battles become epic, and the cieling for skil is incredibly high as real world strategies and tactics will get you far.  All the while, even less mechanically inclined players wont find it overly burdensome, even if they don't get all they can out of the game.  Finally, battles often feel unique as different fations play differently, the terrain drastically changes battles, and seiges on cities introduces its own mechanics.
The other side of Total War is the macro.  Players must build troops, build buildings, and manage finances.  While simple, I found a great ammount of enjoyment building my territories up.  While not in depth to any real degree, the over world system does require some finesse once you expand further and must deal with rebels.  I'm underselling this a degree, because the entire system is extremely enjoyable.
While I'm not up to date on the more decent Total War games, and despite its age, I would recommend Tota War Rome as a great entry point into the franchise.  It's a large, expansive, moderatly deep experience that you can get lost in for hours.
If you are a fan of the strategy genre and have't experienced Total War as of yet, give this game a try.

This is the 3rd instalment of the Tomb Raider Legend Trilogy. If you're asking how come, well it turned out that TR Anniversary is also part of it and chronologically TR Legend is a sequel. I don't want to get into details as it might spoil few things which I want to avoid. Graphically the game is good although it's nothing spectacular but still nice to look at. It is worth to mention this is the first ever TR game which uses motion capture technology for Lara's animation and I must admit that it was a good idea as her movements are very natural like never before. There are also some new graphical features like dirt sticking to Miss Croft's body. So generally I got a very positive impression. When it comes to voice actors they are very good as always so nothing new here also the music got better, more epic (as it is the last chapter it had to be). Just like with every Tomb Raider game Lara visits several countries and also will use her bike but this time It's not like in TR Legend where you had driving section but it's more like an additional mean of transport or just to simply get into one or two places to continue the level and you can get off it any time you want. Another change is when Lara equips dual weapon and there are 2 enemies she will target and shoot both targets. Secrets are still physics based and quite interesting. Of course Lady Croft got some new moves which is always the case with new game so there was no reason otherwise. To sum things up Tomb Raider Underworld is a solid game which closes the story for good and too bad this is the very last game with up-to-date yet still classic Lara Croft and presumably we won't see her in the series again unless in another Lara Croft series with isometric view.

The review that will answer your questions....
Concept: 64 players battle it out on the ground or in the air. there appears to be 2 types of battles much like battlfront 2. You have on the ground warfare and space battles. Lets start with the space battles. There are different space stations and ships you can spawn in. They are HUGE, with AI running around on them and AI sitting at different little computer desk as if they are busy. If your ship gets hit, lights flicker, alarms sound the whole ship or space station shakes as you run up and down the hallways. Oustide is a war going on very similiar to battlefront 2 space. People will launch boarding parties and before you know it, you are fighing firefights down hallways like a CQC Battlefield game as you attempt to defend your capital ship or whatever you are in. At the same time there are alot of ships fighting in space and your buddy could be out there in a fighter protecting the big ship you are on as you fire your machine gun down a hallway. It really is battlfront 2 on crack. As the big stations and ships get hit massive explosions and damage are visible on the models. ALL models from the smallest ship to the biggest space station take awesome damage. The battles are bigger then 64 players,,,you have massive capital ships that clearly carry hundreds of people on them (we have all seen star trek). so even though that may only be 1 real person driving it...it stands for like 100 poeple in game and has many many guns firing off of it. The AI brings in some things aswell that arent includded in the 64player/bot count. There isnt any waiting period for a ship. IF you want a fighter from the hangar and so do 10 other people...well just go up to it and click it. even if all 10 of you do it at the same time it will launch 10 fighters, not the stupid waiting game. I cant stress enough if you liked battlefront space battles then you need this game. Yes you can gun a spaceship while someone flies it and vice versa. Infact if you are in a bomber, you can get up out of your seat as a pilot and walk around it even though its small, that option is really cool to me. You may also play with the AI in offline mode, They are very competent. The AI is on point. I read that in someone elses review before i purchased this, and I am now confirming it too. They arent dumb. You can also issue commands if you are a squad leader. And if AI bots are in your squad you can command them with things like follow me, free roam, attack here, etc. (even in multiplayer) Its almost impossible to find someone alone. This game is very much a group game. A real player or AI commander will issue orders to you and your squad. They may differ from the orders the squad to your left has, and they may be in cunjunction with the orders the squad to your right has. Its not a free roam team death match, there are objectives drawing players into big battles. (like chivalry)
Ground warfare.....you can crouch lean left or right around corners, and the way you earn vehicles is through points from kills or objectives etc. the better you are the better vehicle options you get, Guns can be customized just as much as bf4. different barrels, sights, bullets, attachments. Lots of customzing. However there is only 3 sets of armor, heavy medium and light. Lets talk maps, there are 10 or more maps so far. And this is my favorite part of the game. I love the maps in the city. For those that played killzone mutliplayer on ps3 and ps4 the cities resemble those maps in looks. However these maps are rather big, very intricate, alot of detail. I find myself very very happy with the maps. None of that call of duty sniping where each building has 1 window and you know to look there when you turn the corner. These maps have 8 story buildings where you can go on every floor and fire from every window. The maps are just..i dunno i was high playing, but damn i love the maps. They seem plausable, the terrian is very uneven instead of super flat and boring.
Sever pop: i have seen about 10 servers, only 1 even close to full. That might bother some of you, it would me except the game throws in AI to offset the player count. for 13 bucks....i am not complaining at all even if i eventually end up just like battlefront 2 is now and I end up playing just offline mode. I guess a slight concern would be if the devs abandon the game due to low player count. How do we uop the count? you buy it! This game gets good reviews, so why not??? However, game still needs work..which brings us to cons.
cons: Sound is not as good as it should be, some guns flat out suck in sound. The dropships that drop vehicles etc dont even have sounds yet. Snipers will smile as 1 shot kills are available, machine gunners will cry as it takes more shots to kill someone then a halo game. Gun damage needs to be upped some. But then again you are in some kind of futeristic suit, but still...takes some time to kill people with basic assault rifles. Other then that, a few polishes here and there and fellas...we got ourselves a rocking game. SO i leave you with this... if you miss battlefront 2 concept...this is your game. any questions, ask below and i will respond to help you.

I have not played for long, so my experience of the game is not complete, however I do feel that I can write a review on the topics which concern me the most. This game is fascinating, and has tons of potential, the gameplay is engaging, and the space battles demonstrate the combined arms approach perfectly. Whether you are going toe to toe with battleships, piloting a bomber, or sneaking through the corridors inside, you feel as if you are integral to the battle. And this is amazing. The weapons and vehicles and character design is also very good, if a bit single-tone (the entire game feels drab, there's very little color). However, this game is not without it's issues. Mostly, polish or lack thereof. I feel that the graphics, albeit good, are somewhat rough, the same going for the animations (movement feels wobbly, for example). The game is poorly optimized, I find it more difficult to run than just about any other game I own. (Which is to be expected, it's in early access. Not harping on the devs)
Overall, this game is already fun and (mostly) playable, and it has great potential which it needs to expand into. There's a great amount of content already in, and the concept is very solid.
PS: The name is seriously badass.

This is not perhaps the most challenging puzzle/exploration game out there - there's perhaps a few puzzles that required me to double check all that I could do and missed a climbable platform, but otherwise the solutions seem pretty simple. That said, the puzzle elements are introduced in a good "platform learning" manner with no writtent text and only minimal on-screen prompts so that you can recognize how certain things will behavior to quickly figure out how to solve the puzzles. There are some nice ideas used in the puzzle designs, particularly with the play of light and shadows, that could make for a more fulfilling game. There are a number of collectables to find with additional exploration and/or level navigation to give this replay value.  The core game took me about 6 hours to complete, and I felt that's about the right value for the price.
What does make this game excel is the relatively simple story. It might be straight forward when you start, but the game uses a number of sublte tricks that lead to a great end-game twist. It is an emotional-driven story and the suprise at the end caught me off guard.  The music and setting all plays perfectly to that tone.
I've seen other reviews that complain of performance issues. I didn't encounter any save for two unreproducable crash-to-desktops early on (this was mid-August 2017) and the rest worked smoothly. It is a bit graphically taxing so low-end computers might have problems, but I don't think it suffers the performance issues that appeared to be a problem when this first launched.

It feels like participating in some kind of Animal Planet show as you navigate a lonely slugcat separated from his family through the vast post-apocalyptic world. The food is hard to get, predators are stronger than you and you are always threatened by approaching deadly rains, so you have to get a meal and hide before storm comes and flushes your progress.
Although the Slugcat is weak, eventually you will learn how to defend yourself and even pose a threat as you explore the world on your travels. No, you'll hardly get much new abilities and level-ups, but you will learn how to benefit from the environment. You will be amazed on how complicated the world is and how much things you can use for your favor! I'd advise you not to read the guides but to explore yourself - feels extremely rewarding when you learn a new trick.
The world seems to be quite open - the only things which limit you movements are Karma Gates - they let you through only if you possess the required karma level. Karma is increased if you rest well-fed at shelters and gets decreased when you die. "If" and "when" words are used to display an estimation on how often either of these is expected to happen. You die a lot here - the game is quite hard and punishing, almost to the point of frustration at first. It is way less fair than Dark Souls - sometimes you die not because of your own mistakes, but due to pure♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ass luck. Still, you wont consider it a big deal as you learn that karma is meant to come and go away. Yet unlike Dark Souls it wants you to rely rather on uninterrupted series of succesful runs around the checkpoints, than on single lucky no-matter-how-much-tries-it-took ones. Consequentive deaths hurt your karma, negating your progress and making Rain World a more challenging game thus way.
Moving to a new area feels like a solid adventure: usually the way is long, while the time is short; you'll often get killed before you reach a new shelter; at times you won't manage to get enough food along the way to register a check-in at new place; sometimes you even lose all your karma before you reach a gate, so you'll have to spend another few hours wandering around the place and accumulating karma again. It happens a lot, so reaching the new place feels like "phew, that was close". On the other hand - it often seems like a hopeless situation and you are about to die, but you end up sound and safe instead. And as you learn how the things work here you'll manage to turn things that way more often. The game progresses slowly - I have 52 hours in-game registered atm, yet it feels like the game is hardly half-way beaten! And hey - it is a single player game!
I won't bother praising the visuals - just check out them screenies. And it looks even better when in motion!

Finished five times so far, excellent game. After every update, I check the game out and update this thing accordingly because I love it so much. Here is a quick summary:
Pros:
+ Price:Worth ratio is very, VERY high
+ Melee combat is very satisfying and very well executed for an FPS game
+ Upgrade system allows firearms to perform differently
+ Skills system allows you to tailor your character the way you want to play it
+ Online co-op (but there is a big negative to this as well)
+ "Semi-procedurally" generated maps
Neutral:
o No level cap
o Loot oriented game
o Great successor
o A lot of weapons
o Attention to detail is amazing
o Excellent graphics
o Level and art design is very well done
o Soundtrack is awesome
Cons:
- No endless / wave based arenas
-
(patch 1.1.7.0 added filtering options)
- Some upgrades have big drawbacks, especially at early levels to make then worthless
- Some game mechanics require (more) explanation, and some don't make any sense
-
Currently, anyone that joins a game is an "apprentice" in essence, and the host is the "master". Apprentices don't progress in the story line as far as I can tell. While I appreciate online co-op, not allowing players to progress in their own game will probably keep them away from joining a co-op game till they finish their game at least once
Personal/Extended Points:
+ I don't know why they added "semi" in front of "procedural". This is what a lot of games out there already do, and they just call it "procedural". Technically, "semi-procedural" is right, but still. Compared to other games that semi-procedurally generate maps, this one has bigger chunks, but the detail went to them is great
o Loot! You grab a lot of loot. In addition to upgrade gems that go into your weapons/armor, some weapons and some skills are also loot. Some may dislike it, but personally I like loot-oriented games
o Not exactly like the previous game; new additions and changes may not be well received by those who love the previous game, but personally I like every new addition and change
- Some sort of wave based arena mode would be awesome for this game. A free DLC added some arenas, but they're 1-shots, and not wave based. You do them, then you can do them again, and you aren't rewarded with loot.
Overall, I enjoy the game a lot. There isn't much left to do for me, so I decided to go on multiplayer a little, and it becomes much more fun in multiplayer of course. I really hope they'll release free & paid DLCs, because this game has insane potential. As I've said, money well spent. I'm looking forward for the future updates and DLCs as this game has become one of my favourites.

I've completed most of this game's "story" for starters. I'm just about done with it, having only the very ending to get by. Thus, I feel in this moment, it's time for me to review this game, and what I personally enjoy and dislike about it.
For starters, let's talk about the positives. Rain World is a colourful, yet gritty survival game that attempts to create a system in which you are being hunted in a hostile world. This game succeeds in this aspect. Every time you enter a new area, you are presented with a puzzle of sorts to work out, dealing with the various creatures around the room, and the constant ticker of the predicted rain timer compels you to hurry yourself up getting to the next safe area before you are unmercifully drowned to death in the violent rains. This means that you have to puzzle out how to get around your enemies without dying, yet you must not tarry for too long. In addition, the enemies and you follow a system of movement that can look extremely janky at times, yet provides an experience not felt in really any other game I personally have played before. When looking to survive in an area, this game can be a ton of fun, and death doesn't feel as much of a chore, as a lesson.
However, the "story" is the one thing that ties alot of negatives together for me. For starters, while in an area with many branching paths to go, an enemy in your way is a great challenge; it forces you to think about how to approach the danger in front of you, sometimes requiring you to think outside the box to deal with it. However, when going down the story lane, the areas you traverse through no longer feel like an environment that can harbor any sort of real life, and more like a "♥♥♥♥ you, try getting through this" to the player. Most of the time, there is only one single path to go. Enemies that are in your way in these areas you usually have to pray don't get you, with most strategy in the branching path areas beforehand being thrown out the window. Several times throughout these areas, I started just mindlessly throwing myself at the exits without much a care for what randomly spawned in front of my path, mainly because there was no real conceivable way around these foes. After all, why care if the exits don't require me to have a level of karma, and the game feels like it gave up too with these stupidly ridiculous enemy spawns.
In addition to the negatives, some techniques aren't even described to you in the game's tutorial, having to seek outside help for. Most of the time, these techniques were unwelcomed, and I would find my slugcat cartwheeling off one of the countless instant-death cliffs later in the game.
Regardless, I finished with the horrid story areas and got back to the more open areas, and found myself having a blast. The thing is, however, that unlike other games that demand challenge of me, Rain World gave me no satisfaction for beating these difficult areas. This was because there was no skill required in beating these areas, just crossing my fingers and hoping the enemy wouldn't be there this time, or that their pathfinding would glitch out.
In conclusion, regardless of the negatives I put forth for the game, it still has elements that are immensely entertaining to play about in. When you are simply surviving for the sake of surviving, this game shines with brutal difficulty. Those first 10 or so hours without a guide, freely discovering new areas completely out of order made the journey in this game amazing. However, once you head into the areas the game expects you to go to to see a specific npc
the game takes a massive nosedive into annoyance and in my honest opinion, stupidity.
I will keep this game recommended due to the truely unique experience of interacting with the world around you, yet just keep in mind if you want to complete the story, that you're in for an agonizing face-grind.

On a more serious note, this game is very fun to play in a relaxed way. Combat is very micro managy (or it can be) which can be both a good thing and a bad thing. Although, I've found myself spending most of my time so far watching my hunters hunt while I wait for buildings to build. Still a very fun and in depth game.
Pro's:
+In depth and micro managable combat if you want to, click and swarm units if you don't want to micro.*
+Fleshed out races with personalities.
+Great soundtrack.
+Fun animations and ai things to keep you entertained while things build.
+Customizable city lay outs (for the orcs anyway, not sure about other races).
+Good variety of units and upgrades.
+Good PvP.
+Very in depth lore that gives you a good feel for the world.
Con's:
-Buildings can take a very long time to build (as in a few hours real time).
-Skirmish mode has to be bought.
-Can be very dull at times.
-Most of the quest dialog is text only, but there are still fun unit battlecries.
-Graphics are about on par with Warcraft 3 (but then again, it's just as enjoyable).
Overall, I recommend this game as a fun strategy game to play as a relaxing "watch your city grow" type of game. Especially now that it's only $4.99 USD.

In many ways, I view Rome Total War as the high point in the Total War Franchise.
Set in ancient, take control of one of many factions (Italian, Barbarian, Mid-Esteastern) and conquer the world!  It's a large game with the map covering Europe and parts of Asia and Africa, and a single game takes more than a small investment of time.
The core gameplay focuses on war and empire management. Battles allow for auto resolves, but the real charm and strength of Total War relies on taking to the field and commanding large numbers of troops in massive combat.  It controls great, even when the scale of the battles become epic, and the cieling for skil is incredibly high as real world strategies and tactics will get you far.  All the while, even less mechanically inclined players wont find it overly burdensome, even if they don't get all they can out of the game.  Finally, battles often feel unique as different fations play differently, the terrain drastically changes battles, and seiges on cities introduces its own mechanics.
The other side of Total War is the macro.  Players must build troops, build buildings, and manage finances.  While simple, I found a great ammount of enjoyment building my territories up.  While not in depth to any real degree, the over world system does require some finesse once you expand further and must deal with rebels.  I'm underselling this a degree, because the entire system is extremely enjoyable.
While I'm not up to date on the more decent Total War games, and despite its age, I would recommend Tota War Rome as a great entry point into the franchise.  It's a large, expansive, moderatly deep experience that you can get lost in for hours.
If you are a fan of the strategy genre and have't experienced Total War as of yet, give this game a try.

I thought I would give this game a negative review after seeing all the problems everyone else is talking about.
Note that I game on PC.
- I have not experienced any disconnections from any games, or even any lag. Ive read multiple times that dedicated servers are terrible for fighting games, so I dont mind the P2P considering I havent experienced problems.

Summary - overall this is a pretty good, expensive game. I dont think this game is worth almost 100 Canadian dollars, because its just a fighting game. Arma is one of the best games on steam. The sheer amount of content the game has from the massive range of guns, to the crazy amount of mods is enough to keep you occupied forever. The base game itself is a very tactical military game, so if your not into the military style of game I wouldn't buy it. However there are dozens of gamemodes to choose from that can fit your style. The singleplayer aspect is fun but extremely hard and tedious. The missions are filled with AI that can instantly spot your location from hundreds of meters away and pretty much have auto aim at the lowest difficulty. But the multiplayer aspect is where the game gets really fun. As I stated there are several gamemodes which you can choose from, some mission based, with clear objectives, others with a style of free for all combat in massive open world. The base game uses plenty of mechanics in the gun play which can be very tactical. Zeroing distance, How far the target is away from you (in meters), Bullet drop, ect. are all very realistic and an important aspect in the gunplay. Arma 3 is typically not a run and gun game, you have to pretty tactical at times and always stay aware of what's around you. There are a large amount of guns to choose from, you have several Snipers, Rifles, LMGs, Pistols, DMR's, and SMGs to choose from as well as a large amount of attachments such as scopes (dozens of different kinds each with different ranges and configurations), flashlights/laser pointers, bipods,  and supressors. The guns and attachments also have several different kinds of skins. There is also a large amount of character customization. The main areas of character customization are as follows: Uniform, Vest, Backpack, Headgear, Glasses, and Nightvision. The Uniform, the Backpack, and the Vest can all hold a varied amount of gear, and there are several kinds of clothing in each area providing different appearance and different armor protection in the case of vests and headgear. There is also a large amount of vehicles, there are cars, mopeds, trucks, armored vehicles, tanks, helicopters, and jets to navigate the massive open world of the 3 main maps that are included in the base game: Altis, Stratis, and Malden. These maps are giant and would take hours to run across without a vehicle. There are also DLC, although a bit overpriced they do contain a lot of additonal content, inclding guns, clothing, vehicles, and even a massive tropical map. All of these aspects of the game come without the use of mods, and are just the core elements of the base game. The best thing about this game in my opinion, is the massive amount of mods availiable. Once you get bored with the base game and the DLC you can delve into new modded versions. There are several launchers for the game (A3Llauncher, CCGLauncher, A3Sync) which display modded Arma 3 servers and have the mods required for these servers ready to download. Many of the modded versions create entirely new games with the Arma 3 mechanics at the core. Some of the mods include DayZ mods, Survival Mods, and (my personal favorite) Arma 3 Life mods. They can add entire new maps to the game, with a bunch of new items. Some of the downsides of this game include the fact of the massive FPS drops that can occur. The sheer amount of  details in the game plus its massive map can be a huge strain on your PC. Even if you have a pretty good computer you can still experience a ton of lag in the game. I have a GTX 970, I7 Core, with 8 gigs of Ram and I get some lag, especially when starting up the game. And the gunplay can be frustrating, because it can be hard to hit someone from longer distances. Otherwise if you have a relitively good computer, and like more tactial, realistic-style war games Arma 3 is a great game which I highly recommend. 10/10

This game is something very special. There's simply so much to it: the maps are huge with many of them being asymetrical attack/defend levels; the terrain varies between vast fields where tanks and aircraft dominate, tight CQC urban battlefields, and even maps fought in space; and the interaction between units to do something greater than themselves is wonderful to take part in. Even the progression system lets you unlock new builds over time without artificially locking any equipment away from new players.
Make no mistake, there are still very rough edges to this diamond but it is still a great example of what Early Access can be: games with a good framework that are worth playing now but that can become so much better. I am hoping (expecting, in fact) that many new and amazing things will be added to Angels Fall First over time, but honestly I would still be happy with it if it never received another update.

Although I don't have a lot of hours on this game, I think this is probably one of the best Co Op zombie survival games. The run and gun aspect is really fun, and some of the guns and melee weapons are really cool to mess around with. The workshop for this game is really good, ranging from hentai noises for witch to a different, more epic ending to The Sacrifice. It also includes like 18 mutations, and it comes with the Left 4 Dead 1 campaign, too. I mean, come on. You're basically getting two incredibly great games for 20 dollars (Or 1.99 if you buy it on sale, like I did). The campaign on its own is great, for both games, mind you, but it also has other game modes. Survival, Versus, and Scavenge (I'm pretty sure those are the only other ones, but there are realism variations plus Mutation). It might sound like a small amount, but you'll be playing Versus trying to master the Special Infected, or Survival trying to get the best time to flaunt off to friends and players you meet online. There are a lot of achievements that seem like a waste of time to get, but to me I like getting achievements. A lot of the hours at the time of posting this are basically only from trying to get achievements, survival, and versus. The comedic aspect is really nice as well, with Ellis' random stories in the middle of the apocalypse, to the song available on Jukeboxes Re: Your Brains. If you ever find a way to master EVERY valve made survival map (Which is highly unlikelay, but probably very possible), then go back to what I said about the workshop, check the workshop, and voila, new maps to get annoyed at. The graphics, while not as great as a 2017 game (obviously) are actually very good for a 2009 game. The co op is so great, whether it be from strangers or with friends you already know. You can always find something to do in Left 4 Dead, and chances are you might never be bored. Seeing as a lot of my friends have hundreds or even a thousand hours on this game, I think that probably proves the point I'm trying to make. Another masterpiece by Valve. Thank you for bestowing this beautiful game upon us.
TL;DR - Definitely buy this game, great co op, great gamemodes, 10/10.

This is an absolutely beautiful experience. One large seamless, lovely world, full of moments of wonder. The puzzles, while not yet terribly difficult, are well-constructed, and the level-design has a great sense of flow. I'm rarely frustrated by puzzles or traversing the landscape, and there's very little backtracking.
Despite having a pretty similar control scheme to a 3D Legend of Zelda title, they've refined the controls to better fit a game filled with puzzles, but no enemies. While I'm a huge fan of Zelda games, Link seemingly has little regard for self-preservation, and likes to hurl himself off of every available ledge, whether I tell him to or not. Our nameless hero in Rime, on the other hand, notices ledges, and stops himself.
The music should be remarked upon as well. A mix of traditional and modern elements, with some beautiful cello work. It's wonderfully atmospheric, and makes you feel as if you're playing through a studio Ghibli film.
As for complaints, I have very, very few. Originally when I played, the camera was super buggy indoors, and would clip through walls, obscuring your view of the level and character. This has been fixed. It was also poorly optimized, and did not run well on my machine despite it exceeding the system requirements significantly. This too seems to have been fixed. ---A new favorite for single player shooters---
5 playthroughs complete, just finished on Insanity 4 (current hardest difficulty).
---VS SW2013---
Vast improvement over SW2013 in gameplay. No tedious crawl into decent abilities, rebalancing makes previously crap abilities worthwhile, and the element system makes everything more fun especially on harder difficulties.
Major letdown in story. While the story in SW2013 was a pleasant surprise, your new companion is simply obnoxious now and the animations/voice acting seems mostly worse. Personally, don't really care, others will.
---CO-OP---
Co-op works great when you've got a decent host. Zero issues with friends, though some lag issues joining random matches.
---Free Updates---
Devs have been excellent with the free updates so far. Solid balancing changes, new difficulties, new crafting components, and tons more on the way.
---General Thoughts---
Mostly, I'm impressed that they managed to turn this into a "loot shooter" without actually having much verticle progression, and avoided (and mostly actually reduced from SW2013) the bullet sponges.
Faster. More weapons. More useful playstyles. Element system works great. Crafting. Lots more challenge. Different from what I expected, but still impressed and excited with a few exceptions.
Would like to see the massive death penalty (lots of lost cash) reduced. Otherwise, will be waiting on the new challenge mode and crafting stuff.
