-- PROS --
+ The loot system is really great. You find your weapons from special bosses (marked as a skull on your map), or occasionally from chests (potentially from other monsters, but I think I've only seen that once). You then find upgrades for your weapons, which is the loot that largely drops throughout the game modes. The weapons have set stats, but the upgrades do not, so that is what you farm for. They give you a lot of loot, so you have a lot of chances to find something valuable. The highest rarity drops at frequent enough intervals to keep you from getting frustrated, but not so often that they rain from the sky.
+ The shops are actually done properly. You can find real hidden gems in there, and as soon as you progress through the story enough you can find some really great high level upgrades. At the moment I am posting this review...you can do something pretty cheesy...  get to the end of your first playthrough (after finishing the final boss), then bump up your difficulty to the highest setting. Go back into your game and visit the shops. There will be higher level gear in there than what you should be getting (at least that's how it worked for me).
+ The combat is a blast! I dislike first person shooters usually (mostly because they give me headaches, but also because I suck at fast paced shooting). This game is great because they have a very viable melee combat system. In fact, right now it's more viable to be melee than it is to use guns (a common complaint that will at some point be fixed, I presume). My favorite weapon is a chainsaw, because the melee skills feel much more pleasant with that weapon than with any other type. My boyfriend plays this game with me, and he solely uses guns while I solely use melee. It works out very well for us, and he loves the gun combat.
+/- The humor...lots of sexual inneundos (which is a negative for me - I don't like this style of "funny" - but a positive to others, and is trademark to this series). But the game did keep me laughing (mostly AT it). There are a lot of genetalia jokes, so enter at your own risk. There are also Fortune Cookies which are really cute and usually have a funny message.
+ The environments are randomly generated, which I like.
-- CONS --
- The story... I'm not going to go into detail (there are plenty of reviews that do that for you already), but the story left me wanting. The ending in particular left me with a WTF look on my face. I was really angry about the end cutscene. Anyways, if you take out the humor, which is in 75%+ of the questline, you're left with a very lackluster story.
- Ammo can be hard to find. If you don't like switching weapon types (because there's a chance you'll run out of ammo of a certain type), you won't enjoy this game as much. There are skills that help combat this. On that same note, you also need to have elemental weapons set up and a physical weapon. There are enemies that are completely immune or just resistant to certain types of damage. There is a lot of weapon switching. I personally don't like to switch weapons, so I just set up my melee to physical, have one back up elemental melee weapon in case of a physical-immune enemy, and then power house through Physical Resistance enemies with my main physical melee weapon.  I have only elemental range weapons, which I primarily use for big story bosses where melee can be rough.
- Crafting is a waste of time and money. You'd rather just reset the shop and hope to get lucky. This might be changed eventually.
Overall, this is a really fun game! The positives far outweigh the negatives. This is worth a purchase, in my opinion. The devs patch frequently and balance the game, so you'll see a lot of changes throughout the upcoming months.
Note: If you intend to play this game ONLY cooperatively, I do not recommend this game YET. I would wait a few patches for them to clean it up before getting into it. The experience for me was...very lackluster and incredibly frustrating. And there were changes in patches that completely infuriated me. I wish I had waited to play this game and not bought it Day One.
-- My COOP Experience --
My boyfriend hosts. We go through the entire playthrough, all the way to the end. The entire time, my progress did not not save in my story (this is an intended feature). So, if I wanted to play my own game without him, I would have to start all over again from the beginning.  It is absolutely a HUGE waste of time to go through your first playthrough if you have already gone through it once cooperatively, which I'll explain in a moment.
Throughout that playthrough, I missed out on a few skills that were rewarded from quests (perhaps a bug, I received some skills, but not all of them). At a certain point in the story the shops reset and get great loot. At this point, the player that does not host (probably due to the fact that your own story progress does not save, so it thinks you shouldn't have access to these shops), you cannot talk to shops. This means you cannot buy ammo (which can be scarce, especially if you don't hunt down chests). This means you cannot buy any skills. This means you cannot buy any weapons that are added to the shops in the late game. This means you cannot sell anything. You cannot buy anything (and the shops have great loot sometimes). This is a bug, and presumably will be fixed. But for my experience on day one...this SUCKS.
Also, when crafting is unlocked for the host, it is not also unlocked for the coop player. So, you'll need to go through the first few hours of the game on your own save game, where you won't get anything for your time other than low level upgrades and some XP and gold. Then if you wanted to craft you could. I'm not sure if this unlocks the crafting in coop or not (I haven't tested it), but if it doesn't, you can always just go into your own game when you want to craft. But, crafting sucks in this game, so don't do it.
And the coop specific performance issues...oh gosh...CONSTANT disconnects from the server (even with good internet connection). Constant huge frame rate dips... every patch improves these things. But it still isn't what it should be.
So, since I was missing a handful of great things from not hosting myself... I was frustrated and quit the game. A few patches roll out, and now they have added these Orbs. You get them from quests after your first playthrough (basically to give you a reason to go through different playthroughs). They will help you boost the stats on a chosen weapon with the next patch. But for now you can just collect them. We think "let's play Shadow Warrior 2 again and horde some resources for the next patch!"
We launch the game, and since I'm still frustrated with missing out on skills (that are actually useful), I decide to host. We go through a few quests...and then I realize that I'm not getting any orbs. Because, duh, the game thinks this is my first playthrough...meanwhile, the host from my last playthrough is getting a lot of them. Since I've already done these quests once, I don't get any rewards from them other than the ones that bugged out. Fantastic. So, I get to go through this entire playthrough, really only to gain XP (there is a cap at some point, which I haven't hit yet), gold, and some very rare upgrades. Because, as I said, the upgrades are tied to story progression. I go through most of the playthrough finding really garbage loot, with nothing useful in shops until the second half of the game. That entire first half I find maybe one upgrade that I ended up equipping. But, hey, at least I could pick up the skills that I should have gotten already and purchase the weapons that I should have already been able to buy!
Frustrating and a huge waste of 13hrs to go through that playthrough. It's annoying that you are penalized for not hosting, even though you have completed every quest once!

Okay, I'm going to explain the good and the bad about this game. Keep in mind that this is my first review.
The bad: You cannot manuelly place buildings, they are all automatic. If you're hoping to leave your workers to gain resources for you while your offline then you'll be terribly mistaken, while offline you gain 50% less resources than you did before. The game is terribly buggy, Some units walk across the sky in sieges, some walk over mountains and the pathfinding is not that great. The AI are some of the worse I've ever seen; While doing a custom siege I sent my reinforcements to attack the army that was besieging me and after they killed my reinforcements what did they do? they stood there for the next 45 mins doing nothing when my castle was rype for the taking. Some of your troops wont attack certain troops when they're standing right in front of them unless you right click on them to attack. The game also has a terrible learning curve and you will ofen get bored playing this game. You WILL spend most of your time in the world map traveling between cities and to new strongholds to attack. Also when starting off in southmont players can attack your townhall from outside your double layered walls and immediately win the battle since battles are won by destroying the town hall, not the army nor the city. The town hall. Mods are also usually never on, I've never seen one on anyways or one that would actaully do something productive and help players.
The good: PVP is fun. Sieges are fun and battles in general are fun. The storylines are decent. Though you cannot manuelly place buildings it is always nice to finish your city and admire its beauty. ((UPDATE: As of "Garruk's Revenge" expansion, some of the negative points I brought up are no longer valid. For example, aside from the expansion pack, cards are no longer locked behind paywalls (though they do require multiplayer play - which may put off some). In addition, the expansion bringing in new cards has done a remarkable thing for the depth of the card pool and possible strategies - 70-120 or so new cards are much more impressive in a game with true, free deck building.
That said, I still cannot recommend this game over the previous installments unless you already own them and are looking for something a little new, for all of its flaws))
I am currently an avid MTG player, having been brought in to the game via DoTP 2013 about two years ago, but mostly playing physical tournaments and drafts at my local store.
Previous Duels of the Planeswalkers games were great ways to learn the game and some examples of cards and strategies from it, as well as experience a non-competetive, easy matchmaking service and a nice little progression aspect, even with a little light story thrown in. Ultimately, they were all greatly restricted in scope, mostly to avoid treading on the toes of MTG Online and the physical card game - Duels is, and always will be, an advertisement for the CCG and a great tutorial with some fun games to be had.
This newest iteration allows you to build decks from scratch with the full pool of cards - something that, shockingly, was never in the previous 'modify an existing deck' design of the series - and has a slightly stronger story and cinematics than the previous ones, in my own opinion. It showcases some nice mechanics and visuals, and has EXCELLENT AI at the highest difficulties (with one or two questionable judgements every now and then), given the complexity of the game. The game also has some nice artworks and background lore/information for people new to the MTG universe, who are so interested.
However. Even without DLC or Expansions, large amounts of cards are strictly locked behind a paywall. PvP players will note a distinct lack of multiplayer modes compared to previous games, and people seeking to grind cards to complete their collection and enhance the number of strategies will find the largely randomized nature of card acquiring to be infuriating - particularly since previous games allowed you to see which cards, in sequence, you'll unlock for each deck. The UI, while pretty, is clunky frequently when navigated with a mouse, scroll wheel and/or keyboard, likely a mark against the limited effort putting in to porting this game year in year out, when it appears to be gaining traction on tablets/iPad more than anything else.
Finally, the card pool is...horrifically shallow. Multiple strategies exist, certainly, but its smaller than any previous Duels game - even before the DLC and expansions are taken into account, EVEN if you include this game's paid-only 'premium' cards. In addition, previous modes and game formats have been completely stripped from the game, and some of the most interesting mechanics in the planes/blocks/sets the game features are completely absent - or at least, not available to players, only the AI.
All things considered, this series has taken one step forward and two, three or four steps back. There was never really a noticeable improvement with this series, year by year, but for long time fans this is, frankly, insulting. To call this an 'iterative' series is doing the word a disservice, as 'iterative' implies some kind of development, improvement or progression, which this game lacks. Just buy one of the older ones - there's no reason to get this one for a lot of people.

This man was an absolute hero. I loved him. Everything he did, I would obsess over. I soon got to the point of worshipping this man religiously and trying to get others into my cult. I spread the word about this man just like Ignatius Loyola spead the word about Reformed Catholicism. I created many large quizzes dedicated to him. The man I have previously been talking about loved the game Total War:Rome. It is a strategy game, much like another of his favourite games, chess. Finally finished this a little while ago but only just now decided to write a review because it's hard to talk about this game in a way that doesn't make me seem like a double standard making jackass. Plus the standard negative stuff about DNF has been beaten to death over and over again in a way that would make Duke himself blush. So I'll try not to fall into that trap.
It's hard to talk about Duke because the games and the man himself is 80% gimmick and 20% one liners. This was no exception. So I can't just say it was too gimmicky. Because no♥♥♥♥♥♥Sherlock,  it's Duke Nukem. Problem is, there was 98% gimmick, 10% one liners and 0.5% things to kill. That was the big negative to me. There was too much focusing on memes that were sometimes not even duke related. There was too much gimmick happening and not enough shooting stuff. Like the minigames that are almost memes themselves at this point. It was like the game was trying to make up for lost time in the self-referential humor and thus you got huge spans of non-action sequences like the strip club. Make no mistake, Duke has always been about being cheesy and awesome and killing swathes of enemies. But this didn't have much of that all things considered.
Now let me get something straight, I'm a straight man and like any straight man I like women and I like boobs. I've seen and touched many of both in my time. So believe me when I say that there were way,
too many instances of "omg look boobs!" Just way too many, it's what you'd expect either a kid or a sexually frustrated adult to put into a video game. Like I said before lots of boob is perfect for Duke because he's Duke. Which is why the strip clubs in the original games were just fine. It was over the top and just great. But this is over the top to the point where someone fell down and broke their neck.
Other thing that almost made me create a review just to rant was the ♥♥♥♥ing hoover dam underwater ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Holy crap. This level frustrated me almost to the point of just stopping right then and there. I don't like underwater levels in 3D games in the first place but I do acknowledge they can be done right. This wasn't. It brought the pace of the game to a screeching halt even worse than the non-action sequences. I died more times in the leech fight and the area near it than anywhere else in the game including the final boss (which I actually died 0 times on so that should say something). Simply because I couldn't move fast. I know you're  thinking "you just have no skill". Maybe that's true, but this was not a matter of skill. Skill cannot be used when you move like a bug through taffy. It gives you little opportunities to artfully dodge like you could in just about every other game.
That said, the final fight made up for it and it was suitably epic. Still, not sure I can recommend it. Even though I think the absolute nail biting hate towards it is kind of silly I do understand to an extent. It's not faithful to the material. Even though I love hearing Jon and all that. It just lacked the gameplay. Which was a gigantic part of Duke 3D and such. If you liked those there is no real guarantee you'll like this one. There's just not enough gameplay and too much pandering and meme-whoring and not enough of what made the series great in the first place: Killing things. Killing lots of things and killing lots of things in a smooth and flowing manner.

This game should have more negative reviews, so I will write one.
There are no berry bushes. There are no flint rocks lying around. There are no fish in the water. There is no tap root on the ground. There is no animal that walks around, yet somehow they can still end up in your snare. The entire game is spent aiming at blank looking tiles, using skills like "look for food", "catch a fish", or "find a flint stone", and hoping that you will get one. There is no way to visually see where any of these things are. The entire game world feels empty and desolate, because you cannot actually see any of the things that you are going to have to go gather. For example, you can gather the berries from anywhere, so there isn't even incentive to find a location that has say... many berry bushes, because the berries come from searching any grass tile.
Basically, you are running around an empty world, and you are expected to imagine all the things that you are interacting with. Someone called it a progress bar simulator, and that is pretty accurate. I guess while the progress bars go by slowly you are supposed to imagine the thing you are interacting with. Like imagine my guy wondering if there are some berry bushes over here, and then when he finds some I can imagine that some are sitting there on the tile. I'm glad the trees at least made it into the visible world, because that would be funny if you had to go around trying to cut down trees, and you couldn't even see them. Its really not that far away from that.
oh... and a 45 minute load time? hahahahahahhaha. since when has that become acceptable?

Rain World is a survival platformer, but it's very peculiar and unique. You play a cute slug-cat creature who is exploring the sodden industrial post-apocalyptic wastes of long-existinct humanity. Immediately you get the sensation that you're a relatively weak creature in the middle of the food chain: many predators above you, but also prey below. The objective of the game is to survive and explore, to find your kin and possibly unlock the secrets of this world, a world which becomes more mysterious, strange and enigmatic as you explore deeper.
The creatures (including yourself) of Rain World are "animated" using a unique procedural physics-based engine, which gives everything a disarmingly-realistic appearance. Some have complained about the difficulty: but if you truly were a small mammal in this situation it wouldn't be a walk in the park. There are infinite respawns, and deaths rarely seem unfair.
I've poured many hours into Rain World and yet I've barely scratched the surface. The game world is gigantic, overwhelming and non-linear and there are countless branching paths for slug cat to explore. The ambient soundtrack is subtle, fitting and unique; the world is full of surprises. I still can't tell whether this is a game, or a digital sculpture, or a simulation. It's really quite incredible, and even players who don't enjoy the gameplay would probably still find themselves drawn deeply into this world even if they're just spectating.
Update: On the Steam discussion board for Rain World the developer has posted a pinned thread titled: "Helpful tips for the healthy Slugcat." There are a few little bits and pieces in here to get you started, and the final dot point says, mysteriously:
"There is more to this world than you know."
I think this captures the game perfectly. Originally I thought this was a cute and unusual platformer, but I underestimated how deep the slugcat burrow goes. Regardless, I'm 50 hours deep and I can't put it down. This is truly a masterpiece.

I wanted to like this game. It looked really cool, and the story was great. Kill animations are seamless and look awesome, the voice acting is great, and War is a great character. The music was good, the collectibles were cool to try and find, and each level/area looks great.
However, the gameplay itself kills it for me. Combat is more or less mashing the same button over and over. You can change timing and directions to execute different moves and you can switch weapons, but each different weapon feels like pretty much the same thing. Building up combos and introducing move variety has no tangible benefits, at least not from what I saw. It started out interesting and I was always entertained watching kill animations and stuff, but by about 2/3 of the way through the game I realized I just wasn't enjoying combat anymore, and hadn't been for a while. I just wanted to finish the game for the sake of completion, not because I was having fun.
Part of that is from the puzzles. The puzzles are pretty easy to figure out, but a real pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to actually execute. You can almost immediately see what has to be done at any given point, but actually doing it can require a lot of tedious running around and platforming.
Boss fights, as well, are really hit or miss. Some of them were really cool, but others were just an excuse to force you to use some new ability you just got, and just went on for way too long without adding any new attack patterns or anything to keep the fight interesting.
On the whole, Darksiders looks like a really good game, and it's enjoyable for the first half or so. If you like hack n' slash and don't mind button mashing you'd definitely like this game. However, going to this game from Devil May Cry just left me wanting more out of the combat in Darksiders. No amount of great animations can make up to me the lack of variety in moves and weapons. This game is also hurt by the fact that building combos is much harder than in other hack n' slash titles, and without any of the benefits of using stylish combos or move variety. Darksiders does a lot of things well, but I can't rate it favorably due to the issues expounded upon above.

I played both the open beta and the closed beta and I've found For Honor to be a great experience. It's a pretty refreshing game bearing in mind how much fun I've had playing this with my friends. I haven't felt so satisfied defeating someone in a game in ages, with of course a neat little execution as a cherry on top. There are obviously a few glaring issues in terms of connectivity though I find it to be more than bearable and haven't really run into too many occasions where it's really had a huge negative impact on my For Honor experience.
I would reccomend this game to anyone who enjoys brawlers and learning how and when to attack, also you should have some patience to learn the movesets of the characters. I would further reccomend this game to anyone who generally just wants to feel like a badass on a medieval battlefield. The combat feels really fluid and you really do feel the weight behind your attacks when taking a swing at someone. For Honor has some neat little cosmetic customisation options for your heroes and also some skill customisation primarily used in 4v4's, which to me is a welcome addition in sort of setting for example your Warden apart from other Warden's.
I feel like it's a worthwhile purchase especially for someone like me who enjoys the competitive aspects of games and who enjoys a change of pace, in terms of learning to be patient in fights rather than the typical "be as fast as possible to win" which is commonly seen with twitch shooter type games and other competitive pvp titles. While For Honor does have a single player story mode that you can play co-op, the multiplayer is definitely where this game shines.

Definately not worth 15 dollars. Not a terible game, but not a very good one either. At and usually below this price range, you can buy other games that give you a similar experience and deliver it way better.
Graphics look very good for 2005.... aside from wide open areas. In-doors, the visuals hold up well. Outside they look ugly, which is to be expected from a game made in the *early* days lof id Tech 4.
The same can't be said for the gameplay. Q4 rustled a lot of jimmies in the Quake community back when it first came out.
The guns feel very unimpactful, and your movement feels really slow and sluggish, almost like you're playing Halo (no offense to Halo), which absolutely does not belong in a Quake game.
The weapon sound effects and animations do a poor job of conveying a true sense of power behind them to the player. They don't have the same kick to them that we saw in prior Quake games, or hell, even Doom 3.
This game tried to emulate the much more slower paced Doom 3 formula (A game that *I* personally enjoyed, but many didn't) and give it a Quake and non-horror twist, but it just didn't work out for them. Yes, it isn't as slow as Doom 3, but comparing this to other id games.... the pacing feels... wrong. Enemies aren't exciting enough to fight individually like they are in Doom 3. They don't pose a challenge to you in any way, and your guns are not fun too shoot.
This game does have its moments. I like how squad members can heal you and replenish your armor. That's cool... it's too bad all of the characters are unintentionally annoying and the plot is absolute garbage.
If you like slow-paced FPS, pick up Doom 3 instead. If you were looking for an action oriented and modern style id game, pick up Rage. I'm well aware that those games are very devisive, but if you're already thinking about getting Quake 4 after hearing all of the complaints, you'll get a better experience with one of those games.

Hoo boy, this is one tough♥♥♥♥♥♥cookie. Where to begin, where to begin... ok, how about the beginning of the game.
You start the game (after a stupidly easy "boss" fight) by having your♥♥♥♥♥♥sucked by two clones of the Olsen twins with zero facial muscles and incredibly annoying voices. You then attempt to play pool with balls that defy all known laws of movement. A quick strut down an ego-hall leads you past a bunch of women (who still have no facial muscles) grabbing their boobs at the sight of you, down to a TV host (who still has no facial muscles) who tells you your interview has been cancelled due to aliens lining up to get a hamburger. No, seriously, the first thing this intergalactic menace does is go pick up some burgers.¹
After this, you get about 20 hours worth of incredibly linear shooting galleries with brain dead AI, poorly executed sex jokes, and one of the dumbest ideas in video game history, which I will describe after the line break for emphasis.
OK, that was the line break. Now, one of the major selling points of this game was the variety of weapons. All the trailers up to the ones just before release advertised the huge variety of weapons. Well, Mr. Pitchford, if you're so proud of the game's wide weapon variety, WHY THE FLYING ♥♥♥♥ WOULD YOU IMPOSE A TWO/FOUR WEAPON LIMIT?
OK, that's the single player out of the way. The multiplayer nearly - NEARLY, you understand - made the game recommendable. Good maps (mostly), fun mutators, a wide range of customization options, low lag (mostly), quite fun. Now I know what you're thinking: "But you seemed to like it, why would you not recommend the multiplayer"? Well, it's quite simple. I liked the multiplayer because it reminded me a lot of Unreal Tournament, one of the greatest multiplayer games ever. It then struck me that it would be a much better idea to just go buy one of the Unreal Tournament games instead of buying this for its multiplayer component. Plus, unlike this, the Unreal Tournament games still have a strong playerbase.
I've heard that the 'Doctor Who Cloned Me' DLC was decent, better maps, actual funny jokes, facial muscles, but... I dunno.
TL; DR version: Meh at best single player, good multiplayer, but you'd be better off buying Unreal Tournament for multiplayer purposes.
(Oh, in case you're wondering, no, there is not a single facial muscle in the entire game.)
¹ - OK, I admit, that bit was funny.

This is the best horror game I've ever played. It is all about the atmosphere, ambience and the story. The way that Frictional Games keep pumping the tension during the game is just brilliant. The game is really immersive and if you get into it, you get into the story, get into the feeling of the main character, you'll be fully immersed and will feel all the horrors and fears that awaits behind every corner. That's what happened to me. Being adult, I have never been so frightened by any of the media content: either it is a movie or a game. But the Amnesia: The Dark Descent literally made me be afraid and really swet because of the tension.
And there are no cheap techniques like so-called "jump scares" or anything I can remember of. All the scary feelings are invoked by the game's atmosphere built by amaizing art and graphics, brilliant ambient and sound effects, intriguing story and gameplay elements. It is your mind which, upon this all, will build inside the conclusions of the upcoming danger, which will may or may not happen. But you'll never know what is it this time: true danger or you're deluding yourself.
Worth to mention that gameplay is built upon the idea, that you can't fight and directly resist your enemies with weapon. Therea are no weapond, no direct fights, no health bar, no danget indicators. And me personally like this idea and gameplay philosophy of Frictional Games, which they evolved from the great Penumbra series (in the first game you actually could fight, but avoiding it was the best option all the time). And alongside the dark atmosphere and unknown danger, when you don't know what is happening, who you may face with, and what it will cost you, the best idea that you would come up with in such situation in real life - is try to hide, or somehow avoid the danger, or run as fast as you can. You wouldn't stop to check out whether that butcher is gonna slaughter you or give you a hug.
If you liked what I have described, you should definitely grab and play this game (it's free right now)! There is much more! And I'm sure that upcoming SOMA will be another horror masterpiece. Thank you Frictional Games!

Many people will rate this game down for being unconventionally difficult and I understand that, but this is a game that requires the player to have some patience and to get used to things before it becomes truly immersive. It took about 10 or so hours for me to feel comfortable in how to manage my time, pace myself, avoid predators, and know how to navigate areas properly.
Once I did however this game became very fun and very worth it. I play it every day and it's worth every penny
Pros:
- Very unique gameplay, you won't find a survival game like this anywhere else
- The enemy AI is very well done, they react to you differently depending on what you carry and do and even adapt hunting strategies
- The world is big and fun to explore, every area is its own ecosystem, this means even your predators have predators
- Beautiful art, music, and environments
- Combat is very fun once you figure it out and get comfortable with it
- Lore is surprisingly very well immersed into the game once you start exploring it, things start making a lot of sense but you have to put in effort to find that out and it feels very rewarding
- You can make friends with many creatures! Even the ones who want to eat you can be your buddy if you try
- When you get everything down it feels very rewarding to play since you will know exactly where to go to avoid or trick things that want to hurt you and you'll be able to turn the tides on some creatures that wrecked you real good in the beginning of the game.
Cons
- The difficulty is brutal. Many things that you need to look out for or avoid will kill you the first time you see them. Many areas will be hard to navigate the first time around. You'll have to re-do a lot of days and sometimes due you just won't be able to go to a certain place that day because there are too many enemies that spawned in that direction. But this IS the point of the game, to make you feel as helpless as the creature you're playing as. But this is not every person's cup of tea and thats okay.
- Swimming, while improved from day 1 release, is still pretty difficult. Even if you get a lot of practice in, water physics will push you around, sometimes you won't be able to reach a platform in time because the tide's too low, ect.
- Controls aren't too touched upon and are sometimes a bit wonky. You know what to press to eat, jump, and run, but the game won't tell you how to backflip, how to turn around in pipes, how to speed up in pipes, ect. it won't tell you that crawling is more quiet, and jumps will sometimes not work out as well because you didn't hold up/forward long enough
- It's possible to lock yourself out of some content if you're not aware. There are some sections that don't tell you the direct consequences of your actions or where you'll be at a loss with what to do. In some places, performing an obvious action has very bad consequences that you're not warned about or aware of.
- You have to put in time and patience for this game to feel comfortable. This isn't a game for people who just want to blaze through the story or just explore everything right away. This is a pacing thing, and its made that way to help you get more familiar with where things are and how the world is connected. This is very much not something everyone will enjoy doing.

This game is extremely punishing but is an amazing experience the I will undoubtedly never forget.
Pros:
- Enemy design is incredibly sophisticated. For example: certain enemies will rush at you while others will wait for you at a pipe. Other enemies will hide and run away from you but will attack when cornered. No 2 types of enemies feel copied and pasted (asside from the obvious different types of lizards, but even they feel unique.) Enemies fight amongst eachother in extremely organic ways that really make them feel alive. The enemy design is easily IMO the most interesting part of this game
- Art style is beautiful
- Sound design is one of the best I've seen in any game
- Music is often subtle but kicks in during battles and chases. When there is music, it's crazy good. Plus it has the bonus of being procedurally generated based on the enemies near you making it always feel unique to your experience
- Universe is super interesting
- The entire game can be backtracked upon, making it an almost open world game. There are also several paths through each region making the game feel non linear while in reality still being pretty linear
Cons:
- This game is very punishing. I don't mean it's like kinda hard. It's ♥♥♥♥ing brutal. There are several sections which, if performed properly, should take about 5 minutes, but instead I replayed them over and over again for hours
- Controls are not very well conveyed. I'd suggest looking up some controls you may not have realized existed (like down+use to drop items)
- Swimming feels very rough (hard to time swimming jumps, difficult to swim into pipes, etc)
- Very little replay value
Final Thoughts:
If you like extremely punishing 2D platformers with unique everything, get this game. Also, I've seen a lot of reviewers say that the controls in this game are bad. I couldnt disagree more. Aside from the slightly iffy water controls I belive the controls in this game to be very good, infact better than many platformers. I think the biggest thing this game suffers from is not giving the player enough breathing room early on. If you can get past the initial learning curve, this game is very VERY good. Don't let this game slip by. Get it.

I'm giving this a bad review simply because of the atrocious menues. If you want my opinion of the game itself, it's Magic. It's no different from any of the years before it besides the card library.
=======================================================================================
The intro is simply annoying. It plays the same whispering wind four times in a row for each of the devs or publishes and their alienware advertisement (because I need top of the line equipment for a digital card game) before finally getting to the intro custscene which repeats the same whispering wind. This one, you have to sit through a few seconds before being able to skip it. We then hit the Start screen where the player is prompted to click start. There is then a two second delay before the fog ever so slowly begins to engulf the screen and take me to the main menu.
I know this sounds like nit-picking but the menues are beyond awful to navigate. Rather than a standard push button menu or even a left and right option, it's uses a front/back layout so you can see the icons for the options behind your current selection, but the icons are just card portraits. How am I to know that "Dictate of the Twin Gods" is "Restart Battle". How about a clock or a back arrow or a curved arrow or something to symbolize restarting. Anyone familiar with the card will tell you that the card has nothing to do with reversing time either, the icons are simply arbitrary to look pretty leaving you to one by one, scroll through your options one by one and read the text underneath until finding what you want. Oh and guess what. The lingering fog is back.
Even if you do happen to manage to memorize the icons, it doesn't make enough of a difference. The one you're on is selected and focused, you cannot see any options you have already passed and any yet to come forward are out of focus and slightly to the right so you can easily click on them. Guess what, it doesn't matter. I can see that icon in the back and I know it is the one I want to click so I'm going to click it but it only shuffles over once to the next option forcing me to click four times just to open the option I want to get to.
2014 gave me a loading screen inbetween menues that lasted maybe a full second at most. I have a 4 gigahert processor, it loaded and then the game started. That's it. Quick and simple.
The game itself has become increasingly annoying as well. The table pulls itself apart like an antique dining table that has an optional insert every time your attack phase comes up and it makes this god awful clang of a forge when it does this. This all happens regardless of whether or not you are attacking. And guess what. That whole nonsense takes another three seconds per turn.
=======================================================================================
In the end, I used to play M14 to kill a few minutes while waiting for my friends to finish whatever they were doing so we could all play the same game. This terrible design couple with these nuisences have ruined that for me as I spend more time looking at WotC's pretentious smoke effect than actually playing the game. Do not bother with this purchase, just buy the movie "The Fog" instead. You'll get about as much entertainment out of it.

Pros:
*Nearly full deck customizability with some limitations.
*Large campaign to complete to unlock cards before entering multiplayer.
*People with good luck get to steam roll people with bad luck due to RNG Deck Shuffles.
Cons:
*Deck customization has some weird and non explained limitions on "how to" manually create a deck.
*AI can be EXTREMELY hard at times, and most of the times has best possible RNG Deck Shuffles.
*If a player leaves during a multiplayer match before game is over, an AI will replace them and can possible destroy you. (leaving should forefit the match completely, not spawn an AI, leave that for Single Player.)
*The "loading screen" between menus is extremely annoying and wasteful. Too slow.
*Harder difficulties seem nearly impossible and don't seem to reward anything different then playing lower or lowest difficulties.
*[Glitch] When starting the game, after closeing after editing your sound settings, everything before the Start button is super loud (back to default) until you click the Start button
*[Glitch] Sometimes when selecting menu options your click isn't recognized and you need to click several times to activate the menu.
*[Glitch] You can click menu options spamming the sound continuously until the menu starts changing.
*[Glitch] When using Travelers Amulet, if you close the screen to select a land card without confirming by Escaping or other means it freezes your turn and you can not do anything else nor bring the land select screen back up. This is a huge bug and has cause me to lose some matches.
*People with bad luck get wrecked by people with good luck due to RNG Deck Shuffles.
My notes:
*$10 sure, $35 just to get cards you would have gotten for playing the campaign, no.
*Not having all the cards from all the starter decks after tutorial is kind of lame. I would have liked to have been able to switch my decks for certain battles without farming all the Explore missions for cards I should have started with.
*The game has its flaws, but for a $10 card game, its well worth it, even if I have the worst luck in the world. Better then spending 100's of dollars on real world card packs to build decks and play physically.

This game is a super huge let-down. On it's own, it's still a pretty bad game, but compared to the previous MTG games it looks even worse.
1. 2015 has no two-headed giant mode. Two-headed giant is the main reason why people play these game. Who wouldn't want to team up with their friends? It's really stupid for Wotc to take it out for no reason. Would it really be that hard just to add another game mode?
2. 2015 is also missing the revenge campaign, challenges, and planeswalkers. Basically, all there is is multiplayer (free-for-all only) and campaign mode which is too short on it's own and becomes really easy really quick.
3. The starting decks are a joke. There is no other way to say it. They're literally the worst decks I've ever seen, and trust me, I've seen some really bad decks. In fact, they're worse than the $15 starters you can buy in real life. (If you're a MTG player already, you know what I mean.) Just how bad? They're packed with heaps of common creatures with no special abilities and almost no spells. Playing the first portion of the campaign is literally painful.
4. You get treated like a baby. If you've played MTG before you can skip the tutorial, but you still have to beat the tutorial boss. Then, after that, you aren't allowed to customize your decks until you beat the first "real" boss of the campaign.
5. The difficulty curve is totally skewed. In the begining, before you unlock enough cards, the game is IMPOSSIBLE. Once upon a time this game had just started, I was decent at it, having fun, and gave it a good review.
Then time went on.
First off, the graphics are nice. Ubisoft makes good looking games when NOT making a buggy piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥like certain Assassin's Creed titles. There's not a whole lot else to say about that.
This game had a lot of potential but squandered much of it. The successful launch of this game was rather obvious as it offered an interesting and new combat dynamic. The combat, which was fresh and interesting, thinly veiled how the system actually heavily lacks options during combat. It's not so much a fighting game as it is almost a scripted game of chess. What I mean by this is simple: If the enemy does X, you do Y. Then the enemy follows up with Z, and you do A to keep it going. Whereas in most fighting games there are a slew of ways to counter attacks and such For Honor actually only has a small handful of methods of decently countering enemies, reacting to new threats, etc. What this results in is highly formulaic combat from pros and very one-sided combat experienced by newer players. Also it's worth noting that there are various bugs in animations and certain combat moves that should have been removed but never were, and instead a new character type was built around exploiting this bug. (The ninja, whatever it's called) When the combat a game is centered around cannot be bothered to fix bugs and instead develops character types to EXPLOIT those bugs you might need to rethink the combat entirely.
Then comes the microtransactions. While not entirely a deal-breaker, they got annoying rather quickly. Sure, they DID stand to give you some kind of edge over your enemy but, well, remember that formula during combat? In general so long as you maintained that you didn't really NEED tons of new gear, though it sure helped if the constant grind of combat came down to pure attrition. Other bits just looked cool, which is sorta "meh". Honestly, it's hard to get attached to a particular look or appearance in For Honor when so little of anything actually matters in the long run.
The faction system is an interesting idea, but it's actually been done before. MAG did it on the PS3, but no one remembers MAG. (I do) However, remember that while some skill plays a part in the victories it REALLY boils down to the following: Which demographic is pumping more numbers into the game? Seriously, victories in the larger arc don't matter as much as sheer numbers of people in the faction feeding into their factional superiority. As for the factions themselves, and the aforementioned demographics, you got Vikings (Try-hards, counter-culture, metalheads, and fans of "The Vikings"), Knights (alt-right, normal right, "DEUS VULT", some metalheads as well, history buffs, and Christians), and Samurai (weebs, liberals, weebs, Japanophiles, weebs, furries, weebs, weebs, and weebs). The faction combat more-or-less becomes something of an online culture war where no one really wins and what victories do occur don't really count for much.
Level designs are pretty decent, but there wasn't a whole lot needed to make them decent in the first place. Various "main areas" for larger fights, some smaller side areas, and verticle portions as well. Honeslty, the level designs are pretty nice and work well with the limitations of the combat.
The single-player story is just stupid. A woman wants the three factions to keep the war going, a war that has been raging when the Vikings, Knights, and Samurai all were forced into a small area of the world and decided not to get along, not to really learn a damned thing about one another, and SOMEHOW kept themselves isolated enough not to advance in response to the threats of... well, the other factions. How did these three factions live so closely together and never, in any way, co-mingle, work things out, learn from one another, or anything else is beyond me and obviously not addressed for the sake of making them basically remain the same so that people can live out their long-lived argument over "Who would win?!". In other words, don't try to apply logic to the story, it doesn't hold up.

P2P ruins what is otherwise a great game.
I have dual interfaces, one public and one private. When I start the game, it assumes I'm on a NAT (Strict NAT at that) and nothing works. I disable the internal interface and while the game things I now have NO Internet connection, it works. If I restart the game with the internal NIC disabled, the game again assumes I'm on a NAT (Strict) and nothing works even though the only IP I now have is a public IP.
The networking in this game is atrocious. There are critical game aspects that require timing that simply don't work because of P2P latency. I attack and because another peer has decided I'm already hit, my avatar will just stand there while I hammer the attack button for 2-3 seconds. I dodge or block but my avatar just refuses to do anything. There can be a good 2-3 second resolution delay in which, if you are on the wrong end of it, your avatar will simply stand still and do nothing while you impotently issue commands.
The game itself is beautiful and fun but it is easily ruined for some by the second rate networking. This is primarily an online multiplayer game and the poor choice of peer to peer networking in an effort to make the code easily console portable and save a few dollars on not having dedicated servers could well sink an otherwise brilliant effort.

I've enjoyed and overlooked the errors in previous versions/years of Duels of the Planeswalkers, but 2015 sort of jumped the shark for me.
a)  Don't buy the premium bundles that include all the cards of various planes.  As soon as you do, the game stops giving out the booster packs for that particular plane.   A lot of the fun just drained from the game at that time.
b) The game cheats.  Playing through the entire series I never saw the computer muligan.  Never fought it where it had a flood or a drought of land.   This became particuarly evident when fighting the sliver deck as every game.  *every game* I played of the 20+ times to get past it, they had 3 different mana colors by turn 3.  Perfect curves.    Yes, I know this is necessary for AI's to stand a chance against humans but it still rankles when it's so damn obvious.
c) The new layout is not convenient.   I'd much rather look at options and navigation on one screen then have to slide through a whole bunch of other options first.   This lay out seems designed for phones where a swipe of the finger is more convenient than the click of a mouse.   If you're on a PC it's just tedious.
d) The card choice is poor of the cards given.  Yes there are some good cards and some favorite cards, but the cards that become available to build your deck are mediocre at best.   Nor do they allow you the cards that their own decks are built.   This causes (at least me) to feel like I've been given stone-and-stick tools to face foes outfitted in iron.   It's another means of giving the AI a necessary boost to make it competitive.   It still feels lame.
e) The auto-adjust of land is either on or off.  In 2014 I could put my deck together and click on "suggest land" and then tweak as I want.   In 2015 you can either accept what MTG2015 says you should have or you have to do it manually.   This wouldn't be so irksome except that to change the option to auto-adjust you have to leave the deck building screen, find the settings, make the adjuistment, and return to the deck building screen.
f) I'll say it again:  Don't buy the expansion card sets that just give you all the cards.   It really did ruin a lot of the fun.
I played 2014 all through 2013 and up to release of 2015.   I'll probably play 2015 whenever an expansion comes out but to be honest it just doesn't inspire the urge to continue playing.   Even with the chance to build my own deck, I feel like the mediocre decks I can manage just don't warrant excitement.
Buy for the 9.99.  Don't spend much more on this and be happy updating the included decks with whaterver wheat you can seperate from the dross of the booster packs.

This game is seriously underrated, but the game's not that bad, allow me to express it with a wall of text:
Let's first talk about the singleplayer, this is basically a sequel of Quake 2, you're fighting Strogg, it's the US army fighting monsters and that's pretty much it. Unlike Quake 2, you actually have soldiers to back you up, some of them being main characters on which you won't be attached to them that much (and you shouldn't, really, you'll find out why when you play the game), you have the regular grunts to die for you, the medics to heal you (obviously) and the technicians to recharge your shield.
The overall story is actually okay, even for a Quake title, the weapons are sort of balanced and the enemies are not too hard or easy to kill. My biggest complain, however, is how you're known as a killing machine not fearing of anything. Like seriously, every single marine talks about you, everyone knows your name, there was even a soldier who thought you were just a myth to scare off new recruits, even though you're just a regular corporal doing his job, which is my major reason of why it bothers me, compared to the other Quake games. The fact that you're considered a hero in Wolfenstein, Doom and Quake is acceptable, since you had to fight through hell in order to be like that, but Quake 4 just slaps it to your face right in the beginning before you even get to kill things. This is unnatural, I don't like that, especially when you're A FU CKING CORPORAL, it would be more understandable if you were a captain, or a lieutenant or something...
Now, for the multiplayer, this is where things get in the sh itter, brace yourself, because I am going to complain really hard on this one. Alright, where do I start, first of all, this does NOT feel like Quake multiplayer, not one bit. I know I should say the same thing for Quake singleplayer, but the multiplayer has just gone too far, let's talk about gameplay issues: the movements suck, they really do, it's slow and it's bouncing around, it's not as fast and straight as the regular Quake MPs and it feels like I'm playing Duke Nukem Forever MP with Quake skins, at least I can still bhop okay. Secondly, the weapons, well, they're not as powerful, it takes more hits than usual to kill someone, and you'll still have some ammo left if you're lucky enough to kill the guy first, their hitboxes are really small too, sometime I keep wondering how did I kill myself when I wasn't aiming at the wall or ground and how am I not hitting the player when I'm obviously in front of him, more on that later.
Now, for the technical issue, we have the network problems, where they keep giving you hiccups of ping from 40 to 120 while you play the game, which is probably the cause of the horrible hitboxes. I only played a single server in Quake 4 before writing this review, so I don't exactly know if it was just the server or the game itself, but a friend also told me that the network problem was even worse than in Quake 3, and also said that it was due to the compatibility with consoles, which doesn't surprise me at all, and while we're at it, that also explains the DNF quality graphics (but it's forgivable, since it's a 2005 game, this time), because of fu cking console ports! I HATE CONSOLES, THEY'RE THE PLAGUE OF GAMING! Ahem, sorry about that...
Anyway, in conclusion, it's still a good game, but it's not a good Quake game, it's worth playing it if you're not going to be an elilist complaining about Quake 4 being far fetched from the other Quake games, you can also imagine that it's just a Doom 3 expansion or whatever you want to think about.

Tomb Raider: Underworld has to be my favorite out of the three. Apart from the graphics, a lot of other things were updated quite nicely as well. The ability to have a variety of secondary weapons was a nice touch that I didn't think I needed. The inventory system is the cleanest and easiest to manage, especially with the elimination of the large and small health packs, and making it just one general health pack size. The HUD was simpler and the analog button commands also were boiled down to the basic extras like the binoculars, flashlight, weapon toggle, and health pack. This made controls simpler as well and didn't bog me down with so many button presses.
Combat was so-so, and once you get the
in the end-game, battles become like nothing. But it was still challenging in some areas, especially in the tighter corridors. Levels were generally much larger than in either of the first two. If in Legends you have small, easy to manage stages, and in Anniversary you had areas that connected to each other creating a seamless transition from level to level, Underworld brought levels of such massive size that the whole scale of things were beyond me. One stage had you climb up a tower with revolving sections (which arguably wasn't that tall, considering how fast you could finish that puzzle), while another was so large that you needed a motorcycle to get from one end of the area to the other. The entrance to the final area was located underwater, and you had to swim such lengths just to finish it.
Despite the large areas though, traversing them never seemed like a long hassle. The obstacles along the way surely provided some break from the back and forth that was sure to happen, making sure that you were paying attention even in those parts.
Underworld did a good job of wrapping up the connecting plots, even providing a short cinematic that I can only describe as a "Previously on Tomb Raider..." type of reel. Everything was resolved quite nicely, leaving just enough unresolved for a neat open ending for some issues.
Not much to say here other than I loved it. I haven't played a good dungeon crawler in a while, and this was really fun to go through. I fully recommend this game. Best appreciated in order though, so play the first two before this one.

Ah Rime, Rime, Rime, you had so much potential. I can see why both Sony and Microsoft dropped this game as an exclusive. Rime is a glorified running simulator, the games vast areas have you running from point A to point B solving annoying puzzles where, get this, the boy has to scream at statues?! Summary: Beautiful game, not too hard, only frustrating bits result from some unfortunate camera decisions, but the atmosphere is silent and melancholy and strange and ultimately quite sad. Don't play this one if you're depressed.
The puzzles in this game are environmental/atmospheric - figure out how to get to this place, move this object a certain way, what can I drag to put on this floorplate switch - that sort of thing. You will not suddenly have to stop and break story to do a math or logic puzzle. Platforming elements are jumping and ledging; grabbable ledges are always very clearly marked by what some sites and walkthroughs call "chalk marks" but to me looked like bird droppings. I am a lousy jumper and I only missed maybe one jump in the course of the whole game, so that should tell you how forgiving the jumping is.
You don't get voluntary saves; the game saves at checkpoints (look for the shell icon to appear at the top right corner of the screen briefly). They're frequent enough, and it's hard enough to mess up, that this isn't much of a problem in practice. Note that there ARE one or two places where you can blow past a collectable or achievement easily and you won't get another chance at it without replaying the game - which would likely be pretty tedious, once you've seen it all once you likely won't want to see it again.
The only annoying decision is that the game sometimes locks you into a particular fixed camera angle for whatever perverse reason of its own, and this can make some of the jumping and so on in that area much harder. Also, if you're playing with keyboard you'll find that the keys change depending on your orientation, so you ledge around a corner by pressing D, then stop moving for a moment, and now the direction you were going is "up" so if want to keep going that way, now you press W. This matters for backward jumps in particular. Fortunately, the character gives good visual cues, looking over his shoulder when he's ready for a backward jump or reaching out to the side when he's poised to jump sideways to another ledge.
Also, some of those fixed camera angles require you to move diagonally with precision, particularly two long bridges where you could easily fall off, and this is nearly impossible with a keyboard. Bottom line: Playing with a controller is probably better.
Note that Denuvo has officially been removed from the game.

ABZU and RiME are two games I've played recently that feel very similar: really nice/simple/beautiful aesthetic, wondrous exploration, and story telling without a single printed or spoken word. and I love them both! I wish there were more games like these!
since the games seem so comparable in my mind, I may as well compare them more: RiME is a little more platform-y and puzzle-y than ABZU, but never anything that requires any crazy reflexes. both have lots of hidden goodies to find, and they're hard! when you find one, you feel good and smart. RiME is a longer game. I do not believe that more length == more value, but having said that, RiME is not longer because it's padding the gameplay with mindless tasks; I feel like the game is constantly throwing new mechanics, or settings, or... "characters"? at me. which is great! I keep thinking "surely this is the end," but it's not, and there's yet more cool stuff I've never seen before!
the only bad thing I'll say about RiME is that it has a couple things that make me go "did they have to rush this part?" the menu has some weird issues (every time you go into the controller settings, it reverts to keyboard, even if you've previously selected gamepad), and the swimming controls are a little janky? they're fine, it just feels less polished than the swim mechanics of most 3rd-person action games, and it's weird to see that when the rest of the game is blowing my mind on so many other fronts. maybe they just decided their time was better spent on the game itself. or maybe the keyboard+mouse swimming is PERFECT - I haven't tried it. who knows!
again, it's a super-minor point. this game is beautiful; it's amazing. the world feels like something out of a Miyazaki movie. I recommend it 100%. play RiME. play ABZU.

After four hours of trying to find the flow of this game, I think I'm going to give up. Rain World is charming, beautiful, and the main character is cute and full of character, but the gameplay simply doesn't work.
On one hand, I often get stuck because a lizard is sitting on top of the only exit (tried and failed to find a way to kill one, and there's only so much you can do to avoid them). On the other hand, there are so many red herrings and things you should be told but aren't. I'm pretty sure I've just spent an hour trying to get past an obstacle that's actually a dead end, because a spot I found earlier and thought was a dead end was actually a passable obstacle (only I didn't realize I could only pass it with nothing in my hands - and no, I didn't find that one out, I saw it in a walkthrough).
It's one thing to make a game that doesn't hold your hand, but it something quite different to make a game that doesn't even give you means to explore it. This game is trying to do too many things at the same time: there are enemies, a maze-like environment, AND a time constraint. The level design is the main culprit here:
- there simply aren't enough alternate routes, and you often end up just trying to wait it out
- there is almost no visual language to help you navigate,
- there are huge parts of levels that serve no purpose beside luring you away from your shelter (which you have to reach before you run out of time),
- and on top of that challenges stack, rather than balancing each other out (which means that a bad random roll results in a ridiculous combination of dangers, such as four lizards swarming the surface and a fire bird attacking from above).
This could be such a marvelous exploration game - but instead it punishes curiosity. It could also be a great survival game - but instead it forces you to gamble. It could also be a great puzzle game, but instead of that no trick I've come up with seems to work. A major disappointment.

This game; this game is hard. Know that going in.
Also know that this isn't Dark Souls hard, where all the enemies wait for you in the exact same spots; but without saying too much, they aren't randomly strewn about either.
I don't reccomend the use of a joystick with this game, Controls are super fluid with a D-pad or the keyboard. There are only 4 directions you can go, and it's either full or nothing. Knowing for certain which way you're trying to go really helps you figure out how to make the Slug Cat more nimble.
I have a few suggestions to help you learn, things I did just intuitively because I explore everything in a game;
Do a war dance occasionally, celebrate your victories. Slug Cat would; be the Slug Cat. Let it teach you it's moves.
Observe, learn, experiment. Everything that happens happens for a reason, and normally it's a reason that you can make use of. Yes, even those things that you thought totally didn't have a reason for happening, or don't think carries any weight in the game's world, *especially those things you might otherwise overlook really easily* have a huge significance just waiting for you to discover.
Death is not as scarry as you think. It's not that you need to get good to progress, I mean, that helps, but that you're letting yourself get frustrated by this obstacle, and aren't trying to explore. Go explore, you'll discover things and say "Why did I ever think that was hard?, I knew so little back then." Gates aren't barriers, they're there to silently suggest that you haven't explored the area you're in yet, and should maybe go do that. There is always another way, Food is everywhere, you just need to find it, Shelters are everywhere, you just need to find them, don't bash your head off something that feels impossible, find the way around. Never be afraid of trying to interract with something, you might be surprised.
This game seems super punishing when you first start out and don't understand it, and you'll still die even when you do, but the more you learn about it the more you'll fall in love with it, especially if you love exploring, because your brain is rewarded for exploring everything, and interacting with everything, and really, that's kinda the point, I think.

This game is a massive beatiful work of art. I myself have not played many platformers, but this was by far the best.
This game is challanging because it forces you to think while acting, there are some "rules " in this game that you will learn as second nature. I disagree with the idea that this game is RNG heavy, for instance many people will argue that most of the monster related deaths were unfair, however most of the times the monsters are completely avoidable. for instance when traveling between screens its easy to tell if there is somthing waiting on the other side and you can peek into the next roon with no real danger if you simply crawl into the room and then leave, if somthing chases you you can simply retreat or better juke the enemy by entering the duct when they do (the duct will light up another color if somthing is traveling through it). you just got to remember to always keep a look out for these signs. as for platforming, this game is very difficult and you need to learn your small slug cats abilities. I hate when people complain that this little guy cant jump high enough. Trust me slug cat is agile and , if played properly, can dodge danger like a ninja, but hes not a superhero that can jump triple his height.
This game is addicting it will leave you fusterated to the point of rage but it will always bring you back with its sense of exploration and wondering whats at the end (trust me the end is worth the fustratiion). Rain world is mainly broken up into sectors that must be acessed through gates that require that you have a high enough "karma" (karma is practically how many days you have survived without dieing, i.e if you survive 3 day and die once after the third day, your karma will be 2,). Each of these sectors pose there own challanges that slug cat and you must identify and figure out how to overcome (and they can be overcome!). P2P ruins what is otherwise a great game.
I have dual interfaces, one public and one private. When I start the game, it assumes I'm on a NAT (Strict NAT at that) and nothing works. I disable the internal interface and while the game things I now have NO Internet connection, it works. If I restart the game with the internal NIC disabled, the game again assumes I'm on a NAT (Strict) and nothing works even though the only IP I now have is a public IP.
The networking in this game is atrocious. There are critical game aspects that require timing that simply don't work because of P2P latency. I attack and because another peer has decided I'm already hit, my avatar will just stand there while I hammer the attack button for 2-3 seconds. I dodge or block but my avatar just refuses to do anything. There can be a good 2-3 second resolution delay in which, if you are on the wrong end of it, your avatar will simply stand still and do nothing while you impotently issue commands.
The game itself is beautiful and fun but it is easily ruined for some by the second rate networking. This is primarily an online multiplayer game and the poor choice of peer to peer networking in an effort to make the code easily console portable and save a few dollars on not having dedicated servers could well sink an otherwise brilliant effort.

The quest system works in a way in which you pick up main and side missions by speaking to people around the main hub. You can see the quests on your minimap and map marked with yellow exclamation marks. Each mission is set in a semi-randomised level which you fast-travel to via your map. They tend to be a bit simple as they will ask you to go to X and kill Y or go fetch X and find Y & Z. Rewards are usually new weapons and money which can be spent on buying upgrades and more weapons.
The game has over 70 weapons all hand crafted and animated. Every weapon feels good to use, and they look great. I am partial to melee myself as it's very satisfying to slice demons in half and see their body parts fly everywhere. There's also an upgrade system in the game. You pick up these different statues that drop from enemies or chests and they can be used to imbue your weapons with different effects like fire damage, extra critical hit chance or health point regeneration after killing an enemy. I do feel that there's a bit too many drops that give you small percentage increases though. As of writing this review they have released a patch that makes the loot suck a bit less, but I hope to see it improved upon in future updates.
Wang jokes, upgraded weapons and katanas... The story still manages to stay cheesy but yet remain serious. Just like the prequel it starts off quite lighthearted and eventually gets more and more serious as you get further into the game. This time Lo Wang has the soul of a young woman named Kamiko in his head. They are very different from one another personality-wise and don't get along to well. I found their conversations to be quite amusing to listen to. However, I do wish they had used her a bit more to convey the lore and such instead of making most of it books you have to pick up from enemy drops and then read as she felt a bit underused. There's also a skill system in place. You gain karma (xp) from doing missions and killing enemies and when you level up you gain a skill point. You can use these skill point to upgrade your skills such as having medkits heal you more or drop more often, heavy melee attacks do more damage or different elemental effects be more effective.
Most enemies in this game have got some sort of modifier to them. By modifier I mean of course that they either are on fire,  have different kind of resistances (against toxic weaponry, physical attacks etc.) or can move very fast and so on. I have mixed feelings on this. Sure it's fun to change your tactics and have to use different weapons with different elemental effects to defeat your enemy, but I do not find it enjoyable when several of the bigger baddies are
to physical attacks, making melee useless or when they teleport behind you and instagib you. This is more of an issue on the higher difficulties, but I find it disheartening that you cannot use melee on so many enemies when you have put many skill points into a melee-based build. Making an enemy completely immune to a certain type of attack is kinda stupid in my opinion. There's a variety of enemies in the game, from dog-sized rats to robotic sexbots repurposed into combat droids. It does sometimes feel lacking though, as you'll often fight many of the same type of enemy just with different modifiers. I think it would be more interesting if there were more enemy types with different attack patterns instead of 5 big rats with different elemental auras, for example.

Other than that, I am glad to say I am having fun playing this years game. I'm very interested to see what expansion sets they come out with. I would reccomend buying the vanilla version, as the extra money paid for unlocking cards won't feel justified in the long run.

I don't feel like doing a review full of gushing like I did with DOOM, so I'll just keep it simple and stupid with a pros/neutrals/cons list.
The good:
☯ the most satisfying and meaty combat out of all first person shooters ever released
☯ over 70 unique weapons to utilize, including double shotguns, katanas, spiked clubs, miniguns, Wolverine claws and rocket launchers
☯ loads of gems you can insert in weapons that allow weapons to be used differently - dual wield, sticky projectiles, renote detonation, explosive ammo etc. - and you can combine them
☯ mobility that puts even Doomguy to shame - sprinting is redundant, you can zoom around the map like friggin' Sonic
☯ no fall damage
☯♥♥♥♥♥♥jokes are everywhere
☯ huge variety of enemies
☯ pretty damn stunning visuals
☯ runs fantastically on pretty much every setup
The neutral:
~ The game features a karma system, which is basically an experience bar. Each time you level up you get a skill point you can spend on an upgrade - maximum health/karma, more ammo found, more powerful attacks and so on. Personally I have no problem with that, but some people might find it pacebreaking
~ Unlike the 2013 prequel, this game is more akin to Diablo in regards of gameplay (except being in first person perspective). There's missions, a hub you return to after completing quests, experience/money/weapon rewards, shops, and LOADS of upgrades you can apply to your character, weapons and abilities. Again, some people might find it pacebreaking and overwhelming, since the game almost literally drowns you in upgrades, and let's be frank, most of the time they're♥♥♥♥♥♥br>
~ The game features five types of elemental damage - physical, fire, ice, toxic and shock, which may be applied to your weapons and be found (as either weakness or resistance) on enemies. Some people might find that off-putting, since you have to switch weapons around a lot on higher difficulties (Insane and up)
~ Every optional mission takes place in a randomly generated area constructed from pieces of one of several presets. Again, personally I have no issue with it, but it might get samey if you happen to run into maps made of identical pieces twice in a row
~ This might feel controversial, but it would be a shame not to address it: many, many people claim that enemies in this game are too bulletspongy, and from what I've seen, it's the kind of people who use wrong elemental damage on wrong enemies, spam quick melee attack and ignore special melee powers entirely, can't aim for♥♥♥♥♥♥and skim over the game's features and then complain that it's too hard. It isn't, you just need to follow the Dark Souls Two-Step Guide.
The bad:
💩While the visuals are great, this game enjoys vomiting particles at you. This, combined with rather excessive foliage on some levels and the massive hordes of enemies you'll be fighting makes it extremely difficult to see what exactly is even going on and why 75% of your HP is suddenly gone.
💩The menus are a bit of a cluster♥♥♥♥, I'm talking Microsoft Excel levels of indecipherability. The game drowns you in upgrades, there's very little you can do to sort them (And I don't quite get how the sorting actually works), you can't pick favorites, so each time you remove a gem from a weapon you need to find it in the massive pile of crap the game has thrown at you. Technically you can tag gems as "junk" to sell them with one button press, but you get like 50+ gems per mission, nobody in the right mind will sit in menus comparing all of that stuff while you could be running around blowing♥♥♥♥♥♥up.
💩Replayability is questionable. New Game+ is pointless unless you missed an optional mission (Which, quite honestly, shouldn't happen) or choose a higher difficulty setting, and even with that it might get boring pretty quickly.
💩SW2 is rather disgustinly easy compared to the 2013 prequel unless you're playing on Insane, which is where the game becomes challenging at all - you either get a wepaon for every single element or you're ♥♥♥♥ed.
Overall rating: 🍆🍆🍆 🍆🍆🍆 🍆🍆🍆/ 10

If you're a fan of MtG, and you feel that Planes has always been lacking becasue of deck customization, then you'll likely enjoy 2015 (you'll probably want all the cards unlocked tho).  If you're new to the series, or want to only pay $10 and be competative in MP, then perhaps there are some things you should consider & understand before jumping blind into 2015.
Everyone seems to be hung up on the premium booster packs; or they don't know which versions to get...  Buy just the $10 core game? Spend $20 to get the card collection in the in-game store?  Spend the $35 on the Ultra Super Mega Version?  Do I really need premium boosters?
Here's what to consider if you're not sure which way you want to spend your money:
As of right now, there are like 14 or 15 premium booster packs.  If you pre-ordered, you'll get some free.  Honestly, it's cheapest to NOT spend the $20 on the card collections in-game, and put that money towards premium booster packs.  For like another $8 or $10, you can buy the rest of the premiums and just unlock ALL the other normal collections in the campaign; it goes pretty quick, really.  That's the cheapest route to all cards.  Just remember, as of right now, you can not get premium boosters from any gameplay.  It's micro-trans only.  If you go and buy the card collections in-game, then buy all the premium boosters to unlock all remaining cards, you're going to end up paying almost $60.
Do you need the Premium card collection?  Depends on how confident you are in your deck building prowess, and whether you plan to play a lot of Multiplayer.  If you do, you'll likely be at a disadvantage.  If not, then no, the premiums are not "needed"; they just add a nice variety of options to the decks you'll be able to assemble.
At the end of the day, if you buy the core game, and all the premium booster packs, and unlock all the other cards in campaign, you'll have all the cards avaiable in MTG:DotP for less than the price of a FatPack.  You even get custom deck boxes... if only it would've came with a sweet 20 sided D15 dice.  ;)
