It's hard for me to not recommend this game, not based on it's own merits, but on the merits of its predessesor, Quake 2. I absolutely loved Quake 2, even if it barely had a story. Granted, its "story" wasn't too much of a factor, and not a big deal was made out of the character. You were just an ordinary marine, and you soon learn why you should have called in sick that day.
Quake 4 tries to have a massively important story and really tries hard to improve on Quake 2. It tried not to hold my hand, but to cause me endless grief as I pinned against the wall trying to shoot down rockets AND deal damage to a monument to arachnophobia so I don't die. The difficulty was appreciated. Trying to nacigate to my objectives was frustrating and confusing at times.
The story was kinda forced, really, and there were moments where anyone with half a brain could have avoided death, but no, no it is absolutely necessary to stand next to a brainwashed comrade so he can more easily kill you. You are a vaguely legendary marine, and for some reason everyone expects you to do the killing.
The final boss is also a joke. The Macron is hard, which is good, but then killing the boss immediately after him may as well be a cutscene.

If you're looking for an atmnospheric, plot-twisting, cliffhanging, not-always-with-the-making-sense-ing...yeah thats a word, anyway, if you're into all that and Star Wars..this is the game.  Just as I left Peragus, the first gaming area, in a wake of explosions and blasterfire, I noticed that story-hooking sensation, like when you turn the page on that book you're reading and feel it's plot hook you and pull you in.  Best to get into this with the Sith Lords Restored Content Mod installed, the story becomes a bit less disjointed and you can appreciate the creator's intent.
Highly Recommended!!

Going from Quake III to Quake IV is like going from a car to firing yourself out of a canon.
Quake IV takes place after the events of Quake II where Bitterman decided to just bunny hop his way through the Strogg base in fifteen or so minutes. After the big gun and Makron from Quake II are destroyed, the Terran Coalition of Man begins a full scale invasion of the Strogg home world.
You play as Mathew Kane, a man so far removed from other Quake protagonists it's almost like he showed up last second and they mistook him for the actual protagonist. Mathew is part of the elite Rhino Squad which consists of nine members, each of them has their own name and voice.
I won't name them all. Because I don't care.
Quake IV takes the same route Doom 3 did and steps away from the fast and frantic action of the previous games. While Ranger, Bitterman, and Sarge were these fast super gods that ran on a strict diet of steroids, poon, and Capri sun Jammers. Kane is more human, he's much slower and chunkier than his predecessors.
This actually gives credence to my theory that in the Quake universe, people actually get stronger and faster depending on how many other people are around them. The less people, the stronger they become. And since Kane spends the entire game with fellow marines, he's nowhere near as fast or as strong as Ranger or Bitterman, who dealt with everything by themselves because they are manly men.
But this isn't to say that Quake IV is bad, it's just different. Ravensoft did a good job fleshing out the universe and lore of Quake II while still adding their own pizass to everything. The Gothic sci-fi environments and chunky meat robots have been replaced with a more industrial horror science fiction setting.
Quake IV's interpretation of the Strogg is this grotesque fusion of machine and human, a macabre rendition to their 1997 counterparts that are almost tame in comparison. The implants on even the most basic strogg soldier looks painful, like someone just kind of smushed metal limbs into a human body. The slack jawed look on the average grunt makes it look like the person that thing used to be checked out some time ago, and the larger forms all look so roided up and enraged that you can't help but be almost afraid of them.
It's sad as to how under appreciated the Strogg are in this day and age. Everything about them is just kind of terrifying. When you are inside a Strogg foundry or any building in general, you can find humans mutilated and strapped to machines, used like batteries or filtration systems, or even just a basic form of processing. The Strogg are completely anathema to humankind and Ravensoft did a good job getting that across. They're like the Borg but without the Borg's budget or those light show things from Spencer's Gifts.
I like using the word anathema because it makes me feel smart.
Like mentioned before, Q4 is much slower than previous games. But the trade off is you get some meaty feeling weapons. Each weapon feels impactful, makes loud noises, and does a decent amount of damage, making basically everything useful throughout the entire game. No weapon feels useless and you're rewarded with these big red splats whenever you hit your mark. You can also continue the time honored Quake tradition of turning your enemies into chunky soup, so that's also good.
Part ways through the game, Kane is captured and turned into a Strogg. This would be a spoiler if they didn't keep advertising it in the trailers. As a Strogg, Kane is faster, has more health and armor, is bilingual, and is also less meaty. But what remains is very meaty. I like to use the word meaty because it makes you uncomfortable. Kane can also use those gross things on the wall and drink some sweet sweet Strogg juice to regain health.
It's actually a nice change of pace and makes the game feel like a more traditional Quake game. But you have to remember that Bitterman didn't need to get Strogg'd inside, he was just a man and a half right out of the box.
But the thing that got me is that very few people seem to mind that Kane is Robocop if Robocop was RoboKane. They just kind of radio out that Kane was Stroggified and, outside of a few mean comments, no one seems to care. You'd think Marines would see you from a distance and accidentally open fire or point their guns and go “Oh, it's you, Kane.” or something.
The mean comments don't even make sense when you think about it. It's not like you went all Locutus of Borg and blasted a bunch of humans, they saved Kane before they got to install the “Kill all humans” stuff into his brain. So they're just being mean and/or jelous because you can properly bunny hop now and they cant. You'd think they'd be more sorry for you than anything.
Quake IV has multiplayer as well, but there were only 3 people playing when I checked so I didn't bother. Just play Quake III: Arena for MP.
Like the other Quake games, there are different versions of Quake IV. And by “versions” I mean “version.”
Quake IV also launched on the Xbox 360, which is the first version I played back in the day. It controlled like crap and it couldn't hold a framerate, but it was still pretty fun to play.
Quack IV also has mod support, with one of the big mods these days being False Dawn, a rather new mod for the game. It's pretty neat, you should check it out.
There is also Quake Wars, which is almost like a companion piece to Quake IV. It's a multiplayer focused battlefield style game set during the Strogg invasion of Earth. It's hard to come by, but last I checked there were still a few people playing it. I wouldn't mind Quake Wars suddenly making a comeback.
All in all, Quake IV is still a pretty solid game. It's not as fast and chaotic, or even as good as Quake or Quake II, but it's still a fun experience. Ravensoft did a good job nailing the atmosphere and fleshing out the Quake II universe, but it's just such a departure from the other games that it will probably ward off some people. But if you see it as more of a spin off to Quake II than a main sequel to the Quake games, then you'll probably have a good time.

The final battle of the Mandalorian Wars took place near the Sith planet of Malachor V. Since the rest of the Republic's fleet could make it to the battle in time, you decide to utilize the Republic's ultimate weapon: The Mass Shadow Generator, designed by the Zabrak technician Bao-Dur. The Mass Shadow Generator activates, pulling the planet, the Mandalorian armada and the Republic fleet into a gravity field. The death of the planet and all parties involved was so great that it gave you a Wound in The Force, severing and deafening your connection to The Force.
However, unlike the rest of your Jedi colleagues, you were the only one who did not fall to the Dark Side. When the war was over, you decided to return to the Jedi Council on Coruscant to face judgement. The Council, both butt furious over your insubordination and incredulous at your voluntary return unanimously chose to banhammer you from The Order. You were then exiled to wander the outer reaches of the Galaxy. Oh, and they took your lightsaber as well.
-
Fast forward five years later. The war with Darth Malak and the Sith was so costly the Republic can barely defend itself. Strange, phantom-like Sith assassins have dogged the Jedi, hunting them down in an effort to completely destroy the Jedi Order. The crime syndicate known as "The Exchange" has put out a bounty for any live Jedi. Strange, durasteel droids have integrated themselves into the Republic government.
Meanwhile, the Republic attempts to rebuild Telos IV, a planet bombarded to near destruction by the Sith Admiral Saul Karath. An unknown figure contacts Republic Admiral Carth Onasi, requesting that you be brought from the Outer Rim to act as a diplomat to Telos. Who made the request, and why, are a mystery to you, but other external forces have plans for you...

This game is one of the most moving pieces of Star Wars history.  Kreia your wanabe teacher says very true statements that you are actually lulled into trusting her judgements (that are VERY worth listening too).  You also can change the personalities of the people you travel with by just talking to them in a positive or negative fashion (reinforced by your alignment (Jedi or Sith)).
This game actually makes me feel more intelligent by Kreia's speaches and opinions.  She also reveals a great deal about backstory and possible future events at <removed due to spoilers>.
The gameplay itself is actually pretty nice.  It has a lot of combat options and things you can personalize.  Whether you want to fight with a lightsaber or not.  The armor you wear can compliment your characters abilities, and your companions aren't typical support characters.  They actually add some welcome and very real context to the game, as well as great combat efficiency.
As for the level designs they could be better, but they remain pleasing to look at.  Even with the polygons that the game had to work with (considering it was put on an older disk).
Also the companions never feel dull because they actually go and talk to each other.  Their conflicts add to the suspence.  Their personalities actually collide, and in the end every mission is a real experience with each of them.  Hell each one has specially added dialog for whenever you use them.  (keep in mind this data is still all compact in an older disk).
All in all?  Worth it.  Story is great, characters are inspired, gameplay feels good, and it leaves an impression on you.

Literally an old school combined arms FPS from the days when 'games were good'.
Think Battlefield 2142 meets Battlefront (the good ones) meets ET: Quake Wars meets EVE: online meets Freelancer?
Whatever, it's a very solid combined arms FPS that has no barriers, From an infantry soldier to a capital ship captain.
You can do it all!
Best thing is that it is NOT class based. You have 3 types of suits with different capacities and from there you just add whatever and customize them to your liking. There's lots of freedom and this customization extends down to vehicles.
The gunplay feels a bit unpolished but it can be played very tactically, utilizing the lean system and smoke grenades you can push your squad through the pretty awesome looking environments. Be it a war-torn sci-fi city to the interior of a battleship, hastily retreating to the fighter bay as the core threatens to blow the entire ship in two.
The art direction and faction design is beautiful and a lot of effort has been put in, vehicles and ships have articulating parts on them that respond to the ships movements, It's just very neat and visually pleasing.
The game has been slowly developed in free time for seven years, while it has lots of content, there is a noticeable lack of polish you would expect, it also means this is built on an older engine, UE3. It plays in DirectX 9 and there is an DirectX 11 option you can turn on with a launch line command however I advise against it for now as it is very unstable.
There are glitches, server instabilities, a poor UI and most importantly: a very small player base (probably due to it's only recent EA release)
But, they are small gripes and the enjoyment of the game trumps the flaws it has.
Don't waste your money on the new cash grab Battlefront, get this!

I think that the most important part of deciding to purchase this game hinges on your expectations and patience.  This game is not a joyful romp through magic lands of make believe.  The game's idea of a tutorial is showing you some buttons to push in the first minute, a couple of mechanics, and then throws you out into the wild.  Your little computer flower buddy will nudge you in the proper direction from time to time, but ultimately you're wandering through the hellish post apocalyptic world that has been reclaimed by beasts.
I hope you're keeping track of your karma, the amount of food so you can sleep, how much time left until it rains, if there are monsters on the other side of that tunnel, if there is a roof above you or not, etc.
And how many of those mechanics are explained?
One of them, kind of.
Rain World doesn't hold your hand and instead drops you into a sprawling open world so that you can learn how to survive as a cute little slug cat in a world where the majority of things want to eat him.  Even the environment wants to digest you.
It does, if you came into this expecting a cutesy little platformer.
On the other hand, if you enjoy free roaming puzzley platformers that makes you earn every victory, this is the game for you.  You'll get to traverse gorgeous environments and discover strange and majestic creatures in your journey through a world forgotten.  No promises on if those creatures will try to take a bite out of you or not.  And hey, you might just unravel a mystery or two in your adventure.
And boy what an adventure it is.  I put in about 20 hours or so and that is with some advice from viewers of the stream AND using a teleport ability to streamline my experience.  If you're one of those 'gotta learn all the secrets' people, you could easily clock in 100 hours in this game, I imagine.
Just to make a note, which I find rather important to point out.  The developers are actually following up on this game still, making quality of life fixes and streamlining some of the more frustrating mechanics.  From my own experience, I ♥♥♥♥♥ed about something on Twitter to the devs and in the next patch it was adjusted, so I like to think my consumer feedback directly affected the game.
(Yeah, it was probably in the works already but hey, it's quite possible that is just stellar customer service.)
If you like your game to make you earn your rewards, rather than handing you your ending and achievements on a platter for pressing right stick, you should pick up Rain World.

I've put about five hours into the main game now, plus about 4 hours into the beta. So here is a couple warnings and info before you choose to buy this game.
The game runs beautiful on my machine. 6600k (overclocked to 4Ghz), 1060 6GB and 8GB of ram. I get a solid above 70FPS on the extreme preset, it rarely dips. The only time I ever drop frames is network issues. I will say this, I've had disconnection issues when attempting to join games but in game, it's almost flawless. (EDIT: After reading some more reveiws, my connection issues are probably in the minority. The game doesn't have dedicated servers and based on a peer to peer system. Many people are experiencing problems with crashing to the menu from the network. So be warned that the network system may make your game almost unplayable)
\
The game itself is a Medieval fighter, there are 12 charcters scross the three factions. Each of these chracters has their own unique set of feats (abilities) and moveset. Though, i will say that some of the classes like my favorite "The Warden" has a much smaller move set than some of the other classes, it feels limiting to what you can do if your favorite style of fighting isn't one of the harder heroes.
If you want to buy this game with the intention of just playing the single player then I'm sorry but this isn't your game. I'm about a third through the story and it took me just over 2 and a half hours. It's short and I don't find the writing to be that great, it's more of a long tutorial to prepare yourself for the multiplayer in my opinion. But the multiplayer, is magical. It's a well put together set of modes, Dominion being my favorite. If you can get four or so friends in a party and play as a team then you will have a blast. It's the perfect game to work together as a team against your opponents. Though don't think that you lone wolfs have no place here, I myself don't have any friends to play the game with so i play with random people and I still have mass amounts of fun. No it's not as coordinated as the chat system it limited to quick commands, team chat and open chat which is fine but the game can't take the stopping and typing experience becxause it's so fast paced. In my nine hours of play, I've never been in a team where the voice chat is useful.
So lets talk meat, the fighting. How is it? It's fun. No it's not for everyone, there is alot of waiting and timing in one on one battles. But I've got to give it to Ubisoft, the controls are just good. On keyboard and mouse, it works perfectly, i never felt limited by it. The controller is definetly what it was made for though and it works smoothly and I never felt like I was forcing an awkward control scheme down my throat. Word of warning: I use keyboard and mouse and it does feel a bit twitchy compared to what I think it's best at, but i havent tested changing the sensitivety for guard mode.
The worst part of this game is the customization system, it's layed out very well. Your hero has armor that you can switch out, each piece of armor (or weapon) has different stats making you able to skill your chracter to your playstyle. Oh and you can switch actual stats to a diffent looking set if you'd like, so you can still look how you want while having the modifications on your items that you want. The reason it falls apart for me is because of the microtransactions, they're connected to the main currency of the game. You can buy armor packs with this, cusomization items that aren't unlocked through the confusing but good leveling system. The nail in the coffin is the rate of earning of just playing the game, each match gives you between 15 and about 45 currency (in my experience), while most of the things to buy are in the thousands. There are other ways to earn currency, which are the daily challenges which give you about 100 currency but in my opinion (you may think differently) these daily challenges take a little too long to complete, making people who can't play the game solidly for a couple hours out of luck.
There are alot of different systems I didn't talk about, so my advice to you is to try and rent the game or play it on one of your friend's pc's before you buy. To see for yourself if you enjoy the game, or if the way you earn currency bothers you. I find this game extremely fun, and in my opinion, if it goes on sale and you can find it for a lower price then its a must buy.  Even if it never lowers from $60, I think it's a worthwhile purchase for anyone who thinks they'll enjoy it.

You can most likely make more than 10 unique decks which is more than what you get in previous games, but the power level is lower and the decks play out more like draft decks, which some may or may not like. I liked the campaign, because all enemies use real decks which are different from each other and the story was okay. Few of the duels did have some special conditions, but the duels for the most part played like the standard duels and less like challenges which I liked, but it's just a matter of preference. The UI looks nice...
... but it's very hard to use. Navigation through the menus is slow, and it feels like it was made with only the touch interface in mind. There is no 2HG, but what's worse is that there's no other special mode neither, like Planechase or Archenemy. I'm glad I got this game for free so I can feel no guilt as I decide to probably never play it again.
It can't decide what it wants to be - a stealth game, an action game, or a shooting simulator.  And it's bad at all three.  The game attempts to encourage players to utilize stealth by giving them a rock to throw to distract Nazis so you can creep past them in the poorly designed levels that oftentimes funnel you directly into Nazi crosshairs in a decidedly un-stealthy manner.  So there might as well not be a stealth aspect.
So you can shoot your way through, right?  Well that's decidedly un-sniper-like, but that's the other option the game gives you.  Well, your pistol and thompson both only have one clip of ammunition in them, so you run out of ammo pretty much instantly.  And apparently times were so hard in Berlin that Nazi soldiers only had three bullets a piece even though they all carry MP40s, an automatic weapon that needs decidely more than a handful of bullets to function.  Which it has, when those Nazis are shooting at you.
So you try to use your sniper rifle, which has some ridiculously stupid idea of what "bullet physics" are.  The bullet drop from 100m is like five feet for some reason, when in reality it's basically neglibible.  It's almost impossible to hit anything while being shot at because your scope is flying all over the screen, which would be ok and make sense if your sniper weren't your only option to fight the enemy with.  As to set-piece shooting, they make a big deal of the "one shot, one kill" moniker, and you're supposed to fire at range and take into account bullet drop, wind speed, etc. - the things that a real sniper has to consider when shooting from extreme distance.  Except you have no tools with which to calculate any of that, and you have to just kind of guess which level of your crosshairs corresponds to the proper distance to get a kill.
The Cabela's-like X-Ray YOU SHOT A GUY GOODJOB camera is pretty nifty, but pretty useless when the game itself isn't fun.  All in all it's just frustrating, and I think I'll play Wolfenstein to get my fill of Nazi-killing now.

I'm glad I skipped Quake 4 way back when it was released. I was put off by Id's previous release of Doom 3 that left myself and a lot of others wondering wtf happened to Id and their ability to make fun games. At first I was having an enjoyable time, happy to find the gunplay that was absent from Doom 3 while still having an incredible amount of attention to details in the world building, design, and even the military atmosphere. Characters have decent dialogue and good characterization that is very realistic, although it does have a Call of Duty feeling sometimes.
However, there are segments that started to wear on me. The tank segment was more of a chore than fun. Controls are floaty (well, I guess it IS a hovertank) but not in a good way. Your weapons feel anemic in vehicles with slow firing machineguns and turrets that take several shells to knock out even some of the smaller Strogg infantry. The walker segment was just frustrating. Strafing becomes extremely slow and clumsy, and you just feel incredibly limited in mobility. It's a really slow, tactical battle when you face off against one of those giant enemy crab things that ends without much feeling of achievement. Special vehicle segments should make you want to do it again! They should feel like a theme park ride that was over too soon.
There are also some cheap deaths like getting knocked off a platform when a Strogg crab thing kicks a car at you and too bad if you didn't save you'll have to trek all the way there and find out where the little safe spot to stand is. Or how about running through a tight catwalk and having a hidden barrel around the corner shot at just as you come around, killing you instantly? You may also find yourself committing suicide with the grenade launcher a lot, a weapon that apparently has a blast radius bigger than its range. Not a good weapon for the mostly tight corridors you fight in. And a lot of the other weapons seem pointless, at least on higher difficulties. The railgun is less effective than your shotgun. Rockets do barely any damage. The lightning gun is so weak. Basically a good sized arsenal, but they all get pushed to the side for the machine gun and shotgun which are just insanely effective from the start.
Some strong points though are the atmosphere. Wandering through the Strogg facilities fills you with dread as lovecraftian horror permeates the Stroggs architecture. The segment where you yourself are transformed into a Strogg through surgical means is absolutely horrific. And that's the strength of Quake 4 is being scary and nervewracking without relying on jump scares like Doom 3 did. Wondering what greater abomination the Strogg will unleash generates enough fear.
But despite its strengths the game just feels lacking and mediocre. It came out in late 2005 and has no excuse to have such shortcomings (even in places like its menu) when big name titles like Halo set the standard way back in 2001. A game like that still holds up today while Quake 4 feels antiquated and tedious to play. You can tell Id was just on a downhill slope, trying to copy aspects from other games but never really figuiring out how to make another fun FPS. Just look at Rage. Good concepts, but often mediocre executions with some bad design decisions here and there.

Quake IV was released at the point where ID games started sliding in quality. While I personally adore Doom 3 for its immersion and focus on slow horror, I completely understand how it alienated fans. Quake IV, however, was an almost undisputed dip in quality as it felt more like Call of Quake than the masterpieces that preceded it. Even more than Doom 3. The multiplayer was still fast and frantic, but somehow less spirited. The campaign, though, echoed Quake 2 more than the original... and with graphics sharing to the same engine as Doom 3, the games could actually be mistaken for each other at times. The only difference, unfortunately, being that Quake IV has a distinctly more bland future-army style to it.
That said, it is still a cool fps, with some sweet moments that may seem bland today, but were pretty awesome at the time. To avoid spoilers, the "surgery" scene was shocking at the time, and needs to be taken into account.
Overall, in 2017 it is probably outdone by other games you can get for the 14.99 asking price. For less than 5 bucks though? Absolutely go for it. It's a decent romp that is well produced and has a good bit of gore and grit, just don't expect multiplayer or anything other than an eightish-hour corridor shooter with some decent atmosphere.

This review is about the vanilla version of the game (without mods). I was a huge fan of the first game and I also like other Obsidian games, but I was rather disappointed by this one. The first few hours of the game are pretty repetitive as you lose your ship two times and have to recover it. After that the game opens up - you can choose what to do next and your goal becomes clearer. Some of the planets you will get to see are quite interesting (Dxun, Dantooine, Korriban) others I found rather boring (Nar Shadaa, Onderon). The lowlight for me were the arena and the maze on Nar Shadaa where you hunt down Visquis. The  characters which will join you are interesting for the most part, especially HK-47 who you can reactivate by the end of the game. A wasted potential  are the two main antagonists Darth Sion and Darth Nihilus. Their design is really interesting, but you do not learn much about their motivations and also the battles against them are not really a highlight. All in all the game is not a complete waste of time, but it could have been so much more. The potential was there, but in the end the good ideas combine only to an ok game experience. A final word regarding bugs and glitches: I had no problems playing the game on my rig (Windows 7, Intel Core i7 870, Nvidia GTX460).

With DNF you get a very classic first person shooter, that first of all tries to convince with its iconic protagonist. Ironically, the  bad quality of this element of the game was one major contributor to the fact that in 2011 fans didnt get what they were hoping for. A more elaborated Duke theme  could have been a success proven key that made DNF a great timeless game. However, after playing the game for 1 hour effectively, you start to realize the ever repeating same superficial sayings.
In terms of gameplay you will find very differently worked out maps. Some of them looked like badly made community maps for CS 1.6 or some other generic shooter that were only created to  s-t-r-e-t-c-h the game . In other parts however (a hotel and a strip club) you could feel the work that was spent into it.
The big bosses were pretty ok, but i would have wished to have more impact on the fight. Certain weakspots that created different reactions by the enemey would have greatly improved the feel of the duels.
I was thinking about comparing the game with Quake, Doom, Prey or Bioshock. It has similar normal and big boss sequences.
What has made Quake a better game back in the days  is a deeper storyline and simply the fact that it was very up to date graphically. DNF lacks both.

Rain World is without a doubt an adventure that breaks the traditional mold so many games utilize.  As a result, it's one of the more unique (if not a bit rough) games I've played in a long time.  You're a slugcat that got separated from your family in a rainstorm.  Simply put, you're to eventually meet them again.  Past the short tutorial, you're dumped into the world and everything at that point is your experience.
Even though Rain World is a metrovania, thinking of it just like an average one is the mistake many players are going to make.  It's all about surviving more than traveling as you'll have to become accustomed to predators such as lizards, hazards, food locations, and all sorts of tricks that can only be picked up with time.  Getting from one hibernation area (save point) before a rain storm hits (time limit) can be a trial all on its own.
Speaking of lizards, get used to them because they're not just the “goomba” of Rain World, but each type has adapted to the area(s) they reside in.  Green lizards are the bulkiest of all and can take quite a few hits before showing signs of distress.  Purple lizards can climb poles and as a result have an easier time chasing you down.  Blue lizards can climb upon the walls in the background and can use their tongue to pull you in, which makes getting away from them far harder than the other two; and the list goes on.  They're not the only things that want a tasty meal...
Possibly for the first time ever in any metrovania title, item and enemy placement in game is randomized.  In one area, you may find a few lizards of variety threatening/fighting each other and a stone nearby that you can use to agitate them; or you could use said stone to lure them away from the next room you need to get to.  Other times, it may just be an absentminded one sitting in a corner not doing much of anything, allowing an eventful trip to the next room.  In other times, you may have several ecosystems such as bats and cicadas attempting to eat said bats while lizards are trying to chomp at said cicadas and a bird may find you appetizing in the middle of all of that.  Said randomness keeps even older areas feeling like new long after you've become accustomed to them.
Each new area goes beyond just being its theme and feels like you're really in that particular spot. Outskirts has a little bit of everything and once you've learned the ropes, you'll be better prepared for the increased challenge up ahead.  Garbage Wastes has you traversing piles and piles of garbage which change the layout of the map and make predators harder to deal with.  You also have water to contend with and newer predators that spice things up just when you were getting used to everything else.  The Wall is a mostly vertical climb to the top of an ancient building and predators in that area have adapted to wall hanging tactics; which allows them to chase you down with greater fervor.
As much as I like the ingenuity of the game, there are quirks and nitpicks I could say about Rain World.  However, they pale in comparison to the four things I'm going to list:  Map consistency, overly aggressive rooms, instadeaths, and karma.
In an average metrovania, when there's a fall that would damage you or otherwise prove fatal, then there would be some way to tell.  No such luck here.  As a matter of fact, there's quite a few rooms that have hanging berries below them in what would otherwise appear to be an area you could go down to.  In other cases, map transitions to lower areas can be dangerous if you fall slightly higher than a certain point.  The Wall is a great example of this as in one part there was a pole I could see jutting from the tip of the bottom of the screen.  Jumping from half a screen away resulted in my death.  Doing said jump again from only a quarter of the same screen transitioned to the next area proper.  In that same area, certain falls that look like your doom actually transition to screen to otherwise unknown areas.
You know how I said that everything in this game is randomly generated on the map?  Sadly its greatest strength is also one of its weaknesses.  For the most part, when everything works, it makes for a legitimately satisfying experience that most games have a hard time achieving.  On the flipside, there's cases where you may get too many enemies surrounding the path you need to take; or in an even worse case scenario, you'll enter a new room only to be greeted by a chomp to the face by a lizard.  The former can usually be worked through with your wits or proper item use while for the latter, you'll need snake-like reflexes or absurd luck to survive.  Even if you survive either encounter, that may have been all that was needed to reduce your rain meter to a lethal amount.
Hell, I've even had my progress halted by one of the deer-like creatures in Farm Arrays due to it “camping” its massive body against the door for some odd reason.  Attempting to push it away from the door resulted in nothing, and in the previous room the game didn't spawn a spear for me to use as a platform.  There was no crawlspace nearby that I could use to get out, nor could I make the jump to retrace my steps back to my older hibernation area; which also leads me to another point:
The karma system, which for each cycle rewards you a level for keeping slugcat fed with four points of food.  You lose one every time you die.  Said levels show your “progress” as a whole, as slugcat doesn't actually gain any extra skills or abilities.  It's also necessary to gain passage to newer areas.  Often though, getting to said new area(s) is a challenge in itself; which makes the whole karma system for opening doors moot.  If you can get to said karma door to begin with, you've most likely mastered said area; or you're at the very least good enough to take on your next challenge.
In closing, just like the alien and unfamiliar lands in it, Rain World is worth exploring.
Just don't get caught too many times by monsters or you'll realize how little you lose and you stop being afraid.

RiME is a simple puzzle game with a backstory that you won't understand until the end of the game. I recommend this if you're looking for an easy-going game.

Rain World is a place filled to the brim with subtle lore, mystery and adventure.
From the moment when you begin; falling and washed away from your family.
To the final moments of greatness, You explore. You befuddle your foes. And Conquer entire areas with your own two sticky front paw-pads.
Along the way you'll make new friends, both trip out and chill out by the shorelines, and even go so far as to search the very depths of your being;  all the while looking towards the moon for guidance - as the gaming world's best soundtrack to date sets a pleasant mood for the area.
If you haven't guessed already; this is a survival game first, exploration game second, and thriller game third. If you are expecting to have an easy time... you're either a dragonslayer or an outlaw - that or high on rushrooms.
That being said, here are some cryptic hints to get you on your way in Rain World;;
+Nothing ventured, nothing gained.
+Batnip will earn you more than an easy catch - if you can avoid being caught out with it aswell.
+For what does a slugcat need of wealth? Glory and friendship to those whom give freely - and scorn to the one whom crosses with spears.

Alright, so this is a new direction for the DotP series.  Has a slew of pros and cons, but the main thing is to not go in expecting the same old DotP.
Pros:
The major pro is the new deckbuilding.  In the tutorial, you'll pick two colors.  Each color has a starter package, and the two packages you pick are your starter deck.  After you clear the first chapter with this starter deck (took me about 40mins, but results may vary), you unlock full deck building and can earn booster packs from winning battles.
Each chapter in the campaign offers boosters built from a different pool.  You can check your unlock progress in the main menu. Takes a while to build up, but it's decently well done.  I'm not sure if there's a limit to decks that can be built, but they don't try to sell slots like Magic 2014.
Some nice QoL touches here and there too, like being able to customize your deck from the campaign menu (without going all the way out and back in every time you want to swap a card out) and a much cleaner battle UI. The menu UI animations can be a little slow though.
Cons:
On the cons side, the pool for deck building feels limited.  It's especially noticeable once you get into the second chapter and start taking on the AI's high synergy theme decks.  A fair amount of the cards used for these synergy builds aren't available in the card pool.  Your synergy options are pretty limited--they were clearly more focused on basic variety--and that leads to a lot more brute force/control building in deck design. Kind of a let down for high synergy builders like myself.
There's an additional smaller card pool for 'premium cards' as well, which can only be unlocked via purchase of booster packs ($2 each).  You get one prem pack free if you own Magic 2014.  Not too keen on the pay wall when the main pool is so tight already. Half of the prem cards are game specific fodder cards (like the rings in a previous DotP), but there are a handful of nice synergy options in there for particular builds. Equipment guys will pine for Stoneforge mystic, aura gnarlid is a sore spot for Aura decks, etc.  $2 would buy a couple expansion decks in previous DotP games, now it'll buy 10 cards you may or may not even need/want.  Not a great move if they plan on making these cards inviable again in a year--most people will just get by without and hold it against them.
Some people are miffed by the lack of certain multiplayer modes, like 2HG.  Should be expected with deck building though, it'd be rough to incorporate the unified deck rules without forcing prebuilt decks.  Typical case of making one group happy resulting in upsetting another group. FFA is the only multiplayer option.
_ _
Overall, the fun factor outweighs the cons for me.    It's magic, it has deck building, and there's enough there to make a variety of viable (if not particularly amazing) decks.  It's by no means perfect, and hopefully it's just a stepping stone for Magic 2016. If they drop some affordable expansions to really buff the card pool, the value will greatly increase.
I like it enough to recommend it to people who are into Magic. The asking price isn't too high, and there's some room to grow. If any of the above doesn't sound appealing though, then caveat emptor.

Today I played this game with my friend.  I hadn't played it since April of 2015, and hoped maybe the game had improved since then.  The developers had been posting updates occasionally, so I thought I was justified in being hopeful.  We started with a simple task-  to get some iron so we could build basic things since everything useful requires nails.  After spending half the day prospecting which involves right-clicking the ground and waiting for a progress bar, then moving and doing it again and again until you can pai- I mean exitedly hone in on an iron spot.  The game doesn't tell you that the distance to the iron will be measured vertically as well.
The game doesn't tell you a lot of things that are necessary to know to do anything.  The game has available tutorials online which may or may not be relevant anymore.  The tutorial, for instance, says you can fuel a campfire with boards, which isn't possible anymore.  Oh, fueling a campfire is the funnest thing.  It takes more sticks than will fit into the fuel inventory to finish cooking a fish even on the quickest setting.  So you have to keep adding sticks from your inventory(better have at least 70 to cook a single fish).  Billets work too, but it's so much more fun to make it more frustrating needlessly.  That's what this game is all about, right?
So after about an hour we think we honed in on our iron and started a tunnel.  Moving soil out and dumping it on the ground is the most fun I've had in a game ever.  If by fun I meant horrible, slow torture.  We finally found iron after spending the entire morning and most of the afternoon.  We then looked up how to build a furnace to smelt iron.  We gathered clay and water just the way it said.  This was the easiest thing we did.  I was surprised just how easy it was to build a furnace.  I thought the game had gone soft on us...
Oh, just kidding guys!  The furnace needs a special skill and tools to use it.  How do you unlock this skill?  I don't know.  I may never know.  I murdered my friend with a shovel and then drowned myself in the lake rather than play this game anymore.  My friend was incredibly grateful and thanked me for the merciful killing.  I wish this game never was.
*In short, this is the bone cancer of survival sandbox games. *

Magic 2015 is hard to reccomend.  On one hand, if you're a fan of magic, you'll enjoy the single player experience...somewhat.  This incarnation has some pretty bad AI that won't attack you when they clearly have the upperhand and the mana usage on your part is spotty at best when selecting spells.  The  AI will legitamately use all the mana from one color to cast a spell when you still have other cards of that color in your hand.  You need to hit control to change this but it shouldn't be that way, the AI should be smart about it.  There have been countless times when I raged at my screen when I forgot to hold control.
The graphics and all that are fine.  THis time around there are very nice cut scenes and some kind of fog effect on each screen.  Its REALLY annoying and slow to navigate.  If you want to exit the game, you have to go back through 3 seperate screens, all with fog fadeaway's that take forever.
I own every DOTP Magic game except 2014 so I dont know what MP modes if any, are missing from that one.  But in 2015 many people are annoyed that two headed giant was removed.  I personally don't care.  I play this for the SP mode.  It seems like the devs spent more time fleshing out the SP expeirence and didn't have time to add all the mp modes.  These Magic games are coming out like new cars.  1 every year and always 6 months prior to the new year they're listed for.
Lastly I'd like to talk about the microtransactions.  You don't need to buy cards although its available right away.  I wouldn't waste your money to buy all the cards right away.  It doesn't take long to unlock most of them.  Play the game you paid for and grind the cards out yourself.  It's actually not that tedious or boring.  My major complaint is there's no tracking system for each level you complete telling you if you've already unlocked a booster from that level or not.  Normally you have to complete each level in order but when you arrive at a new plane, there is an option to explore it or move on to the first boss.  The explore option unlocks a booster but there's no way of telling if you've already done that level when coming back. I personally cant recall what I ate yesterday, let alone if i unlocked a booster pack from a video game.  But now, you can make whatever deck you want and this was badly needed in every other iteration of MTG.  This is without a doubt the best SP expeirence for Magic besides playing Magic Online and buying digitcal cards with real money.
For 10 bucks this game is worth a buy I"d say if you're a Magic fan.  If you're just a card game fan, play Hearthstone.  It's free to play.  So it's really hard to suggest this as a buy or not.  Alot of reviewers on here are raging that the MP mode was gutted.  But I don't care about it.  So buy it if you just care about the SP experience.

Magic 2015 is one of the games that I've been looking forward to. I've noticed that many people would not recommend this game on steam due to the "pay 2 win" accusations. The truth of the matter is that, if you like to play Magic and don't want to pay a lot for the cards, then this is the game for you. At first the game is really hard and it does feel like a pay 2 win game. But, after playing more and more, I've made my very own deck, because that's a new feature in 2015, and I feel like I'm having a lot of fun.
Pros:
*Customizable decks (build your own)
*Feels and plays like the card game
*Makes you "grind" like an RPG to get better cards
*Good viusals and is great for new players to learn the game
Cons:
*Resolution issues
*Buggy in places here and there
*Rather hard even in the tutorial
*You start with one pre-built deck that you can't review
So I'd say that this game is made for new to veteran players. It's fun and doesn't cost a lot to play. People are complaining that the game is "too hard" or "pay 2 win" but, in reality, you just need to play the game and you can change the difficulty of the game in the options menu.
Another issue people are complaining about is that the Lands get tapped for you when you are playing a Spell. Let's say a card costs one green and then any other and you have two green Lands and a red. In your hand you also have an Enchantment that costs one green as well. The computer, most of the time, will use the two green Lands to play the first card leaving you with the red Land left over causing you to not be able to use the Equipment Spell that turn. To fix this problem, just hit the CTRL key on the keyboard. It will go through a cycle of combos of Lands that you see fit to the situation.
Overall, I believe that Magic 2015 is NOT a bad game at all. They may have removed and changed things here and there, but it's still a good game. I'd give Magic 2015 a 7/10 score. This is because of the lack of the first deck's information given to you and how hard the tutorial is.

I cannot help but adore this game. Ever since that epic cinematic slow-motion teaser trailer came out, with it's haunting classical music theme, culminating in a pretty "What the ...?" cliffhanger making you wonder "who?, why?, is that her?", I was in love with this game.
It turned out to be one of the quintessential cornerstones in the franchise's reign, bridging the gap from old-school graphics to the now more dated beginnings of 'Next Gen' graphics, this game just blossomed with fantastic setpieces, creative puzzles, envigorating score, and epic story that even to this day I dream of playing again and again. I can look past the now age-dusted graphics to see one of Croft's finest games of the old-style. The new games are fantastic in very different ways. Their gritty realism and nearly movie-worthy cinematics bode well for a knuckle clenching adventure, but Underworld was a final bow with a standing ovation to a time when the games felt a bit more like a game.
I've nominated it for the 2016 Steam Awards 'Test of time' award because it is a game that has stuck with me for almost a decade as one that I would brag about to others as being a game that i've played more than once and still have aspirations and daydreams about playing again.
There were other good contenders for this same award, such as Mirrors Edge, for its breaking of the mould and stunning design esthetic; Deus Ex: Human Revolution also for its design detail and depth of ways to approach each playthrough; to lesser known gems like Robot Roller Derby Disco Dodgeball, that just brings you back to elementary highschool Dodgeball, but the satisfaction of making the impossible hits from across a obstacle-riddled arena; and the more popular Warframe, who's devoted development teams continued involvement in the evolution of the (truly)Free-to-Play mod-heavy and extremely co-op friendly environment makes the game ultra satisfying to sink hours upon hours of your life into (unfortunately, that very overwhelming aspect of that game's continued expansion and risk of keeping me from growing and exploring other games makes the love of that game a bitter-sweet pill to swallow, and why I found it hard, even after sinking litterally the most hours i've ever played a single game (now over 200 hours), to give the Test of Time award to. Because at some point, i can see myself years from now, playing through another few hours to finish another round of Underworld, whearas Warframe, and all it's changes will every single time become such a fight to catch up and learn all the new features and ways to play.)

RiME is an adventure game which carries on the tradition of popular contemplative adventure titles, such as "Journey" or "Abzu", while succesfully pursuing its own distinct identity.
You are tasked with exploring and solving puzzles inside a dreamy set of landscapes in order to unfold the real reason behind your journey; the contemplation of the incredible level design is of course an integral part of the experience but RiME, unlike the games mentioned before, offers a very satisfying and layered exploration gameplay which at times resembles the popular "Legend Of Zelda" saga.
The worlds you are going to visit aren't simply vast corridors to traverse, but intricate sets of structurew filled with collectables, secret passages, hidden treasures and very engaging puzzles.
Just like the mentioned "Zelda" saga RiME offers some very pleasent puzzles which won't proove to be too hard to solve, but most of them definitely showcase some very intelligent designs, specially when it comes to the handling of light sources.
I'm not saying more on that simply to avoid giving spoilers.
Since the very beginning of the game it's clear that most of the areas are very vast and intricate, and sometimes you are even treated with some breathless views of the landscape you just traversed; it feels like exploring "small" worlds, rather than separate maps, and the level design is alkways top notch.
Of course the second biggest appeal of the game are the "dreamlike" qualities of the experience; the worlds you are going to traverse whisper you of ancient worlds, mind abstractions and physical manifestations of fears, ranging from ancient ruins caressed by the sun, to shady hallways roamed by dark spirits, and while you'll be busy taking in all of this, a superbly melancholic soundtrack will guide you to the end of the adventure.
It can't be denied that RiME is a game that is made with and speaks to the heart but, while still recommended, i have to describe its evident shotrcomings.
The game is simply a bit rough on the technical side; the graphics themselves are delightfull, but the game simply doesn't seem to run well, not even if you have a decent PC or try to be humble with the antialiasing.
A recent patch made things better and there's no Denuvop working in the background anymore, but unless you lower all the settings you have to be prepared for some stuttering here and there.
Also some of the game aspects, like the climbing mechanics (not used that much, fortunately) aren't nearly as smooth as in "Uncharted" or "Tomb Raider", leading to a couple of frustrating moments, when the character doesn't respond as intended.
If you don't mind a couple of rough spots i still highly recommend playing RiME, specially because it shows that you don't always need to sacrifice gameplay to create an engaging dreamlike experience.

What makes this scary?

There are currently three races to choose from, the empire/town emulation is fazed out quite quickly as you discover a drawn out grind fest to level a single army and any heroes you earn or buy. You can earn heroes and elite units buy generating gold and buying premium crowns or simply buying them with money, you will end up with a single army with a hero or two and several camps generating gold. The PvP will only include a hero setting fires to kill your non elite units and a hero that can solo any regular elite units, you will only have the option to counter a certain hero or just ending up co oping PvE sieges to gain crowns faster.
I recommend simply clearing your home town map of quests and enemies then upgrading your resource gathering tools and start trading off extra resources you do not end up using on 2nd/3rd tier units. You want any upgrades that increase your gold income and you want to travel to neighboring towns and find which resource they pay for the most and setting up a camp nearby with that said resource. After you have three maxed camps set up generating resources set up another of all storage traveling units to trade and a single army of 25 2nd/3rd tier tanks, 25 2nd/3rd tier ranged DPS and either 9 town workers to gather resources off dead bodies or 5 of them and 4 storage traveling units. The last slot will be for either your starting hero or a crown bought one, leave your army out of your hometown so no one will attack it but if they do make sure to either have a single hero there or walls with long ranged dps mounts. Gold is key.
Support is weak as they run with a small team so wiki and check forums for any issues or wait for the newest Empire Expansion to come out.

So many games try to emulate
's success, but none of them manage to do what this game did right. Its legacy is well-deserved.
From the get-go,
establishes presence. The game's dark asthetic, sound design, and setpieces inspire paranoia in your heart from the very beginning. Its atmosphere plants horror in your brain without resorting to Dollar Store jumpscares or oversaturating you with gore. Sometimes the game is subtle with its horror, but when it isn't, it makes sure that you never forget each chase as monsters are right in your face.
Truth to be told, the monsters aren't the most grotesque thing you'll see in a video game. In fact, you've easily slain scarier monsters in action games that excited you more than they scared you.
does such a great job crafting and framing its world in a Lovecraftian manner that you can't help but fear
.
The gameplay itself is solid and does what it needs to do. There's some inventory and resource management as well as the lightining system. The game accesses your fear of the dark and forces you to use your lantern and tinderboxes wisely. As far as the puzzle-solving goes, it's good and accessible. You won't have to Google astrophysics to advance the plot, but you'll always feel satisfied getting yourself out of a rut.
If you have the guts, give this a shot. It's also fun to play with a group of people who know of the game's reputation, but are too afraid to tackle it alone.

It is profoundly frustrating to carefully navigate around random enemy placements when you'd rather spend that time searching for the next save point. The going only gets easier when the player learns to bait, juke, stealth past or fight enemies, not only effectively, but in a timely fashion.
Being motivated enough to tackle the challenges that each new area brings must come from one's own desire to explore and unlock the secrets of a game that heavily favors its own stylistic integrity and obscurity over clarity and streamlined play. It makes no up front promises about its narrative and the slow pacing lets the story fall deep into the background behind the gameplay where it is almost forgotten. Sparse fragments of lore explaining the world are further locked behind a yet higher level of tedium and they perpetuate an old, troubling trend of telling a player about interesting things instead of showing them.
The visuals in Rain World range from ornate, beautiful, and awe inspiring to desolate, bleak and depressing, but it is everywhere inhospitable and unrelatable. Between mountains of trash, intricate machinery and stone statues there isn't a single item that looks like the remains of a personal possession or place that appears to have been lived in.
I've seen people make some solid comparisons to other games, but if I had to compare this game to anything, it would be the film 2001: A Space Odyssey for reasons that involve too many spoilers and layers of explanation to do here.
It is hard to recommend Rain World (unless you enjoy soul crushing loneliness and despair), but if you like tough games, have a wealth of patience and are willing to step outside your comfort zone to experience something unique and experimental, then you might have the mindset needed to enjoy it. I have nothing but praise for what this game tries to do in its story, style and mechanics. The physics based movement and creature interactions alone are reason enough to check it out.
I feel that a lack of QA testing is one of the major things holding this game back. With difficulty adjustments and bug patches, I think it could be accessible to a wider audience, but as of the time that I'm writing this, it is not an easy recommendation.

I didn't expect a good game. I expected a Duke Nukem game. I didn't get either.
I've always been a Duke Nukem 3D fan because it was my first game I've ever played. I've played countless hours of DN3D through the years and was finally hyped for DNF. I've preordered DNF and even thought about getting myself the Balls Of Steel Edition. I've counted every day, hour and minute for its release. When it was finally released, nothing else in the world did matter.
I finished the game in just ONE sitting, in the hardest setting. Got 60% of the achievements in one swoop. I wasn't even rushing, I was taking my time to enjoy the game. I was dazed and confused. What went wrong?
Well, I got it down what went wrong AS A DUKE NUKEM GAME:
- The game offers no challenge whatsoever. Everything feels easy.
- I could only use two guns per time. TWO guns. Screw you, you're only holding 2 guns at a time.
- The game is linear. No keycards, no switches, nothing. Just straight forward.
- No puzzles. I only got like one or two of these and they weren't memorable. You won't be spending your time with them.
- The level design is just awful. As I said, the game is a corridor, so don't expect those rooms and layers you're used to on a normal Duke Nukem game.
- The soundtrack didn't seem fitting. I miss that bassy MIDI songs.
- Health recovery like CoD or Halo games killed 50% of the fun. You won't be begging for medikits, you just get behind a cover and wait.
- Gun impact felt bland. Gunplay was very dull.
- Shooting sections feel cheap. They lock the room and throw enemies at you. That's pretty much it.
And what went right:
+ I like the new guns.
+ Multiplayer was a fun mode but it was condemned since day one.
+ It's Duke Nukem. He's that guy full of one liners and wrong jokes.
But that's about it. Duke Nukem Forever feels and plays like a unfinished and unpolished game. It feels like a beta through the whole game. Get it for REALLY CHEAP if you're a hardcore fan, if not then just don't.
Play LoK instead.

9.5/10 A Spiritual Experience & The Hardest Platformer I've Ever Played
Introduction:
Don't let Rain World's cute, peaceful, and even dreamy science-fantasy exterior fool you; this game demands the highest level of skill, patience, and problem solving ability around every corner.  Rain and cats are the two things my fiancée and I find most relaxing in this world, so I bought it for her thinking it could be something atmospheric we could calm down to in the evenings.  I was so painfully wrong.  This game put me in a constant state of fight-or-flight mode to the point where when my friends asked me why I seemed so stressed, all I could think to answer was "Rain World".  I loved it.  You'll have to trust me when I say I'm no thrill seeker, and stress is the last thing I look for in a game, and yet Rain World is easily my favorite game from this decade and one of my favorites of all time.  Let me try and break down why.
In Rain World you are at meercat level in the food chain: one above grub.  Everything, and I mean EVERYTHING, wants to eat you.  More than that, the world itself from the ground up is designed biologically to be able kill you quickly and effectively.  Everything one-shots you and you have no real effective ways of fighting back.  I dove into this starry-eyed after just playing through Shovel Knight, expecting that there would be enemies but also that I'd be able to combat them as easily as they could combat me, or even better.  After all, I'm the protagonist!  One does not get that luxury as a slugcat.
The first frightening realization is that spears do basically nothing, at least not until you get very very good with them, and that their primary use is (I kid you not) to create platforms in walls to more easily escape danger.  Some things can be killed, but they usually take many spears to do so, and most of the time spears will just briefly stun your enemies... very briefly...  This is because of a key dynamic that players must get used to very quickly and that is as a slugcat you are prey.  This is a post-apocalyptic ecosystem and it is harsh and unforgiving to those who are at the bottom.  The only way to survive is to understand your position, then seek to deny it.
Gameplay Breakdown & Guide:
Rain World is a metrovania style platformer built primarily on survival and exploration.  Slugcat must travel to new, unfamiliar, and increasingly dangerous lands in a quest to find his family, whom he got separated from in the opening cutscene.  Getting to different areas means finding and passing through mechanical gates on this primarily machine-based planet.  However, gates will not open for slugcat unless his "karma" is at a certain level.  Karma goes up whenever you successfully spend a day eating enough food, not getting eaten yourself, and hibernating within a water-tight sanctuary before the bone-crushing rains fall each night.  Karma goes down whenever you die.  Not only that, but the gates themselves rarely have sanctuaries near them, so wandering all the way out to one when you don't have enough karma usually means death, and with it less karma.  This simple system I feel like is what turns people off to the game most of the time, but I thought it was beautiful and the primary reason I kept returning to Rain World.
See, viewing the different areas as "levels" is probably the fastest way to get discouraged with this game.  Expecting that with enough skill one can sprint through every area in one go is going to make for a slow, painful, and disappointing playthough.  You must instead find value in taking small steps, and realize that even with every seemingly random death from sneaky and surprising predators, you are still making progress.  First off, karma never goes below a certain threshold, so whenever I find myself at the lowest level I enter the first of three modes of gameplay that I've constructed: scout mode.  The game's difficulty comes from an almost borne-souls system at times where sometimes the only way to know how to get past something is to have died to it once already.  This is why scout mode is so essential, so that one can learn the layout of an area without fear of consequence.  Use low karma as an opportunity to fill out your map and learn where predators live and how they hunt, rather than fruitlessly trying to raise it.
The second mode is forager mode.  Again, this is not something that's literally in the game, but rather a method of playing that I've constructed.  Once you've thoroughly scouted and feel like you know where the safest and most food plentiful spots in an area are, it's time to build up karma.  Food and predators move slightly from day to day and can take several days to respawn, and will actively hunt and flee from you and each other offscreen, so even if you hibernate successfully one night successive nights can prove difficult, but this is why you scout.  Once your karma is suitably high, it's time to enter the final mode, the marathon runner, and make a mad dash with all your karma to the nearest gate.
All that now said, let me summarize and defend.  Each area of the game CANNOT be mastered on the first run through.  The game is about testing, poking, prodding, learning, surviving, and ultimately preparing before inevitably continuing and exploring.  Only after practically memorizing an area can one surpass it, which at first glance seems like grinding and relying on good rng, but I've come to see the gates and karma as methods of actually mitigating rng's involvement in a player's success.  It's not enough to just by chance reach the end of an area to move on.  The game is asking you to prove that if asked to do so you could reliably and confidently reach the end of that area again and again and again.  Only then, only after literal mastery of an area, are you allowed to move on, and to me that's beautiful.  Rain World isn't just the hardest platformer I've ever witnessed; it's trained me to be better at it in ways that no other video game has.
The Conclusion:
There was a distinct moment in my playthrough where I remember confidently switching gears from flight to fight; where survival itself was no longer enough and I had to bend this world to my will in order to move on.  In time I realized that my slugcat had become even more monstrous that the many monsters he had feared for so long, and towards the end of my playthrough I realized that things could have gone differently.
Rain World only has one ending, and that never changes.  I won't spoil the ending, but I will say that approaching it felt like approaching St. Peter and the pearly gates.  The build up to the end of Rain World felt like the buildup of unimaginable weight upon my shoulders.  I held my breath throughout the entire final experience, but when that final scene ended all that weight was lifted.  As my tears flowed it felt like my sins were being washed away.
What you do along your journey doesn't change what the ending is, but it changes its meaning.  Rain World pushes you in such a way that you're forced to decide on whether or not in a harsh an unforgiving environment if you too will become harsh and unforgiving in order to reach your goals.  The journey becomes not about what ending you're going to earn, and instead about if along your journey you were a benefit to the lives you touched or a curse.  The weight of the ending comes from remembering why you set out on the journey in the first place.  Rain World teaches the value of others, the pain of isolation, the importance of finding a family, and the interconnectedness of all souls, passed or living.
Rain World doesn't get a perfect score from me unfortunately due to glitches, lag, and clunky controls that are to be expected in such a massive indie game.  However, v1.01 fixes a lot of those issues and lessens artificial difficulty.  I hope this game continues to be polished, but its challenge doesn't get mitigated so far as to lose its unique charm.

In the first 3 or so hours the game might feel very punishing, you'll need to learn the controls - some of which the tutorial doesn't explain at all (you can turn around in tunnels, pressing down and "pick up" drops what you are holding quietly at your feet, double tapping "pick up" swaps which hand an item is in and you throw what's in your slugcat's right hand first). You will also learn how enemies behave and how different items (plants, gems, rocks/spears and many more) effect them. Lastly you will find that you require karma to pass to the next zone (again this isn't explained) and to get karma you need to hibernate without dying. Don't stress out about karma, enjoy the zone you're in and naturally try to progress through zones when you feel ready.
The game is quite slow paced but with bursts of action. When you first enter an area, you'll probably try to slowly map the area out and retreat before you die until you have a good understanding of the area, which allows you to move much more quickly. This isn't as important with the new update which lets you remember the map after you die.
Much like games such as dark souls, death is not a big deal. It can be frustrating at times if you can't find the next hibernation spot or if you need to pass a karma gate as death will set you back one karma, however death can be a chance to check another path or instantly head back with a new plan on how to defeat the challenge ahead.
I have very rarely found the game unfair as there is pretty much always an item you can find or a tactic to use which will avoid situations which feel unfair. Things such as dying to a lizard as soon as you exit a pipe can generally be avoided by not leaving the pipe before you see there isn't a lizard, and quickly going backwards if there is.
The parts I love about this game are the art/music, the creature AI and the level design. Every area is so interesting that I never felt bored. The creatures all interact with you and other creatures in different ways, and react to how you behave. If you attack a creature which isn't trying to kill you, it will remember and be more aggressive in future, and likewise if you help an aggressive creature hunt it might become your friend.
To conclude, I love the exploration and interaction in this game. It's thrilling to explore, but expect to die a lot and it can be frustrating at times - although this can often be solved by exploring another path which will often lead to more items or another way around.

I was very excited for this game, as the previous Shadow Warrior game (the 2013 reboot) was easily my personal GOTY when it released. The change from a linear shooter with pre-made levels to a procedurally-generated shoot-and-loot-em-up made me skeptical. Being a fan of Borderlands, I knew it was a formula that worked but I wasn't sure how well it'd translate into Shadow Warrior. It didn't.
In games like Diablo or Borderlands, gear tends to have trade-offs to make them somewhat "equal" (outside of level differences). In those cases, whichever the player decides to use is entirely subjective. In Shadow Warrior, that's not the case: you'll find a shotgun that's objectively better than your other shotguns. And eventually you'll find the best shotgun. It's not the best because it suits your playstyle more, it's just the best because it deals the most damage. And that's all the depth there is to the loot system: what deals the most damage is what you use.
The element system feels tacked on, and like an annoying way just to get players to change their weapons. Using Borderlands as an example again, I feel that did elemental damage better. The use of elements is entirely in their usefulness in combat - you swap to them because they're useful. In Shadow Warrior, you swap away from them because they're useless. And it's very clear that the game just looks at the element of whatever gun you were just using and gives every enemy in the next area resistance to that element.
The final nail in the coffin of the loot system was the gem system. Never have I ever experienced such a tedious upgrade system in a video game before. I mean holy♥♥♥♥♥♥this was the worst. There are so many ways they could have made this better, like just general ease of access stuff like small icons to know what the gems affected when sorting through them. Swapping them out with new gems became a slog that I absolutely dreaded before I was even 25% of the way through the game. While there are a few of these that are actually cool, the novelty wears off quickly.
The level design of the first game was replaced with procedurally generated levels in the sequel. I've never been a huge fan of procedurally generated game worlds, but for the most part the game did them fairly well. I did encounter a few issues where I could see outside of the map, faced many invisible walls that were in places they shouldn't be, experienced dozens of floating rocks and platforms, and even found entire structures without any sort of collision. Just in general it wasn't bad though - but I really would have preferred levels that were actually created by level designers.
The writing and story were pretty good. Nothing ground-breaking, but still pretty good and it was a solid story to follow the first game. It had a lot more♥♥♥♥♥♥jokes, of course, as that seemed to be their entire marketing for the game. But some of those♥♥♥♥♥♥jokes were genuinely clever, and most of the non♥♥♥♥♥♥jokes were pretty clever as well. There were a lot of collectible journals that could be found, which gave backstory on the world and characters (and by "characters" I mean mainly Smith and Smith alone, he has like 100 journals dedicated to him and his past). I felt the handling of major characters from the previous game was very rough - specifically the Kyokagami Twins and Zilla. Hoji definitely deserved more recognition for his significance in the first game, but the closest you get is a couple of references and a sword you'll likely replace because its DPS isn't high enough.
I don't feel like Shadow Warrior 2 is a bad game, it's just definitely not a good one - and moreso not a good Shadow Warrior game. The combat, writing, and world shine - everything else not so much. I don't regret my purchase but unlike the first I can't recommend it.

The game description for Life is Feudal: Your Own refers to itself as a "realistic medieval multiplayer sandbox". Sadly what has been delivered so far is a grind intensive RNG experience in frustration. While I have quite a few criticisms about this early acces game, in this review I will cover my initial thoughts, focus on my attempt at making a torch, and present my conclusion for the game in its current form.
The player starts off with a small amount of food and some clothes resembling a cloth sack. From there it is up to you to start living your life any way you want. I was initially surprised by the depth of options presented in the tool tips. I could prospect the ground for ore, strip the bark from a tree, collect sticks, search for edible food on the ground, and much more. I could already picture the village I would build in my mind, bustling with life and promise. How wrong I was.
Most actions in Life is Feudal are painfully slow or based on random chance. Each time you search the ground for food the action takes a significant period of time and often turns out no results. If you don’t find food you don’t skill up. If you do find food you gain a skill up, yet seemingly don’t increase your chances of being successful in future searches. My friend and I tried with default settings and with skill gains set to high with the only benefit being additional skills unlocking faster. The only things in the game that are close to realistic are extremely frustrating. Digging a tunnel  or terraforming takes a very long time and requires you to go drop all your dirt in a different location after every 5 or so digging actions.
One of the most pointless grinds I have experienced is trying to create a torch. Torches are often one of the first items crafted in a sandbox game and usually one of the most simple. This is not the case in LiF:YO even though only two materials are required. The first material, a stick, is easily gathered from a tree. The second, naptha, is synthesised from herbs. The process is as follows:
- Create a sickle,
- Search for herbs
- Gather the herbs
- Discover their properties by combining random herbs
- Gather more of the herbs that have the correct properties
- Create the naptha
While this initially doesn’t sound too difficult it is important to note that all the herbs look the same. You are given a random herb each time you gather so you cannot focus on collecting a certain type. Each herb was taking around 10 seconds to pick up and there are also a lot of different herb types which makes the odds of geting a specific one a lot worse. Due to poor inventory management/UI it takes a long time to combine herbs to discover what properties they have. After devoting more than half an hour to nothing but gathering and combining herbs I had not found the correct ones to make torches. In comparison It was far easier to build a house.
To conclude, my biggest problem with LiF:YO is that the developers seem to equate realism with random chance. If the game were more realistic a player would be able to identify herbs by sight before gathering them. Players would be able to locate berries and mushrooms visually instead of having to click on a tile hoping for the RNG gods to award them something to eat. While the idea of the game has merit and the future of the game does not look entirely grim it is my hope that the developers shift a focus more towards something that is more user friendly and gives rewards based on work and skill rather than random chance.
