QUAKE is a series with as much of an identity crisis as well as raising the bar of id Software’s capabilities of creating landmark titles for each game. From the shift of enemies and tone from Shub-Niggurath to alien Borg race of the Strogg in the first two games; from the changing focus of single-player campaigns to various multiplayer-focused FPSs of Quake 3, Quake Wars, and Quake Champions; all these games have made deviations as sequels, and Quake 4 is no different by allowing Raven Software to take up the helm of creating a game of their own.
Like with Prey (2006), Q4 would improve upon the flaws of DOOM3 by utilizing its engine’s capabilities to create a more traditional old-school FPS experience with unique qualities of its own, which makes it feel the Obsidian equivalent to id Software’s success. In spite of these improvements, Q4 is a polarizing game because it doesn’t stick closely to the rocket-jumping ways of old and rather seeks to improve upon the merits of D3 to create an atmospheric experience. If you enjoy the single-player experiences of id Software as well as D3, however, it is imperative you should experience Q4 to see how the small adjustments made to the overall experience goes a long way to make a greater FPS.
Of all the greatest deviations from its past games, Quake 4 heralded the idea of adding modular changes to weapons in old-school FPSs that added additional functionality. The most ironic of which is the flashlight added to the machine-gun after the complaints of DOOM 3. While RPG-FPS hybrids like Deus Ex and System Shock added modable features to weapons via stat bonuses and upgrades, Q4 chooses instead to add more functionality to every gun over time from simple ammo boosts to additional firing-modes and more. Its best purpose to the game is to keep every weapon relevant over the course of the entire game while also adding new weapons on top. This is an idea future games like DOOM (2016) would later capitalize on with more player agency and progression systems to add more features in the gunplay.
As a whole, the gameplay of Q4 is a much more competent FPS game with various enemy types, most of which are different from Quake 2, that blends the horror elements from D3 with the action of classic Quake. Whereas D3 felt restrictive with the amount of enemies it would spawn, encounters in Q4 feel more lively with the diverse enemy cast as well as the constant threats that come in as cleverly disguised gauntlets. Level-design, while perhaps the only greatest misstep it makes in feeling too linear, still remains engaging by having various means of exploration and ambushes to keep players on their triggers. Sound design, lighting and the atmosphere are still highly polished to make the player panic at the slightest sound-cue down the hallway. Overall, if D3 was a tech-demo to showcase the engine’s capabilities, Q4 feels like the refinement of this engine in terms of making a more interesting game.
Other less impressive, though technically interesting, features added to the experience was the vehicular combat sections that had varied the experience with a tank or mech-walker. In execution, these sections add something beyond gameplay variety to the sense of world-building from the levels’ enormous sizes and scenes of destruction. These mechanics were perhaps added in to proceed Quake Wars as neither the multiplayer nor the single-player capitalize on utilizing vehicles whether for competition or allowing the player to choose between various levels to choose from with the additional mobility. It’s rather a shame the game hadn’t made more use of these features as mods like False Dawn for Quake 4 showcases how truly better of a game Q4 would be if it allowed more agency for the player.
Probably the biggest complaint fans have with Quake 4, aside from players demanding for more faster mobility that doesn’t work in these levels without making them into pinballs, is the game’s many scripted moments that borders on feeling like a COD game.
This aspect is perhaps true for the initial third of the game before the infamous, though visually amazing and immersive, Stroggification scene. What these players don’t realize is once they are separated from their squad is where Q4 truly shines by having mesmerizingly alien, colorful and haunting environments in dimly lit corridors that have personality in every level. It doesn’t help in this game’s case that a majority of the time the game allows the player to get free health and armor supplies via squad-mates when these types are present; however, they can be killed if the player is not mindful about them, so they don’t break the game’s difficulty, they make it feel like a nanny is always there watching you when they’re present.
Even on the hardest difficulty, which does present a fair challenge in spite of these issues, Q4 allows these squad mates to sap away the enjoyment D3 created by letting the player become immersed when alone. Whether this was done to emphasize the storytelling or give the player a sense of direction, which had already radio communication to address both issues, the amount of scripted set-pieces as well as squad mates present throughout the game is something that does take away from the experience.  This is the only complaint I do agree with fans is a problem; however, it’s when the game lets you off on your own and/or kills your allies is when it really begins to shine to the days of old.
After the success of Quake 4, the prominent designers and heads of Raven Software continued to put out great games like Marvel: Ultimate Alliance and Singularity, yet following these games the people of Raven Software left to form Human Head Studios where they would create another cult-hit on the same engine, PREY (2006). The remnants of this once great legacy behind Raven Software were left to become Call of Duty’s osmosis into other studios to refine and polish the multiplayer components of other games, probably never again to create their own games while under Activision. The same could be also said of Human Head Studios.
While it’s by means not the last game of either studio, Quake 4 feels like the beginning melody of the swan-song of these once prominent titans in videogames, only left now to ponder every night, weak and weary, staring upon forgotten lore, nearly napping before there comes a tapping on the craven door, only with the same messenger as before to speak that name once more.
Quoth the Raven, “Nevermore.”

Really disappointed in this offering of Quake. The first three games in the series all broke new ground and offered unique gameplay plus atmosphere. Quake 4 really doesn't have anything new to offer in either department. Basically it feels like a Quake 2 themed arcade light gun shooter in the category of Area 51 and House of the Dead. It probably would have been much more successful as a light gun game. But it's not, Quake 4 is a first person sci-fi shooter picking up where the story of Quake 2 left off. On the plot line I'm unclear if this is supposed to be a second wave of human invasion on planet Stroggos or if Quake 4 simply picks up the story right after Quake 2 amped with Doom 3 style graphics. Regardless it's stale and boring. I missed this game when it first came out and thought it might be cool to finally have a go at it. Now that I completed the game I'm thinking I should have skipped it entirely.
Quake 4 begins with a lack of player mobility. Jumping is a joke and there's no ability to sprint. I found it to be slow and aggravating. That changes slightly after the 'Capture' point in the story which made the game controls feel a bit better. Enemy positions always felt predictable and it was easy to overrun their spawn points. It's fairly sloppy work to have a half dozen enemies spawn into a hallway corner one after another but that's exactly what takes place in many spots. So once you discover those it's easy to just stand in front of the spawn point and one-shot every space fool with a shotgun blast to the face as each one appears. You can generally anticipate where enemies are going to come from in each section and that does not contribute to any kind of feeling of tension or fear, unlike Quake 2. That tension and atmosphere was sorely missed in this game.
Another major problem I have with Quake 4 is the emphasis of being part of a squad or team. The constant radio chatter and silly NPCs running around did nothing to foster any sense of a large operation or a feeling of being part of a big team. Instead it's just a cheap way to advance a story line without any real level design or clever challenging gameplay. A better solution would have been to allow team co-op on the single player campaign minus all the NPCs. Quake 2 for example had the ability to start a team co-op server for the single player missions and that was brilliantly executed. The catch was only one player's worth of resources were available so the team had to ration supplies and work together closely to be successful. It does not look like id or Raven gave that any consideration for Q4. I would have preferred that over all the irrelevant radio chatter and otherwise meaningless NPC nonsense. Frequently once tasked with finding a console or switch to activate you're forced to backtrack through previously explored areas. There's nothing new to see there, just keep moving on to the next tedious task.
Another thing that bugs me is Q4 includes the space janitors by default. I hate that junk. Space janitors come through the area you just killed everyone in and they clean up the bodies free of charge. That really dampens the feel, game devs take note. The only way to fix that is though a console command to leave the carnage on the floor where it belongs. Let's give the space janitors the day off, shall we?
As far as the graphics and look of Q4 it's not bad. I liked Doom 3 alot and Q4 is very similar in many ways to it. There were a few spots where I stopped to look around some and hang out and I think that holds up alright. The various weapons also looked pretty good although I did not find any of them to be particularly ferocious. Outside of the dark matter gun everything felt mediocre for dishing out damage. I did not use the blaster at all, and hardly ever used the machine gun except for finishing off a punk when I was low on every other kind of ammo. Rockets seemed to be king for clearing out the hallway mazes lickety split. Not much fun in that though.
Quake 4 does not appear to play well with newer versions of Windows. There's a significant amount of complaints on the Steam Q4 Discussion forums about that so I'd strongly recommend if you are not keeping around a dedicated vintage machine running XP to think twice about buying this game.

WE NEED MORE GAMES LIKE RiME!
I just finished the game, and I gotta say, this is a masterpiece in every sense of the word. RiME manage to hit the right notes in music, aesthetics, narrative and gameplay in order to compose a beautiful melody of a game. From the moment I started playing, the hypnotizing atmosphere, relaxing and melancholic music and flawless and fluid animation of the child protagonist, kept me glue to the screen until completion, this was amplified as I start to encounter murals, hints and key hole paintings, that slowly revealed the tragic story behind this apparently light-hearted game.
As most gamers out there I'm used to the usual interaction mechanics: drive the car and win the race, fly the plane/ship and shoot the bad guys or kill everything in sight with your sword/gun... it was a pleasant surprise to see that most of the "combat" and puzzle interaction in RiME was render entirely through sounds and vocal cues made by our main hero. I've never felt more connected with a video game character as I felt with this little kid. The sense of wonder and loneliness I felt as I call out for anyone in the deserted beach at the beginning of the game, or the oppressive feeling of despair that I felt crying every time I clicked towards the end, were feelings that I rarely get in a video game.
RiME is a piece of art, an introspective journey across innocence and fantasy. An intense yet relaxed experience that will take you through very adult feelings like sense of lost, acceptance and hope, through the skin of a child. This is an experience that I wish to share with all my love ones, the same as a movie or a good book.
In a sea of carbon copies of the same Action/Adventures, RPGs, FPS, RTS and all that we've been cater as regular video games, RiME breaks the rule and go directly for the art behind the game, giving us an entirely new experience of joy, sadness, bonding, wonder and adventure, all wrapped up in a beautiful and unforgettable package!

EDIT: Revised review as of 29/09/2016.
Recently decided to dig out Kingdom Wars and take another look to see if anything has changed. I can say there have been some fairly drastic changes since I first played Kingdom Wars, notably the crown store being the biggest.
The crown store from what I can see is now completely gone, crowns are now used as a means of upgrading buildings and then making units that may require crowns to be made. The only benefit you can obtain from the game in a buying sense is by using "Premium Time" which basically gives x2 crown income (this includes quests, sieges, co-op etc - i.e quest giving 2 crowns would give 4 instead). This is quite cheap, and in honesty isn't even a necessity to enjoy the game. (The starter pack DLC's they've added are pretty good, and one even gives all the additional single player content they added in after I had stopped playing).
I would also say that despite still being a small company, I contacted their CS regarding my old account and how I had lost my older progress, and despite the age of my account they still helped me get some new cities up and running, which has allowed me to play and edit this review.
I would warn that there are some bugs in the game still, during sieges enemy reinforcements can literally run through your palisade wall battle camp, which can prove quite problematic, hopefully this will be getting addressed. I haven't had a chance to try Co-op just yet, once I have I will update the results, as there used to be sync problems which I believe I outlined in my original review.
I would now recommend Kingdom Wars, if you can get beyond some of the annoying bugs the game itself is definitely worth trying, and it does bring something quite different and refreshing.
Also, don't rely on the path finding the bit about that in my original review definitely still stands!
**Original old review below - left for comparison**
I played this game quite a lot when I bought it and thought it was great at first. The economy side of the game is interesting and well thought out, the unit selection is acceptable. The idea of sieging and the length sieges can take when you aren't using armies of fully levelled crown store units is also fun (we can get to that later).
The game does have the potential to be really good, there's no disputing that, but please note kingdom wars is basically a name and an expansion - this game has been in development since 2011 and if you pair that with its current state, you may have some worrying thoughts of the direction the game is taking.
One of the biggest gameplay flaws in this, is basically the crown store - unlike other games where your armies are limited to the amount of epic units you can have - this game isn't. You can make entire armies of the most powerful crown store units in the game, level them freely and just annihilate any city within <30 minutes to farm even more crowns. These can then be used in PVP if you wish to do so.
PVP - Basically we have a strength system here - if your PVP protection is down you can be attacked by player armies that are in the current area. The system isn't well balanced, for instance you could have an army of fully levelled regular units which can then be attacked and killed by a far smaller army of one or more fully levelled crown store units - this means you can essentially lose an entire army to a few units of crown store elites.
Then we go onto the bugs that I started to get plagued by, for instance each time I loaded into my cities I found my resources half wiped, when loading out from areas I'd have my resources completely wiped.
The gameplay is buggy, the path finding on units is atrociously bad (they can easily get themselves killed, so you can't really command them to go one way then quickly go to manage other units elsewhere, since they'll likely get themselves killed with their own poor path finding.
You can use the forums for this game for help, but help isn't really what you see there. If you look at the development logs, you see such silly developments and changes like prices of units etc - when this game has serious fundamental core game flaws, a game that calls itself an MMO, but can't even keep your data secure.
They use community volunteers as mods, since they can't afford to actually employ objective people that will provide you with proper service. I think anyone reading this can agree that community volunteers should be kept to forums at most, and not given any sort of power within a game environment at all - you don't see this logic applied here.
Also, something that really irks me when I was scouring the forum where the mods/devs do actively post on this game was the way they kept saying "this rare bug" this seemed like some sort've half hearted euphemism that i've never seen any development companies say. If you're experiencing crippling bugs, you don't want to be told it's rare and of low importance - you want to be told it's going to be dealt with asap.
My view of this game is essentially - could be something amazing and it could be something different. I just think the developers are either too young, or too new to their field of expertise and this has just been a mammoth undertaking that they haven't taken up with enough maturity and focus. With some proper direction, and better management in regard to the games running, perhaps that could change.
I recommend this game to anyone who has a strong chin and can put up with some of the annoyances I mentioned above in regard to the bugs, perhaps some of you can see a game that's been out there for this period of time with such core game issues and still enjoy it.
For those who are looking for a casual game you can play without any issues, I don't recommend this game in the slightest.

Two Worlds 2 is a game that is pretty much unfinished. How do I know? The map, the story, the map.
I first played the original Two Worlds back in 07. The game was strange to sat the least. The story felt unfinished with entire cities not even used within the story. There was a lack of polish but it did feel like an journey, as well as offered some new things for it's time. Now the 2nd one. Eh...
So at first it seems more polished. The story feels more a part of the game world and not just an after thought. The story is still weak. Your character has to save his sister again, while getting transported to different areas for whatever reason. The story also starts and ends all of the sudden.
Gameplay wise it is a third person hack n slash. Nothing wrong, nothing good either. The boats are nice but needless due to the world mostly being shut off from you openly exploring. Horses are also lame since you only use them on smallish islands.
Sound is ehh. Voice actors try, but their tones don't fit their scenes. Think Oblivion with even less feeling.
Graphics are decent for 2011, not on par with Witcher 2 but also no where near as demanding. I play this game at Ultra except AA @2160p 60fps no dips on a 4790k/980ti. The performance is great. Visual options are fairly vast and some advanced setting as well.
The game world is dull and much smaller than the first game. You have a semi large island and two smaller islands. There is a huge hunk of land in the middle of the map but you can not get on it. Atleast not center of it. It is reserved for multiplayer. What a load. You can sail around for hours in a boat, that if you get it stuck on rocks you're stuck. This a mostly empty world.
Atleast they got rid of the old english from the last game. All in all this is a skipable boring RPG. Get Witcher 3, Skyrim, or beer instead.

If you like the Team Ico/genDESIGN games like the recent The Last Guardian, but specifically Ico, then you'll like this game without a shadow of a doubt.
The gameplay, story telling, characters, music/sound, atmosphere, and even the puzzles take inspiration from Ico, with the art design and some animals reminding me of TLoZ: The Wind Waker.
The awesome story's beautifully told completely through imagery, as there's no dialogue in the game whatsoever, but even so it simply means that there're no language barriers holding people back. It's a story that some might find slightly challenging to follow, but what you are shown is easy to remember, and everything makes sense when it gets tied together in the end.
Game time is roughly 5 to 9 hours depending on how long you want to spend exploring, taking screenshots, collecting everything, and achievement hunting. I will say that you should take your time with it though, it's not a game that you should rush, even if you can.
I highly recommend it, especially if you can get it on sale. 8/10.

RiME is about a boy that wakes up stranded on an island after wrecking his ship. Your goal is to find out where and who you are through a series of puzzles that lead to sometimes breathtaking vistas and beautiful music scores.
+Soundtrack
+Art style, notably the water tesselation, is eye-catching
+Lack of text or any sort of dialogue builds on the immersion that really helps you dive into the world of RiME (reminiscient of Journey)
+Decent replayability. The game offers a chapter select option after finishing the game, while also providing a list of all collectables (these range from music to outfits) that you can find there.
+I personally didn't have any issues with this game, but there have been reports of it running pretty poorly on certain rigs. make sure to check your specifications even if they are above recommended.
+Controls can be a little clunky at times
+Camera angles are a little awkward at some points in the game (this has been mostly remedied by the movable camera angle added in a post-release patch
+I don't regret spending 40 dollars on this game, but the argument that the content doesn't match the price is a valid one. Maybe wait until a sale.
Overall an excellent addition to my library. Check it out!

First things first, I LOVE For Honor.
I am a big fan of it, have been waiting for its release for years, and have tested and played its beta and enjoyed it.
And don't get me wrong. I love medieval games, and revel in the thought of Samurais V Vikings V Knights!
And that is why I was patiently waiting, and hoping that the game's flaws were all ironed out upon release and can become better than its own beta test.
But upon playing the release, I cannot reccommend this game to anyone, seriously. Please highly consider a few things before you sink your money into this developer-forsaken game.
Pros:
-Amazing graphics
-Awesome gameplay
-Concept is just badas & cool
-Quite a bit of customization
-Story single player isn't bad
Cons:
-The matchmaking system STILL SUCKS. Yes, I cannot stress this enough! It uses Player to Player connection (P2P), and it still does. What this means is that finding matches is going to be at least 10 mins long, and when you do miracolously find and join a game session, you will be disconnected for no reason other than the game's stupid system, even if you have decent or even good internet. Why? Simply because the Host of your game session does not have decent internet connection. Random disconnects, SUPER EXTRA Long wait times on game matchmaking, LAG LAG LAG, and  worst of all: It WILL disconnect in the most inappropriate times.
-Bugs, Yes BUGS. and A Lot. It's like it's saying "Fak the Alpha/Beta test, Nothing has changed and nothing will." You join a game of Dominion and what happens? You are stuck looking at the top view of the entire map like a God, with NO option of spawning within the game...wth... or you spawn, the game starts and....your stuck...just stuck....as other soldiers whisk around you frantic on the battle they are about to face, you just stand there...armor and all....like an idiot...then of course you get disconnected...classic. yay.
-The battle system is fun and innovative but it is not without its flaws. From spammable combos on certain heroes, to bugs that will not allow you to parry or block, to exploitable gameplay mechanics that will leave other honest players at a disadvantage, and many more. It is sad to say, that Ubisoft has done nothing whatsoever to fix these problems even after beta testing, heck I think personally it just got worse in the release. (P.S Fullscreen is still mistakebly being put on Full Windowed Mode, freakin lazy arses)
-What I was dissapointed at the most probably, is the fact that many people pay huge amounts of money, especially to pre-order this stupid game, BUT WE DON'T EVEN FULLY OWN IT. What I mean is that, most in-game stuff is locked and can only be bought by an in-game currency called "Silver". C'mon, try and guess what Ubisoft did to this "In-Game" Currency. Like a freakin troll, they made this currency extremely hard to get, and requires hours, if not, days to muster up enough silver to even buy anything cool (fine for a hardcore gamer, but not for casuals). I mean we already bought the game, why dafuq do we have to bear with most of the cosmetics, and equipment being locked away until we grind ourselves to death. I thought gaming was supposed to be fun. Although, you don't really need the cosmetics to perform well in the game, but it just pisses me off to see an uber expensive game being treated like it's a free-to-play game model. Even if you do want to buy silver with real money, it costs a fortune (almost as much as the deluxe edition of this game) to get most of the things you'd probably want to buy... (e.g. Executions, Emote, Effect, Costumes, Equipment, Blah blah blah...) It's stupid and I feel tricked personally, I mean, buying the stupid Gold Edition or even Deluxe does not get you a lot of stuff to be honest...rather you save your money and use it to buy more stupid silver.
-The game is made for some heroes to be better or a counter to other heroes, and although its not like this means you can't win against these odds, it will just be really hard. Especially since the game is built upon 1 v 1, and not really meant for a free for all.
-If you are getting the game for the singleplayer, DON'T. It is not made for a single player experience. Although the story campaign wasn't bad, it was still short, and not exactly amazing. This game's multiplayer is where it shines...or was supposed to at least...
(a connection error occured returning to main menu)
-I don't know how, but upon release, they have made revenge mode incredibly buffed. Not only is it a bit harder now to beat a guy with a revenge buff, it is also extremely EASY to get into revenge mode now. Making it possible for 1 guy to beat 3 or even 4 people at once by just spamming revenge mode over and over. This doesn't make sense, 1 guy shouldn't be able to beat multiple opponents so easily, this isn't dota. Even the best players MUST run away when faced with such an ordeal. But somehow now, any troll can just take you down just by defending a few attacks and then activating revenge mode and completely annihilating your team. Or sometimes even, your team member activates revenge mode as well, and you get a battle fest of super saiyans duking it out... wtf...
-Ubisoft nuff said...
Well, overall For Honor is still my favourite game at the moment, even with all these flaws. Just goes to show how much potential this game truly has. It has depth, it has style and everything needed for an A class game. Shame its flaws are shining brighter than all those good things I've just mentioned...

What is my opinion on Magic 2015? I have very mixed feelings about it.
First off, I love the Duels of the Planeswalkers series. Most of my friends are too “poor” (or just cheap) to get into actual paper Magic with me. The closest FNM location to me is almost an hour drive away and I end up spending more of fuel than I do paying at the door. A group of acquaintances play regularly but they're too casual, and that's coming from a casual player. So while I enjoy collecting Magic cards I seldom have anyone of my same caliber to play with. DotP is great for my friends an I because while they can't afford to spend the money necessary to build a strong deck, they can buy this game though sales or ask for it as a gift. In short, this is how I get my Magic fix.
Over the past few installments there have been some serious changes. Starting with D12, the game didn't allow you to remove cards from the base deck, meaning if you wanted to add anything you'd end up with a 60+ card deck, and the balance was chaotic (but still fun). D13 introduced a far more balanced environment to play in, as well as the ability to truly change each deck any way you wanted, removing base cards and replacing them with newly unlocked ones. D14's balance and deck structures were a step down from those of D13, but the game had a more story focused approach and featured the Sealed Play game mode which paved the way for D15.
And lo, D15 is finally here.
Typical of Wizards, information on the game was either sketchy or non-existent. I had to take everything I heard about the game with a dose of salt. A few things caught my eye, those being the entire game would be run in the Sealed format and 2HG wasn't going to be in the game. Hooray for the first, boo for the second. These opened up a flood of questions: How do we unlock cards? How does the campaign work? What do I do if I unpack really bad cards? WHY ARE YOU REMOVING TWO-HEADED GIANT?
Wizards score for answering these questions before the release: 0-4
Moral of the story being don't expect much from the Wizards PR department when it comes to DotP.
Even with these and many more questions looming about, I still pre-ordered the game. Thankfully, when the game was released most of these questions solved themselves. As the game begins, you are placed into a tutorial that walks you though the five colors, creatures, instants/soceries, enchantments, artifacts, lands, etc., etc. This tutorial is clearly for new players, but I appreciated it none the less. At the end of the tutorial, the player picks from any two combinations of colors. I opted for Black/Red, but not before I experimented with each of the combinations. For some reason, Wizards decided that the final fight in the tutorial should be hard as balls, especially if you're on Planeswalker difficulty. Not fun. Once you finally muscle your way through that, though, the game is much more enjoyable.
Upon defeating the tutorial, the next chapter in the campaign is unlocked and ready to play. The player travels to Innistrad and duels several different challengers themed around that plane. For some reason, the first challenge in this chapter was the hardest for me, which was very discouraging considering you have very few options as far as deck editing are concerned. As you progress through the chapter, you unlock several booster packs which add 1 or 3 cards to your pool (which makes finishing the chapter much more manageable) until you beat the final boss of that level. Once Innistrad is complete, the player is allowed to open any Premium boosters they have purchased (More on these later.)
Moving on from Innistrad, the player has the option of tackling the Theros chapter or returning to the main menu to edit their deck or even create a new one with the cards they have unlocked so far (Finally!).
As soon as the player finishes the Innistrad chapter, the game truly begins. Your options as far as deck creation widen, you can farm for booster unlocks, change your persona and title, or battle others online. However, pushing past both the tutorial and Innistrad can be very disheartening, so I encourage any of you who are hung up on this part to continue giving it your all until the real game begins.
Now. Let's tackle a few of the negative comments on the game I've seen so far:
Two-Headed Giant
Yes, there's no 2HG mode in the game, which sucks. However, the public outcry at this during the development was severe, and I can't imagine Wizards won't throw us a bone and add it as a DLC or expansion.
Premium Boosters (AKA Pay-2-Win Boosters)
Yes. They're pay to win. Don't let anyone else tell you otherwise. These boosters cost $1.99 and unlock 10 new cards for you, featuring a few you can't get from regular boosters. Playing the campaign without them is hard, but read my comments on Card Collections first.
Card Collections
In the store you can purchase each of the five card collections (Innistrad, Ravnica, Theros, Zendikar, and Shandalar) which will unlock all of the non-premium cards from that collection for you without having to grind them. I pre-ordered the edition of the game that came with these collections, and I highly regret it. Grinding out boosters is a part of the game, just like playing to win boosters from FNM is a part of the experience of paper Magic. Now read “Card Collections or Premium Boosters?”
Card Collections of Premium Boosters?
As I said, the cards came unlocked for me, which I regret. Personally, I enjoy the part of the game where you have to grind out new cards to improve your deck, and I really really miss that. I would actually recommend buying Pay-2-Win Boosters over purchasing a Card Collection.
The card pool is too small!
Yes, the card pool is pretty small, but that's what expansions are for! In the past games, Wizards has released expansions featuring several new decks to play with. Since there aren't per-constructed decks for you to use, I'm calling it now: Wizards will release expansions featuring new Card Collections for players to unlock!
Edit 1:
As I continue to derp about with deck creation, I keep thinking to myself how limited the pool is. There are a few combinations that work really well, such as BR Control/Sacrifice, GW Landfall, Pure U Control, and even BW Lifegain. The problem is once you've seen that particular strategy, there's not much you can do to create a better variation of that. Now, some of the different strategies are really fun to mess with, like Pyxis of Pandamonium Landfall, or RGU/UBR Defender, but they get old pretty fast. I've started equating this to playing paper Magic within only one expansion. Right now, D15 only has the first part of a three part expansion (I hope, anyway), so it's like playing with only Return to Ravnica or Theros expansion cards, leaving out the rest of the block. The more I play, the more I want to reinstall D13. Heck, I'd even reinstall D14 for the custom mod decks.
The sad, sad irony of D15 is that this is EXACTLY what the player base has been asking for. In my opinion, DotP should stay as far away from MTGO as possible, but MTGO could be made to look a little more like DotP.

It's beautiful, it has pretty tight controls, it's really immersive, and it's an experience you can't get from any other game.

Everything about this game is trial and error. Every area you enter will kill you repeatedly until you understand every reason it kills you. Then they will keep killing you repeatedly because you can't know where to go. And occasionally it'll kill you because it decided to spawn a centipede in the only corridor you can take and it never goes away.
That level of unfair difficulty does well to serve the game's atmosphere. But it makes it awful to play, for a more important reason. You have no idea what you're doing. You have no idea where you're going. You have no idea whether you're going the right way, at any point. The level design is so obtuse and ambiguous that everything looks like a death trap. There's a story to follow, but you have no idea where to follow it. This makes the entire game feel aimless.
It turns out, frustration combined with aimlessness leads to a terrible experience. The atmosphere and uniqueness could've carried one of those flaws. But not both.

I actually enjoyed the game.  I was happy to finally see a Magic the Gathering video game with full card customization after all of these years.  Many people don't seem to understand that in order for this to work, it is necessary for us to begin with a chosen starter deck, and then earn the rest of your cards.  You can easily farm new cards in the first node of every level to enhace and perfect your deck.  Also, many do not stop to check the default settings in the options menu.  I found it best to try different settings that would benefit my playstyle the best.  For example, I believe that you should be allowed to adjust the amount of lands by default on the deck creation screen.  Also, it should be easier to understand how to choose which mana to tap for all spells, rather than let the game choose for you.
With that being said, of course I feel there some grey areas that should be addressed.  I do not mind if WotC/Hasbro wishes to sell extra booster packs, but all of the cards should always be available to earn in game at a reasonable drop rate.  We already payed for the game.  We should not feel forced to pay more for it. The artwork is very nice, but whats up with the brilliant white screens?  I didn't check but also can I change the card table?  Also, I imagine there will be an expansion pack with more things to do like two headed giant, but will there be more new cards?  I would also like to see a few more of the older edition cards like lightining bolt, and classic counterspell cards.  One final gripe is that I seemed to have trouble connecting to a multiplayer game.  It just seems to time out.
Anyway I would recommend this game if you like Magic the Gathering, but I would probably wait for an expansion pack or two to come out to fully appreciate it.  Especially if you are new to the game, or have only played the previous versions of this game.

An extremely enjoyable medieval combat game, whilst not a free form fighting game such as Chivalry or Mount and Blade, it still delivers a massive amount of fun with it's combat system that is easy to learn, but hard to master. First off, anyone saying this game is "Pay 2 win" is just downright wrong. They are mistaking gear, for skill. I haven't put a penny into this game other than the base 60, and I have no problem winning. If someone buys IN GAME CURRENCY THAT YOU CAN ALREADY GET with their real life money, so be it. They can open crates (Which are found throughout the story, or bought with in game currency that is laughably easy to accumulate) and they can then get gear from these crates. Gear that changes your stats. I know what you're thinking "Oh god, he can have +20 attack, he's OP and pay to win" But that isn't this game. If you have a piece of gear that does give you +20 attack, then it will also give you -15 defense and -10 stamina. To be completely honest, I find gear is most of the time a handicap, as it takes away from 2 stats to give a boost in one, not to mention the fact that GEAR CAN ONLY BE USED IN THE 4V4 GAMEMODE. So go ahead, and tell me that microtransactions are ruining this game, this game is pay 2 win. People that tell me that, I just nod my head and laugh, because no amount of gear makes up for SKILL. If someone beat you, It is either for 2 reasons: 1) They are more skilled than you (Which is most of the time true, as a lot of the people playing release, such as myself, have devoted many hours to games such as Dark Souls, Chivalry, Mount and Blade, and even the Closed Alpha and Betas for this game) or 2) You were kicked off of a cliff. The whole thing about being kicked off of a cliff or wall is kind of a problem, but I see it as this. It's a fighting game. There are no rules that state you can't kick people off, in fact, it is ENCOURAGED. They even teach you about it in the tutorial. There is a reason that there are so many spots to kick people off. It's a game mechanic. It's not unfair either, as both parties can do it. Hell, you can even counter it, as long as you have proper timing. Most of the people I see complaining about the game, consequentially, aren't very good at it. Hence why they resort to chanting "Pay 2 Win" as seen by so many of the negative reviews. One problem that a lot of users say, however, is the Peer 2 Peer network. If you don't know, Peer 2 Peer is when one of the players in the lobby is selected to be the "host", who is then in charge of "hosting" the server. What people don't know, is that a lot of games have this system in place, and don't have problems. Almost all the Call of Duty games had them, I never had a problem with any of them, Grand Theft Auto V's multiplayer is Peer 2 Peer as well. During the Alpha and Closed Beta, I had a few disconnection problems, but during the Open Beta and Release of the game, I have yet to have any major networking problems like people are describing. Maybe I am an isolated case, but I still think that this game is just getting a lot of hate simply because it's a Ubisoft game. Don't get me wrong, I REALLY dislike Ubisoft, especially what they've done to huge pieces of my childhood as a gamer like the Splinter Cell series, and the Ghost Recon series, but I feel that I really do enjoy the game (Other than the EXTREMELY salty and toxic community, may be one of the worst I have ever seen)
Thanks for reading, and have a good day!

(06/02/2017 addendum: As I look back several months later, I realise I never recovered from the menu-induced whiplash, therefore my recomendation has changed to: Do not buy, stick with SW1!)
: If you love Shadow Warrior but hate Borderlands, then proceed with caution (at least wait for a sale), as this game is one concerted effort by the latter to ruin the former.
But is this better than Shadow Warrior 1? Yes and no!
1) No more stamina, which is great because unless you're called Dark Souls/Bloodborne then don't bother!
2) No more falling damage, thus no more splattering yourself on the floor by dashing down a six foot flight of stairs!
3) Although it's still more advisable to just dart in and out before the enemies hit you - a much more viable tactic with the lack of stamina and fall damage, combined with the more open spaces - you can now parry with your sword.
4) Excellent animation quality, with different animations playing each time you fire/reload.
5) The Lo Wang brand of humour. He's hardly Oscar Wilde (whose quotes can be found on fortune cookies, incidentally), with most of his jokes falling flat but still amusing, in fact I probably wouldn't have made it to the end without them.
6) Kamiko. Wang's new head-tenant provides a more effective counterpoint to his behavior than the trickster Hoji ever did.
7) The controls for chi powers and special sword attacks have been much-improved, with the former requiring only single button presses and just a
directional input + right click for the latter.
8) Much greater variety of weapons, more than I suspect I've managed to find so far.
9) Combat is fast-paced and
be satisfying which brings me to....

Plus, you'd think that the purpose of a colour-coding system would be so that you can tell at a glance, which ones would be more effective but no, in this game it is possible - and all too likely - for that level 50 "legendary" red gem (red>yellow>blue>gray) you just acquired from that difficult boss fight to offer
dps than say, your level 45 blues, probably because it got -damage as one of it's downsides!
The only gem types that are actually
are the different ammo types like explosive or piercing and the alternate fire modes - which actually
, instead of supplement, the primary fire - like rapid-fire, dual-wield and turret, none of which I have ever used because that would mean wasting one of the 3 valuable slots I need to improve the
stat that matters:
!
Probably the most damning part of this system is the constant - and sometimes
- gameplay interruptions that will inevitably ensue as you tediously scroll through the list of gems, trying to optimise your weapons to counter the increasingly bullet-spongey enemies and their random grab-bag of arbitrary modifiers, mainly elemental resistances/weaknesses.
For me, this got worse when I realised I could have the Ninja Touch amulet equipped for +30% melee damage and the Marksman Soul for +30% firearm damage and I got into the habit of swapping them out when switching between sword and gun, since opening the inventory pauses the game.
In short: Shadow Warrior 1's weapon upgrade system was far superior; quality over quantity! I would actually rather suffer those invulnerable-everywhere-except-the-chicken-pox-on-the-back trolls than this alternative!
So what about plot and level design? Well after a promising start, in which you progress linearly and loop back around to Wangs' car after collecting the artifact, you arrive at the hub area and upon embarking on your first mission, Wang goes to enter his car, only for Kamiko to inform him that she can take us to and fro more efficiently which, after only one mission, I took as the developers saying "Oh no, linear progression through coherent levels is so last year (or 3 as it were), teleporting back and forth between the hub area and the same 2 or 3 copy-pasted play pens is what the cool kids are into!". This makes the game a disjointed sight-seeing tour compared to the journey that was SW1 (the same issue I had going from Dark Souls 1 to 2).
This, combined with the side-questing, completely kills the pacing and gives no sense of momentum or progress - which I'm guessing is why they felt the need to flat out tell you your completion percentage on the character select screen - leaving me with little to no investment by the end due to the stupor it had lulled me into. And as for the ending: abrupt, unsatisfying and they may as well have just
!
Upon finishing SW1 on normal, I immediately and gleefully restarted on hard whereas SW2, I started on hard mainly because of the promise of decent drops (I dread to think how bad they must be on lower difficulty levels!) and now that I've finished it, have no immediate desire to go through it again.
Ultimately though, I did still enjoy it but that came in
of the Borderlands influence, which has rendered merely
what otherwise would have been a
game if it had kept the weapon upgrade system, plot and level structure that previously served it very well.
For this reason, I'd say it is worth getting but definitely
at full price.
There is nothing wrong with linearity, Flying Wild Hog! Better to forge ahead with certainty than to flit back and forth and meander around. Put that in one of your fortune cookies!

I want to start by saying.  I love Magic the Gathering.  I have never played Magic The Gathering Online.  I play the real card game and I've played all of the steam released Magic games.  Also this is pretty much a single player review, I don't do multiplayer personally. That being said.

This game does a great job of evoking some moods and sensations I haven't felt in video games in many years. The game is massive, and unlike most triple-A-titles, is not in a hurry to rush you through cinematics. Like other great indie games, Rain World lets you explore and enjoy the world and its mechanics. There is no rush, even though you inevitably have to hide from the rain.
Many reviews blames the game for being too hard and unforgiving. Whenever I get trapped by predators and killed, or get caught by rain too far from a safe place, I blame myself. I blame myself for being too cocky, or for forgetting to conserve movement and going too far.
There is a real penalty for dying, unlike other hard games, so you actually have to be careful. As your skill grows, the game rewards you for being brave, yet there is a fine line between brave and foolhardy. That difference is the difference between nimbly dodging a lizard, seeing it getting dragged away by something bigger, and getting caught in a pit between beasts, all escape-paths blocked.
The nature of the game engine is that all beings are alive, moving around according to their instincts. The physics allow for unforeseen behaviours which can be very pleasing, like impaling an enemy against a wall with your spear, not killing it but letting it squirm in place. This adds to the fun of the game, as you can use these mechanics to succeed. Pitting the different animals against each other is another vital tactic that you will learn by playing, and watching.
As harsh as Rain World is, it is a beautiful place. Vast and hostile, but still a nice place to be.

SW and Doom were the biggest shooters of my childhood that i was a fan of, and now, they were both getting a new release on the same year!  How cool is that?
At the time of writing, i run a gt960, i5-4460 and 8gb ram. The game runs smooth 80-100fps on low/med settings and still looks very beautiful. My fps haven't dropped below 60 even on the big bosses with their mobs and i haven't encountered any bugs. Started playing this at the day of the release, so in that aspect this was a job really well done!
NOW! On to the game itself:
The stages are procedurally generated, i'm an old schooler myself, so i didn't really like this part. The levels look the same after a while. There's the forest setting, a cyberpunk city, a normal city and some random little village's with few houses and agriculture. So sidequests get pretty boring after a while, and there's a good chunk of them.
Secrets are also generated in those levels, that was the only thing i personally liked about generated levels. Just not my thing, seems too repetitive :D As illogical as it sounds when saying that randomnes is too repetitive.
Guns, there is a lot of them and you can carry 9 at the same time, others stay in your inventory whenever you want to equip them. They aren't just the same ones with a slight tint of different color either, but uniquely crafted, and you have three slots on each one to modify with powerups. Since some enemies are resistant to some elements, and others to other elements, it brings a little bit of tactical thingy. Powerups are plenty, and you can apply/take them off from weapons how you want, no penalty at all.
Skill system is more streamlined, and more diverse than before. I liked this version better than the last one. More fine-tuning of my Wang.
Between this and Doom, Doom takes the cake for me for better action and more interesting levels, but this is easily the second best SP-shooter for this year.

Other reviews will tell you about this game and how good it is, but I can tell you some good tips when getting started.
1. When given a choice of your first faction, you can only choose a roman family. I say play on medium difficulty for battles and the main map (But easy is acceptable). Also, play as either the Julii (Red) or the Brutii (Green). The Julii will take on Gaul, Spain, Brittainia, and maybe other factions like Greece or Carthage, but mainly barbarians. This lets you get used to how the roman armies work before taking on major nations. The other good option is the Brutii. The Brutii fight mainly Greek forces and later eastern nations. You will start out trying to take the richest cities on the map, which means it is easy to maintain a great economy.
2. If given the choice between killing a rebel army and another nation's army (If they aren't yet at war with you) go with the rebels. Rebels can be beaten easily and are great for leveling up your generals and troops.
3. DO NOT FOLLOW COMMUNITY GUIDES AND UNLOCK THE OTHER FACTIONS TO PLAY AS FIRST. You can edit a .txt file and unlock all factions immediately, but if you have just bought the game, I suggest you do not do this. You should play as a Roman faction first, as they are the most powerful and will help you get used to the game. Besides, other factions have to deal with the roman's at some point...

I really want to recommend Magic 2015, but I can't. This game is really a sad case of "one step forward, two steps back." For example: the new "open" deck building system is a great new feature which is marred by placing too-strict limits on how many copies of cards you can use and also makes the single player campaign a chore as you have to grind to get new cards so you can compete with the overpowered AI decks. Another example: the new black/white design aesthetic is clean and appealing, but actually navigating the menus is clunky, gimmicky, and obnoxious--it feels like a console port. This point is particularly annoying to me since I thougt Stainless Games had learned their lesson when Magic 2014 finally had a clean, simple, easy-to-navigate interface.
After weeks of playing, my opinion has only gotten worse--constant crashes, disconnects, and glitches with cards. Stick with 2014.

Sniper Elite V2 puts you into the WWII setting in Berlin, 1941. You obviously should play the first game before this, but some of you didn't, which I'm guilty of too. I feel that after playing the first 3 missions of the game, the review was ready to be spit out. I personally like this game, and the reasons so I will say. Now the gameplay is very nice, giving you a challenge the whole way through the mission, which I like. Unlike COD, this game takes the use of your brain and putting it to work. You can't run in throught the mission and shoot, hell no, not in this game. You can easily die running into the mission, which I'm guilty of the first couple times. You can easily be picked off by one or two enemys by running in, but in COD you can take on 10-15, which is insanely absurd. Which is mainly why I don't like COD too much, but the zombies mode and campaign are alright. So, in order to not get killed so much is to have the enemy come to you, you don't come to them because 2-3 shots can kill you right off the bat.
Now to talk about the graphics and the enviroment. The enviroment is great, it gives that vibe to the whole WWII scene, having to do with flying planes, destroyed buildings, tanks, roadblocks, exploded vehicles, you name it, the game has it. The graphics are beautiful, running Sniper Elite on a 1080p resolution and the ultra settings preset made this game look beautiful, which contributed to the game being so good to me personally. But, the water and smoke looks like poop! The water looks like a plastic sheet put over the ground, not to mention that stepping in it had no splashing effect which made the water so lifeless like it wasn't even water. The game developers need to put some physics into the water and smoke, or it'll just make the enviroment seem more lifeless and bland. The smoke from a far distance looks good, but up close it looks like it was made with the Microsoft default Paint program you have in the Start menu. The smoke also has no density to it, making it bland just like the water. Again, the developers should've spent more time on the smoke and water effects. Anyways, I forgive it since the rest of the enviroment looks next-gen with great PC optimization giving a full 60FPS on ultra with this last-gen GeForce GTX 550 Ti Gigabyte OC that I carry in this PC.
Now the background story, which this game doesn't really have any. The backstory to this game makes me say "What"? Now, what I mean is that there's no backstory to this game, as in the cutscenes before each mission for example Grand Theft Auto, Half-Life, and Mafia II have a backstory, which gives it's background that promotes the fuller understanding of the game, although there's a brief saying of the mission you are about to enter in this game. But, still there really isn't a backstory to the game. Now, if you don't understand what a game's "backstory" is, I'd go look up backstory on Google or whatever search engine you use. Anyways, Sniper Elite is still good even though it has its flaws to the game. Every game has its flaws. Like Grand Theft Auto IV, which has sort of a horrible PC optimization to the game.
The heartbeat system consists of mainly two things, your lung capacity to use focus time, and your health. When your heartrate goes above 80BPM you can't go into focus time, there's two reasons as to why it is over 80BPM. One: You've been shot, which brings up the heartrate, but not necessarily all the time though, there's a few times when I been hit 3 times and it still was at 70BPM. Two: You've have been either jogging or running around, which would always raise your heartrate. So, that's the heartrate system in a nutshell.
HUD elements like your objective and your weapon and ammo will disappear after an amount of about 5 seconds, which can be helpful if you need to see at the corners of your screen. That's a plus in any game.
Overall, the game's nice, the music is good. The gunshots are satisfying when you snipe someone overhead. The overall rating of this game is a good 8.7/10.

Seems like the previous storylines were all related to each other. But after finishing this one I don't see it going anywhere from here. Will see what Anniversary has to offer but I think it ended. Great story.
Puzzles were not too hard but nice to figure them out. So it kept the mood up to keep playing, not to quit cuz rage or something like that. Also if got lost, no idea what to do, can ask for hint under Tab, which was nice. They had this relic hunt in there as well but since there were so many of them and they were really tiny it didn't work for me. Had no mood to look all of them. If had 3 in each chapter and something bigger would had been nicer.
Combat system was kind of boring. New enemies which was nice but there was no challenge killing them. It was same in previous game as well. So yeah, they have still improvement space in that area. Secondary weapon was kind of useless, they let you choose one at the beginning of each chapter but ended up never using them. She had on autoaim that had 100% acc so yeah. Lots of tiny spiders came. If 10 then just 10 shots and done. No challenge, kind of pointless to add them then at all. Also her kick was so op. No matter what enemy got close, kick them, they fall on floor, shoot, if they still not dead, kick again as soon as they stand up.
Graphics improved hellalot comparing to previous game(s). Lot of more little details, surroundings.
I was really bothered by character movement. The speed of her actions were really off to me. Looked really odd. All wall climbings, jumping, you name it. Got stuck in the at between places and had to reload or kill myself with nades to continue. Also the interactions with items such as boxes, placing them on the pressureplates were very glitchy. Press E to pick up cube, it flew off nowhere or she went underground and appeared again. Placing cube on the pressureplate, it flew of as soon as touched it. So had to find that not glitchy spot on it.
Overall, game was great. I am recommending it with both of my hands. But you should play previous ones first. Otherwize story is kind of off.

Okay... let's put it this way. I am going to say yes, but it is yes with a HUGE amount of caveats!
I'm NOT going to defend it's glaring, straight-up sickening misogyny, it's juvenile humor, and the fact it shows just what happens when you have too many cooks at the pot (so to speak). It is a game from another era, one that should have grown up with it's peers, but it didn't.
Still, if you can get past all of this, it actually is kind of fun. I know that is a LOT to get past, but I played "Send in the Clones" and enjoyed a few good chuckles, and it was just kind of fun to step back into the shoes of the narcissistic Duke. The main game is a little tedious in places, but it is still fun, the achievements are actually fun to go after and it has a sense of humor about itself. Don't get me wrong, I think the cutscenes in the alien hive were some of the worst the game has to offer (trust me, hit youtube and look it up if you haven't played this... you'll understand why).
This also isn't a game I'd let my kid play (if I had one), as it has some SUPER adult themes (and if you don't know what a glory hole is, maybe you shouldn't be playing it either), and I wouldn't want any kid thinking that Duke is a role model in any way, shape or form (especially for his treatment of women). 3D was more fun back in the 90s, but there is a little humor, charm and a halfway decent FPS under all of this crap.

★★★★☆ - "Worth your time, give it a bash"
PROS:
- The enemy in this game is monstrous, everything about it is terrifying.
- An interesting story told through minimal cut scenes and notes.
- Creepy environments which you can roam around, each very atmospheric with superb lighting and design.
- Restrictive gameplay means you interact only with objects, this adds to the tension as you can't fight back but only run and hide.
- Amnesia is just one big puzzle game, one that doesn't hold your hand and is very challenging. You learn by dying and by reading, listening and experimenting with objects.
CONS:
- As you can only interact with objects I would have liked to had seen more of them, some rooms feel repetitive and if they were to be more dense it could have only added more character.
- A tiny complaint here are the loading screens, as you enter certain areas there are loading screens, they are overly long but as you play more there become more. On a positive note it doesn't distract too much away from immersion as its all just one big place too explore.
VERDICT?
A very tense experience, not for the feint hearted nor the impatient but a rewarding and intriguing game.

I tried really hard to enjoy this game, and there are bits of enjoyment to be had here and there, but after trudging through the base game plus the expansion, I couldn't help but feel like I just played through a poor man's Oblivion or Witcher.
The game actually looks pretty nice, and the music is some of the nicest I've heard in awhile out of an Action RPG.  The crafting system was also pretty interesting, but that's about all that's good to say about Two Worlds II.  It's a pain to manage all your items, and the UI was very clearly designed with consoles in mind.  Combat feels slippery, and character animations are awkward looking.  Despite being a bright, colorful world artistically, the characters that drive the story forward, with the exception of one or two, are uninteresting, cliched and/or poorly fleshed out.  The worst offender is our protagonist, who instead of being dark and mysterious (which I think they intended), just comes off as dull and devoid of personality.
With a bit more polish, I probably would've been able to like Two Worlds II enough to recommend it, but I read somewhere that a lot was cut out of the game for whatever reasons.  And unfortunately, it shows.  Not a total failure, but there are many other games of this sort that do it better out there.

Early Access Review:
As many others have said, it's a Battlefield/Battlefront-esque game from the delightfully named "Strangely Interactive Ltd." The game, still in early access, has fair/good graphics with occasoinally beautiful levels (I've had a few crashes to desktop, but not in the middle of a match) which feel somthing like a cross between Homeworld and Halo. The fps elements have an excellent degree of customization ...and oh yeah...you can fly battleships!!
There's some squad-based elements, and the bots are actually very good for this. Whoever did the AI, should be proud. I'll see a bit of oddness in long hallways where they just break off, or where they'll clip into a rock formation and fire 'wildly' but people might do that too.
The game may not be overly kind to new players, with some questionable UI decisions, and little or no explanation of the 'points' system used to grant more/better gear. I also found that my old xbox360 controller (which I like to use for vehicle combat) will occasionally just lose key bindings before/after/during a match, which can be frustrating, but hey, the keyboard always works and this is early access. For $14, that's a steal.
With as little time as they devote to it so far, I'm actually pretty engaged with where they could take the story elements.
Do you like fps games? Have you enjoyed Battlefield or Battlefront? Have you ever wondered what it would be like to execute a commando raid on one of your homoworld levels?
You couldn't ask for a better price. If for some reason, you just can't stand a game that lacks polish....jut buy it and wait. Congrats to the developers!

I don't think I need to play much more to come to a conclusion: pricing and server issues aside, I think this game is very unique both in mechanics and in most other things. I don't know if the game is worth $60 just for singleplayer--which is good in its own right--but if you play that and both singleplayer, I find it to be a decent price.
Here's the money issue: a $40 season pass to get more than 4 or 5 maps on each gametype. While the vanilla ones look great on their own and have different weather/time effects, I was a bit disappointed to see there weren't many more than what there were in the closed beta. Even though what they've promised sounds good, it makes me skeptical to buy the DLC, no less the season pass.
This has been discussed many times before but peer-to-peer connection isn't a great idea. Maybe there won't be any servers to inevitably go down in 5+ years like most other games, but usually this type of multiplayer leads to glitches that leave you in match-starting screens until the end of time... or you Alt+F4. I haven't seen signs of a system where it picks the host with the best connection; if not that's where I'd start. Despite that, the issues I've experienced have been fairly rare, but again, I haven't played for too long.
Honestly I can stand these things, but that's just me. Hopefully I don't get tired of it, or their updates are consistent enough to keep the game alive--much like The Division. It's a lot like said game where I actually enjoy playing it, the feeling of moving is nice, the graphics are lively, and the mechanics are enjoyable. I have some amount of faith in Ubisoft despite their expected money mongering, but I think this game delivered what I wanted and I don't regret my $60 spent for this.
All I can reccommend: if you're skeptical, wait for a sale of at least $40 on the main game.

First of I played this in 1080p on a keyboard and on Easy. I wanted to finish it quickly so i can move onto other games.
I have put in a few hours and have reached near the end of the game and i'm not going to be finishing it.
This game has such great potential to be an excellent game but it suffers from huge design flaws. I was really looking forward to enjoying this game and wanted it to be a good game, but its not, small annoyances riddled throughout this game build up and render it unplayable towards the end. One of the biggest downsides is the "Trap Rooms" which seem to be every second room each one having a 2-5 waves of enemies in them, which is completely unnecessary and don't add any reward for the player once completed, not even a small amount of health. The Health is very sparse only coming in one use only chests and is not drop by common enemies. The only enemies that drop health are smaller "Action Kill" enemies, one of which only spawn in the overworld/hubworld. The others being bats and birds which again are Action Kill enemies which if you kill normally give you a reduced amount of health, the normal amount is quite small.
The Story i feel isn't as important as what this game is about, Killing things and making you feel quite the baddass while doing so. It loosely revolves around you redeeming your reputation as a Horseman by doing things for Demons.
Dungeon Design is reminiscent of The Legend of Zelda, so i will loosely compare to that. The dungeons have the normal elements of Fire, Water and Earth along with a Heaven and a Hell, I haven't seen a Hell Dungeon in a Zelda game yet but a Heaven/Sky one though. (I only got upto the Heaven part but i'm guessing you get to hell from where the game was heading) The Dungeon puzzels are quite easy to figure out although not every well explained from the entering fly though. If you were to play a board game you would read the instruction on how to play, the fly though at the start is the instructions for the player if they are not clear then the puzzle needs to be rethought. The Puzzles are often just throwing your boomerang though fire light a bomb, pushing blocks into place or hitting a switch to move some platforms to jump on. I should also mention that there will be instances were you get stuck and fall though the world, happened to me about 4-5 times causing me to reload a save file.
As mentioned before the biggest problem with the game are Trap Rooms in what seems like every room. They have no variety or strategy to them, the same 2-5 monsters come in 2-5 waves per room. The smaller monsters all have the same predictable attacks which are easy to dodge and finish off with an Action Kill. Some of the larger Monsters, not all, are the problem. Their attacking rage is greater than your dodging range so you have no choice but to soak the damage and continue slashing your sword on them until you kill them. After each Trap Room in a game like Zelda you would expect that classic tune to play and you unlock a chest with some loot in it. In Darksiders Trap Rooms you get nothing, no reward no health absolutely nothing, so what is the point of having a Trap Room there? Why are you trapping me in there, there is nothing of value, there is no chest of gold or health (which is the same as gold in Darksiders), its just a hallway with literally nothing in there. This is one of the best examples of the awful design. If you find yourself with little health and your unable to beat the next Trap Room, then congratulations your stuck and cannot progress until you get more health (more of this later) When you reach the end of a dungeon your faced with a "Boss".
The Boss fights are boring, easier than the dungeon itself and a good few don't include the item that you got whilst progressing though the dungeon. If your going to make a dungeon based game, make sure that the Bosses inside each dungeon use the item they hid away because its their weakness. You use it against them to defeat them, not just wack 'em with a sword a few times and they they say 'f**k it, you win'. That means any old person with a sword can do it make the player feel special and as if he/she was the only person who could have done it and not Divorced Doug with the failing lawn mowing business from across the road (no offence to any doug's). After you have "defeated" each boss you go back to the same guy and he says go to this place and kill this Monster, you get the point you've played Zelda before. You go though another repetitive dungeon, solve a few puzzles, kill the "boss" and head back.
While you are exploring the dungeons you might end up doing some platforming, if fact you will. The platforming is nothing special just your standard Jumping, Climbing, Swimming, Sliding and Grabbing. The game does a somewhat nice job of this each dungeon is varied but it still similar to the last in terms of enemies. When preforming said platforming acts sometimes, not all the time, your button presses are unresponsive and you will fall to your death. Which brings me to my next point, Life and Death.
Death is a good thing in this game. If you die, you will spawn with more health then you started with. Some Monsters will do up to 2 whole health bars/skulls in one attack on easy. Health comes from smaller enemies like zombies, bats, birds and spiders, killing them will give you a small amount of health. You can also get health from one use only treasure chests, which don't completely fill your health bars/skulls. because of the shear lack of health in the game you will find yourself stuck in numerous locations, usually before an unnecessary Trap Room. If your in a situation where your on your last bit of health, find a cliff and jump off it your better off, really your are, you will respawn with 3 and a half bars ready to fight again.
The Art style for this game is great. I love it. Its reminds me of Warhammer 40k crossed with World of Warcraft crossed with Gothic Architecture. Its just a shame it was wasted on a game like this.
The PC Port for this game is better than most, the controls are okay, not the best but okay. The frame rate is great sitting on 60+ FPS. What bugs me is the lack of options for graphics, there is none. Just select your Resolution and if you want VSync then apply. You can't select Texture detail, Anti Aliasing or Model Detail. I have a low end system so i was pretty happy to be getting 60+ FPS in this game. Key mapping works good, the only problem i have is that Num Enter should be normal enter as well, i just like it like that so i don't have to move my hand off the mouse. I know i'm lazy.
In conclusion this game has its fun parts, but its mostly bad. The design of everything is bad, the story is forgettable and unengaging to say the least. What the games tries to do it fails in and it doesn't fail in the bad design will make you put the game down and never play it again. The best part about the game is the Art its everything i like Dark, Gothic and gritty, It really does complement the game but not so much im going to start playing it again. If you already own the game just avoid it and if you want to play it look up a Lets Play on youtube its not worth your time, just play a Zelda game again i would suggest Twilight Princess as its the closest to a game like this. (I didn't proof read this so it might be unintelligible nonsense, i wanted to go to bed.) Thanks for reading.
TL;DR - 3/10 Good Art style wasted on a game that is badly designed.

Duel of the Planeswalkers 2015 is a casual Magic experience that finally includes an aspect that players have been looking for; deckbuilding and collecting has returned. The game plays out a little like the old Microprose game. After a tutorial, you are handed a deck of two colors of your choosing, which is somewhat mediocre, and from there, you can explore the planes of the multiverse, and face the unique challenges of the campaign to collect cards, and improve your deck.
The experience overall is pleasant, even if some color combinations are a bit more challenging than others, and with the option of unlocking the card pool early, you can have interesting and challenging duels with other players online. Overall, you get a lot of value out of this title. The challenges are fun, and the little campaign story is a nice tie-in with the Meta Story, which is a fun touch.
There are the typical DotP complaints here. The Interface is confusing at first, and there are times where you are forced to wait when you would rather be skipping, and there are probably settings that let you change this somewhat, but they are not easily seen. The game also feels like it wants to use a control pad over key and mouse, but it works fine either way.
Graphically, we are pretty and we are boring at the same time. The Battlefield is a dull silver/gray that becomes a bluish tint when you react to the opponent's spells. The cards are nice looking, and I get a thrill when Guttersnipe attacks with it's little lightning attack. Overall, if you are patient, the combat animations, while repetitive, feel good, particularly if you have board wide effects going off.
Overall, if you are into card strategy games, Magic the Gathering, or are just looking for a casual fantasy experience, you likely will enjoy your time with this title.

this game is quite different from the past few online magic games. This game gives you the freedom to make whatever kind of deck you'd like for your kind of style from booster packs that contain common, uncommon, rare, and sometimes mythic rare cards. At the start of this game you get alot of weak cards to play with but the more battles you win the more booster packs you earn after every battle (even playing online) after progressing in the campaign you get the choice to build decks from scratch, or base decks that choose the best cards you have and allows you to either keep it that way or you can tweak it. I have some decks that i built from scratch and some that my computer generated for me without even tweaking it. If you're the kind of person you automatically needs a pre-made deck right from the start then I'd say stick to an older version but if you give it some time (or some money for collections giving you all the cards in that plane) the game can make powerful decks for you.
Now onto the online, you can only play with free-for-all, there is no 2v2 or other special modes. To me this part stinks because i loved 2v2, even in real life. Also there is no way of changing your deck without leaving the online session once you join a game. I hope they fix that problem in the future and maybe add a few more modes to play but i also like to play 1v1 so I can live with it but in my opinion the game would be a lot funner if they made more modes to play.
There are a lot of bad reviews about this game because people were caught off gaurd by the fact that YOU have to make the decks, the decks aren't made for you. There are a lot of really good cards like i got Kozilek, Butcher of Truth (got it in a premium pack when i bought the game). In real life that card is pretty rare anda great card if you have to mana for it.
Overall I'd recommend this game even though it has a tough start and limited modes, it has a lot of cards to for you to choose from to make decks of your own and i beilieve they're going to make some DLCs to add even more cards to play from.

I honestly think that a lot of the negative reviews towards this game were written without considering the game's spiritual predecessors: Wurm Online, Haven & Hearth, and whichever others gave way to inspire the mechanics in LiF. This game maintains the same level of grind as Wurm, assuming a 1.0 skillgain multiplier, while making every last accomplishment feel wonderful. When I got my first tunnel dug to ore, it was a great feeling, and then smelting the ore, and so on.
The only agonies I face in this game really come from trying to play solo, terraforming (even with other people I imagine it's dreadful to flatten out a cliff face, as it really should be.) the occasional bug and probably loss of life and items from PvP encounters. I don't quite appreciate the way the skills work, with the prerequisite skills and all that, due to the fact that A: there's a(n) (adjustable) skillcap, and B: some of the sequencing doesn't make sense. IIRC, use of chainmail is restricted to after you reach level 30 in warhorse training, and other armor skills are thrown after other random combat skills. It just doesn't feel right. Lastly, if you're playing alone, just absolutely forget about making real progression with the skillcap at its default settings, because nearly every skill is required to make a nicely functioning settlement.
Is this game worth the price tag? That's debatable. At this state, I'd personally say yeah, but I understand others that aren't as seasoned to the type of game this is might want to hold out for a sale or for more content to be ironed out and implemented. At the time of writing I've had ~40 hours in the past few days, and I've got to say, nothing feels more satisfying than seeing what all I've managed to accomplish on my own.
