Quake 4 feels like the illegitimate love child of Quake 3 and Doom 3. Add to that the feel of someone who once read about what a cool game Quake 2 was, attempting to create an edgy modern tribute.
The game is pretty bloated with annoying and unnecessary friendly AI, who's main purpose usually consists of swinging by just to say something pointless and/or die. They also enjoy shouting mean slogans at the Strogg! Theres also laborious vehicle segments that are always a drag.
The game wasnt THAT bad, but it frequently felt like work, and by the end i just wanted it to be over. Pick it up on sale if youre a long time fan of the series and a completionist, just dont expect much.
EDIT: More fun stuff! Also spoilers probably
The guns are fairly bland, most the upgrades feel like they simply make a poor gun usable rather than doing anything special. The gravity gun is just a BFG knock-off, the nailgun doesnt even make any sense appearing in the Quake 2 arc of the story, the assault rifle and shotgun are both basically as generic and lifeless as it gets.
The horror aspects of the game are also delivered poorly. Their idea of scary seems to largely consist of disembodied torsos. I mean theres only so many torsos you can see before it becomes tiresome - like seriously theyre everywhere. The main characters stroggification procedure was one of the few saving graces.
The first(?) boss where you get the gravity gun was pretty good, but the rest were kinda meh, and the end boss was utterly dissapointing. You shoot it a couple times with the gravity gun and it just drops. Then you get a second phase where you essentially do the same, except theres a momentarily confusing shield/generator phase to get through. The overall difficulty of the game was pretty easy, even on second highest difficulty. The only reason i didnt play on highest is a melee unit kept 1shotting me with its special as soon as it came on the screen at the start of the game.
Vehicle/rail shooter segments consist of spamming the fire button in the general direction of enemies, and hoping they die before you do. Theyre neither rewarding or enjoyable.
The enemies Quake 4 provides were actually one of the better features. They all feel pretty good and show clear progression and strategies to deal with.

AFF has immense potential - the core promise of infantry/ship/armor combat is already there.
These are my initial thoughts, made on WEEK ONE of release. Obviously the game will change drastically during Early Access so please treat my comments as such.
Positives
+ Unique mix of combat - you can board capital ships and destroy internals as your friendlies attack the ship exterior.
+ Unique combat roles - players can choose a bunch of different roles, including the Commander and Squad Leader role.
+ Immense customization - weapons, vehicles and ships have extensive loadouts, available right from the start.
+ Vast and varied environments - the levels are large and can be beautiful at times,
+ Huge battles - 64 players online is impressive and caters directly for clans.
+ AAF has been made by a bunch of modders since 2005, surely that deserves a thumbs up?
Negatives
- User Interface - UI needs visual overhaul, the text placement and scaling can be downright ugly
- Not friendly to newcomers - new players may feel lost when starting a game
- Performance - framerate hitching and low FPS, though may be my dated rig
- Sterile environments - levels are lacking in detail and have bland lighting

This game finishes the story set up in Legend and Anniversary. Whereas the other two games displayed polished gameplay, controls, and story, Underworld seems to have been created by the developer's B team with no quality control checks implemented.
The controls and jump/grab detection are atrocious and the game seems to arbitrarily decide when the player gets to make a jump or die miserably. I would estimate about 2-3 hours of my playtime are due to this recurrent situation and I promise you will experience many hours of frustrating restarts, as well.
The camera is horrible, as well, and twitchy angles serve to compound the issues the controls and detection failures create.
It is also a buggy game. For example, if you fall off a ledge while crouching, you will not die no matter how far the fall. Another example, which is far worse, is if you die at certain times during puzzles, the game will simply reset your puzzle. Minor spoilers:
Combat is awful and plentiful (overly so for a Tomb Raider). Good luck dodging.
The puzzles were great. I really enjoyed the puzzles. They could be pretty tough relative to the previous two, which was a nice change of pace.
The story is all right. The story is the second reason I was able to slog through this otherwise tortuous experience. There were some good moments and the big reveals towards the end were cool. Don't get me wrong, the actual resolution keeps in tune with the rest of the experience: still pretty lame.
Honestly, my finishing this game is really a testament to Legend and Anniversary because the whole time, I kept thinking I would be doing a disservice to those two if I didn't finish the trilogy. Overall, Underworld is a frustrating, buggy mess and I would encourage the reader to avoid it. If you have to buy it, get it on sale and be prepared.

A really great game, definatly deserves the score and it's probably one of the best RPGs of all time. Very close to being as good as the first one. Though... There are some problems with it. I don't know if this is the game in general since it was rushed (We'll get to that later) or just steam in general but when I first started it, it kept crashing. ALLOT. It may not act up for you if you have windows XP, or vista, but anything above 7 you probably will experiance crashing. How I found to fix it, is go into your options and fix your resolution. If you have an HD monitor, having it play below HD will cause it to crash, aswell as having it 1080p if you have a 720p monitor. Long story short, just use the resolution your screen was meant for. I also oddly experianced frame rate drops from around a solid 35 FPS to around 15 when I was around smoke or fog. There might be an option for it, but I never bothered. Also, a downside is in some cutscenes, and even for a few characters in game from time to time, the audio was completely gone. Like some others have said, it doesn't have the "full audio" checked off, but that's not a game breaker.  The story itself is suprisingly good, before I got it I'd heard allot of hate on the game. It's not bad, I actually really enjoyed the story except it felt a bit... rushed. In some places you'd have a very slow intense buildup, then all of a sudden you'd be rushed through waves of enemies and boom. You're done with the mission. It was somewhat annoying. Also, devolopment with other characters is really screwy... Some characters are completely numb, and the others that you can devolop a close relationship for, you seem to never have the time for it. To devolop a relationship with a character you need to gain influence, the best way to gain influence is to appeal to them while they are traveling with you. You can only have two other people with you, and you'll soon find that some characters hold themselves in combat FAR better then others. The combat is as smooth as ever and you'll use the same tactics from one, nothing has really changed in that aspect. Yet it's far from the first. In the first KOTOR you'd be fighting both sith and jedi, having epic lightsaber battles. You do have a lightsaber, and some of your companions can use a lightsaber and the force, but it doesnt feel right. Lightsabers are meant to fight other lightsabers, though throught the whole game (Untill the litteral last part) Maybe like... 12 people? Yeah, around 12 will have lightsabers. They compensate for this by having these "Sith assasins" that use staffs to make up for it, but they throw them in WAVES AND WAVES AND WAVES; to the point where it just becomes a damned chore to fight them.
The very begining planet, is very slow, which is nice since it teaches the new people to play, but if you are like me and have played the original hundreds of hours you will get frustrated with it. The game is great, but the devoloper obsidian was rushed to produce it, so allot of things fall flat, and many things that should be in place. aren't. There's a mod to fix this, called the restored content mod, which even adds a new planet and hours upon hours of new content to enrich the story, you may want to check that out.
Overall I got about 30 hours out of the main storyline and some important sidequests, I didint finish all the sidequests, so adding those would probably add another two or three. Also this game brings back the 'organic meatbag' slaughtering HK-47, so that's a plus on its side.
All in all heres an overview
Story: 9/10
Combat: 7/10
Character Devolopment: 6/10
Customization: 7/10
Replayability: 6/10
Overall, I'd give it a 7.5/10 If it's on sale, pick it up. But I wouldn't be too keen on buying it full price, even though it is ten dollars, for that you should either buy the original KOTOR if you don't own it, or one of the Jedi Knight games. Those are good.

RiME is almost certainly worth your time, but it's less likely worth the price for most people I know.
Much of it is comparable to a game like Journey or Abzu - very good and very consistent visuals, and an entirely nonverbal story. There's some puzzle-solving, but none of it is anything that will tax your brain so much. It's a relaxing game to play, which depending on your mood may be just what you need.
Ending thoughts for me are mixed. I disliked that you basically know nothing about the game's meaning until the reveal at the end. To me, that didn't really feel like satisfying pacing - like each scene before the ending just resulted in mental confusion, like "This could mean anything".
I actually think Tequila Works' other game this year, The Sexy Brutale, pulled off this kind of eye-opening twist ending much better, with little hints and other little stories spread throughout the early game, as well as more satisfying writing/gameplay even when it's not contributing to "the reveal". Basically, RiME often felt more empty - which may be okay for a lot of people.
In spite of misgivings, I can still recommend the game for a playthrough, and I know the ending hit some people harder than me, so it may be a more valuable experience to you. I think it's safe to wait for a sale on it, though.

It's 9 years old and still one of my favorite games of all time (The original and skyrim being above it)
First, the graphics are timeless. It looks just as good relative to other games of its time on 2012+ hardware in 2014 as it looked on an original xbox console in 2005. While there aren't really any graphics customization options, there doesn't need to be.
Second, the gameplay is amazing. The combat system is simple yet very satisfying. (I use the same attack move every single time and it never gets old) And the rpg elements are really good as well.
Third, the story is really well developed. While I admittedly didn't pay much attention to the story, there is plenty out there for you fanatics, such as extended dialogue options, journals (holopads) and sidequests.
The ONLY downside to this steam purchase is that the PC compatibility is bad. You have to do some tweaking with the config files to get this game to run on a newer operating system. That being said it's well worth it!
Now to address the "rush job" arguments that everyone makes. Yes, this game could have been much better if obsidian had the chance to work on it longer. But if you consider this game independent of the first, it is definately still a great game!

I got this from GS for 3 bucks in a box and everything, figured I'd give this game a try, I heard ...really only negative things about it. Till this day I like me some Duke3D so I was hoping for some good times here.
Turns out the game isn't that bad, it's by no means great, the visuals are dated and there's some silly parts but it's more amusing than the slew of games trying to be as real as possible. Is DNF a dumb game? Heck yes it is, it's dumb as hell and that's why it's good- it's not trying to be story driven, it knows what it is and rolls with it like a good b-movie.
Since it came out it's clearly been updated, 4 weapon limit instead of 2 (that's a nice fix there) and I've not had many crashes so far. The guns have a nice feel to them, the alien weapons less so but the guns really feel powerful, and if that's not your thing you can always hurl weights into the faces of aliens which looks even more hard hitting.
The visuals are dated but that's how Duke 3D was, Quake was out shortly around Duke 3D and that didn't stop it from being fun eh? The game looks fine, I don't get the hate for this stuff especially with the slew of retro games that GoG puts out that get so much love. Yes this game came out looking like a slightly nicer Doom3 years later but screw it that's not what makes a game.
For 60 the game would have been a major let down, but for 3? I'm MORE than happy and I'ds say even up to 15 it's not a bad time. I'm not saying this game is great, I'm saying it's good, it's not bad and it's certainly not as crap as the reviewers lead you to believe. See it on sale? Nab it if you like silly shooters.

*** EDIT at 278 hours played ***
Another year, another MTG Duels of the Planeswalkers game. As always the game offers an arcade style way of learning how to play the classic 1993 card game, which is easy to learn and hard to master.
-DECK BUILDING AND CARD POOL-
This edition finally features custom deck building, although you start off by selecting two colors and receiving enough cards to start playing with those colors. At multiple points, later on in the campaign, players are enabled to pick starter packs of different colors (called 'archetypes'). Winning additional cards is achieved by winning single- and multiplayer games, at which point players receive a booster pack that contains random cards that can be used to adjust your deck or build new decks.
As a player I'm personally very happy deck building is introduced, because in the previous edition certain decks were way too popular to my liking, making the multiplayer rather boring (decks like Avacyn's Glory and Chant of the Mul Daya).
At first glance a card pool of 300 different cards - plus a so called 'premium' card pool of 40 or so that can only be accessed by buying booster packs for real money - may sound limiting, but seeing you'll receive some of these cards 2-4 times, it all adds up to plenty of chances to express your creativity as a player in deck building (EDIT: since writing this review the premium card pool has been made available to all!). Newbs can also use an auto completion function in the deck builder if they are unsure on how to finish up building a new deck, but remember trial and error and streamlining your own deck is part of the fun of the game. Nevertheless, a card pool of 300 cards for an annual edition is a rather limited number when compared to the over 600+ cards that real magic introduces every year.
Speaking on deck management, this function has been greatly improved in this editon with plenty of filters, like the ability to only show newly won cards. Also, last edition would not handle alt tabbing very well. Magic 2015 handles alt tabbing perfectly: when you enter the game again after al tabbing the changes on the table are updated properly. Also, I haven't had any disconnects or opponents disconnecting so far, so the netcode might have been improved as well.
-GAMEPLAY AND GAME MODES-
As in last edition the campaign is split up in a number of chapters, each comprising of 5 duels and an exploration event featuring 5 duels. The game also comes with a good tutorial that, sadly for veterans, is mandatory. Apart of that there is of course a multiplayer mode that features 1vs1 quick matches and 2 to 4 player ffa. Although this game certainly enables players to enjoy single- and multiplayer Magic, the small number of game modes and a lack of a decent lobby system to continue playing with the same players after finishing a game feels limited when compared to last year's Magic 2014.
Especially the 2vs2 co-op type experience will certainly be missed, which perhaps was necessary to prevent partners from using identical decks or perfect combinations and ruling the leaderboards. Why this game mode, as well as sealed deck mode, is ommitted is unclear. Why not give players the choice to play the game modes they enjoy the most?
-USER INTERFACE-
One of the biggest downsides of this edition, however, are the menu structures and animations. Very banal things turn into such a drag with the horrible way these menu's are designed and animated. It takes too much time to go from gameplay to the main menu and to the deck builder, and then back at it again. Players with multiple decks who win a couple of boosters will have to spend a lot of time in the deck builder to update their decks with the newly additions, watching the clock tick while they have to go back to the main menu after editing a deck each time to start working on the next, unable to simply switch decks from the deck manager.
Similar problems become apparant throughout gameplay. Another example is the fact players cannot simply pick a deck from the lobby before a single- or multiplayer match. Instead they have to 'equip' a deck before hand. Also, when a player restarts a match he should be able to immediately choose whether he wants to pick another deck or do a quick restart with the same deck. In reality a couple of seconds are spent every time to watch the menu's pop up or disappear using mist forming animations that, seeing players will have to do this a lot, become very annoying after the first half hour of gameplay. It's cumbersome stuff that reminds me of the way Gran Turismo 5 on ps3 handled it's menu's (EDIT: browsing through the menu now goes a lot smoother after patching!). In fact the menu's have been made worse in comparison to Magic 2014, with big icons players have to click through on a full hd resolution pc monitor instead of having complete menu's written in letters on a single screen.
As stated before, also lacking is a decent lobby system. After playing a game both players get thrown back into the multiplayer selection screen, and do not go back into the lobby to pick a deck and go at it again. This was a bad design choice, limiting social interactions in the multiplayer environment of Magic 2015 and it really makes you wonder how much love the designers have for this legendary card game. In the last edition the lobby's were always full of afk hosts coming out of games in which all the other players had already left and going afk while loading up the lobby. In this edition, there is no real lobby system at all. Why this option was picked over the installation of an afk timer for hosts after each match? I have no clue.
It seriously is hard to imagine the designers of this editon played last year's Magic 2014 at all... A very sad thing indeed.
-CONCLUSION-
All in all, some very odd design choices from Stainless Steel that have been in the business for many years. There's no decent lobby system, the menu's have never been worse, as well as missing game modes.
Still, looking at pure gameplay mechanics this game is a great strategy game that can be recommended to anyone. And as a whole Magic 2015 is a functional video game, offering many hours of great strategic gameplay with deck building for only 10 bucks. There's a reason this trading card game has been around since 1993! Sadly, this edition hardly feels like the next annual chapter in a long running series. However, at the end of the day the core gameplay is more or less perfect and this game does offer an accessible yet rewarding Magic The Gathering experience to all. Recommended!

I enjoy the Duels of the Planeswalkers games for what they are: digital alternatives to solitaire. As the official MTG Judge for my Local Game Store, I sometimes want to get away from the crazy worlds of standard, draft, and EDH to set sail to the magical christmasland that is DotP. It's quick, casual, and mildly entertaining. So, how does the newest installment measure up?
My god this is awful.
The game started right off on the wrong foot with its clunky options menu clearly designed with consoles in mind, low default resolution, and just about every unnecesary gameplay option defaulted to "on". After running through this foolishness, I then attempted to hop into a game, but DotP informed me that in order to play through the campaign, I must first complete the tutorial.
Okay. Simple enough.
Wait, did I say tutorial? I meant Tutorials. Plural. As in SIX of them.
The tutorials are ridiculously hand-holdy even for beginners. The annoying lady-voice assumes that you have only heard of such ephemeral passing concepts as "mana" and "attacking" from some distant melody as if in a dre- GODDAMNIT STOP! I'm L1 for crissakes! How much more of this must I endure?!
After you get past the tutorials and jump into the game, it doesn't get much better. Deck building has been introduced, but it is so fundamentally flawed that it astounds me how they could get such a thing so wrong. Remember Sealed Mode from 2014? It's basically that, but for the whole game.
The main problem is that while the game will let you build a deck, it won't let you build a GOOD deck. The starter decks that you get in the beginning are absolute trash, and the "Booster Packs" that you get for defeating opponents aren't much better. To describe them, imagine all of the least playable commons and uncommons from Innistrad, Theros, Zendikar, Return to Ravnica, and the last four Core Sets. Well, that's pretty much what your pool is gonna look like after an hour or two of grinding each plane for boosters.
On top of that, some of the selections for cards are just baffling. Black Spot removal at five mana? Every other DotP had it at two or three! Sorcery-speed unsummon and lightning bolt? Four to five mana for counterspells? Your only real option if you want to play any kind of reactive deck is to splash red for removal early on, but that gets derailed by the fact that every creature has a ridiculous amount of toughness for its curve (thanks Theros) and you won't get any boardwipes before the fourth plane unless you pull really REALLY lucky.
But hey, is that what's bugging you? Luck got you down? Can't pull the cards you need? Well don't worry! The good ol' wizard on the coast has the solution!
Just buy 'em! With real money!
That's right ladies and gentlemen, Duels of the Planeswalkers 2015 has built-in Microtransactions for ingame boosters or card collections.
(flips table)
What else is wrong? Well for one, challenge mode is gone. The encounters have all been turned into regular opponents with randomized decks. All the old problems are still around: The AI that taps your lands for you and orders blockers for you is downright awful, AI in general is pretty lacking throughout, the game's difficulty is still completely artificial with the AI stacking your opponents' decks while making sure you always draw exactly what you don't need for the situation. At one point I actually caught the opponent playing a land without actually decreasing the number of cards in their hand. In paper Magic this wouldn't just be cheating, it would be physically impossible!
The matches with random scrubs are mind-numbingly boring until you hit the boss for each plane, which each present so sharp a difficulty spike that you could equip it to an invisible stalker and knock off half your opponent's life with each hit. The encounter with Teysa Karlov, for example, damn near gave me an aneurism. The only way my deck could beat her was to restart the game until I got a Stormbreath Dragon in my hand, and half the time she would either (A) Kill me before I could cast it or (B) Make me discard it. On top of all of this, whether boring or difficult, NONE of the AI decks are fun to play against.
Anything else? Hell, I dunno. Do you like the new borders? Not really? Well they're around. They even put the holofoils on all the rares. You know, in case someone tries to counterfeit these digital cards that don't even have collector numbers printed on them. And challenge mode is gone. I know I said that one already, but damn that one pisses me off!
The hell with all this. I'm done. Don't buy DotP 2015. It's not even worth it for the paper promo (25 cent mythic for Xbox owners, 1 buck mythic for everyone else). Go play Cube or EDH with your friends at your local game store instead. And if you know anyone who microtransed for a booster pack in this game, slap the bejezus out of them.

Wow. I have like a hundred hours on this game and i still haven't written a review. Well, better late than never... (sorry for cliché)
This game is... mmmmwah! (immagine an italian chef being impressed) Its trait system for family members is great and quite realistic, all the campaigns are fun, and it lets you pretend like you are the ruler of your empire-soon-to-be. This let me imagine and theorise what the future would have been like (e.g. win as carthage, what would the world have been like today?) which is always a fun exercise. Also, the managing of cities and maintaining public order is both realistic and very deep. For example, don't make people happy = settlement revolts, turning to rebel hands.
The AI for this game is also surprisingly good, considering its era. The AI actually has the capability to fight back, or, like in many of my games, they all dogpile on you when you start to get good. That can become annoying, as over-expansion of one's empire can be disaterous at times.
The diplomacy for the game is also quite in depth, allowing you to form alliances, ask for ceasefires (if you are at war with someone), make trade agreements, exchange map information, and a few more that i have forgotten.
Finally,I'd like to commend The Creative Assembly for balancing all the factions so well. All the factions have their strengths and weaknesses, except maybe for the roman factions (although, those campaigns are quite boring. I suggest playing as Germania as soon as you unlock them, as they are a nice and diverse and fun). Even the unplayable factions are fun!
And so I conclude my reveiw. I would say like and subscribe, but this isn't a YouTube video. Goodbye.

I'm not usually very verbose on these things but I felt that this game needed a much deserved boost. This is a labour of love and I can tell from the small details like the star maps in the briefing room. It all helps conjour an atmosphere, and the briefings do just that. It feels like your inside the setting.
But enough of that. If you take Planetside / Planetside 2, a bit of Elite:Dangerous, Call of Battlefield Ops (you know, the whole overplayed first person shooter genre with loadouts and numerous weapons etc but with a grander feel) with the feel of a hollywood film, then you have the gist of Angels Fall First.
It's very early in the early access lifecycle, and player have a lot to master. It's more of a mech/battle machine style flavour to it where your equipment takes x number of 3 different categories to equip and you can't overload. You can have any weapon straight away, but chances are you'll have no secondary weapon, additional armour etc until you level up. It's not a linear levelling either. If you command troops more than actual fighting, then only the yellow Command bar goes up. You level up the 3 main "skills" in order to carry more equipment, anmd it works surprisingly well.
I've only played the bots so far, and it's very entertaining just with that. Reminds me of the old days with Unreal Tournament where I would train myself up against bots before embarrassing myself against human players. I really love what this game represents. Real feudal life. Hard, unkind, and taking effort to eke out a living. You get to experience struggle. But then, that's where the dream goes horribly wrong. I understand that they had to make concessions with the interface becaue they wanted to keep the servers from getting loaded with crap on the ground and have it crash. But the methods they came up with to deal with that aspect are painful to work around. Please note that *my friend and I played* this game with the server set on default settings. I wasn't solo.
Let's go from the experience of making a house. The first little hut that you can make at the begining. So how would you make a house/hut in real life? Well, first you'd get some tools. Then you'd use the tools to gather the resources. Then you'd use the same tools or other tools to refine said resources. Then finally you'd assemble said refined resources in some fashion to construct the final product. Also I should include the reality of dealing with the terrain by preparing it. This is both an acceptable convention and a logical one. However, the developers of LiF:YO have decided that they wanted to do it their way.
The LiF:YO way. First you start off by gathering the tool components. I'm with them at this point. You grab some branches, flint, and plant fiber and away you go with your tools. But here's where it gets convoluted. You don't now get to walk up to a tree, small or otherwise, and start smacking it. You have to "know" how to cut this tree down. So start learning. So grab some branches off a tree and other things to learn. Ok, you now know how to cut the tree down, but not all trees, because an axe on hardwood works differently than on softwood. Ok, fair enough, there's something there I won't argue with. But now I want to refine the wood into the construction materials. I have the tools, but again, I don't know how to cut a log into planks or construction posts. So to learn this, I pull more branches off trees and grab saplings and peel bark and cut down more trees. So finally I know how to make a log and planks and I get the materials I need to make the house. So I can make the hut right? Wrong. Now I need to go dig a hole in the ground, over and over and over... Why, you ask? Because I need to learn how to construct a house. The skill required to construct this house is called Construction Material Preparation and you need it to a pretty high level. So appearently digging a hole in the ground and dropping the dirt over and over again teach you something about building a hut. But the digging part is only for the prerequisite skill. Once that is high enough, you start digging rocks. But this does not get you the skill you need directly. You must "refine" this rock into smooth stone to learn the art of building. Eventually you finally get the skills required to build said hut and can relax with a Mojito on the porch looking into the forest you just razed to build it.
My other complaint is that what do you do with all the rock and stone and wood that you didn't use up in this endeavor? You can't put it in storage, because that would require nails and stuff that requires iron ore that requires... Ok, I could go on, but the point is, this game requires you to do things that make absolutely no sense to level up without connections to other things that make sense. One last thing. I can respect the fact they don't want a pile of dirt to fit inside a sack that you drop on the ground as your only means of storage early game. But they already broke that convention with the planks and smooth stone and trees that you can stuff in the sack unrealistically. So make up your mind. You can't have it both ways. It's annoying as hell to have to walk away from your work just to dump dirt and rock on the ground while the capenter has filled his sack to the brim with a forest of goodies. Which by the way, if I wanted to give my buddy a rock to make a cooking pot, it can't happen early game. He has to dig his own rock, which also takes grinding a skill.
I should further note that the majority of people currently enjoying this game are bypassing this entire process by using Admin commands. Doing things like creating resource piles of infinite resources because the mining is still broken. This hardly makes the game as epic and good as they are letting on. If you aren't willing to play the game the way it was meant to be played, at least have the decency to note that in a review. Also, if you are bypassing all the "broken" content with changed server settings. What does that really say about this game?
TL:DR I feel like in the end, if I play this game I feel I'd make a better use of my time making an actual hut in my backyard out of the same material this game uses in far less time. I also wouldn't have to learn how to swing an axe for each type of tree I want to cut down. I'd like to know how this character made it to adulthood not knowing how to dig holes and catch food. If this is the direction they want to go for the final product, there's no way I can say "Well done." Please rethink the skill tree and material aquisition aspect of this game and I will revisit your fine work. But untill then, I'll be in my backyard finishing my castle.

Angels Fall First is a great and fun game, even at this stage in Early Access. Apart from some bugs, it almost feels as if it's a full release, not an EA game. I've only played singleplayer with bots, haven't tried any actual multiplayer, so account for that when reading the list below
Pros:
- FUN Gameplay
- I love the art style, some folks don't care for the textures and all that, but they work well for me
- The switching between between ship to ground combat on several of the maps is something that most games don't do, and is done beautifully here, even if it can be a bit glitchy at times (for now).
- Minor atmospheric things; consoles displaying the health status of turrets in real-time on capital ships, viewscreens that display the outside of dropships when in their module, or that display the outside of a capital ship when in the crew quarters
Cons:
- Some bugs (Camera view clips through the Swift's hull when using lower railguns, sometimes dropping through the world. Bug with the biggest issue for me is that when docking a strike craft for refit/repair, I try to board to switch into a dropship or another class of strike craft, and my infantry character spawns still on the space map, and I can float/fly around. Kind of amusing, actually =P)
- Lack of maps with space/ground transition (Currently only two, although if you count the base map and their Territory variety, you have four. Not the biggest con, by a long shot. Each game can go entirely different.)
- Ranks/levels gained are not currently persistent. (Makes weapon/upgrade choices somewhat limited. In game you can increase your "star" level, and gain more requisiton points in the Combat, Command, and Supply tracks, however any rank increases or point maximum increases you gain disappear at the end of the round. If this is just in singleplayer, or is how it is in Multiplayer, I don't know however it would be nice to have it be persistent.)
Overall, seriously, get this game, it is completely and utterly worth the price.

Random ramble: Lackluster and short story, but that's fine because Ubisoft focuses on the online aspect of this game. That being said; This is by far one of the most infuriating and unbalanced pvp experiences I've had. The game comes out, feeling like it's an early access pvp game, with a lot of gamebreaking glitches, clunky controls and even worse balancing. The game has an amazing artstyle with some of the best animations I've ever seen, however that doesn't justify the horrible online experience it has given me for the ridiculous price it gave us.
The game is going to have the same seasonal progression as R6 siege has (heroes coming out season-by-season), with 4 gamemodes currently.
Duel - 1v1 without gear stats (which is a good thing) on rather small maps. Problem with the maps is that most of them have a lot of cliffs and hazards that makes the gameplay feel unfair and unbalanced (viking tank can literally push you 12 yards without you being able to do anything).
Brawl - 2v2 without gear stats (Great and fun most of the time) which places you and your teammate in separate 1v1s on a medium sized map, sometimes small. This is where you either act ''honorably'' by doing separate 1v1s or gang up. Lots of salt from this mode btw.
Dominion - 4v4 which was supposed to be the main mode for this game and is basically just a zone capture with respawns until team break points. This can be a fun experience, but is mostly horribly annoying due to all the perks and traits and gear stats (Samurai and vikings get perks that gives a situational ranged option, which hits wayy to hard btw, and knights gets a weak healing spell with limited charges...)
Elimination - 4v4 elimination is a mode if you're either too bad in 2v2s/1v1s OR you just have one-two many teammates and have to queue some 4s. This basically puts your team on different places of a map in seperate 1v1s at start. You can obviously run away from ur 1v1 and team up etc. There are also buff pickups on the map which seem pretty damn strong. I usually get queued up against a premade team and end up ragequitting the game. Gear, traits and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t are all included in this mode.
Overall the appeal of the game for me is the immersion, artstyle and sometimes the gameplay. Do I recommend for the price? Not at all, this is by far one of the most disappointing releases for me last couple of years, on par with no mans sky(I didnt care much for NMS). But if you're competitive and will do ANYTHING (using OP characters and exploiting) then it's still not worth due to the heavy price. If you expected ''the next Chivalry'' I'd suggest you go back to chivalry and have some fun with your friends.
Take note: This game got released recently, with very few beta tests for balancing. So I've got my fingers crossed for the dev team to make this game what it deserves to be; A great medieval fighting game.

1. So I wanted to play a 2x2 game with my friend (a gamemode in which there are 4 players in 2 teams). He made a lobby and invited me to it, but every time when we make the lobby, then always random players automatically join it before me. To be with my friend in the same team, I had to join my friend's lobby as the first player. When I joined as second or third, then my friend had to be in opposite team with a random guy... When there are already 4 players in 2x2 game lobby, then one of the players starts the 20 seconds countdown and every player has to hit "Ready" button to accept the incoming game. BUT even if you don't hit that button, you are joined to the game anyway. The funnier thing is that during the countdown you just can't exit the lobby, so you have to exit to the ♥♥♥♥ing operating system, run the game again and try to join with your friend to the same team AGAIN.

I have to say the game is really good. The way slugcat handles CAN be frustrating at times but ive learned to work with it. Im nearing the end of the game and havent had too much struggle except for really far jumps and the five pebbles region for reasons I wont spoil.
Here are some tips i learned that may help others.
-food replenishes every 2-3 successful hibernations.
-food eaten in the current "life", and you die before hibernating, gets reset.
-jump over the green lizards!
-the vultures helmet scares creatures! Use a spear!
-go veeery slowly around monster kelp.
-dont reset too soon if a lizard gets you. You might get saved by it getting attacked.
-you are only truely dead if 1: slug cat has an x.x face, or 2: you dont come back on the screen (I.E a lizard makes it to a one-way pipe and comes out without you.)
-There is almost always a hibernation chamber somewhere near a gate, with food nearby to get you to the karma you need.
-i have yet needed to use the shopping from those tribal guys. I stole light from a guy i found randomly. Saved me a lot of trouble.
-items remain in hibernation chambers forever! Dont be afraid to leave valuables in a chamber you will come back to. (At least i found my old light stone was still there after coming back.)
-blue flash seeds kill spiders.
-blue rock-like seeds that seem to only be thrown actually become edible bubbles when placed in water.
-double tap shift to switch hand held items.
-slug cat swims faster while submerged but will auto swim up and get stuck if low on air. Be careful. (Hardest thing to control to be honest)
-steal those weapons from the tribal guys. Sone are really powerful!
-you can kill lizards with enough spears!
My best strategy was to forgo trying to survive in a new area. Focus on exploration. If you die, map out the area in your head and try to find a gate or a hibernation chamber. When you find it, take a mental note where it is and then spend your time feeding on your way back to it (or while there.)
Also save your survivor achievement. You get a special something that will prove VERY handy later on! Dont use it unless you absolutely have to! I wasted mine and found out its a one time use. Period.
All in all i do highly recommend playing this. I hope this review helps many.

I loved this game. I have the other two in the trilogy - Anniversary and Legend. However, this one is for the PC, my others for PS2. To compare them:
Story is best in Underworld, but also great in Legend. Anniversary I found did not have enough story, with a basic plotline, but I get it was a remake of a classic. There's always something happeneign in Underworld, cutscenes in every level. So many surprises in Underworld, and I like that it takes a darker turn.
Rewards are not as good. There are a larger amount of treasures to find than in Legend, but I can't remember in comparison to Anniversary (are there more in Anniversary?). The rewards are all concept art and character designs. No unlockable outfits, bringing me to ...
Outfits. Smallest selection available in the trilogy. You cannot 'unlock' any, but the selection is available from the start. At each level you are given a choice of 2 - 3 outfits corresponding with the location (you can't play with winter clothes in Thailand).
Graphics are amazing. I love the difference. I'm not usually one interested in graphics, but this changed me. I don't know if it's just PC vs PS2, but they helped so much for me. Seeing Amanda again with better graphics really changed the game for me. Although, seeing Lara in some scenes she looks so much older!
Moves have definately been improved. Lara is able to do more with the controls. More jumps, climbs, etc. Fantastic, everywhere. She can now walk/balance on the poles you only used to swing on.
Weapons are interesting. With the entire selection available from the start, unlike outfits you can use them all anywhere. They all (except her classic pistols) have limited ammo, and ammo cannot be found throughout the level.
Levels are a good length as well. They are fairly restricted (corridor levels), but it's better than Legend. Longer than Legend, not as big as Anniversary.
Overall, this one is my favourite. I couldn't decide between this or Legend, but this is great. The story is so intense and exciting, even though ocassionally predictable, I liked it. It tied together all loose ends, and didn't leave anything hanging. The level replay style is quite different to Legend and Anniversary becuase once you have played all levels, you revisit them exactly as you left them so there are no more enemies (except regenerative ones) and the puzzles are all already solved. Welcome to Justaposition: The Game.
For every single thing that Rain World does right, a massive price is paid for it. It's an interesting creation, being the result of a developer/artist/programmer who apparently played few games before beginning work on this. Like every other feature to this game, that proves to be both a good and bad thing; good because it offers a chance for a new perspective of what a game can be into the industry, undiluted by over-saturated game mechanics, unimaginative structures and generally the toxic of the CoDs and EA games of the world, yet bad because it offers no experience for spotting the subtleties in game design, the small things that can make the difference between a masterpiece and a deeply, deeeeeply flawed experience with a short lifespan.
Initially I listed all the most prominent features of this game, followed by the pros and cons of each one in a fairly rigid structure - but I exceeded the character limit. So instead I'll leave the other reviews to go into more specifics and I'd just like to try and be helpful to the developers and list what I think could be done to vastly improve the game:
Give the ability to throw objects vertically & diagonally as well. Just do that. That can be patched. Just do it. For Christ's sake.
Make the days the same length, or at least the same length within each specific region. Just do that. That can be patched. Just do it. For Christ's sake.
Either nerf or remove the Daddy Longlegs. Just do that. That can be patched. Just do it. For Christ's sake.
Make it so Slugcat can't go backwards in vents, remove some of the pointless other passages that serve only to hinder and possibly give Slugcat just a slightly higher jump. Just do that. That can be patched. Just do it. For Christ's sake.
Don't make the grapple-bugs weigh you down, and also don't give them the ability to latch onto you with their tounges. Just do that. That can be patched. Just do it. For Christ's sake.
Make slugcat a bit brighter in water BEFORE you get the light after finding the alien. Just... you know.
Fix, fix, FIX the Karma mechanic. It, along with the controls, seems to be the number 1 most complained about aspect of the game. Instead of having to have a certain level to progress to the next zone, why not just have a set target of times to hibernate in one area before you've "conquered" it and can move onto the next one? And the amount of food in the region can be built around that. Just do that.
Remove some of the falls. A game with controls as unreliable as this should not have as many opportunities for falling to your death as it does. Just... do... it.
Rain World leaves me feeling broken and depressed. It boasts such a beautiful and endearing world design, and the simple and simply told story of a young, cute creature trying to return to its family is more than enough motivation to play and push through the apocalyptic wreckage. However that motivation is slowly savaged and worn away by the repetetiveness that comes with being stuck in one area unable to progress, with no hibernation point ahead in sight and still dying to the same creatures or awkward jumps over and over again. Rain World gets extreme difficulty extremely wrong in that respect. To make a game challenging but fair two key ingredients are needed: Tight controls, which this game just. Does. Not. Have. The wobbly physics ruin that, and it also requires the opportunity to master, to "git gud", to learn by trial and error, which is rendered impossible by this game's unpredictable nature. I made it to just the beginning of The Underhang, and have experienced 20-plus deaths trying to get to the next hibernation point which I haven't even determined the location of yet. Sometimes I get way ahead only to be rained on to death, other times I get snared by the completely unfairly omnipresent Daddy Longlegs on the very second screen. It makes me sad to think that I won't be able to enjoy the remainder of the game because of the broken shards left in it, and the most annoying part is this game lures you in with its beauty and actually makes you want to play it before you begin to realise you probably won't ever complete it.
EDIT: I got to the Five Pebbles area. This game is awful. Utter garbage. Don't buy it. They botched that part up so terribly it ruins the entire experience. Complete waste of my time to spend hours on an already patience-stretching game to get to a part so broken and hair-pullingly frustrating and unfair that it halts you in your tracks. The people who made this game don't understand the intricacies of high difficulty at all. A load of crap.

If you pay the $35 for this game, you will be paying to skip content. The "pick a deck, but you're stuck with it" gimmick is bad design and the devs are bad for doing it. No preview of the decks, just a vague description that in my case was totally misleading. I chose Red->Black which was described as "focusing on stealing your opponent's creatures and sacrificing them for fun and profit". Yeah it was just a plain RB aggro deck with 2 Act of Treason and 2 vampires that could sacrifice creatures for a +1/+1 counter...in a 60-card deck. 4 cards does not a focus make.
But that bad design was merely irritating, not game-breaking. I could live with it.
The deck-building feature is good, it's about time that they added it. However, they didn't actually add it. They replaced all other features with it, for a net loss of game. Let's see what the trade off was for something that should have been a standard feature years ago:
No more Two-Headed Giant, either co-op vs AI or multiplayer.
No more Planechase multiplayer.
No Challenge puzzles.
No Sealed campaigns.
Is all that worth it? Hell no.
This is a blatant money-grab by Wizards, who clearly fear losing players from MTGO if they add too much actual gameplay here, which is completely stupid as the two games serve two different fanbases.

Nether is the true answer to online first-person survival games. Being only in early access as of this review, this game is already a match for DayZ.
Like DayZ, you start with very little and are forced to search the deadly, infested world you probably once called home. Scrounge for food and weapons to keep yourself alive, always sneaking to avoid alerting the horrors that stalk the streets, or at least make that trigger-happy player not hear your footsteps as you come up behind him with a kitchen knife.
Unlike DayZ, however, the enemies are just as much of a threat as other players. And also there are a few RPG elements strewn about like levelling your character's skills to make them more effective in a few categories including but not limited to melee combat, guns, and survival.
In DayZ, you would find the zombies to be hardly any threat at all because they were incredibly easy to sneak past and if you /did/ somehow alert them you could give them a good clean poke and they would fall to their knees and immediately commit ritual seppuku...Ok that might be a bit of an exaggeration, but the point is the zombies in DayZ were almost no threat at all to anyone who got the basics of the game down and all they had to worry about was players Killing On Sight (KOSing).
But in Nether, the ever-lethal abominations that roam the streets (also called Nethers) are akin to some demonic abomination you would find if you fused together DOOM and Dead Space. Did I mention they can teleport?
Most of my deaths in-game have actually been from the Nether, because they come in all shapes, sizes, and ways of killing you in the face. Not to mention if one spots you then it lets out a howl or shriek or some other disturbing noise and alerts all other Nethers in the immediate vicinity to come help in kicking your♥♥♥♥♥ But that's not to say the players aren't an equal threat.
Indeed, players are always very trigger-happy, and some are always just out to be a giant sack of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and ruin your day for the hell of it. However, by comparison to the Nethers, death by KOS is few and far between in my experience but that may just depend on which server you play on. Believe it or not, you will actually WANT to go to the higher populated servers because most people will band together to take down people who KOS if you ask nicely. And I've heard some rumors that the development team may be working on ways to impliment punishments for people who do KOS. Which is all the more reason to buy the game now since the early funding will aid in the completion of minor tweaks and balances before full release.
After all is said and done, Nether is an outstanding game that went above and beyond my expectations. If you are a fan of games like DayZ, then this is a "must buy". If you are interested in these types of games but have never played them before, I would still highly recommend Nether over any other simply because it is an exceptionally well-made game and it isn't even in full release yet. Of course you'll find some odd bugs and glitches, but that's to be expected.
For those of you who prefer actual rating systems, I would personally give this game 8/10 in its current state (Early Access), and I would not be surprised if it got an even better score upon full release.

When I first bought this game I was scared that I had once again gave my money to an under experienced developer team but that changed quickly. The team over at Phosphor Games has got some great talent and I was actually amazed to see such great scenery, graphics textures, and lighting as soon as I entered a server. Altho the game is still in an "Early Access" state, It feels solid and runs great. The survival aspect has greatly been captured along with the feeling of being in a apocalyptic world. Almost every building or structure can be entered and searched for food, water, and weapons to help you survive against the dangers lurking around every corner. With the world being so vast with buildings to explore, it can become quite exhausting looting at times.
The alien creatures know as The Nether were designed fantastically. They are somewhat difficult to fight and kill at first but once you get the hang of it, it becomes much easier. Altho you do not want to find yourself up against more than 2 or 3 them at a time as that can result in a very quick death with how much they teleport around you and even spit at you to block your vision. Stealth is definitely the way to go in this game. I found avoiding them completely made the game alot easier, especially at night time.
As for the PvP in this game. I've only come across a few people and most were easy to kill if I had a gun of some sort. You do sometimes get your lone range camper who's window shopping the hotspots for guns waiting for someone to come walking by so they can get a cheap kill, just like you would any survival game though so watch your back entering military zones and popular spawn areas. The whole game is played in a first person view and I really hope it stays this way. I personally think 3rd person has ruined alot of other survival games with PvP combat in them. Aiming down the sights in this game may come off a bit different than other games giving that it has that "Real" feel to it. You will have to make up for gun sway and your stance you are in. Also as of now there are no hit markers to confirm to you that you have actually hit the person you have just shot at. You will have to have a good aim and patience to get the kills here. Unless of course its just some lvl 1 guy that spawned in with a kitchen knife right in front of you.
Overall I highly recommend this game right now. It is one of my most played and most enjoyed. The developers also seem to have a great bond with the community about the game.

First off, don’t listen to all of the nay sayers. There is a lot of false information floating around and a lot of people who can’t handle the new deck building process. There seems to be a flood of negative reviews and some of the information provided is false or misguided.
I am going to address the negative issues before I go into my review:
1.	This game is pay to win!

This right here is 100% completely incorrect. When you pay your $10 you can play through the entire game and unlock 88% of the entire card collection without ever paying a dime. The other 12% you do have to pay for in booster packs ($28 worth of packs). These “Premium” cards are not game changers either. No one is going to have an upper hand with these cards, there are only a few that matter anyways.
2.	The game is Impossible / Too Hard!

Again, this is incorrect. While this game is a bit harder, it is not nearly as hard or impossible as everyone is making it out to be. The big change up from previous versions is the capability to build your own deck. You are no longer getting your hand held with premade decks.

When you start the game you get a single premade deck and that is it. From there the choice is yours. I beat the entire game in 8 hours with nothing but a slightly modified starting deck. I slowly changed it as I unlocked more cards. I then proceeded to beat all of the explore nodes in another 8 hours.

What people need to do is stop complaining about it being so hard and actually seek advice on deck building and tactics. People complaining about not having all the cards unlocked right away is just like people complaining about not having the best gun unlocked in Call of Duty right away.
3.	There is no Co-op!

Correct! This is true as of right now. Currently there is no Two Headed Giant. While this is one of downsides of this new iteration, it is not a major game changer. With the amount of negative feedback, I feel that it will be making a return in an update possibly. Here is to hoping.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
So after addressing those 3 major issues, let’s head into my actual review. If you don’t want to read my detailed review you can scroll to the bottom for a list of Pros and Cons…

Magic 2015 starts off with an in depth tutorial for anyone who has never played magic before. It is painstakingly slow but it addresses every major point of the game and some decent tactics too (such as waiting until main phase 2 to play permanents). For any players that already know the basics, you can skip the tutorial entirely and go straight to the tutorial boss fight.

Before you start the boss fight you get to choose your first and only premade deck. You get a selection of any 2 Color combination deck you want and then you jump right into the boss fight. This selection determines your starting pool of cards. After you beat the tutorial boss you start the long process of unlocking the entire 88% of the card collection that is attainable without spending money.

You now have 5 Planes to go through beating bosses and collecting cards until you finally meet up with Garruk in the ultimate showdown. For anyone who bought the Complete Pack, You must beat the final boss in Innistrad to unlock your cards and that is also where your card collecting ends. Each Plane has an explore node that you will want to visit multiple times as well (Until you face the Planeswalker from each Node) for more card unlocks.

After you’ve collected your cards (Or bought for some of you), it’s time to head on over to multiplayer. Currently multiplayer consists of 2 Player, 3 Player, and 4 Player free for all’s. Sadly there is no 2 Headed Giant (2v2) for good old co-op fun. I’m hoping they add that later. You can choose to create your own match or join someone else’s via quick match or searching player lobbies. Multiplayer is the place to showcase your deck building skills. This is where you get to see how good you really are at this game.

This brings me to my favorite new addition to the series, deck building. You can finally make your deck however you want to. The deck building options are real easy to use and it’s easy to find the cards you want using the multitude of filters available. As you unlock new cards, you will find them here ready to be placed into your decks. If you have no idea how to build a deck you can rely on the computer to auto complete your deck for you with whatever cards you currently have selected. I recommend getting help from the community or paying attention to card tactics you see in game for deck building though.

You also have the option of browsing your entire card collection from the card collection menu. You can see all the cards you currently own, how many copies, and more importantly, which cards you still need. If you want 100% of the collection you are going to have to fork out another $28 after collecting all the current cards.

Navigating the menus in this game can be tedious. At first everything looks nice and clean and ordered. After you spend some time in the menus though, you start to get annoyed. There is a slight lag when you transition from menu set to menu set. You have to go through multiple menus just to get where you want to. It’s like trying to get to a picture on your computer and going through 3-4 folders to get to it but each time you click a folder there’s a fancy transition you have to wait for. It would be nice of the developers to also change the menu navigation in the future possibly.

Overall this game is well worth the $10 you pay for it. You can spend some extra cash to skip the card collecting if you want as well. I got a good 16 hours out of the single player campaign alone and will spend many more hours in multiplayer and practicing with new decks against the AI. If you are looking for another magic game then this is the game for you. If you are new to magic, then this is the perfect learning device to get into the game.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Pros
-	Real deck building
-	In depth tutorial for newcomers
-	Single player encounters that require creative thinking
-	Options for aesthetic customization
-	Multiplayer that truly tests your ability as a player
-	Chance to play with 2015 Cards
Cons
-	No coop currently (no two headed giant)
-	Annoying menu navigation
-	Amount of misguided complaints
-       Need to pay extra for complete card collection

Magic 2015 - Duel of the Planeswalker is, I think, a 5th installement in the series. It's a great way to get into Magic - the game gives you your first starter deck and after each win you get a random booster pack with new cards. Just like in paper Magic you create a 60 card deck out all the cards you have a and battle opponents on 5 different planes. After you unlock enough cards other deck archetypes become available - this is really only a suggestion as you can modify these decks however you want. As you progress further the opponents get way more powerful. To the point where your regular aggresive deck is not enough and it is better to play control/discard deck. I haven't played all the encounters yet but Liliana was hard for me and Garruk boss fight is actually two fights that you have to win one after another.
The deck building is a little diffrent from real Magic. You can have 4 copies of any common card, 3 uncommon, 2 rare and 1 mythic. In paper Magic its 4 copies of any card. I understand this though, a player who grinded the game for hours will have 4 of many rare cards and would get a real advantage over newcomers. It's like in World of Worldcraft high level characters can't slaughter new players freely. Overall deckbuilding is easy and fun to do. There are filters for colors, cost of the cards and the type. There is even an autocomplete button. You can customize land numer if you want (has to be enabled in advanced options)
There are no challenges this year, which is ok but the feature doesn't seem that time consuming that they couldn't add it. Challenges where premade play situation in which you had to usually win in one turn against the odds. They were nice but, really, you could only play them once.
Also missing is 2headed giant mode in which 2 players compete against another pair. Each pair share a life total of 30. Since multiplayer was always laggy and it was almost impossible to connect, I don't lament this omission. Usually at least one person of the loosing team would disconnect and you would get a win and card unlocks.
About card unlocks - new game is superior to 2014 and earlier. You get a random booster of cards that can possibly help your deck. Before you could only unlock single card and most of the ulock were useless. So you had to play, say, 15 games to unlock 2 useful cards and the rest was just a grind. Now each win can be a gain.
The Planes themselves are nicely designed. Each deck has a theme corresponding with it. Vampires and Zombies in Innistrad (horror plane), Allies and Kor people on Zendikar and so on. It is just exciting to play against them. Unfortunally not all the cards that opponent has in his deck are playable (can't get them in boosters or anywhere)

Some of the cards are only available from premium booster pack which have a real money cost (microtransactions). They are not game breaking and I'm not planing to buy any of them as I didn't buy sealed slots a year ago. Also when you complete the campaign there is really nothing to do. Apart from multiplayer which is quite pointless.
On the graphic side they did a complete overhaul this year, consisten with current line of Magic graphic design. The menus are ment for consoles and tablets (they always were) and some spinning wheel movements are not that easy with a mouse.
I play with a controlle and it is very comfortable.
To sum up, Magic 2015 is a very good game. It captures the Magic spirit of openning boosters and tuning your deck (though experienced players do not buy boosters :) and makes it a challenge to both create a deck and win with it. It might be a bit challenging to beat late game encounters for new players but overall I think they will be fine if they are patient. I reccommend this game to anyone who wants to get into Magic or wants to get back from a long break.

Let me preface this review by sharing with you what this game has done for me.
Skip this, if you want the actual review.
I've received a copy of this game from my brother, as I was rather excited by the gameplay and he was kind enough to notice it and went out of his way to gift it to me.
I started playing this game and finished it on the highest difficulty, but I rushed it, since I want to leave all the good stuff for multiplayer.
Now, this is the only game that hooked me up for 24h straight in four years. Four years.
I've enjoyed every aspect of the game, at least to an extent, each mission left me wanting more, the lore tidbits were a good reading. Do I have to mention the gameplay? No, I don't think so.
Thanks to this refreshing experience I was able to regain the joy that once came with playing games, as before that I thought I was getting to old to play games anymore.
Thankfully, it wasn't the case.
Now I know that because of my very refined and particularly specific taste I cannot enjoy every game I play (although I very strongly believed I could). This realisation has put me into a rather introspective mood, which furthers my self-improvement - that was my goal, long forgotten. Rediscovery at its finest.
I want to thank my brother, again, for buying this game for me, otherwise I wouldn't be able to get this far (heh, me bruder es gud nig o/).
The developers put a lot of care into this game, as it is able to combine different aspects - from gameplay to storytelling to graphic and map design - in a way it is enjoyable for people of various gaming backgrounds, be it roleplayers, arcade nuts, or simply shooter lovers.
-
+ Smooth combat
+ More unique weapons than in Borderlands 2 (I am comparing the arcade nature of these games here)
+ A variety of builds to choose from (melee, chi, ranged - the three main categories)
+ Fair death penalty at all difficulties (although No Pain No Gain isn't punishing enough)
+ Slightly complex, yet comprehensible attribute system (stat changing effects, elements, resistances, enemy types)
+ Every weapon is useful throughout the whole game (play with whatever turns you on the most while killing)
+ Multiplayer difficulty settings ranging from 2 player to 4 player even when you DUO
- Meh gem system - you'll find a lot of the same gems with slight variation, finding the 'perfect one' is annoyingly frustrating. Yes.
Some amulets are worse than others and you can equip only one - possible 'balance' issue?
- Weapon specific upgrades, some that cannot be taken off (personal grudge, they create unnecessary clutter in your inventory)
- Not enough melee weapons and special attacks - there are a lot of ranged weapons, which make melee weapons look like sidearms only (in my experience they also had inferior damage)
- Enemies have copy-pasted abilities (#NotAll), resulting in less challenging gameplay
- I'M FREE FALLING (I am handicapped and kept falling over the edge)
- Miss Rate - it seems like a very unnecessary detrimental stat, though it can kick your♥♥♥♥♥when you least expect it
Overall one kitten out of three in the oven for dinner. No need to be needlessy cruel, right?

This game is veeery frustrating. As other mentioned, it requires heavy exploration to find:
- Progress route
- Food
- Shelter
But basically punishes the player for doing so by:
- Map get "forgotten" upon death
- A "karma system" (which acts like a key sistem progressing over daily counter) that upon death get re-winded, so you'll need to grind one more day just to get back to the point before the last death. Efficiently generating endless, purposeless grind.
- Unlike the explored map sections and the karma system, consumed food is gone for good even if you die and the day get re-winded.
- Flora instagibs you
- Fauna instagibs you
Moreover, the day is short (+/- 20 min) and the punishment for not finding Progress route, Food and Shelter in time is:
- Rain, which guess what... instagibs you. :D
TL;DR:
- IF you appreciate an EXTREME and sometimes tedious challenge: look no further and find a new definition to the word "pain" by grabbing one of the most brutal experiences available on the market, seriously, this game one-shots cringe-generators such as Flappy Birds and Dark Souls.
- IF you don't find the idea of spending your evening getting mad over your screen appealing: wait for a "rebalance" and until then pass this. Or buy it and smash your screen for the frustration, I couldn't care less.
For the aforementioned reasons, and considering the needs of an "average player", I cannot recommend this game. This does NOT means that the game is bad, it's just very very mean. :D

I prefer more action-oriented games (i.e. Uncharted series). But this was an enjoyable change of pace because as expected, it's more about solving puzzles then shootouts like the Uncharted series.

People say this game is way too difficult. I've read one or two reviews regarding the controls, saying they are iffy and they ruin the game. Let me say right off the bat that you can change the controls, and the default controls aren't that bad themselves. But then on to the gameplay. People say that it is beautiful and the character and NPCs move amazingly. I agree with both of those. But the difficulty?
The difficulty is hard. Yes. But it is a GOOD hard. It is challenging enough to make you try your hardest but not too hard to make you stuck on rung 1 the WHOLE time. In the beginning, I loved it but thought it was too hard for me. But it was SO addicting I kept playing and eventually, I got the hang of it and without dying once got to area 3 and Rung 5 section 2, or whatever those little things are called. Then I died a few times and got back to rung 3, and back to 5. It is fun but hard, and sometimes it may seem WAY too hard but you find a way around the that and take another route. And this game is rewarding when you get a rung higher or move on to the next region. Discovering all the new creatures, concepts, plants, and terrain is really fun too.
But is it TOO hard? Not it my eyes. If you really try you will make your way up those rungs and move on to new regions. At times it may be frustating, or rage filling, or make you feel like you want to break you keyboard, but you will move on and find new mays to get on with the level. This game is addicting, beautifully made, but challenging, but I reccomend it to you guys. Enjoy Rain World!!

This is an amazing game, but there's some problems with connectivity. The servers are p2p and it takes a long time right now to find matches, and when you do there's a chance you'll lose connection for no obvious reason. Also, staying in a group of friends is a pain because of the invites and it dispersing the group whenever a game ends due to few players and the disconnecting servers. Also there's a few things that are a bit irksome to me personally.... Not being able to customize or do anything during the crazy long queue times is a big one.
There aren't many gameplay elements that are too bad. Reviving players seems like it's too fast and is really powerful, and run speed (lookin at you, Peacekeeper) is a pain to play against when they can just run away and leave you and revive their teammates with little you can do about it. Executing enemies is a way to prevent revives, or camping their corpse until the timer runs out but usually your teammates need your help. HOWEVER
The gameplay is amazing when it is working. This game has some of the most immersive combat I've experienced and it runs so smoothly and everything looks great. You can feel the weight of your attacks and the sounds are so satisfying when you land them. There's so much detail in every player model and the animations are great. All of the classes look amazing (especially Lawbringer) and I can't express enough how great it all comes together when it works. None of the classes feel more OP than other ones right now and they all play so uniquely, which is nice for once in a game.
I'll recommend the game to anyone who is even remotely intrigued by the looks of it. They just have to do some things to fix the server issues and lag and bugs....Once they have it up and running decently, you won't regret your purchase.

In KotOR I, the underlying question was always "Are you good or evil?" In Obsidian's KotOR 2: The Sith Lords, the question quickly becomes "What is good? What is evil?"
This is the key difference between the two, because otherwise not much has changed. There are little improvements, such as being able to influence your companions in more meaningful ways, perhaps even in ways they don't agree with. But the main differences, which sets it apart from its predecessor by miles and miles, are the characters, the story, and its almost critical treatment of the Star Wars universe.
KotOR I was an amazing game that faithfully translated the Star Wars Experience. You have a crew, you travel through space, you become a Jedi, you face the temptations of the dark side, and challenge an evil force in the galaxy. But for all its achievements, it was a very black/white experience with very little gray area. In fact, BioWare seemed to draw some novelty of the fact it introduced a "Gray Jedi" in the form of Jolee Bindo, who was neither good nor evil.
For Obsidian's outing, *everything* resides in that gray area, not just one character. Every decision you make will be called into question; your profound acts of charity will be deemed selfish and ignorant, while your outrageous acts of tyranny will be deemed weak and cowardly. If you go by the morality scale KotOR I favored, you will not be able to win, and that's really the point. There are no absolutes in life -- giving some credits to a beggar on Nar Shaddaa will get him beaten and robbed later on, and treating the same beggar with malice will encourage him to treat others in the same manner -- and the game's characters will encourage you to make informed decisions over choices made solely to improve your good/evil alignment.
This makes Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic 2 - The Sith Lords a tremendously engaging experience as far as immersion, choice, and consequence, with memorable characters who strive to be more than the SW archetypes we've become familiar with, and a masterful story that dives into dark territory that few storytellers in the Expanded Universe have bothered to touch. It's a very unique experience and, in my opinion, boasts some of the finest writing in a video game, period.
It's an old game, but a great one -- and one that's stuck with me for nearly a decade. If you decide to take the leap, be sure and download the KotOR 2 Restoration Mod for the definitive experience.

This game is great. Better than the first game? Yes and no. In terms of gameplay, this one takes the old combat engine and gives it a huge upgrade. Storywise, though, it is lackluster. While the original was simple and to the point, but with many twists and lots of character development, this one falls short. It had some enjoyable characters, but others were boring and received little development. Some were introduced so late in the game (depending on what order you play it in) that I didn't get to see if they had any development. The hands-on and easy to do character development of the original is replaced by a strange system that is difficult to use. However,some of the character interactions were interesting and immersive. The overall plot is interesting and raises good qeustions, but there were many points where I was unsure what was happening or why. At the end of the game, I was left very confused as to why certain things had happened. On a more positive note, the gameplay is excellent. While sometimes many characters seem as though they couldn't hit the side of the barn, the overall fluidity is great. The leveling system is great, and can be very immersive. All in all, if you can over look a few problems with the story, you have an excellent, entertaining, and immersive game that will give you hours of gameplay.The other big problem is the glitches. They are intolerable at some points. They vary, from skipping through entire important conversations to simply crashing ffor no reason at all. This game is very unfinished. From what I've heard, this is due to the developers being rushed by ther sponsors. These glitches aren't really deal breakers, especially sense there are many mods that essentially finish the game. The sad fact is that this game could have been even better then the original-quite a feat-but it is left in it's shadow because of this lack of polish.
Overall this game is worth getting, especially sense it is only ten dollars, but if you want a more finished game, you'll have to download mods on your own time. 7/10 for the Vanilla.
