I like this game.
Now, can I say I really like it?  No.  Is it acceptable?  Unlike every other review I've read for the game by people who are immidiately unpleased by the UI or Gameplay, I say it is acceptable.
Firstly, lets discuss what they did well.  Now, they did nothing exceptionally, but, a lot of what they did do they did on par.  The UI, often credited by even the haters as 'fancy'(although sometimes to a fault), does a good job of reflecting the set the game was built around.  As a matter of fact, I feel the team that put together this game was in much closer contact with the group that made this core set of magic.  However nice it is seeing old cards and gimics in a Duels of a Planeswalkers game, it isn't really reflective of magic at the time, and if some one would use this game as a learning mechanism to get into magic, I believe it is more important for them to know what to expect from the sets of cards they are getting into.  Not some crazy infinite turn combo that they will never be able to pull off without putting in time and money to get old cards that they can't even use in standard which is a common starting ground for new players.
The gameplay is exactly what I'd expect from a Duels of the Planeswalkers game, it plays just like its predecessors.  With their special scenarios and silly at times AI.  The story, unlike past versions of this game, does actually exist.  Is it deep?  No, but, the fact that it exists at all is a step in the right direction.
I haven't dabbled in the multiplayer as of yet, but I'm certain that plays just like past versions of the game as well.  The lack of 2-headed giant is a negative factor, but not game breaking.
The "Pay to Win" controversy that seems to be surrounding this game is unfounded.  Looking at the cards you can get by buying the premium booster packs the game offers you is simply a way to 'step up' your game.  Not skip the staircase all together and become a god of the multiverse.  If you've played sealed, it's simply exanding your sealed pool with cards of similiar or worse value.  You do not need to buy packs to win, and can be just as succesful with the game if you don't want to open your wallet past the 10$.
Tied in to that "Pay to Win" mind set people are getting into is the deck building, which is exaclty what they promised.  I for one am more excited for future DLC that expands the card pool in this game then I ever was waiting for new pre-made decks  in previous games.
The most important question for many of you though is, is the game worth the 10$ pricetag?  If you've been a purchaser of past magic DOTP games upon release, I'd say yes.  This game offers a unique experience, which seems to be off setting to many people who have played past games, but I've become fairly fond of the game.  Hopping on and playing it as much as I did any of the previous versions.  If you are some one who would otherwise usually wait for a sale, wait for the sale.  Overall, I do recommend this game.

The best installemnt of DotP so far, in my opinion anyways. This is the first one that actually lets you fully build your own decks, and play with them in the campaign and during multiplayer play. For me it took about 10 hours to fully beat the campaign, and unlock a mojority of the cards, which is about the same as the previous games. Add in another couple hours to unlock the rest of them, and have fun building various decks. One downside to the game is that, deck building is a little limited, you can only have one of each Mythic, two of each Rare, three of each Uncommon and 4 of each Common. That does make the game fair though. Another major downside to the game is that there are only 1v1, and free for all game modes in Multiplayer, no Two-Headed Giant, no Planechase and no Archenemy, just plain old free for all and 1v1. The only other downside for me, is that you have buy boosters (at $1.99 each) to unlock some of the cards, with no other way to get them. Overall, I give the game an 8/10, if there was a wider collection of cards to unlock, more multiplayer game modes, and a way to get the Premium cards without paying money, I would definetly give it a 9/10, or maybe even a 10/10
Pros/Cons
+ Actually build your decks
+ Decent lengthed Campaign
+ Decent Variety of cards
- Some deckbulding restrictions
- Only way to get some cards is with money
- No special multiplayer modes (ie no 2HG)
Overall, I really enjoy the game and look forward to DLC, and highly reccomend it to anyone who either loves Magic, or wants to get into Magic.

This game is amazing! It's like a mix of Devil May Cry, Legend of Zelda, Portal, and Fable The Lost Chapters and balanced nearly perfectly. Combat is fluid and fun and the insane amount of combos and moves makes itfresh and not repetitive (unless you make it repetitive by just spamming the mouse button :P) Power ups are cool and are utilized well IMO. There's a lot of action but also a lot of puzzles and many oppurtunities for exploration. It's an open world and many paths to other areas require puzzles and such and most of the puzzles don't feel tedious and are challenging but very intuitive. There are few exceptions (freeing Azrael took FOREVER and was kinda tedious). Boss fights were a highlight in this game. Bosses were tough but had patterns that you'll pick up on after a while. But using the patterns to your advantage takes skill and precise timing. There are collectibles that help you, like finding artifacts that you can trade in for currency, 10 pieces of armor you can find, chests that include either currency, wrath, health, health or wrath shards to increase your total capacities, trinkets that show you where chests and artifacts are in the area, keys, etc. Cool gadgets and gear offer more variety and also help in puzzles such as a grapple, the voidwalker which is essentially a Portal gun, the shadow mask to go back and forth between the shadow realm and your realm (no this isn't Yu-Gi-Oh in any way), etc. Plus you get to ride a horse that can even help in combat. Controls are great IMO, and I played on the keyboard. Left Alt for dash felt weird at first, but after finding a good placement of my hand on the keyboard it became easy and flowed well. It took me about five minutes or less to get used to. The using CAPS LOCK + 1, 2, or 3 for abilities was the only thing I thought was a bit tricky. I rarely felt the need to use them, though. Also underwater movement was fluid and fun, which is rare I think in a game. The story was really engaging. The ending also had a great little twist. Voice acting was great, save for a few parts, with Mark Hamill doing a full-on Joker voice for the Watcher and Liam O'Brien, the guy who voices Gaara in the english dubbed Naruto series sounding like an ancient version of Gaara as War, the main character. Yes, it's just as awesome as it sounds. The added ability to pick up items in the environment such as cars or telephone poles and use as weapons only added to all the chaotic fun. The boss death scenes were all brutal and soooooo satisfying. I highly recommend this game, it is amazing and the exploration and hidden places and objects adds to replayability.

I feel fairly certain that this game took a few years off of my life. I mean that in the best way possible.
Amnesia: The Dark Descent is a first-person survival horror game from Frictional Games. Now let’s get rocking.
The Good
When a game is so nerve wracking that I start cringing when I see corners/closed doors and almost have to pick up an alcohol habit to get through it, it’s a pretty damned good game. From my first encounter with a Servant Grunt to the end of the game A:tDD kept my painfully aware of how deep of water I was in. But this game wasn’t just jump scares, oh no. There is an omnipresent feeling of “I could be brutally murdered at any moment” that tags along with you the whole time.
You never know how big of a coward you are until the game you’re playing won’t allow you to fight back when there are a plethora of abominable creatures coming for you. Sure, you’ll probably try throwing things at the Grunts or the Brutes, but it won’t do you any good. Your sanity will be draining away and, when your feeble projectiles are rendered worthless, you’ll try as hard as you can to run or hide.
The atmosphere was intensely creepy; palpably so. The music was on point and made the immersion that much better. The story was also fantastic; easily the best of the games that I’ve reviewed sense our return. Well written dialogue, Lovecraftian themes, and sense of dread throughout.
The Bad
I don’t really have anything I found to be “bad” about this game. Let’s just move on.
The Meh
I found myself wishing I had a map once or twice or that I could check the fuel level in my lantern without opening the inventory screen every time.
Verdict: Yea
Full price, sale price, whatever; this game is worth the cash. If you’re looking for your next foray into the abyss, look no further. Just go ahead and pull out your wallet.

Seems to be a lot of bad reviews for this game and I will attempt to address most of them.
First and formost only free for alls in multi-player mode. Yeah thats a hard hit for fans of 2 headed giant, hopefully the negative feedback about its absence will force an update (Keep your fingers crossed)
Second, terrible starting decks and no way to change them. This is like schrodingers cat, both true and false at the same time. The starting decks are under powered but they are not unplayable. I believe the starters are designed to force people to consider new strategies instead of the typical rush, control, or burn play style that they may be used to. And you are allowed to change the starting deck after completing the Innistrad plane (A person just has to take the time to beat the first "Boss"). After Avacyn is defeat return to the Main Menu>Deck>Create Deck, all of the starter decks should be unlocked.
Third, "Stupid AI tapped the wrong lands for my spell! / Targeted the wrong thing!!!" Any time you can use different combinations of mana to pay for a spell you can press the left Ctrl key to cycle through the lands to be tapped (says so right in the controls tab). Like wise if the target of your spell is in a stack, like equipment on a creature, you can use the scroll wheel on the mouse to zoom in on the stack and select the proper card you wish to target.
The Game is so slow. Yes but there are things that can be done to speed things up, turning off combat animations, turning off zoom played cards, and spamming the continue button. Myself I am kind of thankfull that things move a little slow and we are allowed time to respond to everything, in a "Real World" duel you can always ask your opponent to wait or hold on a second. I think a lot more people would be upset if they lost duels because the AI played too fast for them to counter.
Its such a pain grinding for cards. Yes it is but if a person does not want to pay a little more then the price of a booster pack in the "Real World" to unlock an entire set of cards then it is good that they have the option to grind for the complete set. Unlike the previous versions where we were pretty much stuck with what we got. Which brings me to the next complaint.
The game has just turned into another pay to win money sink because "Richies" will just buy up all the premium boosters. That statement just isnt true, most of the cards in the premium set have counter parts in the other sets that do the same thing or better stuff. A person just needs to know how to maximize each cards potential.
The interface is so clunky. I have to agree with that, it seems to be designed for touch screens, which in theory makes it sleek. However theory and practical application are two very different thing. There is good news for those of us without touch screens, the arrow keys can still be used to navigate most of the menues, instead of using the mouse to click and drag.
Now that most if not all of the "bad" stuff has been addressed I'll move on to the great things.
We can now BUILD decks with our ENTIRE collection of cards!!!! Our collection is actually OURS to play with and do as we wish. Finally we are masters of our own destinies.
For less then the price of a fat pack we can now own 5, yes 5 complete digital sets!!!!
Yes we will miss 2HG but just because that format isnt CURRENTLY supported by the game doesnt mean that we as players cannot unite and talk to each other and make our own player created formats, like maybe "common chaos" where each player can only use common cards in their deck, or some form of 4 player assassin and stuff. As long as everybody playing has agreed to the rules, arranging private games with player created formats shouldnt be a problem at all.
I have been playing MtG since Fallen Empires was released and what drew me to the game was the fact that it pushed me to test my creativity and ingenuity. This game is a huge step in getting back to the roots of MtG. So what if a deck we make doesnt win every time. Whats the point of playing if you just snag a deck template some one else created, and every duel plays out the exact same way? Personally that sounds much more boring then grinding cards for a couple hours.
In closing I would give this game 9 stars out of 10. IMO it is a huge step in the right direction. While there is room for improvement, the same can be said for any game in existence.

First off, to see the original review and all of my reviews, go to
And we begin:
Think of what War Z was supposed to be, but add lots of bloodthirsty demons and less fail. Nether is a First Person survival MMO based loosely on the city of Chicago, it involves main survival techniques, such as
The need to eat
The need to drink
Shooting demons in the face
Stabbing people with kitchen knives and
Finding weapons and ammunition.
Unlike other survival MMOs, there are Objectives and Safe Havens, where players cannot attack each other; these areas are used to buy supplies from Markets, or even trade supplies with players, they’re are also good to group up with friends, or find new ones.
In my opinion, Nether could be a really interesting and fun game, but in reality it’s very frustrating. You spawn with a knife and little to no supplies. If you find another player, don’t expect to be friends, because odds are you’ll get shot in the face instantly. If that isn’t enough, you also have to worry about the Nethers, while you’re expected to reach the safe haven with a kitchen knife.
I’ve played the game for a total of 6 hours and I’m still yet to find a gun, food or water.
With that aside, the game is still in Beta, so I suspect it will improve by the full release. Don’t get me wrong, it’s a great idea for a game, but it’s just plain impossible to play solo.
I have to admit, the game is alright; even though you have an inevitable demise, it’s quite a suspenseful experience, for instance; you have to be quiet when moving through buildings, otherwise the Nethers will find you, and if they don’t, you have a pretty high chance of a player hunting you down.
My advice; if you plan on playing Nether, make sure you have friends to play it with, otherwise you’re not going to have much fun, unless you’re really lucky and find a gun in the first few minutes, in which case I hate you.
As for graphics, the game is improving with every single update, and already we can see that the graphics are going to be amazing, they really tried to make it look good, and they pulled it off quite well.
Overall I’d give the game a 6.5/10, but if I played it with friends, it would get a higher score than that without a doubt.

Difficulty setting : Hard mode
Time played : 20 hours (on Steam, because of Photo mode), 15/16hours ingame. 100% Completion (altough I missed some Elite mobs)
Shadow Warrior 2 is refreshing while still going for an oldschool gameplay. This is a fast FPS mixed with Diablo. A Borderlands on drugs, without the boring side. You have plenty of quests to keep you entertained, and the game has a huge replayability since you can use your finished save to go on NG+ and even change the difficulty setting.
Actually, you have : Easy, Normal, Hard, Insane, Insane 2 to 4.
Since the game can also be played in coop, you also can adjust the difficulty with the amount of players you'll have in your game.
Example :
Insane 4 =/= Insane 4 +4 players difficulty.
Also, be sure to have taste for this kind of game because since it's like Diablo, Elite monsters can be a little too bullet spongey if you're playing a very high difficulty and you don't have enough DPS on your weapons.
Speaking of weapons, I've found 50+ weapons in the game (there are 70+ weapons) and they all have their unique skin and personality, especially when you're doing your backward special attack with a melee weapon. the effect won't be the same between a Katana, circle blades or claws, for example.
Graphically it's very good, like really beautiful and you have a good set of options to tweak if you want the smoothest experience ever. The game is somewhat good optimized although it could be better. I noticed a lot of framedrops because of elite corpses on the ground, although the game was running fine when said elite was ALIVE and moving.
In conclusion, the game was really fun to play, and I'll go for my NG+ Insane run, waiting for the coop to be fixed (the host has a saved progression while coop guys don't, i don't know why, but you can lose your loots if it's not loot from your save).
Still, Lo Wang is a funny character and Shadow Warrior 2 is a real improvement after the 2013 version. It's brainless, lots of bloody fun, tons of weapons and customization (with gems), it has a good soundtrack, the jokes are cheesy and funny. Grab it if you're interested!

Shadow Warrior in 2013 surprised the hell out of me.
I'm a story fanatic; a good game is centered around the story and graphics, gameplay, etc take a second place(Not distant, but still second)

Graphics: Great. Settings can be repetative but that's something you get accostomed too with a grinding co-op. Quality is airtight.
Sound: Sure. Music, great. Sound effects, wonderful(I love the WarSSAWWWW)
Gameplay: It's okay. Melee weapons outclass guns in every way EXCEPT...you can't really duel. Just being near enemies gets you hurt and they're everywhere. So range is your friend unless you're tweaked pretty well.

Story: Here we go....

The end result is explained and the sense of near-tragedy continues fairly well enough, but it's not the SURPRISE and I can't directly fault Flying Wild Hog. I wish it was the same, but we always want more of what we loved.

As many have pointed out, the pricing for this game is a little suspect. My first playthrough took 6 hours and I managed to find maybe 50-60% of the collectables without trying that hard. That being said, I would recommend this game (but perhaps when it is in a sale) for the general experience.
The launch was apparently marred by framerate drops, however as of 11 June, this game ran wonderfully on my rig: i7-4790K @ 4gz, 16GB RAM, GTX-980TI on a 1440p monitor set at 85hz at the time of playing. Graphics set to High/TXAA, no noticable stutters at all through 6 solid hours of play.
No spoilers, but essentially in order to understand the full extent of the story, you will have to go out of your way to find the collectables and pay attention to details dotted through the game. It will not spoonfeed you much, except for the cutscenes between 'acts'.
Honestly, half the time I felt like I was playing a game which Studio Ghibli could have made, especially with some of the imagery looking similar to elements of Spirited Away and Princess Mononoke... this is no bad thing of course, as Ghibli makes wonderful imaginative movies, but still... I had to double check who made the soundtrack as it sounded like something Joe Hisaishi would put together. On the subject of the game soundtrack... beautiful! I love classical themes which are heavy on the cello and violin, and this has it in abundance.
Visually I found the game to be bright and beautiful, but behind it is a tale quite dark and emotional... just like a Studio Ghibli movie really!
Anyway, to sum up, I found the game to be a largely enjoyable experience, even if the 'puzzles' were all a bit obvious. It was visually and audibly beautiful at times, with smooth animation which emphasised character (a big need for a game with no real spoken dialog)... but do I feel compelled to return to it and finish finding the collectables? Not right now... so I would recommend the game for the experience, but do not feel it is long enough to justify the full-price tag at the moment.

So at this point I've played 32 hours and can safely say, this game is fantastic, it has some teething issues that need to be solved such as the UI, AI, hit detection & performance issues but all of these can be ironed out to leave the fantastic gameplay & atmosphere of the game.
On the subject of atmosphere, it is done very well, the planets could do with some work for weather events such as rain, thunder and fog slowly creeping into the battlefield but other than that it looks surprisingly good for an UE3 game but the meat and potatoes of this game, at present, is the space combat. The ships are large and expansive with intricate details everywhere, medbays, barracks, a kitted out bridge and all sorts make you want to explore the ship before you even get into combat, I've yet to actually completely map any of the ships due to being fired at before I can get half way through!
The individual fighter, bomber & assault ships are also very fun to use and are pretty detailed, they handle surprisingly well although I did have to lower my senstivity quite a bit to get them to perform well and they can also be customized to a large extent to make each fighter plane unique.
The infantry combat is surprisingly good as well, with many options in your loadouts to make your character as unique as possible from plasma assault rifles to grenade launchers and even undermounted flamethrowers & shield generators that allow your team to push a charge, there is a lot of potential here to create some incredibly awesome squad-based synergy and to truly lead an epic charge with your team using multiple shield generators, grenade launchers & assault rifles to break through an enemy position. Or perhaps some flamethrowers, turrets & explosives to stop the incoming assault, detonating the enemy as they walk into the killzone of your explosives & turrets.
Having played 32 hours I can say without a doubt that this game is fantastic, easily a 7 or an 8 out of 10 for me, this game reminds me of all the good times I had in Enemy Territory: Quake Wars, it can only go up from here and I do look forward to see where this game goes in future, the only issues at present are some hit detection, netcode & UI related issues but besides that this is one of the best Early Access games I've played in a while.

Rain World is a really good game but I don't think it is for everyone.
This isn't a metroidvania, you aren't going to be gaining new abilities (In the classical power-up sense at least) and increasing your stats. The improvements come from gaining understanding of Slugcat's abilities and the world around you.
When you start out nothing makes sense and you will die often, when you die you will lose a symbol that you don't understand what it means, this may make you upset but don't let it, if you don't know what the symbol is for then what does losing one matter? Short answer; No. Longer Answer; You have nothing to lose, get out there!
As you progress you will learn how to play, not through a forced tutorial or someone telling you but by experiencing it yourself, you discover the many moves Slugcat has (Far more than the basic movement and jump the game does tell you about), you will start to understand why you rolled instead of doing what you wanted to and then you will learn how to control the game correctly and it will feel lke a breath of fresh air.
You will see animals, you will not know if they are friendly, neutral or hostile. You will not know what their colour or size or number of horns means, you will not know how to interact with or escape from them. But you will LEARN those things yourself if you try.
You may enter an area where food is scarce and hard to find, but is it really? Perhaps there is food you just don't know how to eat yet? The game provides everything you need, it just doesn't spell it out for you and that has caused a lot of frustration for many players.
My advice for anyone who thinks that this game looks and sounds interesting is to persevere, when the game starts you have nothing to lose, die as much as you like to learn the mechanics because you're in no rush to get anywhere yet!
Understand that slugcat has mass and weight, slugcat's stance, speed, direction all factor in to what will happen when you press a button; will you jump? will you do a slide-tackle? Will you roll? Will you back-flip? None of those are explained but they are there for you to use from the very start, you just have to practice.
This game has depths the like haven't been seen in a game for a long time, if you persevere you will get an enormous amount of enjoyment out of it.
If you have friends to play this with than buy it, If not I do not reccomend. Also definitly buy on a sale.

Many people have probably already talked about how graphically beautiful the art style and story telling of the game is. So I'm going to avoid that and talk about the mechanics.
This game is honestly more fair than what people give credit for. Yes, the game is difficult, but it is mechanically simple. Yes you are going to die a lot. And it can be pretty damned frustrating. But if you've ever played a game like Dark Souls, then you can understand what I mean by it's actually -fair-, and that the player has a few advantages that the enemies often times do not share.
It requires a deal of patience, and there will be moments where there is an amount of luck in play. But such is the way of life.
The monsters in this game are persistant entities. They are not actively looking for you however. In most cases they are just casually prowling the world. But the moment they catch a sound of you just trumping around, or see you (which you need to be pretty close for some of them), they will gun it for you. And it is hard to shake them. But they don't always know where you are. They still need to search for you. Which forces the player to learn the stealth mechanics on their own. Something that a good deal of reviewers might have failed to pick up on.
The monsters are smart enough to actually be tricked. You can lure them away from your path and sneak around them in an alternative path.
That's not sayin that there is not a single moment of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. There is. Sometimes when the AI sees you, they always know where you are. An instance of this is when a flying predator swoops down and sees your running into a hole. When you quietly crawl your way into a small underground antechamber, the damned bird will press himself up against the ground to try and get you, despite that there is no way for it to even get at you.
The game is incredibly hands off as far as it goes to teach you the ropes. The most it will teach you is basic controls, and then you're pretty much on your own to figure things out. But fear not, the game is not terribly cruel. There is a helpful little critter that follows you around.
For the perceptive players, they will catch on to what this creature is doing. It will point you in the correct direction to go, usually the fastest (though not always the safest). It will point you to the closest food supply, however it seems to be primarily limited to pointin out moths to you. It will give you subtle hints about the ecosystem through flickering images, And it will even warn you of danager that might not be immediately discernable, or out of sight.
The creatures in the game are capable of using all the same shortcuts, tunnels, and passage ways that you can. However, you do get a warning before you move to the next area when a creature is near a doorway, or when something is coming through.
I hadn't followed the game's progress for the years it was in development. In fact I only just heard of it on the first, which peaked my interest.
So in short. The game is frustrating as hell sometimes, but it is deceptively fair. More advantage is given to the player than you think. And their are some things left for the player to discover as you try to survive. Trial and Error comes with a cost, but it is not too terribly significant when you concider that each death is merely a baby step in your experience.
The game makes no attempt to hold your hand, nor to patronize you. The frustrated are likely the ones who try to go the same direction over and over, instead of attempting to find a different route. And those who quit are likely the ones whom have tried to rush through the map like rambo, instead of taking their time to scope the area, and observe how the creatures behave.

At this point in development, the enjoyment you get out of this game is pretty strongly correlated to the quality of the group (guild) you play with and the server. This game is really one where you HAVE to work together, especially on servers where the settings are close to what the MMO will be (600-1000 skillcap, 0.5-2 multiplier). However, now that the guild claim system is implemented it can be very rewarding because everything within your guild monument's claim is protected.

As other people have said, it is a pretty slow paced game, which makes it realistic, but I find a lot of newbies don't seem to grasp that. You have to put in a lot of time and have patience in order to get a settlement going and get armor and weapons. And even then, if you're playing on a pvp server, you still need to put work and time in your settlement to improve your defenses or another guild is going to surpass you technologically and wipe you out.

If you're doing multiplayer (where most of the fun is to be had), I would highly recommend using teamspeak, mumble or the like for your group. Communication is essential in multi.

All in all, I've definitely got my money's worth out of this game. This style of game and the way the devs have implemented most things so far seems perfect. I can't wait for the MMO.

Holds up much better than I might have expected.  I replayed this in 2016 on a lark because I was wondering if I could get some insight as to why an old school id shooter like Quake 4 was well received but didn't blow anyone away at the time but an old school id shooter like Doom (2016) is one of the top games of the year.
Turns out, the premise of that question was fundamentally flawed because there's actually a ton of difference between "Quake 2" old school and "Doom" old school.
The movement speed felt really sluggish at first, but that didn't bother me once I got into the groove of things.  It's slower than Quake 2 which itself was slower than Doom.
This game was developed by Raven, but has that "punch" to the combat that is the trademark of an id game.  The Doom 3 engine is put to great use here; the visuals (mostly) hold up pretty well even by today's standards.  The overall aesthetic might be similar to Doom 3 since they're both sci-fi action games with cybernetic monsters on the same engine, but it's pretty distinct and there's a lot more variety.  Think more Starship Troopers instead of Aliens.  The game gets dark and creepy at times but other times you're outdoors in trenches or in more open and interesting areas indoors.  Doom 3 was going for relentless claustrophobic dread pretty much the entire game, but this game has a lot more variety in color, tone, and emotion that it's attempting.
The overall level design philosophy is very close to Quake 2 both in the Strogg architectural motifs as well as just the design of the combat areas and layouts.  Except for some reason the sky isn't orange - maybe they thought that would make it look too much like Doom 3's Mars?  Also the maps are maybe a little more linear and there's a much lessened emphasis on secret hunting.
The story and characters aren't really engaging in any way.  The stroggification scene was cool but they didn't really do anything with that concept afterwards and it was spoiled in the trailers.  The story that is there is functional in that it builds the tone and feel they're going for.  This is an area where the game excels.  Fighting alongisde other marines in trenches while explosions go off around you creates a strong, early Call of Duty-esq war feeling to the game, but more Starship Troopers than WW2.  There's also a strong element of body horror as you work your way through the game, see the stroyent creation, the stroggification facilities, see biomechanically crucified marines merged with computers, etc.  The  soundtrack is more cinematic than Quake 2 and less memorable (outside the main theme), but builds this atmosphere better.  Just overall, Quake 4 feels less bland and brown than Quake 2 did at times.
This game picked up some bad habits of the games in between the old school shooters and the more modern ones; exposition-powered doors, NPC's standing in your way until you let them finish talking, forced turret and vehicle sections with bad looking outdoor areas and clunky controls to "break up the monotony" - there's gameplay variety from strong central mechanics that give the player interesting choices, like Dishonored or Doom 2016, and there's insecurity that your players will get bored so you force them to do some other type of gameplay for a while.  There's weapon upgrades, but unlike Doom 2016 or Rage they're just gated based on your progress through the campaign and given to you at specified times so that feels kind of pointless to not just make the weapons have all the features to start with.  Unlike Doom 3, this game is more straight action, without any real puzzles or environmental interaction, but that means the handful of times the game expects you to do anything but just "shoot the thing until it dies" it's frustrating not because it expects you to do anything hard to figure out, but because you're not in that mindset.  There's some frustration from having a handful of old school big arena fights but now you have to contend with drastically reduced movement speed and reload times and no sprint mechanic.
Most of the weapons are very satisfying to use, but some of the weapons feel nerfed, like the grenade launcher, the railgun, and the BFG.  Weapon reloading was fine early game, for the assault rifle and shotgun, but when you have 10 weapons it's annoying to constantly cycle through all of them after each fight to make sure they're ready to shoot.  The railgun is already a slow firing weapon so adding a long reload animation after 3 shots was excruciating.  Keeping the reloading for the human weapons, and maybe the hyperblaster would have added to that more realistic war feeling the game was going for without hurting the gameplay for the rest of the large arsenal.
So there's some flaws and frustrating / dated bits, but it holds up well as a game from that last generation of shooters on the evolutionary tree of games like Doom and Duke Nukem - games like Doom 3 and Prey - before the genre split out into different directions with games like Far Cry or Cod4 etc.

Make a habit and figure things out before setting out into the dangerous rain world. Once you get the hang of it, this slug can dance. For real. (figuratively)
This f*cking game, is the most frustrating game I have played in recent years. Now, I'll be honest, look at my play time, and I'll say that when the frustration finally channeled into accomplishment, the game feels great. But are you ready to put up with tens of hours of brutal work? I could've finished several other games that makes me HAPPY with that amount of time. Let me explain why this game is so flawed:
The game is way too punishing. I ain't no wimp. If I fell, I get back up. If you fall in Rain World, you fall into a literal pit. With every death, you not only revert progress, you LOSE progress. Grinding karma is quick once know how, but grinding IS grinding. It is to proof that you can survive the region? Well, I don't have repeat it 4 times now?!
Knowing is 80% of the battle. The creature spawns, the annoying cvnt meat eating plants, the optimal paths, the shelter locations. This game is made for people who already knows the game. Coming in fresh? Prepare to get lost, prepare to fumble around not know what to do, prepare to progress painfully slow, because every time you don't execute something well, you are forced to lose progress. Got bad RNG spawn? Tough luck, prepare to die. Without information, you can't reliably practice, you can only wing it. Go through an area, again and again and again and again, until you can spot the consistency, then only you can try besting that area. Lost time adds up, and this game has no respect of your time.
The level design is trash. Utter. Garbage. Sprawling mazes that leads to loops are the worst. You just went through HELL and noticed that you are back to map #2. You got to be kidding me. You missed a crucial jump (or intentionally fell to explore), guess what? You can't get back up, now you got to push onward to some other maps until you found a way back. Didn't bring a spear? Hah! Tough luck, this corner just became a dead end for you! Oh right, did I mention there's a lizard camping on this one pipe? Better detour again! But hurry! Rain's in 2 minutes! Where the food and shelter's at? Oh! At that area you were trying to get to...
Now, now. The issue significantly lessens when you got things figured out. As I mentioned, this game is made for those who already knew the game well. I had to put up with tens of hours of sh!t to come to this point when I'm no longer facing aforementioned problem, I don't think EVERYONE should go through the pain I've been through unless that who have similar SHEER ♥♥♥♥!NG WILL.
This is a great game. The core mechanics are amazing. However, many design decisions have made this an immensely frustrating game, with satisfaction only coming after dealing with said frustrations. This isn't healthy. There must be better ways to enhance the experience while keeping the spirit of difficulty and brutality. For the path they chose, I don't feel is the best one. Peace.
P.S. I've unlocked my inner mastery of whine and cuss while playing through this game.

This game is great. Better than the first game? Yes and no. In terms of gameplay, this one takes the old combat engine and gives it a huge upgrade. Storywise, though, it is lackluster. While the original was simple and to the point, but with many twists and lots of character development, this one falls short. It had some enjoyable characters, but others were boring and received little development. Some were introduced so late in the game (depending on what order you play it in) that I didn't get to see if they had any development. The hands-on and easy to do character development of the original is replaced by a strange system that is difficult to use. However,some of the character interactions were interesting and immersive. The overall plot is interesting and raises good qeustions, but there were many points where I was unsure what was happening or why. At the end of the game, I was left very confused as to why certain things had happened. On a more positive note, the gameplay is excellent. While sometimes many characters seem as though they couldn't hit the side of the barn, the overall fluidity is great. The leveling system is great, and can be very immersive. All in all, if you can over look a few problems with the story, you have an excellent, entertaining, and immersive game that will give you hours of gameplay.The other big problem is the glitches. They are intolerable at some points. They vary, from skipping through entire important conversations to simply crashing ffor no reason at all. This game is very unfinished. From what I've heard, this is due to the developers being rushed by ther sponsors. These glitches aren't really deal breakers, especially sense there are many mods that essentially finish the game. The sad fact is that this game could have been even better then the original-quite a feat-but it is left in it's shadow because of this lack of polish.
Overall this game is worth getting, especially sense it is only ten dollars, but if you want a more finished game, you'll have to download mods on your own time. 7/10 for the Vanilla.

I am really enjoying my time with this game so far. It reminds me in some ways of Limbo. I'm only a few hours in and haven't made much progress, but overall, the game is meeting my hopes and expectations.
What I'm enjoying: Beautiful environments, solid world-building, and learning my place in an unforgiving ecosystem.
What detracts from the experience: A very weak tutorial/in-game learning, controls that don't always feel responsive, and some quirks that I'm assuming are caused by highly randomized elements, such as enemies that jiggle in place rather than resting or path-finding smoothly.
Regarding the controls, I'm unsure if using a controller will help - that is my preferred way of playing these games - but so far, even some relatively simple jumps and maneuvers can require several attempts. Compared to Ori and the Blind Forest, which I think played like a dream, this game is a little on the clunky side. It's far from unplayable, but it can be a bit challenging to pull off the maneuvers you want, and I've run into at least one minor area where the game did not behave consistently (it was having trouble detecting a fruit that I was trying to grab). More an issue of level design than controls, there are also some areas where numerous small hiding nooks have been placed right beside tunnels leading to other areas. Getting the slug cat to enter the tunnel seems to be complicated by these other semi-usable surfaces.
You are mostly set loose to experiment and die. The tutorial covers some bare minimums, but I learned more in the 3 minutes that I just spent glancing through someone's tips post than I probably would have learned in hours of play. The game doesn't really do a great job of building lessons into the environment - if you like learning through experimenting, that's great, but it's looking like you'll have a lot to learn.
I'm not going to lie, I have a soft spot for creatures. Not just the cute little slugcats, but the monsters in the world as well. This game makes it very clear that you need to pay attention to your environment or it will kill you (it may even kill you while you're paying attention). But when you survive a dangerous encounter, it's extremely satisfying. The story is bare-bones, but I think that the world that the adventure is set in and the way it is rendered more than make up for that. I'm looking forward to spending a lot more time with this game.

Many parts of Rain World feel tough, but fair. The survival mechanics create a feeling of urgency and make progression extremely rewarding. The monsters are terifying and formidable, but smart play and a bit of skill in maneuvering around them make them managable. In most areas of the game, there are branching paths allowing you to take a different route if one is too treacherous. These are the parts of the game that work.
The frustration comes from things that feel arbitrarily difficult. There is a particular area in the game that forces you into one linear path, and that path takes you underwater. Not only is it difficult to track where you are underwater, but slugcat behaves very inconsistantly. Sometimes he moves swiftly, and other times he is sluggish and floats upwards. The real kicker is that slugcat drowns in about two seconds. In these moments I do not feel like I can get -better- at the game to progress. I feel like I am at the whim of the stars aligning just right to allow me to progress through this area. This strips me from any agency as a player, and it is only out of stubborness that I even continued after these parts, despite really liking other parts of the game.
This game feels like it needed some additional playtesting before release. Hope the devs take note of the feedback on this game and patch it as I think the changes needed to make these parts of the game  less frustrating would be pretty minor. In the mean time, I can't reccomend  putting yourself through the torture Rain World will inflict upon you.
Edit 4/9:
Recent patch fixed the specific issue with the part I mentioned as well as some of the other more frustrating aspects of the game. I have put a few  more hours in and have been having a much better time  with the game.

The game is gorgeous. There is a single player campaign, so there is a story to the game. It sounds nice. It looks nice.
But I won't be seeing much of it if I get my refund.
The "guard mode" mechanic is terrible, especially on a keyboard and mouse. Everytime you move your mouse, you change guard positions. If you have a laser mouse, this is going to do nothing but frustrate you. You can bind other keys to "change guard," but you CANNOT turn off changing guard via mouse movement.
Meaning, if you want to be exact in your fights in guard mode, you need to move everything bound to a mouse button to a keyboard button, and never touch the damned mouse.
You can of course use a gamepad. However, even with the gamepad, the direction of the guard isn't very accurate, and it will switch often enough to STILL frustrate you. This won't be much of a problem if you don't get past the first part of the story, or if you never run in to someone attacking from your left in multiplayer (fat chance), but it will be a problem otherwise. If you can get over the goofy mechanic and deal, you might love this game.
For anyone who would rather not spend $60 to be frustrated, I don't recommend this game at all.

The Good:

The Average:
Though the game tries to vary up the gameplay and feel between each level, the last few levels start feeling repetitive very quickly.
The Bad:
- Graphic settings is broken, you must go into the config.ini files to manually adjust many of the settings.
- No subtitles
- Multiplayer dead
Conclusion:
It uses the Doom 3 engine and it has the same look and feel as Doom 3 as well but just plays out much faster. Quake 4 seems to successfully combine some old school gameplay with newer level design.

They removed all the good multiplayer modes there is only FFA now, 50 of the 300 cards are behind a paywall (and not just pay 5 bucks...pay them 1.99 for a CHANCE TO MAYBE GET THEM), the UI is slower than ever and the game crashes a lot.
Also, the "open ended deck building" is also a lie.  You are limited to 3 of one type of uncommon, 2 of a rare, 1 of a mythic.  While this does help make more decks viable...its false advertising to say its completely open when its not.
Also, playing versus the AI to get more cards is frustrating.  They give you a hodgepodge deck that has virtually no synergy, and no endgame cards for any of the options you can choose from.  Then you are facing fully completed decks with tons of synergy and they have not only the best premium cards...but cards that players can't even access (even though they are legit MTG cards).  Why even have these cards coded in the game but only for AI?
Finally, this game was hyped to have the M15 core set in it, but really most of it is not M15.  And in terms of the 300 cards in general, 95% of them are absolute trash cards.  This is likely due to them limiting deck building, but still.  This isn't even a true magic experience.  I would say its "fair" in PvP at least, if there wasn't a clearly pay to win mechanic with permium boosters.
Moral of this story is that since 2013, Stainless has been striping this game of features and now has proven to be comfortable with false advertising.  Don't make the mistake I did and buy this out of hype for deck building.  Its the worst trading card game released in years.

I would suppose the most popular analogue for games such as this is Day Z, and justifiably so for it is the first truely successful open world apocalyptic experience as far as I know. Nether is quite similar, and though in its early stages demonstrates an already seemingly expansive world to explore with an overgrown nature engulfed city being telegraphed with such an immersive execution. The ambiance of the desolate city scape only further ensconces the player in the shoes of the survivor as both natural and unnatural sounds coalesce in echoing harmony. Combine this with post apocalyptic often fully explorable structures, and the perpetual looming animosity of other survivors then you can have a rather tense survival experience. However, the current state of the designated enemy is rather at times frustrating. The teleporting variants of the predominant enemy known as the Nether seem to teleport consistently throughout an engagement, however they do so in such imbecilic and interspersing fashion that during the course of the conflict they will at times simply not be visible. Teleporting a floor above you, in the room next to you, outside of the building you are in are common occurrences. This problem is largely absent when fighting outside, but many battles take place around structures or inside of them (hence city). Aside from this obvious blunder there are other problems which I'm sure will be fixed or reimagined as time progresses toward a completed product. Disconnecting from a PvP engagement will also pose a problem, as in the current state it is an overly viable strategy which is only propagated by the reset of all level progress upon death (and of course the loss of all items on your person). The latter I hope remains apart of the game for it adds the edge all games of this sort require to remain suspenseful. I believe this game will resolve most of these, and other problems as I said for it is still quite a work in progress although a worthy one for any of those interested in an immersive apocalyptic experience.

I had a huge number of problems with Shadow Warrior 2 that did a number on its overall fun facto due to the tedium, but the developers have been taking care of their game with consistent patches, making it a much stronger title than it was at launch. I can give this game a more confident recommendation now despite some of the issues that still remain as a part of its foundation.
The loot is still not the most interesting thing on the planet. The only gameplay changing one are the various ammunition types that you can experiment with such as turning a gun into a turret, adding dual wield, or explosive rounds. Unfortunately, you can be discouraged from using them if you’re trying to create a pure elemental weapon since you’ll spending much of your time creating specialized weapons to capitalize on enemy elemental weaknesses. That’s a vital aspect that becomes more and more prominent when playing on the higher difficulties which is one of the major weaknesses of the game.
I already have to react quickly to what’s going on in front of me, but expecting me to quickly read enemy traits that only pop up when aiming at them makes for a messy situation. You can expect to do plenty of weapon switching on the fly to take advantage of enemy weaknesses or to at least stop using a weapon they’re resistant or immune to since dealing reduced or no damage doesn’t result in victory. The enemy traits become more complex on the higher difficulties which can hurt the replay value of the game if you like finding better loot and gaining more experience due to the time to read (TTR) of enemy traits. The TTR is my biggest gripe with the game, especially when being assaulted by groups.
However, despite that complaint, the gameplay and performance were both great at launch and better now. I noticed they performed some optimizations where Chi Blast is concerned since that could destroy frame rates depending on where it was performed. It’s much better now and that was the only performance issue at the time in my experience. The game has a rock solid foundation with its PC version and that scores very well with me considering how many times I’ve been burned this year by AAA games that ran like crippled gazelles. Those consistent frames on Ultra means the swordplay and gunplay both benefit and feel great as a result.
Obviously, the swordplay is where the game shines. Sure, there are guns and I’ve used them for a good while and still do, but the sword skills mean melee combat is ultimately the way to go for most of your loadout for a first playthrough. Some skilled socketing can keep guns relevant, but the sword skills can be upgraded while guns only can have more ammo capacity.
The revamped crafting system can potentially allow for some very crazy things since you can remove negative traits from gems through purification, add a fourth gem, or increase base stats. The first two are game changers, but you’re not going to have access to them until NG+ or if you repeat missions on a friend’s playthrough since the first time through awards skill points. That’s how you can collect the new Orbs of Masamune crafting currency. Acquiring those Orbs can be a more time consuming experience depending on the strength of a gem. The highest cost I’ve seen so far was 700+ to add it as a fourth and missions were giving 32 -62 as a reward.
The new crafting options are the only things I’ve noticed. They added a Sell All Junk button which was a much needed addition. I no longer have hundreds of items sitting in my inventory. The loot filter makes everything easier. You can find items with more ease now as you can select the type that appears in every single item category. It also works with crafting which cuts down on time spent in the menu by a godlike amount. They even added colors to the elemental upgrades for quick identification. What’s funny is that the time saved with the filter and the other UI and QoL changes can go into the new crafting system since you have more things to consider and tinker with, but that time feels better spent versus the soul draining experience that was there before.
Co-op works well and functions, but you’re all end up with similar Wangs. That’s okay, I guess since the story only stars Wang, but I wouldn’t have mind an exclusive set of trees that people could pick for the sake of variation. Playstyles can differ depending on the upgrade(s) they choose for their powers, amulet slot, and armor slots. You could make yourself a melee or ranged monster with upgrades that alter the powers – Chi Blast, Vanish, Healing, Spikes – to support the player’s preference.  Anyway, yes, the game is fun with friends and slicing up enemies together makes for some good times.
I greatly enjoyed the graphics after turning off blur effects. I definitely took some time to just stare at the swaying grass and loved it when It rained. I’m a big foliage fan. Dismembering enemies and seeing the blood stain the grass and flowers red is a nice touch. The level design on the other hand could have used a more personal touch, less recycling, or a better type of procedural generation. You’ll revisit the same place multiple times to talk to the same character again, run into a door that then makes you backtrack to find the enemy that has the key to unlock it, and recognize areas pretty early in the game. The game could have used more one-off areas. There are some, just not enough to keep things from becoming visually bland which makes it appear like a money saving tactic. The Christmas theme the game is rocking now is a nice little touch. They did reuse a map, but the snow and holiday enemies were nice for the special mission. The rewards were really good too.
The writing is filled with a bunch of♥♥♥♥♥♥jokes, puns, and references. The main story is good enough to provide a reason for all the killing. However, it did fall apart at the end in the last 15 seconds with its nonsensical resolution. It was serviceable until that moment. On the lore front, you’ll find dozens and dozens of books (text entries) and fortune cookies. I’m not too fond of having so much text that can provide large amounts of backstory for major characters being delivered in such a boring manner. That and the tone clashes with the dialogue’s writing. It’s super weird and out of place, especially since many of them are depressing diary entries with a suspicious lack of Wang.
The QoL changes I mentioned earlier helped fix the pacing for Shadow Warrior 2. You’ll still stop occasionally to look at the loot and decide on what to equip, but it goes by much faster now. I don’t recommend stopping to read the text entries unless it’s a fortune cookie pop-up, especially if you’re in a co-op game. Also, being in NG+ means I don’t look at the drops until I’m done with the mission since I have the weapons in a good place already. I just need those sweet Orbs.
So, Shadow Warrior 2 deserves a recommendation despite the messy immunity business, repetitive level design, and disappointing ending because it understands how to be a fun game with satisfying slashing mechanics. It’s a game that only became better with time due to the support from the developers. I appreciate their efforts and I like what I see. You might too.

Now moving on to the review.
Pros:
-Deck building; I love the customazation in this DotP. I love the ability to filter your search for cards and see more information about your decks. This will definitely help me get better at buidling decks--not a talent of mine.
-In-game UI; the layout when actually battling is gorgeous. The way the characters and health are represented are fantastic. I kinda like the split battle thing, while it can make the game a little laggy. I think they might've done it to symbolize the 'red zone' that some people refer to when attacking. While it could've been done better, it's a pretty nifty idea.
-Large card pool; while there are microtransactions there are still plenty and plenty of cards to choose from as you go through the game. The first plane's booster packs are nothing but skin and bones but as you move along there are more cards in your pack to reward you. By the end of the game--and defeating the expore nodes--you can get 300 something cards. While you do have to buy 14 more packs (for a total of $30) to get the "full" experience, that's still a lot of cards for casual players just looking to get their magic fix.
-Foilstickers!: While yes this is a microtransaction, this is my favorite kind. I spent a few dollars in DotP 2013 foiling out some decks. I like the idea of being able to make SPECIFIC cards foiled if I so desired. I also just like shiny things.
-Eldrazi: Haven't gotten to Zendikar yet but from the videos I've watched there seems to be some of my favorite plane wrecking babies in this game. +1 for annihilator!
-New cards; as a fairly new Magic player--I'm going on my third year of cardboard magic--I love seeing cards I've played with in cardboard magic on my screen. Brimaz, guildgates, artifacts that are in my Ulagmog EDH deck, etc etc. I love the card pool for this game thus far.
-Opening decks; while they are weak, I didn't have a hard time against the AI even on the hardest difficulty. I lost a few times but that's expected, this game is half skill half luck in my opinon. But once you trudge through the first plane you start unlocking cards you can start tweaking the deck to your liking. I also really love being able to pick your opening colors, even if it's multicolored. I feel like it kinda balances out with the weaker cards. I had tons of fun playing a deck with colors I chose from the begininning. Also you still have time to change it before you move on from the tutorial.
Cons:
-Microtransactions; they have collections so you don't have to play the actual story line. Wow. It's actually hilarious when you think about it. There is an option for lazy ♥♥♥♥s who don't actually want to play the game. As for the "preminum packs" it's kinda crappy. I would have definitely prefered to have unlocked all the cards instead of having to pay for them.
-Menu; It's awful to navigate with a PC. It seems almost as if it was built for the mobile platform and Wizards was just too lazy to make a different menu for PC. While it definitely looks nice it's clunky to navigate. Although I use the avatar diamond in the lower right hand corner to navigate between the campagin and deckbuilding so I'm not entirely bothered by it. But that being said it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥ that I have to use shortcuts to avoid long♥♥♥♥♥menus.
-Opening decks; as much as the opening decks were nice I disliked having to go multicolored. I would've liked a mono color option as I love playing mono green. Beggars can't be choosers though I suppose.
Note:
-Two Headed Giant; I never liked this format, neither in DotP or in cardboard. It's not there and for those people who are head over heels for it, this might be the reason you don't buy the game. Personally, I don't really care. I don't play multiplayer to win as I'm not competitive, I play it when I'm bored and have nothing better to do.
Overall: Buying this game really depends on how you view the DotP games. It's a matter of personal preference. I wrote this review to enlighten others. While I was browsing through the reviews last night a lot of these reviews seemed to be knee jerk reactions to the game. Hope this was helpul for you. It's not the best DotP game but honestly, they could've done a helluva lot worse. 7.5/10

Game is a solid 9.5 out of ten. This is one of those rare gems that just makes playing single player Great again! Multi Player is also great. It was a little touch and go for a while due to some dodgey patches but everything seems to be working again for the most part and the devs are working actively to try and make sure this is one of the best streamlined game experiences you can have!!!
You play as Lo Wang, a wise cracking mercenary who never learns to be socially acceptable but has a great sense of humor that helps off set the world of blood and guts and demons that make up his life. The game is like Conkers Bad fur day when it comes to jokes and cheesy one liners that keep you smiling or at least gives an occasional chuckle here and there.
The weapons do not get old quick. This is really great. All weapons are customisable with three different stat modifiers that vary between players skill and playstyle. They also scale with difficulty and level so you always have some fun and something to work towards. You periodically obtain new weapons from missions or find them on your travels after defeating eneies. You can also purchase some from stores in the game. You also have armor that also featuress similar customisation slots. One specifically for multy player to help you deal with more enemies. There are many different difficulties and they sclae well without feeling like a pointless grind. The game is actually rewarding!! Weapons range from hand guns, to mini guns and missle launchers for firearms and katana's to pantera claws for hand to hand combat!!
The game also features a crafting option to build items that modify stats on weapons by recycling three other stat modifiers. This almost always offers something better and half the time, more useful!
Fights are great and feel rewarding. There is not bullets sponges to be had unless on very high difficulties or playing against bosses so you feel like a challenge is to be had still without getting bored . You wont have to shoot at a guy for 10 minutes to kill him, unless it is a boss and you are too low a level. :P The fighting system is slick and streamlined. The controls are flawless! You also have a few powers including a chi blast that knocks down enemies buying you time to reload, a vanishing act that makes you invisible for a short time allowing you to make a deadly accurate strike to a weak spot or escape to fight again another day. You have a health regen power and a paralyzing attack known as "grip of darkness" that emobalizes your enemies if you get overwhelmed allowing you to strick first.
Leveling up gains Experience that allows new skills to be unlocked! You can select what powers and skills you wish to use making the game feel far less linear than most shooters.
The game also has some great Easter eggs and secrets! Some more notworthy secrets include cameos for Stranger Things, and Mine Craft as well as various other games developed by the publishers and developers. You will see Serious Sam, an Ed-209 knockoff and what looks like a a hologram of Sailer Moon in a room full of cocaine at one point. Periodically you will also notice fortune cookies to be collected that have various quots and much needed wit in the middle of fights. Notedly, many Hunter S. Thompson quotes are thrown around as well as some from philosphers throughout history that embellish actual Quotes and have some real quotes as well. They are as amusing as they are wise more often than not.
Speaking of Hunter S  Thompson, There are tons of drug refferences in the game! Lots of pot plants and piles of cocaine can be found periodically as well.  So if you cannot handle lots of sex jokes, drugs , junkies, violence and gore, then this is not for you. This game is for all the classy people who can take a joke and love seeing how the wild and crazy adventure unfolds.
The graphics looks great and play fairly well too. Most of the issues people had early game are now corrected and more content is in the pipeline to add to replay value! You may still notice lag spikes when playing with many people with maximum enemy counts spawning at the moment but they are imporoving upon that already! I will say that is where the higher difficulties because irritating performance wise. Everything else seems to perform very well. I only get occasional dips in frame rate and one almost freeze in the last 8 hours of play which means most of the issues like memory leaks and such are being fixed!  You wont regret it. The game is great for everyone who loved the 80's and 90's and loves a trip back in time. You even have an option to change the resolution scale to make the game look like an 8 bit commodor 64 game! Just for laughs of course but still fun none the less.

Much faster than the first game in terms of movement, and enemies are generally less bullet-spongey. The levels are pseudo-procedually generated, basically there are sections which are combined together to form a level, sort of like Diablo 2. Thatnkfully there are still secrets, and because the levels are more open-ended they encourage exploration. The performance is mostly good, with some minor lighting bugs and sometimes the UI glitches out. Sometimes it slows down during heavy fights with lots of enemies or explosions on the screen, although that's probably not the game's fault, just the amount of stuff going on. Visuals are nice, a bit better than SW2013 although the character models are kinda eh. Still the enviroments and guns look great. The story and background lore is interesting but the characters themselves are all massive♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ which I suppose is the point. The humor, well that will be up to you. I found a lot of the jokes funny just because of how childish a lot were but I can understand if someone would be annoyed by the relentless amount of jokes. Overall this game was extremely fun, especially if you don't mind the loot-based mechanics.

I recommend this game but with a caveat.  Early Access is early access.  Don't expect a ton of shine when you load this up.  There are networking issues, the tutorial essentially needs a complete reworking (which sucks because there is a lot to this game), and the UI needs cleaning up.
That being said this is a game that shows what passion can be when put into a game.  There is plenty of atmosphere when you do anything in this game.  You don't just turn into a ship and fly off, instead you may get lowered into a launching bay and shown a little camera scene of you leaving.  You get mission briefings on what you're doing before you ship off to fight.  It's really neat!   Also, the ship/vehicle design is really awesome.  Love the look.
Things I would adjust outside of the glaring bugs/issues:
-Time to kill is longer than I think it should be.  You have this visceral atmospheric warfare going on, it should be gritty and intense with infantry combat.  Keeping cover and moving up when you suppress the enemy!  Make weapons have a harder impact!
-The vehicles in the ground game need fixes in their controls.  The Drakka (I think; the dual plasma hover tank) moves it's turret with the hull.  I should be able to move independantly from the turret.  W/A/S/D to strafe and move forward and back while using my mouse to move around the turret and shoot.   Right now when you aim, your hull turns to face that way.  Really unnatural feeling and janky.  Might as well get rid of the turret.     The gunships are the same way too.  Really hard to control.  End up flying all over trying to acquire the target.  You end up fighting your own ship than the enemy.
- Animations for infantry weapons.  Some of the models/animations don't look up to snuff to a lot of the other art in the game.  Feels like you're not firing a weapon, really chinsy.  I don't like some of the weapons.
-Better tutorial.  Normally in an FPS you get beaten over the head with no brainer stuff.  "Press the crouch key to crouch!"  Yeah, no kidding.   In this game it's different.  The controls aren't the problem as that's easy to figure out.  How do you board a ship with a drop ship?  What are those support, command, and combat bars for? How do I get points for those (I didn't know that's why I couldn't equip stuff).  What is the strengths of each fighter?  What's their special ability listed in the options?  etc etc.        I would recommend a 20-30 min tutorial video where you break♥♥♥♥♥♥down Barney style and explain all of those nuances that are specific to the game.
*Wipes brow* For the price and what this game can certainly be, get this♥♥♥♥♥♥

Alright ♥♥♥♥ers, here's the deal. This game is obviously about you versus nature, and it won't be pretty. Except it will be, the game is gorgeous....where was I again? Oh right, the game is brutal. But it's a kind of brutal that has not been seen in a long time. Instead of most platformers, where you die over and over again and finally memorize a map, you die over and over, but you learn how to adapt with each death. You put yourself in the place of a slugcat, a very tiny creature compared to the blood thirsty inhabitants of this broken ecosystem. But there is a much larger story in place, one which you can choose not to follow if you so believe, and turn it into your own experience. Want to sneak past predators and be a white ghost? Check. Do you want to scamper your way to every checkpoint, Check (my first playthrough was doing this) do you want to hunt the deadly predators...well, you can! But it's difficult.
Back to what I was saying though, if you have the patience to learn, this game will reward you. Everything was so thought through by the developer I am blown away, to the point where I FEEL like a curious animal, wondering about the interactions I should take through the enviroment. There have been times where I felt defeated, one death too many. But Rain World is such a fascinating place, every creature evolving to their environment..how can I just walk away and not do the same? I just can't. Sometimes I WISH I could, but this game has too many mechanics, too much I can adapt to, I just have no excuse not to. If you are looking for a game like this, you will not be sad about your purchase..be aware though, it isn't for the feint of heart, how long can you survive?
EDIT: forgot to mention, all these reviews for gripes about the map not being saved etc, the developer has already said he is going to get rid of that next patch. That's the thing, he is such an amazing dude, he is constantly listening to feedback and reviews, so if you come back to this game later and find that all your complaints have suddenly become invalid, FIX. YOUR. REVIEW.

Tomb Raider: Underworld is an entertaining treasure hunter adventure with some overall minor flaws.
The story is a typical Tomb Raider plot with known characters from previous Tomb Raider Games (especially the direct predecessors Anniversary and Legend). Lara seaches accompanied by her partners Zip and Alistair for Avalon, the mythical place King Arthur's sword Excalibur is held and her father searched for years ago. Concluding the Tomb Raider Legend storyline she furthermore is on a treasure hunt for Thor's hammer Mjölnir, an artifact which holds superhuman power and shouldn't fall into the wrong hands.
Overall the story is pretty mediocre. It delivers enough reason to visit exotic places around the world and to raid sunken temples and long forgotten tombs. But none of the characters actually does more than to serve their purpose in being the villain, the more or less funny sidekick or the friend who gets killed. It's a pity that Underworld fails to deliver a compelling storyline with interesting and charismatic characters as the original Indiana Jones movies or the Uncharted series (PlayStation exclusive) did. Nevertheless the story clearly isn't the main acpect why you play a Tomb Raider game.
Gameplaywise you get everything you'd expect from the successor of Anniversary and Legend: Cool setpieces around the world with puzzles, enemies and gunfights. The combat feels really dated and does not deliver any actual thrill resulting in a total revision in the series next entry. But the jumping and climbing mechanics work - besides some glitchy and buggy situations - really well. Unfortunately some settings get recycled meaning you don't encounter the exact same levels twice but you get two pretty good underwater levels (don't be scared, they're really nice) and you raid a big overgrown jungle temple twice, one at the coast of Thailand and one in the jungle of Mexico on a motorcycle.
Graphic and Sounddesign are obivously dated because of the game's age but still are good enough to deliver the joy of being on a world-spanning adventure. I played the game on full settings and use Windows 10 (64-bit) as an OS and did not experience any major bugs, only in one level I had some strange and extraordinary frame drops. Apart from this I played constantly with 144 fps, my screen's limit.
Altogether Tomb Raider: Underworld is not a really surprising adventure and does not deliver any really new features to the series but this isn't always required to give you a good time. The story is forgettable boring but the gameplay itself holds this adventure alone. I've played better games but I also played games much worse. A worthy addition in the Anniversary-Legend-Underworld trilogy. If you like the old school Tomb Raider games you get what you'd expect and possibly what you want.

I can't quite remember how I came to own Amnesia: The Dark Descent (fitting); survival horror isn't exactly my genre of choice. In fact, the last game like this I remember (properly) playing was Alone in the Dark. The first one. But despite it not being 'my genre', there is a lot about this game I enjoyed (or at least appreciated. ;)
The atmosphere is superb. (I did start out with the lights out, but they were turned on again pretty quickly.) It sucks you in, and while you are playing you /are/ Daniel.. which meant that I had to take frequent (and in some cases, prolonged) breaks. The 'insanity' system adds so much to the experience and is something I really appreciated (well..) about the experience. I also appreciated that it didn't rely too much on jumps, but on suspense. Because we're our own worst enemies when it comes to anticipating things.
The story is also interesting/engaging. I enjoyed learning more and more about where I was and what had happened there. The voice acting was good. I enjoyed the puzzles, even though most of them were relatively straightforward (how complicated do you really want them to be when you're scared, anyway? ;). I'd say that the weakest point probably was how linear/straighforward things were, but then I wouldn't have wanted  towander around that castle with no clear aim or idea of where I was going anyway (because I would be the type to walk myself in circles, get too scared, and quit). So.. in the end, I guess I don't really see it as too weak a point. Everything else more than makes up for it (and diminishes as a weak point for the reasons I just gave).
So. Yes, I would recommend Amnesia: The Dark Descent as a thoroughly worthwhile experience. I probably won't be playing it again, despite wanting to know about certain variations and being curious about the custom story option. Once, for me, is enough. But I'm definitely glad I played it because it is a great game.

If you like RTS fantasy games then this is a great one to start with! You can play offline single player modes but the online version is so easy for new players. You can literally spend the first 24 hours of in game time just building up your city and levelling up units WITHOUT worryinging about being attacked. Your 12 hour immunity to attack BEGINS when you decide to build walls and you can hold off on the walls for 12 hours so you have a nice army and city ready to give any attackers a run for their money. The game matches you based on army strength so even when you do finally decide to PVP you will not be getting owned by players with much stronger armies, this is not the D-Bag gank festival that other PVP oriented games tend to be. I am Namaste in game if you have any questions! there is tons of helpful posts in the steam forums to help get you started.
