Of the few Ico-inspired games to come out in the last few years (Toren, Submerged, The Girl & The Robot, Fossil Echo) this is the one I was most skeptical of. It seemed like it would be too on the nose to have its own identity. And yet, this turned out to be the best of the bunch and more original than it appears on the surface.
The game is mostly climbing puzzles like Tomb Raider (and Ico), but there's a few puzzles were you push blocks, carry objects, or pull levers. There's no combat, but occasionally there's areas of danger to avoid. There are a few companions, but they're nothing like Ico's Yorda, and your main interaction is to activate beacon by shouting at a short range. The pacing is great and it does a great job of wordlessly leading you through its unique logic. The game feels like it sheds nearly all of the most clever puzzle elements, by the end in favor of pure navigation. It turns out to be engaging enough, but it's also strange learning how the game works only to have it devolve into a platformer.
I'm mixed on both the graphics and audio. Sometimes it looks incredibly beautiful and sometimes the lighting is weirdly flat. The character animation is amazing and you really believe he's navigating all this terrain... and then other times there's harsh pops between animations. The attention to detail in the music and its ability to dynamically cue based on your progression is incredibly well done! It's a nice enough score, but the instrumentation is also very bland. One of the things I liked about Ico was how alien it sounded, but the music in this seems much too normal (though probably is trying to channel the style of Miyazaki's animes). Audio itself is generally very good at getting the reverb of large chambers right, but there's very little breathing room to soak in that atmosphere with the soundtrack being a near constant.
The story begins as if someone literally said, "Let's make a direct sequel to Ico." You begin washed up on a beach near what reminds of a crumbled bridge. Hmm. By the end it ends up pulling the rug out from under that concept, and it becomes it's own story about something entirely different than I expected. It's sort of a bait and switch, but it's a really smart way of handling the homage without directly taking the idea. I don't think it quite earns its emotional punches, but fair play to the devs for trying.
In conclusion, I liked it a lot and would strongly recommend it to Ico fans. In many ways it's an improvement through modernization.

Great game!
For fans of Planetside 1 and 2, Battlefront, Republic Commando, and even Freelancer, this is a treat. Though not without its rough edges in early access, AFF brings the heat to the sci fi genre with some of the most spectacular game design and levels ever seen.
The city levels evoke the sprawling Blade Runner-esque metropolis that many of us instantly conjure in our minds from decades of novels and films, and unlike most games past in the scifi genre, actually manage to faithfully recreate the same level of scale seen in a blockbuster movie.
Capital ship gameplay is also highly innovative with first person control of the ship, the ability to board and repel boarders, take out bombers and fighter craft etc., all while completing objectives against the enemy spacefleet with your team.
The AI bot support is second to none, and as advertised is able to take on *all* roles in the game, and even has quite good strategic level coordination for taking objectives or flanking out human players.
AFF also launches with a large amount of content for any indie game, much less the first day of an Early Access: 9 (huge) maps complete with multiple shifting objective points, lots of infantry and vehicle weapons and mods/addons for weapons and vehicles/infantry.
----------------
Now, I'm sure you're wondering what the catch is, and if there is a catch.
No catch, but the game does suffer from a bit of a lack of polish. Sounds, particle effects and performance can all be improved.
But for an Early Access game in a day when most early access games launch with barely any content or gameplay to speak of, it's already well worth the price, and is far more ambitious (and delivers!) than most indie games can rightfully lay claim to.
AFF doesn't do the easy thing, and it shows both in the fun of the gameplay and the places where it can improve.

Nether is a first person post apocalyptic MMO survival game. It features multiple servers with (never ever had any trouble logging in, and its extremely quick actually getting into a game) 64 player games, in a world space that feels neither cramped nor oversized. As it’s still early access there are features that have yet to be implemented (hoping for a larger map, more players and creature variety). It is very well done at this point; all the core elements are there it’s just in need of polish. For instance clutter (Tables, Rubbish etc) does appear to be floating in some cases as well as loot. The loot can occasionally feel a bit random and is also a little too shiny. Some of the more advanced graphical features like FXAA (Lighting I think) need refinement. However the general graphics/Textures are excellent with a world that feels similar to The Last Of Us in its apocalyptic tone.
The combat is very solid with a good variety of weapons that you can usually find pretty quickly and guns after an hour or so of searching. Although it can take longer to find guns there are plenty of melee weapons to choose from. The EXP levelling system is solid with a good selection of perk trees and what not (Your EXP/Level does reset after each death). The PVP can be frustrating at times as when you die all of your loot is dropped (there is a storage system though) and I feel this needs refinement (PVP specific servers for instance). The enemy AI from what I have experienced is very good, with the most common foe teleporting all around you. Forcing you to be on constant watch, front and back. Although the enemy variety at this time is limited.
Overall this is an excellent game. The mechanics are solid, with a well thought out loot/combat system that doesn’t put you off retying if you suddenly die, and you will die often, usually as a result of other players than the monsters. It’s not DayZ but then it doesn’t want to be. It’s a lot more approachable for one (you can’t break bones or bleed out) and leans towards a combat/exploration focus rather than Simulation/Survival.
I’d say at this time 3.5 stars (it’s an excellent game at its core it just needs more refinement). However id be very happy once all the little bugs are gone to give this 4.5 or even 5 depending on new features. A must-buy if you’re looking for an a more action orientated game similar (With a very solid loot/collection system) in concept to DayZ

This is an Early Access title at the time of writing this review.
::TL/DR Version::
Single (solo) players - Game is overpriced and not worth the purchase. Development is too focused on the MMO that is being built from this funding project.
Multiplayer/Co-op Players - Game is still overpriced, but somewhat enjoyable with the right server and players.
:: The LONG Version ::
After a little more than 50 hours of playing this game, I have to honestly reject recommending this game. The videos and screenshots look great and I could not help but be very hopeful about this game. While that hope is still there for the potental of Life is Feudal and most of it's features, it has dwindled very rapidly. The fact that this game makes you work for everything, instead of just handing you everything like Minecraft, is the strongest reason why I was so interested in playing. With that said, this game feels more like an unenjoyable job than an enjoyable game at the time of this review.
Life is Feudal: Your Own gives the impression of being the fantastic single-player little brother to the anticpated MMO version to be released later. I bought into the dream, and watched it crumble as soon as I tore into the wrapper. There is no single player experience to this game.
Er, wait, what? Yes, you heard that correctly. The only way a person can play this game and enjoy it, or progress, is by using boosted server settings (skill rate, tunnelling rate, skill point limit) and GM commands. I tried this route, and the game had no enjoyment for me because I didn't feel that I had accomplished anything on my own, regardless of having a house and some walls. I started a second server, to play solo, with all default settings and found no enjoyment for a multitude of reasons.
Life is Feudal: Your Own has no NPCs, other than wildlife. For a solo player, this makes building walls and gates for your settlements pointless. And while there are the combat skills, they are pointless against wildlife. I found myself killed by a boar several times because I was lacking any combat skills to be able to land a hit on them with melee or ranged weapons. Utilizing the GM commands, I gave myself some armor and boosted my skills, only to still die after just a few hits (usually 3-4). If there is no difference is survivability with armor, and no increased chance to hit with better skills, then what is the reason for attempting combat with wildlife? I guess the only thing left is to just be a Lumberjack and a Farmer, right? I will say that the Lumberjack role is about the only role that seemed to work for me. You can strip trees of their branches and bark, and even a few saplings. Sure you can cut down those trees, and even turn them into boards and building logs. However, you can't do anything with it without the supporting crafting skills. Most everything requires some form of metal component to build, so you also need those supporting skills. Suddenly, the skill cap is looking smaller and smaller. Farming is a mixed bag of ideas. The system to find random plants (crops) works to help you find food that you can cook on a campfire to keep you alive or plant to start your crops. That part of the farming skill system works great, but also leads into my issues with the server side of the game.
The problems that do not work for me as a solo player, is the fact that the server has to run almost 24-hours of real time before you are able to harvest those crops that you have planted. Planted trees also require the server to run for an extremely long time period of real time before they have grown enough to be of any real use for the player. The server side is a mixed bag of confusion. The systems used to determine decay and time of day (in-game) will progress between the time a server is shutdown to when it is restarted. This takes place even if the server settings for decay are set to 0 (disabled). A person that is not able to play everyday, like myself, will find this to be quite annoying. Monuments that are used to protect your items from decaying, are not able to be managed while they are damaged. (See Update Note 1) If the monument reaches the end of it's hitpoints before the server is restarted, then it will be deleted upon server restart. This is the same with any other items (dropped items, campfires, snares, etc.) that are not protected or held by the player. Systems such as the growth of crops and the growth of tamed animals will not progress or update while the server is offline. It must be ran non-stop for these to progress. The slightest amount of items will overburden your character to the point you can not pick up anything, or even swap equipment. While there are storage options in the game, the storage limitations on the smaller, yet easier to craft items make them almost pointless. The larger storage options are impossible to obtain for a solo player, due to their increased material requirements, skill levels to craft, and the rate of decay for the numerous dropped items while collecting the other components. This basically adds up to the single player being a lot of the "let the game run, while I go play something else" type of scenerio. For these reasons, I have to warn all players looking for a single player experience to avoid this title at this time. Especially for the overpriced tag of $40 USD.
I found the multiplayer side of this game to be just as much work, with a lot more frustrations. I tried several public servers and found the combat against other players to be just as annoying and unbalanced as my single player experience against boars. There is also the inability to progress on public servers (in my experience) because you are constantly being murdered and robbed for usually crappy primative tools, or the log on your back. Talking to other players, I was bothered by the need to have scheduled shifts between players to guard their settlements from being attacked while others were offline.
Overall, this game made me feel like an over-worked, under-appreciated, non-paid employee that wished I had never even tried. If there was an option of getting my money back on this game, then I would love to use it. WIth the experience that I've had with this game so far, I don't think I will ever re-consider Life is Feudal: YO or the MMO in the future.
UPDATE NOTE 1:
--- Update 0.3.2.6 added craftable repair kits that can be used to repair damage cause by players and decay.

Gonna start this out with H1Z1 is a competitive Battle Royale style game.
I've played this game since Pre-Season 1, Skipped Season 2 which is why I don't have 1,000 hours play time because of queue time hehe
It's come a long way from what it started as, and it's still getting better.
It's meant to be a fast paced battle royale shooter. emphasis on the FAST part.
Getting a Win (1st place) is the most important, but it's not just about winning. It's about the Kills on the way to the top. I'd suggest playing slow at first to learn what to do about shredding, the shoe tiers and basically learning what everything does. Everything is scored on your top 10 placements plus however many kills you have. Whether it be in Solo's Duo's or Five's although each are seperate. So don't worry about deranking.
Once you're confident in your plays start playing aggressive. How it used to be was land, get a shotgun, challenge, die. learn what you did wrong and start another whole game and lobby. Now they have a Combat Zone, where you spawn and respawn loaded with spare helmets, First Aid kits, and the 3 main guns alternating the close range weapon for practice. The AR-15, The AK-47, and Alternating The Shotgun and the SMG "Hellfire". Now just like every game this game has a shooting system you need to learn before you say this game is "trash". The Combat Zone allows you to work on your aim extremely fast compared to playing individual games like it used to be. Take advantage of it, and trust me you can be putting up kills in a game.
- It's not meant to be slow and tactical moving from house to house hiding. you can't hide in the grass in a field when you run Ultra graphics, everyone else can still see you. Although cover is extremely important.
- Sound in this kind of game is exremely important so if you're stomping around looking for loot in a house, expect someone like myself to come straight into that house looking to challenge you off the spawn or even late game.  Although foot steps sound drops off at a certain range. Gunshots can be heard much further, so every shot is useful information on where your enemies are and possibly how many.
- H1Z1 is legit a 100 Square Mile map, it takes time to get around (especially if youre walking). Bunch of different kinds of terrain and "Points of Interest".
- Don't forget to check your map for the safe zone, because you'll need to start moving towards it pretty fast depending on where you land compared to the zone. The toxic gas has been moved up in how fast it advances, so you need to keep it moving.
I really enjoy this game because it's not as time demanding as CS:GO per game, so kinda casual. but also competitive and will get your heart going the further you make it into the match. It only counts you're top 10 so I don't really care if I die of the spawn because it doesnt count against my top 10. Each game should only last around 30 minutes at the most. The Short:
Its Battlefield 2142 all over again. You say it like its a bad thing.
The Long:
Angels Fall First, despite its strange and seemingly unrelated name, is an absolutely stellar game and a sure buy for anyone who enjoys any of the Battlefield games or even the Battlefront games. The gameplay is spot on out of the gate, but will need some minor tweaks as we go through its time in Early Access. Overall this is a solid early access game that is more fully featured than some AAA games that have come out recently, and is extremely well done in its 7 years of creation and refinement. I look forward to sinking many weekends into this learning its special mechanics and mastering its gunplay.
The graphics are great for an Unreal 3 game, and its runs buttery smooth maxed out on my rig (which is a bit of a power house with its i7-4790k, 16gb of RAM, and a GTX 980) but thats more that can be said about some PC games. The textures could use some work, but the draw distance is impressive both planetside and in space and the visual flare of lasers and♥♥♥♥♥♥wizzing around you in a multi-squad firefight are amazing. Vehicles and character models take visual damage as they get shot up, which adds a wonderful touch to the game.
The sound is my biggest gripe about the game so far. Some of the weapons lack the punch that we've come to know and love from our first person shooters. Lasers don't sound "lasery" enough and gas-operated firearms lack the meaty bass that makes them feel like more than a pea-shooter in your hand. I really hope the developers focus on improving their sound design overall with better voice acting, sound effects, and music to really bring the game together.
Gameplay is where this game really shines, as all games should in a perfect world. If you've played a Battlefront game, you've played a stripped down version of this. The time-to-kill for the weapons could use a little tweaking, namely in reducing the amount of CLIPS I need to put in someone before they keel over. The weapon customization is on par with that of a Battlefield game with a tad less guns. You can customize sights, barrels, ammo, and more including your armor and grenades. Lots of potential to change it up every so often if you get bored playing a particular role. Tired of running in with a LMG and heavy armor? Change it to a shotgun and light armor for a totally different experience in terms of engagement. There's plenty of possibilities and the game's lack of a class system helps the player truely play the role they want to with the equipment they want to use.
There is two real map "types" with plenty of large and varied maps to choose from. The first is your standard fair land based map with small cities and towns, with spawnable vehicles to drive around and blow stuff up with. There are a few that take place within a single massive compound or city and those tend to be my favorite levels due to their smart layout and intense CQC skirmishes. The second type are space battles that kind of play out like Battlefront space battles but with more varied objectives than "Blow up the enemy ship". One notable map has one team defending a space station while the other tries to land dropships that act a spawn points on it in order to take it over. And all this is happening while other players are in fighters and bombers and even HUGE frigates with interiors and everything are duking it out outside the station. The scale in all the battles is wonderful and really makes you feel like its a huge fight and you're just a tiny cog in the war machine.
My favorite feature by far has to be the ability to play a full match with up to 63 bots, all with scalable AI levels and even equipment levels. This is a godsend, especially in the early days of the game when there may not be many servers or players on said servers. The AI is just good enough to keep you on your toes and can still move rather coordinated offensive moves or defensive lines. I had a single match with just AI last over 2 hours with constantly changing battles. It was more fun than the few multiplayer matches that I played with much more intense combat senarios and with no risk of being disconnected or lag.
Overall, you'd be a fool to not pick this up at a price of less than $15. Its a steal for the value that you get in the game and I look forward to what the developers add and refine in the game.

Nothing could be further from the truth. Rain World is a perfect balance of beauty and brutality. The artwork is a colour palette wetdream, and I've found even more immersion by turning up the sound effects of the game, so that I've learned to distinguish environmental factors by ear.

It just takes observation. There are so many tiny nooks and crannies that you can hide into, and then just observe a good majority of the scary♥♥♥♥♥beasts that will make a lounge rug out of your fur.
Rain World removes any sense of hand-holding. I can understand why so many people would hate this, but what it offers in return is the most genuine sense of exploration and wonder.
Buy this game, and embrace it with an open mind, and I'm convinced that you will ♥♥♥♥ing love it.

While I consider this a great game, I would only recommend it for a certain kind of player. Although it is a platformer, a good deal of patience and perseverence is needed. The game will often seem unfair to the point of brutality and frustration, as much of the other entities are procedural in nature and governed by their own internal factors. Initially the controls will feel muddy and imprecise, and you won't even be told some of the most useful basic interactions. However the game ultimately grows beyond this. It explains little, so those who enjoy mystery while also being able to appreciate mastery over an admittedly arcane control/game system will probably love this, but if you require more immediate enjoyment and better telegraphed mechanics then it may be worth skipping. Even I had to play in 30 minute bursts to begin with, but it quickly grabbed me (and occasionally spat me out, and then grabbed me again). For how intense and strange the game can be, I would suggest playing it casually. Think of it like hardmode Super Meat Boy at a slower pace and with a far steeper learning curve, none of the arcade styling, and a Team Ico approach to storytelling (zero to little verbal or written instruction or narrative, with the world itself and the expressions of the inhabitants telling the story themselves). You will also want to look up some of the advanced controls that the game never tells you, because without those I imagine the game would be incredibly frustrating. Things like double-tapping the grab key to switch your items in your hands, or holding down and tapping the grab key to quietly drop the item in your primary hand.
The basic idea is that you play the role of a lost slugcat, a slimy quadrupedal thing with the ability to slide, climb and wriggle your way about an unforgiving natural world in search of your family (and for others of your kind). The rain of the world falls so heavily that it utterly demolishes most living beings exposed to it directly, so the flora and fauna have adapted to hide and hibernate, with brief periods of busy activity during the dry spells. You must eat enough to ensure you can hibernate, and then find your way to a saferoom to last out until the next activity cycle. It sounds simple, but you are low on the food chain. While agile, you are weak. While clever and adaptable, your tools are limited and your predators many. With a few exceptions, the creatures in the world aren't conveniently immortal threat entities just used to usher you around, meaning that the unfolding of any one encounter can be painfully stacked against you, or conquered with strokes of brilliance or luck. This game rewards exploration and bravery just as much as it punishes it. If you can deprogram your thinking of "I cannot defeat this" or "I absolutely have to go this way", you can usually find alternate routes or new survival strategies. Sadly the game doesn't elaborate on this, and someone who tries to overcome challenges by just throwing themselves at the brick walls may eventually find that some walls just don't crumble. Sometimes there is no trick. Sometimes it isn't a glitch. Sometimes certain approaches or routes are supposed to be unfair, and it is upon you to investigate for a new way around, even if that means slight backtracking. But sometimes the 'impossible' encounter can be conquered with a strategy you never tried before. Sometimes a resource can be hiding in plain sight until you realise its uses.
The game eventually goes beyond just exploration, giving you cryptic opportunities to dig into a little of the backstory, with a mind-boggling ending that I can appreciate people may hate if they never found a way to tap into some of the lore. By the time I was finished, I was both relieved and awestruck. Such a melancholy but brilliantly original feeling little gem. Definitely not for everyone, but I'm damn glad this kickstarter got funded. Now a piece of me hopes for expanded content or a sequel of this world somehow.

To keep this short and simple, since very few if anyone will read it, and I tend to ramble and rant randomly, I'll simply list a few ways this title compares with similar games, from my perspective.
I have played most of the TR games since the original on the playstation.  I always enjoy them to at least some extent, but often gave up on finishing them, rather than look up walkthroughs and strain my eyes and/or nerves for hours and hours.
This game, however, I truly enjoyed.  I watched part of one video walkthrough, because of confusion, but it was my mistake as I simply wasn't fully aware of the inventory system (since I had the item the entire time, but am quite used to notifications these days.)  I played on the easiest difficulty, but that almost exclusively affects combat.  The new functions available made the fighting even easier at times, but also tempting to fool around with, resulting in Lara's untimely demise more than a few times.  To be honest, I tend to dislike the combat systems of tomb raider games most of the time, but looking back I can clearly state that if they had always had some of these abilities in earlier titles, especially the dedicated melee/spinkick/jumpkick/etc, I would have enjoyed them all much more.  To me, the best parts of this "original/non-reboot" Tomb Raider series, was the adventure aspect.  Earlier titles varied greatly in their adventure/puzzle/combat ratio(s) but never quite like this game.  Some was frustrating, even a couple parts that took dozens of attempts, but the issues were mainly my own.
All things considered, the puzzles were quite easy, levels often quite linear, and plot twists that weren't often surprising.
But the most important thing about each of those "negatives" is if you are comparing this game with others that specialize in one or two aspects.  Despite simplicity at times, the puzzles often required thought, patience, and were fun.  Any "linear" issues are irrelevant to me for this game, as it was more of an interactive movie, not an open world RPG.  And the story, despite it not being perfect, and often described as anti-climactic, felt more real and understandable than some big end fight.    tl;dr. enjoy it for what it is.

Potentially 2017's Ubisoft hit, as long as the developers do what they did with Siege. Siege in its early days was quite a mess, rampant with hackers, and generally unbalanced. Over time, it was molded into a great and must buy FPS for anyone who enjoys the genre, and with the many free weekends and sales, its hard to find people who dislike Siege.
For Honor is a fighting game, disguised as hack and slash. Its amazingly addictive and intense, with great customization for characters. The animations are incredible, and all transition in and out of each other very nicely. The game is VERY well optimized, coming from someone with a GPU thas the equivalent of a 750ti in 2017. There was a lot of care in making this game look appealing. So, does it PLAY good?
The game requires reflexes, reactions, and mind games which is a staple of any fighting game. There are 3 character types: vanguards, heavies, assassins and hybrids. Vanguards are balanced characters, comparable to Ryu from Street Fighter. Heavies are usually slow, but either hit hard or have a lot more defensive options. Assassins are fast, aggressive and reflex oriented, but tend to be low on health. Hybrids are a combination of any of the 3 types, usually no more than 2. Despite sharing similar archetypes, every character is different, making character knowledge absolutely vital. For Honor can be very frustrating as you are learning the ins and outs and getting accustomed to its unique control scheme, but its insanely rewarding puting all that knowledge and practice into play and coming out on top.
Lastly, story mode... story mode here isn't anything particularly interesting. Its a glorified tutorial, with an interesting set up and and good presentation, but it feels quite tacked on, like many singleplayer campaigns in MP focused games tend to be. Its worth a playthrough for unique emblems and customization that you can't get elsewhere, however.
All and all, For Honor has a lot of potential. Its very fun, its very addictive, and very rewarding. If you are still on the fence, its safe to wait a month or two and see how it plays out, but I think if you are looking for a new multiplayer game to grind out, For Honor is a very good choice.

After playing most other Duels of the Planswalkers, this is the first one I cannot recommend. Even as a learning tool, this version may leave you bitter and disilusioned in magic as a whole.
After the first deck you recieve, all other cards have to be obtained through booster packs, which you earn by playing. However, the idea of booster packs is only an illusion. You recieve the cards in a set order depending on which plane you play on. So if you want Brimaz, you have to unlock every other card on Theros because he is the last. And after you unlock every card on a plane, THERE IS NO REASON TO CONTINUE PLAYING THERE. You cannot gain additional copies of cards, so you'll only ever get one Brimaz.
Additionally, not all cards can be found in free booster packs. Some cards can ONLY be obtained through "premium" packs bought for real money. These cards include:
-Kozelik
-Stoneforge Mystic
-Maelstrum Archangel
-Kitesail Apprentice (Really?)
-Blasting Station
Being able to construct your own decks is supposed to be a major draw this time around, however it came at the expense of all pre-made decks. You can ONLY use the first deck you recieve (nearly all commons and uncommons) and decks you've built out of a pool that only reaches 300 cards. This ends up with you having a lot less variety and synergy in your decks, especially if you're new to the game. Additionally the constructed deck mechanic fails in that you're basically building a 60 card sealed deck to face against pre-made decks until you reach the point where you've unlocked enough to make a confident constructed deck... but at that point you've probably beaten most of the single player campaign.
Additionally there are cards programmed into the game that you as the player cannot use. TONS OF THEM. Now, older versions of the game have all done this, it's not new. BUT in those versions it kinda made sense as all you had was pre-made decks and perhaps those cards didn't fit in any of them. But now when you can make your own decks, every card programmed into the game should be avalible to you at some point. There's no reason not to give the players cards like Grey Merchent and Honor of the Pure when you already put them in the game!
There's no secondary game mode this time around, such as Planechase or Archenemy. Also gone are the entertaining and sometimes even tricky challenges that would give you one turn and a set of cards to get out of a bad situation.
On a plus side, the game looks very pretty. Backgrounds and menus look very stylish as do all the booster pack arts. The downside is this comes at the expense of actual functionality. Even the escape menu during a game is a mess, and is really more form coming before function.
The game runs slow unless you turn off shadows and the audio is always popping for me.
The game is also very buggy. Often, when too many triggers are going on the stack and some form of lifegain is involved the game will break and make whoever was gaining life invincible. You can tell this has happened because their life total won't change. I've had to happen to the AI as well as myself.
Additionally a lot of cards don't work as they should (Ajani's pridemate still only gets 1 counter when there are multiple lifelinking creatures dealing damage) and targeting creatures during combat can get messed up by some strange bug that returns a "cannot target creatures in that zone" error.
So, once again, do not purchase this game. Purchase duels 2014 or 2013, they are much better and worth it especially if you're trying to get into magic.

I've been a Magic player for 20 years now, almost since the very beginning. I love the card game, its intricacies and depth, which puts to shame other trading card games like Hearthstone at the moment. There's so much work behind each set, it's nothing less than amazing.
Sadly, Wizards seems determined to destory all of their reputation with their DotP series, and this is one of the top fails.
It is curious to me that throughout each and every iteration of DotP, I've felt as if the games were beta versions at best. They had an unfinished feel to them: as if they were not tested by actual players, but only by the developers blind to their own shortcomings. This game has exactly the same feel, but worse. The menus are horrible to interact with. They're slow, unresponsive, inelegant. The system and the game itself is slow even on my new computer, the AI is taking the wrong decisions, and the land tapping is messed-up so that whenever I want to cast a spell I have to manually adjust the lands being tapped, or the wrong lands would be chosen.
Now compare this to Blizzard's Hearthstone slick inteface, their attention to every minute detail (even when you need to wait for online players to connect, there's a 'wheel of fortune' that revolves with good music, so that you feel like you're actually doing something), and their willingness to actually change the format by ignoring things like 'lands' and thus making the game less dependant on chance and shuffling than MtG.
I used to think that Wizards could've made the DotP series much better, but they didn't want to because they simply don't want players to be hooked up on DotP as opposed to Magic Online. This is no longer the case, or not completely. For games as badly wrought out as DotP 2015, which 1st year design students (or anyone with skill...) could probably have designed better, I must come to the conclusion that Wizards just couldn't find someone competent enough to program it for them. Obviously, there is a management fluke somewhere here, and it reflects on what Wizards think of their audience. That's us.
When somone in the street asks for my money and then screws me over, I will not buy from them again. When a company asks for money to create a game, and then provides me with a shabby, barely-coherent result, I will not buy from them again. And I do not see any reason to buy DotP 2016 (or for you, kind readers, to buy DotP 2015) before Wizards have shown their commitment to the player base and the game by fixing the huge, glaring problems with DotP 2015.
Sad that I do not believe this will happen.

Let me start out by saying that the game isn't bad. It's a great concept, and it looks pretty great. Further, the game is still in Beta, so don't view the game -too- harshly.
But it has a long way to go before it's worth buying.
1. Too much emphasis on PvP, to where ultimately the game feels like a chore to play. It's impossible to rally any sort of human cooperation a majority of the time, which while fine in a game like DayZ, is a serious flaw in a game like Nether (where safe areas have to be defended and survival typically is best in groups).
I'd suggest making two (or more) seperate teams/groups, of which the player has to choose from on character creation and cannot change unless they rejoin the server.
One is the "survivor" group, in which members of the group cannot hurt other members, and people inside gain exp boost (or some other form of incentive [maybe hunger slows down?]). The other group is the bandits, which is the free-for-all side of the game, offering no incentive beside being able to hunt whoever they want. The two groups should be easily distinguishable.
2. Safe areas are not safe. People often camp the entrance of a safe haven and shoot anyone approaching. The ideal solution is extending the area of safe havens and giving combat a cooldown (10seconds?) upon exit.
3. The level system feels pointless, as it resets after every death. It should be account bound, much like how gold-items are. Or removed. Either way, as it stands, there is no reason to level up.
4. Collision issues are everywhere. Crouching often gets you stuck on objects, especially while on a roof.
5. Name tags are displayed when you hover over another person, which is a real big issue when trying to hide/avoid other people. This feature should either be removed or it should be changed to only display in extremely close encounters.
These five issues, amongst numerous other glitches (gun delay, scenary bugs, etc), make the game not worthwhile yet. I hope to see these things changed very soon, so that it feels like playing the game is worthwhile.

This game is ver challenging. For anyone who likes Amnesia Style monsters and atmosphere combined with a Fallout-sque setting and Day-Z concept.
This game is basically a first-person Day-Z with monsters, known as the Nether, instead of zombies.
The game can be hard at first, as you are spawned randomly in the map with nothing but a kitchen knife. But as you look around, you will find weapons, food, and medical supplies. The hardest part of the game however, is not finding supplies, but keeping them. If you die in Nether, you lose all your items and skills/experience. The biggest challenge is gaining experience for your skills while trying to stay alive. Run across a small group of nether, no problem, maybe one level or half a level there. But run into a bigger group, maybe five levels, but without any friends, you are guarnteed to die.
Even after successfully farming Nether and gathering a good amount of items, there is still the threat of other players out there. Some are friendly, some are two faced, and some will kill on sight.
In short, if you can grab some friends or make some online, you will have a better and easier time in game.
But the solo experience is also very tense and fun if you like survival-horror games. Defintely worth the buy.

Nether is an amazing combination of spectacular post-apocalyptic survival, and very well put together First Person Combat. It does update rather often, so you need to be installing new things quite a bit, but honestly, the updates only make the game that much greater, so the updates are worth the wait.
This is a strict Multiplayer only game, so if you don't have good enough internet to play online, I don't recommend getting it just yet. Multiplayer is quite amazing in this game, and really gives the player a more intense experience when exploring and surviving the world, because now you aren't just fighting mutants, you are also fighting real time players around the world. You can either team up with friends, or be a lone wolf, the choice is completely up to you.
The graphics in this game are absolutely incredible, are give the game a whole new depth to surviving. The game features a full day to night system, moving water simulation, grass and tree movement, and actual structure movement in certain objects. The games graphics can be turned down if it is too much for a weaker computer, but if you have a beast computer, I definitely recommend playing this game in all it's glory, because it truly looks amazing.
The gameplay mechanics in this game are also quite cool, such as the combat, movement, and interactions with other things. First off, the combat system is very well made, and gives players the choice of certain weapons they'd like to use. More of a close combat fighter? go with a deadly hatchet or a baseball bat. Want to snipe from atop a building? Find a sniper rifle to pick off your enemies, the combat choice is all up to you. The movement in this game is very nice and fluent, and has just the right amount of bobbing and motion blur, just enough to feel real, and not enough to annoy you, so it's very well balanced and playable. Interactions with other things is a very cool thing in this game. Finding random objects such as a sowing kit is actually important, even though it doesn't sound like it. You can find and interact with so many different items in the game, and it really gives the player a bigger survival feeling, instead of just having no hunger or thirst.
Finally, the most important thing, this game is VERY fun. Games are not just about fancy guns and graphics, which this game has, it's about the fun in it. What's a game with no fun? I found myself staying up until three in the morning, running from monsters, and exploring the vast open world. There were many jump scare moments, and awesome fights. I realize that not everyone enjoys the same game, so that's why I'm about to put a conclusion of what kind of gamer would enjoy this game.
This game is meant for the people who enjoy exploring an open world, with not any objective except for surviving. It's a First Person Shooter, which means you are seeing from the perspective of a man's eyes. This game is scary in a lot of ways, and can scare people who are not good with jump scares, or very ugly and scary monsters. This game is also violent, and has killing of mutated monsters, who spray blood when hit, and die in a pool of blood like goo, and also the killing of other humans, who will fall over when dead, but only drop their items, and not lay in a pool of blood. This game is also Multiplayer only, at the moment, and requires that you are online at all times, possibly on a server with no people, or on a server loaded with people, so you will, most likely, be playing with strangers most of the time on this game.
I've had a lot of fun playing this game, and I hope a lot of other people will help support this game to help make it even better!

Shadow warrior 2 is an absolute amazing game. The combat feels realy great and fluid, you just slice and dice your way through the enemies, get loot, get good.

So why do I not recommend this game ?
After the Patch on the 21/22 of Oct there were new stuff added and some stuff changed. For example a heavily overpowered weapon was made 66% less overpowered but still staying as one of the best in slot kinds. The thing leaving a very bad taste in my mouth is the invention of immunities to damage types.
Immunities to me are a somewhat lazy way to increase the difficult of the game but offer little to no complexity added. I've reached the point prepatch where i could outright ignore physical resistant mobs and just use any physicaltype weapon to my pleasure through stacking crit% critdmg% and dm% values overall on my gear.
I realy enjoyed the moment reaching that level. Just beeing able to nobrain through the level / map / missions / campaing all over again. Times were great.
Now dont get me wrong. Usually thinking while playing games is involved but I realy miss games where you just dont need to focus on the fact that in a group of X enemies you have atleast 1 guy immune to 3 diffrent damage types which regenrates health, atleast half of the group is immune to a combination of 1 - 2 diffrent damage types, 90% of the group is immune to any chi power, and they are pretty much able to exhaust a decent lifepool in no time.
I mean yeah, i could totally use ranged weapons in that situation. Just let me reqeuip all of my usefull gems to re-slot them into my go to guns. re-allocated my armor upgrades / amulett. And enagage the group of bullet sponges.
Damn the guy with immunity to fire has moved infront of the guy with ice immunity, better switch my weapon. Ah crap I ran out of ammo for that paticular weapon as they sponged realy heavy on my bullets. Lets just vanish and reallocated to another weapon.
Dang where did my upgrades go again, gotta search for the name...
Ah man i found it. Whoops an enemy is attacking me. Good thing i have a rather large healthpool, Dang it oneshotted me. How unfortunate. Better go down in difficulty. Hmm playing hard instead of T3, Too easy, still Immune enemies show up from time to time.
Well lets fight on insane instead. Yeah with constantly swapping between elemental and physical weapons i am able to do that. Lets go up to Insane T2. Hmm yeah common enemies are immune to stuff. Let's just grind Insane for exp then. Takes forever. You can't gain exp past a certain level on a certain difficulty unless you go upwards in difficulty. Also no exp-bar you gotta lookup the values yourself in your savefile... wat
TL;DR;
I realy enjoyed the heck out of SW2 prepatch 21/22 of oct.
Afterwards it's just like any other game with lazy difficulty / oneshot mechanics once you reach a certain point. Better save your money and play the unpatched gog version.

Alright, now that STEAM has somehow decided to make some words censored. Might as well re-write this into proper review. And trust me, ol Dukie will get the royal bolloking he deserves...
Duke lounges on his fat backside in a casino, getting his nob gobbed by suspiciously barely-legal looking schoolgirls. Whilst the aliens from Duke 3D return, promising peace and cookies instead of butt-probing and war.
And take a wild quess actually happens.. They do come in peace.. Just to f*ck you over if you actually believed it.
No seriously, i cannot talk about the story because Duke Forever decided to take the good ol' design decision of shooters of yore, to actually have no story at all. And even if Forever had a story, it still would have been a pile of w*nk.
Seriously Duke Forever is a decent in the shooter department, and pretty much s*it at everything else.
Mostly impaired by the design decisions, made in the mythical eons ago when they decided to create a sequel to Duke 3D. Looking at the shiny newcomers and quite sadly trying to ape all of them and trying its hardest to innovate with the concept.
I'm suddenly reminded of an old picture in the ICanHasCheeseburger sister-sites. Where there was a photo of a pre-order receipt for Duke Forever, i cannot now help to think, whether said man would be happy of Duke Forever, or come to realisation that his long awaited decade would only produce a complete dissappointment .
But with that PADDING of the review, make mental note since it is the whole theme of Forever.
The gameplay is horrid, Duke clunks around like a arthritic senior citizen. Jumps with a ridiculous "hungh!" That i bet sounds like all the other Dukes "effort" noices. Only open his flappy mouth to spurt one-liners, that although some were mildly humorous, they still did not fill anything in the enjoy department.
Gunplay, although being the only part that is even with the slightest redeeming value. Feels anemic as all hell and even after they patched the stupid design decision of only carrying two (2) guns, to the extreme number of four (4), wont make it any better, since all the weapons are about as interesting as pea-shooters, with annoyingly limited ammo and not enough ammo in the levels to justify carrying four (4) butt-violators to battle. Indeed i had to continually change my loadout after i noticed, that certain level either had no weapons and enemies, or only having two (2) or three (3) weapons that i did not have in my loadout, and had to change my most explody weapons into these anemic pea-shooters..
And the level design.. Although i could pull the argument that Duke 3D also had somewhat bleak areas and generally dark themes, I still feel that Duke 3D still has lot superior level design than Duke Forever, surpricing no one ever. I feel that i should plaster the "evolution of shooter levels"-Picture here, but i think i'l just let you google that... Anyway where was i ?
Oh yes levels, BORING.
In all and all, Duke Forever is terrible, but in a good way. I'm going to pull the Terrible good movie argument here.
Duke Forever feels like a terrible late 80's early 90's action-film and is that a bad thing, not really unless you use that as the only response in a debate. Duke Forever fills the BS-Meter all too well, and is in the level many terrible movies, with equally sh*t jokes, terrible storyline, shooting and deaths of useless extras and minor supporting-roles. But as a game, Duke flops flat..
And he requires ton of "little-helpers" to get into working order. Unfortunately for Dukie, the helpers are console-generation tropes and design decisions that are more butter-buttons than actual medication.
Duke Forever, get the all too generous: D+

Well, I finally sat down and played it, and I have to say that I loved it and all the bad press it got was unwarranted! Duke Nukem Forever was a blast to play! Everything from the strip club mini-games to the hardcore gunning action to the anti-air missions. For those of you who aren't familiar with the textbook case of "Development Hell", Duke Nukem Forver was a sequel planned almost immediately on the heels of its acclaimed predecessor, Duke Nukem 3D. Unfortunately, stuff happened, legal stuff happened, and a game was spat out around 2011. After seeing bits and snippets and reading up on some negative reviews, I finally bought it and played and, like I said, LOVED IT! Duke Nukem, having accumulated fame, fortune and everything else (a casino, a restaurant franchise, a strip club, etc.) from saving the Earth, gets his mood ruined when ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ aliens show up with less than diplomatic intentions. Duke Nukem has aspects of the Gears of War, HALO, Doom 3 and every other big name shooter instilled into its mechanics and is peppered with mini-games on the side (some pointless, some cool, some kinky), all the while staying true to its original origins of one-liners, violence, machismo and BABES. The mechanics were smooth, the gameplay was a little hard but not too hard, the graphics were beautiful, the weapon selections was great and the setup for everything was beautiful. So why did it get negative reviews? Not sure, but if I had to nitpick what may have been wrong with it, I'd say it was a little too linear. It had a very clear plot and story that the player has little choice but to follow along with. It's reminiscent of games like (2006 sleeper) Prey and Bulletstorm in this sense. Aside from that, it's everything you'd expect from a Duke Nukem sequel, so give it an honest try. It'll be in the bargain bin for the rest of its days, so what have you got to lose?!

Duke Nukem Forever is a first person shooter 15 years in the making. Back in the 90s most of us fell in love with Duke 3D. Not for its movie cliches or paying women for money, but for its non linear levels with a lot of exploration and guns. Well Duke Forever took away the non linear level design. Now Duke is stuck in some one dimensional levels. You'll visit the desert, a damn, a bar, an alien hive, his underground complex, get shrunk in a Duke Burger all on your journey to a tower. Duke isn't as fast as he used to be, so now he has vehicles every so often. You'll sit on and drive remote controlled cars and a giant monster truck that squashes enemies and uses nitrous boost for the jumps.
I think my issue with this game is the first two hours felt like everything but first person shooting. The game throws a lot of distractions at you. An interactive museum dedicated to Duke, punching, playing pinball, driving, first person platforming and a turret section. It just seemed like the shooting was 15% of what Duke Forever was.
Once you get over the giant hill of the first two hours, the game feels like a Half Life 2-ish game and that's good. Duke's world has been taken over by aliens. If it didn't sound Half-Life 2 enough for you, Duke walks and drives his way to a massive tower with a beam of light extending to the sky. There is a checkpoint system and no exploration or secrets. There are a few simple physics puzzles here and there. Moving barrels to weigh things down. Stuff like that.
The game uses a typical Unreal / Gearbox with controls to thumbstick crouch, thumbstick sprint (forward only), weapon switch, grenade, trip mine, zoom aim, fire, melee, jump and actions / reload. There are quick D-pad controls for Duke's night vision, holovision (duke clone to distract enemies), steroids and beer.
You can only carry 2 weapons and switch between them. There is a good variety of weapons. A laser sighted pistol, alien laser, shotgun, triple barreled ripper machinegun, rail gun to snipe, RPG, chaingun, devastator, freeze ray, triple stinger missile launcher, trip mines, grenades and so on. Nothing feels like it has impact.
The enemy intelligence is pretty good. Berserker pigs will charge, pig soldiers will shoot at you, and if you hide, they will grenade you. Alien soldiers hover, teleport in and out and actually try to flank you. It makes for a nice dynamic. The only problem is a lot of the maps are so straight forward, they don't allow for being flanked. The boss fights are pretty easy and that's not a complaint. Just RPG them until they're low on health, run to them and uh button mash them to death.
Other enemies from the franchise make their return. Octobrains swim, hover and shoot projectiles at you. Preginators jump and face stick onto you so you'll need to button mash to take them off. Hovering assault commanders that fire missiles at you. Overall, it seems like there aren't that many enemies, just different versions of them.
There are a few sections that confine you to an area and just have enemies flood in. It feels like a cheap way to extend gameplay, even if it does highlight enemy intelligence. Some enemy rooms are so simple that you see the enemy dropping in, so you can be there to shoot them point blank, taking away any kind of challenge or fun.
If this game wasn't Duke, I would have kept playing to realize there is an enjoyable game here past the first 2 hours.

This game is a 'survival' exploration platformer, in that survival is more a theme than in any kind of exceptional game mechanics. You can wander about from place to place, making sure you can collect at least four units of food before you find a new shelter, all the while avoiding enemies and other hazards along the way. At each shelter, when you have food, your game is saved, and you gain a karma point. With enough points, you can progress past doors to other sections. Dying causes you to lose a point.
That's this game in a nutshell, but that's not what the game is about. It's how it expands upon and details all of these mechanics that make the game much more. The environments are diverse, the enemies are unique, and around every turn there's something new. Finding out that I could
, as well as encountering certain items and interactions, like finding
, or realizing that
were the kinds of experiences I initially felt the game would be all about.
The game continues to build on that, adding more dynamics, more enemies, and more hazards along the way.  The initial excitement came from being able to investigate options by tinkering with objects, routes, and by observing enemy behaviors. However, as time goes on, this excitement will fade, or will come in small bursts as new areas are unlocked or new bits of the game and its mysteries are revealed.
You will become frustrated. The random enemy placement that will cause you to die before you can react, or force you to wait until your time runs out. The fidgety nature of the physics platforming and inaccurate controls, which, while they make sense, will lead to your doom on more than one occasion. The incredibly frustrating rooms full of things that will kill you time and time again as you spend hours trying to work your way through a single section. These kinds of complications aren't readily present in the trailer or the game description.
At the end of it all, I have 'beaten' this game, which, judging by the achievements at the time of writing, is roughly 0.6% of all players. It was no easy task, and my journey was a hateful, spite-filled one, as I drove to overcome the challenges this game presented. I was satisfied to have seen what I set out to accomplish, but it was not a happy and fun experience. It is definitely not the game I initially expected.
It seems a fair number of the more popular reviews are from people who haven't even really been to the game's 'halfway point' which means they're still kind of reviewing only a partial experience. I don't mean to call into question the validity of other people's opinions, because they're still fair points, but there's still more to it than just that, and trying to detail it out would ruin most of the game's actual experience.
Edit: Thankfully with patch 1.01 several of my initial concerns have been addressed, so I have revised this review to reflect both this patch and my completion of the game, with more a focus on the game's overall experience and tone, which can't easily be described through breaking down specific mechanics alone.

You need to tweak some GFX card settings before launching the .exe to get this game to run the way it was made to. Most importantly to turn V-Sync ON, with the port from console to PC you need to nerf the FPS for the ingame physics engine to behave the way it was designed to. A lot of people don't give this game a chance because they ran a buggy game without really optimizing the settings. If you run this game above 60 FPS then it will perform very poorly with twitchy gameplay.
I love this game and this is what Tomb Raider should really be about. Not killing deer to craft handbags or making a one-time campfire, or lamenting over tear-jerking drama. TR:U is full of puzzles but like it's predeccesor (Legend) it was rather short; I reached final boss in approx. 8 hours. There are still lots of places to explore and find secrets for replay value. I liked the new engine especially with the now-added gimmick to rock climb up a wall. Human combat was a bore but thankfully there are only two levels with it. If you like the original Tomb Raider games then you'll love TR:Legend, TR:Anniversary, and TR:Underworld (in that order).
It's a shame that Crystal Dynamics felt the need to reboot Lara into a "hyper-realistic" girl-next-door. We were really approaching something great with TR:U. Instead of rebooting into a "Last of Us" copy, they should have just taken the AC:Black Flag route with an open-world tomb-raiding experience and a pulled-back camera. R.I.P this future series.

pros:
Set it and forget it farming (offline resource gathering)
Each unit is actually a squad.
Semi-persistent world
You don't notice when units die because there's a pile of corpses everywhere and the victor can make get some loot. (you were the victor right?)
Problems:
No attack queueing (can't tell units to attack more than one target)
Units who are told to attack, move to the target units position and will run right passed the oncoming hoard to reach their "destination" which usually ends as being a corpse.
Unit control is next to non existent, often with some sort of resource allocation group there's a couple of government workers just standing around.

Personally, I like 2015 well enough. Granted card selection is limited, and it is even moreso, if you don't get premium boosters (I did not), but I actually like the decks I built near the end of the game. I mostly played mono white with decent amounts of life gain, and it turned some of the hardest duels into a joke (I removed and locked down Garruk's deck before he could even hit me). I have heard quite a few people complain that trading 2HG for such limited custom deck building is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, but imagine what the game will be like after the expansion(s) come out; I can only imagine that the payoff for getting them will be far superior to that of buying the expansions for previous Duels titles because you will be able to use the new cards in whatever decks you want; that seems pretty cool to me and I already really enjoy the base game. Heres my pros and cons since you guys like that stuff:
PROS:
Cards unlock quickly enough (I unlocked them all, and it did not feel too grindy)
You can design decks as you please (YOU CAN EVEN SET HOW MUCH LAND IS IN YOUR DECKS!)
Single player offers a good amount of challenge
CONS:
Menus and animations are slightly annoying
Some people will find single player too challenging (I feel like CPU decks are stacked somewhat on the hardest difficulty)
The CPU uses cards you cannot get (this is kind of annoying)
I think the CPU decks have more of the same rares in them than you can put in your decks (not sure about this)
The starter decks are not the best (should they be?)
That all being said I should say that many complainers are ill-informed. The land system is not screwed, the game simply no longer gives you good suggestions, but you can still pick what land you wanna tap; it's just that in the previous games the computer kinda helped you pick better land combinations as defaults, but, as someone who plays with real cards, I always hated that anyway. I would also say that unlocking everything takes less time than it did in 2014, but maybe that is just my experience; I unlocked all the cards after sitting down to play the game twice (granted I did play for several hours each time). I get that it is annoying that you have to play through the first chapter before you can really start deck building, but the first chapter was kinda easy (especially in camparison to the rest of the game), and I think that it (the first chapter) takes maybe a couple of hours (if even) if you are hardcore struggling with the difficulty. Also, I have won plenty of matches without buying premium boosters, so I do not really think the game is pay to win.
Anyway, I really like the game, and it is a fine time to move on from 2014, which I played the ♥♥♥♥ out of.

Yes, this is worth getting.
I've noticed a lot of negativity about this game since it's release and frankly I don't understand where it is all coming from. What you have here is a solid, fun, online RTS game, with some innovative original flourishes.
Pros:
= Three distinct factions with very different play styles both in terms of city building, unit disposition and battle tactics. They are further differentiated by their own distinct unit, building and UI art, quest lines and voice acting. Each faction can also recruit a variety of mercenary units to further enhance army customization.
= The battle pacing is just right. Look I'm an old fart, so I prefer a game where I can actually see the action unfold rather than everything be over in the blink of an eye. The pace of combat is somewhat slower in DoF than in other contemporary RTS games. I think this is a good thing becasue it allows for more tactical options and also negates any ping advantages in multiplayer.
= Heaps of single player content. Each faction has a very generous quest line which I estimate to be around 30+ hours worth per side, not counting replayable missions. There are also countless NPC skirmishes to explore in a variety of landscapes against varied NPC elements.
= The quests are involved and interesting. They have put a great deal of thought into felshing out details of the fantasy world. It's not a testiment to originality, but it's a top notch effort for a video game setting. I love how half of what the elves say is made up gibberish with no explanation offered, but after an hour or so in the game you find yourself understanding it all.
Cons:
= There are a few technical issues especially with pathfinding, but nothing that some patience and practice can not overcome.
= Multiplayer is a mixed bag. You can grind out a very formidable army against NPCs and newbies can get crushed if they dive in unprepared. That being said, when the balance is just right, they battles are a lot of fun.
= Speaking of grind, there is a bit of it. It's an online game so the pace of progression is sedate. You won't max your units out over a weekend. Your rank and file units can also be permanently lost, so you need to be paying attention. I personally like the perma death touch for some units (hero units take an xp penalty instead when they get "KOed"), but I can understand why some people would consider it a negative.
All in all I had a great time with DoF. If you're an RTS fan and looking for something a little different and long term, you should definately pick this up during the sale. It's a steal for seven bucks.

I've been buying these games for the past few years and each year there has been a improvement on the last.
Each year the game had multiple game modes, single player and multiplayer game types.
Cards unlocked through the course of gameplay or for a additional fee if you didn't have time to play to unlock the cards and just wished to get into the duelling fun.
The DotP games never had the best deck building in card games but I believe this was on purpose to create a easy and accessible game for newcomers and seasoned magic players just to pick up and play a few games without having to spend hours making a perfect deck.
But each game has had fun mix of modes and cards that gave me a lot of enjoyment, Duelling friends and overcoming defeat in the scripted duels with certain hand of cards where the AI would always play the same set of cards so even if you failed the first time you could learn and adapt to what that opponent did and be able to defeat them.
The puzzle challenges which would have you die the next turn and only by using your pro MLG magic skills and thinking outside the box you would be able to turn it around and win before the end of your current turn.
Working with friends to overcome insurmountable odds in the special modes like Planechase mode and Archenemy mode which change each year as fun twist on the traditional magic formula where only by working together you could overcome the enemy.
It is with that knowledge that I bought this game without looking into it as all previous game have been brilliant and this would appear to be my down fall as in this year's Magic: DoTP they seem to have taking a gigantic leap backwards in term of available content within the game.
They have striped it down to a 1v1 format with a basic single player duel against AI(which does have an interesting story tied with it) and 1v1v1v1 for the multiplayer that's is it, no unique game modes or fun additions just a very basic dare I say it cash in title.
This game has an UI that seemed to be designed with either tablets or consoles in mind. absolute worse pc port I have ever seen, (maybe even worse than dark souls 1) now the DotP games have always had let me say... clunky menu systems but when I have to click the start button on the tile screen and it takes me 28 clicks before It goes to the next screen that immediately raises flags in my mind of what to expect.
Now, I am all for artistic flair but if I have to endure a delay every time I swap menus or exit to main menu which is then proceeded by a light that is brighter than the light Gandalf shines from his staff to stop the Nazguls from attacking Faramirs men in LotR every time I go to a different menu it kind of puts me off playing the game as my time is being wasted at every turn and as my goblins pals say "time is money friend".
Now I think this review maybe long enough as it is but to sum it up because most of you have probably not read it anyway. :)
Pros:
Interesting overall story within the single player experience
Better deck customisation
Cons:
Puzzle modes gone
Challenge modes gone
Multiplayer modes gone only basic 1v1v1v1 left
No two headed giant multiplayer mode
UI takes ages to move through menus, mouse doesn't seem to react sometimes.
Better deck customisation seems to have taken away the good starting decks the other DotP games had now you choose a starter deck and it doesn't synergise with the card in the deck, without extensive modification.
Premium booster packs (bad starter decks might not of been a mistake but a calculated decision)

Play Length: About 80% through the game.  Lacked the enthusiasm to finish it.
Positives: I like the general atmosphere of the castle.  The design of the game's primary monster is decent.
Negatives: I didn't find this game particularly scary, and I don't really understand why other people do.  The main problem is that there are no consequences for death, at all.  When you die in this game, you get sent back to a checkpoint which is usually very close to where you died.  Even stranger, you don't lose any items you picked up, or any progress you made.  Strangest of all, the game has a habit of removing (!) the enemy that kills you.  So not only does dying have very little effect on your progress, it can often benefit you... something that absolutely should not be the case for a horror game!
The job of a horror game is to make you feel like you are in danger.  It's impossible to do this when the monsters are paper tigers who can't do anything to you, and you the player are practically immortal.  This is a strange design, because the game does not give you any weapons, and forces you to avoid or run away from enemies.  You would think that this is because the game designers want you to feel vulnerable, which is all the more ironic considering how player-friendly the death system is.
There are other problems with this game.  Generally, I don't like horror games where you can't fight back... it's a good idea to make the player feel vulnerable, but the problem with not being able to fight back is that it makes the gameplay too one dimensional.  If all you can do is run away, then it leaves nothing for the player to think about.  And part of being a good horror game is creating tension through forcing the player to make choices.  A better approach is combat with limited effectiveness.  Ideally a player should have three options that they have to constantly consider: combat, stealth, and running.  More options creates more tension.
I also think that the level design in this game is a bit weak.  The castle has a nice ambience and a cook look to it.  But after awhile it starts to feel samey.  There's not enough variety or creativity to how the environments are designed.  There's also a disturbing lack of enemy variety, with one particular enemy being the main enemy you will see for 90% of the game.  Lack of surprises is a huge problem for any horror game.  I'm also not a big fan of this game's soundtrack.  It is atmospheric, and works on a basic level, but there's no variety to the music and it never feels memorable.  So while it may work in a superficial way to build fear, it doesn't elevate the experience the way other really good horror soundstracks do, and it really gets stale after awhile.
Overall: I don't personally find this game scary, and yet, some people do.  I don't fully understand that... certainly, the game has atmosphere, and being chased by scary monsters is something that should be scary.  But it wears thin very quickly in this game, and the lack of consequences makes everything feel much more like a video game, and less like you're really there.  I would guess that roleplaying is a factor... even if you are basically immortal and the enemies pose no threat, some people may find the game scary by role-playing their character.  But for me, personally, merely simulating a horror experience isn't scary; I need a game to have mechanics that actually create tension.
If you are heavily into roleplaying a horror experience, then this game may work for you.  But if you are like me, I would highly recommend not wasting your time on this game.  There are far better horror experiences out there.
About my rating system: I have two things I rate on.  Overall score, and soundtrack.  Personally, I feel like game soundtracks are tremendously undervalued; to me, it's a vital factor in getting me into the game.  For the score, I grade on a scale of 1-10, and I try to grade in such a way that each number has a meaning and equal importance.  The meaning of each number are as follows:
0: Garbage, 1: Awful, 2: Poor, 3: Underwhelming, 4: Mediocre, 5: Decent, 6: Good, 7: Great, 8: Excellent, 9: Phenomenal, 10: Masterpiece
Amnesia's score:
Game Rating: 3 (Underwhelming)
Soundtrack Rating: 3 (Underwhelming)

Business Tour - Online Multiplayer Board Game  is a free to play virtual boardgame that is a modified clone of Monopoly.  It works on Win 10, looks ok, sounds ok, and plays ok.  It looks and plays sort of like Monopoly, but changed enough to not be sued by the owners of Monopoly.  Has a short tutorial and rules manual.  In the Offline mode, you can play with four players that can be AI or other players using the hot seat method.  Of course, the computer take care of the bank and automates the whole game and provides a 30 minute timelimit, and speeding up the game.  Sort of hard to tell who turn is it, there is a diamond over the head of current player and slight blinking of player's nametag.
The rules are More Aggressive than the boardgame that i remember from long ago.  Chance cards are a mixed bag of attacks on other players, bad happening, and boons to you.  You can turn the background music down to off, once you get tired of it.     The AI is aggressive so you might lose more often if you play vs more than 1 AI player.
Has a multi-player mode that you can play with other users over the Internet.  The dev makes their money off the multi-player mode, with the fact that you can buy gold and chips in the store.  You can spend gold to reroll a throw of dice, or roll dice with even, odd or pairs results.  New players accounts start with 20 gold.  Chips are used as bets on multi-player games, where some tables are charged large amount of chips.  You can post your own table with several options.  Has a 2 vs 2 option, so that 2 player help each other win vs the other side. I don't suggest you play the multi-player mode much, except with real friends.
Worth a try, if you liked the boardgame Monopoly.

Shadow warrior 2 is an absolute amazing game. The combat feels realy great and fluid, you just slice and dice your way through the enemies, get loot, get good.
The Story has somewhat of the original humor, also adds new stuff here and there. The end is most likely the worst part.
So why do I not recommend this game ?
After the Patch on the 21/22 of Oct there were new stuff added and some stuff changed. For example a heavily overpowered weapon was made 66% less overpowered but still staying as one of the best in slot kinds. The thing leaving a very bad taste in my mouth is the invention of immunities to damage types.
Immunities to me are a somewhat lazy way to increase the difficult of the game but offer little to no complexity added. I've reached the point prepatch where i could outright ignore physical resistant mobs and just use any physicaltype weapon to my pleasure through stacking crit% critdmg% and dm% values overall on my gear.
I realy enjoyed the moment reaching that level. Just beeing able to nobrain through the level / map / missions / campaing all over again. Times were great.
Now dont get me wrong. Usually thinking while playing games is involved but I realy miss games where you just dont need to focus on the fact that in a group of X enemies you have atleast 1 guy immune to 3 diffrent damage types which regenrates health, atleast half of the group is immune to a combination of 1 - 2 diffrent damage types, 90% of the group is immune to any chi power, and they are pretty much able to exhaust a decent lifepool in no time.
I mean yeah, i could totally use ranged weapons in that situation. Just let me reqeuip all of my usefull gems to re-slot them into my go to guns. re-allocated my armor upgrades / amulett. And enagage the group of bullet sponges.
Damn the guy with immunity to fire has moved infront of the guy with ice immunity, better switch my weapon. Ah crap I ran out of ammo for that paticular weapon as they sponged realy heavy on my bullets. Lets just vanish and reallocated to another weapon.
Dang where did my upgrades go again, gotta search for the name...
Ah man i found it. Whoops an enemy is attacking me. Good thing i have a rather large healthpool, Dang it oneshotted me. How unfortunate. Better go down in difficulty. Hmm playing hard instead of T3, Too easy, still Immune enemies show up from time to time.
Well lets fight on insane instead. Yeah with constantly swapping between elemental and physical weapons i am able to do that. Lets go up to Insane T2. Hmm yeah common enemies are immune to stuff. Let's just grind Insane for exp then. Takes forever. You can't gain exp past a certain level on a certain difficulty unless you go upwards in difficulty. Also no exp-bar you gotta lookup the values yourself in your savefile... wat
TL;DR;
I realy enjoyed the heck out of SW2 prepatch 21/22 of oct.
Afterwards it's just like any other game with lazy difficulty / oneshot mechanics once you reach a certain point. Better save your money and play the unpatched gog version.

Though, on its face, Rime might seem derivative of games like Ico or Journey, with subtle touches from Shadow of the Colossus and The Last Guardian. To say the team at Tequila works took inspiration from Team Ico and thatgamecompany would certainly be an understatement. For the first possibly third of the game the mechanics and the narrative seem to meander with little direction and even less reason to feel the need to deeply explore any of the environments. It really isn't until you get to the central tower where the game opens up and you begin to experience the more overt aspects of the narrative. Everything in this game is important. This is a game about interpretation, so the more you invest, the more you seek out, the more you lose yourself to the character and the world, the more the game will reward you in the end. Though I might have had my issues with the early game, it really does come together. The narrative, informed by an amazing score, does something few other games dare do. For many adventure games of this ilk, the journey is just as important as the destination, and while the jouney in Rime might not intially feel like anything to write home about, its when you arrive at its conclusion that everything falls into place.
