It really shows that the developers want as much flexibility and freedom in each match for players to have that ultimate SCI FI battlescape.
You can fly fighters -> to capital ships.  You can board or prevent boarding of said large ships, attack stations and really work as a team.  The ground battles in my opinion are great, just not as epic as the space fighting. My only Criticism of the ssaid favoured battles is that the flying of fighters/bombers feel a bit clunky and akward.
The UI has been updated and still being tweaked, the leveling system for the the areas (Command, Combat and Support) are so so, but does give you flexibility on what roles to use - and earn xp through it. Plenty of damn weapons and customisations for both ground troops and vehicles - and no stupid Loot Boxes/Pay to Unlock.
As the developers are still trying to turn this into the dream they envision, the advertisment side of it is not pushed, therfore the player numbers are low.  This can be negated by being the first one on in the mexican wave and joining a server (and fighting against the excellent bots - YES THEY ARE STILL A THING!), or popping onto their discord and having a chat with them as they are very active, and alot of the loyal playerbase are just waiting in the shadows for an excuse to jump on.

A lot of reviewers are citing the game's controls, randomly spawned enemies, and save system as reasons to hate this game's guts. The problem is, they're overblowing the game's issues by orders of magnitude and almost completely ignoring the upsides in a lot of cases. A basic list here -
Pros:
+Looks amazing
+Runs at 60 FPS, even on this ♥♥♥♥♥♥ laptop*
+Difficult, but in a way that makes you go "Dammit, I didn't grab the pole!" instead of "Dammit, it didn't let me grab the pole!"
+Actually makes you feel like a cat (especially the long jumps)
Cons:
-Occasional weird control issues, but I've not had them nearly as often as others claim to have. (e.g. accidentally crouching, sliding off cliffs while trying to jump)
-Doesn't tell you about a couple things (namely, the ability to backflip and to stick poles into walls to serve as platforms)
Now, allow me to talk about the criticisms of the game that I rather doubt. The most common complaint is about the controls. People keep ♥♥♥♥♥ing about how the game feels clunky, unresponsive, and hard to play; the most frequently cited example is the fact that, when crouching on the edge of a ledge, you will instead slide right off if you're too close. That, honestly, is true; it is kind of frustrating when that happens. The other common one is that slugcat's jumping sucks. Slugcat does indeed have a very short jump, only around a block high, which will take some getting used to if you're a Mario fan. But this doesn't make the jumping suck; it just makes the level designs work. If you had a Mario jump whenever you hit A, a lot of the game's platforming and climbing challenges would be negated. Instead, your small jump means you need to take advantage of your surroundings to get anywhere.
But Slugcat isn't restricted to one jump, oh no. If the player is crouched, and holds down the jump button, they will (invisibly) charge a jump; when the button is released, Slugcat will still not travel very high, but can cover quite a bit of horizontal distance with a long jump. Slugcat can also perform a backflip if you turn and jump while running; this gets more height than the other two, though is more situational and harder to pull off.
Another common complaint is the lack of, dare I say it,
Yup. The game tells you (most of) the controls and then sends you off on your own, with only occasional hints as to where to go. This leaves you free to explore the world as you see fit, without feeling like you're being railroaded by the little yellow hologram guy. Apparently, not being told where to go immediately means the game is committing some kind of cardinal sin. The only lack of information I can complain about pertains to the backflip, the ability to temporarily ingest inedible objects for later use, and the pole-platforms; the game never actually tells you how to do those or even that they can be done, which definitely should be changed.
Saving is... different in Rain World. You hibernate in special waterproof chambers after collecting enough food. This increases your karma and saves your progress. Death will return you to your most recent save, undoing any and all changes on the map and re-randomly spawning enemies. It also demotes your karma level by one. Karma is important for a couple reasons; one, it can gain you achievements under certain conditions, and two, high karma is required to progress through the game to new areas. Certain "gates" will not open until you have high enough karma, so you have to make good use of the resources in your current area until you can hibernate enough times without dying. That sounds tedious, and it can be if there's a particular That One Screen for you or something, but fear not. Every once in a while you come across a golden flower; eat it, and your current karma level will become protected. Should you die, your karma will not revert (the flower will be lost, however).
That's about all I have to say. It's not a perfect game; it does have a couple issues that need addressing, and its intense difficulty (REAL difficulty, might I add; not inflicted by the game's controls or systems but by clever level design and the requirement of critical thinking) is not for everyone. But if you're into games like I Wanna Be the Guy, or Super Meat Boy, or even Mirror's Edge-like parkour platformers, and don't need mommy to walk you across the street so that you don't get hit by a bus and then ♥♥♥♥♥ about mommy not being there, you'll probably enjoy this.

First, the game does have its issues.  Nothing like running down a hill and taking enough fall damage to kill you, but if you press jump you can take a 50 foot jump with no damage.  Just weird and inconsistent.  And yes, you have to enter a key when you first run the game or get a DLC for the game, which is unusual and annoying at this point in time.
That being said, the land is interesting and fun, there are tons of creatures, a lot of flexibility with the story line but the biggest plus is the magic system.  You make your own spells from components and rearange the components later to suit other needs.  For instance I have created spells that shoot out a spray of missiles. The missiles blind when they hit and summon undead warriors where they land.  Another shoots a huge spray of fire missiles which bounce around filling an area with fiery death.  I've used water walking and feather fall to weasle my way into areas that, later, I realized I was supposed to get to later in the game, yet I was able to make it work.
Another oddity of the game, which from my perspective, Im not sure is a plus or a minus is the multiplayer.   It has multiplayer, but unlike other games where you play the same game single and multiplayer the multiplayer game is a different game.   Same game mechanics but you gather in a city, and choose a storyline that has nothing to do with the single player game, gather your comrades and play through that scenario.  On one hand its extended, unique game play.  On the other you cant use the single player character you built up, you dont get to explore the extensive single player world and questlines with a friend and the multiplayer game has much less content.  I can still say I've had fun in multiplayer and built up a powerful multiplayer character, but its worth noting that when you read that the game is multiplayer its probably not executed the way you probably think it is.
All in all I've enjoyed it an think its a game well worth exploring.

At first glance Darksiders looked to me just like any other 3rd person adventure. In fact in the first level or so there is nothing more to it, but after that the game really picks up and gets interesting. I was mostly drawn in by its great setting that takes place in a post-Armageddon world where both angels and demons deem you as an enemy. The art style and the environments were really beautiful as well, what enhanced the atmosphere. After you've gotten past the first level, that's when your character starts to learn new moves, making combat very fun and engaging. In addition you get some new weapons as well, like the Scythe, for more crowd control, and also a Tremor Gauntlet, if you fancy power punching. Among all the combat, the boss fights especially stood out for me. Each and every boss fight was both challenging and enjoyable at the same time and this is perhaps the game's biggest strength in my opinion. The cool cutscenes and the special kills were an icing on the cake. Although there are so many good things about this game and although I've given it a 9, I also have several criticisms. First of all, the game is not exactly a very good console port. The keyboard and mouse control scheme was more or less playable, but it's the fact that you couldn't change graphics options apart from resolution. Of course this isn't much of a problem for someone with a powerful PC, but for those of us with average machines, even on low resolution there is a noticeable drop in framerate in some areas of the game, making it quite stuttery. Another thing that I disliked - some areas were just a bit too long, like the Hollows and the Ashlands. Not sure whose bright idea it was that the sewers and the desert are good candidates for lengthy levels, since those usually tend to be amongst the most boring of the environments in any game. The Black Throne level was perhaps the biggest offender. Although it was a very beautiful level with some cool battles, it had way too much backtracking and also made you do the same thing 3 times! And my last criticism would be towards the puzzles. Although there were some great puzzles in the game, some others were really annoying. They weren't hard or anything. You could figure out most of them right away. It's just that to execute those solutions usually took too long, requiring too much running and jumping about, as well as tonnes of trial and error, and hence that was breaking the pace of the game. All those criticisms are quite strong for me and I guess if I wasn't so charmed by the game's setting and art style, I probably would've given it an 8 rather than a 9. Overall the game is highly entertaining and worth checking out. Going to be trying out the second one no doubt...

After just finishing this game, I have time to give a little review.
So here it is, real brief; if you are looking for a good story, with fun characters and pretty good gameplay, come on over, get the game. A typical hack-n-slash combined with dungeon adventure (often and not-inaccurately compared to Zelda games), Darksiders is a pretty good game.  The oversized weapons, the lack of fall damage, the incredible feats of strength, and the executions all make you feel pretty powerful, in a very God of War-like fashion.  My personal largest complaint is that the control scheme, specifically when it comes to using powers or consumables mid-combat, is a bit less than ideal, though it is possible a controller could help with that.
Is it worth the $20 price tag? Sure.  In no way could my playing be described as masterful, and oftentimes not very efficient, but as of just completing it, I have 20 hours of gameplay.  That is about a dollar per hour of entertainment, so it's much cheaper than a movie in that case.  If you can't bring yourself to spend 20 bucks on it though, wait until a Steam sale or see if it ever shows up in a Humble Bundle or something, get it for 5 bucks.  No reason not to swing 5 bucks at the game, it's well worth your money at that point.

SOOOOOO many bad reviews on this game and some of them are just complaining about stuff that isnt true ^^
1) Starting Decks  ( NOTE: You choose your deck after completing or skipping the tutorial )
I really like the game! It is true that at the start you decide for a deck by choosing a main color and then a second color to get a mix of cards that are not great!
But really do you want to start a game with a deck that can beat every opponent in 2 turns ?
The fun about magic is collecting cards and then build a deck with what you got in your booster and then try out these decks against friends or against campaign Decks!
Your starting deck just means that you will get some cards of the color of your choice!
The only way to change your starting deck is between the moment you picked it and the first duell against the tutorial boss!
Afterwards you have to live with your cards and you need to unlocke new cards by getting booster!
2) Campaign
After completing a turtorial you can start the  campaign which is seperated in 5 Planes! Each Plane consist of around 5 enemys! You have to beat the first one to get to the second and so on!
A in my opinion great change in the campaign compared with Magic 2014 ( the only other part i played ) is the fact that the enemys dont play the same hand everytime!
In 2014 they had an order of cards they wanted to play and if you didnt prevented it somehow you could predict what card they would play with a 100% chance!
Now it really feels like they play a normal game, so they can have bad starting hands with few mana or no creatures to play in the first 4 turns! So it was fun to play the campain even if I had to repeat a duell because i lost!
3) Collecting Cards
This was a very important point for me and i am glad they made it that easy to collect cards, yet you have to work for it!
When defeating an enemy in the campaign for the first time you will get a Booster with cards! Most booster constist of the standard cards you will get in a normal Magic booster ( Some commons, uncommons and rare or mystic rare cards )
but some booster, for example the first booster you will get in the campaign are are skripped to drop special combinations!
So the first campaign enemy will give you a booster with only 3 commons in it, the next with 3 uncommons up to an booster with 3 rare cards!
From then on all enemys in the story of the campaign will drop normal booster!
Now there is the problem that after defeating an story AI he will not grant you a new booster if you challenge him again!!!!
To get more boosters you need to explore the Planes!
The button to do this is unlocked after clearing the first Plane!!!
The booster you get are always defined by the Plane you are in! So in Theros you will get Theros booster and in Ravnica they will be Ravnica booster!
( Tip: Completly exploring a Plane will let you face with a Planeswalker! Defeating these will grant you a special booster with some skripted rare drops )
4) Deck Bulding
Not much to say here! If you got the cards in a booster you can put them in a deck!
To create a deck thats a different color than your starting choice you will need to collect a few cards and it will take some time!
There is a special limit to the use of uncommon, rare and mysticrare cards in one deck!
The same card is only allowed X times in a deck. ( Uncommon: X=3 ; Rare: X=2 ; Mystic: X=1 )
4 )Multiplayer
I havent used it yet! Because i wanted to finish the campaign first ^^ ( which took me around 7 -8 Hours so far! )
5) Conclusion
I really liked playing the game so far! The ability to create a deck freely is in my eyes a great Improvement!
You are able to collect almost all cards simply by playing the game and on the highest difficulty the game is challenging and fun to play!
Cons: There are around 50 Premium cards which are ( as far as i know ) only accessible by buying Premium Booster!

THIS REVIEW IS VERY LONG AND RAMBLEY, SEE THE END FOR A TL;DR ON MY PRIMARY REASONS FOR THIS REC
Now I never really got into the hype of this game, nor did I ever really want to pick up this game until my friends told me about it and asked me to play with them. Reluctantly I said yes. And ironically, I don’t play with them at all. I never bought into the team aspect but I enjoyed the aesthetic of warriors from middle history battling each other. So going forward with this review, I’d like to say I came in with no real concept of the game and a clear conscience.
Upon opening the For Honor Open Beta, I was met with a tutorial. It introduced you to the simple mechanics with clarity, and allowed you ample room to train and even learn some of the more advanced mechanics such as parrying and countering guard breaks. I have to give Ubisoft some credit to this because not many games introduce a player to its core with a tutorial and some tools to help them practice. In a sense, the tutorial made the game and its more advanced mechanics much much simpler to understand…Or perhaps the game itself was already easy to pick up (I’ll get into that later). The next thing to do was join multiplayer, and that’s where I met my first gripes with the game.
While I enjoyed the concept of a cross platform faction war, I didn’t really enjoy matchmaking at all. While I’m basing some of my experiences with matchmaking on the Open Beta, my opinion still stands strong. Previously in the open beta, it took quite some time to enter a game, and even then, there was no guarantee that the game itself would start. Sometimes people disconnected for no reason at all. Sometimes I disconnected for no reason at all. Entering the official release, this problem only seemed to make itself clear. Countless times have I run into the problem of being booted from matchmaking due to a connection error that I had no solution to. Countless times was I trapped in an endless loop of players joining and then failing to join. Needless to say it was frustrating. There’s also the problem with the fact that this game solely relies on P2P connection. There are no dedicated servers whatsoever, and for a game that touts a potential competitive scene, it’s downright discouraging. For Ubisoft to skimp out on dedicated servers for a game that relies on cooldowns, stuns, and timing, it’s a bit disappointing.
Speaking of game mechanics, when I actually got into the game, I thoroughly enjoyed it. Sure, the first few games I ran around like a headless chicken. I understood some aspects of it, but definitely not enough to take on more experienced players. When I began to pick up on the game’s flow, I started to really enjoy it. Hacking and slashing is a fun thing to do, especially when you’re a Knight. However, as I began to play into it more, I noticed the game’s mechanics were kind of easy. You had the same premises of stuns, blocks, light attacks, heavy attacks, combos, and finishers from fighting games like Skullgirls, Mortal Kombat, and Tekken, the main difference being that the pace of the game is slower due to windups of each attack. Now this may not seem to make a big difference, but it gives players ample time to counter, and also perform their own combos. To me, this makes the game significantly easier, and more casual.
This observation led me to conclude that the game really didn’t have a lot of depth. Like I said previously, the game was very easy to pick up. I was initially unsure of whether that was due to the tutorial or simply due to how the game was.
However, looking into it, and comparing it to other fighting games, which really are its most direct comparison, I was convinced that the game didn’t have a lot of depth. Where Skullgirls contained a plethora of hidden strategies, and required great predictive skills in order to truly master it, For Honor gives you a UI that reveals all the information quite blatantly. Couple that with the slower pace of the game, it makes it even easier. This can be seen as a good thing, but for me, and probably for those who wanted to get into this competitively, I only see it as a way of lowering the skill ceiling.
That doesn’t make the game undesirable though. The prospect of chopping heads off and fighting knights as a dainty samurai lady is pretty cool. Or fighting a very thick, bat wielding samurai with a petite knight. All that is very amusing and really fun to play out. There’s also a sense of satisfaction that I don’t get with any other game when I get a kill in For Honor. None of what I said up above detracts from the fun of this game.
What does detract from the fun are the microtransactions. When a studio decides to use their money to implement a system only seen in fee to pay games on a fully priced AAA title instead of dedicated servers, it makes me a little bit mad. I’m not like other people who give a negative recommendation immediately after seeing microtransactions, but to see money that could’ve been spent to enhance player experience from the get go, go towards something that reduces the importance of a core part of the game (the progression system) it pushes me to be like those people.
It really is a shame.
All in all, I’d give this a cautionary recommendation. As it stands now, the game is fun. It’s great to get into. But with the shallowness of the game, the problems with matchmaking, and the microtransactions, it really isn’t worth it until two out of the three complaints are addressed by the developer. At least to me.
TL;DR
-----------------------------------
The game is pretty easy to get into, and it’s very enjoyable. But keep in mind that it’s a bit on the shallow side in terms of mechanics, and that it relies on P2P connection and has some problems with microtransactions. I caution you buying this, because I don't know where Ubisoft will take it.
Give it a strong 6 to a light 7.

The level of sh*t this game got when it launched is unfair to say the least; especially since Quake 4 is the only FPS game to tell the story of a futuristic human invasion of an alien planet and do it decently.
The first half of the game you play as “regular” soldier Kane. I use quotation since there’s nothing regular about him. Your character is somehow the same as in Quake 2 (or of equal fame) and a silent protagonist, so not much is known about him besides the fact that he is super awesome no seriously u guys.
But even with your Samsonian power, it all goes bad during a cut-scene in which you're knocked out (thank's Opposing Force!). Because of course, you’re invading an advanced alien race, what did you think this was? Somalia? Things go south and most of the human army is killed, but NOT all of them (unlike Q2) and you will find and fight alongside small groups of soldiers, doing their best to stay alive. This is probably the most immersive part of the game.
Indeed the invasion part of Quake 4 feels truly unique, with humans clinging desperately to survival while higher command keeps yammering about them advancing in the fray. Of course, as games go, both sides agree to call it a day and send you in.
Even so, it doesn’t take long until♥♥♥♥♥♥go fully up and your entire assault squadron is routed, with you captured by the Strogg after a failed boss fight; one of the first true main issues of the game, since, while this is a fight you are meant to fail, you must fail in a SPECIFIC point and after a SPECIFIC time, making the whole thing a major pain in the♥♥♥♥♥
After that, you pass a few (spoiler-free) steps that make your character quicker and more prone to working alone, turning the whole thing into a slightly more classic affair of quick-pace shooting. Pew-pew forward and you might notice the game beginning to get a bit bland. You will still get exposition and sometimes even find colleagues, but the suspense from the beginning will be gone.
The ending is also a bit flat, with it finishing on a cliffhanger that still hasn’t delivered (2016). Even so, the game is still worth it if you enjoy military SciFi themes, The Quake 2 lore or simply find it at a discount.

I'm loving this so much, I've been playing it till 4 in the morning and it's been an absolutely amazing treat to me, and worth every penny. What do I love most? The characterization of the protagonist and the the artistic experience that is RiME. Whatever you do, do not run through this game attempting to solve the puzzles because you're focusing on the game - the way this world is constructed is just absolute magic, from the way the fox glyphs light up with you as you run around the stairs, to the way the stars shimmer in the sky, or the little particles in the water. The artist behind this game has a truly rare gift for picking up little organic details of the world and emphasizing them to make a cartoon world feel so very rich and alive (they're also very creative). Sadly, to keep the magic and play with your own emotions, the character tends to run when I often wish he'd just walk. Speaking of the protagonist, that's the other thing I loved. The character doesn't just have a set of animations, they react to their environment in a way that's not often seen. They'll express a rich range of emotions throughout the game based on the situation (those times when I sent my poor character blindly running into a wall he couldn't see XD). And it's not that these were necessary for gameplay reasons, but, they're just THERE. They're details that are there purely to make the character a little bit more real, more likeable and the experience, far more rich and rewarding. And that's the thing that shines about RiME, it's an experience and for me, it focused nicely on quality over quantity. I might not get 40 hours of original game-play out of it, or a full-on fantasy novel, but I will probably have actual memories from it when I'm done, and really neat ones at that. Thank you for this!

Grand strategy game which heavily suffered from pathfinding issues, amongst other things. All these issues have now been solved, however. With the free Arcana Expansion released, now is the perfect time to grab the game.
A persistent online RTS, or MMORTS even. There's been only few attempts at these over the past decade, and each has had it's own values. But Dawn of Fantasy: Kingdom Wars stands out from the few in the genre. In a good way, that is. This is a game of pure quality, you can experience the love the developers put into the game first hand. Apart from the issues which have haunted this game, the core gameplay is sheer fun. Building up your small settlement into a mighty fortress while managing your armies, sieging massive pre-made strongholds, or just going out on a looting trip, no challenge is ever the same.
While I have not played the game in quite awhile, I do remember there to be an in-game shop using premium currency. Nothing essential, but plenty of things which cannot be obtained otherwise, including the mighty Dragons. I am, however, quite sure you were able to gain premium currency ingame, which becomes considerably easier the stronger your economy gets.
Edit: The cash shop has been revamped. The currency can no longer be bought but only earned in-game. As such there are no longer microtransactions possible, removing any P2W brand the game could possibly have had.
These devs are really responsive to the community and actually willing to change their model to such an extend. Kudos for that.

Rime is simply, a brief but beautiful game.
You play as a boy shipwrecked after a terrible storm ruins you journey home. You're left on a beautiful island to explore it's wonders and mysteries. The game is beautiful, using bright colors and simple textures to paint a magnificent world and a soundtrack that matches the Pixar esque beauty of the visuals. It's an absolute joy to explore and play in. The story is completely without dialogue but towards the end it'll pull heavily at your heartstrings.
Rime lacks any combat, but rather has you puzzle your way through everything. None of the puzzles in the game will leave you stuck so the pacing never dies, everything is pretty straight forward but if you want to find all of the optional collectibles, you'll have to venture off the beaten path.
I spent a good amount of time searching for stuff but I missed a ton, but even with all of my searching I still beat the game in under 6 hours. Yes, going back to collect everything will yield more hours but I'm going to get most of my playtime from other playthroughs, the game is short enough to beat in a single sitting and would be an absolute joy to do so. I look forward to playing it again.
At $30 it's kinda hard to recommend on gameplay alone since it's so short but the story, visuals, audio and a poignant story on top of all this makes it an easy recommend.

If you want a new Battlefront game, but didn't really like the newly announced Battlefront 3, then this is a game you should look in to.
Here are some of the pros and cons of the game so far:
+A large variety of maps featuring space, ground and infantry combat (there are a lot of maps, really).
+A good amount of loadouts  for infantry/vehicles, rockets, rayguns, miniguns, sticky grenades... basically most of the popular gun archetypes are covered in the game.
+Dedicated servers! That you can customise! Yay! Being able to host a server is a rarity these days for some reason.
+LAN mode.
+Offline play is also included, you can play on all of the maps available with bots, you can also play online in co-op with people against bots (or with bots against people, your choice really).
+Space battles! Yeah, the game has a really fun space combat thing going on where you can get in to dog fights and blow up infantry transports.
+This one is a bit subjective, but the game has a pretty good artstyle in my opinion, the maps even have an optional mission briefing that's been fully voiced.
Now... let's get to the "cons" section.
-The ironsights are a bit♥♥♥♥♥♥ sometimes it's just easier to use the hip fire, though that may make you lose some accuracy. (After playing for a while longer, I found out that you can change the ironsights in the weapons loadout and some of them are not entirely♥♥♥♥♥♥ :D, though some work is still needed)
-There seem to be some optimisation issues for some people, I have a 290X and there are times when the game tanks below 60 when there are a lot of bots on the screen, lowering the amount of bots seems to fix that.
-The interface can be very confusing, a better tutorial for the commander mode (and the general interface) would be appreciated. The loadout screen can also be a bit confusing since you have to manage point bars in order to equip different things.
~This one is more of a personal opinion, but I feel like the default TTK (time to kill) is a bit high for infantry units, a 1v1 firefight can take a bit too long sometimes.
Still, overall this is a solid game for all of the Battlefield/Battlefront fans out there and most of the current problems seem to be easily fixable. Aside from a single crash I had the game is also very stable (so far at least), so already it's better than some of the recent AAA games on release lol

Shadow Warrior 2 is an explosion of fun, blood, guts, guns, blades and mobility. A ridiculously over-the-top massacre with the sole purpose of being enjoyable. Stuff explodes and breaks apart everywhere all the time as blood and viscera sprays all over the place and there's this juvenile sense of fun in it. It has a strong 90s feel in those areas. It's a kind of a game that has tons of shortcomings but I just didn't care and enjoyed myself all the way through. The slaughterfest that it offers is just really satisfying. Not to mention the game looks absolutely stunning.
With that said, the open nature of the game with the overworld map, side quests, loot and leveling is a double edged sword. It has potential but feels subpar and rushed. The non-combat areas are pretty lifeless and dull, especially when compared to the lore that's incredibly abundant in the game. You're constantly drowning in upgrade gems that kind of blend together too much and it's easy to lose track of your stuff. The semi-random levels do not have a whole lot of pieces to offer so you're gonna see the same bits over and over in seemingly different parts of the world and, to be perfectly honest, the diversity of the environments is not as high as in the SW'13. The game has a decent amount of content but the story lacks any kind of meaningful conclusion.
Compared to the previous game though, it has a much better feel to the combat. The enemies are no longer bullet sponges that take forever to kill (might still be the case on higher difficulty levels). Guns are, for the first time in a FWG game, actually fun to use and as far as melee goes, watching enemies getting sliced into bloody pieces is as fun as always. Especially the movement is a huge step up from SW'13. No more pointless stamina bars: you've got an infinite sprint, double jump, dash and ZERO fall damage. That let's you just glide and fly through the environments like a badass ninja should be able to.
I think the best way to go about it is to approach this game as a stress reliever and stick to Easy/Normal. Do not overthink it, sit back, laugh at cringe-worthy jokes and enjoy the carnage.

I've been following Rain World's development for a while now, and it has not disappointed me in the slightest! As a small and vulnerable prey animal, death is always only one snap of a predator's jaws away. And yes, you can only travel between areas if you've survived several days consecutively, meaning you can (and will) set out and end up further away from progressing than before. I can see the frustration that this causes many players, and it's true that the controls are a bit awkward sometimes, but it doesn't ruin the experience for me - I'm quite happy to abandon hopes of moving forward and focus on survival for a while. It's grinding, sure, but what a world to grind in! The detail that has gone into the levels and their weird and wonderful wildlife, with a unique procedural animation system, is really something special, and this has always been the game's draw for me.
It's definitely not a relaxing game, and can be quite unfair - Mother Nature is cruel and random, and this game pulls no punches in illustrating that. As it stands, I probably would not recommend this game if your time is precious and you don't want to be frustrated. However, if you are interested in spending time struggling against nature in Rain World's beautiful pixel-art wasteland and uncovering its mysteries, do give it a try. The devs seem to be paying close attention to player feedback, and hopefully with a few patches they can polish up some of the rougher edges and help this game get the recognition it deserves!

Well, there's a reason for all the mixed reviews. I've only played a little, but I think it's enough to give you an idea of what to expect.
This game seems to be likened to dark souls for its difficulty, but I disagree. It is far closer to Prince of Persia (the original). You control a slugcat who has a very realistic way of moving around. If you've played Prince of Persia, you already know that your jumps suck and platforming is a slow, methodical game. Rain World is a little faster, but it is definitely not a Mario or Metroid.
Critics are also pointing out that the random enemy spawns are unfair and can halt progression. Yes, the spawns are unfair, but I don't really view that as a detractor. The ecosystem in the game does not revolve around you. The other creatures have behaviors of their own which they will follow regardless of you. It's realistic, and I love/hate it, but I wouldn't change it.
Others have also complained about the controls. Most platformers have tight controls (mario, metroid). This platformer has loose controls. Again, think of Prince of Persia; your character reacts immediately, but cannot accelerate quickly. You cannot stop on a dime. Waves will mess with your ability to navigate in the water. You will jump just short of the gap.
Finally, I would suggest watching a few episodes of Thesparrowjourney's let's play of this game BEFORE you buy it. It helped my decision and the first few episodes do not contain any real spoilers. I think that most of the detractors here went in expecting metroidvania or Ori, and were thus disappointed.
[UPDATE]
Once, you've learned that you AREN'T Mario or Samus. The game is not really that hard. Sure, you get stuck sometimes, but you will eventually overcome the obstacle. The hardest part is determining which paths to take. Even then, just follow the last instruction you recieved! Keep going in that direction until something happens.
I reached the end of the story in about 10 hours following the instructions the worm gave. Never did I encounter an area in which I was truly stuck and thought the game was unfair.

I can understand the fascination of building up a civilization from nothing. But in this case, the building up is so agonizingly slow that there's not much fun in it. By default, XP accumulates so slowly that you'll find yourself doing many, many hours of repetitive busywork, just to get to the point that you can build your first hovel to live in. Or make a
, so you don't have to sit around all night with nothing to do. Searching for berries and other gathering tasks are painfully slow click-and-wait operations, with no in-world visual feedback, just a progress bar. Getting your skills up to a point where you can do something meaningful will take many hours of mind-numbing activity.
When I played with a friend, we set the server for faster and faster progress on our crafting and gathering XP. Eventually, we got to a point where the game was just about playable. But it was still a pretty empty experience. Plant crops. Wait. Gather stuff. Wait. Sit through long, dark nights because you
can't make a #$*%$& torch. 'Feudal'?? More like "futile." In feudal times, everyone had candles or oil lamps or flint and steel -
to give them
at night. This is more like the Stone Age.
On top of all that, Life is Feudal: Your Own suffers from the increasingly prevalent problem of all 'sandbox' games: it's just a big empty box with sand in it. There's no actual
here - no quests, no higher levels of activity at all, other than building stuff yourself. (I'm sure someone very soon is going to package up the Unity engine and a C compiler, and sell it (for $60) as "the
sandbox game!")
On top of all that, the UI is unbelievably clunky. There are so many open world games out there, and just about every one I've seen has a slicker and more convenient UI than LIF:YO. Sorting and managing all the junk you gather is really annoying, and will take up a big part of your time. Figuring out simple tasks (like planting seeds) will require extensive reading of FAQs and user guides, and even then will never seem intuitive or natural.
Yes, this game is in Early Access. (All except the price; that seems pretty complete!) But after watching recent progress, I've lost hope that it will ever become much more than it is, possibly with a few glitches fixed. Forget quests, storyline, adventure. It's up to you, the player, to literally make your own fun. I think for the money you have a right to expect a little more.
So, while I love the
behind LIF:YO, the execution leaves me unsatisfied. And the roadmap leaves me with little or no hope that this will change. I'm not saying it's worthless. I admire the hard-core approach, and I like the feel of the world. But for me, it's not enough.
This is a game that
players will enjoy, but I don't think I'll ever be one of them. Considering the steep asking price, you probably want to be very sure which category
fall into before taking the plunge.

A truly well-made game by every sense of the word - unique enough to be the new revolutionary standard of melee action games.
With that said, some reviews for this game are simply just downright unfair. I don't mean this in a sense of "people are being too mean." Nothing is perfect and this game's no exception. But when you say things like "This game's really good, and I really like this game, but I can't recommend it because of X", first of all: that's contradictory. Second, if your X reason is "balance" and connection issues, there are some things you should think about:
-First off, the whole "passive play meta! Just turtle 2 win LOL" problem has pretty much been fixed with one nice clean patch. Guarding is still easier than attacking, but you don't just dodge and guard to win games. That's not how it works, and people who say "this game only rewards passive play" are making gross oversimplifications. The actual skills required to play well in this game are reaction time and mind-games. You can break someone's guard consistently if you're good enough. At very high-level play, you sometimes do see players parry/guard each other with 100% accuracy in 1v1s, but good thing 4v4 mode is the most popular mode, huh?
-The game runs on P2P connectivity. That's not a flaw. It's the developer's choice. Yes, P2P means that if one person quits, the entire room might get crashed. That's the tradeoff: P2P ensures high quality connectivity, but it compromises stability. And it makes sense that For Honor utilizes P2P connections - the gameplay is highly reliant on accurate timing (down to milliseconds) AND it's incredibly sensitive to FPS changes. That's why this "dedicated servers" thing is really just a meme. It's not a good thing. It increases the risk of lag, and that's going to be absolutely terrible for the game. Right now, when you see someone complain about "connectivity issues" in For Honor, they're not talking about high ping or high latency traffic. They're talking about disconnects and crashes. But this isn't Ubisoft's fault. It's not Ubisoft's fault that some guy who has no idea how latency works decided to play For Honor with his 1MB/s 3GB/month capped latency with a stock modem and a bunch of anti-virus firewalls on and gets auto-booted every game. You're not supposed to have terrible Internet in P2P games.
And that's how nearly all of these negative reviews are: "Hi, I played a bajillion hours in For Honor (probably because the game's fun and good), but I can't recommend this game because of X". And that X reasons is always "balance" or "connectivity issues". Throw in a good mix of "Ubisoft is terrible" memes, and you get the Steam reviews page. As a final note, this whole "le Ubisoft xD" is simply just a bad meme. Ubisoft was never a giant company, and compared to their previous titles, this is technically the best game they have ever made. They are not a lieing, thieving, evil corporate goon company that Reddit would have you believe. They're not exactly a smart and wildly successful company, either. Let's be fair: they're just trying to do what they can to get the least flack and pay their own damn bills.

Gonna go against the grain and recommend the game.
We've all been asking for customizable decks in this franchise and they're here.
What some people are missing is that this DotP is not supposed to compete with paper or online magic.  So the card pool is not particularly deep, and if you understand that going in, you won't be disappointed.  If you want ALL the cards, pay a heck of a lot more to play Magic Online.
I'm gonna make clear what the pay model here is.  In DotP 2015, for your $9.99, you're getting most of the experience.  You'll need to do a little grinding as you play through the campaign to unlock the planes and all the cards from them (in the form of booster packs when you win).  I think these battles are pretty fun, especially since the computer decks use more powerful cards than you have access to.  So it's a bit of a challenge and your deck can't be garbage, especially against the bosses.
You should NOT buy the plane unlocks that are $4.99.  Those are just a shortcut to unlock all the cards in the plane, but it doesn't take long to unlock them on your own.  Plus you're killing whatever incentive you may have had to play the campaign.
You also should NOT buy the special edition, collectors edition, or any of that crap.  They don't include the "Premium" cards.
The "premium" cards aren't necessary to win but they tend to open up a lot of deck archetypes you couldn't build effectively otherwise.  To get all the "premium" cards you will need to purchase 14 boosters at $2 each, or $28 in all.  If you pre-ordered, you get two boosters for free.  If you own DotP 2014, you get one booster for free.  The most you should ever spend on this game is $9.99 + the $28 from boosters, if you so desire.  But the game is fully playable for $9.99.
Personally, so far I like DotP 2013 and 2014 a little more, because of the powerful and interesting cards at your disposal in those titles, but this version offers the ability to truly make a deck your own and I'm very excited to see what the metagame in 1v1 duels will be.  As others have mentioned, 2v2 isn't included, which is a terrible decision, but I didn't play that mode much in the past regardless.

Not a bad game but I can't recommend buying it when the price is 20 euros. I've had a great time playing this shooter but only after installing some mods. Let me put this straight - this game is not properly optimised for Steam. I have a good graphics and enough RAM to run most games but this Quake 4 game even when put in Ultra Quality settings has crappy textures. Add an overall gray-brown-black-metal surrounding and your graphics may look like well, mud.
I have most of the same gripes with this game as I've had with Serious Sam 2 - the vanilla game didn't age well. Graphics are not optimised for High Definition, the main character is moving pretty slow for a cyborg, some encounters seems heavily scripted, weapons sometimes don't pack as much punch as they should.
But after installing SIKK MOD and PARALAX MOD the game just got better. Graphics are finally nice - dynamic lights, most of objects are retextured to some HD textures, we get some blur effects, etc.. But we also get some problems with levels loading and game crashing after modding so this is a mixed bag of goodies and uglies.
Let's try to sum up all of pros and cons for Quake 4
Pros:
- modded graphics look really pretty
- enemies are grotesque, mechanical monsters with solid design
- sound is fine
- plot is ok for a single player mode
- weapons have nice design - Nailgun and BFG both look nice and have a considerable power
- sometimes we can control vehicle like tank or mech suit
Cons:
- although vehicles are fun, those levels with vehicles are pretty long and boring
- some of weapons are underpowered - I think that grenade launcher, rocket launcher and most of all railgun are somewhat weak
- graphics without mods
- most weapons have clips that you need to reload every now and then - really, who thought that would be a good idea in a Quake game? For example Railgun has a 3 ammo in a clip. Most stronger enemies take 3-5 hits with a railgun. Same goes for shotgun - we need to reload it slug after slug up to the point where we get a magazine upgrade and then we can reload a whole magazine (about half of the game). Luckily, we can remove clips with a SIKK mod
- character moves really slow and enemies move fast. That can escalate rather quick... - we can change that with SIKK mod
- no replay value - single player campaign is scripted and multiplayer is possibly dead
- buggy as hell when modded - I needed to move config files manually every now and then when some levels didn't load. It was pretty annoying to save game just before next loading screen, then exit to desktop, move files, run game, load saved game, pass through a loading screen into a next level, save game, exit to desktop, move back those files, run game, load saved game and finally play it. Really, this is pain when you need to do this about 20 times during whole game.
After all I can recommend playing this game after modding it a bit (if you can grab it for let's say 5 bucks/euros that is) but if you're not a Quake fan then you can skip it. It's definitely not worth 20 euros, it aged poorly and looks bad without mods. I've had fun but I would not play this game a second time. It's barely playable without mods and thus I can't give thumbs up to a game that requires mods to be fun.

Pay to win?

Quake IV is an OK game, to start off with this mini review, let's focus on the campaign since multiplayer is dead and Quake III / Live is a better option for that, this game lacks of replay value due to its linear nature, similar to Doom 3, but i felt like this singleplayer was much shorter compared to the other, in Doom 3 there are some secrets and stuff to collect like the codes and PDAs, but yeah, it took me 7 hours to beat it, but it was still a enjoyable experience, the level designs are really good except for those horrendous turret/vehicle sections, there is a nice roster of enemies and a extense weapon arsenal, although the BFG is missing here (I was expecting it to be here since it follows the Quake II storyline) but you got a nice replacement, there are bosses too, some of them become regular enemies at the end of the game and you have a couple of "final" bosses, but they are not that exciting to fight, just run around them shooting them till they die (like some of the Doom 3 bosses). The story isn't that deep but is good to explain more about the QuakeII/IV lore and the graphics are really amazing (for the time). I think this game could have been better if the campaign was more deep and long, maybe some alternative endings or paths, even the final boss is not that threatning and easy to kill, leaving a really weird and anticlimatic cinematic. I would recommend this to people who wanna try something different on the FPS genre, not the best of them but it really shows how oldschool shooters were back then when all that mattered was the fun of shooting things with overpowered guns while running like a madman.

IF YOU ARE EXPECTING 2 HEADED GIANT DO NOT BUY THIS GAME!
I knew this before I got the game but there are so many upset people posting in the forum about this I figured we should get this out of the way from the start. There is no 2v2 mode in this year's edition of Magic. If that is your favorite style of play you should probably stick to 2014.
Here is what I do not like about the game:
The user interface is slow and clunky. It may be only a second delay here or there, but it is noticeable.
The menu screen is in a scroll format and not a list. That means only one option is displayed on the screen at a time and you may have to scroll 6 times to find the sub menu you are looking for.
During the combat phase the battlefield actually splits open partially, exposing a red glowing divide between the players. It closes after the combat phases, but this animation still takes a small portion of time and happens every time. As someone who plays with card animations off I find this mildly irritating.
The game forces you to play the tutorial (on the hardest difficulty you still have to play the tutorial boss) even if you have played Magic a lot. Seriously, the game asks you how much Magic you have played and choosing "a lot" then immediately dumps you into the tutorial.
You have to play through the first plane to get any extra cards you paid for. People who pre-ordered got a free premium booster pack (these packs are not free unlocks, you usually have to buy them) and people who own Magic 2014 also get a free premium booster pack, at least at the time of writing this review. People who paid for the complete version may be upset to find all those extra card unlocks they paid for are not available until after the first hour or so of gameplay.
What I do like about the game:
I like being able to customize my own deck. My biggest problem in 2014 was that I played among a small group of friends. After playing my first card or two they knew what deck I was playing and what they needed to do to counter. Now I can keep them guessing.
I like that you can buy the regular $10 version and play the game to unlock all of the base cards in the game. I can get the same content as the people that bought the Complete version just by playing the game enough.
After getting used to all of the things I don't like about the game they all kind of became background noise and I found myself enjoying just playing the game. If I weigh the pros and cons of the game I would say that the $10 version is worth picking up. I would definitely buy again and do not regret my pre-order.
Tl;dr - NO 2hg, some additional cards you have to pay to get. Buy $10 version for better value. UI is bad, but playable.

I haven't been so enchanted with a game in a long time.
I'll start with the negatives:
Sometimes you get bad RNG (an enemy completely blocking your path) and in very rare situations can not leave the screen to re roll them, resulting in a bit of a lame death unless you can get really lucky and get by that enemy.
This game is brutal, and your deaths usually dock you about 5 minutes of your time, but can be much more punishing/frustrating -- especially if you die to rain after a ton of exploration :/
This game does not teach you a lot of very helpful survival tips -- or even all of the core mechanics.
This game has difficult controls at first, ESPECIALLY WALLJUMP SECTIONS
Sometimes the physics can do some silly stuff, since mechanics are very physics based and you're really counting on them to work. This hasn't really killed me or anything thuogh.
Onto the positives.
If you haven't already spoiled the experience by watching a bunch of trailers, please play this game completely blind.
The attention to detail and the worldbuilding of this game is something unique and fantastic that I have not seen done so passionately in a long time. The game invokes the grim feel of a hostile world in a manner _very_ similar to Heart of Darkness.
There is a lot of joy to me in learning a new way to cleverly exploit the world around you. As you play, you will go from this little white lizard-food ♥♥♥♥ to a wall jumping grenade throwing squid riding acrobat with a mastery of his environment.
However you're still weak. You still can't really fight some of the horrors that are after you, but you can always come prepared ;)
This is a tired comparison but after enough dying it started to remind me of Dark Souls. That being, once you've been through an area a few times, you just fly through these zones that kicked your♥♥♥♥♥with ease, and it feels really nice.
Also because it doesn't teach you ♥♥♥♥ all about the specifics. but that's a neato experience if you're ready for it.
Artistically you are probably already aware that this game is unique and amazing. Its music can be weird in spots -- not bad though, just strange.

This game is absolutely abysmal, even by 1997's standards (the year they first started working on this).
To start, on the upside, you are a badass throwing out cheesy one liners whenever you kill enemies. That's pretty much it. From here on out, it's going to be nothing but downhill. I had to force myself to keep playing and even then, I simply couldn't take the pain anymore. The story goes - aliens attack and it's up to the Duke, an aging sterol junkie and narcissist to defend Earth. That sounds cool but in reality, the Duke rarely speaks and there is little humor (forget Bulletstorm, Borderlands, or Portal - this isn't even a warm up to comedy). The gameplay is nothing more than equip yourself with generic assault rifles and blast linear swarms of generic aliens. You do this several times before the pace is abruptly halted by generic platforming or unnecessary dialogue. The reality is the game doesn't know what it wants to be (think Postal but worse) so it tries to be everything. It tries to be humorous, fast, witty, serious - but it's not any of that.
The Duke is living in the past and you can clearly tell by the random ideas lumped together right before release. At best, this game was average for 1997 but by 2011's standards, it has fallen way, way, way below average. The score is nothing more than a bland overtune that puts you to sleep. The graphics and textures are very pixelated, bland, blurry, blocky, and poor. The AI is broken and commonly gets stuck on things. The multiplayer servers are deadier then Jake Lloyd's acting career. You could probably get it to run on a toaster but I doubt it (which is a good thing because the toaster might blow up and you'd need a new one). What's funny is the game is so bad, the developers realized it and took the time to make jokes about it. This does not excuse the fact that you had 14 years to make a game that played like it was done in just 14 days. I realize most of us got the game for cheap (<$5) but even then I felt I got ripped off. If I was paid to play this game and I had no other source of income, I would gladly take to the streets. Every attempt the game makes to succeed ends up in utter disgrace. I should also mention that this is my first Duke game so I went in expecting nothing. I ended up getting nothing (but grief).
Here are some other words to describe this game: faulty, soulless, broken, inadequate, inferior, unacceptable, pitiful, wretched, destitute, deficient, unbearable, weak, disgraceful, insidious, malicious, malignant, failing, failure, failed, EA, Call of Duty, Battlefield Earth, The Third Reich, and the Biebister.
I give this game a 2/10 (+1 for power armor, +1 duke voice).

I went ahead and picked up this game up during it's sale cause I was simply curious + it had a adorable little creature as the main character, a little weak Slug Cat. You go about a ruined world that is split up into regions which can only be accessed during certain days. Each region holds different rooms with different layouts and different monsters to keep you on edge while playing this game. Firstly, the graphics are overall a job well done. The character model you play as is adorable and innocent while everything around you is destroyed in rottten ruins. Secondly, the AI in the game are smart to the point that you will find certain monsters actually camping or hiding around your only way out. This degree of intellgence ends up making the game Hardcore driven since there are fair penalties upon death (you go back a day which causes certain gates to regions to close, yet you can avoid going back a day upon death by eating rare golden flowers). Hardcore in this game is really a two sided-coin, either you like it the difficult Hardcore aspect or you don't (the game does not get easier, but seemingly gets more difficult). The one issue I'm seeing according to other reviews are the controls and key bindings. I'm personally using a controller and facing little difficulty with moving my little Slug Cat around the map, yet other people also claim the character you play as is too slow or clunky. Yes, the character is slow and clunky since it is a Slug Cat and you will find yourself being chased down by faster monsters since your slug tail is dragging you down. Overall, I reccomend this game to those who use controllers and are fine with a Hardcore driven game that will screw you over despite your best efforts. I give Rain World 8/10 Yummy, Juicy, Mouth-Watering, Slug Cats

WARNING: THIS GAME FEELS RUSHED TO THE MARKET AND HAS A LOT OF BUGS (SOME OF WHICH ARE GAME BREAKING) AND GLITCHES
Gameplay:
The areas you explore are much larger than in Legend and Anniversary and it makes the exploring more amazing in my opinion. You even explore some underwater areas, which you couldn't in the previous titles. Lara has many more options with climbing and platforming and it's amazing. You can climb on poles, jump from wall to wall and the grapple is now much better. The game saves checkpoints a lot more frequently than Anniversary, so it makes it less annoying to die from a bad jump or bug (which can happen a lot). The puzzles are good, although sometimes they are not clearly presented.
The most annoying thing here is the camera. It's even worse than in Anniversary and will make you fall to your death a lot (though because of the better checkpoint system, it's not as annoying). It moves on its own and doesn't allow you to see where you need to jump next most of the time.
The combat is less frequent here and most of the time you'll only battle animals, which can be dispatched quite easily with adrenaline system and because you have all the weapons from the beginning, the difficulty of these encounters are really low.
There are no boss fights in the entire game.
Music: Although not bad, it felt worse than Legend and Anniversary.
Story: The story finally resolves the cliffhanger from Legend and is also a fitting conclusion to the trilogy. Still, it's more like it was in Anniversary, with story being more on backseat with occasional cutscene. X360 version also got two DLC that weren't released on PC.
Technical:This game was obviously rushed to the market, because the amount of bugs and glitches I encountered in this game is among the biggest in all games I ever played. Some can break the game (in which cases the best solution is to download saves from the internet (tombraiders.  net has a full collection of them). These bugs are not as much seen in the first half of the game, but as you get to Mexico, you will encounter them more and more. This results in many jumps that will not connect, or make Lara stuck in objects. Another really annoying bug is that motorbike disappears from you, making you unable to continue and the only option you have is to start the level from the start. I also had problem with seeing what could be climbed on and what couldn't, because some objects look climbable (a lot of blocks).
On the other hand, the game looks amazing for its age. Some people had trouble with fps, but for me it ran 60 fps all the time, apart from some weird slowdowns when I turned on flashlight underwater (at which point the game slowed down to 40 fps).
Finally the game supports the controllers normally, so the on screen prompts are controller buttons.
Overall: The game is good, but is set back by horrible camera,lack of combat and bugs, which make the game frustrating later on. If it wasn't this unfinished, I would have probably liked it more than Legend. Only buy this if you don't mind bugs and a really bad camera.

Quake 4 is an excellent FPS game that has a great singleplayer campaign and an excellent multiplayer component.  This is a worthy sequel to Quake 2 (with some caveats).
The singleplayer campaign picks up shortly after the events of Quake 2.  The Strogg's planetary defenses have been disabled and a second invasion operation by the humans is underway.  I thoroughly enjoyed the campaign.  There's a stronger story this time around, named characters pertinent to the story, medics and techs that can heal you and provide armor recharges between fights (on occasion - and try not to let them die), and you get to fight using an assortment of heavy weapons - including a tank and a battlemech (they call it a "walker" *pff*).  A f'n battlemech!  They had me at tank...  *tear* *sniff*
The graphics are very nice, running on the impressive ID Tech 4 engine introduced with Doom 3, and while there have been advancements with graphics technology in the last 10 years - they still hold up extremely well.  The architecture in the game is very detailed and the texturing very well done.  There are some large open areas on the planet's surface, but most of the game you're running around inside of the, often tight, corridors of the enemy compounds.
The sound design is solid, with ambient sound permeating and creating much of the mood for the areas you'll traverse.  And throughout you will hear radio chatter that gives you an impression of the scope, cost of the war being waged, provide you with story points, and levy objectives on you.  The sounds of weapons' fire and impact are all very good - no whimpering shotguns here.  The music is sufficient, but it lacks the unnerving moodiness of previous Quake titles.
The weapons you get all have their benefits and deficits.  For instance, some enemies will take bullet after bullet from your rifle when another is quickly turned into swiss cheese, but they all seem to be more susceptible to certain weapons over others - one enemy type in particular will explode almost immediately when hit with the lightning gun.  You start out with a pistol with infinite ammo that is actually quite useful in certain situations.  You will also gain a rifle, shotgun, hyperblaster, nailgun, grenade launcher, rocket launcher, lightning gun, and a dark-matter gun.  Throughout the singleplayer campaign you'll get little upgrades from techs in your unit that add new features to some of these weapons:  a bigger clip, increased damage, a targeting scope, etc..
The developers clearly tried to add alot of combat flavor to the game, arguably absent from the first game (a minor quibble).  There is a portion of the game where you have to man a mounted gun on a moving tram and take down enemy aircraft as well other vehicles.  In another you have control of a hover-tank and have to quickly maneuver and destroy an assortment of enemies and armament whilst trying to navigate to your objective.  In another you get to man a battlemech fighting off the enemies with it's heavy caliber guns and rockets.  Yippee ki yay mutha♥♥♥♥as!!
There are around 20 or so different enemy types, not counting bosses and all fairly disgusting, especially the zombies that puke acid (this might explain why I need pills to sleep at night).  They get similar weaponry as you, though some have unique energy weapons, flamethrowers, and whatever the hell the Iron Maiden's awful scream attack is supposed to be.
Quake 4 does drift away from the feel of Quake 2 a bit too much, imo.  The Stroggs of Quake 2 lived on a planet with a thick blood red sky.  Their installations were dark, gritty and minimalistic.  The architecture was authoritarian with big red banners draped on their exteriors that reminded one immediately of the Nazis during WWII.  Their technology was function over form.  It had dangerous fauna and some truly memorable enemy types.  Exploration (which often required some puzzle-solving) was rewarded, you could swim underwater, you could throw a grenade - using it's tick-time once activated to good effect, the hyperblaster was like a gatlin gun that shot lasers and made a unique piercing sound when it was fired, you were given objective information by a computer that notified you with quirky voice, etc..
Meanwhile in Quake 4....
...the sky is blue and reminiscent of Earth, their installations are often well-lit and incredibly high-tech.  The architecture barely resembles that of the previous game.  There is no dangerous fauna you'll come in contact with and most of the enemy types have been completely reimagined and some are just completely missing.  The story is supposed to take place after Quake 2, but everything looks and feels just too different.  There's almost no exploration to be had and it never involves puzzle-solving, there is no water ANYWHERE and so no swimming either, you can't throw grenades, the hyperblaster here makes a sad whoomping sound and seems more like the plasma gun from Doom, and there is no computer updating your objectives.
I'm sure I could think of more if I sat here long enough.  I just don't understand why Raven felt the game world needed such a makeover.  Updating the graphics using new technology - awesome!  but this level of reimagining was totally unnecessary.  The upside is that the game is just as dark thematically as Quake 2 and includes some very gruesome, gory content - arguably more disturbing than what Quake 2 was able to convey.
In the end this is an excellent game that just falls short of reaching the level of awesome of it's predecessor Quake 2.

This is hands-down one of my favorite games of all time. It's typically called a mash up of God of War and The Legend of Zelda and if the sound of that makes you feel a little tingly, make the jump! The combat is 3rd person hack n' slash at its finest, just the way I like it! There is also a great deal of platforming and puzzle solving weaved into this fine tapestry. Prepare to pick your jaw up off the ground after stepping into gloriously apocolyptic environments of varying degrees, whether it's the ruins of a great city long past or a massive desert made of the ashes of millions of dead people.
The theme of this game combines elements of various religeous mythologies, primarily those of Judeo-Christion myth, to craft an epic world full of very powerful entities and monsters intermingled with elemnets of modern human society. You play as War, one of the 4 Horsemen of the Apocolypse, who has been blamed for the premature destruction of Earth in an eon's long war between the forces of Angels and Demons. The Horsemen are extremely powerful enities who serve as judge, jury, and executioner, also serving as the middleground between the 2 warring sides, led by the mysterious Charred Council who attempt to maintain balance between Heaven and Hell. All throughout the adventure, you will move Heaven and Earth(sometimes literally) to clear your name, leaving a mountain of bloody corpses in your wake.
As the embodiment of all that is War, you weild the mighty Chaoseater, your weapon of choice, cleaving your way through Angel and Demon alike. Along with your signiture sword, you will find other powerful weapons along the way like the powerful Harvester Scythe borrowed from your brother Death, Mercy, a pistol borrowed from your brother Srife, the Crossblade, and the mighty Tremor Gauntlet. On top of that, there are varois abbillities and other objects of power, used in similar ways to items in Zelda games, to help you progress as well as gain advantages to certain enemies. There is also an upgrade system for abillities and your 3 main weapons level up and gain experience as you use them. They can also be augmented with various runes found throught the world. Later into the game, you gain access to your horse, Ruin, who you then be able to ride in amany places in the game map. If all of that isn't enough for you, the deviously selfish creature called the Watcher, an entity bound to you who acts as your guide and a leash for the Council, is voiced by none other than Mark Hamill! So what are you waiting for? Give it a try!
TL:DR: Fly like Link, Sting like Kratos!

Amnesia: The Dark Descent is vastly overhyped game, but nevertheless one people should still play for it's unique mechanics and style. It's not a horror game purely based on jump scares or other cliches. The art style is great, and the environment is presented really well. Another thing that stood out was the soundtrack; great timing and some beautiful and haunting arrangements that fit the mood of the game.
The game isn't without it's complaints though. For me are the voice-acting of the main character, overall story, and repetitiveness really bring this game down. I found the voice of Daniel to be outright annoying at times, and really overdone. The story itself could have been interesting, but I felt like it took way too long to unravel. And on top of that, the conclusion is a bit shark-jumpy in my opinion. (I do appreciate the multiple endings, and how the player goes about choosing them though.) I also found that each horror encounter wasn't too difficult after you progress through the game, as it was pretty much the same each time. There's great tension for sure, especially on your first few times with any of the monsters, but there is almost no difference between each encounter, so it can get stale and predictable.
Overall, I'd give this game a 6.3/10. It's pretty decent, but lower your expectations, and buy it on a sale.

As a huge Quake 2 fan, after dealing with some initial graphic problems, I jumped into the game. And about an hour was enough for me. It's really, really boring. The level design is lame, enemies encountered in the first hour are lame and mostly huge hp sponges, weapons are lame and not very satisfying to use. DISCLAIMER: Anyone who claims the story in this game is "lacking" simply didn't spend any time actually thinking about what was going on, observing the symbols and motifs, and were just busy worrying about being told what's going on. If you like to be told what's going on at all times, you probably won't enjoy this game. If you enjoy thought-provoking story that requires some in-depth thinking, then you probably will like this game.
When I first started playing, I didn't really know what to think about it. I really love games like this.
The beginning was rather slow, like it was meant for little kids. Because of that, I was thinking to myself, "Oh, this is one of those games that tries to emulate something like ICO, but will ultimately fail at establishing a meaningful or consuming story." In short- I underestimated the developers.
Well, I just finished the game and I have to say that it is probably one of favorites of this genre. The team who made this was absolutely brilliant. Was it very slow in the beginning? Absolutely. But once you open up to the "actual game", you become very consumed by what's going on. The progression of the story is meaningful, thoughtful, and very unique. The symbolisms are rich and the story turns on its head in terms of the feelings it inspires.
The art/graphics were amazing, but there are some optomization issues. I have a 1070, 16gb RAM, and an i7, I should be able to run it on max everything and not see the kind of stuttering I saw when turning the camera. If you put everything on "medium" and turn the advanced settings on, it should look gorgeous and eliminate the stuttering/framerate drop. I was just a little irked I couldn't do everything on ultra. But that's a very MINOR thing, as everything was still gorgeous and breathtaking on medium.
I was constantly annoyed that the ledges had this bird-crap looking stain on them through the ENTIRE game, I wish they had maybe come up with something different. It actually ruined my immersion more than a couple times as I mildly thought, "That poor kid has to jump face first into bird sh*t." I think it's supposed to be wear on the rocks, but I just couldn't get it out of my head. Lol.
The puzzles in general were quite easy, but the experience is really what you are paying for. The amazing music, the scenery, the characters, the story- it's all well worth the $30 I paid. Absolutely breathtaking game. I'd say it's my third favorite behind Journey and ICO.

RiME is a puzzle adventure game with a story about loss and regret. There's no dialogue. It's a decent game but in my opinion not worth the price. Note that these puzzles are on the easier side of the genre... There is very little direction given to the user, but not much that really leaves them scratching their head for a solution.
PROS
- Visually pleasing with high contrast colors and imaginative worlds
- Interesting non-playable characters
- Easy puzzles leads to casual gameplay
- Camera gives a cinematic feel
- Some nice character animations not seen in most games (falling from a great height, running downhill, etc)
CONS
- Character runs slowly, which drags the game out.
- Controls are clunky. Often have to stop moving and reorient position to interact with objects
- The parkour is clunky as well. Some blocks you can climb, others you can't. They try to indicate some of them with markings on a ledge but it's sometimes arbitrary what you can climb and what you can't
- The roaming cinematic camera forces user to change their direction. Users may have to unpress a key and then press it again to reorient the character to that direction.
It was a good, easy, casual game but I found myself fighting against the controls (e.g. forcing myself to run, intentionally come to a complete stop in front of an object, then spend two seconds to reorient the character so he can interact with the object).

As a long time player of this franchise, going back as far as DoTP2012, I am severely disappointed in this game. It brings only 1 new thing to the table, while removing a massive amount of other things for no apparent reason.
Pros:
This has been asked for ages, and finally it's been implemented, just the way we want it! Fully configurable decks, lands, cards, and all.
This has been the main selling point of the DotP games for me personally.
Cons:
Let's take Ravnica as an example. The Ravnica plane in game has a 59 unique cards, including 10 guildgates. The 'Return to Ravnica' release in real life cards has 274 unique cards. The whole block (which the plane is based on) has 679 unique cards. Some of these cards
in game, as the AI uses them plenty, but the majority of cards remain unavailable to players. Just to show how bad this is: There is a
dual colored card for each of the Ravnica guilds in game accessible to players.
Some of these modes such as Two Headed Giant have been part of the game ever since the beginning, and have had a massive appeal for Online play. I personally realize that it would be ridiculously hard to balance things like these, but I still wish the game mode had been left in.
Again, this is something that has been in the series for a long time. But in this version, there are no challenges. By challenge, I mean certain pre-configured scenario where you have to use a certain mechanic of series of cards to win the scenario.
This has also been a part of previous game, but is not in this version either. For clarity's sake, the Revenge campaign was a campaign where you redid the old campaign where the AI had improved decks.
There are 43 'Premium' cards which can only be unlocked through the purchase of booster packs. These boosters cost 1.79 euro in Sweden, uncertain about US based pricing.
