I bought the game as a pack on a sale. As a long time fan of the franchise, this is a solid title. For those who never played the series before, here are some things you need to know. First, this isn't the Tomb Raider from the reboot. The gameplay is a bit different, a little less cinematic in it's story telling but the game is still an eye candy that will make you stop to look at the scenery despite it being a little graphicaly outdated. It is overall a good game and I recommend it.
That said, here are some of the issues that you may want to know. Because of its age, it is highly unlikely that there will be any new patches to fix it. First, the framerate. The framerate throughout the game is not stable. You will often find yourself with slowdowns under the 20fps mark. If this occurs to you, alt+tab out for a second and returning will usually fix the issue until it happens again. Secondly, I encountered a few crashes during my gameplay. Due to varying fps, I'm assuming it might be due to a few memory leaks. It's a bit annoying but only occured about 3 times during my playthrough. Then there are a few minor issues that I encountered along the way such as invisible collision (may annoy you if you are also the type to explore everywhere), a few camera collision and odd angles, a few streaming issues (unloaded textures until you are right against the object, possible issue if you are a speedrunner).
The issues stated above may break the immersion and lessen the appreciation for the game but the overall experience is still enjoyable. I recommend this title if you feel like revisiting the franchise or want to see experience the series pre-reboot.

Rain World is indie developer Videocult's new survival platform title published by Adult Swim Games. Taking place in a world of deadly rainstorms and vicious carnivores, players take charge of a single lonely slugcat, who must evade and survive long enough to reunite with it's family. Will you be able to get back to the safety of your home, or be pounded into oblivion by a torrent of crushing water?
It comes down to is this: Rain World is a gorgeous game with great storytelling and a very slow pace. It has some bits and pieces that are more in favor of art than fun--such as non-skip-able animations and a dreary color palette--but there's still great gameplay and a huge amount of content for all that (over 60 hrs on a first play-through!)
If you're the kind that likes to sprinkle some art house movies in between binge-watching cartoons, then you ought to consider Rain World a must-have, a 10/10, an insta-buy. However, if you're just looking for the average Mario-Meat Boy-Hedgehog experience, then consider that you'll be getting a game more focused on careful planning than twitch reflexes. Consider also that you'll be getting a beautiful story, though--for us, that's worth it.
Pros:
+ Great storytelling
+ Tight controls
+ Excellent design and animation
+ Huge amount of content
Cons:
- Some unnecessary ledge-clutter
- Dreary colors
- Visual disconnect between environs and cutscenes

Raven Software's Quake 4 is often regarded as the black sheep of id Software's famous FPS series and while it does have its shortcomings, it's well worth a playthrough, so let's get out the Nailgun and kick some Strogg♥♥♥♥♥
That is if the game worked properly to begin with. When I first started the campaign, the game's graphics were terrifyingly... bad. It seemed to have issues streaming textures in, giving the game a very washed out and comicbook-like look. This problem is a common occurance according to many Steam users but don't you worry, Sikkmod not only fixes those problems but makes the game look incredible to boot. I recommend everyone to download that mod, here's a tutorial on how to set it up:
Sadly, the FPS lock of 60FPS can't be circumvented, which is a shame, and for a game with competitive multiplayer a rather questionably decision. However unlike Quake 3, the multiplayer is pretty much dead which is to be expected.
The story is set right after the events of Quake 2. The Makron has been killed by some lone Space Marine (heh!), the Strogg's defenses have been weakened and it's the perfect opportunity for the Space Marines to strike. You take on the role of Cpl. Matthew Kane, a "certified badass" for reasons unknown, shooting your way to the communication hubs with Rhino Squad to destroy them and cripple the Stroggs' communications. But things never go as planned and you get captured by none other than... the Makron? After having some "enhancements" done to you, you get rescued in time by your squad and the real fun begins...
One of the things you'll notice at first is your movement speed, which compared to earlier entries of the Quake series is quite slow. This can be circumvented with the console parameter "pm_speed x" and should be binded to a key as the game reverts your changes after loading a save or new map (bind key pm_speed x). I suggest increasing your running speed to 230, the same amount after your character gets "enhanced". FOV is good enough to begin with and can be increased further by typing in "g_fov x" in the console. Again, bind it to a key. The shooting in this game is very satisfying though I found the hit registration to be somewhat unreliable. I often found myself having trouble to kill even the weakest enemies as they seemingly absorbed most of my bullets. This only happened with the Machine Gun and Railgun however and it may as well have been my own incompetence so take this info with a grain of salt. The combat is what you would expect from a oldschool shooter: fast paced, mostly projectile based and alot more difficult than todays games. I'd consider myself fairly competent at FPS games (the genre I play the most) and Quake 4 isn't gonna go easy on you. I died quite a few times on Lieutenant Mode (Hard) and reflecting on my playthrough I can only think of 1 or maybe 2 times where the game decided to be cheap (like getting knocked into an abyss by a homing rocket). Quake 4 also has a few vehicle sections which mark the lowpoint of this game. They are just boring and cumbersome, luckily they don't last for too long.
Quake 4's levels are more linear than its predecessors which may be a turn off for some people but Rave Software did a great job designing them. Stroggos is a biomechanical nightmare you don't want to experience in the flesh. One level in particular titled "Waste Processing Facility" is especially unnerving and creeped the ♥♥♥♥ out of me (a gorehound). Quake 4 does feel a bit "cinematic" and sometimes hinders your progress (Marines blocking your ways, doors not opening) but it's bearable and doesn't destroy the pacing. Kane's squadmates are a likeable bunch and some of the events in the campaign are very memorable. The music is a mixed bag, rangin from nice ambient level tracks to standard action oriented songs. The main title by Chris Vrenna is nice to listen to.
Quake 4 is a damn fine game. Now move out soldier!

Quake 4 is an anomaly in terms of game design. Released more than ten years ago, it still manages to hold a special place in my heart for its interesting, old-school mechanics and its interesting attempts to wrap up the "storyline" that began in Quake II.
By no means does that mean you need to play Quake II to play this one, as Quake 4 does a very good job of giving you an overview of what happened previously before you're shoved into the perspective of a Corporal Matthew Kane, a man that everyone seems to know of for some reason. Earth is finally taking the fight to the homeworld of the Strogg, a grotesque group of biological/mechanical hybrids who seem to design every aspect of their planet for maximum defensive and warlike means.
Gameplay is a combination of what one would expect in an old-school corridor shooter and what one would expect from a squad-based fps. For some reason, however, they abandon much of the squad-based nature of the game about a third of the way through the game. After a major plot point, the player character is seperated from most of his fellow marines, and remains mostly seperated from them for the rest of the game. This is also the same time that many of the more powerful enemies are introduced.
The game's pace is very inconsistent for the middle part of the game, as I expect the developers were struggling to adapt to the new style and designed levels that wound've worked a bit better with the squad-based system. These transition levels were always less fun for me than the rest of the game, as they seemed to rely on the difficulty inherent in fighting large enemies in enclosed spaces.
However, the game really holds up despite all of this. I personally love the game's art style and the voice acting is top notch. I haven't played the multiplayer in years, so I can't vouch for how well it has held up, but I remember it playing like a much faster Quake III.
If what I've discussed above appeals to you, why not pick this one up? I'm sure you'll get a dozen or so hours of fun out of it at least.

- Review written at the state of the game on the 23rd of October 2016. -
Fun, lots of fun, but a little easy and unpolished, and gets repetitive.
Not a lot of replay value.
If you'd like a game thats a bit of a throwback to the old Duke Nukem/Doom style 90's shoot-em-ups, this game has a lot of oldschool play feel (I can't remember the last time I pushed up to #8 to change weapons?!)
= The Good =
- Fast fun, energetic action play
- Quippy funny dialogue (if you have a 13 year old male sense of humour like me, otherwise you'll hate it)
- Interesting levels that each have a different feel to them (until you find you've played the same one 3 times with a slightly different objective)
- Cool weapons, and the ability to slot upgrades into them (until you realise they didn't really put that much effort into the upgrade system and its fairly randomised)
- Decent melee combat (whole game with melee challenge anyone?)
- Interesting story and characters
= The Bad =
- After the first two hours of play you'll start to realise that the game is actually fairly repetitive in its playstyle.
- The minimap makes the game TOO EASY.  It could have been interesting if I had to find my way through levels but you just follow the little 'auto direction' thingy in the map and you get to your objective.  So you don't really explore the level at all, and a lot of work was put into the design if you look at them.
- Even if you had to search for loot- the loot system doesn't really reward exploration anyway.  Loot drops in level seem completely randomised   If they had specific hidden upgrades you had to search for that gave unique rewards, exploring the level would be much more interesting.
- Your shift key will be mashed to bits.  The 'dash' aspect makes the game way too easy.  You can kite enemies forever, until you run out of space to run into, which is never.  Get hurt, press shift a few times and run away, heal up off chi, return and fight.  Repeat.  I heard there used to be a limit to how often you could use it like an endurance bar, what happened to that?
- Although the melee system is fun, having 3 special attacks in a way is a bit limiting.  Some sort of fancy WASD combos with slashes could have made it a bit more interesting.  Parrying is somewhat worthless.
- Enemies have no weak points, you just shoot/slash at them till they die, doesn't matter if you hit them head foot or whatever, doesn't matter, there's no damage different.  Same for bosses.
Summary -
- After 15 hours, I finished the game on the second most hardest difficulty.  I think i died about 5 times, but you become way too strong for the enemies toward the end of the game.  It really becomes more about how much fun you can have killing them.
- No intention to play further, there's no point.  I don't think I'll gain anything by doing it in the hardest mode.  There's nothing more to do in it, I did multiplayer for a bit with my friends, but it's the same thing, just more enemies.
Can only recommend if you want to pay the price for about 15 hours worth of play.  Overall, it's fun.  But I don't care about the money to afford it that much, however, you might not want to shell out for it.

I have watched this game's devlog since the very beginning. I did not recieve this game for free, but that kind of dedication to something may have colored my viewpoints on the game. With that out of the way, let's go.
First off, understand that this WILL NOT be for everyone. It's punishing to a T, the world is absolutely out to kill you, and learning how to control the slugcat in anything other than generally flailing twoards your goal will take some time. In addition, even mastery of the core mechanics does not guarantee your own survival. And then, there's the obfuscation of information. This game is VERY hands-off, and will leave you to figure every single nuance of the world and the controls outside of the most basic aspects of movement, and the absolute vitals.
So why do I still recommend it, in spite of all of this?
Because I'm just utterly in love with it. Not just the beautiful graphics, or the world, but the concept and its execution. For me, the difficulty is in exactly the right spot. It is my opinion that the game SHOULD stop you from progressing into its harder, more lethal areas if you can't even survive a few days back-to-back in an earlier one. This game feels like it's not revolving around me until I prove that I'm worthy of its attention. And more games should do that. I don't want my success handed to me through game mechanics and lore. I am not some predestined hero come to save the land, more powerful than everything I fight. I'm just another animal in a world I can barely understand, and the only thing on my mind is how I'm going to survive in it. And I love every second of that.

A lot of folks are somehow entirely missing the point - this game is a war of attrition in a chaotic, living world. You are going to die - be thankful you don't start over from the beginning. If there is any advice I can give you, embrace naivete, and experiment with your controller. You can do a fast roll, quickly turn around, and a backflip with a couple different inputs. This game wants you to learn it, to explore it at a comfortable pace - if you smash into it as fast as you can, you're going to have a bad time. If you get it in your head you have to kill your enemies all the time, you're gonna have a bad time.
Relax, and brace yourself. This game is incredibly difficult. It won't even hand anything to you. You will have to focus on surviving as much as you focus on advancing - sometimes that means hunting in a safe place for a few days (half an hour in the real world) so you can get your footing back - relax, play it safe, experiment.
Also, if you don't like highly difficult platformers, this might not be for you.

RiME is a visually stunning game. The colours are bright and even the darker scenes are beautiful. I was especially impressed by the water in this game.
The music and sound is also amazing. The soft violin and oceans sounds make this game very relaxing and enjoyable.
The puzzles in this game are not difficult but at the same time, the combination of puzzles and platforming make this game very interesting to play.
RiME is also a surprisingly long game for what it is. I completed it in 5hrs (Probably 4.5hrs if I hadn't got confused).
The story of this game is complex and meaningful and is very much based on how the player interprets the story. The game does not force a certain plot upon you; it leaves you to decide what a certain character is feeling and why they are like they are.
The most amazing thing about RiME is its ability to portray feeling and mood through image, colour and posture of characters rather than through words. This is a very unique skill and has to be applauded in RiME.
Overall, I would highly recommend this game as a casual puzzle game but also as a deep story and visual masterpiece. Well worth the money.

I completed Rime in about 5 hours, and I take my time on games, so I'd estimate average playtime to be about 10-12 hours, to complete the game once. You could rush through in less, but wouldn't want to. Once you've completed it, the level select option is opened up, along with info on which collectables you have found in each area. The design and art direction is nice enough, as are the levels and puzzles. The music and sound effects are decent too, but the game is also quite frustrating. There's a little bit of heart-string pulling towards the end of the game, although nothing too out of the ordinary.
The main distraction are some serious and frequent frame rate issues; just running through a corridor or panning the camera results in drops. Shadows on walls can also look atrocious, with serious pixelation and flicker. This game is pretty, but by no means graphically stunning, and there is no excuse for these issues. Strangely the frame rate issues were mostly concentrated in the first few areas, but they did crop up throughout. If a game like legend of zelda breath of the wild : Cemu Emulator (which does have stunning visuals and much more happening at once) can maintain a solid frame rate on a low end pc, 99% of the time, then so can this, with its much simpler graphics and levels.
There seem to be issues with some of the achivement. I did exactly as required and didn't receive some. They are also extremely ambiguous, and in one case could have meant one of two things, which was a real pain (you're hiding from one creature by using the shade, while also trying to avoid other creatures which may or may not be called "shades"...). Lots of the achivements seem to be things you'd stumble upon more by luck rather than through skill or exploring. A little annoying as it's nice to know what you have to do, even if not where, instead of just a random riddle alluding to something you have no clue about.
This is a good, and not stellar, game. The 9/10 rating from Edge is their way of saying they want more games like this compared with FPS's and open world collecting / shooting games, which would be nice, but they don't have to show that by inflating a game's score. I'd give it 5/10. The reduced RRP helps, but even for $20 or so, 10-12 hours isn't a whole lot of playtime, and I'm not sure I'm that fussed about playing each level again (collectables would be fine - toys, costumes etc, but for the achievement which I have no idea at all how to get, it's a waste of time).
It's great to see developers making games like this, I was just hoping for a little more. It's a lot of lovely ideas, nicely put together, but as some other reviewers have commented on, we've kind of seen it all before. You can see what they were trying to achieve, but some fresher ideas and a little more to do wouldn't have gone amiss, along with maybe a few more levels. It's very bare-bones, but in some ways that's nice, without superfluous and vacuous NPC's, pages of stats, having to craft items, keep an inventory, and have a huge laundry list of objectives to tick off. Still, a good effort, and anything that's not a Marvel cash-in or new Call of Duty is definitely worth a look.

Quake 4 is yet another linear old-school'ish FPS in a Quake franchise. A franchise where no previous games were connected to each other, think of Final Fantasy. Quake 4 is proud exclusion, being a direct sequel to Quake 2, where space marines battle against cyborgs made of steel and human flesh on their planet. It was developed by Raven Software in 2005. And uses Doom 3 engine, so beware of sharp dynamic shadows.
There also was Collector Edition which came with Quake 2. As you expect, Steam version is not one. And there also was X360 port, that had Quake 2, some achievements and a bad optimisation. Not missing much there.
So, as for technical side. You will notice that textures are low quality even on Ultra Setting. That's because engine doesn't recognise mordern hardware for what it is and thinks you have very little memory and refuses to put correct settings in. You have to edit config files for textures. I recommend you to take a look at Steam community guides, there is a good one that tells you what commands to change.
I also would still have some small glitches with lights/shadows after playing for a while, but very minor and rarely, unlike what I had in Doom 3.
Another thing is that it had an awful lot of stuttering, especially when opening door to a new room. As if it tries to load something but for some reason has a lot of problems.
While game has options for widescreen aspect ratios, not all widescreen resolutions are there. Edit config for those too.
No alt-tab in fullscreen and no Steam Overlay.
As for multiplayer community, it's tiny. There are only few people, I only got to play in 3-player deathmatch. But in all honesty, since Multiplayer is similar to Quake 3 Arena one, it can be quite enough. You know, game where people tend to duel.
Apparently a lot of servers use Q4Max mod. It's low size anyway, and only seems to add more server options for competetive scenes, like full-bright skins, while not changing core gameplay itself, so it's OK. And some fixes. And gamemodes.
And in this plot you play as Kane, a silent protagonist and a badass who already got famous for things we don't get to do in this game. You are part of Rhino squad with who you will spend some of game time too, occasionally.
The Earth launched a second invansion on Strogg planet, hoping to fully clean it up while they are in supposed chaos as the certain badass killed their leader in Quake 2 (and another badass destroyed base on asteroid and another sissy blew up Gravity Well). Sure thing it was about as effective as assassination of political leaders, especially when we are talking about polished army of machines with purpose to kill, so you are about to get some more of hot time.
But at least this time 99% of marines weren't immeditly killed.
Not to mentioned that this time you will have some small cutscenes, radio chatters and NPCs to give the world more of living feel and to move a storyline. While still mostly focused on action and gameplay.
And yes, while it's not mazes, rather being what you would call a corridor shooter, it still can be considered old-school action. While having badass graphics. Frankly it didn't try to be spooky or dark like Doom 3, instead deliviring some shooting and aciton that Doom 3 didn't. And if you measure quality of FPS by how effective shotgun feels, then buy it immeditly, because shotgun in this makes ragdolls hoversault and just blows.
And yea, it's continuation of Quake 2, so you will see some familar elements from that game. But I feel that this one realized them much better. Which wasn't hard, seeing how Quake 2 felt unimpressive and somewhat generic even for a year of it's release. I mean, what tech advantages of Q2 would matter if you can't see anything past color red of art style. Anyway, Quake 4 isn't red, it actually has a art style that can show you dark grotesque images of creepy meat factories while staying colorful. Everything was slightly redesigned to be more badass too.
Gameplay also can be counted as superior. This one seems to pull weapons from Quake 3 arsenal though, with lighting gun and such. Well, with blaster instead of gaunlet. Don't worry, they are balanced around each other for single-player, having need to reload and special abilities of some. Monsters aren't as lame either. Melee berserkers can actually chase you down instead of never being able to hit a walking player. Monsters aren't as hitscan based either, having plenty projectiles to shoot and tactics to employ, making it more varied and fun too.
It's just shame that I can't say that it's music is better than Quake 2 soundtrack. I mean, main menu theme is nice and such and very Quake-like. But during actual gameplay you will be only occasionally hearing some kind of orchestra of sorts. Something from generic non-interesting heroic movies soundtracks. It still pumps you up during game, so it works.
And most awesomely, Raven Software took a few lessons from then-modern games and used them to improve pacing, variety and overall enjoyment of this linear campaign.
That includes masterful mix of rest moments and high-action ones. Sometimes you shoot many baddies, other times you are crawling over conveyer belts. To that extend it also employes parts where you are stuck on a turret of venichle or have to actually control one and get to another point. Thankfully, those sections are simple to control, aren't hard, short and fill quota on explosions, so they are most welcome.
Another thing that it takes are teammates. No longer you have to travel in Strogg world all alone, while failing to get immersed because you don't belive that every marine would become insane just from managing to land onto planet. I am referencing to Quake 2 again, yep. Sometimes in some sections of a game you will be followed by one or even up to three of marines, who will help you to effectively clear out the rooms, while rarely getting under your crosshair. They also don't suck, don't die easily and can kill stuff. And just make it feel more alive and that you are part of team. And some can heal and give armor. Don't worry, there is enough of lone wolf action, like one-man-army you are.
It also keeps on changing in player abilities, and not only by giving you weapons. It even updates the existing ones, giving them new propereties. Like turning nailgun (yes!) into scary weapon with projectiles that follow target. Or giving lighting gun ability to spread on others nearby. Thus also making you thing of how to balance your weapon choice and usage through the game. Even if railgun and lighting gun feel underwhelming.
It also even once updates your character, diving game into slower-paced half and into more of solo faster-paced one. Well, I am mostly talking of character speed. Let's not spoil the cutscene.
And yes, it has a few bosses. Not many, most are put together in the end of a game. But still some and they are nice, even if final boss feels a bit dissapointing. Maybe. This is usually a game I'd pass up as I do with most indie sidescrollers as theres so damn many of them but boy am I glad I gave this one a chance. A lot of my liking for this game has to do with the fact that it scratches an itch of mine that I find I can't get in many other games in that you play as an animal in the food chain and have to prey on animals beneath you and flee from animals above you. If that kind of gameplay appeals to you then this is the game for you.
Another thing I like is the difficulty, a lot of games these days are catered to casual gamers so that nobody will have trouble beating the game and it makes for a lot of really simplistic and downright boring gameplay to people like me that enjoy a challenge. And boy is this game challenging, a split second decision can mean the difference between life and death in this game as you try to escape animals that would have you for breakfast. If you're looking for a mellow exploration game where you explore the games world at your own pace thats not something you'll find here as each day is spent looking for food and finding shelter before the rains hit as rain is the biggest killer in this game. Thats not to say exploration isn't a huge part of this game though, as the overarching goal is to travel from region to region looking for new food sources and taking in the beautiful landscapes. Just don't expect to admire the landscapes for too long before getting chased by a hungry lizard.
Early on the controls may take some getting used to as its physics based so the position of your character effects what your movements do, it took me about an hour or two before I felt comfortable with the controls and after that I haven't had any issues. But if you're the kind of person who expects super meat boy esque accuracy where when you press the button the exact same thing will happen every time you'll be out of luck, because its physics based a jump from one ledge might be angled differently than another and you have to take that into account by paying attention to your character and surroundings at all times. That might be a dealbreaker to some hardcore platormer fanatics but for me it just makes me feel more immersed in the character as it makes them feels weighty and real instead of just floaty sprites gliding over whatever surface they're on.
So far in my playtime the only negative I've found is that the location of enemies can be unpredictable since they're being simulated all at the same time, sometimes you might come out of your shelter only to be surrounded by things trying to eat you almost immediately and that can feel unfair. Thankfully the punishment for death isn't too harsh, the game has a "karma" system where surviving a day adds to your karma and dying takes it away. Gaining access to new regions requires a certain karma level but beyond that its not used for anything that I know of, so even if one of the rare unfair scenarios I've come across does happen I'm not too bothered by it as I can just play it safe the next day to be right back where I was in terms of karma.
Overall though I give this game a glowing recommendation and thats high praise from me considering I almost have a disdain for indie sidescrollers at this point because of the over abundance of them.

Is it difficult to play? No! Is it difficult to survive? Not if you can think quickly. Is it difficult to progress? No, not if you're patient enough to learn from your mistakes and can bear some repetition to figure out how to overcome a challenge. Is Rain World rewarding to play? Absolutely!

The biggest gaming disappointment I've had to deal with in a long time.
As a Kickstarter backer I instantly fell in love with Rain World's animations, art and sound. It looked great 3 years ago and still does. It's an amazing look that echos Another World, Flashback and Prince of Persia but with more grit and something unique onto its own. Rather than explaining much to you the player is left to their own devices to figure out the world and its dangers, which is fine and works really well for a lot of titles and it suits this game well too. The game is a cohesive package that goes for minimalism but still has a lot of depth as well.
Sadly the game only looks and sounds good but the gameplay falls apart and is just a massive exercise in frustration. Foremost, the controls are not that great, the Slugcat controls really, really poorly. It's movements can also be quite random when it comes to going into holes or getting it to do what you want. The biggest issue I have with the controls is that ducking is a toggle, for what reason I don't know, but like every other 2D platformer where ducking is something you hold they went against the grain for no reason on this accord. This becomes frustrating because when you're crouched down you're noticeably slower and a lot of the time when you exit one of the many pipes that connect this massive world you're automatically placed into the crawling animation. In a game where death is a one shot deal, you need the character to be as limber as possible at all times. This is really annoying. The Slugcat can only throw horizontally left and right and you cannot aim at all, which coupled with the jaged terrain all over, leaves you missing most of your shots. Slugcat also has a terrible jump height, literally one of the lowest jumps I've seen in a platformer. While the game doesn't want you to jump over everything and wants you to climb the various pipes strewn about there's many times where a jump becomes more of a headache than anything else because your jump is so weak.
I'm not going to complain much about RNG and how it can lead to your deaths since that's half the fun of the game, but there ARE times where your death is incredibly cheap because you come out of pipe and right into the jaws of a creature that just happened to be there and you can't do a thing about it.
Lastly, and the biggest irritation of the game is it's "point" system. Across the world are hybernation rooms that are basically small bunkers that will keep Slugcat safe for the evening while the violent rain will kill everything outside and cause a giant flood. If you're outside during this you better hope that you're close enough to a save hybernation room to survive or you'll be dead as well. In order to use a save room the Slugcat needs to eat 4 smaller animals (bat like things) or fruit. These are usually easy to attain, so isn't not big of a worry but sometimes you just won't find anything to eat. After you eat and wait out the storm you'll gain a "point" or "rank." A small wheel with various symbols will rotate and change. These points won't give you any abilities, a higher jump or health to allow you to survive more than one bite. What they WILL do is open new doors in the world and allow you to explore further. However, upon death or even quitting the game when you're not in a save room will roll back you rank requiring you to farm food again just to hybernate and raise your rank. You will also lose any part of the map you uncovered since your last save which is irritating.
The game punishes you too heavily for death or even quitting the game in the middle of it incase life happens, a lot of the time I've spent with the game is regaining ranks and essentially wasting time in areas I've already seen. Over. And over. And over again. This isn't just about getting good, death is sometimes out of your control and the sloppy controls only add to the frustration. Hybernation rooms can also be incredibly far apart.
Ultimately I can't recommend Rain World to anyone except those with a lot of time on their hands and enjoy repetition while they feel like they're bashing their brains against the wall. I'm saddened with how the game turned out, this could have been amazing.

I'm curious if Rain World will find it's niche group and become one of those cult classic, brilliant super-challenging games that streamers play endlessly. I personally don't really have an opinion about the difficulty, because frankly I'm not into difficult games. So yeah, buy it and see for yourself :)

I guess you already know if you’re going to like this game but if you feel doubt after reading some of the reviews, let me remind you:
-The game is not that hard, it just requires an entirely different approach from what you’re probably accustomed to, think on how the Oddworld series or Alien: Isolation works, if you liked those games you will love Rain World.
-The controls are not bad, they just work different, they’re not janky or unresponsive at all (I’m looking at you The Swindle), they were designed for keyboard first, then for controllers, so don’t be afraid if you don’t have one.
-There’s very little hand holding, but all the important mechanics are organically explained if you pay attention. But then there’s always the internet so ask away, PCGamer already has an article with good tips for your journey.
-This game has a whopping 1600 screens and some of the areas are probably the most beautiful places you’ll ever visit on a videogame. The music is also top notch and the intro succeeded at making me feely even when Ori and the Blind Forest failed to.
-The karma system is ok, but some people (including me) have problems with the checkpoint placement, I would love it if there was checkpoints next to every gate.
-The karma system will tell you how hard is a place, if opening a gate requires a high karma symbol beware.
-This game commits the cardinal sin of having death pits that are very hard to distinguish from normal pits, it’s only on one area, in the “harder” part of the game, but it is a problem nonetheless.
-You can drop items without throwing them too far away with down + throw, you can also switch hands by double taping the grab button, you can also eat a non-edible item for use latter, just hold the grab button like you would to eat something and do it again to regurgitate.
-There’s a lot of small things that make the experience easier but I wouldn’t want them spoiled for me, so I won’t spoil them for you.
All in all I highly recommend this game as a unique experience that doesn’t just play it safe like so many others platformers (just this year we’ve had Hollow Knight and Owl Boy). This game is bold, fresh and truly innovative, but it also has some very rough edges… And yet it stands a much better chance of not just being remembered (and copied at nauseam) but also of deeply resonating with its core audience.
(At the time of writing this review I have probably 10 hours clocked with the game, I played offline at college, yes 7 hours, and yes I missed three classes)

One of the most interesting games I've ever played. Rain World plays differently to just about everything I can think of, and while I don't think it's a game for everyone, I do think it's a game that will receive more and more attention with the passage of time.
Play is divided into cycles, in which you wake up from hibernation, hunt or forage for food while avoiding predators, gradually uncover more of the map, and then go back to shelter and sleep again. The mechanic that makes the game so interesting to me is one that seems to be frustrating a lot of players- the karma system. Karma is a persistent resource that increases by one when you live through a cycle, and decreases by one when you die. In order to enter- or exit- different areas of the map, you have to have enough karma.
This can be seriously frustrating. If you find yourself in a difficult area, you can end up dying over and over- losing all of your karma- without actually making progress. Imagine a roguelike that gets harder every time you die! That's what Rain World can feel like sometimes.
But it starts to make a lot more sense the more you play. From moment to moment, your purpose as a player is not to explore the world and make progress, even though the game feels a lot like a metroidvania. Instead, it's about finding ways to survive- consistently. It's about finding enough food to make it through the day, and often, rather than running to a new shelter, you'll end up heading straight back to the place where you started the cycle.
And eventually, you get better at it. You start to understand the way the map fits together without having to look at it, you get a feel for what areas are dangerous, you can feel where the food is going to be this time- you start to actually understand the world from the point of view of an animal that lives in it, rather than a Samus Aran or an Alucard who just wants to move through it.
A few hours in, I found myself completely stuck in the Chimney Canopy area. I would wake up, throw myself into the world, and die, over and over. My karma was already at rock bottom- I didn't feel like I had anything to lose. But then I found a little golden flower- if you eat it, it protects your karma from decaying after a death. But only once. All of the sudden, that life mattered. I couldn't die, or I'd lose it. I knew I had to find food, I had to play safe, I had to get back to the shelter. And I did. And I did it again, and again, and again, until my karma was maxed out. That kind of experience- that kind of sudden rush of hope and overwhelming will to survive- I've never felt that in a game before.
There are also some obvious things to love about Rain World. The presentation is spectacular, the combination of intelligent AI and procedural animation makes the game look like a nature documentary, and the level design is quietly brilliant. But I think every review makes note of these, and you can see most of that for yourself just by watching the game.
If you're on the fence about buying Rain World, keep in mind that it's not a game for everyone. It is brutal and occasionally downright unfair, the karma system can be very frustrating, and checkpoints are few and far between. Pretty much every criticism reviewers have thrown at this game is well-founded, and if those throw you off, you may want to save your money. But if you give this game a chance, I think you'll find that it's not like anything you've ever played, and a lot of the frustrations people have with Rain World are rooted in the fact that the gaming community has never really seen anything like it.

People say enemies are too spongy? That's if you're playing on the harder difficulties, it's kind of the point. Playing on normal you will find some enemies spongey, but many small enemies dying in a predictably short (and glorious) fashion.

I can't wait to play more, I'm only stopping long enough to write this then I'm going back for more.
Flying Wild Hog, well done, now crank out some DLC, cause god damn, I'm gonna need more of this.
Update : First playthrough finished. Zero crashes. Only the most minor bugs encountered. They fixed most of them before I completed my first playthrough though (flickering textures).
I'm still having an absolute blast with this game. Now the fun is in getting all those left over achievements and finding all  the secrets I missed, as well as unique enemies and weapons.
The achivements list does a good job of showing you which unique enemies you've missed so it's not a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to find them.

Starts out strong, but sadly turns out to be a sub par sequel. All side quests take part on the same 3 or so maps slightly reshuffled, and even the short main story recycles levels. That story itself doesn't really hold up  either.
This game has some interesting weapons, but because of the stats, bullet sponge enemies, and combat system very few of them actually feel special while using them.
Coop quest progress doesn't count towards your single player game, although you do get to keep the found gear.
In the end I found myself getting bored, and this game has a borderlands pre sequal sort of meh vibe at best.

An overall fun platforming-action-puzzle-shooter.
I've played Mirror's Edge so I'm used to the old "dying and retrying" trial and error way the game works. You'll die, a lot. But it's mostly caused by bad grab/jump point marking on the developers part. If you go slow and are deliberate in your joystick movements you'll learn the mapping pretty well.
The combat system does get wonky when there are more then two enemies on the screen. I recommend equipping the right secondary gun for certain enemy types to help stun them to buy more time for dogging around. Shotgun up close to knock back quick movers or leapers helps.
The puzzles do not hold your hand in any way. If you need a hint you can look in the in-game journal but how you accomplish it is up to you to figure out. No detective vision here. But I found most puzzles to be fun and some were a blast to figure out.
The music was fantastic. Each environment had its own theme and the ques for any sort of action or discovery were always on point.
The story was good. I cant help feeling at the end of the game though that some key details were being left out. Or were rushed over in the story. In the end I didn't feel it concluded but wanted to tell me more and just, ran out of time.
I have played this game twice and got just as much fun out if it the second time as the first.

Mixed reveiw here. Gorgeous character, level design, and story. But slightly poor execution of the game. Handfull of bugs towards the end. I found myself dying more from falling b/c the game didn't recognize that I was facing a ledge completely and the jump looked plausible to make, but I fell to my death at the last moment because the camera kept shifting or because I kept getting randomly hit by Natla's fireballs. Solution to this problem would problably have to use a controller instead of a mouse to get the camera angles, straight. And another solution would have been to make being able to stun Natla from hitting you. The tutorials in game explain fairly wel how to run,jump, swim, climb, and shoot etc but the Head-shot mechanic could have been better implemented. It took me a bit to get used to looking at where my heatlh meter was as opposed to where my adrenaline meter was and I had to use Youtube to figure out how to properly use the mechanic The game's in-promptu moment weren't entirely clear to me when you could use it during the heat of battle.  But thanks to helpfull  gamers out there once I practiced it was a flawless tactic to use.
My last and particular thing though, that I will say about Underworld which gripes me beyond the simple glitches is the so called DLC that was released after the launch. Apparently after the game there's two continuing, chapters explaining more if not totally concluding the game in it's own right.After a little reasearch, apparently Crystal Dynamics had intensions of including the chapters but due to a small layoff of the deves, caused it to be DLC since Microsoft wasn't sure if the sales would cap. I've yet to find if there's a Steam port of these chapters. The ending by itself feels rushed and watered down compared to the other Tomb Raider's. There's no real explanation as to what happens to Lara, Amanda, Natla, and Croft manor when you escape Avalon. Not to mention there's no real showdown you get to have with ol' Natla who's impervious to any attack. That being said, it's a shame there wasn't better communication with the development and marking team during the release of this Tomb Raider cause it's got some really nice features that just could've been improved over time.
Overall 7.5/10

Finished first playthrough on the 3rd difficulty.
Pros
1. Its fast-paced, enganging combat with switching between ranged and melee, moving, jumping and dashing around quickly to avoid damage and its fun to do it.
2. Tons of weapons to play and customize with. That includes dual wielding, explosive ammo, charge shots, elemental effects and etc. And various weapons have different unique attribute.
3. Run's pretty well on a mid range GPU (GTX 960).
4. Environment graphics and level design is great. With various video settings to add some spice to the overall experience and tweak to your performance liking.
Cons
1. Cluttered loot system. Inventory drowned with weapon mod pickups, lack of item sorting thus everything is in a list and you need to go through them 1 by 1.
2. Finished in roughly 20 hours, I'd say it's rather short for a loot shooter type of game similar to borderlands. Eventhough the first Shadow Warrior is roughly at the same playtime, the game should have more end game features like for example endless horde survival, arcade mode and so forth.
3. Despite environment graphics looks good, the models does not. Models texture looks blurry and not stylized like most of the 2016 titles, body parts clipping, thus not much immersion to the overall experience.
4. Lack of boss fights variety compare to the first Shadow Warrior. This one is sort of a disappointment.
It was said that there will be content updates soon. Will update more after trying out.
For now, do I recommend people buying this?
If you love loot shooters, dashing around like a ninja and hacking enemies to pieces with your melee weapons or blowing up enemies with many ranged weapons. Then yes.
If you prefer a story driven shooter like the previous title, with no fuzzling with items and loots, better character design and development, more enemy and bosses variety, then it's a no.
If you're somewhat in between, I recommend getting it on a sale. Although the full price it offers isn't as expensive as AAA titles.

So, i just finished Shadow Warrior 2. I played on Insane difficulty and ended with lvl 27.
Gameplay
Combat system is pretty good. It works as intended and its extremely satisfying. But the thing i came to hate is the bullet sponge. On Insane difficulty everything is insanely tanky, making it sometimes even more frustrating than satisfying. Also mobs with random generated stats. Sometimes the game generates an extremely powerfull npc, which is killing you on 1 or 2 hits. And the only thing you can do is either avoid it or go through extremely painfull fight. Basically NPCs can generate stats countering all of your weapon's stats. Making you switch the upgrades to be even able to do some DMG. Frustrating.
The thing i found the most ridiculous is how easy bosses are in this game. Boss fight is much easier than a fight with NPC with OP stats. Boss fights are literally only about dodging to one side and shooting, while dodging. Nothing more. Even more sad thing is that there are 4 bossfights and 2 of them are with the same boss....
Loot system
Ridiculous. You have upgrades and with them you upgrade your weapons. On Insane difficulty you are forced to do it, unless you want to bullet "spongeness" to be even more painfull. Every weapon has 3 slots and the only purpose of upgrades is to select the one with the most DPS stats. Thats all. Upgrade system is pain in the♥♥♥♥♥and it shouldn't be here in the first place.
Weapons
There is a lot of weapons and i found all of them interesting in some way. So in that aspect the game is pretty good.
Crafting system
This has to be a joke. You can't even call this "Crafting system". This whole system is based on combination of 3 mods and getting 1 mod of higher lvl with RANDOM stats. Thats it. Nothing more, nothing less.
Soundtrack
In this aspect the game is perfect. Soundtrack is extremely fitting, making the fights more bearable and satisfying.
Story/Characters/Humor
Dunno how others. But i found this story very cliche and its characters plain. The ending was as open as it could be. I didn't like any characters except Lo Wang. Even Wang's jokes became more and more boring as the story progressed. This game isn't about story, but still SW1 had at least likeable characters, here i couldn't find any.
Enviroment
Absolutly, utterly terrible. It felt like i was running through 4 maps 5+ times over and over again. I heard this game is procedurally generated and well, it looks like it in the game. Some maps look identical, or so it seemed like that to me. This game should've been hand made.
Technical issues
Don't buy this game. Wait for it to be fixed. When i tried to start this game for the first time, i couldn't even start it. I had to look up for fixes on google. In the end i fixed it, but still... Then during my playthrough i got stuck in fence or walls. And had to restart the whole mission, because going back to town and back to mission didn't work. Making me even more frustrated. Then at some point of the game i couldn't load my save and had to restart several times before it started working.
Overall
If you like Borderlands, can bear a horrible upgrade/crafting system and can get over technical issues, buy this game. Oherwise don't buy this game. Even though the technical side of combat system is perfect, the horrible bullet sponge/OP NPCs are ruining the whole experience. Soundtrack is godlike, but it isn't good enough to save this game. This game may be worth 10-20$, but 30+$ is too much for what you get.

Amnesia: The Dark Descent is a great game for all the horror players out there, it is very atmospheric, and has you on the edge of your seat for the entirety of the game. People who don't like the concept of running and hiding, and rationing your supplies should NOT get this game, but for the people who do, this is a must have.
One of the best horror games you can play.

If you're a fan of the survival horror genre, get this game. Amnesia came out just as that genre of video games was really building in popularity, and it did a damn good job of kicking it off with a bang.
Amnesia borrows a lot of the successful elements from the Penumbra series (made by the same company), but it easily stands on its own. The survival-horror elements in Amnesia are really quite well done; the atmosphere in the game is some of the most interesting and genuine I've experienced, and it really pairs extremely well with the fascinating and unique story that begins to unravel as you delve deeper into Castle Brennenburg. I won't elaborate on the story, but it, combined with the atmosphere, made for one of my all time favorite game experiences.
Enemy ecounters are scripted, and while this does limit the game to about two really good playthroughs, it does work quite well while the experience is still fresh. Even still, Amnesia's fairly unique "phychological horror" approach has won this game over most other in the horror genre; instead of a steady stream of jump scares and gory imagry, Amnesia goes another path and lets players look into the darkness, imagine what's in there, and sometimes struggle to find out if it's real or not. The first hour of the game involves the player exploring the castle, solving puzzles, and gaining an introduction to the story - that's it, but it works remarkebly well, because as you look into a dark room you expect something to be there, even if it's not. This only makes the real encounters all the more frightening. Beyond that, you are defenseless in the game, weak, and all you can do is hide, which brings in the sanity system.
One of the more interesting aspects of the game is your sanity meter. There are several light sources in the game (you have a lantern that uses scarce fuel, and tinderboxes to light stationary torches), but light is not always your ally. In order to hide from the enemies in the game, you must remain in the darkness, but stay in the darkness too long and your sanity will deteriorate. As your sanity goes down, your character begins to hallucinate, the environments change, your vision and motor skills deteriorate, and it becomes easier for you to be spotted. This is a very unique gameplay element, and I wish more games in the genre used similar systems.
Even once the scripted encounters render the main game stale, you're not nearly out of luck. Frictional Games allows players access to a free level editor, and there is now a good community with custom stories, which are downloadable "levels" that can be accessed from the main menu of the game. These have made Amnesia's replay value tremendous. Some of these user created addons are quite lengthy, and actually surpass the main game in their quality.
If you're a fan of horror games, Amnesia is arguably one of the best out there. Plug in your headphones, turn the lights off, and enjoy (or crap your pants).

Darksiders remains one of the criminally underrated games I've ever played. Sure, it is a little too sluggish to be a full-blown slasher, the platforming is not especially inspired, and the plot is very standard.
But the devil is in the execution.
Combat feels just solid enough to believe we control a 9ft tall god of war who rips monsters apart with his bare hands, and the combos are visually pleasing. The traversal and platforming are clear, leave little doubt where to go and fully use the gadgetry we collect throughout the game. And the plot? It's very well voice-acted, the world is interesting and creative.
Visually, the designs are very vivid, created by one of the more distinctive comic artists of modern era.
Overall Darksiders are a great game I love coming back to, even if just for a moment.

The first banyon of hope amidst the onslaught torrent of Minecraft / WURM clones, "Life is Feudal" stands out -a beacon of fury- weathering the early access storm, fighting the gale with stern resolve.  Dungeon mastereque parameter settings for the world, plus the promise of modding, shows the trust the devs have in their player community allowing unprecedented control or troll terror chaos.  The servers are similar to "Neverwinter Nights" in that each is uniquely dangerous.  It is clear that default craft timers were not built for a solo experience without epic struggle, as status determines many harvesting / crafting / building times.  Menus & protocol are sensible.  The music is pleasant.  The natural pace of the game is such that (at first) the player may wish to multitask, & always can.. provided they are safe.  As the game builds, this is no longer true, with survival taking up every moment.  Banning together is vital to success in so much as each character will possess stats vital to your defense against others.  "Life is Feudal" stands far above any of the horror-survival zombie-box games, making the terror not about PVE, but about what is truly frightening:  real players.    A beautiful day on your farm can turn into a viking raid party holiday in moments.  From Zen to War in less that 60 seconds... & back again.  This is what WURM should have become.  The Minecraft kids whom were into raiding, looting, & PVP will find a natural home here, a logical progressing from their all but decimated survival servers.
POTENTIAL GREATNESS ABOUNDS.

Quake IV is a almost 10 year old FPS that still holds up quite well today. The core gameplay is quite linear and baisic, but it does make up for this with some excellent shooting mechanics thanks to the briliance of the Doom 3 engine, each ounce of lead (or lighting, or dark matter, or nails, etc.) you pump into enemies feels satisfying. Couple that on top of the wide enemy variety (complete with bosses), the very diverse set of weapons you find (with upgrades too!) and ragdoll effects on enemies that never quite get old, you got yourself a very entertaining shooter at it's core.
Now as for everything else:
Level design: Probably the next best thing about this game, while quite linear, it does provide a very good sense of atmosphere with the
♥♥♥♥ed up things around you. The lighthing and effects of the game really do help you feel like you're in a very bad place. I can't say much more without spoiling it, but expect to feel uncomfortable with places that make you go "What the ♥♥♥♥ is THAT?" or "That's seriously ♥♥♥♥ed up.", and belive me, you will have a ton of those moments.
Soundtrack: It's okay, nothing really special about it, the soundtrack fits the moments I guess, but you'll be too busy kicking♥♥♥♥♥that you'll forget what's playing in the background.
Story: Also not much to say about it, you are a marine that has to kill aliens and destroy thier main base to save the earth, something happens in the middle of it but that doesn't stop you from kicking♥♥♥♥♥and saving the world.
I'd also like to note that the moment around the middle of the game
leave you remembering it for the rest of you life.
Graphics: You'd think it would look particularly bad thanks to the game being 10 years old, but with the engine it was made on, this is far from the case, while it is low in polygon count compared to newer games, it has much better lighting and particle effects then most of the games I've played, that's very good considering it's age. Look up screenshots of the game on max settings or play it yourself on max and you'll see what I mean.
Misc: Voice acting is good, nothing spectacular. Game has little or no replay value due to it being linear, however there are plenty of mods that offer new campaigns and levels that should keep you going if you want more.
Overall I give Quake IV a 8.5/10, it's excellent at what it does. Anybody looking for a amazing fps with it's own unique identity must check this game out, if they do not mind  the baisic and linear "kill anything that moves" style that comes with it

Remember:- life is feudal!
Positives:- LiF:YO caters to a wide range of interests.  Ever wanted to be a town planner in medieval Europe?  Love farming simulation but kinda feel like a cheat sitting in a John Deere?  Fascinated by the history of feudal times and want to live it just a little?  Know the theories of Marx, Durkheim, and Weber and are interested in the sociological concepts of individualism and collectivism and want to try living in an age with a whole other mindset?  Or just love gearing up in metal stuff and hitting people with swords?  You will enjoy this game.
Negatives:- This is where it gets hard.  Having played over 1000 hours before making this review.  just about all the things that I would have seen as a negative have improved or been fixed altogether.  The dev team has been brilliant, and if they keep delivering like they have, LiF:YO will go from being a great Alpha to a fantastic release.  Anyone who wrote a review not recommending the game essentially because it is Alpha should do the honest thing and try the game out again, then adjust their review if the problems they experienced have lessened or gone away.
Gameplay:-  The most important thing to get right playing this game is to play it with other people.  Seriously.  If I had a thin leather for every player I've seen try to solo this game, and after a day or three depart forever leaving nothing but a tiny plaster shack, a furnace, and some unfinished wattle fencing, I'd have enough to armor 100 novice archers.  Remember, life is feudal.  In feudal times the average serf lived within spitting distance of at least a dozen other average serfs.  "Ah!" I hear you say; "serfing isn't for me, I'll be a Lord or at least someone rich enough to own flanged mace!".  Sure, in which case you'll need to be around even more people.  Coz heres the thing ok, Life is Feudal is about feudal life.  You ain't going to build any legends or awesome stories on your own.  Join a community, build a community, invite your friends, make new ones, whatever it takes, play this game with as many other people as you can.
What could be improved:-  We're still waiting on a number of important features to be added, but LiF developers have been consistent in delivering updates and have issued a time frame for key updates to come.  In terms of adding to gameplay, all I'd suggest is added variation to life events.  Given there is no specific end game, interest in the game comes through experiencing different things.  Therefore the game is improved through increased variation of features and of random events.  Weather could have more influence on a range of gameplay aspects, illness (and alchemical medicines) could be introduced, random OP animals, NPCs in distress, custom weapons crafting, random disasters, and above all anything that enhances group-oriented and co-dependent play.  Why is there no specific end game?  Because this is about life... is... feudal, remember?

Been playing the last few evenings, finished it last night.
Gameplay wise it's a nice change of pace to say Prey or Skyrim, which I've been playing lately. Nice cel-shaded style game, reminiscent of Zelda's Wind Waker game, but that's where the comparison ends really. There's no combat whatsoever, and where there are threats, it's quite clear how to avoid/deal with them.
Puzzles are relatively intuitive, if at times a little simple, but not tedious - there's no pointless repetition.
There are four stages/chapters and an epilogue of sorts that are quite clearly delineated in terms of theme, and quite clearly so once you've finished the game and find out the names for the chapters.
As there's no dialogue whatsoever, apart from a little tension in the second chapter, until that final chapter everything's pretty chill and cheerful, it's only the glimpses of the story through murals and hidden "keyholes" throughout the game. The end of the final chapter however, and the epilogue were to me a kick in the guts. It was quite impressive how much the devs could portray without a single word.
On the technical side there's a few complaints, not the best optimised game I've played lately (had to turn down a few settings, whilePrey was a lot smoother on my rig with all settings maxed out, and seemingly more a technically demanding game) but for an indie game I guess that's not unexpected. Only had major slowdowns once partway through the first chapter as a distant building was being rendered and the occasional stutter that I'm used to seeing in most games I play - a 9 year old Mac Pro with a GTX 960 somehow keeps up pretty well at 2560x1080 in my opinion. Performance might be different on consoles.
Recommendations for this game are tough - for the most part it's a pretty enjoyable game, especially as an intro to gaming for a kid, but that ending might be a little much for some, but maybe that's because it hit home for me if I were in that situation (writing this review with my 16month old on my lap)

RiME is a weird mix of puzzles, platforming and storytelling, that appears to fit together, but always has a few gaps where you can spot the flaws.

Text:
the big bad here is twofold: Performance is.. spotty. While I personally have had few issues, those few I've had make me do a double take when the game stutters for a moment, or FPS suddenly get halved mid-platforming segment. Quite annoying to say the least.
That said, I was fully enthralled by the games art-style, that mostly reminded me of a world ripe for exploring and sightseeing - and that fits to a T. With the games vista, locations, canyons and caverns all around inviting you to look, but often not to touch.
The games puzzles are a bit of a mixed bag - enjoyable if you view them as an experience, and less if you view them as a challenge to overcome, as they are not very challenging at all. Each can be solved in a pretty straight forward manner when you figure out the games moon logic demands.
Further, while this is an enjoyable experience, if a bit of a mixed bag - the real enjoyment of the game comes from the way the story culminates. Provides bits and pieces hidden around the levels that all come to a head from seeming nowhere and tie every note together immensely well.
While not a challenging game, its an immensely enjoyable story and gameplay experience.

Is the current version of this game worth $40?
In a word? ... no
but it has the potential to be. So if you have the $40 bucks to spend on the possibility of this game being awesome then by all means spend the money and support the devs. just be aware it is a gamble and if it pays off you will already have the game upon release.
The developers have stated frequently they want to continue developing this game no matter what and thus far I have seen few reasons to doubt them. What they have so far though is a start and a lot of work to finish to be released Q3 2015 which I do not see happening seeing as the alpha has so many features untested such as:
-guild system (number 1 for a reason)
-ability to burn towns, destroy buildings etc.!!!!!!
-horse mastery
-build seige engines ... you can build the workshop
-potion usage (you can make potions but are unable to drink them currently)
-shifting terrain from tunneling to terraforming or vice versa
-crafting balance
-weapons balance
-various skills and special moves etc
At this stage of the game the worst armor for protection (padded) is also the most difficult to make due to the limitations of farming flax. Whole fields of this stuff (100's of plots) plowed, fertilized, harvested, tanned, spun and then loomed (days of work) deosn't give you enough cloth to make 1 piece of armor .... as opposed to leather which is almost as free in its movement and offers better protection can be made quitre easily in an hour or 2 as can plate, scale etc.
That is just one example of balancing issues needing to be made in the limited version of the game that is thus far playable. There are many others ... not the least of which is combat. Right now there is no reason to level up anything other than leather and bows (which means you have to level up slings /cringe) but once you and your friends get there no one can fight you. A 100 quality royal plate wearing, shield using beast can be easily kited out and killed in only 4-5 shots by a bow user who doesnt get scratched. The plate and/or shield should offer more protection imho and don't even get me started on item quality ... or the difficulty of mining granite (I single handedly built a keep just about) but I digress.
Now that I have loaded up the bad news .... the many things this game has going for it are varied, and individually they are good reasons to support the devs. Putting them all together is why I will recommend this game despite the negatives listed above.
-character customization via attributes and skills. There are so many ways to make a useful character within the proposed skill cap it's actually kind of daunting. The complexity is mind blowing.
-terraforming (I know it is a grind but the terrain flexibilty is awesome)
-variety of buildings/structures to be made .... they actually have so many they need a better way of organizing it.
-the immersion into the seamless world ... or in this case, island
-real time combat
-ability to use strategies and build accordingly with the flexibility of the sandbox
-the need for friends ... while not strictly necessary, it is an MMO and life is feudal. Having friends makes things more enjoyable. Many mmo's these days obfuscate that point. Not here. It's in the title.
-limitations are what you expect them to be ... for the midievil times.
I would highly recommend convincing some friends to make a village with you.

So far I've really enjoyed Rain World. It's incredibly unforgiving, to a very frustrating degree sometimes, and I can understand why that could turn some people off, however I love for that feeling of satisfaction when you finally get past that incredibly difficult area, and I'd say it's rather similar to Abe's Oddysee in that regard.
You really are dropped in the deep end, the tutorial will show you the basic moves, what to eat and how to find shelter but aside from that everything else is up for you to discover. Which is nice for the whole new experience feel, but it leads to a lot of trial and error (I still don't have a clue what causes a Scavenger to become aggressive and sometimes I get slugcat to do a real fast cartwheel which I can never seem to replicate.)
The controls can be a little sensitive at times, you need to be very careful with the trigger or you will go tumbling off a ledge, usually at the worst possible moment, and the movement of slugcat can be a tad unpredictable; I somehow always end up making slugcat go backwards through tunnels, though this can be fixed by holding "a", it takes a few moments which is a death sentence if you're evading a lizard. But once you've mastered the controls you can pull off some really nice moves to escape the variety of creatures chasing you.
Combat is a tad awkward which actually works quite well, it encourages you to flee rather than try to fight the monsters head on, and as you are near the bottom of the foodchain I'd say that makes sense. The few times I use stones and spears was in an attempt to draw attention or hinder the enemy, not kill them.
There is a form of skill progression in the game, I'm not entirely certain if the different trees are unlocked from the beginning as I only achieved my first lizard kill very very late into the game. But carrying out different tasks, such as only eating fruits, will progress you in a specific tree and then once you've completed the tree you can get a "passage", which you can use to move slugcat to any shelter you've been to.
I think the standout feature of the game is the fact that you do feel like you're part of a huge ecosystem and it can lead to really exciting encounters. You might be in the middle of running away from a huge green lizard when a vulture swoops down to your rescue, only to be eaten by something you originally mistook for a pole. You can distract the vultures by running into a group of scavengers and hope that it takes one of those instead. A huge centipede blocking your path? Lure a lizard to follow you and hopefully they'll take it out for you.
Despite it's flaws I still think Rain World was definitely worth backing and I've had a great time with it so far. Yes it can be very frustrating and if you don't want to be seriously challenged I would say this probably isn't the game for you. But I really really love it and if it wasn't for the fact I need to sleep I would probably still be playing.

Game is great so far. There is a strong element of RNG that does detract from the skill-based gameplay, and the controls are sluggish. The difficulty is pretty brutal and checkpoints are spread far apart. The game does not hold your hand and is absolutley beautiful.
The feeling of surviving in an opressive world is captured beautifully. Slugcat is just another cog in the ecosystem, the difficulty combined with the vast, open world makes for exhilirating gameplay. Your heart will be pumping when a vulture partially rams it's head into your hiding hole. Or when the sky becomes grey and the ground begins to shake as you frantically attempt to recall where the nearest hibernation chamber is.
One thing I want to really gloss over is the AI. Each individual creature has it's own personality. Some predators will be more persitant and viscious than others. A wounded lizard will be more cautious of you in the future.  All NPCs on a given run will be actively living their lives as Slugcat attempts to survive, hunting, scavenging and having territorial disputes.
I will update this review in due time, but for now all I can say is buy it if you can stand the difficulty, and are a sucker for atmosphere and world-building.

Alrighty then. I'm giving Duke Nukem Forever a "conditional" thumbs-up and by conditional I mean get it if it's on sale for five bucks. If you buy this for $20 you'll most likely be kinda sad but at $5 it's pretty great. If you are familiar with the previous games in the Duke Nukem series this one is the same old story. Sex crazed aliens invade the planet and steal all our women. It's up to you to wipe out the space vermin while saving hookers and strippers from unpleasant deaths. There is nothing new or inventive on this one as far as the gameplay is concerned. Gunning your way through each area is linear and there aren't any well hidden secrets or divergent levels to explore. It's fairly straightforward as far as first person shooters go, but I really dig the junior-high school humor and trashy one-liner jokes throughout Duke Nukem Forever. As Duke you can enjoy a beer, take a pull off a cigar, blow away some green skinned intergalactic perverts, and slap a few bOobz along the way. It just doesn't get much better than that. The raunchy dialogue and huge b00bies everywhere made me laugh and made up for some of the dull aspects of gameplay.

I was so stressed out because whenever I would pick up a block and try to set it down it would fly hundreds of feet in random directions. So I was reading some tech support forums and found that some people were saying that if they turned the graphic settings or anti aliasing all the way up, it seemed to help but not cure the issue. This got me thinking. Maybe it has to do with framerate?
I usually display my framerate in an OSD with a monitoring app and realized that I was getting hundreds of frames per second even with the graphics and AA settings maxed out. So I started experimenting with VSYNC. This fixed the issue.
Turn on VSYNC to solve most playability issues.

Shadow Warrior 2 is a slick first person shooter / looter hybrid that fuses the sites & sounds from Doom & Painkiller, trash talk from Duke Nukem & role playing from Boarderlands. You'll get to explore a stunningly detailed underworld whilst rampaging through your foes using the bullet, bomb or the blade with blood splattering pace as you go. Ignore the daft dialogue & non-existant narrative because this is a game of carrying out errands that usually involve dispatching various villians & collecting valuables. The thumping 80's era rock & traditional oriental soundtrack really works well which breathes life to the whole gameplay experience. Of all the FPS's on the market these days, few match the satisfaction you'll get from it's gore & a combat system that never feels tiresome, you'll be rewarded to a variety of wild outlandish weapons on offer & useful loot that boost your character stats in various ways. So, if you're looking for a game thats fast, brutal, yet fun ... you've found it.

This game is a barrage of nonsense. A good kind of nonsense. The AI is great, the creatures act like they're supposed to (♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ly), and the humans act like how they're supposed to (more or less intelligent). However, there are some drawbacks.
PROS:
+The game is set in a beautiful world, the environment is great, the reflections are realistic and the voice acting is fine. +The controls are superb and even moving around is enjoyable.
+The swordplay is basically perfect, definitely better than any other game I have played in my lifetime.
+The gunplay is great and hearing your shotgun blow a person's head off really is a treat. Not to mention, every weapon is unique and there are tons!
+The creatures are detailed and the stronger creatures are fun to fight against.
+The jokes (although mostly crude) are great and don't get boring.
+The music is top-notch.
+The optimization is almost perfect (much like MGSV's but with more options). I'm running on a GTX 1070 and my FPS rarely went below 100.
+ Weapon models are gorgeous.
+Upgrading your weapon is easy.
+There's a great skill tree.
CONS:
-All of the human character models are not good. Much like Fallout 4, the characters are bland and need refining, while the world is beautiful.
-Multiplayer is buggy and doesn't have a ping indicator.
-Some of the voice acting sounds bad and/or doesn't sync with the mouths of the characters.
-The story is mediocre, but not a chore by any means.
-Some gun sounds aren't as good as the others.
-VSync doesn't work properly (from my experience)
