After completing the main storyline and exploring all the different planes I'm going to write an honest review. Unlike the majority of the reviews on here I actually enjoyed this game, putting in almost 17 hours since release. I'll go through a few positives and negatives:
- Clunky, touch optimized interface
- Grindy nature of collecting all the cards
- A small subset are premium cards, which you need to buy 14 booster packs to unlock
- Forces you to pick a deck at the start without knowing any of the cards, then restricts all customization options until you beat the first plane
- Most of the starter decks are borderline unplayable
+ Full deck customization i.e. you can make a deck using any of the 976 cards
+ Premium cards aren't any more powerful than the normal cards
+ Limits each deck to 1 of any mythic, 2 of any rare, 3 of any uncommon and 4 of any common card, so people that have just bought all the cards don't have as much of an advantage
+ Multiplayer mode is very fun
As you can see there are a lot of negatives for this game. The most frustrating part for me was they should either give you the option to change your deck after you've beaten the tutorial with it, or tell you that your choice was final and you won't ever be able to change it again. Luckily the deck I chose was strong enough to beat the campaign with, but if I'd have been stuck with a garbage deck from the start it would make progressing through the campaign to unlock decent cards almost impossible. You don't get a large enough range of cards to make any actual other types of decks until you've pretty much completed the campaign mode unless you get lucky through boosters.
Overall I found the game very fun since I didn't have any problems completing the campaign, and the grind to unlock the cards wasn't that bad for me. I'm really enjoying the large variety of fun decks you can make on this game, and trying them out against people online is very fun. I haven't spent anything more than the original asking price and am having just as much fun competing with people online as I do with the deck's I've spent 100's on MTGO. Of course the game only contains a finite number of cards so the online meta will get figured out soon enough and the game will become stale and boring, but until then I'm getting a lot of value out of the small purchase price.

Let me start out by saying I am in general a big fan of Magic and the Duels of the Planeswalkers games. But this is by far the worst DotP game, and there is a few reasons for that:
First of all we need to address the menu controls. DotP games have always had clunky and annoying menu's and they seem to get worse every year. You have to scroll through pictures and every time you click on something the menu fades in and out instead of just going to the desired submenu, which gets very tiresome in the long run. There is also small annoying problems like how you play games to unlock boosters, and when you open a booster and get your new nice cards you can go into your deckbuilder from the booster-unlock menu, but you can't go back into the campaign from the deck builder menu, so everytime you unlock one card you want to add to your deck you have to navigate through all the menus again to get back into a game. And with the fade-in and fade-out this gets extremely annoying.
There's also the fact that the decks are bad. Now now, hear me out, I know that the starting decks in DotP are always bad, but never like this. I had to complete around 60% of the campaign (Around the end of Ravnica) before I unlocked my first Mythic from a random booster, and it was green while I play U/R.
In this game you get to create your own decks which is great and works rather well, but what they don't tell you is that you have to farm boosters (unlocked through 'exploring the planes' aka doing challenges and mini-encounters) and the boosters are completely RNG, so either you play a very underpowered deck or a very overpowered deck. I think this is rather sad since DotP is meant to teach new players Magic and be a casual game for us older Magic players, and a steady balance in all the decks was what made that playstyle work. In previous games the decks were balanced off each other, here it's all RNG.
And when it comes to the AI... oh boy... You remember how in the elder games it felt like AI's drew exactly the right cards at exactly the right time? Yeah, here that becomes a normality.
All in all it's still a DotP deck but I wonder if the 10euro+extras won't be better off just creating a Magic Online account and get a deck started there. This feels like playing Magic Online with draft decks, so I would rather recommend the real deal.

Kudos to developers for building something unique, but the death system and inability to tune the punishment after it ruined my experience.
In Rain World, you play as a small animal, slugcat, which got separated from his family (pack?). Wander through post-apocalyptic world, where you are both a hunter and a prey. Avoid larger animals that try to hurt you and try to gather fruit / smaller animals for you to sustain yourself. I really had high hopes for the game and tried to like it. Admittedly, it gave a lot of reasons to do that.
•	Great post-apocalyptic styled graphics, amazing backgrounds
•	Amazingly, responsive controls
•	Immersive ambient sounds that create a unique atmosphere
•	Cool innovative style, which tries to mimic a real eco-system. To add to that, it is somewhat supplemented with a physics mode, where bodies behave according to the in-game laws of physics
•	Vast world to explore
But after 3 hours of playing, I had to throw in the towel. What went wrong? Obviously a game like this must be a no-brainer to pick? For me, what spoiled the fun is terrible punishment for death with no way to cancel it. Here’s how the game “levelling” system works: the level is not written explicitly, but every time you rest, there’s a symbol that “bumps” upward. To enter some areas, they require that symbol to be at the certain height (that’s why I call it level). You gain levels by catching lesser animals (sometimes spread through different rooms). To gain one level, you need to get 4 types of food and then find the resting place. Sounds reasonable and fair so far. The catch is: whenever you die, you lose one level.
Bear in mind, I don’t mind the unforgiving combat / hunting difficulty, because it fits the harsh world perfectly. The hunt and hide mechanics are nothing short of excellent and they throw you in a world where the tides can change in a second: at first you hunt, then you become the prey. There’s just this anti-pattern of game design that grinded my gears: heavily punishing the player for death in a game that requires player to explore, meet lots of dangers and actually die quite a lot (from developer’s press release: “Rain World is truly a brutal place, and it is important to accept that death is an inevitable part of life.”). Well, I could accept it if it did not have this way of punishing me with repetitive grind for food in order to get to where I was (and probably lose it again). That’s where frustrations began and fun ended.
It could be easily fixed: add an “easy” mode option that does not take the level upon death and I’m sure I’d enjoy the game more. But since there’s no such thing – the game really became a repetitive experience with focus on mostly hunting the same stuff instead of exploring the world (due to the risk of losing everything). If you like incredibly punishing games – get it, you won’t be disappointed, because the gameplay execution is actually great. If you hate the feeling of losing your hard-earning level progress once you die (and then repetitively grinding to get it back) – this game is not for you.
Again, I loved the rest of the game, but I have no idea how this level punishment came through and what was intended with it (if there’s a comment from developer: I’ll gladly publish it beneath the review; I don’t mind being wrong – I actually want to be wrong this time, because I want to like this game). It absolutely killed the experience. I don't think the game should be dumbed down, but an option to disable death penalty (i.e. "easy mode" where you don't get any achievements) would come in handy. At this point - I can not recommend the game unless you are a fan of super-punishing games.

I respect a lot of aspects of this game.  The production is pretty nice, the visuals are great, and the animations of all the creatures look really good.  Also go into this understanding what this game is, it's a "cinematic platformer".  Not a Metroidvania. The problem for me is that the game isn't fun to play at all due to a mixture of weird controls and bad design choices which try to mask itself under the guise of challenge.  Hopefully I can explain what will probably be a minority opinion on the game.
Now before you flame me as a "Filthy Casual" or whatever else, I'm a twitch streamer who has spent thousands of hours playing "I Wanna be the Guy" fangames, I have also deathless Super Meat Boy cotton alley.  I've probably forgot harder things than most people will ever see, but I also recognize the difference between legitimate challenge and fake challenge created by silly design.  The thing about challenge is that good challenge is rooted is a sense of fairness and good controls in platformers.  That's why games like Meatboy work, and this game falters.
The game basically has you going through these platforming areas which look stunning, and forces the player to rush to the next save point before the rain arrives and insta-kills your character.  The entire rushing aspect alone is kind of silly given that you are running through these areas blind trying to frantically find a save point.  It's just not the fact that you have to find a save point, but even if you do get there in time, you need to pay a cost in food to save.  Sometimes there just isn't enough time to get to the save and find the food you need, and in a few cases where the stages were fairly linear, there just wasn't any at all.  This creates a needless level of frustration for no other purpose than to make the game harder just for the sake of it, without any thought to the design.
There is also a level of RNG to a lot of the aspects of the game, that when layered on top of the other things, just sucks whatever fun could be in the game right out.  Monsters that hunt you can appear in random places each time you try to replay a stage.  They kill you in a single hit, which is fine.  What is not fine is when they either spawn right at the entry of a new room and instantly kill you with no chance of counter-play, or spawn on the only path to the next save while the clock is ticking to the next rain storm.  The cool things about this part of the game is you get to see some interesting and dynamic situations with the creatures, but that joy is quickly gone when the RNG essentially robs you of any chance to progress because you appeared on top of an RNG placed baddie after the transition to the next room.
The controls for me were another source of frustration.  The character can't jump very high at all, and the only way to jump far is to crouch first, then press jump to perform a "pounce".  The problem with this is that some of these required long jumps have to be done from either a small platform or at the very edge of one.  Pressing down in these situations causes the character to climb down from the edge instead of ducking, thus dropping you into pits causing massive retracing of your route or into death.
Another aspect of frustration isn't so much the fact that when you die, you return to the previous save, or that parts of the map you discovered since are wiped, or the fact that time gets rolled back one day.  It's the fact that there are doors that can only be passed if you are on certain days.  So early in the game there's a door that only opens on the 4th day, so the more you die, the more you have to wait for that door to open.  This means you need to spend days gathering food before the rain comes each day, because the only way to advance forward a day is to save, which costs food.  If you get past the door and die before you can find a save, you are back to gathering food again, so you can save, so you can advance a day, so the door can open one more time.  It's just layers of bad design like this that make the game feel super tedious.
I haven't been following this game for years like some others around here, so I'm not emotionally invested in the hype of the game.  I suspect my opinion of the game will probably be a minority point of view, but I feel this game could have been amazing if it were not for some of these design choices.  Who knows, maybe underneath all of this, there's a massive and amazing game to be found, I'm just not patient enough to deal with the design to see it.  Maybe you will.

First let's get this out of the way: This game takes time and is quite a slow paced game. And expecting otherwise and getting this game will be entirely on you, because it's very much said to be right off the bat :P
Now, with that said, we can talk about the game itself. I think this game is at a great start for early development, and the potential is phenominal. I've easily no lifed this game (No really... I got the achievment and everything.) and am still looking forward to playing more. It mixes RPG and Sandbox surprisingly well, making them both interdependent on one another. You need to level skills to build, and you need to build to level skills. Then there's the fact that other than using prefab structures, you get to design everything else to your liking. You decide how big or small your settlement or even castle will be, given if you're willing to put the time and effort into finishing it. This game won't be for those who like to get right in on the action, and if that's your cup of tea, I don't advise expecting it to be so. Though I will still suggest it, because you never know. This game makes you feel like it's the simulator that it is.
If I could change anything about this game, it would be the green bar. But I'd change it to something they already plan to replace it with, metagames; something to keep you occupied and alert instead of staring blankly at a loading bar. There are a few bugs here and there, though I can't remember examples since I haven't played in a while, but I know there was. And that's to be expected, it's early alpha. VERY EARLY. It really is obnoxious to see how many kiddies whine about bugs or the fact that it's not done in some areas, because it's exactly that; early alpha development. It's like wanting a diamond out of graphite; It's not, but in time it can be. But I digress, this game is still fairly polished compared to other alphas, some even that are near beta.
You will also find this game is NOT to be played alone, for extended periods of time. While it can be done, it's soon apparent that you'll need friends to aide you in your endeavours. So, get your guild/steam group/clan ready and get to work!
So concluding my review, I'll rate it on categories:
Bugs(Expected to change as it's developed): (few crashes, nothing else that's game breaking) 7/10
Graphics(doesnt effect overall rating, but some people play for graphics): 10/10 (If you have the rig to support the graphics on max)
Optimization: 8/10
Replayablility: 9/10
NewUserFriendliness: (Not going to lie, this game requires out of game sources to actually get the ball rolling.) 5/10
Potential: 10/10
Update Frequency: 7/10
Overall Rating: 8/10
*EDIT: So I forgot to take into account the sheer price of the game. If this is your kind of game, it will be worth every penny spent. However, if you don't know what you're getting into and don't like it, then you may find you're out $40.

I bought RIME on day 1, and I like RIME so far. I'm up to the point where I'm trying to get past the Roc and find a key (I think). The kid in RIME reminds me of Ico (the "B" side of Shadow of the Colossus). To me, the music seems more appropriate for an elevator, but I guess it fits the ambience of this game okay. My two biggest complaints are (1) the way the camera either flies around on its own or locks itself at a stationary position and you can't move it (especially when you're trying to walk across a narrow bridge or ledge), and (2) you can't save when you want to, but have to restart from "checkpoints" that the game determines. On the plus side, I really like that I can use my USB XBOX controller on my PC -- too many indie Steam games don't map the controller buttons in a useful way or don't let you invert the Y axis, forcing you to use the KB and mouse -- RIME handles the controller perfectly! True, the puzzles are easy and not too challenging, but it's nice to play a relaxing "adventure/puzzle" game for a change that doesn't confound me every step of the way and make me take sneak peeks at spoilers regularly to continue on with the story. If you want an uber challenge, there's Antichamber and The Witness and The Talos Principle (three puzzle games that I really like a lot) -- but if you want a relaxing stroll, there's RIME.  For instance, if you like "walking simulators" like Drizzlepath Genie or Firewatch or The Path (three other games that I also really like a lot), but with a little more challenge, then RIME is perfect for you.  Nuff said?

Shadow Warrior 2 is going to be a special kind of casual game for me.  Yes, the upgrades are underpowered and overplentiful.  You "don't" need to be constantly updating the upgrades and weapon configurations once you've found the 8 some that please you.  But you will need to frequently go through "mass inventory management"; assigning junk upgrades for sale and replacing outdated ones...  you'll know when you need to this... when enemies start to become bullet sponges.
That being said...  Shadow Warrior 2 is a great game.  It relives the single player FPS experience of Shadow Warrior while making some minor upgrades to controls, gameplay, and graphics.  It reminds me of borderlands 2 in it's customizability and preset explorable regions populated with procedurally generated enemies.  This isn't a bad thing...  some far cry influences regarding weapon selection sidesteps the issue borderlands has with damage scaling... kinda.  It feels like a far cry adventure stuffed in a borderlands styled zone-based universe in the setting of Lo Wang's destruction.
Graphics, gunplay, gameplay, and feedback are all excellent.  The monotony of inventory management is this game's one true failure.  Otherwise I love it, and the prospect of co-op with friends!

Some games get better with each chapter or sequel, I'd have to say that the Tomb raider series is a bit of a hit and miss affair in this matter. However, Underworld is in my opinion better than the previous two in the Anniversary/Legend/underworld trilogy.
An honest and accurate review? This is the Dark souls of Tomb raiders. You will die plenty, not by enemies but mainly ....well just stupid crap that you may or may not have pressed on your controller/keyboard. A seemingly obvious jump just won't hit the mark and you'll plummet to your death. This has been an inherent problem in the Tomb raider series and no matter how accurate you think your jumps may be, sooner or later you'll do something that should work but doesn't.
A big gripe I have is that the two chapters of DLC are xbox exclusives and they wrap up the Underworld story and tie up some lose ends, some big loose ends. If you decide to get this game and finish it, I'd suggest checking out a letsplay of the DLC chapters if you're interested in the story.
On that, the story itself is not too bad, a nice dose of Norse mythology and a few surprises...and anti-climaxes.
The graphics for a game of it's age are still pretty impressive, some nice textures and shadows, decent enough sounds and the music isn't overbearing.
Kinda felt that this game went back to it's Tomb raider roots in the feeling of adventure, epic levels with decent puzzles and a feeling of awe when you enter a huge room or area and see where you are and where you have to be. Also, there are plenty of opportunities for treasure hunting!
The gameplay was ok when I wasn't dropping off cliffs and dying by not even pressing the wrong button.....
I enjoyed the combat, the headshot ability is a little to un-used once you get mjo....I mean towards the end of the game. The motorcycle was a bit lame, I hated having to get off it every few seconds to pick up relics or treasure and the levels didn't even feel big enough to necessitate a motorbike....ok some areas it was fun.
All in all, I think if you're a huge fan of the series, get it!

This is not as good as the previous game.  It feels unpolished, incomplete.  Especially given the previous game.  They went more Borderlands style with this one, looter shooter, only it's lacking some elements that made that work.  The loot in this comes not from weapons, but from gems to slot into said weapons.  The problem with that is that most of these gems are just stat boosts.  A slight increase in a stat or two, and the "better" ones all come with a drawback.  There ARE some elemental ones, but again, they get slightly better as the game progresses, that's it.  The only ones that are actually good are there are a few that actually change the behavior of the weapons.  IMHO the system would be better with only those gems, and only one slot per weapon.  AND NO ♥♥♥♥ING ELEMENTS.  Seriously, I hate those.
The recent patch 1.1.3.0 only made a few things worse.  And illustrates that the game is still, effectively, in beta.  They've been asking the community what they want to improve, and using that to balance the game... slightly.  They nerfed a couple things that were admittedly overpowered, but they also reduced the effectiveness of some things that weren't that powerful.  And on top of that they increased the difficulty of enemies, AND reduced the amount of skills players can get.  Enemies can now spawn resistant to everything just by the nature of having so many modifiers put on them in higher difficulties.  Combine that with removing one of the major reasons to even bother with New Game+ - that being gaining skill points from repeating missions (you only get the skill points once now, no matter how many replays), and it just feels like they're poking blindingly and hoping the game will eventually balance out.
There's a lot of base weapons in the game, more than 70.  You won't use most of them.  I don't even really like the flow of combat in this one versus the previous game.  The previous game was quick, responsive, and you could do a lot with combinations of movement keys.  Double tapping a direction to prepare spells etc.  The new one puts them on different buttons, which just adds to the complexity of the controls.  And not in a good way.  Controllers are not able to be freely customized either.  This makes this game more complex, needlessly so.  The levels as well are pieced together procedurally generated to add some randomness.  However, the pieces do NOT always fit together well, creating a lot of seams and places where you could jump out of the map entirely, or get stuck.
Even the story feel like a bit of a rehash, and a let down, from the previous game.  The previous game's was very interesting, and kept me sucked in.  This one feels disjointed, not helped by the fact that there are side missions.  The cut scenes as well are VERY badly animated.  Like they are filled with placeholder animation, with wild, exaggerated movements that in no way match up with what is going on.  It looks absolutely awful.
All in all... no.  I don't recommend this.  Maybe if they fix it, but this game right now feels like Early Access... and I don't see it actually ever being completed.

Magic 2015, a game I have looked forward to for quite some time, and showed great promise with having the ability to build completely custom decks and a card pool from sevral of the newer blocks, it saddens me to say however that in it's entirety the game is lack-luster and all in all a disappointment.
The first thing you notice when you get into the game is that you have basically no choice but to go through the tutorial, granted you CAN skip most of it, but the final match is no choice you have to go through it, from there you get to choose a starting deck and go up against the final round of the tutorial, after that you can choose to change your deck for one of the other starter decks and do it  again, or continue into the main game, though be careful about this, because you won't be able to change your starter deck for a while after you leave.
To unlock more cards you gotta win games, which will give you a booster pack that contain rand om cards from the plain set in which you just fought, so if you fought n the plain of innistrad you will unlok cards from the innistrad set.
The main issue with this, is that the cards you get from them are random and might be useless to your current deck, to top is all off, there are cards you can only get out of the Premium Booster Packs, which you have to buy in the store, FOR REAL MONEY, even if you bought the most expensive special edition do you have to buy them, which is a frikkin Rip-Off, though not as much a rip-off as the 9,99€ those unlucky enough to not own most expensive Special Edition have to shell out for each of Card Collection.
The campaign are extremly hit and miss, some of the matches completely and utterly demolish certain starter decks, for instance if you pick the black/red started deck you are going to be stuck on the final battle in Innistrad for quite a while, and you have to beat this battle to unlock your special edition content, I might ad, so if you where hoping having those would make it easier, think again, wheras others are so easy I literally never lost a single card, a perfect example of this are against a certain mission that pits you against your own deck, if you play a mill deck and put to Elixirs of Immortality in, you can't loose, it might take some time but the AI are basically programmed try to bash you to death, so a Wall mill deck (using the wall humunculi and the myriad of other Blue defender cards, will leave the A.I literally incapabale of doing anything, throughout my entire game the AI smashed me for 12 damage, cuss I simply dind't feel like blocking as I knew I would win, and milled 6 cards using Hedron Crab.
So the variance of the matchups are hit and miss, which is slightly annoying, but what really ticks me off is that there are so many cards programmed into the game we probably will have to shell out coin for later, even though they are already in the game itself, the final boss of Innistrad uses cards you do not have acess to at all, they are not even listed in the card collection, so if we want them it's probably DLC.
The card pool contains many cards, sure, but there are so weak and unfocused absolutely no way to build a themed deck out of them, want to build a goblin deck? there are about 5 diffrent goblins in the entire game, and none of their lords, want to use elves, same problem only that there are about 3 diffrent ones, milling? hope your not looking for Traumatize or Mind Funeral, cuss they aren't in the game either, Artifacts, let me be blunt, there are a grand total of 2 Artifact creatures in the entire game, one of which is a Defender. infact the best deck I have been able to construct after nearly 6 hours of constant building and testing are a burn deck, and that's solely because most of the critters in this game tend to be glass cannons unless you want to go above 6 mana in cost, you really know the card pool is weak when Shock can kill most of the critters you get in the starting decks without any assistance.
Meanwhile the Campaign features fun decks like Allies, Demons, Slivers and Soldiers and other such highly focused highly effective decks, which you have to beat with the deck you build from this junky card pool, it does make it more challenging, sure, but it also makes it frustrating, knowing YOU  could have been using those cards instead of whatever you have managed to claw out of your Boosters.
The Card-pool issue gets even worse by the fact that they put out cards that are meant to be used in such specific decks but have so few cards to go along with that they simply can't work, a perfect example of which are Vent Sentinel, which you would use in a Defender deck, most Defender creatures are in blue in this game and they support a Mill strategy much better than a burn strategy, infact Vent Sentinel is the ONLY red defender in the game.
To make matters even worse is the fact that green is all but unplayable on it's own, green has a ton of stompy creatures, don't get me wrong, but in total there are only 2 sets of cards that can accelerate your mana, first of which is Cultivate, and the other is the elf that puts a basic land from your han onto the field when you summon it, there are Travelers Charm, which puts land into your hand, but that's it.
While you do have Meteor, or if your lucky enough to score a Darksteel Ingot out of the Premiums you will have some more mana acceleration, but those aren't exactly viable since Ingot are a Rare card and Meteor costs 5, and have to be gotten from Theros Boosters, which are the halfway point of the campaign.
Then we have the game modes for single and multiplayer outside the campaign, we have 2-player Duel, 3-Player Duel and 4-player Duel, that's it... no puzzles, no special game modes, no special campaigns or anything of the sort, what it DOES sport is a store locator, which is useless if your not into the physical card game, a Leaderboard, which, considering how weak the card pool is are also pretty useless, and a Gallery.
The games story, what little there is, are OK I guess, mothing super but nothing flat out bad either, though the ending was a bit... wierd, not sure what was up with that.
Multiplayer.... well it's what you expect right now, those who bought the most epxensive special edition and as of such have all the cards can easily produce decks that stomps those who dare try to be casual and no-pay-standard-edition about it, good ol' pay-to-win in other words, I suspect this will improve once players finish up their card collections the hard way, or break down and buy them in the store, but until then, I would actually suggest staying clear, not fun having a starter deck when your oponent are using a deck that actually has atleast a wee bit of streamlining behind it.
And then there is the forced tutorials, while you CAN skip the gameplay tutorial, aside from the final battle of it, which you choose your starter deck in, the tutorial for the deck builder are unskippable and starts automatically the first time you enter AND a 2nd tutorial starts once you defeat the final encounter in Innistrad, the first Campaign Zone, and you have no choice but to go through both if you actually want to build your deck, but do NOT click too fast during it, or the tutorial will bug out and freeze, forcing you to ALT + F4 the game and restart the game, which will force you to watch it all over again.
Addendum:
Hit-and miss campaign, no extras outside it, weak card pool and pay-to-win multiplayer, I really wish I could recommend this game, but I really, REALLY can't, do yourself a favor, stay clear until it goes on sale or something, this is simply not worth it, trust me.

I'm changing my mind. I'm really enjoying the card pool. There are some rather interesting complexities and intereactions within the seeming restrictions. It can be a neat way to play.

I will never understand the people that made the decisions involved in putting together this years version. I really want to like this and I've waited months and months to do so. But the following points are incredibly difficult to get past.
- Dead Giants.
Removal of Two Headed Giant due to lack of budget and/or questionable priorities
- Menus of Eternity.
One at a time icons that fill your entire screen. What should take five seconds to navigate can easily take over thirty seconds.
- Menus of Sexy.
Lovely fading effect that likely drained an unjustifiablly large percentage of the budget. Who sexys up the least important part of a game at the cost of everything else? Definitely a questionable priority.
- Themeless Themes.
They describe each deck like they do all of these amazing things together, but only the most laughably small amount of cards that reflect each theme appear to have made it into the card pool. This is even more pronounced in contrast with last years distinct and solid themes.
- I've Got Bugs.
Should be a super-fun tribal deck, not a constant pain in the UI♥♥♥♥♥
- Deck Select.
You cannot change decks as you set up a multiplayer game. You must equip a deck in a previous screen, requiring you quit out and try get back in. So just to get an arbitrary language tie-in with an artifact type, we now have to do things the hard way.
- Lobbying for a Lobby.
Where is the multiplayer lobby after a game? It seems like it just drops out to one of the main menus after a game but once in a while it will go back into the game set up screen. Which one is it? Do we have a real lobby or is it just random?
- Yawning Pool.
I understand a good balance of card power, but it feels like I've been zerg rushed with meh. While there are a couple of fun and interesting cards, it feels like you have to use scraps dancing around them to complete a deck. Card synchronicity is really quite lacklustre. Gimme some of the AI's cards.
- Bigger is Not Big.
The entire marketing spin is spearheaded with 'Hunt Bigger Game'. If you did an audit and comparison of mean and/or total creature size between this and last years version, I'd probably be willing to put money on us actually hunting smaller game this time around.

Rain World is a 2D survival platformer with a vast world to explore. You play as a slugcat who has been separated from your family. You are trying to find your way back to them, but you encounter a whole lot danger along the way. There seems to be more going on in Rain World that what appears at first glance, and I find it intriguing.
One key thing to keep in mind about Rain World is that you are always battling against the clock. There is a constant countdown until the next rain storm, and these rainstorms will kill you. Hibernating is the only way to reset the rain timer, but you can only do this in special safe rooms. In addition to being in a special room, you’ll also have to make sure that you have hunted or scavenged enough food first. Food you forage is limited and will not respawn, but after hibernating food you hunt for does.
Some creatures, like the bats, are your prey, but the majority of creatures are predators that will hunt you down and devour you. Avoiding predators is an absolute must since you are extremely squishy and vulnerable. Expect to die a lot if you try to venture far out into unexplored areas too quickly. If you play more on the safe side, then you can expect to do a good amount of backtracking to hibernate in safe rooms you’ve previously discovered. In addition to avoiding the rainstorms, hibernating also ranks up your current rain cycle icon by one each time. Dying deranks it by one. These icons match specific gate icons, that will allow you go into other regions. If you rank up to the same icon enough, then you can permanently unlock all of those gates.
When I first started the game, I felt sort of bored and think others may feel the same way. I kept playing though, and realized this game is not as easy as it looks; since then, the game has really grown on me. Despite my innumerable deaths, I keep wanting to try again. Rain World is a niche game, and will certainly not appeal to everyone. However, those who love somewhat challenging exploration platformers, and don’t mind that there isn’t much in the way of combat are sure to get a lot of enjoyment out of Rain World.

Rain World is a survival metroidvania game (not a traditional platformer though!), in which you take control over a slugcat trying to find his family that he was separated from. Now that we have this out of the way let me tell you this: this game is a masterpiece. And I'm gonna tell you why.
1) your main character is almost at the bottom of the foodchain in this world. That means avoiding predators and trying to get food necessary to survive. As you might expect, that premise leads to a lot of deaths. There's no lose state in this game though, you can try to pass any point of the game as many times as you want.
2) controls - at first you might think that the controls are awful. Slugcat can't jump very high and his movement feels clunky and weird. But the more you play, the more you begin to realise how incredibly precise, fluent and consistent the movement is! I had to rebind the controls to unleash the full potential (A - jump, W - throw, D - grab, SPACE - map), but once I understood the rules, I can safely say that it's one of the best designed controls in any videogame.
3) game size - this is a MASSIVE game. It has about 12 big regions with subregions, every one of them is immensly vast, you can literally stuck in one place for good few hours not making any progress, walking in circles. Sometimes you will think that you make progress, just to discover that you were just doing a big loop leading to the previous big location :) I would describe it as trial and error done right
4) creatures - they don't only look great and scary, but they make sense in this world. Flora and fauna in this game is just amazing to look at, study and learn about (mostly by sticking your paws into every situation and seeing what happens). Animations of the creatures are amazing. Sometimes I was just mesmerized by some new animal and I was just staring at it for 5 minutes, looking how fluently gorgeous its movement looks :)
5) sense of amazement and accomplishment - new locations are breathtakingly beautiful. Pixelart in this game is spot on. Finding a hibernation chamber after 2 hours of struggling with particularly difficult task is one of the best feelings that I've had in ANY videogame.
6) hardcore feel to it all - every second of this game brings 3 questions: 'what am I doing, where do I go now and do I even make progress'? :P This game gives you basic map and nothing else. No big arrows pointing at the direction of the next mandatory checkpoint or 'corridor gameplay'. Trial and error, that's the name of the game. You have to learn how the cogs of this world work. What can you eat, how can you make something edible, what is hostile towards you, how can you tame it, what can you jump on, what's going to instakill you, etc. There's also rain mechanic and hibernation mechanic bound to it. You need to find food and find hibernation chamber before the rain comes and kills everything on the surface. The cycle takes about 10 minutes to complete, so while exploring, you are always forced to look for shelter aswell. And it works brilliantly! You go explore unknown terrain, sometimes you find a new shelter (and you never know if you came any closer to the end or not :) and most of the times you die. Deaths can be frustrating, especially when it feels cheap (with predators spawning near the entrances of new areas and stuff, but honestly, they are predators, they instinctively feel where can they find prey), but overall, with unlimited continues, it's not a problem.
I have only one pet peeve with this game. And it's the minor one. If you perform some special task, you're granted the ability to teleport between 'big areas'. The thing is - it's one time usage. So if you don't know that, you might just foolishly teleport yourself to the first location ('eh, let's just try it for ♥♥♥♥♥ and giggles, oh...') and get stuck there, because you can't teleport back. Making it to your original location would take hours, so you have to perform another special task in order to earn next teleport.
All in all, Rain World is one of the best games that I've ever played, it looks amazing, it feels amazing and it feels incredibly rewarding despite its insane brutality.

My review was orginally posted on Brash Games:
Rain World is one of those games that can be recognised from a mile off. From the gloomy pixel-art environments to the to the adorable protagonist, Slugcat. While some people are getting tired of the resurgence in pixel-art, Rain World should be an exception. Light and shadow drift across the screen as the day goes on, water ripples and surges with an unbelievable level of realism. Dark caves shimmer from the light of luminescent mushrooms, scattering shadows onto the backdrop.
Environments are complex to look at, foliage covers every surface, however they are satisfyingly simple to traverse. Careful use of colour makes it easy to distinguish what is important and what isn’t. Nothing feels out of place, the heads-up-display is suitably minimal and as a result you are never pulled from the experience with any inconsistencies in the design.
The naturalistic environments are complemented with the procedural animation. For those who don’t know; procedural animation uses artificial intelligence to control the minute movements of your character. Therefore you won’t be seeing the same animation over and over again. Slugcat’s little arms tense as (s)he dangles from a pole or when a piece of fruit is just out of reach. Since the movement is directly related to the physics engine it will take some time to get used to. The sheer charm of simply watching Slugcat will get you well over the learning curve. Every creature in the game is animated in this way too, each with their own methods of traversing the terrain. This adds an uncanny level of realism, the giant centipedes in particular made me squirm.
Without spoiling too much I’ll return to the creatures, but first, what do you actually do in Rain World? At it’s heart Rain World is a survival game, you need to find/catch food and hibernate. While you could spend the entire game in the first area searching for food and sleeping day after day. Slugcat is nomadic, ever moving onward to the next area. Each time you hibernate you “rank up” in a chain of karma symbols. However if you die, you will respawn at the previous hibernation point and go down a rank. You are never explicitly told how these ranks work, figuring them out is a large part of the enjoyment to unlocking many of the cryptic achievements.
Guiding you along is a small hologram, it will direct you to some key locations and teach you some basic controls without being too intrusive. You can even scare the hologram away if you don’t want it’s help. Rain World is all about working things out yourself, watching a detailed guide will frankly ruin the experience. However discovering all the mysteries this game has to offer will require a lot of discussion with other players. It respects your intelligence, making it all the more satisfying when you do work something out for yourself.
The design of the levels and the systems are so naturalistic, overcoming an obstacle does not feel like the intention of the developer. It’s hard to explain, it’s like the developer just created a world and plonked you in the middle of it. This world is cruel, Slugcat doesn’t feel like the center of all attention and to succeed you need to be resourceful. You don’t have a specific goal, for all you know there might not be a way out, you’re just pushing onward and trying to survive.
This unique feeling of actually belonging to a world is owed directly to the “ecosystem”. The creatures I mentioned earlier all have their own agency. They will go where they want, fight each other, hunt for prey, you name it. While the species of all these creatures are made by the design of the developers, individuals are procedurally generated at the beginning of your playthrough. If you see a purple crocodile for the first time, you won’t know it’s behaviours. Maybe it’s good at climbing, perhaps is fast on the ground, what if it isn’t very aggressive?
The only way to find out is by observation, and probably getting eaten, that too. Some creatures are easier to kill than others, but more often than not you’ll be frantically jumping over them trying to find some high-ground. The position of these creatures changes with each cycle too (each time you hibernate). Sometimes a crocodile will be guarding the very place you need to reach. This can be frustrating at times, however it’s the nature of such a diverse and unpredictable world. You will be frequently required to change up your plans, adapting just to stay alive.
There is always a way around these situations, it might involve distracting the crocodile, going a different way or simply hibernating for another day and hoping the coast will be clear. It certainly isn’t for everyone, if you don’t keep an open mind you will feel like you’re headbutting a brick wall for hours. Many people will argue this is unfair, but it contributes to the overall concept of the ecosystem in such an intrinsic way, you could argue one way or the other. In my opinion it provides such an original experience of survival any frustrations fade away.
The more you play, the more you’ll learn, slowly building up a catalog of what’s dangerous and what isn’t in certain circumstances. This makes venturing into a new areas exciting and terrifying in equal measure. You are constantly against the clock, if you don’t find a hibernation spot in time the rain will kill you.
The music has some procedural aspects too, different tracks will fade in and out depending on the situation. At some rare instances the music will swell giving you an opportunity to stand back and observe the desolate beauty of this place. It’s a short but welcome change in a world that is so against your existence, or rather, everything’s existence. Moments like these you truly forget you’re sat in your pants, playing a videogame.
I did not think a game could be simultaneously; cute, terrifying, funny and awe-inspiring, but videocult have managed to pull it off. There is one part of the game that will unfortunately make or break it for some people. One way to compare it would be Blighttown in Dark Souls, it’s not for the feint of heart, but the rush and the struggle of overcoming the impossible makes you feel warm and cosy when you finally reach a hibernation spot.
Rain World is a difficult game to review, some will argue the unpredictability of the world makes the game hugely unfair. Those people wouldn’t be wrong, but for each “flaw” with the game there is a counter argument to be made. The moment to moment interaction with the world is so compelling (partially thanks to the procedural animation) getting stuck only gave me a larger opportunity to spend more time in this world. Sitting back and watching all the other creatures scrabble around hunting and interacting with each other is mesmerising. This isn’t just a bizarre simulation, you have to harness these interactions to progress through the game, all of the systems interlock.
Rain World is a vastly solitary experience and you will probably feel lonely at times, especially considering completing this game will take most players about 30 hours. There are plans to introduce local co-op and versus multiplayer too as a free update. Co-op would greatly change the experience, for better and for worse, but it’s impossible to say for certain until I try it for myself. However, no game has had me glued to the screen like Rain World has. I don’t know how Videocult have managed to preserve such a fascinating simulation of an ecosystem, while maintaining playability. Rain World is the definition of emergent gameplay, Slugcat will go down in history.

Rain World is a unique survival game with beautiful pixel art.
The main premise of the game is to gather food, survive predators, and move forward throughout the world.
It can be very hard, and sometimes even frustrating if you don't know what is going on at times. Which is what I will try to quell through this review.
The game starts off with a very nicely drawn cutscene that sets the basis of the story. Then it throws you into gameplay, explains a few basic things and leaves you to figure out the rest. Which sounds great to me, but I feel like 1 or 2 more important things needed to be taught. So in the first 30 minutes of my gameplay, I felt a bit frustrated trying to figure out what kind of game this is, but after that it was great.
As you explore the world, you need to feed yourself to fill your hunger meter. Once you've gotten to a certain point, you can then hibernate in a few specific locations. Upon doing this, you progress to the next day, and level up your character.
If you die, you will lose any progress you've made since the last time you hibernated. You will have to re-do the day and you will lose your level progress. The game can be quite difficult at times due to this, but it's nothing keyboard-breaking worthy.
Most of the times, you will die to predators. They are quite clever for the most part. They follow you through small vents, up poles and can sometimes even cut you off from where you're trying to go. It can be really scary, and the fact that the game most of the time has no music, but plays an intense percussion rhythm around enemies makes it even more intense.
The one other major threat in the game is rain. It basically plays the role of a timer in a day. You've got a set time to complete the day, once that runs out, rain will come pouring down from the sky and kill you. If you are underground, it will flood the place and drown you. Now this is really terrifying. The only way to survive it is by hibernating, so you need to gather your food fast throughout the day.
The movement and climbing is quite intuitive. You just use a jump button to get around, and move in the direction you want to. The pixel art looks really great, and the physics and animation look very fluent and work well together.
Overall, I'm having a lot of fun with the game. It's very well made, and once you get over the initial bump of learning how it works, the difficulty can be very fun and rewarding!

Quake 4 is fun. The story is shady, though. It's essentially Iraq/Afghanistan War propaganda. The story is that you're part of the marines invading a desert planet fighting the locals, much like what the US was doing when this game was released. The graphics still hold up fairly well considering this game is just about a decade old. There are a lot of well realized technologically, industrially advanced locations filled to the brim with details. The setting is gritty sci-fi and the aesthetics really sold the dark atmosphere. There is a fair amount of gore in the game. The game certainly has some similarities to Doom 3, which was released around the same time. Quake 4 leans more towards sci-fi where Doom 3 more towards super natural horror. The lighting is really well done. The colorful lights from the computer screens and machines contrast well with the mostly otherwise pitch dark rooms. Think of the lighting at a rave and you've got it. When first arriving on the planet, the main character can't understand the alien writing on computers and it just looks like jibberish, but a little ways in something happens to him and then the computer consoles start displaying messages in English, like the character learned to understand the language. The main character looks like Robocop without his visor on and it looks bizarre. The combat is decent. There are a lot of corridor battles and the 'ol trusty running backwards in a circle, shooting up the enemy tactic still works a bit too well. The weapons were standard issue. There wasn't anything too exciting, but they were suitable for the game were fun to shoot. The level design is mostly simple and straight forward, but combat was never boring. The boss battles were challenging, yet not too bad. I will say, the final boss was much more difficult than I anticipated. It took me a while to figure exactly what I needed to do. There are some on rails sections and some where vehicles are controlled that break up the on foot parts that make up a bulk of the game. Frequently NPC marines will join the fight and every one of them gets a name and so I always felt bad when they'd inevitably get mowed down. It took around 10 hours to finish. Quake 4 is not the revolution that the first one was two decades ago, but it is still a fun game that holds up today.

There are many negative reviews out there about this game, so many people say it's a terrible game and poorly made. Hearing those things made me a little hesitant to try it out but it looked good to me and I saw it was on sale so I decided to give it a shot. Due to all the negative feedback this game has received I expected to see some serious problems with it.... glitchyness, boring gameplay, bad graphics, just something that would really make it too undesirable for me to want to play and finish it. I played and played, waiting to find the reason(s) so many people dislike this game but from the beginning to the end I found nothing significant enough to justify the hatred so many people have for Duke Nukem: Forever.
The gameplay was fun, the environments were interesting, the graphics and physics were good, the weapons were pretty diverse, the difficulty was well balanced, and most of the jokes and puns were funny enough to give me a little laugh. The game kept me interested enough to play it through to the end over the course of a few days and it never disappointed me or made me feel like it wasn't worth the money I paid for it. It was really an enjoyable experience and pretty much the opposite of what all these negative reviewers made it out to look like.
So, the question is; why was this game so bad in the eyes of so many? My best guess would be that it's due to a few different aspects. Maybe the game had problems when it was first released which have since been patched. Maybe it was hyped up so much that many people were expecting a groundbreaking game and were disappointed when they saw it wasn't. This game was supposed to be released many times over the course of about a decade and each time it was announced that it was to be released soon it ended up not happening each time. The reoccuring disappointment from that would be enough to make many gamers critical on it when it was finally released.
There were a few negative things I saw in this game, minor though they are, they're still worth mentioning. I saw a few small glitches such as that the pigcop freezes for a second in mid-air when he lunges towards you if you move out of the way. I also didn't find the characters in this game(other than Duke Nukem himself) particularly interesting or memorable, they were all pretty bland. The enemies didn't exactly have colorful personalities either but in a game like this they really don't need to do much else than look fierce and give you a good fight and those were two features they certainly had. Another thing is that to me there doesn't seem to be much replay value in this game, you pretty much see everything the first time around. Though after beating the game it unlocks a few bonus options and cheats which you may find interesting enough to play it through once again.
Everything considered I feel like this is a good game. It's no Halo or Half life 2 or grand theft auto or Shenmue or Max Payne or Resident evil or any other groundbreaking game with a terrific storyline that will make you sit back in your chair once it's all over and say "Wow, that was an incredible game" but if you want a non-serious shooter with some comedy, pleasing visuals(B00BIES 0.0), fun gameplay and stupid things to play around with(dry erase boards, minigames, turds in toilets, light switches, microwaves, etc.) then this might just be the game to suit your needs. Just remember that game reviews are simply based on the opinions of that particular reviewer and a game they call bad could be a game you will thoroughly enjoy. If this game looks good to you, give it a shot. If it looks good but you're pessimistic due to the negative reviews you've seen then wait for it to be on sale and pick it up. I enjoyed it, maybe you will too.

Okay so this is my first review ever, so keep that in mind.
Also keep in mind, THIS GAME IS NOT FINISHED YET!!   A lot of people may trash one thing or another without realizing that this is not a complete product.  For an unfinished game, it's fantastic.  For a published game, it's got some work.
Things to expect: Bugs bugs and more bugs.  Again, this is not a complete product.  So yes, there's bugs.  There's quite a few annoying ones.  HOWEVER since I have purchased this game a lot has been done to fix these bugs and to improve on the game.
If you like simulation type games/RPG based on crafting.  You'll love this game.  Very few games come close.   I would argue some of the skills don't make sense when it comes to unlocking certain skills..  Like Tailoring is unlocked through..  Cooking?  ..  wha..??  Procuration is also a requirement as well as farming..   ?!?!?!    I think that needs to be re-evaluated.  However, the way the skills work in terms of leveling them up is great.  There's basically a few "Teirs" to skills.   0-29, I would call this untrained.  You don't know completely what you're doing, you can't do very much with it, and whta you can do will result in terrible products.   30-59.  I would call this an apprentice.  you know some stuff and you can do some useful stuff, things you make or produce with this skill is not great but you're learning.  60-89, journeyman.  You can pretty much do what you need wit hthe skill and have descent items created from it.  it doesn't take too long to get to 60 in most skills.  Once you're there, you don't really NEEEEED to go any further unless you want to specialize in that skill.  Keep in mind you have a limited amount of skill points so you can't do everything in the game (unless you're on one of those servers who pretty much get rid of the skillcaps)  Getting to 90, which I would say is master, 100 being grandmaster, takes time.  so, skills are cool, the unlocking part needs work.
Combat is gross right now.   plain and simple.   The idea behind it though is amazing.  If you get wounded, doesn't matter if a healer can heal you, tha'tll just keep you alive, you're done.  Unless your suicidal.  This makes for a fantastic combat system where player skill mixed with character skill could land a blow that takes someone out of the fight.  Killing also shouldn't be taken lightly as you will loose karma/alignment.  the lower alignment you have, the more skills you loose when you die.  ALSO if your alignment drops enough, anyone can kill you WITHOUT penalty.  So careful.  People do have the opporunity to yeild.  I would highly suggest letting them live.   Again, cool ideas with the combat system, can't wait till the kinks are worked out.

No game ever will live up to 12+ years of development, that is impossible.  The game is tremendously under rated.  The campaign does start out a little slow aside from 1 encounter and it's really not the same style as Duke3D, but it's the same spirit and humor.  Where Duke3D took the FPS concept and made it better, Duke Forever didn't have nearly the impact on the genre that Duke3D did.  Success it not easily repeated.
The Doctor Who Cloned Me:
If you even somewhat enjoyed the campaign for Duke Nukem Forever then you should buy this, it starts off right where the campaign ended and it adds a heafty amount of gameplay for the money.  You can really see where the developers that the developers improved on what they already had.  The game just seemed to flow better, in terms of combat sequences, sections of finding things to boost your ego bar.
Multiplayer:
Aside from the occasional lag and the hackers, this part of the game is extremely fun.  It's fast paced, aggressive, and there is the Jetpack.  There are plenty of maps especially if you get the DLC.  Everyone is on equal ground, it's multiplayer plays slightly like Quake, weapon spawns, power ups.  Back in the 90's when this game was announced I wasn't even thinking about buying this game for the multiplayer, but what a gem it turned out to be.  Most of my multiplayer playtime came when I owned a copy of this on the PS3, but I have played some on the PC too.  I loved it so much when I stopped playing I was top 15 in the world on PS3, I'm sure by now I've dropped off the top 100 but it was great times.
When considering if this game is any good you have to consider it as a whole, did you have fun playing it at any point?  Ignore the fact that it was in development for so long and forget about the way Duke3D was, we all know how great Duke3D is, and no Duke Forever is not better than Duke3D, but it's still way more original that many of the other FPS that get released now a day.

Cool game overall. Basically a later 3D Zelda, with art and writing thats more "Warcrafty" in tone.
The overworld is pretty empty, but at least the zones looks different. The early game has alot of filler, in the form of combat challenges that have to be completed to progress. The late game has you return to empty areas for a very short, not that involved, triforce hunt.
Dungeons are a linear series of rooms that have to be tackled in a certain order without any opportunities to break from the script. Occasionaly after beating the midboss, and picking up a new item, you can backtrack to get a heart piece in an earlier room but thats about it. Most dungeons have some sort of gimmick or set piece moment to stop the game from feeling too repetitive, which does work, but the dungeons are still super linear.
Combat is good, not amazing, but good. Attacking enemies is satisfying, you have access to a large diverse tool set, all of which has a variety of uses, not all of which are telegraphed, enemies don't just constantly bum rush you, and upgrades aren't so good that they nullify combat altogether, so... none of the glaring issues that usually bog down western action games. No real pros other than a lack of cons, I would put the combat somewhere between God of War and DMC1 in terms of quality.

This game is an interesting mix of hack and slash and Zelda-like adventure.
Pros:
Hacking and slashing away at your enemies is fun.
Buying the weapon and move upgrades feels comfortable and utilizing each one makes you feel more accomplished like you're actually growing as a character (at least it did for me).
You're always unlocking new abilities and items at (seemingly) random points in the story. That element of surprise always intrigued me.
The story and voice acting are pretty good. Normally not something I look for in a game like this, but I stayed with it.
The finishing moves on bosses and most enemies felt really satisfying.
You can get a lot of playtime trying to 100% the game your first time (~20 hours for 100%? Give or take a few hours)
Neutral:
The difficulty can be a bit sharp at times, especially since health doesn't drop from enemies until your health is critical and earning enough currency to buy health supplements can be risky. Could be good if you like the challenge, but it could also be frustrating.
Cons:
Game crashes sometimes out of randomness.
I felt the dungeons dragged on a little bit sometimes.
There isn't really much in terms of replayability.
Overall, Darksiders is a very solid game and anybody who likes Zelda or Devil May Cry should at least look into this game when it's on sale.

Surprisingly, this game is well-crafted and enjoyable.  This is surprising because the first Two Worlds game was a commercial and critical flop.  Somehow it got a sequel.  As a fan of the Elder Scrolls series, this game felt right at home.  The graphics are great.  The combat is satisfying.  I particularily like that fact the any piece of equipment can be dismantled into raw materials at any time.  Also, those raw materials don`t contribute to your weight limit.  See an axe that you don`t need?  Pick it up anyway and dismantle it.  There is literally no downside.  You might need the materials later.  The magic system is pretty neat as well.  Rather than having specific spells, you have cards with various effects.  The game makes you build your own spells with card combinations.  You can make spells like a fire ball that splits into smaller fire balls that all home in on a target.  I didn\'t use the magic system a lot, but I can tell it has great potential.  At 20-30 hours long, it\'s not overwhelming.

(Enemy AI will see through bushes and whatnot and kill you). Bullets, well, here's the cute thing. In real life, a tree needs to be about 40 centimeters thick to stop a 5.56. This is not as good as the previous game.  It feels unpolished, incomplete.  Especially given the previous game.  They went more Borderlands style with this one, looter shooter, only it's lacking some elements that made that work.  The loot in this comes not from weapons, but from gems to slot into said weapons.  The problem with that is that most of these gems are just stat boosts.  A slight increase in a stat or two, and the "better" ones all come with a drawback.  There ARE some elemental ones, but again, they get slightly better as the game progresses, that's it.  The only ones that are actually good are there are a few that actually change the behavior of the weapons.  IMHO the system would be better with only those gems, and only one slot per weapon.  AND NO ♥♥♥♥ING ELEMENTS.  Seriously, I hate those.
The recent patch 1.1.3.0 only made a few things worse.  And illustrates that the game is still, effectively, in beta.  They've been asking the community what they want to improve, and using that to balance the game... slightly.  They nerfed a couple things that were admittedly overpowered, but they also reduced the effectiveness of some things that weren't that powerful.  And on top of that they increased the difficulty of enemies, AND reduced the amount of skills players can get.  Enemies can now spawn resistant to everything just by the nature of having so many modifiers put on them in higher difficulties.  Combine that with removing one of the major reasons to even bother with New Game+ - that being gaining skill points from repeating missions (you only get the skill points once now, no matter how many replays), and it just feels like they're poking blindingly and hoping the game will eventually balance out.
There's a lot of base weapons in the game, more than 70.  You won't use most of them.  I don't even really like the flow of combat in this one versus the previous game.  The previous game was quick, responsive, and you could do a lot with combinations of movement keys.  Double tapping a direction to prepare spells etc.  The new one puts them on different buttons, which just adds to the complexity of the controls.  And not in a good way.  Controllers are not able to be freely customized either.  This makes this game more complex, needlessly so.  The levels as well are pieced together procedurally generated to add some randomness.  However, the pieces do NOT always fit together well, creating a lot of seams and places where you could jump out of the map entirely, or get stuck.
Even the story feel like a bit of a rehash, and a let down, from the previous game.  The previous game's was very interesting, and kept me sucked in.  This one feels disjointed, not helped by the fact that there are side missions.  The cut scenes as well are VERY badly animated.  Like they are filled with placeholder animation, with wild, exaggerated movements that in no way match up with what is going on.  It looks absolutely awful.
All in all... no.  I don't recommend this.  Maybe if they fix it, but this game right now feels like Early Access... and I don't see it actually ever being completed.

I backed Rain World on Kickstarter ages ago and have waited patiently for it for many years, so disclaimer - I might be a little biased.
First up: The game only supports 4 low resolutions, 1024, 1280, 1360, 1366 all x768 - it doesn't allow you to run in anything higher or lower so you better have a 16:9 monitor that's friendly with those resolutions, and not have a really high desktop resolution or you're playing in a small window.
Once in game the tutorial rooms aren't too bad, there's some nice scenery and a helpful worm thing projects holograms to show you what buttons to press to do the basic moves. Standard tutorial type stuff. The issues only really begin after this.
Hibernating for the first time ends the tutorial and lets you set out to explore the world for yourself, having introduced you to the game fairly competently. Unfortunately several issues jump out rather quickly once you're given free reign, which I'm going to bulletpoint for easy reading.
I'm sure I'd have more to say if I played more but frankly between the issues I've run into so far Rain World is just an example of how to make an exploration game like this not fun. Is it cute and unique? Certainly. Is it fun to jump around and eat things as Slugcat? Yup. Is doing anything else fun? Nope.
Unfortunately, it's the way the game's designed, a patch concievably could fix these frustrations but it'd require a lot more development time while the core of the game and its rules are rewritten so it's very unlikely that it'll change. The best advice I can give to someone who's interested in the game is this: It's like marmite - you'll either like it or hate it, you won't know if you don't give it a try but be prepared to spit it out in disgust.

Easily in the top five for my Favorite Games of All Time, for two very specific reasons: Morality, and Choice.
Most RPGs tout freedom of choice and moral dilemmas as main gameplay mechanics. Nearly all of them, to put it generously, are stupid. Games like Fallout 3 and even the beloved original KotOR offer choices such as 'disarm the nuclear bomb and be rewarded with the praise of a grateful town, or blow it up, killing dozens of innocents for a paltry reward,' and 'deal politely with the NPC, or call them names, use racial slurs, and belittle their profession, and then threaten them with physical violence until they hand over ten credits and a crappy blaster.' Contrary to what the game would have you believe, this is not a choice between good and evil. This is a choice between saintly, and stupid. It can be argued that even an 'evil' character would want to act suave and courteous, because they're smart enough to realize acting like an adolescent bully is actually counter to their aims. Unless you are one of those 'for teh lulz' gamers, there is no good reason to be 'evil.'
KotOR 2 on the other hand, presents choices like 'side with the rightfully elected but possibly inept queen, or support the violent coup staged by the strong, visionary general,' and 'Help improve the lives of the helpless refugees and make an enemy of the most powerful criminal organization in the galaxy who will hound you for the rest of your days, or turn a blind eye to the oppression and ensure your own survival.' Often, the 'good' choice is not immediately apparent. And when it is, you can be assured that it will be a difficult one. Good will usually mean sacrifice, while evil often means survival. With this far more mature and realistic approach to moral choices, this game accomplishes two things: It allows much greater flexibility in roleplaying your character. You can be a good person doing bad things for good reasons, you can be a bad person just earning everyone's trust, you can be a mercenary strictly out for yourself, and yes, if you really want to, you can be the beneficent saint beyond all reason, or the violent pyschopath (but expect characters to scold you for it, on both counts). And secondly, it becomes a thoroughly smart deconstruction of the 'Light Side/Dark Side' dichotomy that typifies Star Wars, and in many ways, latter-day RPG gaming as a whole.
While I have never once played an 'evil' character in any other RPG, this is the one game where playing a Dark Side character is just as fun and interesting, if not more so, then a Light Side one. Thus, despite being buggy and unfinished, it will forever be one of my favorite games of all time.

Do you like games like Kingdom Rush but want something a bit different? Tiny Guardians promises just that. Instead of building towers along a lane and controlling 1 hero, you are following your hero through the lane while controlling up to 6 guardians of various classes. Sounds good so far, yet the execution and actual game play and tactics are pretty lacking, unfortunately.
Let's start off with the guardians:
All in all there are 12 guardians available over 4 different classes (Warrior, Range, Magic and Stealth). These "classes" can be upgraded with stars you earn from beating levels (up to 3) and challenges. These can also be upgraded several times during battle. Each hero and upgrade costs resources that are earned by killing enemies. If you want more heroes that will also cost ever more resources. Higher Tier heroes cost more resources to deploy and upgrade.
Tier 1, which you unlock in the first few missions (Knight, Archer, Magician and Rogue) are actually pretty good for most of the game. The Knight is a sturdy tank with a stun, the Archer a ranged DD with good DPS, the Rogue a hybrid melee/ranged DD, who's not really all that necessary, and, what I found to be THE bread and butter hero in the game: The Magician, the only one who can dish out reliable AOE damage with each shot, slows enemies and causes massive aoe damage every few seconds with her spells. Seriously, this unit is so overpowered that building nothing but Magicians with maybe 1 tank (and later a healer) is enough to destroy most enemy waves. Of course they are fragile, but who cares if the enemies are often dead before they even reach you.
Tier 2 heroes (Berserker, Hunter, Cleric and Assassin) unlock gradually in the mid to later levels. The Berserker is a moderately ok unit with an AOE special, more HP, but less Defense than the Knight, so I never really used him. The Hunter deals a bit more damage than the Archer, but is slower and has a crappy special ability, yet you ABSOLUTELY NEED her for 5 or 6 levels, because she is the only one who can spot stealthed enemies and traps, which can deal tons of damage. So it's kind of annoying that she gets shoehorned in there like that. The Cleric is a dedicated group healer, but only after being upgraded once in battle. She is essential later on, unfortunately. The Assassin is a melee crit damage dealer with quick attack speed, but is weak without the expensive upgrades.
Tier 3 is where the game loses ANY appeal whatsoever, however. These heroes can ONLY be unlocked with the ingame premium currency "coins". I assume that in the mobile version (yes, this is a port), these could be purchased for real money. Here you get coins after every mission or so. If you just stick to the main campaign (about 14 missions I think) you should be able to unlock ONE of them about half way or 2/3s through the campaign. That is if you want to play with the Paladin or the Sentinel, which cost 8 coins. The Wizard costs 12 and the Dancer a WHOPPING 20 coins, which means you will be grinding challenge missions for quite a while (artificially lengthening the game). Challenges force you to play a map with no reviving heroes, only certain types of heroes, a maximum of x upgrades or just at a higher difficulty (always a combination of 3), which makes a victory anything but certain. This is unacceptable in a SP game for which you pay full price. Moreover you have only a vague idea of what each hero does until you unlock or deploy them. Only then is the entry readable, so you could be saving 20 coins for the Dancer, hoping to unlock the most powerful hero (because it's the most expensive), only to find yourself with a hero you won't ever use. Personally I unlocked the Pally, which is just a better Knight with a heal instead of a stun, but also twice as expensive almost. Deals a lot more damage as well, but I've heard the Sentinel and Dancer are a waste of time and the Wizard is supposedly a Fire AOE mage. I'm fine with my discount Ice mage though. I assume the Wizard is too expensive to effectively use anyway.
Which brings me to my next point: At least on the 1st difficulty setting Tier 2 and 3 heroes are just not good enough to warrant the expensive upgrades. I usually just went with 1 Paladin, 1 Cleric, maybe 1 Assassin and 1-3 Magicians in the end, upgraded the first 3 once to get their special abilities and then just focussed on the Magicians (not in that order). What point is there to include all these options if there's no viability and the game is not balanced? I'd rather have a Level 5 Magician than a Level 2 Paladin for kinda the same price. This is one just one of the flaws of the game.
Next up, enemy variety:
A new type of enemy gets introduced with each level. Basically these are for the most part mildly interesting and fun, but also pretty standard, apart from the carnies. Nothing you haven't seen anywhere else before. There are also a handful of bosses, which are just super annoying, but we'll get to that later.
Levels:
Not too many and nothing interesting. Why you traverse the levels instead of just standing there and waiting for enemies? Cause the game says so, but it doesn't make a difference. In other TD games the level plays a vital role in your strategy. The only tactical decision here is "take a Hunter or an Archer?" based on the enemies in the levels (mid section of the game). Shame.
Graphics, Sound, Music:
Decent flash graphics, ok sound, subjectively ok music, but gets repetitive.
Controls:
The best for last...*sigh*. The game was clearly designed for mobile users. Heroes are controlled exclusively via drag-and-drop. Same goes for upgrading them. For the most part this is "ok", but in any case really obnoxious and irritating. Maybe assigning each hero a number key or just changing the whole pace of the game in general might have been a good idea, I don't know. I can clearly see how on higher difficulties the slow input could be a real problem. The controls aren't too precise either. Especially in boss fights you need pretty insane reaction times to hope to avoid the boss abilities. Speaking of boss battles: ♥♥♥♥ me, are they boring and bland. You basically just fight a tough enemy with an insane HP pool, who regularly charges you and then "leaves" the battlefield to "bombard" you from afar. EVERY boss does this, they all follow the same pattern with various variations. I've beaten them all on easy, but some of those abilities ONESHOT your heroes (especially the Troll Warlord!) and you can often not even avoid them, because your heroes are too slow and you're already being hindered by the clunky control scheme. Big no!
All in all the game is not worth the price of admission for barely 4 hours of gameplay in my opinion. And also pretty much a waste of time. It's not particularly fun, offers little new and doesn't even have any semblance of a story. For the most part it's: Build x and y, upgrade, win, continue. It could have been something better, but it isn't.
