I wanted to like Darksiders almost as hard as Darksiders kept trying to be God of War. I tried really, really hard.
The concept is cool. Book of Revelation, four horsemen of the apocalypse, yaddayadda. Like any brawler the point is simple: smash dudes. Lots of dudes. Even if I don't much care for the Warhammer 40,000/World of Warcraft proportions and pauldrons fetish that Darksiders's art direction makes ample use of, the visuals are pretty good. The voice acting is fitting, given what script the VAs had to work with. And on that note, the characterization is about as shallow as either W40K or WoW's; angry guy is angry, thus, he does angry things. I didn't expect masterful writing going in, but when even mediocrity counts as a positive bullet point in a review, it heralds bad things to come.
There's only one category where Darksiders really shines, and that's the boss fights. The introductory cutscenes are great, the battle mechanics themselves are usually pretty neat, you feel great for fighting and winning, you get to watch War perform some pretty brutal finishers on the bosses at the end, and there is no annoying underwater fight to speak of. A+.
The final boss is the worst, though. No, not The Destroyer. The
final boss.
The protagonist, War, and the final final boss, the camera, are introduced in the same cutscene sequence when you first fire up Darksiders and select New Game. And if you know anything about the camera angles in pre-rendered cutscenes, it's that you can't actually move them. Get used to a lot of that; Darksiders is an ongoing and constant battle of atrition against atrocious perspective shots, awkward lock-on phases, and jarring transitions.
Entire swaths of the puzzles in Darksiders feel unnecessary. There's a lot of time-based puzzle mechanics that involve a lot of waiting to reset if you make a mistake.
Toss in an uncooperative camera that won't let you look up to see when it's safe to proceed until you're already hanging from the ceiling and the time-slowing Chronospheres to make you wait that much longer when the spinning fan blade you couldn't see coming knocks you down, and you've got a recipe for half an hour wasted on multiple, identical, really badly-designed obstacles in the Ashlands.
Or, worse than player-controlled timers, there are entire rooms in the Dark Throne area in the later part of the game with floors that automatically build and remove themselves in cycles. If you miss the chance to step onto the path when it appears near you, you have to wait for the cycle to circle the entire room in order to continue. At least one of these also features a player timing puzzle.
Darksiders features what most gaming circles call "artificial difficulty." The harder game modes bump up the damage enemies do and, possibly, the number of enemies and the number of waves of enemies you face, but they don't become more intelligent or actually more challenging to destroy; they just take longer to finish off. My first run was on Apocalyptic, the hardest difficulty setting. When I briefly tried again on Easy to see what the differences were for this review I noticed a stark difference in survivability- mine and the enemy's- but I didn't play long enough to really see if there were fewer enemies to fight. It felt that way but I can't confirm.
My biggest complaint with the artificial difficulty is that it's irritating to be one-shot by some of the bigger baddies in the early game when you don't know how to fight them. Dark Souls players might find the challenge enjoyable, but the difficulty spike feels out of place in a brawler like this one. As I played, however, I picked up more Lifestones and was able to mitigate this problem. But it's still a problem.
In the beginning of the game, when I was instructed how to toggle between running and walking, I was ecstatic. My joy quickly turned to despair when I realized that the player's default state
running. War's movement speed is agonizingly slow. This could be mitigated by Ruin, the demonic steed depicted in the game's promotional matierals, but Darksiders has a huge problem: you play one of the four horsemen, but you don't get many opportunities to
It's unfortunate because everything in the game is either far too speedy or War is much too slow, though I suspect it's a combination of both. The result is a lot of chasing enemies around or trying to wade through piles of mooks to deal with the real threats and failing because everything can strafe circles around you. Thanks to a really jarring pause at the end, your dash is useless as a way to close real distance and seems to feature variable invincibility frames on top of it. I could never figure out what I did differently when I succeeded or failed; dodging always felt like a gamble.

The maps aren't bad to look at, but all they have are a few trees and a bridge or two, maybe a cliff, that's it. There's nothing more to see on those maps. You can maybe find a village or two, but they are all abandoned. Overall a very boring environment.
To wrap it up:
If you only want to senselessly smash your car against a wall or a tree, then this is your game - For 22,99€, which is extremely pricey for what the game offers. For me, it was not worth the price.
If you want a realistic driving experience with a steering wheel or at least drive a car for longer than 3 seconds without it going complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, then this is not the game for you.
Since it's still in Early Access, I hope the Developers can make this game playable, because in this state, it's just plain boring, unrealistic and overall nothing I would recommend.

Summary
Shadow Warrior 2 is a game that excelled with its combat that paired up with a raunchy set of humor for a ride that despite its numerous shortcomings was an enjoyable game. The majority of my enjoyment stemmed from the fast paced and visceral combat as I sliced my way through robots, demons, and the Yakuza in their multitude of forms. You'd think everything is fine then, but outside the combat and the accompanied visuals everything was just lackluster at the best of times.
Each character in the game struggled to be anything more than two dimensional. Unlike the first game no one had any character development, Wang himself has seemingly reverted back to how he was before the beginning of the first game dropping only raunchy jokes and arguing with Kamiko. To the games credit the jokes were enjoyable from start to finish, but a poor substitute for actual character development.
Resting solely on virtue signally the story never warms up nor is remember able for anything other than the women are all victims of men, and a bad cliff hanger that the game itself explained would be an extremely bad idea but is done because, you go girl.
Gorgeous looking yet shallow levels plague the game as well. Procedurally generation with only a handful of set pieces means you will within 4-5 missions have seen most of what is to be seen. Fortunately the game focuses on combat and fills these levels with respawning but a lovely variety of enemies that you'll have a workable slew of weapons and powers to slice, dice and murder the hell out of with.
The Good
-Fast Paced Combat
-Plenty of enemies to fight
-Useful Powers
-All play styles are plausible
-Best Menu Music Ever
-Good Sound Track
-Visuals (not counting levels)
-No Denuvo
The Bad
-Game is easy even on Insane
-No replay value
-Bad Multiplayer connectivity (as of review)
-Virtue signaling story
-horrible cliff hanger ending
-Procedurally generated levels have no staying power and become incredibly dull fast
-Lack luster boss
-Bullet sponge enhanced (read larger) enemies
-Random Spawning enemies during a fight
-Cheap Deaths
-Have to read the lore to find out what happened (I like lore but forcing everyone to do so in order to know what is going on is a negative)
Long Review
Shadow Warrior 2 is a mixed bag of emotions for me, on one hand from the start to the finish my experience was generally favorable despite the constant negatives of the game. Combat was executed sublimely well allowing me to really get into it The movement system, the weapons, all came together to create a fast paced experience interspersed with some intense moments. Every play style was viable thanks to the upgrade system and various powers. Leaving you to choose what slew of instruments you wanted to dispatch your murderous rage with. The 8 weapons you had to select at time, that can be switched out in the middle of combat, often felt suffocating when compared to the multitude of your options from swords, to heavy weapons and everything in-between. Only downside to the selection is the same you'll find in all ARPGs, after you find a better option in the same ammo type there is zero reason to use the weaker weapon. The game tries to balance this by not having overtly more powerful versions that you need to acquire in order to progress. In doing so they also sucked some of the ARPG fun of acquire new weapons out.
Like any ARPG you have a selection of pickups to gather, the majority of which you'll sell for mad money that you'll use to buy ammo or meld upgrades together later in the game to produce ones with higher stats. With upgrades you can decide what elemental value you're weapon will have, how much of its damage will be converted from physical to that element, what extra benefits and penalties will you take. Missing from the game is the standard ARGP comparison tool for switching out upgrades. Unlike most ARPGs where you feel you are collecting an incrementally more powerful set of tools and upgrades making your character incrementally more and more powerful. This feeling is utterly missing from Shadow Warrior 2. That's not entirely a bad thing for on one hand it lends to keeping the game's combat balanced from start to finish, but on the other it robs the player of that excitement from each new upgrade discovery being the one they absolutely need. I played on Insane granting me the best selection of upgrades and even then it didn't have that ARPG feel.
Greatest part of the game is how they open with you having the majority of your abilities. You can double jump, shift in any direction (which will become your go to moving method because running is to slow), and able to do both stab enemies and swirl around to knock out entire groups. Within the first couple missions with the exception of the rage power you will have all 4 of your primary powers. While they don't work on Supreme enemies they are each actually viable options.
After completely quests or murdering a few dozen, hundred, thousand enemies you are awarded with enough karma (EXP) you unlock an skill point. Skill points are also awarded for completing quests, so you will get enough to deck out your character. The trouble comes from which options to choose from as with powers they're all useful, so it comes down to which powers you use or feel will benefit your play style that you're going to want to go for.
Speaking of Charon's new customers; enemies are divided into three categories: Zilla's forces, Demons, and Yakuza. Each come in a wide variety of flavors and temperaments for your killing pleasure. Demon's come in a different forms from humanoid to decidedly not humanoid, Zilla's forces are augmented super humans and robots, and the Yakuza come in various forms of guns, swords and drug addicts. Supreme enemies are scattered through their legion and the only thing different about them is their size, their health, and they're immune to all your powers. On higher difficulties that you'll definitely use if you want a challenge they spawn frequently throughout the levels.
As for the levels, they are all procedurally generated for a small amount of set pieces. About 4-5 missions into the game I had seen the majority of pieces in the selection with any meaningful difference. These levels were advertised to create replay ability by offering a differing layout each time you go through them, but in practice that doesn't entice you in the slightest. Handcrafted maps with carefully placed secrets from the first game were vastly more enjoyable and remember able than this game's procedurally generated variety.
You don't need to remember the first game to get into the second game, but if you played the first game you'll likely remember Wang's character developed from a mercenary who would do anything for the right price, to growing a conscious, to deciding to save the world and help his friend. It was filled with fraught moments, drama, and deep characters who did things for thought out reasons and personal motives that ranged from reasonable to self serving. That's all gone in Shadow Warrior 2. Literally all of it, Wang is back to being an♥♥♥♥♥♥♥dropping only sex jokes and murder jokes every 10 minutes, none of the other characters have any motivation for their actions and even writers didn't know why Zilla did what he did to start the plot in the first place.
Immediately they shove Kamiko into your body because we have to do this stick again, and it comes across entirely forced. What proceeds is a plot about how none of the women are at fault for their actions except Kamiko's Grandmother, but are instead all victims of the men. I'll spare spoilers but arranged marriage is brought up frequently and constantly called♥♥♥♥♥♥ All culminating in an ending that the game explicitly tells you will destroy the world entirely, that you do for no other reason and I do mean no other reason as you could have legitimately just left everything alone and things would have been fine, becau

To start with, for me the two biggest problems with this game are the intro, which is one big tutorial that always feels way too long and painfully slow to me no matter how many times I have gone through it, and the fact that this game was released unfinished. Not due to any problems with the developer really, but just an inability to finish their vision by the productions release timeline, resulting in a relatively complete, though sometimes painfully obviously stunted form. There does exist a patch with the remaining content (though also a bit buggy) if one cares to find it, but the game as is still stands as an impressive sequel to the original KOTOR.
Now, with those two big flaws in mind, this game still was able to deliver an amazing SW experience that pushed the degree of player influence in their team and world beyond what the original felt capable of doing. You awake with no real memory of yourself (of course), and find yourself escaping a mining station with new found companions: a rouguish character, droids, and a mysterious old woman who is strong in the ways of thr force. Employing some similar character relationships that were present in the first KOTOR, this sequel makes it possible to influence your allies to the degree of taking a vast majority of them on as jedi (sith) apprentices, giving force powers to almost your entire team, based completely on the personal dialogue choices and interactions that you pursue with each of them. On top of that, the setting of being chased by a shadowy Sith force, trying to piece together the stories of the torn worlds you find yourself on, blanacing the sides of the force, and assembling your crew as you continue on your adventure is fun everytime and exciting I play through it.
In all, this is a gem of a game, tarnished and incomplete, but even so it holds up to its predecessor and even some of the big budget finished RPG's I have played.

Business Tour is what you get when you take Monopoly, and strip out almost all mechanics. The only thing you do in this game is roll the dice and land on property, you aren't allowed to trade, aren't allowed to mortgage, and can only build houses when you land on a property. There's always been this kind of stigma against Monopoly as rolling the dice and just seeing where you land, but that's not really the case if you know the metagame and play strictly by the real rules, but Business Tour basically embodies everything people perhaps wrongly hate about Monopoly. Since there's no trading, players who have enough money can buy properties they land on, even if another player owns it, which is a necessicary mechanic because of how they reworked the rules, but lengthens the game out horrifically, since the win conditions are to either have 3 sets of monopolies, completely own one side of the board, or own four special properties (or bankrupt everyone else). The only mild element of strategy is the chance cards, which let you do thing to other people's properties, otherwise this game is pure Dice Rolls. There's also microtransactions that let you affect the outcome of the dice. I know microtransactions are the hot thing in free to play games, but you can't just put microtransactions in a game that's been around for almost 100 years and expect people to choose your version of if over someone else's. The one good thing I'll say for it is tha tthere is a decently sized playerbase and it didn't take long for my game to fill up, which you can't say for the Steam version of Monopoly Plus. Overall, if you want to play online Monopoly, either get the Console version of Monopoly Plus, Tabletop Simulator, or Rento Fortune, they're all more engaging and fun than this is.

Let's start with the bad: What you heard is true. The game is BUGGY. I mean very very buggy. Before you go, install the latest version of The Sith Lord Content Restore Mod (TSLCRM). It fixed a lot of bugs and restored some content that was not presented in the game because Obsidian rushed the game to the market. Yet, the game still feels unpolished. SIde quests may be bugged out, your characters will be randomly stuck in odd locations, and the companion AI is very dumb.
If you can standl the bugged out quests in your journal and all the other weird bugs you may encounter, Kotor 2 is a very unique Star Wars and RPG experience. The story did not take the straightfoward good-defeat-evil cliche like in the first game, instead, it is very deep. I think it's probably one of the best Star Wars story out there. It also looks very cinematic. Some camera moves during cutscenes are very well done. The ending is left to be desired however.
Gameplaywise, the game is pretty much the same with the first one with some new skills and combat animation. You can mess around with almost all the items. If you played the first Kotor or other DND games like Dragon Age, you won't take too much time to get your hands on.
To be concluded, it's a very good game. Buggy, but still good. I will give it an 8.5/10.

Do you know anything about Heartstone? Is it that it's kind of a ripoff of Magic The Gathering? Well, Blizzard were not the first ones to rip those damn cards. Etherlords did it first, and I personally think this game still holds up to Heartstone, if what you're looking is a singleplayer experience. As usual I'll start talking about the things the game doesn't do right:
The game has a story on it, a story that seems somewhat deep for a card-based game... However, it never got hooked to it. Seriously, it's quite boring. It also doesn't help the story that most characters have less than average voice-acting to them.
Another issue I have with it is the difficulty. Most of the enemies in the game are okay, offer a good challenge, and being defeated usually means that you should look at your deck and change your cards, as there's probably a better way to deal with this sh#t. However, one of the races on the game seems to have some balance issues: the Pale race. These guys don't f#ck arround. Some of their monsters are hilariously broken, as they're insultingly hard to kill (they usually just go hollow when you kill them, becoming a ghost but being able to return to life in exchange of mana or other stuff), and some of them deal insane amounts of damage, while also draining your HP. Seriously, build yourself the most broken and lame deck against those ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
The last thing is that the multiplayer is long dead. Now there are ways to play with people, even while the servers died years ago by using third-party software... But there's barely anyone who has the game. I HAD IT YEARS AGO WHEN IT RELEASED AND EVEN THEN IT WAS HARD TO PLAY WITH SOMEONE! This game did not get any attention during it's life-time, and it shows.
However, is the game good? Holy crap, it is.
The gameplay is a real good challenge, an entertaining strategy game were you're always trying to build your deck to get better, but also a game were defeat is usually just the perfect chance to get better. Something like that is hard to pull off.
The amount of different cards, races and monsters is also quite great. There are tons of different strategies you can build to yourself, along with the tons of different enchantments, traps, artifacts and other crap you can get your hands on.
The level system is also interesting, and I liked it a lot. As you level up, you can select extra passive skills such as regenerating some HP each X turns, getting an extra card each X turns and so on. They really make you feel like your deck and character is unique.
Do I recommend this game? Yeah, IF you're a fan of this kind of strategy games. If you like Magic The Gathering, Yu-gi-oh, Heartstone and all of those other weird card based games, you'll like it a lot. If you're not a fan of those but you like strategy games, it might also interest you. If you're neither of those, you should turn arround.
Oh, and ♥♥♥♥ Exile. I f#cking hate that spell. It can go f#ck a d#ck sideways on the shadow realm.
TL:DR Edition: Old card based game that ripped off Magic The Gathering, mostly singleplayer because of dead multiplayer. If you like Heartstone and other card games, give it a try on a sale.
